Title: Aino Bunge: Committee on Finance hearing on the Riksbank's operations and monetary policy
text: Aino Bunge: Committee on Finance hearing on the Riksbank's operations and monetary policy On Tuesday, the entire Executive Board took part in an open hearing at the Committee on Finance about the Riksbank's operations and current monetary policy. This was the first time that the Riksdag had invited board members to a hearing on the Riksbank's overarching operations and the 2022 Annual Report. Date: 14/03/2023 09:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Aino Bunge Place: The Committee on Finance Published 14/03/2023 Governor Erik Thedeen began the hearing by summarising the past year and noted that a great deal has happened at the Riksbank and abroad that has had an impact on operations: "Last year, we saw inflation starting to rise sharply and interest rates have risen rapidly. Raising the policy rate was necessary to safeguard the inflation target, but at the same time, rising interest rates caused the market value of the Riksbank's asset holdings to fall. This unrealised decrease in value has in turn had a negative impact on the Riksbank's financial result and, just like many other central banks around the world, we will report a significant loss for 2022. However, this does not affect the Riksbank's ability to carry out its tasks. In the longer run, however, the Riksbank's capital needs to increase to ensure the bank's financial independence. In addition, a new Riksbank Act has come into force and the bank has new management." Erik Thedeen also noted that digital developments in the payment market are proceeding at a rapid pace. At the same time, the Riksbank saw a temporary increase in the demand for cash following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "It is clear that the demand for cash increases in times of crisis, but it is important to remember that if it is to be possible to use cash in a crisis, we must also be able to use it in normal times. We consider that it must always be possible to at least purchase vital goods and services with cash. As a result of the new Riksbank Act, we have been given increased responsibility for cash management and during the year we have prepared the ground for the opening of new banknote depots. The Riksbank has also launched a new service for instant payments, RIX-INST, and work on an e-krona continues. Digital central bank currencies (CBDC) have become a major issue internationally during the year and Sweden is seen as a pioneer. We are active in various international partnerships linked to both CBDC and international payments". The second part of the hearing focused on current monetary policy. Erik Thedeen began by summarising the decision from February and noted that inflation is still far too high and that monetary policy needs to act to bring inflation back to 2 per cent within a reasonable period of time. He also commented on the ongoing bank problems in the United States. "We are following developments in the financial markets, and we currently consider there to be no risk to financial stability in Sweden. Among other aspects, Swedish banks are subject to stricter regulatory requirements than the agents in the US that have encountered problems. Direct exposure to these agents is also limited among Swedish banks. At the same time, it is not unusual for turbulence in foreign capital markets to spill over into Sweden. We are therefore closely monitoring the situation and, as always, we are prepared to take action in the event of a rapid change". Deputy Governor Aino Bunge then went on to talk about what the new Riksbank Act means for monetary policy. Among other things, a clause has been added under which the Riksbank shall contribute to a balanced development of output and employment without disregarding the price stability target. "Although this can be seen as an adjustment to existing practice, it probably affects how the public and elected representatives view monetary policy and how it is evaluated. We therefore need to be clearer in our communication with both our assessment of the real economy and how we consider it our monetary policy decisions". Aino Bunge also said that it is important to acquire a broad picture based on incoming data and forecasts for the economy and employment, but stressed that it is essential to bring down the high inflation in order to avoid even greater problems for the economy further ahead.

Title: Erik Theden at the Committee on Finance: High inflation and rising interest rates are testing the resilience of the Swedish financial system
text: Erik Thedeen at the Committee on Finance: High inflation and rising interest rates are testing the resilience of the Swedish financial system "After many years of low inflation and very low interest rates, increasing asset prices and rising indebtedness, it is uncertain how economic agents can cope with a rapid rise in inflation and interest rates." These were the words of Erik Thedeen when he today attended the Committee on Finance's open hearing on financial stability. In addition to the Riksbank Governor, others taking part in the committee hearing included Minister for Financial Markets Niklas Wykman, acting Director-General of Finansinspektionen Susanna Grufman, and Swedish National Debt Office Director-General Karolina Ekholm. Date: 31/01/2023 09:00 Speaker: Governor Erik Thedeen Place: Sveriges Riksdag, Forstakammarsalen Published 31/01/2023 Erik Thedeen emphasised that significant vulnerabilities have built up in the Swedish financial system over time. "These vulnerabilities primarily include banks' and bond holders' exposure to highly indebted commercial property companies, although high household indebtedness also makes the system vulnerable," he said. There are also additional challenges to the Swedish financial system, such as the substantial fluctuations in energy prices. Macroprudential measures need to be safeguarded Erik Thedeen pointed out that the macroprudential measures implemented by Finansinspektionen, such as amortisation requirements, help to increase resilience. "However, broad reforms to housing and tax policy are required to enable the housing market to function better and cope with the risks associated with household indebtedness," the Governor said. He also emphasised that the inquiry's proposal for new statistics on household assets and liabilities is an important issue. "Registers of household assets and debts have been in place in Norway and Denmark for a long time and are used by both central banks and researchers. The lack of such statistics in Sweden imposes constraints on the analysis of important questions linked to financial stability and monetary policy, such as how vulnerable highly indebted households are. It is important that the inquiry's proposal, which has been circulated for comment, leads to a change," Erik Thedeen emphasised. Resilience needs to be strengthened in several areas Erik Thedeen pointed to several incidents last year, as well as during the pandemic, that have exposed liquidity risks among financial agents other than banks. The vulnerabilities of corporate bond funds, who are important investors in Swedish corporate bonds, need to be managed. In addition, the Governor highlighted the increase in cyber threats due to the deterioration of the security situation in 2022. It is important to promptly strengthen our capacity to prevent, identify and manage cyber threats, Thedeen said in conclusion.

Title: Aino Bunge: Important for inflation to fall significantly this year
text: Aino Bunge: Important for inflation to fall significantly this year "Inflation is far too high and prices are rising broadly. This is a situation to be taken very seriously." That was the message from Deputy Governor Aino Bunge when she spoke today about the Riksbank's latest monetary policy decision at Dagens Industri's Risk and Return conference in Stockholm. Date: 09/03/2023 09:05 Speaker: Deputy Governor Aino Bunge Place: Dagens Industri's Risk and Return Published 09/03/2023 "It is a tough situation for many people when inflation is this high, and interest costs are rising. But by raising interest rates, we reduce the risk of inflation problems becoming even worse and more persistent. Low and stable inflation is a prerequisite for a strong development of the Swedish economy going forward," said Aino Bunge. Underlying inflation has not yet shown clear signs of falling and it will take time for monetary policy to have full impact. "We have said that it is important to bring inflation down within a reasonable time. And that time perspective should be relatively short if we are to maintain confidence in the inflation target in these challenging circumstances. We have a year of sharply rising inflation behind us, but this year we want to see it start to fall towards the two per cent target," Aino Bunge added. She also mentioned that household debt and house prices have been on a rising trend for several decades. A vulnerability that the Riksbank has been pointing out for a long time. "Swedish households are considerably more interest-rate sensitive than they were when the Riksbank raised the policy rate on previous occasions, not just in light of their heavy debt burden but also due to the short interest-rate fixation periods on their loans. This is something we have to take into account in monetary policy." There are strong indications that inflation will fall back during the year, but Aino Bunge stressed that we live in uncertain times and that inflation must fall far enough and sufficiently broadly. "Our policy-rate path in February indicated that the rate is likely to be raised further in the spring. Before our next monetary policy meeting at the end of April, we will have several statistical outcomes and indicators that could affect the inflation outlook and the shaping of monetary policy. We will do whatever it takes to bring inflation down," Aino Bunge concluded.

Title: Aino Bunge: Inflation is still high
text: Aino Bunge: Inflation is still high It is a good thing that inflation is falling, but there is still some way to go before it is close to our target of 2 per cent. This comment was made by Deputy Governor Aino Bunge when she spoke about the Riksbank's latest monetary policy decision at the Chamber of Commerce of East Sweden in Linkoping today. Date: 15/05/2023 13:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Aino Bunge Place: Chamber of Commerce of East Sweden, Linkoping Published 15/05/2023 Ms Bunge said that the high inflation rate is costly for society as a whole, but has a particularly strong impact on those who have small margins to begin with. "It is really important that inflation falls clearly this year. Low and stable inflation is a necessary condition for good economic growth and for Swedish wage earners to once again experience real wage increases." The household sector as a whole entered the interest rate hike phase with high savings and has been able to maintain its consumption. But as the interest rate hikes have an increasing effect, it becomes inevitable for many Aino Bunge, deputy governor. households to consume less, as we are now seeing in the statistics. Inflation and rising interest costs also affect the housing market and housing investments are falling. At the same time, Ms Bunge pointed out that the labour market remains strong. Cost pressures in earlier production stages have slowed down and companies' price plans have been dampened from very high levels. This indicates that inflation, too, will fall further. But it is still uncertain how quickly this will happen. Monetary policy needs to be contractionary to ensure that inflation falls and stabilises at the target level, said Ms Bunge. "Inflation fell in April and that is a welcome and positive development. We saw, for example, that food prices decreased in April. But we should remember that inflation is still high and still has some way to go to reach the target. Ahead of our next monetary policy decision at the end of June, we will evaluate this and other information that may affect economic activity and inflation prospects and assess what constitutes an appropriate monetary policy to bring inflation back to the target within a reasonable time."

Title: Aino Bunge: The state must take responsibility for future payments  there is neither reason nor time to wait.
text: Aino Bunge: The state must take responsibility for future payments - there is neither reason nor time to wait. "Digitalisation has created great opportunities, but also problems in the payments market that require the state, including the Riksbank, to take action. In the short term, the public's ability to pay with cash needs to be protected by legislation and more people need to have access to payment accounts. At the same time, legislative work on the e-krona should be initiated, in line with what is happening in the EU." These comments were made by Deputy Governor Aino Bunge when she spoke today at the Riksbank's seminar on future payments. In addition, she pointed out that the banks need to take responsibility for modernising their payment infrastructure and developing more solutions for instant payments. Date: 13/11/2023 13:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Aino Bunge Place: Sveriges Riksbank, Stockholm Published13/11/2023 Protect cash - we are approaching a cashless society Digitalisation has created challenges and problems in the payments market that require the state, including the Riksbank, to take action. The possibility to use cash has declined. The Riksbank considers that legislation is needed to ensure the possibility of using cash, not least in situations where other payment methods do not work. "For cash to be used in the future, both under normal conditions and in crisis and war situations, the Riksdag needs to regulate where and how it can be used," said Ms Bunge, pointing out that stores should be obliged to accept cash for socially important goods such as food, fuel and pharmaceuticals. Banks should also be obliged to accept deposits from consumers. Everyone must be able to pay Ms Bunge said that a number of measures are needed to increase financial and digital inclusion, and continued: "First and foremost, it is important that as many people as possible get a payment account. We also consider that the banks shall offer payment services at reasonable prices that are adapted to consumers who have difficulties using digital services. Public operators may need to help individuals with payments, for example at service centres or citizen advice bureaux." Develop more solutions for instant payments Swish enables instant bank transfers and is a valued service used by many. But we need more fast and efficient payment services. "The trend toward instant payments is now accelerating abroad and soon we will have European legislation that regulates these issues. This kind of legislation may also be needed here if the banks are to develop more ways to make fast payments. It is important that Sweden does not fall behind in the development," said Ms Bunge. Work on the e-krona continuing - legislation should be prepared A digital central bank currency, an e-krona, could give the public a continued opportunity to choose between state and private money when making payments. The Riksbank's work on an e-krona is a way to meet the challenges of the future and digitalisation. Many other central banks are exploring the possibility of introducing a digital central bank currency. For example, the European Central Bank has come a long way in its preparations for a digital euro. "Sweden should also start work on legislation for an e-krona. If the Riksdag decides that Sweden needs an e-krona, the lead time should not be too long. It is therefore the Riksbank's clear view that the preparations must continue. An e-krona would preserve the state's role in the payments system and make it more robust," concludes Aino Bunge.

Title: Bunge: Inflation on the way down, but weak krona contributing to uncertainty
text: Bunge: Inflation on the way down, but weak krona contributing to uncertainty "Monetary policy is working and inflation is on the way down. But it is much too early to say that we are done fighting inflation. There is still a risk for setbacks and a weak krona is part of this." This was said by Deputy Governor Aino Bunge at the Swedish Association of Corporate Treasurers in Stockholm, where she was invited to talk about the economic situation and the Riksbank's view of the krona. Date: 11/12/2023 13:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Aino Bunge Place: Industrins Finansforening Published 11/12/2023 In recent months, inflationary pressures have been subdued and consumer prices have risen at a slower rate than before. "This is good news, but changes over shorter periods can vary a lot. To assess future inflation developments, we need to continue to monitor a broad set of inflation indicators, as well as economic prospects." Monetary policy is having a tightening effect and demand is falling in Sweden. "The signals we have received indicate that this has made it more difficult for companies to raise prices and price plans have been revised down. However, it is vital that these plans also continue to be confirmed in actual price developments," said Ms Bunge. Exchange rate matters for the development of inflation According to Ms Bunge, the weak krona also contributes to uncertainty regarding inflation. "The Riksbank does not have a target for the krona, we have a target for inflation. But the exchange rate affects the outlook for inflation and therefore we need to monitor it closely." Moreover, when inflation is high, it seems easier for companies to shift cost increases from the exchange rate to consumer prices, commented Ms Bunge, referring to the Riksbank's studies in the most recent Monetary Policy Reports. Many, including the Riksbank, consider that the krona is undervalued. Economic conditions in Sweden relative to the rest of the world - with strong government finances, a resilient labour market and good competitiveness - indicate that the krona will strengthen. "If speculation has contributed to weakening the krona in recent years, it may mean that it can strengthen relatively quickly once there is a turnaround, and investors take new positions based on the trend being broken. Maybe we are already there. The krona has recently strengthened. But it is still weak and our forecast is that it will strengthen further. Ms Bunge thus sees continued risks for inflation: "There is, of course, a lot of evidence that inflation will continue to fall. But it is too early to say that we are done fighting inflation. There is still a risk for setbacks and a weak krona is part of this. Inflation must go all the way down to the target of 2 per cent, and we must live up to the strong level of confidence economic agents have in the inflation target."

Title: Current monetary policy issues
text: Current monetary policy issues Date: 1996-10-09 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Location: orebro In my speech today, I will briefly address three issues in turn. How does the inflation target work, what does the inflation outlook look like and what role does wage formation play? How does the inflation target work? A central bank manufactures and distributes money and preserves its value. If the Riksbank spends too much money, i.e. sets the repo rate lower than is compatible with the national economic balance, inflation threatens. Conversely, if the Riksbank spends too little money, i.e. sets the repo rate too high, the result could be deflation. Both inflation and deflation are equally undesirable and give rise to unstable economic development. The goal that governs monetary policy is therefore to issue the right amount of money, i.e. to set the repo rate at the right level, so that both inflation and deflation are avoided and stability in price development is achieved. The typically Swedish word "lagom" comes in handy here. The Riksbank's target of 2 per cent inflation, with a tolerance up and down of 1 percentage point, is quite close to what is usually called price stability. Over the past four years, inflation in our country has been between 2 and 3 percent on average. This has meant increased conditions for a better functioning and more stable economy and that we are moving away from the unstable inflation and speculation economy of the 1970s and 1980s, when prices rose every year by 8% on average. It was not until the spring of 1996 that households, businesses, savers and investors began to seriously believe that inflation will remain at around 2% in the future. Inflation has thus increasingly disappeared from our thinking and action. Not least the falling interest rates are a sign of that. Persistently low inflation is also the best guarantee of low interest rates. When the Riksbank decides on the repo rate, it is inflation in relation to its target one to two years ahead that is at the center of the analysis. As a rule, it takes so long for changes in the repo rate to have a full effect on inflation. If the economy grows too fast and the public begins to expect rising inflation, the likelihood of increased inflation increases and, consequently, that the repo rate will rise. Conversely, if the economy slows down and if more and more people start planning and making decisions in the knowledge that inflation will be low, the likelihood of a decrease in inflation and thus a lower repo rate increases. Once a low-inflation regime is established and the public adjusts to long-term inflation around 2 percent, inflation will be determined by how demand in the economy relates to production capacity. This means that a monetary policy which is guided by an inflation target in the long run tends to smooth out the fluctuations of the economy. This applies both if growth risks being too high and the economy overheats, as well as if the economy slows down and risks going into a recession. In this way, growth can become more sustainable and be in line with the expansion of production capacity, which in turn is determined by factors such as population growth, education level, technological development and the functioning of the various submarkets of the economy. Monetary policy cannot influence long-term growth, but well the fluctuations of the economy around this trend in that the policy is guided by an inflation target. What is the inflation outlook? In order to explain as openly and clearly as possible how the Riksbank analyses the future inflation outlook and looks at the structure of monetary policy, we publish special reports four times a year. The analysis in the inflation reports serves as a basis for the council's monetary policy discussion. The conclusions of this discussion are also set out in the reports in a separate chapter. The last Inflation Report was presented a few weeks ago and I intend to start from it because the analysis and conclusions essentially stand the test of time. As I pointed out earlier, the basic elements of an assessment of future inflation are, on the one hand, demand and supply conditions in different markets and, on the other, expectations of future inflation. Since I have already mentioned that inflation expectations have been adjusted downwards towards the inflation target, I am concentrating on developments in the real economy. The slowdown phase at the end of 1995 seems to have been short-lived. There has been some increase in production so far in 1996. This is supported by preliminary GDP statistics, as well as statistics that talk about rising new orders and production in manufacturing. Furthermore, the conditions for a European economic upturn during the autumn seem to be favourable. This in turn means good opportunities for sustainable Swedish export growth. This is especially true as Swedish companies have lowered their relative prices to fend off the stronger krona. However, despite an improved demand trend, it is uncertain how quickly this will affect production development, as companies may want to trim their inventories. Domestic demand also rose in 1996. Investments, especially in industry, have increased and most of the evidence suggests a continued favourable development. At the same time, private consumption appears to have shown subdued but stable growth, despite fears of a decline in 1996. The basic conditions for increased private consumption in the future are now also in place. All in all, we consider it most likely with growth of between 3 and 4%, overall for 1996 and 1997. The emphasis is in the upper range. It is mainly exports and investments that are expected to contribute to higher growth. Private consumption is likely to gradually make an increasing contribution over the next two years. It seems likely that in the next few years the economy will grow below its potential and that the so-called output gap, i.e. the difference between demand and the economy's productive capacity, will not close, creating tensions such that a development that is incompatible with the inflation target is at risk. This approach also appears to be consistent with the evolution of various financial variables such as money aggregates and the volume of credit in the economy. They give the picture of weak inflationary pressures from the demand side. The markedly low inflation over the past six months has largely been a consequence of more or less temporary effects such as the strengthening of the krona and falling housing interest rates. As these temporary effects subside, it is likely that registered inflation will rise in the autumn. However, the faster rise of consumer prices as a result of the ebbing of temporary factors is not the same as that underlying inflation would accelerate. Against this background, the Riksbank expects the outlook to be good because inflation will be in line with its inflation target over the next few years. The information currently available therefore suggests that there may remain some scope for lowering the repo rate. However, it is not always to be expected that monetary policy will follow a certain pattern going forward. Crucial for further development is incoming information and how it relates to the analysis in the Riksbank's latest inflation report. What is the role of wage formation? Any assessment of future inflation is based on risks and probabilities. One such risk, discussed in the Inflation Report, is wage formation. During the first half of the year, wages and salaries appear to have risen by just over 5 per cent, if you correct some temporary and statistical factors, compared with the corresponding period last year. This represents an increase from the more than 3.5% by which wages rose in the second half of 1995. Compared to the inflation target of 2%, a wage increase of just over 5% implies a real wage increase of 3%, which is at least twice as high as trend productivity developments. In the long run, real wage developments that deviate from productivity developments are not compatible with the inflation target as they tend to exert pressure on prices. In the perspective discussed in the Inflation Report, the risks of higher inflation, as a result of the cost pressures coming from the wage side, should be limited. In the long term, however, strong wage growth, while maintaining low inflation, would lead to weaker employment development, which is a trend that, moreover, can already be discerned. The chances of bringing down unemployment are thus made more difficult if wages increase too quickly. The question is how should the high wage increases be interpreted? The pessimistic interpretation is that the rate of wage growth in 1996 and 1997 will continue in the years to come. This would mean that the so-called equilibrium unemployment rate - i.e. the level of unemployment at which price and wage rises begin to accelerate - is higher than the 5 to 7 percent of most empirical calculations have concluded and that the output gap in the economy is closed. Thus, there would be no spare capacity left in the economy. This, in turn, would mean that unemployment cannot be as much lower as it is now, unless a major change in the structure of the labour market is brought about which makes it work substantially better. The main hypothesis that the Riksbank is working on is somewhat more optimistic, which does not exclude the need for an improvement in the functioning of the labor market. Wage outcomes may have been influenced by the fact that the credibility of low-inflation policies was not established when the agreement was concluded. The wage round in the spring of 1995 was marked by the inflation expectations that prevailed at the time and which were up to 4 percent. Therefore, both employers and wage and salary earners expected a possible rate of wage growth of around 5 percent, given that trend productivity is between 1 and 1.5 percent. The situation in the spring of 1995 was also marked by a rapid increase in export demand and a very favourable profit situation in the foreigncompetitive sector. If this hypothesis is reasonable, we can expect a gradual decline in the rate of wage growth as current agreements expire. Next time, however, wage negotiations will not be coordinated in time in the same way as before. As early as the end of 1996, the agreements expire in the paper sector and in the financial sector. There is therefore a need to closely monitor how the negotiations in these areas, among others, will run and what the results will follow. It cannot be ruled out that the process towards wage increases commensurate with the inflation target may be more protracted and costly in terms of unemployment, but it will happen. If, on the other hand, adjustment is faster, the result will also be positive from the point of view of employment.

Hur fungerar inflationsmlet, hur ser inflationsutsikterna ut och vilken roll spelar lnebildningen? Hur fungerar inflationsmlet? En centralbank tillverkar och distribuerar pengar och bevarar deras vrde. Om Riksbanken ger ut fr mycket pengar, dvs stter reporntan lgre n vad som r frenligt med samhllsekonomisk balans, hotar inflation. Omvnt om Riksbanken ger ut fr lite pengar, dvs stter reporntan fr hgt, kan resultatet bli deflation. Bde inflation och deflation r lika onskade och ger upphov till en instabil ekonomisk utveckling. Det ml som styr penningpolitiken r drfr att ge ut lagom mngd pengar, dvs att stta reporntan p lagom niv, s att bde inflation och deflation undviks och stabilitet i prisutvecklingen ns. Det typiskt svenska ordet "lagom" kommer hr vl till pass. Riksbankens ml p 2 procents inflation, med en tolerans upp och ned p 1 procentenhet, ligger ganska nra det som brukar kallas fr prisstabilitet. Under de senaste fyra ren har inflationen i vrt land legat mellan 2 och 3 procent i genomsnitt. Det har inneburit kade frutsttningar fr en bttre fungerande och mer stabil ekonomi och att vi r p vg bort frn 1970- och 1980-talens instabila inflations- och spekulationsekonomi, d priserna steg varje r med 8 procent i genomsnitt. Det var frst under vren 1996 som hushll, fretag, sparare och investerare p allvar brjade tro p att inflationen ocks i framtiden kommer att ligga kvar p en niv kring 2 procent. Inflationen har drmed alltmer frsvunnit ur vrt tnkande och handlande. Inte minst de fallande rntorna r ett tecken p det. En varaktigt lg inflation r ocks den bsta garanten fr lga rntor. Nr Riksbanken beslutar om reporntan r det inflationen i frhllande till mlet ett till tv r framt i tiden som str i centrum fr analysen. Det tar i regel s lng tid innan ndringar av reporntan fullt ut fr effekt p inflationen. Om ekonomin vxer fr snabbt och allmnheten brjar vnta sig en stigande inflation kar sannolikheten fr en kad inflation och fljaktligen att reporntan kommer att stiga. Omvnt om ekonomin saktar av och om fler och fler brjar planera och fatta beslut i frvissningen att inflationen kommer att vara lg kar sannolikheten fr en minskad inflation och drmed en lgre repornta. Nr vl en lginflationsregim etablerats och allmnheten stllt in sig p en lngsiktig inflation kring 2 procent kommer inflationen att bestmmas av hur efterfrgan i ekonomin frhller sig till produktionskapaciteten. Det innebr att en penningpolitik som styrs av ett inflationsml i lngden tenderar att jmna ut ekonomins svngningar. Det gller svl om tillvxten riskerar att bli fr hg och ekonomin verhettas som om ekonomin saktar av och riskerar att g in i en lgkonjunktur. P s vis kan tillvxten bli mer uthllig och hamna i linje med utbyggnaden av produktionskapaciteten, som i sin tur bestms av faktorer som befolkningstillvxt, utbildningsniv, teknisk utveckling och hur vl ekonomins olika delmarknader fungerar. Penningpolitiken kan inte pverka den lngsiktiga tillvxten, men vl ekonomins fluktuationer kring denna trend genom att politiken styrs av ett inflationsml. Hur ser inflationsutsikterna ut? Fr att s ppet och tydligt som mjligt frklara hur Riksbanken analyserar de framtida inflationsutsikterna och ser p penningpolitikens upplggning publicerar vi srskilda rapporter fyra gnger om ret. Analysen i inflationsrapporterna fungerar som underlag fr fullmktiges penningpolitiska diskussion. Slutsatserna frn denna diskussion redovisas ocks i rapporterna i ett srskilt kapitel. Den senaste Inflationsrapporten presenterades fr ngra veckor sedan och jag tnker utg frn den eftersom analysen och slutsatserna i allt vsentligt str sig. Som jag framhll tidigare r de grundlggande elementen i en bedmning av den framtida inflationen dels efterfrge- och utbudsfrhllanden p olika marknader, dels frvntningar om den framtida inflationen. Eftersom jag redan varit inne p att inflationsfrvntningarna anpassats sig nedt i riktning mot inflationsmlet, koncentrerar jag mig p utvecklingen i den reala ekonomin. Avmattningsfasen under slutet av 1995 tycks ha blivit kortvarig. Det har skett en viss produktionsuppgng hittills under 1996. Det stds av den preliminra BNPstatistiken, samt statistik som talar om stigande orderingng och produktion inom industrin. Vidare tycks frutsttningarna fr en europeisk konjunkturuppgng under hsten vara gynnsamma. Det innebr i sin tur goda mjligheter fr en uthllig svensk exporttillvxt. Det gller srskilt som svenska fretag snkt sina relativpriser fr att parera fr den starkare kronan. Trots en frbttrad efterfrgeutveckling r det dock oskert hur snabbt detta kommer att pverka produktionsutvecklingen, eftersom fretagen kan vilja trimma sina lager. ven den inhemska efterfrgan har stigit under 1996. Investeringarna inom framfr allt industrin har kat och det mesta talar fr en fortsatt gynnsam utveckling. Samtidigt frefaller den privata konsumtionen ha uppvisat en dmpad, men stabil tillvxt, trots farhgor om en nedgng under 1996. De grundlggande frutsttningarna fr en kad privat konsumtion framver r nu ocks p plats. Sammantaget bedmer vi det som mest troligt med en tillvxt p mellan 3 och 4 procent, totalt sett fr 1996 och 1997. Tonvikten ligger i det vre intervallet. Det r framfr allt exporten och investeringarna som vntas bidra till en hgre tillvxt. Privat konsumtion kommer antagligen successivt att ge ett allt strre bidrag under de nrmaste tv ren. Det frefaller troligt att ekonomin under de nrmaste ren vxer under sin potential och att det sk produktionsgapet, dvs skillnaden mellan efterfrgan och ekonomins produktionsfrmga, inte sluts och skapar sdana spnningar att en utveckling riskeras som r ofrenlig med inflationsmlet. Detta synstt frefaller ven vara konsistent med utvecklingen av olika finansiella variabler som penningmngdsaggregat och kreditvolymen i ekonomin. De ger bilden av ett svagt inflationstryck frn efterfrgesidan. Den ptagligt lga inflationen under det senaste halvret har i stor utstrck-ning varit en fljd av mer eller mindre temporra effekter som kronans frstrkning och fallande boenderntor. I takt med att dessa tillflliga effekter avtar r det troligt att den registrerade inflationen stiger under hsten. Att konsumentpriserna stiger snabbare till fljd av att tillflliga faktorer ebbar ut r emellertid inte samma sak som att den underliggande inflationen skulle accelerera. Riksbanken bedmer mot denna bakgrund utsikterna vara goda fr att inflationen ligger i linje med inflationsmlet under de nrmaste ren. Idag tillgnglig information talar drfr fr att det kan terst ett visst utrymme fr att snka reporntan. Dremot kan man inte alltid frvnta sig att penningpolitiken framver kommer att flja ett visst mnster. Avgrande fr den fortsatta utvecklingen r inkommande information och hur den frhller sig till analysen i Riksbankens senaste inflationsrapport. Vilken roll spelar lnebildningen? Varje bedmning av den framtida inflationen bygger p risker och sannolikheter. En sdan risk, som diskuteras i inflationsrapporten, r lnebildningen. Under frsta halvret tycks lnerna stigit med drygt 5 procent, om man korrigerar fr en del tillflliga och statistiska faktorer, jmfrt med motsvarande period fregende r. Det innebr en uppgng frn de dryga 3,5 procent, som lnerna steg med under andra halvret 1995. Jmfrt med inflationsmlet p 2 procent innebr en lnekning p strax ver 5 procent en reallnekning p 3 procent, vilket r tminstone dubbelt s hgt som den trendmssiga produktivitetsutvecklingen. I lngden r en reallneutveckling som avviker frn produktivitetsutvecklingen inte frenlig med inflationsmlet eftersom den tenderar att verka upppressande p priserna. I det perspektiv som diskuteras i inflationsrapporten torde riskerna fr en hgre inflation, till fljd av det kostnadstryck som kommer frn lnesidan, vara begrnsade. P sikt skulle emellertid en stark lneutveckling, med bibehllen lg inflation, leda till att sysselsttningen utvecklas svagare, vilket r en tendens som fr vrigt redan nu kan sknjas. Mjligheterna att f ner arbetslsheten frsvras drmed om lnerna kar fr snabbt. Frgan r hur de hga lnekningarna skall tolkas? Den pessimistiska tolkningen r att lnekningstakten 1996 och 1997 bestr ren framver. Detta skulle innebra att den sk jmviktsarbetslsheten - dvs den arbetslshetsniv dr pris- och lnestegringarna brjar accelerera - r hgre n de 5 till 7 procent flertalet empiriska berkningar kommit fram till och att produktionsgapet i ekonomin r slutet. Drmed skulle det inte finnas ngon ledig kapacitet kvar i ekonomin. Det skulle i sin tur innebra att arbetslsheten inte kan bli s mycket lgre n den r nu, svitt inte en omfattande frndring av arbetsmarknadens struktur kommer till stnd som gr att den fungerar vsentligt bttre. Den huvudhypotes som Riksbanken arbetar efter r ngot mer optimistisk, vilket inte utesluter behov av en frbttring av arbetsmarknadens stt att fungera. Lneutfallet kan ha pverkats av att trovrdigheten fr lginflationspolitiken inte var etablerad nr avtalet slts. Avtalsrrelsen vren 1995 prglades av de inflationsfrvntningar som d rdde och som lg uppemot 4 procent. Drfr rknade bde arbetsgivare och lntagare med en mjlig lnekningstakt p runt 5 procent med tanke p att den trendmssiga produktiviteten ligger mellan 1 och 1,5 procent. Situationen under vren 1995 prglades ocks av en snabbt kad exportefterfrgan och ett mycket gynnsamt vinstlge inom den utlandskonkurrerande sektorn. Om denna hypotes r rimlig kan vi frvnta oss en gradvis nedgng i lnekningstakten i takt med att nuvarande avtal lper ut. Nsta gng r dock inte lnefrhandlingarna samordnade i tiden p samma stt som tidigare. Redan i slutet av 1996 lper avtalen ut p bl.a. pappersomrdet och inom finanssektorn. Det finns drfr anledning att noga flja hur frhandlingarna inom bl.a. dessa omrdet kommer att lpa och vilka resultat som fljer. Det kan inte uteslutas att processen mot lnekningar som str i proportion till inflationsmlet kan bli mer utdragen och kostsam i termer av arbetslshet, men den kommer att ske. Om anpassningen  andra sidan gr snabbare blir resultatet positivt ocks ur sysselsttningssynpunkt. Title: Ingves: Monetary policy experiences in Norway and Sweden  a journey over 10 years
text: ANFoRANDE DATE:SPEAKER:LOCATION:MANAGEMENT CLASS: RESTRICTED 2022-03-21 Stefan Ingves Norges Bank SVERIGES RIKSBANK SE-103 37 Stockholm (Brunkebergstorg 11) Tel 46 8 787 00 00Fax 46 8 21 05 31 registratorn@riksbank.se Monetary policy experiences in Norway and Sweden  a journey over 10 years Many thanks for the invitation to speak at this conference in honor of oystein Olsen! The theme of the session is "towards a more flexible inflation target management". I will give my personal picture of how we have thought about monetary policy in Norway and Sweden during the 10 years that oystein has led Norges Bank and I have had similar assignments in Sweden. It becomes a picture painted with fairly broad brushstrokes. The economies of Norway and Sweden have great similarities but also significant differences. This also applies to the institutional prerequisites for the central bank and monetary policy.  A similarity is that we are small foreign trade-dependent economies. But while Sweden primarily exports various products with a certain emphasis on industrial and input goods, oil is completely dominant for Norway.  As a consequence, Norges Bank is tasked with managing the income from oil in a fund that is invested abroad, the "oil fund".1  Another difference is that Norges Bank is under the Government, while the Riksbank is under the Riksdag.  Sweden is a member of the EU, while Norway is only a member of the EEA Agreement. In this way, more degrees of freedom arise in relation to the Maastricht Treaty in Norway when it comes to the requirement for independence in monetary policy. Overall, monetary policy is thus on paper less independent in Norway than in Sweden, but in my opinion the differences are small in practice.2 I would 1 The formal name of the fund is the Government Pension Fund Global. 2 Vredin (2017) mentions in his article that the Norwegian Government's right to issue instructions to Norges Bank had only been exercised twice since 1985: in 2001, when the inflation target was introduced, and in 2013, when Norges Bank was given the task of advising on the countercyclical capital buffer. The article also provides a more detailed review of the differences and similarities between the economies of Norway and Sweden in a longer time perspective. Haugland et al. (2021), pp. 35-46, provide an overview of important episodes during 20 years of inflation targeting Norway. 1 [10] I would argue that perhaps the most significant difference in terms of the conditions for monetary policy in our countries is the importance of the international oil market for the Norwegian economy. Norges Bank and the Riksbank have had many common monetary policy challenges to deal with, but have done so in somewhat different ways. Today I will focus on two issues that we have thought a lot about over the past 10 years and that have a major impact on the degree of flexibility in inflation targeting policy:  how to conduct monetary policy in an economy with a high degree of dependence on the rest of the world, specifically the importance of exchange rate movements and globally falling interest rates  how to address emerging financial imbalances, specifically rising house prices and growing household debt Monetary policy challenges in small open economies  Similarities but also differences To get an overview of monetary policy in Norway and Sweden in recent years, a natural starting point is the policy rate and inflation developments (see Charts 1 and 2). We see that both inflation and the policy rate have generally been higher in Norway than in Sweden, while the direction of movement has often, but not always, coincided. The importance of the exchange rate  "small currency" and "commodity currency" In a small open economy, the exchange rate is an important determinant of inflation. A similarity between our economies is that our currencies tend to weaken in times of economic turmoil  a "small currency effect" (see Chart 3).3 In Norway, oil price developments play a major role for obvious reasons, not least for exchange rate developments. The Norwegian krone is a "commodity currency", where rises in oil prices tend to strengthen the currency and vice versa. The difference in relation to the Swedish krona can be seen more clearly in Figure 4, which shows the oil price and the exchange rate of the Norwegian krona against the Swedish krona. These similarities and differences are clearly illustrated by a couple of episodes over the past 10 years. One such episode began in the autumn of 2014, when oil prices fell sharply. We saw a "commodity effect" in Norway, in the form of a weakened Norwegian krone, which was not visible in Sweden (see Figure 4). This helped to keep up Norwegian inflation. In Sweden at the time, we had to deal with the aftermath of the euro crisis and not least the ECB's monetary policy, which had a dampening effect on inflation via a stronger Swedish krona. Although interest rates abroad also affected conditions in Norway, the monetary policy agenda was dominated by the negative effects on economic activity that the falling oil price entailed.4 Despite the fact that the backgrounds differed, the monetary policy outcome was ultimately quite similar: In both Norway and Sweden, the policy rate was cut gradually, but to different levels (see Chart 1). 3 The chart shows the exchange rates against the euro, but the trade-weighted exchange rates, I-44 for Norway and KIX for Sweden, have developed in a similar way during this period. 4 See, for example, Haugland et al. (2021), p. 43 and Norges Bank (2016, p. 6). 2 [10] During the outbreak of the corona crisis in the spring of 2020, the similarities and  above all  the differences between Norway's and Sweden's currency movements became apparent again. We saw a fairly moderate weakening of the Swedish krona  the "small currency effect" was thus limited (see Figure 3). But the weakening of the Norwegian krone became even greater. The "commodity effect" was huge as a result of the sharp fall in oil prices at the beginning (see Chart 4). It also justified intervention in the foreign exchange market by Norges Bank, partly because the market was functioning poorly.5 A common argument in favour of a small open economy applying a floating exchange rate is that currency movements can act as shock absorbers in economic downturns. One conclusion I draw from these experiences is that the Norwegian krone fulfils this function to an even greater extent than the Swedish krone, through its role as both a "small currency" and a "commodity currency". A world of low interest rates  a monetary policy constraint, but in different degrees In the world of central banking, we have had to deal with a world of declining global interest rates for a long time. This imposes constraints on monetary policy, as the neutral policy rate, which neither stimulates nor slows down the economy, will be lower (see Chart 5). But even in this context, there are not only similarities but also differences between Norway and Sweden. As oystein himself discussed in a recent speech, monetary policy has not been quite as limited in Norway as in other countries, including Sweden.6 This is illustrated quite clearly by developments in recent years. We lowered the interest rate to negative levels as early as 2015 (see Chart 1). At the same time, we also initiated the purchase of government bonds. During the corona crisis, we have also bought other types of securities. In Norway, the policy rate instead reached its lowest level of zero per cent to date only in May 2020 and has started to be raised again recently. As I mentioned earlier, both inflation and the policy rate have generally been at a higher level in Norway than in Sweden over the past 10 years (see Charts 1 and 2). How can we understand that? An important explanation, in my opinion, is the contribution from oil revenues, which has gradually been phased into the Norwegian economy and has constituted a kind of structural financial policy support for the real economy and inflation.On 7 October 194 Despite these differences, we have reached a common conclusion with regard to stabilisation policy: fiscal policy will play an important role in economic downturns in the future. It has already done so during the corona crisis, which was reinforced by the asymmetric nature of the crisis: Certain sectors have been hit particularly hard and required targeted fiscal policy measures. 8 A further common experience is that fiscal policy has complemented monetary policy well in both Norway 5 See Alstadheim et al. (2021) for a thorough review of the development of events in the Norwegian foreign exchange market during the corona crisis. 6 See Olsen (2021). 7 One reason why the inflation target was set at 2.5 per cent between 2001 and 2018 was precisely that oil revenues were phased into the Norwegian economy. After 2018, that element was not considered to be as strong, and the target was lowered to 2 percent; see Haugland et al. (2021), p. 44. 8 See Olsen (2021) and Sveriges Riksbank (2021a), p. 18. 3 [10] and Sweden during the crisis. And this was facilitated by the fact that the strong public finances in both our countries created considerable room for manoeuvre in fiscal policy. Financial imbalances  similar challenges but different Solutions One issue that is linked to the global interest rate situation is developments in the housing market. Unlike many other countries, house prices did not fall very much in Norway and Sweden after the global financial crisis in 2008, and they have continued to increase in trend terms over the past 10 years (see Figure 6). The falling global interest rates have meant that the neutral interest rate in Sweden and Norway has also fallen. And this in turn is a strong contributor to the development of house prices, since home purchases are largely financed by loans, and the level of interest rates affects households' expenditure on the loans. In this way, households have been able to increase their mortgage debt sharply in our countries. Contrary to what many feared, house prices have also risen sharply since spring 2020 in many countries, including Norway and Sweden, despite the deep economic downturn (see Chart 6). But the specific effects of the corona crisis, for example that households have changed their consumption patterns and spent more time at home, are, in my opinion, more important drivers this time than the development of mortgage rates.On 9 October 201 Overall, financial imbalances in the form of rising house prices and household debt are a growing problem, as households become more vulnerable the higher their indebtedness. But we have chosen to deal with this problem in slightly different ways in Norway and Sweden. Norway  monetary policy consideration of imbalances and increased tygslada Financial stability has been given a prominent role in Norwegian monetary policy and at Norges Bank in a broader sense. A joint report on monetary policy and financial stability has been published since 2013. Consideration of financial imbalances has been clearly communicated in monetary policy and is also anchored in the new Central Bank Act in Norway, which entered into force on 1 January 2020. It is significant that, as a result of it, a monetary policy and financial stability committee has also been created . In addition, Norges Bank has additional macroprudential tools at its disposal: in 2013, it was assigned an advisory role for the Ministry of Finance's decision on the countercyclical capital buffer, which was recently expanded to a decision-making function plus an advisory role for the systemic risk buffer.On October 10, 2019, 9 See Sveriges Riksbank (2021b) and Olsen (2021). 10 See Norges Bank (2021). 4 [10] Sweden  few changes In Sweden, despite a similar problem, we have chosen a different solution. For a period, roughly from 2011 to 2014, the Riksbank took some account of financial imbalances in its interest rate decisions. However, we did not assess that it worked when the credibility of the inflation target was threatened, as inflation became increasingly lower (see Chart 2). I described this episode in detail in a speech a couple of years ago.11 To some extent, the issue has been easier to deal with in Norway, as inflation has not been as low (see Chart 2). The Riksbank's mandate for financial stability remained unchanged at the time of the 2013 review, and we were not given any additional tools for managing financial imbalances. Finansinspektionen was given the main responsibility for all macroprudential tools in Sweden. And already in the directive to the inquiry into the new Sveriges Riksbank Act, it was clear that a prerequisite was that the mandate for macroprudential policy should remain unchanged. Not surprisingly, this is also what is stated in the law that will enter into force in January 2023. It is no secret that I think the Norwegian solution is preferable, since central banks have a lot to contribute in both macroprudential analysis and financial stability analysis in general. That said, despite the different political solutions in our countries, we have benefited greatly from discussions and exchanges of ideas on macroprudential policy and financial stability. An example of this is the Nordic-Baltic cooperation on macroprudential supervision, where we, together with a number of other countries in our region, have benefited greatly from sharing experiences, not least because the financial systems in our countries are strongly interconnected. Another example is our annual conferences with Nordic central bank governors, where developments in the Norwegian and Swedish housing markets have been a recurring theme. A Glimpse into My Personal Memory Bank I am now nearing the end of my speech. And then I want to take the opportunity to round off with a touch in my personal memory bank. I have had the privilege of meeting oystein on many occasions over the years. But I want to take the opportunity to share a special one with you, because it shows that oystein can handle the most difficult challenges. The venue was Oslo, in 2015, and it was one of the annual conferences of Nordic central bank governors, which was also attended by a number of employees. It all began with a great treat to a wonderfully quiet boat trip in Oslo's harbor district. But all too easily we wouldn't get away, obviously. The next item on the program was a RIB boat trip. 11 Se Ingves (2019). 5 [10] Something happened to one of the delegates  I think it's well captured by the lyrics of one of history's most classic pop songs: "feeling kind of seasick"... "Face, at first just ghostly, turned a whiter shade of pale".On October 12, 2019, I have rarely seen oystein so committed. But it all worked out for the best. Once on land, the delegate perked up faster than fast. It was all a very memorable stay in the Oslo archipelago, at the fantastic facility in Vindasen, characterized by the great hospitality of Norges Bank and oystein. It remains for me to wish you the best of luck on your continued adventures after your time as Governor of Norges Bank. Maybe there is now time for the occasional boat trip, in calm waters. Title: Breman: High inflation  the interest rate may need to be raised earlier
text: Breman: High inflation - the interest rate may need to be raised earlier "Energy and food prices will probably continue to be high in the period ahead. The main reason is Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The earlier rise in inflation may thus be further exacerbated. This is because Russia exports significant quantities of oil, natural gas and fertiliser and because Ukraine is a major exporter of cereals, mainly wheat and maize." These were the words of Deputy Governor of the Riksbank Anna Breman in a speech about inflation that she gave to a group of upper secondary students visiting the Riksbank. Date: 23/03/2022 09:15 Speaker: Deputy Governor Anna Breman Place: Riksbanken Published 23/03/2022 Inflation is affected by rising energy and food prices Inflation in Sweden has already increased noticeably for many households and companies. Energy and food prices are also rising steeply - basic necessities for everyone but which central banks often disregard when they talk about inflation. "If the gap between how households perceive inflation and how we analyse it and communicate it is too great, this may reduce public confidence in the inflation target", Anna Breman pointed out. The inflation target in focus The fact that inflation is now being driven by things households cannot do without, energy and food, may cause their inflation expectations to rise. The Riksbank is also working on new forecasts for inflation and will present its analysis in the Monetary Policy Report at the end of April. "But we can already say that inflation will be significantly higher than in our last forecast. We cannot prevent inflation from rising in the short term. Our remit does, however, include taking action to ensure inflation is close to target in the medium term", Anna Breman emphasised. As things look now, it is reasonable to bring forward an increase in the policy rate. But we can also wind down our bond purchases more quickly. In order to determine appropriate monetary policy, we need to consider various factors that affect inflation in the medium term: the labour market, growth and inflation expectations", Anna Breman said in conclusion.

Title: Anna Breman: We need to continue to act to bring inflation back to the target
text: Anna Breman: We need to continue to act to bring inflation back to the target "Inflation is too high, it is too broad and it is hurting households and firms. The mandate we have been given by the Riksdag (Swedish Parliament) is to maintain price stability. For inflation to be low and stable again, we need to gradually raise the policy rate and reduce the Riksbank's asset holdings/ These comments were made by Deputy Governor Anna Breman when she spoke at Nordea's AAA seminar in Stockholm on Thursday. Date: 09/06/2022 09:15 Speaker: Deputy Governor Anna Breman Place: Nordea AAA seminar, Stockholm Published 09/06/2022 The high inflation rate is due to a number of different disruptions in production and distribution worldwide, but also to strong demand as restrictions are lifted. "The Swedish economy has recovered quickly after the pandemic. Although there are risks to the outlook, the economy is performing well," said Ms Breman. While firms are showing strong results and are optimistic about the future, households are much more pessimistic. "This doesn't necessarily mean that households will put the brakes on and stop consuming, the labour market is still strong. However, they will probably keep a tighter grip on their wallets if they are worried about both the Swedish economy and their own finances." At the same time, a higher interest rate impacts different parts of the economy to different extents. "The construction sector and the fast-growing tech companies are likely to notice the higher interest rates more than, for example, the manufacturing industry. Young people with a lot of debt are, on average, more sensitive to interest rates than older people with lower indebtedness," continued Ms Breman. "In addition to short-term cyclical effects, we also need to be aware of the major structural changes that are under way," said Anna Breman, and mentioned in this context energy transition, digitalisation and the risk of deglobalisation. "These trends affect inflation and the functioning of the economy both in the short and long term, and are something we need to consider in our analysis". "There are always trade-offs in monetary policy; If we do too little, there is a risk that inflation will stick, if we do too much we risk triggering a downturn in the economy that could cause inflation to fall well below the target in the longer run." "At our most recent monetary policy meeting in April, I said that it is important to act now. Inflation expectations must not rise too far, and we need to counteract the risk of entering a price and wage spiral. I also said in April that I would have preferred somewhat fewer policy rate increases than indicated by the Riksbank's policy rate path. I wish to stress, as I did in the minutes, that it is extremely important that my assessment that fewer increases may be appropriate is not interpreted and/or misunderstood as tolerance for higher inflation in the medium term. If inflation goes even higher and becomes even more persistent than in our forecast, I will support doing what is necessary to attain the inflation target, including more rate hikes than are in the current path and/or a faster tapering of asset holdings.," concluded Ms Breman.

Title: Breman: Inflation needs to become low and stable again
text: Breman: Inflation needs to become low and stable again Rising prices and higher interest costs are noticeable for households and companies. However, it would be even more noticeable for households and the Swedish economy in general if inflation were to remain at the current high levels. As we said in November, the policy rate may therefore need to be raised further. Deputy Governor Anna Breman made these remarks today, speaking on the economic situation and the Riksbank's monetary policy at the Chamber of Commerce Malardalen in Vasteras. Date: 20/01/2023 12:00 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Anna Breman Place: Chamber of Commerce Malardalen, Vasteras Published 20/01/2023 High inflation has required large rate hikes 2022 was another year characterised by dramatic developments, Ms. Breman said. Imbalances between supply and demand during the pandemic and high economic demand, in addition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and problems on the European energy market, led inflation to rise very rapidly over the year. This led to large rate rises both here and abroad. In Sweden, the Riksbank raised the policy rate from zero to 2.5 per cent. Inflation has continued to rise over the winter High inflation and higher interest rates are cooling off the Swedish economy and households have reduced their consumption. "So far, however, GDP growth and the labour market situation seem to have been a little stronger than we expected in the forecast in November. Inflation has continued to rise and CPIF inflation has become higher than expected, very much due to electricity prices." "Excluding energy prices, inflation has been more in line with the Riksbank's forecast, although it is still far too high. In addition, the krona has weakened, which does not help when inflation is this high," Ms Breman emphasised. "At the same time, there are signs that global price pressures have eased and, concerning electricity prices, forward prices show that they may rise less than was feared when we made our forecast in November, although uncertainty is very high here," Ms Breman said. The policy rate may need to be raised further "It takes time for monetary policy to have its full effect. Last year's rate rises will therefore not make a clear impression on the inflation figures until this year. But inflation is much too high and, as we said in our forecasts in November, the policy rate may need to be raised further to make sure we return to an environment in which inflation is low and stable," said Ms Breman. "I have previously emphasised that monetary policy tightening is a matter of adjusting the level of the policy rate, the policy rate path and the pace at which asset holdings decrease. But exactly how monetary policy will be formed in the period ahead is something we will return to on 9 February, when the Riksbank's next monetary policy decision will be published," Ms Breman concluded.

Title: Breman: Inflation needs to fall further
text: Breman: Inflation needs to fall further "The tourism industry has recovered well since the pandemic. Will households continue to prioritise travel, eating out and concerts to the same extent as today? How much will households be able to, and want to, dip into their savings to consume this type of services? How this affects inflation and employment is one of several factors that will be important going forward." These comments were made by First Deputy Governor Anna Breman today, speaking at Tourism Day for the Jamtland Harjedalen region in Are. Date: 19/10/2023 13:00 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Anna Breman Place: Copper Hill Mountain Lodge in Are Published 19/10/2023 High price pressure in industries that were hit hard during the pandemic The hotel and restaurant industry was hit hard by the pandemic. The COVID outbreak and the restrictions imposed caused the demand for tourism-related services to plummet, while many costs increased. With pandemic restrictions lifted, tourism-related services have increased sharply in the last two years. In addition, the weak krona has made it advantageous for foreign tourists to come here. Anna Breman, First Deputy Governor. But the tourism industry is one of many sectors in the economy performing well. Demand in the economy has been high overall, which has made it easier for many companies to pass on their higher costs to consumers. And prices have risen widely, in all industries. "High inflation creates uncertainty and erodes household purchasing power. To return to low and stable inflation, we have gradually raised the policy rate," said Ms Breman. "We can see that the policy rate hikes are having an effect. Inflation is on the way down. Energy prices have fallen sharply, and food prices have moved sideways in recent months. This benefits all households, but especially poorer households, as energy and food are a relatively large part of these households' expenses." Ms Breman stressed several favourable conditions for inflation to continue falling. "Producer prices have fallen, wage increases are moderate and inflation expectations are stable. The Swedish economy is slowing down and demand is subdued. But inflation is not yet at target. Underlying inflation is still high, not least in the service sector. For inflation to be sustainably low and stable, we need to see a clearer downward trend in more price categories. The policy rate may need to be raised further." Future developments affect inflation prospects The service sector, which includes the tourism industry, employs many people throughout Sweden. The employment rate is currently at a record high, but we are now beginning to see signs of a slowdown. The social partners have shown great responsibility, with a 2-year agreement with moderate wage increases. As a result, it will be possible to reach the inflation target with employment remaining at a high level. Ms Breman pointed out that it will be important to follow companies' pricing behaviour now that wage increases are moderate and producer prices have fallen. Household savings and consumption are also factors that are important for inflation. Households' saving rate was high during the pandemic. This has enabled many of them to continue to consume, despite the cost of living increases and higher interest rates. "How much will households be able to, or want to, dip into their savings in the future to consume? Will households continue to prioritise services such as travel, eating out and concerts to the same extent as today? How this affects inflation and employment will be important going forward," said Ms Breman. "Ahead of our next monetary policy decision on 22 November, it will be important to assess how these and other factors affect economic activity and inflation prospects for both the service sector and the economy as a whole," she concluded.

Title: Anna Breman: Inflation is falling, but risks remain
text: Anna Breman: Inflation is falling, but risks remain "Inflation is moving in the right direction, but we are not out of the woods yet." This comment was made by First Deputy Governor Anna Breman, speaking today at the Royal Swedish Academy of Engineering Sciences (IVA) in Stockholm. Date: 04/12/2023 11:00 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Anna Breman Place: Kungl. Ingenjorsvetenskapsakademien (IVA) Published 04/12/2023 "The policy rate hikes are contributing to the fall in inflation. Demand is weak and forward-looking indicators suggest that inflation will continue to fall. But it is important to point out that this will not happen by itself. To ensure that inflation continues falling and then remains at a low and stable level close to the target, monetary policy needs to remain contractionary." Weaker demand is contributing to companies no longer planning to raise prices as much as before. "Quite simply, it is more difficult to raise prices when demand in the economy is no longer as high. We know that companies' pricing is influenced by several factors, such as the balance between supply and demand, the cost of changing prices and competition. And how often companies change their prices varies, of course, between companies, but also over time. In general, prices are rather sticky, but with microdata, we can see that companies' pricing behaviour has changed in recent years." We need to be open to the idea that firms price-setting behaviour may have changed One of the Riksbank's research projects analyses nearly five million price observations from 2001 to the end of September 2022. This shows that individual prices are normally sticky, they rarely change. However, in recent years, when companies have had unusually large cost increases and been affected by supply shocks at the same time as demand has been strong, they have tended to raise their prices much more often. There seems to be a strong correlation between the frequency of price changes and the rate of inflation. It is the frequency of price changes that is the main driver of changes in inflation over time, not the magnitude of the price changes. This is a pattern in Swedish data that is consistent with research from other countries." The correlations between producer prices and consumer prices, between energy prices and consumer prices, and between exchange rates and inflation have not followed historical patterns in recent years. "To understand the dynamics of inflation going forward, we need to be open to the idea that the price-setting behaviour may have changed, and that companies may adjust prices more frequently in the future, partly because new technology makes it easier and cheaper to adjust prices more often. If we could have even better access to microdata, it could give us early indications of when inflation is about to rise or fall," Ms Breman continued. The Riksbank is actively working to gain access to more updated microdata to be able to deepen our analysis. The banks' price-setting behaviour also seems to have deviated from the normal pattern. The banks were quick to raise mortgage rates, but not as quick to raise interest rates on savings. Higher savings rates are part of the monetary policy transmission, i.e., how changes in policy rates affect households and companies via changes in market rates. Higher policy rates should result in higher interest on savings accounts and this usually contributes to households saving more and consuming less, which dampens demand and leads to lower inflation. "Households and companies are now affected by higher interest rates on loans, but it took longer before households also received higher interest on their savings accounts, which had a negative effect on the transmission of monetary policy. One explanation for this could be poor competition in the banking sector, which means that banks do not have to compete with pricing on savings accounts," said Ms Breman. "Ahead of our next monetary policy meeting, we will receive new data on how economic activity, the labour market and inflation are developing. We are seeing a clear slowdown in the Swedish economy. At the same time, the signals from companies are mixed when it comes to price developments. In the National Institute of Economic Research's Economic Tendency Survey, price plans are still at elevated levels, while the Riksbank's Business Survey suggests significantly lower price pressures going forward. All in all, we see good conditions for inflation to continue falling, but we should not underestimate the risk of setbacks/' concluded Ms Breman.

Title: The Riksbank and monetary policy
text: In English Webbarkiv Rosenberg: The Riksbank and monetary policy Date 2007-05-31 First Deputy Governor Irma Rosenberg spoke on Thursday at Nordea in Copenhagen. Rosenberg began by talking about how the Riksbank works today and then presented his view of the economic situation in connection with the monetary policy meeting in May. "In February this year, we presented our own forecast for the repo rate for the first time. The reason we took that step was that we want to be even more open and clear to the public about how the Riksbank views both the future development of the Swedish economy and the consequences for monetary policy. At the same time, I would like to emphasize that our own forecast for the development of interest rates is not a promise on the part of the Riksbank, but is precisely a forecast and is constantly being reassessed. As in the past, economic developments will determine how we will change the repo rate in the future. Our forecast may also differ slightly from long-term interest rate expectations in the financial markets. This does not have to be something strange as we may assess future economic development a little differently. On the other hand, short-term market expectations are of course more clearly affected by our forecast. This is only natural because the repo rate primarily affects the short-term interest rate," Rosenberg began. "By publishing our own interest rate trajectory, we're basically as clear as we can be. The new way of working therefore reduces the need to signal, before monetary policy meetings, how the Executive Board views the level of interest rates. It is normally sufficient to signal clearly at the time of monetary policy meetings. Only in exceptional cases is there reason to give additional signals when approaching the next meeting and interest rate decision. Of course, as in the past, individual Members should in future also be able to express their own views in public. Above all, however, it is a question of clarifying one's personal considerations at monetary policy meetings in retrospect. The fact that we will now also be naming the Members in the Minutes makes it even clearer what position each one is taking. This also makes it easier to review the motives behind the decisions," Rosenberg continued. "I was now going to move on to saying a few words about how I viewed economic developments in the context of the last monetary policy meeting. The new information released in recent months suggests that inflationary pressures have been slightly higher than we expected in the February monetary policy report and at the March monetary policy meeting. This is partly due to the fact that the government's spring budget looks to be more demand-stimulating, at least next year, than we previously thought. Another reason for the changed picture is that the agreements in the contract negotiations so far indicate that wages will increase faster than we previously expected. How high wage increases can be expected depends, among other things, on how the labor market works. Important questions are whether the labour supply will increase to the extent we expected, whether the development between demand and supply of labour is monitored and what account is taken of the labour market situation in wage negotiations. Today we have a strong labour market situation and then it is reasonable to expect slightly higher wage increases than in recent years. But the outcome of the wage negotiations has still been higher than we thought there was reason to expect, given that the unused capacity in the labor market is still quite large," Rosenberg noted. "At the last monetary policy meeting in early May, my view was that the economic picture had not changed so much that there was a rush to raise the repo rate. Inflation was still low and it was estimated that it will rise only slowly in the future. This was because there were still several factors holding back inflationary pressures. Price pressure from the rest of the world was expected to continue and productivity was still improving at a good pace. Corporate profits were good and there were many indications that the profitability of the business sector had continued to improve. Therefore, my view was that it was not necessary to raise interest rates at the last monetary policy meeting. On the other hand, developments suggested that the repo rate needed to be raised more during the forecast period than in the February report in order for inflation to be in line with the target and for the real economy to develop in a balanced manner," Rosenberg said. "The pace of interest rate hikes must now be balanced so that inflation does not pick up faster than expected, but growth in output and employment must also not be slowed down too early. How quickly and how much interest rates will be raised in the future is something we will have to return to at the next monetary policy meeting in June. Then we will have more information about the collective bargaining process and how production has developed this year," Rosenberg continued. "I was going to end with a few words about the consequences of abolishing the property tax and replacing it with a lower municipal levy. The tax change affects inflation by changing housing costs in the CPI. This change produces a relatively large direct, but temporary effect on inflation. There is normally no reason to counteract such tax effects with monetary policy. With regard to indirect effects on inflation via general demand, it can be noted that the reduction in property tax, as proposed by the government, is fully financed in the housing sector. This means that disposable income is not affected overall. However, tax changes can affect property prices. If property prices rise for fundamental reasons, such as a change in property taxes, it is not normally a problem for monetary policy. However, if household demand increases as a result, monetary policy must of course take into account the effects it may have on inflation and GDP growth," Rosenberg concluded.
