Title: Current monetary policy
text: In English Webbarkiv Current monetary policy Date: 1999-03-25 Speakers: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Finance Committee hearing On the first of January this year, the Riksbank was given a formally independent position. According to the sixth chapter of the fourth paragraph of the Sveriges Riksbank Act (1988:1385), it follows that the Riksbank must submit a written report to the Riksdag's Finance Committee on monetary policy at least twice a year. Such a report has been submitted to the committee today and I would like to briefly summarise the content of this and our view of the conditions for monetary policy. I will begin by briefly summarising developments in the Swedish economy and in the area of inflation in recent years. Thereafter, it is reported how the Riksbank conducts monetary policy on the basis of the new legislation. It then looks back at the past year and evaluates the evolution of consumer prices in 1998 and the monetary policy pursued. Finally, I intend to look ahead and present how the Riksbank views the future inflation outlook and current monetary policy. Swedish economy in the 1990s After the deep crisis in the early 90s, favorable export and investment development has laid the foundation for a stable recovery of the Swedish economy. Private consumption has also gradually contributed more and more to growth. Since the inflation target was announced in January 1993, the Swedish economy has grown by almost 3 percent on average per year. Inflation expectations have fallen and the credibility of the overall economic policy has increased, partly as a result of the consolidation of public finances and the stabilisation of the banking sector. Long-term expectations of future inflation have come down to the target level of 2 per cent. There is thus a fundamental credibility to the current macroeconomic regime, which in turn is a prerequisite for lasting favourable economic development. Inflation has remained low since the inflation target was announced. The CPI has increased by 2 percent on average per year since 1993 and by 1.2 percent since the target formally came into force in 1995. Adjusted for interest expenses and the direct effects of changes in indirect taxes (UND1X), inflation has increased by 1.8% on average since 1995. To a large extent, the low inflation is due to the spare capacity that existed, and exists, in the Swedish economy after the recession in the early 1990s. However, the low inflation rate is not exclusively due to excess capacity. To the picture here also changes of a more structural nature both in Sweden and abroad. International competitive pressures have increased significantly in the 1990s. One consequence of this is that it has become increasingly difficult for companies to raise their prices. Although, strictly speaking, these are probably mainly one-off effects on inflation, increased competition may have an impact on global inflationary pressures over a long period of time. Increased international trade, EMU and deregulation of various kinds suggest a longer-term effect. In addition, the credibility of monetary policy has increased and inflation expectations have thus become lower, which is reflected in price and wage formation in the economy. More detailed definition of the inflation target and the conduct of monetary policy The new Riksbank Act states that the objective of monetary policy shall be to maintain a fixed monetary value. The Executive Board of the Riksbank has specified this; The objective of monetary policy is to limit the change in the consumer price index to 2 per cent in a slightly longer, annual perspective. A deviation of /- one percentage point can be tolerated. As a result, monetary policy is characterised by continuity even after the entry into force of the new legislation. Monetary policy is expected to have the greatest effect on inflation one to two years in the future, which is why the Riksbank must base its policy on a forecast of inflation developments during this time period. In the report that the Riksbank has today submitted to the Finance Committee, such a forecast is presented as the basis for monetary policy. Monetary policy is normally conducted using a simple rule of action: If the Riksbank's inflation forecast one to two years from now shows that inflation deviates from the set target, the repo rate should change. The ambition is to adjust the interest rate so that the inflation forecast one to two years in the future is in line with the target. However, the rule of action is not mechanical. Inflation forecasts are surrounded by significant uncertainty. In practice, therefore, policies must also take into account other possible ways of exiting the economy and inflation than indicated in the main forecast. There may also be grounds for allowing a more flexible interpretation of the decision-making rule in certain specific circumstances. The Executive Board has decided that there may be two reasons to deviate from the set inflation target, which in principle implies a codification of the practices that have applied to monetary policy in recent years: 1. One reason is if consumer prices are affected one to two years from now by factors that are not expected to have a lasting impact on inflation. Such factors may be changes in household interest costs or in indirect taxes and subsidies, which for a short period of time affect inflation developments without having a more lasting effect. 2. Another reason for deviating from the decision-making rule may be that a rapid return to the target would give rise to large real economic costs. There may therefore be some reasons to deviate from the time horizon and try to bring inflation back to the target level more gradually. Should any of these situations arise, the Riksbank must clarify in advance how large deviations from the inflation target may be justified in one to two years' time. Inflation developments in 1998 and evaluation of monetary policy In light of this, let me move on to discussing how inflation developed last year in order to comment in this context on the extent to which the Riksbank has achieved its inflation target. I would like to stress that the evaluation is likely to develop in the future in the light of the clarifications made by the new Executive Board. The annual average of the twelve-month CPI figures was 0.4% for 1998. Inflation, as measured by the CPI, thus fell short of the target of 2% and the lower limit of the target. The major interest rate cuts implemented by the Riksbank in recent years and the changes to indirect taxes and subsidies decided by the Riksdag have to a large extent affected the inflation outcome last year, as they did in 1996 and 1997. Adjusted for such temporary effects, inflation, as measured by UND1X, was around 1% for 1998 on average. These are effects of the type that the Riksbank should ignore because we have little opportunity to continuously eliminate the effects that disruptions of this type have on the inflation rate. To respond to a change in the temporary factors with a change in interest rates and then to adjust the level of interest rates accordingly when the effect does not long affect the inflation rate would be to create unnecessary instability in the real economy. An illustrative example is the change in tobacco tax last year, which had a noticeable impact on the inflation rate, which, however, was not lasting. Another important explanation for the low inflation outcome is the lower international price pressure caused by, among other things, the lack of transparency. The Asian crisis and its spillover effects. The fall in the prices of petroleum-related goods and coffee alone dragged down the annual change in the CPI by almost half a percentage point in December 1998. These are more direct forecasting mistakes. The Riksbank - together with most other analysts did not foresee that the international crisis would be so extensive and that commodity prices would fall to the extent that has occurred. Although the inflation rate has been low, the Swedish economy cannot be said to experience deflation. This is reflected in the fact that domestic underlying inflation - i.e. inflation adjusted for interest costs, goods mainly imported and the direct effects of indirect taxes and subsidies (UNDINHX) - was just under 2% in 1998. During my last visit to the committee, I stressed how difficult it is to be clear in politics, since temporary factors - partly caused by the Riksbank's own actions - lead to inflation falling below target. It is because of this that the Executive Board recently decided on certain clarifications of the inflation target and underlined the importance of the Riksbank indicating in advance the occasions when deviations from the inflation target may be justified. This should facilitate evaluation. As I pointed out, the basic reasons for ignoring this type of temporary factor are the concern for the stability of the real economy. Inflationsutsikterna Low international price pressures Since the previous Inflation Report in December, both consumer prices and underlying inflation have developed broadly as expected. In February 1999, measured as the annual change in the consumer price index, inflation stood at -0.2 per cent. Underlying inflation, meanwhile, was 1.2 percent, as measured by UND1X. One of the reasons for the weak inflation trend is the low international prices. There are also many indications that low international price pressures will persist in the future. Weaker international demand, increased competition and overcapacity in many sectors are likely to result in continued low inflation in the OECD area in the coming years. The Japanese economy is still in recession with no clear signs of recovery. Despite several fiscal stimulus packages, combined with strong measures to resolve the banking crisis, household and business confidence has not yet improved. The euro area - an area that is of great importance for Swedish exports - has also shown a more subdued development during the winter than was expected in our December report. However, a consumption-led economic upturn still seems likely for the euro area as a whole, but it may be somewhat more subdued than the Riksbank previously expected. The U.S. economy continues to show strength. In the long term, however, a slowdown in economic activity in the United States is likely. In the Riksbank's main scenario, GDP growth in the OECD area is estimated to be just over 1.5 per cent in 1999. Against the background of, among other things, the monetary policy easing taken in the rest of the world, a certain recovery is expected in 2000, when growth is estimated to be just under 2 percent. The international economic outlook for 2000 has thus moderated marginally since the Riksbank's assessment in December. Gradual recovery in the Swedish economy International developments, with weaker growth in our immediate vicinity, are expected to lead to the Swedish economy growing somewhat more slowly than in 1998. The weakening in Europe affects Swedish industry more than the upward revision in the US. Nevertheless, the growth prospects for the coming years remain relatively good. Domestic demand is expected to rise gradually over the period, partly as a result of low real interest rates. This picture is supported by various financial indicators such as loans to households and the development of money supply. This counteracts the somewhat weaker growth outlook for exports and the deteriorating outlook for the industry, mainly this year. The picture also includes that the restraining effect of fiscal policy on demand is assumed to be smaller than in the fiscal consolidation of recent years. Together with a gradual recovery of the international economy, this means that GDP is expected to grow by just over 2% in 1999 and by around 2.5% in 2000. The somewhat weaker economic outlook suggests that employment may grow slightly less than assumed in the previous Inflation Report. The unemployment rate is expected to fall from 6.5 percent this year to 6.2 percent next year. Pricing in the financial markets and various surveys conducted show that households, entrepreneurs and market participants still expect very low inflation in the coming year. Looking further ahead, inflation is expected in line with the Riksbank's target. Despite relatively good growth, there is likely to be spare capacity in the economy over the next two years. This suggests low underlying inflationary pressures during the period. The Riksbank estimates that inflation, measured as CPI, will amount to 1.1 per cent in one year's time and 1.4 per cent in two years' time. The weak development in consumer prices is partly explained by temporary factors that are not expected to have a lasting impact on inflation and therefore do not affect the structure of monetary policy. Temporary factors, i.e. changes in indirect taxes and subsidies and falling interest costs on own homes, are estimated to hold back the increase in the consumer price index by 0.5 percentage points over one year and 0.2 percentage points over two years, i.e. until March 2000 and March 2001, respectively. Underlying inflation is therefore projected to be 1.7% in March 2000 and 1.8% in March 2001 as measured by UND1X. In the light of the decided operational target formulation, let me emphasise that the Riksbank thus estimates that the years 1999 and 2000 will also be characterized by temporary price movements as a result of the interest rate cuts that have been made and due to decided changes in indirect taxes and subsidies. Overall, these factors are expected to drag down CPI inflation by 0.9 and 0.6 percentage points, respectively, measured as annual averages for each of the two years. Deviations from the inflation target should therefore be expected as a result of these factors also in 1999 and 2000. The risks of lower inflation outweigh As always, the inflation forecast is fraught with uncertainty. It is difficult to predict how the international economy will develop in the future, given the somewhat fragmented picture. The situation is about as difficult to assess as at the end of last year. It is true that the turmoil in the financial markets has diminished. However, the international economic development is a major uncertainty factor, which has rather increased somewhat over the past month with the strong economic figures in the US. These, in turn, have led to an upturn in long-term interest rates globally and also affected cyclical equities. Weaker international development could be triggered by a sudden decline in the United States. The U.S. stock market is highly valued, household savings low, and investments may appear high relative to earnings expectations in the business world. If a downturn in the UNITED STATES occurs in parallel with the weakening of the domestic market in Europe and the recession in the Japanese economy is not broken, the consequences could be serious for the world economy. On the other hand, a stronger development could occur, for example, if the European economy develops stronger than in the Riksbank's main scenario with strong consumer confidence and support from the United States, while the recovery in Asia is faster than expected. Overall, however, the risk of a weaker international economy is considered to be greater. This is also why the Riksbank estimates that the risk of lower inflation than in the main scenario is greater than that of inflation being higher. Monetary policy conclusions The Riksbank's inflation forecast concludes that inflation will slightly fall short of the Riksbank's inflation target over one to two years, even when corrected for temporary effects of indirect taxes, subsidies and interest rate changes. At the same time, as I have recently said, the risk of inflation being lower than in the main scenario is estimated to be greater than that of higher. The Executive Board of the Riksbank therefore decided at its meeting yesterday to cut the repo rate by 0.25 percentage points from 3.15 to 2.90 per cent with effect from 31 March. Penningpolitiken bedrivs normalt med hjlp av en enkel handlingsregel: Om Riksbankens inflationsprognos ett till tv r framt i tiden visar att inflationen avviker frn det uppsatta mlet br reporntan frndras. Title: Hearing on monetary policy
text: Webbarkiv Stefan Ingves in the Finance Committee. Hearing on monetary policy Date: 2016-02-23 Speakers: Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Skandiasalen, Swedish Parliament On Tuesday, Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Martin Floden will participate in this year's first hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. Ingves presents the background to the decision to lower the repo rate to -0.50 percent. He notes that although the Riksbank's very expansionary monetary policy has contributed to a strengthening of the economy, a fall in unemployment and a trend increase in inflation since the beginning of 2014, inflation is now expected to be lower in 2016 compared with previous forecasts. A longer period of low inflation increases the risk that confidence in the inflation target will weaken and that inflation will not rise towards the target as expected. Uncertainty about global developments in the rest of the world also remains high, with low inflation and several central banks pursuing a more expansionary monetary policy with the aim of stimulating the economy and raising inflation. "We have to choose between acting now or waiting for more information. In my opinion, it is better to be proactive because it is much more difficult to deal with increased monetary stimulus in the rest of the world afterwards". At the same time, Ingves points to the risks posed by the low interest rate environment. "Reforms are urgently needed to improve the situation in the housing market and to reduce household incentives to go into debt. Without them, there are obvious risks of very poor socio-economic development later on," Ingves warns. Floden discusses in his introduction the factors that have been decisive for his monetary policy stances over the past year or so. Inflation has long been below target, which, together with falling inflation expectations, risked damaging confidence in the inflation target. In addition, monetary policy in the rest of the world has become increasingly expansionary, and we have seen a downward trend in real interest rates in recent decades. "With lower interest rates in the rest of the world, the Swedish key interest rate must also be low; otherwise, growth and employment will be hampered and inflation will be too low," floden says. But as the Swedish economy now continues to strengthen and resource utilisation in the economy rises and will approach a strained level in the coming year, this suggests that inflation will continue to rise. This was an important reason why Floden expressed reservations about the recent decision to lower the repo rate. "I also think we are approaching the limit at which the pass-through of monetary policy weakens. Therefore, I think it is better to wait with further reductions", floden points out. Title: A year with the new Executive Board
text: Be4ckstrf6m: One year with the new Executive Board Date: 2000-04-05 Speaker: Governor Urban Be4ckstrf6m Location: Nationalekonomiska ff6reningen With the new legislation that came into force on the first of January last year, the Riksbank gained an independent position in its 332-year history in the formal sense for the first time in its 332-year history. It is true that, in practice, the Bank has acted independently for quite some time, but this has rather been based on the prevailing consensus of the politicians in power on the benefits of this and not on any legislative order. I myself am in my seventh year as Governor of the Riksbank and during that period I have experience from cooperation with four finance ministers. None of these have sought to influence the interest rate policy pursued. It would be going too far to say that all the finance ministers have actively supported the interest rate increases that have been implemented in all situations, but no one has, as I said, sought a different interest rate policy. The Riksbank's predecessor, the Palmstruch bank or Stockholm Banco, was founded in 1656 and although it was private, it received royal permission to conduct banking activities. It was also the king who chose the bank management. However, the bank failed after issuing too many notes against unsecured loans. On September 17, 1668, the bank was reconstituted and put under the direct control of the then Reichstag, the Estates of the Reich, in order to prevent the royal house from interfering in the bank's affairs. Kings in those days were often inclined to lead the country into war and war cost money. Thus, as early as the 1600s, it was realized that a central bank could be used for various types of, as they considered, urgent but costly projects. However, the order in which the Estates of the Riksen took control of the then Riksbank proved to be no adequate guarantee against interference. The banco commissioners appointed to manage the bank could never really work as independently as intended. The estates of the reich constantly interfered in the affairs of the bank, and the royal house sought to requisition funds from the bank on repeated occasions. Moreover, with the introduction of parliamentarism in our country in the early 1900s, the distinction sought in the 1600s by reconstituting Stockholm Banco and making the Bank of the Estates of the Realm under the Riksdag ended. As a result, government power came to be emanating from the Riksdag. But this was to some extent more about separation of powers. Independence in today's sense is not about different institutions sharing power. What is at issue instead is a delegation of responsibility and authority. In today's legislation, central government delegates decisions on monetary policy. The Riksbank cannot therefore manage monetary policy completely independently of the democratically elected institutions. This is an important difference. The Riksdag has stated that the Riksbank will be responsible for price stability. An explicit goal delegated to the central bank creates less room for rapid change, or political pressure, of monetary policy and thus gives a greater credibility to the policy. The devolution of monetary policy that has taken place through the new legislation can be said to be based on three parts. Firstly, parliament has defined and legislated on the objectives of monetary policy, i.e. to maintain a fixed monetary value and promote a secure and efficient payment system. Secondly, the Riksbank has been given the task of working independently towards these goals. Thirdly, the Riksbank is accountable to the Riksdag for its actions. This kind of delegation from the political system is not something exceptional in a democratic society. The judiciary is usually held up as a comparable example. The courts also carry out their activities independently on the basis of the laws decided by politicians. If the elected representatives are not satisfied with how the sentences are handed down, new laws are passed. There is no interference in the judgments in individual cases. Of course, the parallel cannot be pushed too far, because in the cases of the courts these are individual legal cases involving individuals and companies, while monetary policy covers all individuals in society. The Riksbank's independence is largely designed in the same way as for the courts. The Riksdag determines the Riksbank's targets, but the new Executive Board of the Riksbank independently makes the day-to-day decisions on the repo rate. There is always the possibility that Parliament will change the objectives of monetary policy if it is not satisfied with the consequences of the monetary policy designed in accordance with the objectives previously set. It is against this background that I would rather talk about the Riksbank gaining independence - and not independence - with the new legislation. The word independence better reflects the order now created around monetary policy. New wiring shape But the new legislation did not only mean a formal increase in independence and that the goal of the policy was laid down in the law. From 1 January last year, the Riksbank also has a new form of management. A management committee of six full-time members has led the bank since last year and will collectively take decisions. The council was given a controlling position and will also appoint members of the executive board on an ongoing basis. Under the new arrangements, a member of the Executive Board will continue to be appointed each year for a six-year term. An important task for the Executive Board is, of course, to take decisions on the shape of monetary policy. But the assignment involves much more than the decisions on the repo rate, although the latter often receives the greatest attention in the media and in the general discussion. The Executive Board's responsibility also includes, as the legislation says, "promoting a secure and efficient payment system", managing foreign exchange reserves in the best possible way, ensuring that the banknote supply functions well and, of course, also ensuring that the Riksbank is well managed in general. The responsibility and collegiality of the Riksbank's Executive Board is thus far-reaching. For example, the Bank of England has chosen to allow the Monetary Policy Committee to decide exclusively on interest rate policy, while the other decisions are taken by other groups. So what consequences can collegiality itself have for decisions? In the academic literature, this has been touched upon, but then focusing on the consequences for monetary policy and other areas has not been touched upon. The motives that are usually given for making monetary policy decisions collectively in the academic literature are, among other things, to get a good balance from decision-makers, but also to ensure good competence in the decision-making body. However, in many of the descriptions made in the academic literature, I find it difficult to identify, as it is often stated that Members act with different preferences and with ulterior motives. In the case of the Riksbank, in my opinion, there is little doubt that everyone on the Executive Board covers the same objective. Price stability is a legislative objective. The members of the Executive Board have jointly agreed that the target should imply an inflation rate of 2 percent, as measured by the change in the CPI, with a permissible deviation of /- one percentage point. Members shall each be responsible for the achievement of this objective. Thus, the preferences should be the same. In addition, as I see it, there is a consensus in the Executive Board on the very framework of monetary policy. Policy-making should be based on the assessment of inflation one to two years from now. If the Riksbank's forecast for inflation during this period shows above-target inflation during this period, the interest rate should normally be raised and vice versa. At the same time, the Executive Board has made it clear that there may be grounds for sometimes deviating from the target. One is if it would entail excessive real economic costs to bring inflation back to target quickly, after a disruption to the economy has occurred. Another is whether CPI inflation is affected by temporary factors that have no lasting effect on inflation developments. For example, interest costs that directly affect the CPI and indirect taxes and subsidies. But monetary policy is far from an exact science. Despite the fact that there is a common understanding of the fundamentals, there are therefore some nuanced differences in the perception of how current monetary policy should be designed. The work of the Executive Board so far has clearly shown this. By all accounts, that's also what the legislature has wanted to capture by making six people responsible for the decisions. How has the Executive Board worked? The Executive Board of the Riksbank has chosen to meet every two weeks. Discussions on monetary policy take place at special meetings about eight to ten times a year. By and large, the processes of assessment and decision are the same as before. The big difference, of course, is that there are now six people who have to make independent decisions. The transparency of the policy, including minutes reflecting the discussions at the Executive Board meetings, means that the trade-offs that were previously made internally are now being made openly. Everyone can follow how the arguments are weighed and how the discussions are conducted and thus evaluate the policy pursued. The nuanced differences that have existed in the Executive Board have so far only concerned monetary policy. As far as the other areas of responsibility are concerned, no Member has so far expressed reservations about majority decisions. The reservations in the Executive Board have concerned both the starting point for the policy decisions - the inflation assessment - and the decisions on the repo rate itself. On two occasions last year, one member of the Executive Board expressed reservations about the inflation assessment. The inflation report then became the majority's forecast. On four occasions, different members of the Executive Board have expressed reservations about the majority's decision on the repo rate. So far, there have been no instances where perceptions of monetary policy design have been based on diametrically different approaches, but rather were nuance in the assessments. We have not yet seen a meeting where one Member wanted to raise interest rates while another wanted to leave it unchanged and a third wanted to cut. However, this has been the case when the Monetary Policy Committee met in the Bank of England. The reservations have so far been due to disagreements about the inflation outlook, about the development of various subcomponents and about when in time a change in interest rates should take place. They have concerned different trade-offs in current monetary policy, which is quite natural given that these are difficult - and often not entirely - obvious trade-offs. After all, the difference in 25 basis points is not a difference that is about black or white. Thus, the effects on the real economy or inflation of such small differences in interest rates should not be exaggerated. There is, as I see it, agreement on the basic policy-making in terms of objectives, and the clarifications that have been made, as well as the framework of thought. The Executive Board therefore does not entirely agree with the academic world's description of individual members with different preferences for inflation developments and hidden intentions to try to achieve their own goals. It is a situation that could theoretically arise in the future, but today's members of the Executive Board have not, in practice, demonstrated this kind of decision-making. How has this been perceived? How, then, has our work been perceived by the outside world? I think some people have been surprised at how much of our discussions, including the differences that have occurred, we have actually shown outwardly. In the run-up to the creation of the Executive Board, some observers speculated about whether the Executive Board meetings would only be well-directed events, without any real discussion. I think we have shown quite well so far that this is not the case. Discussions on policy take place in the Executive Board and their outcome is far from a foregone conclusion. It's also what makes this form of decision-making so exciting. Neither I nor my colleagues can be absolutely sure exactly what decision will be taken. It is also then that the council's representatives are present and the minutes are written. That is also how we have interpreted the spirit of the legislature with the new order. The new independence places greater demands on transparency about policy and that the Riksbank reports on how we think about monetary policy and other areas. Even before the creation of the Executive Board, we published the Inflation Report and the Stability Report. In addition, there are now the minutes of the meetings and the fact that the speeches have been given a slightly different role. Overall, there is greater transparency in the work now, even if we cannot always give as clear a picture as before. It can be said that the new transparency means that the public enters decision-making at an earlier stage than before. With the old model, communication took place only after the decisions - formal or informal - had already been taken. In the new system, the public gets to know each decision-maker's thoughts on the decision that is emerging. It is possible that this arrangement may not be as clear as the previous one, but it is more transparent in the sense that the motivations for monetary policy appear clearer. So here we have a contradiction between transparency and clarity. By all accounts, communication has worked relatively well since the executive board was appointed. Monetary policy measures have largely been expected in advance. Transparency has therefore not been to the detriment of clarity, at least not so far. I also doubt it ever will be. The important thing for market participants should be how the thinking about interest rate policy is in the central bank. With increased knowledge of this, it should become easier for them to predict monetary policy. Chart: actual and expected repo rate. Although the protocols have been created to provide the opportunity for the Swedish people to see how we reason and thus be able to demand accountability, the publication of these has also provided an additional piece of the puzzle for those who monitor our doings and presuppositions and try to interpret our policies. They show both the members of the Executive Board's views on current policy and reflections on how the policy might be designed in the future. If we look back at developments in the autumn, we can note that the fact that some Members expressed reservations in August probably led the market into expectations of an increase. In the autumn, however, we received some criticism for talking about austerity long before any rate hike actually took place. Expectations were built in as early as September, but the raise didn't take place until November. However, the majority of the Executive Board did not see alarming inflationary pressures. This, together with the fact that inflation expectations were anchored around the target, made it possible to take time to try to make it clear to everyone and everyone in the economy that austerity did not mean that the party would be over with this. Our aim with a tighter policy was rather that we wanted to provide the conditions for it to continue longer, but without the guests being too over-refreshed. For those who early on thought they saw the need for a rate hike, the period between words and deeds may possibly have been seen as unnecessarily long. I am happy to admit that the experience of autumn 1994 influenced my own perception. However, the rate hike then, which I and many others with me think was necessary, came as a surprise. This time I thought it was important that it came in a context when the Swedish people saw the necessary in it. This should not be interpreted as meaning that neither myself nor my colleagues would not be able to act quickly with the repo rate if necessary. But there is a clear point in that the Swedish people feel a strong confidence in the interest rate decisions we make in the Riksbank - not least through the experiences that the 1990s offered. During the spring, we have experienced times when the signal to the market does not seem to have reached. At its February meeting, the Executive Board raised the repo rate by 0.5 percentage points because we saw risks that inflation would be above target in one to two years' time. But when we raised the interest rate, we de facto reassessed the inflation outlook on the basis of the new repo rate. In the press release issued in connection with the rate hike, the Executive Board stated that inflation was expected to be on target for one to two years. In addition, there were statements in speeches, when Kerstin Hessius and I pointed out that we saw a more balanced risk picture for inflation developments after the interest rate hike. Nevertheless, expectations remained in the market that interest rates would be raised at the monetary policy meeting, which, as is well known, did not happen. Both we in the Riksbank and the players in the market have reason to take on board what has happened. It is in the Riksbank's interest to continuously communicate the thoughts we have on the inflation outlook so that the repo rate decisions do not surprise. In this case, on a total of three occasions, we had discussed the inflation outlook quite explicitly in a way that suggested that there was a high probability that the decision we would eventually make meant that the repo rate would be left unchanged. Still, expectations were set for a hike. It is normally the inflation outlook over one to two years that determines our actions with the repo rate. Certainly, we in the Riksbank also have to take into account the mandate in the legislation to "promote a safe and efficient payment system", something that may require us to change the repo rate if that goal should be about to be threatened. Normally, price stability is a prerequisite for a secure and efficient payment system, although situations could arise where the relationship between price stability and financial stability does not seem so simple. This could happen, for example, if credit lending is on the rise in such a way that it could lead to a new banking crisis of the kind we experienced in the early 1990s. But in such a situation, we will be very clear that we intend to depart from the usual framework of thought. The credit expansion that is now taking place is apparently too fast to be compatible with socio-economic balance in the long run, but in any case it does not threaten so far the stability of the payment system. Slutord All in all, I can note that the debate around the Riksbank's independence has become more harmonious recently. Independence itself seems to have been accepted and the discussion is currently more focused on substantive issues surrounding the Riksbank's areas of responsibility. I personally think that the legislation we have works very well. It provides formal autonomy, which requires far-reaching transparency. Now the Riksbank has also reached the point where we are one of the most open central banks in the world. Therefore, it feels extra fun that the Riksbank's position is characterized by a greater degree of harmony than a few years ago. I remember so well that I thought about how this could be achieved when I took office as Governor of the Riksbank at the beginning of 1994. But transparency also places new demands. It tightens the requirements for us to make good judgments about the future, which every experienced economic assessor knows is a difficult task. But it is also what makes the work in the Riksbank so stimulating - not only for me as Governor of the Riksbank or for my colleagues on the Executive Board, but for all the talented economists who are on our staff. A greater degree of harmony around the Riksbank and its monetary policy should also make our statements and actions disappear from the front pages of the newspapers. As long as they are part of a normally designed monetary policy, they should hardly belong to the kind of news that needs to be crowded at the front of a newspaper, radio or TV broadcast. That hasn't happened yet, but I think there may come a day when a rate change of say 0.25 percentage points is not front page news. When this happens, monetary policy and the Riksbank's independence have not only found their role in Swedish society, but have also been seriously accepted by a broad public for the work that has been done. I think that day will come.

Title: Speech at BIS 71st Annual General Meeting
text: Backstrom: Speech at BIS 71st Annual General Meeting Datum: 2001-06-11 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Backstrom Plats: Bank for International Settlements, Basel Ladies and Gentlemen, On the occasion of the 71st Annual General Meeting of the Bank for International Settlements, it is my privilege and pleasure to extend a warm welcome to all the delegates from our shareholding central banks, the representatives of non-member central banks and international institutions and our distinguished guests. Before I turn to our traditional review of salient aspects of the Bank's affairs, I regret to have to inform you of the recent death of a former member of the Bank's Management. Maurice Toussaint died on 5 June 2001 at the age of 80; Mr Toussaint was a Manager of the Banking Department from 1971 until his retirement in 1986. I would like first to comment briefly on the financial results for the year ended 31 March 2001. The Balance Sheet and the Profit and Loss Account, duly audited, appear at the end of the Annual Report; a commentary on the Bank's operations is provided in the chapter of the Annual Report entitled "Activities of the Bank". The Balance Sheet total increased by 1.6% during the year to 76.1 billion gold francs, which represents a record for the end of a financial year. The Profit and Loss Account shows a net profit of 271.7 million gold francs, a decrease of 11.7% compared with the figure for the previous financial year. This decline is principally attributable to losses incurred on the early repayment of certain of the Bank's securitised liabilities. Since these losses will be recouped over the period to the original maturity of the claims concerned, the underlying economic profit situation of the Bank remained stable. The factors behind the decrease are described in more detail in "Activities of the Bank" under the heading "Net profits and their distribution". I am pleased to inform you that the Board of Directors recommends that the present General Meeting approve an increase in the dividend from 340 to 360 Swiss francs per share. The number of shares on which a dividend will be paid is 452,073, which excludes 77,052 shares held in treasury, comprising 72,648 shares formerly in private hands, 2,304 shares repurchased from central banks and 2,100 other shares. Accordingly, a sum of approximately 48.6 million gold francs, being the gold franc equivalent of the total dividend proposed, has been set aside for this purpose. As for the remainder of the net profit, amounting to 223.1 million gold francs, it is proposed that the present General Meeting approve transfers of a sum of 44.6 million gold francs to the general reserve fund, a sum of 3 million gold francs to the special dividend reserve fund, and the balance of 175.5 million gold francs to the free reserve fund. Turning now to the administration of the Bank, the major event of the past financial year was the repurchase of privately held BIS shares. In January 2001, an Extraordinary General Meeting decided to restrict the right to hold shares in the BIS exclusively to central banks, and accordingly approved a proposal of the Board of Directors to proceed with the mandatory repurchase of all shares held by private shareholders against payment of compensation of 16,000 Swiss francs for each share. In order to effect this mandatory repurchase, Articles 6, 12 and 15 to 18 of the Bank's Statutes were amended and a transitional provision was included as Article 18(A) of the Statutes. These statutory amendments are based on the special international rules applicable to the BIS as an international organisation, including the Bank's Constituent Charter and its Statutes. At end-May 2001, compensation payments had been released for 82,7% of the total of 72,648 shares which were formerly in private hands. 86,5% of private shareholder accounts had been closed at that time. The remaining former shareholders have been contacted again but have yet to reply to the Bank or to send all documentation required to process the compensation payments. A small number of former private shareholders are contesting the amount of compensation to be paid and the valuation methods chosen and have filed complaints against the Bank either before the Arbitral Tribunal provided for by the Hague Agreement or in national courts. The BIS has requested that all such claims be referred to the Arbitral Tribunal in The Hague which, pursuant to Article 54 of the Statutes of the Bank, has sole jurisdiction to hear disputes arising from the transaction. Among the Board of Directors, Hans Meyer and Gordon Thiessen retired from their positions as President of the Swiss National Bank and Governor of the Bank of Canada, respectively, and vacated their seats on the Board. The Board elected their successors at the respective institutions, Jean-Pierre Roth and David Dodge, as new members of the Board. There were three changes among the Alternates of ex officio Directors. Antonio Fazio, Governor of the Bank of Italy, appointed Bruno Bianchi to succeed Carlo Santini; Guy Quaden, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium, nominated Peter Praet to replace Jean-Jacques Rey; and Ernst Welteke, President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, appointed Stefan Schonberg to succeed Helmut Schieber. As regards senior officials of the Bank, Guy Noppen and Marten de Boer retired from their position as Manager at the end of September 2000 and the end of March 2001, respectively. Peter Dittus was appointed Deputy Secretary General from 1 October 2000. At the end of 2000, Josef Tosovsky succeeded John Heimann as Chairman of the Financial Stability Institute. Before concluding these remarks on the Bank's affairs, I wish to express my gratitude for the support offered to me by my colleagues on the Board and their Alternates in the past financial year. I also wish to thank the Management and staff of the Bank for their continuing contribution to the success of our institution. I would like to turn now to a review of global economic conditions. Let me look back on the main economic developments; look forward, as befits a good central banker, to identify potential risks; and finally stand back to reflect on some broader policy challenges concerning monetary and financial stability. The salient economic development in the most recent period has been the deceleration in global growth. This started with an unexpectedly abrupt and sharp slowdown in the US economy in the later part of 2000, possibly heralding an end to, or a pause in, an extraordinary period of expansion. It was accompanied by a faltering of the recovery in Japan, and followed by a weakening of growth in emerging market countries and subsequently, to a lesser degree, in Europe. By postwar standards, an unusual but welcome feature of the slowdown is that it was not fundamentally induced by tighter monetary policy aimed at quelling strong inflationary pressures. The tightening that did take place may have acted as a catalyst. But the slowdown seems to reflect a more spontaneous weakening in expenditures following the previous expansion and was heralded by sharply falling equity prices, rising credit spreads and tighter lending terms. Indeed, globally, inflationary pressures have remained remarkably subdued at this point in the cycle, despite last year's rise in oil prices. This bears witness to the progress made in the long-standing fight against inflation. No doubt the wave of technological innovation has played a significant role here. But product, labour and financial market liberalisation, both within and across national borders, has been instrumental in bringing this outcome about. Moreover, the process has been underpinned by prudent fiscal and monetary policies in a growing number of countries. We are already reaping the benefits of this success, in the form of greater room for manoeuvre. In response to the slowdown, monetary policies have, where appropriate, been eased. In some cases, where fiscal prudence has allowed more than the use of automatic stabilisers, this has also been accompanied by an actual or prospective relaxation of fiscal policy. Since the slowdown started, the crucial question has been how long and deep it will prove to be. A deceleration in growth in the United States was expected and even desired, as it would allow the economy to avoid overheating and gradually to absorb the domestic and external imbalances built up during the previous rapid expansion. Of these, the negative private saving rate and the large current account deficit have attracted most attention. If the process went too far, however, it could have significant implications for a world economy that, as I will explain in a moment, still exhibits a number of weak spots. By mid-May, the upturn in equity prices, narrowing credit spreads, a firm dollar and the shape of the yield curve were all signs that financial markets were anticipating a relatively quick recovery. Official forecasts have been suggesting a broadly similar central scenario. A number of factors could give grounds for optimism. In the United States, there have been clear signs that the inventory cycle has largely run its course and that consumer confidence has been holding up. The new government in Japan has indicated a fresh determination to implement the long-awaited financial and corporate restructuring. Borrowing in international securities markets was particularly buoyant in the first quarter of 2001. The financial crises in Argentina and Turkey have seen only limited contagion so far. And the room for some central banks to ease policy further as long as inflationary pressures remain subdued can provide some comfort. Even so, we should be mindful of the risks ahead. The road leading to the hoped-for sustainable growth is a narrow one. The real and financial imbalances built up during the long expansion might not unwind as smoothly as might be expected. There is a tension between short-run and long-run dynamics. One example of this tension is how the external imbalance in the United States might be resolved. Paradoxically, if the central scenario actually materialised, it would do little to address this imbalance. Doing so would most likely need to be accompanied by an effective depreciation of the dollar. The question is whether such an overall adjustment would take place smoothly and without rekindling inflationary pressures in the United States and unwelcome deflationary forces elsewhere. Another example of the tension has to do with the nexus between investment and consumption at the current juncture. The key to further expansion in the United States, and to a lasting recovery in Japan, is maintaining and restoring profitability, respectively. This would help to propel investment, bruised by an overhang in the capital stock. But in the short run, sustaining profitability could risk setting in motion forces that might depress consumer expenditure excessively. In the United States, if underlying productivity growth is indeed permanently higher, the current slowdown will entail sizeable job losses, at a time when the household savings ratio is at an alltime low and indebtedness relatively high. Sizeable job losses would also need to accompany the restructuring in Japan. In both cases, the resilience of the consumer might be severely tested. How the future unfolds will also depend on developments in the financial sector. The link between the slowdown in profits, asset prices, financial conditions and the real economy is critical. Here again the picture is mixed. There are clearly some very encouraging signs. In contrast to previous episodes, such as October 1987, equity prices have undergone a major correction without so far causing obvious strains in the markets. Signs of exuberance in property prices seem so far to be limited to a few countries. With the exception of Japan, the banking sector generally appears to be in better shape than before previous downturns. Encouraged by supervisors and scarred by previous experience, financial institutions have tightened risk management practices. And emerging market countries have taken steps to address the vulnerabilities revealed by the Asian crisis, especially with regard to their external debts. Nevertheless, weak spots remain. Since earnings have fallen sharply, equity markets still look high by historical standards. The rapid growth of credit in several countries during the upswing has led to a substantial accumulation of leverage, not least in the telecoms sector, while bank provisions are, as always, comparatively low at this point in the cycle. In Asia, particularly exposed to the slowdown in the IT sector, financial restructuring has not proceeded as speedily as might have been warranted. Large external deficits make Latin America and eastern Europe vulnerable to a sudden change in market sentiment. And the resilience of new instruments, such as credit derivatives, as well as that of markets and intermediaries, recently subject to considerable structural change, has not yet been fully tested. It is, of course, natural for risks and uncertainties to loom large at turning points in economic activity. Upon reflection, however, the character of the risks at the current juncture is rather novel in the postwar context. As such, it also contains clues about the evolving nexus between monetary stability, financial stability and the business cycle. Allow me to make four observations and to outline two broad policy challenges. First: financial liberalisation has resulted in a much tighter link between financial and real economic developments. This has greatly improved the allocation of resources and underpinned the higher growth potential of the world economy. At the same time, it may also have contributed to amplifying business cycle fluctuations. Access to external finance is more plentiful and more intimately driven by perceptions of, and appetite for, risk. And these move strongly with economic activity. Hence the highly procyclical nature of credit, asset prices and market indicators of risk, such as credit spreads. Second: much of the financial instability experienced since at least the late 1980s in industrial and emerging market countries reflects instances in which the above mutually reinforcing processes have gone too far. In too many countries, financial imbalances, and the associated distortions in the real economy, grew in the expansionary phase and their subsequent unwinding overwhelmed the often weak lines of defence in place. The costs in terms of GDP forgone have been high. It seems that we are all better at judging the relative risk of different instruments, institutions and counterparties than at assessing how risk, especially system-wide risk, evolves over time. Third: many of these episodes of instability have taken place against a benign inflation background. Low inflation is necessary for sustainable long-run growth but is not sufficient to prevent financial instability. In fact, low inflation can sometimes allow the build-up of underlying imbalances to proceed further. It can do so by encouraging optimism about the future and obviating the need for monetary tightening to contain rising prices. Fourth: as a result of the present configuration of arrangements in the monetary and financial spheres, the current business cycles may arguably have come to resemble more closely those under the gold standard. For it was then that a liberalised financial environment last coexisted with a monetary regime that enjoyed high antiinflation credibility. There are two key differences, however, that may have the potential for amplifying fluctuations in our modern times, by making the present system more "elastic". One is the presence of safety nets in the financial sphere; if illdesigned, they can encourage excessive risk-taking. The other is the absence of an external constraint on credit expansion in the monetary sphere, such as convertibility into gold. The issue is how far these two differences are offset by the prudential regulatory and supervisory framework now in place and by the discretionary response of the monetary authorities to economic developments. I suspect that in the years ahead we will be devoting increasing attention to these complex issues. The policy goal, as always, should be to put in place safeguards in the financial and monetary spheres to reap the long-run benefits of a liberalised environment while limiting financial instability and its attendant costs. This in turn implies two key challenges, elaborated further in the body of this year's Annual Report. The first challenge is to strengthen the lines of defence in the prudential area. We have done a lot in recent years, with respect to institutions, markets and infrastructure. The proposed revision of the Basel Capital Accord is just the latest, highly welcome example. But more can be done to build on this solid base. A guiding principle is to strengthen further the system-wide orientation of the prudential framework, with respect to both diagnosis and cure. Salient examples include improving the design of safety nets and studying possible ways of limiting the amplitude of financial cycles and their consequences. The second challenge is to assess critically the relationship between monetary policy and financial stability with a view to consolidating the gains on the inflation front without unwittingly incurring costs. The issue is whether there are conditions under which it might be appropriate for monetary policy to respond to the build-up of financial imbalances and, if so, how this could be done. I am fully aware that these are difficult, indeed uncomfortable, questions. Yet tackling them may hold one key to further progress in our search for enduring monetary and financial stability. Doing so will call for close dialogue and cooperation between monetary and prudential authorities. The BIS and the Basel-based community more generally will no doubt continue to play a prominent role in this endeavour.

Title: Swedish economy
text: Be4ckstrf6m: Swedish economy Date: 2002-02-02 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Be4ckstrf6m Location: Aktiespararna, Sf6lvesborg-Bromf6lla Thank you for the invitation to come here to Sf6lvesborg and for the opportunity to discuss the Swedish economy with an interested and well-informed audience. Given that the Riksbank's Executive Board will discuss monetary policy and determine the repo rate on Thursday next week, I would like to take this opportunity to say something about how I currently view the conditions for this decision. When the Riksbank determines the repo rate, an analysis of future inflation in Sweden is at the center. Inflationary pressures normally vary with the business cycle. The stronger the increase in output and the expansion of employment, the greater the risk that prices and wages will rise faster and vice versa. Therefore, it is natural to start the assessment of the inflation outlook with a discussion of the conjuncture. But there may of course also be other impulses to price developments than those related to the economic cycle. In conclusion, I will say something also about such price movements and how they come into the monetary policy framework. International business cycle in line with assessment... In the Riksbank's latest inflation report, we estimated that the international economy would gradually recover during 2002. This follows the rapid decline in activity that took place in 2001 in all three major economic areas of the world. Gradually, the reorientation of economic policy taken in the United States and a number of other industrialized countries is having an effect on demand in the economy. Since the beginning of last year, the U.S. Federal Reserve has cut its key interest rate 11 times by a total of 4.75 percentage points, down 6.5 percent to 1.75 percent. It is not only monetary policy that has extended a helping hand to the economy, fiscal policy has also been conducted in a more expansionary direction. The U.S. Congress has decided on increased government spending and reduced taxes; additional stimulus may be relevant. In Europe, economic policy has also changed and become more expansionary. The European Central Bank's key interest rate has been gradually reduced to 3.25 percent. Fiscal policy, on the other hand, has not been able to be used in the same way as in the United States. Weak public finances in the initial situation make it difficult for many European countries in general and Germany in particular to pursue equally stimulating policies. A reorientation of economic policy, together with the fact that the adjustment of stocks by companies seems to be coming to an end and the fact that more and more of the misinvestments of recent years have been written off their balance sheets, suggest that an economic recovery will take place in the second half of 2002. These were some of the factors that formed the basis for the Riksbank's forecast in December 2001. How, then, does this assessment stand? If you look at the statistics received since the inflation report was presented, the contours of a flattening of the economic downturn, especially in the United States, are becoming increasingly clear. In Europe, too, tendencies in that direction even if they are not as pronounced. Of course, we cannot be completely sure and setbacks may come, but american households' confidence in the future at least looks to have returned. Consumer spending, which accounts for about 70 percent of U.S. GDP, has shown surprising robustness. Productivity development in the business sector remains good. The stock decommissioning looks to have come a long way. Well-stocked inventories and falling sales usually suggest that companies are starting to cut production so that it falls more than demand. The adjustment of inventories is initially driving the economy downwards. As the reduction in inventories gradually draws to a close, companies can raise production again without demand yet starting to increase. It is precisely this positive effect that should soon come. However, for recovery to last, it must be accompanied by a broader and sustained increase in demand, otherwise it risks being relatively short-lived. Here there is reason to be vigilant about developments. Imbalances are large in the US economy and the stock market is highly valued, both in a historical perspective and in relation to this phase of the business cycle. However, a high level of productivity compared to the rest of the world can reduce concerns about these problems. The ratio of households' savings to disposable income continues to be at a record low. Unemployment continues to rise. Against this background, there is a risk that the willingness to consume will moderate and the propensity to save will increase, as well as a delay in the recovery on the investment side, which, taken together, would worsen the prospects for a lasting recovery. The economic upturn in the US economy is thus by no means secured. There are a lot of positive signs, but there are also risks. If we then turn our eyes to Europe, there do not seem to be any clear signs of an early recovery. Yet the euro area has not built up imbalances similar to those in the United States. This makes it easier for the recovery, once it comes about, to continue. If you look at leading indicators, you can certainly see that companies have become more positive. However, the outlook for the euro area's largest economy, Germany, remains uncertain and unemployment is rising. In Japan, for example, the problems in the financial sector are putting a spanner in the works for a recovery. Prices are falling and employment is falling, contributing to negative developments. All in all, there is today hardly any reason to change the assessment that there will be a recovery in the world around us in the second half of 2002. But there is a risk that the recovery will be slower and more protracted in the US, in which case this would suggest weaker economic development than in the main scenario. ... as well as for Sweden The economic picture the Riksbank signed for Sweden in the December report showed a business cycle that is fairly consistent with previous ups and downs. Demand is expected to pick up in the second half of 2002. The assessment is based on a relatively strong increase in households' disposable income - just over 4% in 2002 - partly as a result of lower taxes, increased transfers and a continued high level of employment despite the slowdown. Improved exports as the international economy brightens are expected to gradually benefit investments in the business sector. Overall, the Swedish economy is expected to grow by 1.8 percent this year and 2.4 percent next year. Published revisions to GDP statistics suggest that demand last year may have been somewhat weaker than the Riksbank expected. However, continued strong employment statistics and retail sales figures suggest a more positive development. Households are somewhat more optimistic about the future. Furthermore, the swedish companies' order situation has improved and it looks as if the downturn in the industrial economy has leveled off and perhaps even bottomed out. Even when it comes to Sweden, I think that the picture we presented of the economy in the coming years largely stands. At the same time, some uncertainty remains that above all, it has to do with the economic situation in the outside world and the various factors that affect it. Inflation picture The Riksbank chose to leave its key interest rate unchanged in December. Behind the decision was the assessment that inflation over the 1-2 year term will develop in line with the target of 2 percent. The current high inflation rate was projected to slow down in the spring. A weaker economy, a stronger krona and lower commodity prices were expected to dampen price developments. Furthermore, the various supply disruptions that pushed up the prices of electricity, meat, fruit and vegetables were expected to fall out of the comparative figures and, so to speak, "automatically" lead to a fall in the inflation rate in spring 2002. In the risk picture presented by the Riksbank in its December report, the risk of weaker inflation was the risk of weaker economic development in both the rest of the world and Sweden. In the second wave, there was a risk that inflationary pressures and the pass-through of a weak exchange rate would have been underestimated. Overall, the risk picture was judged to be balanced, i.e. the scales weighed evenly. Incoming statistics since the December report was published show slightly higher inflation than expected. Inflation as measured by the CPI rose by 0.1 percentage point between November and December, giving an annual rate of 2.9 percent in December. Compared with the forecast in the December Inflation Report, the outcome was 0.3 percentage points higher. Underlying inflation as measured by UND1X, i.e. the consumer price index adjusted for interest costs and direct effects of taxes, stood at an annual rate of 3.4 per cent in December compared with the forecast in December of 3.1 per cent. It cannot be ruled out that part of the rise in inflation, in addition to the temporary factors, may be a result of the previous good economy. Rising costs for companies can, when the economic upturn becomes too strong, begin to be passed on to consumers in whole or in part in the form of increased prices. In my opinion, it cannot be completely ignored that such an impact on price formation may, at least to some extent, be behind the rise in inflation. Another factor that may be behind the rise in inflation is, of course, the weak krona in 2001. It is always a problem for a central bank when the inflation rate deviates more markedly upwards or downwards from the target. Today's inflation rate is well above target and the underlying inflation rate even above the upper tolerance limit of 3%. But the matter is somewhat more complicated than that. Let me therefore pause for a moment here to highlight a couple of aspects. Every central bank that has an explicit objective must make a choice. In its most extreme form, this election situation may look like this: Either the central bank aims to keep inflation on target at all times, or it admits that there are deviations perhaps even for slightly longer periods. If inflation is to remain accurately on target, major adjustments to the repo rate are constantly required, which leads to sharp reversals in market interest rates, output and employment. However, if temporary deviations between inflation and the central bank's target are allowed, monetary policy can be conducted in a softer way. A more gradual adjustment of output and employment will bring inflation into line with the target. There are downsides to both of these extreme positions. Large-scale repo rate measures, with the attendant sharp shifts in employment and output, could lead to a build-up of public support for the central bank and the monetary policy regime. However, excessive deviations from the inflation target can lead to a lack of confidence in the inflation target, rising inflation expectations and to the costs of eventually bringing inflation back to the target being high. This means that central banks often choose a monetary policy strategy that lies somewhere between the two extremes. Not too big a rash with the interest rate, but also don't hesitate to change it if necessary. Normally, the Riksbank conducts policy with a view to inflation one to two years in the future, but there may be times when the perspective must be even longer. The disadvantage of it is that the repo rate must be determined using forecasts and forecasts can go wrong. There are constant price disturbances that are not cyclical but that have an impact on the inflation rate. However, the advantage of a forward-looking policy is that monetary policy can be conducted more smoothly, but still with a firm hand. The Riksbank reacts strongly to inflation forecasts, but since forecasts involve an assessment of which inflation impulses are temporary, overreactions are prevented. The supply-side disruptions that have occurred over the past year are examples of price fluctuations that can cause deviations from the inflation target with the monetary policy strategy chosen by the Riksbank. For example, it can be poor access to water in the power reservoirs as a result of a snowless winter as was the case last spring, diseases among cows that drive up meat prices or unusually cold weather in Europe that pushes up the prices of fruit and vegetables. If factors of this kind raise the general price level, it will temporarily raise the inflation rate in the following twelve-month period. Let me underline this: these kinds of temporary effects remain in inflation at an annual rate over the following twelve-month period - they do not disappear after only a couple of months. The fact that temporary factors can influence inflation rates in this way has happened in the past. For example, for a few years at the end of the 1990s, it was the successive deregulations in the electricity and telecommunications sectors that created deviations from the inflation target, but with the difference that it was then a question of the target being exceeded instead. Now the reverse has happened. With our monetary policy strategy, this is something we have to live with. The inflation rate will swing around the target, so to speak - that cannot be overemphasised. But if we look in the rearview mirror, we can see that inflation has been very close to the inflation target on average since it was introduced. It is intended that this should continue to be the case in the future. Thus, it is not the temporary price disturbances that cause the greatest concern, as long as they do not affect inflation expectations. It is different if the krona is weak or if a strong economy is the reason for the target deviation. Both of these factors, as I have just said, may have some bearing on the fact that inflation is currently above target. However, the krona has strengthened somewhat and the economy slowed down last year. Both of these circumstances should mean that price pressures will be dampened going forward. This was the Riksbank's view in the latest inflation report. The fundamental features of this analysis should be able to remain firm in the future, but the Riksbank must closely monitor that price increases will indeed be dampened later in the spring. It cannot be ruled out a certain shift forward in time of the decline in inflation, given the higher outcome so far and possibly continued rising prices for fruit and vegetables. It is, of course, positive that employment has held up in 2001 despite weak production figures, but the flip side is that the rate of increase in productivity in enterprises has slowed down. The noticeably lower productivity growth given that published GDP figures for 2001 stand - has also contributed to higher than expected wage cost pressures. Final words All in all, I think that today there is no reason to adjust to any great extent the real economic assessment that the Riksbank presented in December. There are increasing signs of stabilisation among our most important exporting countries, which usually precedes a gradual recovery. The Swedish economy also seems to be levelling off and the conditions for a better economy usually follow such a levelling off. At the same time, however, some question marks remain about an international recovery and imbalances, not least in the US economy. Here there are risks of the kind that we highlighted in December and that still need to be taken into account in the overall assessment. The inflation picture stands roughly speaking. The pace of price increases is expected to moderate gradually going forward. At the bottom is the falling resource utilisation last year and a good bit into this year. Temporary effects that have driven up prices gradually also lose their impact on inflation rates. In addition, a gradual strengthening of the krona would reduce the risk of imported inflation. At the same time, uncertainty about the exchange in the broad sense between growth and inflation remains. The inflation picture thus remains problematic and cannot be waved away. The Riksbank must, as I see it, closely monitor incoming inflation figures, deepen the analysis if there are deviations and take this into account in the ongoing structure of monetary policy.

Nu har det omvnda skett. Med vr penningpolitiska strategi s r detta ngot vi fr leva med. Inflationstakten kommer att s att sga svnga runt mlet - det kan inte nog betonas. Men tittar vi i backspegeln kan vi konstatera att inflationen har legat vldigt nra inflationsmlet i genomsnitt sedan det infrdes. Det r avsikten att det ska vara s ven i framtiden. Det r allts inte de tillflliga prisstrningarna som orsakar strst bekymmer, svitt de inte pverkar inflationsfrvntningarna. Den mrkbart lgre produktivitetskningen givet att publicerade BNP-siffror fr 2001 str sig - har ven bidragit till ett hgre lnekostnadstryck n vntat. Slutord Sammantaget tycker jag att det idag inte finns anledning att i ngon strre utstrckning justera den realekonomiska bedmning som Riksbanken presenterade i december. Tecknen p en stabilisering bland vra viktigaste exportlnder blir allt fler, ngot som brukar freg en gradvis terhmtning. ven den svenska ekonomin tycks plana ut och frutsttningar fr en bttre konjunktur brukar normalt flja p en sdan utplaning. Hr finns det risker av det slag som vi lyfte fram i december och som fortfarande mste tas med i den sammantagna bedmningen. Inflationsbilden str sig grovt sett.
