Title: Swedish monetary policy
text: Backstrom: Swedish monetary policy Date: 2000-03-17 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Monetary Policy Forum Favourable development in the Swedish economy The Swedish economy is currently developing better than it has been for a very long time. Statistics Sweden reported last week that GDP grew by an average of 3.8 percent in 1999. At the same time, nearly 90000 new jobs were added during the year, which is the largest increase in employment in 30 years. This expansion takes place in an environment where price and wage rises  at least so far  have remained at relatively low levels, despite the fact that the economic upswing has continued for over six years with average annual GDP growth of around 3%. An important reason for this is, of course, the spare resources that existed after the crisis in the early 1990s, but also that inflation expectations have been anchored around the target. This is an indication that this is a balanced process, at least so far. This is further underlined by the fact that the economy is in surplus in both central government finances and current account. Ten years ago, who would have thought that the Swedish economy would enter such a favourable trajectory? The national accounts, which are now available for the new base year from 1980 onwards, show an interesting fact. Investments play a prominent role in the economic cycle that the Swedish economy has been in since the summer of 1993. However, it is not the same investment boost as in the US. Rapidly increasing investments in new production equipment provide a higher production potential in the long run. This is certainly one reason why productivity increased somewhat faster in the 1990s compared to the 1980s. This has helped to raise the potential growth rate of the Swedish economy, which thus makes it possible for the economy to grow sustainably somewhat faster. Historically, however, there has so far been a fairly moderate increase in productivity growth. Graph: Labour productivity from 1870 to 1999 However, a growth trajectory driven by investments can create virtuous circles. The supply side of the economy generates increased demand and favourable demand tends to further strengthen the supply side. As I said, increased investment tends to drive increased productivity growth. Increased productivity growth, in turn, means that expectations for companies' future earnings growth are adjusted upwards, which often leads to rising stock prices. Higher valuations of companies both stimulate these companies to invest further and also enable new companies to access venture capital for further expansion. At the same time, households that own shares experience an increase in value, at least on paper, their net assets. Higher wealth values and optimistic future expectations lead to faster increases in consumption. Graph: Share of investment in GDP Since the 1950s, there are three distinct shorter or longer periods of rapidly rising investments. The first period stretched from the early 1950s until 1967. The capital stock was built up during this period and laid the foundation for a relatively large potential for rationalization in business. Productivity growth was also, as we all know, rapid in a historical perspective and the investment period was long drawn out in time. A contributing factor  but by no means the only explanation for the rapid increase in investment  was the extensive housing construction. The share of investment in GDP peaked in the recession around 1967. Profit shares in companies fell, the first and second oil crises took place in the 1970s, structural problems became apparent in the Swedish economy and the share of investments in GDP fell sharply between 1967 and 1982. A lot of this case is explained by a decrease in housing investment, but even excluding housing, there were clear tendencies towards stagnation of the investment share. If anything, the trend even showed a slight decrease. At the same time, production potential weakened. Sweden lagged behind other countries in terms of growth. Real wages stagnated. The second period of rapid investment growth began after the devaluation in 1982 and extended until the late 1980s. However, it does not appear that the production potential of the Swedish economy was affected. The economy overheated at fairly moderate growth rates in the late 1980s and productivity growth slowed markedly. Indeed, the 1980s showed the weakest productivity growth since industrialism had its breakthrough in our country around 1870. This suggests that during this period it was not so much about productive investments that help to lift production potential. Statistics also show that  at least in the late 1980s  there was a large extent of investment in commercial real estate in connection with the years of speculation. The third investment period began in connection with the turnaround in the summer of 1993. The krona depreciated, the share of profits in the business sector rose, the world economy improved, exports and industrial production picked up. Gross investment played an important role in the process of growth. The trend is also more pronounced if one clears for housing investment. Investment-driven growth can lead to different processes Assessing how persistent an ongoing growth process is, is not so simple. Depending on how the interaction between the supply side and the demand side of the economy develops over time, a few different scenarios can be drawn up: "A first possibility is that the supply side of the economy is expanding too quickly and the build-up of the capital stock goes too far if the investment activity is characterized by over-optimism. It can become a kind of speculation in real investments. In such a process, sooner or later there will be a setback, without necessarily being preceded by an acceleration of price and wage rises. Such a setback could force the real economy into a difficult downward course of adjustment. The question is whether the downturn of the Japanese economy in the 1990s has not had this kind of element. It is also likely that "overinvestment" in real estate contributed to the Swedish problems in the early 1990s. "A second possibility is that rapidly rising asset prices will bring with it a similarly rapid credit expansion. Wealth expansion in this case generates demand for financial investments, rather than for goods and services. The return on these financial investments is initially far higher than the cost of borrowing. One such financial bubble creates vulnerability not only in the balance sheets of households and companies, but also in the financial system at large. Sooner or later, however, over-optimism reverses and a difficult process of financial adjustment sets in motion, perhaps even problems in the banking sector arise. This, too, is something that has been characteristic of the Japanese economy. Sweden and a lot of other countries have also experienced similar processes. "A third possibility is that demand growth will be too fast, despite a faster expansion of capital stock and supply side. Optimism about future incomes will be too great. The result is then a classic acceleration of price and wage increases. A fourth possibility  and this is, of course, the best option  is for the interaction between the supply and demand side of the economy to develop harmoniously and go hand in hand. The investment period from the early 1950s until the mid-1960s is an example of such a long period. What is usually referred to as the new economy is driven by a strong wave of investment in which the new technology gradually spreads throughout the economy and streamlines production, but development can thus take several different paths. Not everything is bright in that world either, although in the general discussion one can easily get that impression, but it undeniably holds a lot of interesting challenges and opportunities for consumers, entrepreneurs, actors in the financial system and, not least, for economic policy makers. But it is important that actors in any part of the economy do not become overly optimistic and make unpremeditated decisions. Then the good circles can turn into euphoria. History teaches us that the process then ends with more or less violent setbacks. For a central bank, it is therefore important to ensure that inflation rates are firmly anchored around the target, but it must also promote efficiency and security in the financial system as a whole. In this perspective, stable low inflation is an indicator that the demand and supply side of the economy develops harmoniously over time. However, as I have just said, we must also follow developments in the financial system as a whole to ensure that no imbalances otherwise build up that could threaten a favourable development of the economy. The experience of the late 1980s and early 1990s still casts its shadow over us. Balanced development in the Swedish economy For Sweden, the development so far seems to be characterized by stability. The figures for the inflation rate have on several occasions come in rather lower than most analysts, including the Riksbank, expected. At present, there also seems to be moderation in credit expansion. However, asset prices have soared in a way that reflects significant expectations of substantially faster economic growth in our country compared to the past. On this point, therefore, there is a case for raising a warning flag. Representatives of the Riksbank have previously said that we are hesitant but not dismissive of the so-called new economy. So far, we have not seen any tangible signs of an acceleration of productivity growth in the Swedish economy, similar to that in the United States. As I said earlier, productivity growth seems to have increased in the 1990s compared to the 1980s, but we have not yet seen any sharp acceleration, even in the latest national accounts. But we are following developments very closely and looking for signs. Sweden is a country that often ranks in the absolute top tier when it comes to IT also in a broader sense than just Internet use among the population where we are actually best placed among all countries. However, the increase in productivity in the second half of 1999 is an interesting observation. Similarly, we note that domestic underlying inflation is low despite strong demand developments. Swedish economy moves towards full resource utilization The fact that demand in the Swedish economy, despite this, is still growing faster than the supply side can handle in the long run is shown by the fact that unemployment is falling. That is fundamentally a good thing, especially after the period of historically very high unemployment that characterized our country during the 1990s. But somewhere there is a limit where companies find it difficult to recruit workers with the right education and professional experience. Already today, such tendencies exist in certain industries and in certain localities. In addition, it has been shown that unemployment among the highly educated has quickly fallen to around 3%, while the unemployment rate for people with lower education has lingered at over 6%. It is not unnatural that a labour market characterised by falling unemployment is gradually becoming more strained. The problem for a central bank is knowing when this risks spilling over into an acceleration of wage cost increases so that the inflation target is threatened. Wages account for the overwhelming majority of companies' costs and rapidly rising wages are therefore a key driver of an inflationary process. But there are two problems here that a central bank has to deal with. An acceleration of wage growth usually comes with some delay after more widespread labour market shortages begin to emerge. At the same time, it takes quite a long time for a rate hike to take full effect. In the Riksbank, we have talked about a delay of one to two years, but of course we cannot be entirely sure of the accuracy of that figure. However, there is currently no evidence that this period would have been significantly shorter. There are arguments that speak in both directions. Against this background, there are two possible development paths that it is therefore important to avoid for a central bank. One is that the central bank acts too early in the economic upturn so that unemployment lingers at an unnecessarily high level and the economy as a whole is prevented from using its full potential. The second is that the Central Bank acts too late. A process of accelerating wages and price rises is about to get under way. Monetary policy must then be designed in a tight way and demand in the economy will be slowed down abruptly in order to bring inflation rates back to target. Both cases involve unnecessary real economic costs and are therefore undesirable. The way to avoid ending up in this type of situation is to make forecasts on inflation so that the central bank can control the repo rate with a view to approximately the same horizon as monetary policy has its impact on inflation. This will calm down both in terms of the development of the key interest rate and in terms of the real economy, i.e. for output and employment. Forecasts can go wrong  but it can be handled As I have just said, monetary policy must be forward-looking. Otherwise, we would be creating instability rather than stability in the real economy. But this places very high demands on both forecasters and macro model builders. Firstly, inflation must be forecast over one to two years' time, which requires, among other things, decent precision in terms of, for example, the relationship between resource utilisation and inflation. Secondly, knowledge is required of how a possible change in key interest rates will have an impact on inflation both in terms of strength and in terms of time profile. It is clear that forecasters and macroeconomists including central banks faced major challenges in the 1990s. For example, inflation forecasts have often been higher than actual outcomes. There are many reasons for this. The Swedish economy, like other economies, is currently transforming rapidly. This may mean that the relationship between demand and inflation changes. One reason may be be that pricing behavior is different when the inflation rate is low compared to when it is high. Another could be that the economy is exposed to increasing competition through internal liberalisation or as a result of general globalisation, or through a combination of the two drivers. A third reason may be that the potential of the economy shifts as productivity growth changes. However, the Riksbank, like other forecasters, is working intensively and continuously to improve its forecasts. The more experience we gain of the new monetary policy regime and its implications for the macroeconomy, the better forecasts and macroeconomic assessments should be. Moreover, in the changing world in which we live, incoming up-to-date information on the development of the economy may need to be given greater importance than more formal model results, which must necessarily be based on historical correlations. Thus, there should be opportunities to better deal with the fact that long-term economic developments can never be made with complete precision, and yet take into account the fact that it takes a relatively long time for monetary policy to fully take effect. The level of interest rates is an important complement to the inflation assessment As I pointed out at the beginning, Swedish economic development looks strong and the task for the Riksbank is to make its contribution to ensuring that this development can continue. Part of this work, as I have just said, is to keep the inflation rate around the target set. The Riksbank can influence the inflation rate in the economy by seeking to adjust aggregate demand in the economy to the long-term growth path and/or influence expectations of future inflation. According to our simple rule of action for monetary policy, the repo rate should be raised when the forecast for inflation exceeds the target and vice versa. However, in order for demand in the economy to actually be affected, it is important that it is the real repo rate that changes, which then affects the real interest rate on loans with longer maturities to varying degrees. However, making decisions on monetary policy requires not only knowledge of what changes are required, but also at what level the policy is based. This is where the reasoning about the equilibrium real interest rate comes into the monetary policy discussion. This discussion is not decoupled from the discussion of inflation forecasts, but an important complement to the assessments. When the economy is in equilibrium, i.e. the expected inflation similar to the target and output on its long-term equilibrium trajectory, then the real interest rate is also in equilibrium. There is thus some level of the real repo rate that corresponds to this level and can be described as a neutral level. Consequently, when the real repo rate is above this level, it can be said that monetary policy is tight and when it is below, the policy can be described as expansionary. But setting this neutral level is not easy because the equilibrium real rate is not directly observable, but must be estimated. The real interest rate depends partly on the interest rate that creates a balance between savings and investments within the country and partly on the international real interest rate situation, which in turn depends on the ratio between savings and investments at global level. Experience shows that the actual real interest rate also varies over fairly long periods, which should indicate that even the equilibrium real interest rate shifts over time. Historical series above the real interest rate show that it was negative in the 1970s, while it was around 4 percent in the 1980s and 90s. Looking at the entire period between 1960 until 1999, the short-term real interest rate was around 2%. The conclusion is that it is difficult, on the basis of historical developments, to form exactly an idea of what level the policy should be based on. However, the Executive Board has made a rough estimate that monetary policy is currently expansionary and that the real repo rate is consequently slightly below the equilibrium level. As the economy grows stronger and we move forward, we can expect resource utilisation in the economy to become increasingly strained. As a result, monetary policy will eventually need to take a neutral position. The question is what level of interest rate this is about and how quickly one should approach it. I can see from various analyses and market letters that many players in the financial market are currently busy with this issue. But it is clear from my reasoning that there can be no mechanics in this movement, no predetermined trajectory mapped out, or any future interest rate steps fixed. The inflation forecast, as always, is allowed to determine the movements of interest rates. A lot has happened here recently. The economy seems to be slightly stronger than we expected in December. At the same time, however, productivity growth looks better. Perhaps one can also be somewhat more optimistic about wage developments. Against this background, after the last rate hike in February, I think inflation risks still look fairly balanced.

Title: Is a new global financial system needed?
text: Is a new global financial system needed? Date: 1999-03-17 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: ForeningsSparbanken's conference Our Economic Situation An extended period of recurrent financial turbulence What greatly shapes the economic situation in the world economy are the consequences of the financial turmoil that has characterized many countries in recent years. The crisis in Japan has been going on throughout the 1990s and the problems in Asia are in their second year. Last autumn, Russia was forced to devalue and also chose to suspend payments on part of the national debt. To this can be added the major problems for the hedge fund Long Term Capital Management last fall. The LTCM crisis led to widespread  but fortunately a temporary  turbulence in western financial markets. In recent months, Brazil has also run into difficulties. All events have in one way or another involved different types of adjustments in each country and the sum has become a dampening of activity in the entire world economy. Added to this is the risk of further spreading the financial turmoil to other countries and that there will be a correction in not least the US stock market. Over the past five to ten years, the road has been lined with financial turmoil in many parts of the world. In 1994, Mexico got into difficulties. Before that, we had banking and currency crises in the Nordic countries and not least in our own country. The ERM system also experienced extensive turbulence in the autumn of 1992 and the summer of 1993. As a consequence, the band borders were forced to widen and several countries to switch to floating exchange rates. In fact, over the past twenty years, there have been more than a dozen serious banking crises, each of which has caused direct government spending of 10% or more in relation to GDP. To this must be added the indirect costs that have followed in the wake of these crises in terms of lost production and increased unemployment. Against this background, the natural questions become what we can do to prevent these kinds of events and, when they occur, what can be done in that case. The title of my speech today is: Is a new global financial system needed? Let me say straight away that I will do no more than touch superficially on several important, difficult issues. The time available to me is short and this heading touches on a very complicated matter of which today we by no means have full knowledge. This is also why extensive work is being carried out at both international and national level to both analyze the financial problems and work with different types of solutions. I begin by briefly describing the background to what has happened, as I see it. It gives a hint of what the problems really are. Only after that is it possible to begin to approach the question of what we can do about it. Some reasons for the financial turmoil In order to be able to briefly describe what has happened, it is necessary to put financial development into a broader perspective. Over the past twenty years, the financial system has been liberalised in many countries. Capital can now once again, for the first time since the outbreak of the First World War, move more or less freely across national borders. In addition, there have been major changes in communication and information technology, which has led to new instruments and methods of risk management. All in all, this has led to the financial system being more extensive and globalized today than ever before. This is true even though capital flows in relation to GDP were also high at the turn of the last century. But then it was other countries that stood as recipients of the capital flows and they also partly had a different form. Rapid financial development and internationalisation are in themselves a logical consequence of the globalisation of the production of goods and services and the sharp increase in cross-border trade in the world economy. This, in turn, has increased the need for new financial solutions for companies and households. As trade and the globalisation of the production of goods and services increase, the development and internationalisation of the financial system is also necessary in order to fully seize opportunities for increased prosperity. But the transition to a more global financial system has not been without its problems. Often the development has been too fast for the system to really "keep up". We remember this not least from 1980s Sweden. Neither the banks themselves nor, for that matter, the authorities were in the right position to adapt to the new conditions of a freer capital market. Lending expansion often took place on loose grounds and the authorities did not follow up the development sufficiently. This was true both at the micro level, i.e. in individual banks, and at the macro level. The economy overheated and asset prices rose sharply. Furthermore, the fixed exchange rate stimulated extensive short-term borrowing abroad. This was channelled through the banking system and led to the build-up of a significant vulnerability. Then, as things turned around, the transition turned violent. Production fell, unemployment rose and the banking system fell into an acute crisis. Although each type of financial turbulence that has occurred in different countries in recent years is of course unique, there are several similarities with what we experienced in Sweden in the early 1990s; immature banking system, substandard supervision, an economic policy that was not designed to take account of the effects of credit and exchange deregulation and a fixed but adjustable exchange rate that stimulated excessive cross-border capital movements. In addition, it has been shown that the requirements for banks' accounting in many countries have been too low. An important factor that has contributed to exacerbating problems in the financial sector is macro-policy. For a free capital market to develop in a stable way, a consistent and predictable economic policy is required. Large macroeconomic imbalances that will sooner or later have to lead to drastic policy measures are causing turmoil in the financial markets. The policies that central banks around the world have been tasked with pursuing have the potential to lead to stable macroeconomic development. A clear and credible price stability objective should have a positive impact on the stability of the financial system. The high inflation, together with credit and currency deregulation, created a speculative climate in many countries. Sweden was an example of this. Similarly, efforts to move away from the high-inflation economy in developed countries have gradually created sharp increases in share prices and bond prices. The shift from high to low inflation itself has led to significant declines in interest rates, which in turn have created substantial capital gains in the stock and bond markets. In fact, over the past fifteen to twenty years, for example, the U.S. stock and bond markets have experienced the overall sharpest uptick in modern times. In parallel with the rise in wealth, there has been an almost explosive expansion of the U.S. financial sector to meet the new interest in investments and other financial activities. I take the US as an example because it is such a dominant economy, but many other countries have also experienced the same thing. Moreover, the U.S. capital market is so extensive globally speaking. Share prices in the US have risen by about 16 percent per year since 1982, compared with the average of between 6 and 7 percent over the past 120 years. Similarly, investments in bonds with long maturities have yielded an annual real return of approximately 11%. The corresponding historical average is only 3 percent. There has simply never been a time in history when both stocks and bonds have been such a good investment over such a long period of time. This, in turn, has created a climate of high risk-taking, which includes a marked increase in interest in high leverage and complex financial instruments. The long period of very high returns on financial assets has accustomed investors and banks at that level. This, in turn, has led to a constant search for business arrangements that can meet the return requirements. This, in turn, has stimulated the emergence and expansion of the financial sector. The convergence of long-term interest rates in Europe has offered attractive investment options for much of the 1990s. An extensive flow of capital from the US to Europe has therefore taken place. When the Danish referendum in the summer of 1992 raised doubts as to whether it would be possible to form a monetary union in Europe, it led to a dramatic reversal of capital flows and a palpable financial turbulence arose in Europe. Gradually, the short-term investors returned and in the spring of 1994 changed their behaviour again. They were then affected by the reorientation of U.S. monetary policy. The increase in short-term interest rates in the US thus also boosted long-term interest rates in Europe for a period of time. The opening up of capital investments in emerging markets created another opportunity to achieve high returns. Between 1990 and 1997, over US400 billion flowed to Asia alone. This corresponds to about 25% of these countries' total GDP in one year. It was a combination of bank lending and portfolio investment. At the end of 1997, international banks had loans amounting to just over US350 billion, of which 60% were short-term. Of course, it is in itself positive that capital moves from one part of the world to another if the return turns out to be higher. However, the problem was that the conditions for productive investments did not turn out to be as good as thought. When the Asian problems later became apparent, capital flows reversed and a serious financial turbulence arose. A third way to maintain a high return was to increase risks through borrowing and the use of complex financial instruments. It formed the starting shot for so-called. Hedge funds, some of which used very high leverage. Long Term Capital Management was one such extreme example. The leverage in this case was more than 50 times the equity. This corresponds to an equity/assets ratio of a modest 2 percent. The international banks engaged in lending directly to countries where yields were high. In addition, they lent capital to hedge funds located in the same countries. In some cases, banks even owned shares directly in these funds. It is fair to say that in many cases the risk-taking was high. This was seen as a natural way to maintain a historically unusually high level of real returns. The good profits, in turn, created a culture of fraudulent security and stimulated further risk-taking. To this can be added that the new mathematical risk models that had been developed created a false sense of security. They proved to work well in normal times, but not when they were needed most, i.e. when the turbulence set in. Sooner or later, the expectations in western industrialised countries of the return on financial investments will have to be adjusted to what is sustainable in the real economy. In addition, the various events that have occurred lead to self-sanitizing actions in the financial system. But there are also a lot of measures that needs to be taken in order to improve the functioning of the financial system. What can we do to prevent financial turmoil? The current problems in the global financial system and its repercussions require both short-term and long-term measures. In the short term  stability-oriented economic policies at the centre In the short term, the problems in the world economy must primarily be solved where they have arisen through a stability-oriented macro-policy. The international community has in a number of different cases provided that the country in question has been prepared to take measures at home that tackle the core of the problems. Financial crises almost always stem from a failed economic policy. The international financial markets may have led to the problems at times coming to light earlier and to its spread, but capital mobility in itself is not the basic problem. Central banks around the world have contributed to mitigating spillovers within the framework of their objective of promoting price stability. For example, the risk of a very serious situation resulting from the collapse of LTCM in the autumn was averted by the swift and resolute action of the US Federal Reserve. The threat of a so-called credit crunch due to the LTCM crisis could thus be avoided. However, the real economic consequences of the Asian crisis and the financial turmoil triggered by the Russian devaluation and default, as well as the collapse of the US hedge fund LTCM, are still dampening growth and inflation in the world economy. They will apparently continue to do so over the next few years, the perspective that is currently relevant to monetary policy. For Sweden, the deteriorating international growth outlook seems to be dampening mainly through a weaker growth outlook for exports. This also has repercussions on industrial investment. However, consumption should develop relatively strongly. Good confidence in economic policy in general, together with the Riksbank's interest rate cuts, may suggest that the external slowdown will be counteracted to some extent. However, in connection with the Riksbank now preparing its report to the Finance Committee, which will also be the first Inflation Report of the year, we must examine in more detail how the inflation outlook is affected by the likely real economic development. One difficulty in this analysis is that throughout Europe, including Sweden, there is a clear difference between households' and companies' views on the future. Households are very optimistic while businesses are more gloomy. Historically, those kinds of differences are very rare and sooner or later the assessments have to converge. The question is whether it then turns out that households have become gloomier or that companies have become more optimistic. Unless the international economy improves, households are likely to gradually become less optimistic. The reason is that the companies' view may be reflected in revised production plans, reduced need for labor and thus make households less optimistic. At the same time, the view of companies may change. The reason would then be, for example, that the US economy continues to be so strong that it acts as the engine of the world economy. But there are risks here too. In the US economy, a number of imbalances are building up. Private consumption and developing significantly stronger than households' disposable income. Business investment is also growing faster than corporate profits. Consumption and investments are supported by the strong stock market performance in the US. There is an important downside risk here when it comes to the world economy. A correction of the highly valued stock market could lead to a significant slowdown in the US economy, which in turn would have repercussions on the rest of the world economy. In the long run, the US stock market cannot continue to provide a real return in double digits. Once interest rates have adjusted to the new environment of persistently low inflation, the return on equities will depend on the underlying earnings trend in companies. Since real GDP growth is a measure of how much wages and profits grow over time throughout the U.S. economy and in the long run the relationship between the two is largely constant, stock prices in real terms cannot grow much more than GDP does in the long run. This suggests that expectations for the real return on equities will sooner or later be revised down to single digits. And this is about the total return that includes the dividends. The decline in these expectations is yet another thing that lies ahead. The so-called P/E ratio for the US stock market remains at historically high rates, indicating a discrepancy between the sum of profit expectations for individual companies and for the US economy as a whole. Even the most optimistic assessments about future improvements in productivity at the macro level should not be able to justify P/E ratios as high as today's. However, an adjustment of real return expectations for equities can take place in different ways; either a quick and major correction or via an adaptation over a longer period of time. These are some of the aspects that the Riksbank must analyse now that the Inflation Report is being prepared. It may also be worth recalling that the Riksbank conducts a monetary policy that is independent of the actions of other central banks. Our analysis can of course be based on the same factors, but our actions are independent of the decisions of others. At the heart of our monetary policy decisions is the inflation outlook in the Swedish economy. They are the ones who determine whether the repo rate is kept unchanged or needs to be adjusted downwards in order to achieve the target of 2 percent inflation in one to two years' time. In this assessment, we correct for so-called temporary price effects all in accordance with the monetary policy target decided on by the Riksbank's Executive Board. Looking further ahead  institutional changes In the longer term, the regulatory framework and the work of supervision in different countries must focus on countering the risks of the kind of turbulence we experienced, especially in the 1990s. It is also important to develop the regulatory framework at international level. In essence, it is the granting of credit that has been at the heart of the events that took place in the 1990s. Extensive credit risks have been the problem and banks seem to repeat similar mistakes time and time again. These may be the generosity of domestic banks to finance private operators' investments in assets or the propensity of international banks to make foreign currency available to their domestic counterparties. The concentration in lending to financial institutions is often high, which aggravates the situation in the course of financial turbulence. There are also reasons to wonder whether the credit risk assessment has been as thorough as one should expect. What is the reason for this? Difficulties for both banks and supervisors in assessing the risks of credit engagement are likely to be one reason. Credit risks are difficult to manage and it is not easy to get a good overview of the actors' credit portfolios. Genuine difficulties in the assessments are thus one explanation, another is that in some cases the banks have not even seemed to make their own independent risk assessments, but only followed the flow. Undervalued credit risks thus appear to be a recurring theme in the crises that have arisen. Therefore, it is up to the banks themselves to create a better credit policy in their institutions. This credit policy must permeate everything from the work of the individual credit officer up to the more comprehensive strategies of the executive management and the board of directors. However, this is not enough, or rather: this is unlikely to happen unless action is taken at the same time by the regulatory and supervisory authorities. Banks' lending and behaviour in general are influenced by their expectations of: how the authorities will act if a crisis arises. Extensive international work has focused on trying to address these problems. Authorities and financial actors work together to formulate and implement international principles for well-functioning supervision, so-called core principles. One part of this is to develop more meaningful capital adequacy rules that take into account what the banking system looks like today. The previous capital adequacy rules were drawn up on the basis of the financial reality prevailing in 1988. A thorough review has been carried out and will be presented in April. In addition to this, efforts are also being made to achieve a greater degree of transparency and clearer accounting. Increased transparency should lead to lenders avoiding taking unhealthy risks, at least in the absence of information. Conclusion The recurrent crises in the financial markets clearly show that efforts to strengthen the system are a continuous undertaking, much to be done. It is true that banks and other financial institutions have done a great deal in recent years to improve risk management, not least as regards the credit portfolio. But the development of the financial sector is so rapid that neither financial institutions nor authorities can be complacent. The developments of last autumn are a telling example. However, we must be aware that the extensive work being done to strengthen the financial system is not the same as the fact that the system will be fully protected from problems in the future. Work must focus on mitigating the effects and trying to ensure that the crises that do occur are not as extensive and socio-economically costly as those we have lived through in recent years. The aim of this work must therefore be to try to reconcile the necessary regulation and supervision of the markets with the advantages that a well-developed financial system has to offer. For various reasons, special regulation and supervision of financial companies is required. However, it must be done in such a way that the development potential that can contribute to higher prosperity in the world economy is not stifled.

Faktum r att under de senaste femton till tjugo ren har exempelvis de amerikanska aktie- och obligationsmarknaderna upplevt den sammantaget kraftigaste uppgngen i modern tid. Parallellt med frmgenhetsuppgngen har det skett en nrmast explosiv utbyggnad av den finansiella sektorn i USA fr att mta det nya intresset fr placeringar och andra finansiella aktiviteter. Title: Is solidarity wage policy possible with the Riksbank's inflation target?
text: Bergstrom: Is wage solidarity possible with the Riksbank's inflation target? Date 2004-03-26 Deputy Riksbank Governor Villy Bergstrom spoke on March 26 at "Union Day" in Vasteras "This year's round of agreements, which covers most of the private sector and the entire state sector, is in full swing. However, the wage settlement in industry is now largely in place, paving the way for a calm round of negotiations. The wages and salaries sum accounts for 70 per cent of the value added in the economy and plays a decisive role in the development of costs and prices, and thus also in monetary policy. Wage negotiations thus entail a risk that the agreements will be concluded at levels that are not compatible with the Riksbank's inflation target of two per cent per annum. However, the fact that industrial agreements have been concluded with moderate levels as a result, together with factors such as the relatively slow recovery in the economy and the weak labour market, militates against such developments, although risks remain in the local negotiations. The statistics received indicate that there is some scope for a lighter monetary policy, which the outcome of the wage movement so far does not constitute an obstacle to," Bergstrom began. "It is the ability of the labour force to produce goods and services, i.e. productivity, that determines the scope for real wage growth in the long term. Real wages can only rise as long as productivity increases. If wages rise too quickly, companies may be forced to raise their prices with higher inflation as a result. The alternative is to curtail operations and lay off labour. It is usually put that nominal wages cannot increase by more than the sum of the 2% inflation target and productivity growth. If, for example, Swedish productivity is trend-wise assumed to increase by about 1.5 percent, an average wage cost increase of around 3.5 percent would be sustainable in the long term. However, this reasoning is based on the fact that the economy is in equilibrium, i.e. that there is both internal and external balance. This is not the case today with far too high unemployment and a current account surplus. If more people are to find work, wages cannot increase to that extent, especially as the current account surplus suggests an appreciation of the exchange rate," Bergstrom said. "However, what constitutes a long-term sustainable wage increase may differ between different sectors of the economy due to different conditions in production technology, competitive conditions and thus productivity development. In the goods-producing, competitive, industrial sector, productivity rise is relatively rapid, while it is significantly lower in the protected services sector and especially in the public sector. This leads to greater scope for wage increases in the business sector and hence demands for at least equal wage increases in the public sector whose wages are lagging behind. This is reflected in recurring low-wage investments, especially in this sector. It is therefore to be feared that there is a structural problem with wage demands in different sectors that do not reflect the productivity increases of the respective sectors," bergstrom said. "Let us assume that productivity growth in the various sectors will in the future be as in the period 1998-2003, and that the average rate of wage growth will be approximately 3.5% per annum. Then it turns out that the Riksbank's target of inflation of 2 percent is quite possible to achieve even in the future. This is despite the fact that productivity development differs in the goods-producing and service-producing sectors. If the low-wage investments do not lead to a higher average wage growth rate than that, the Riksbank's goal formulation is compatible with a solidarity-based wage policy. On the other hand, there may be problems if differences in productivity development increase significantly and the trade union movement at the same time maintains the solidarity wage policy," Bergstrom concluded.

Title: Investments in Sweden instead of capital exports
text: Bergstrf6m: Investments in Sweden instead of capital exports Date 2005-01-18 Deputy Governor Villy Bergstrf6m spoke today about the importance of investments for long-term growth at a seminar organized by Statistics Sweden and ITPS "The falling trend in capital formation in Sweden today may in the long term threaten the upswing we have seen in productivity and thus also growth. As it looks today, with large surpluses in trade and current account balances, Sweden is net exporting capital to the outside world despite the fact that there is room and need for more investments at home," Bergstrf6m began. "Already in the 1970s, when I was researching capital formation in Sweden, I was worried about the decline we then saw in investments as a share of GDP. Over the thirty years that have passed, this concern has not abated, quite the contrary - it has increased as the downward trend in investment has continued. Not least, this is clear when it comes to public investments as the Swedish infrastructure is clearly neglected when compared to similar countries," Bergstrf6m said. "Part of the downward trend in investment is a compositional effect that has to do with a change in the structure of the business sector. The industrial sector as a whole has declined as a share of GDP in favour of the expanding services sector, whose output makes greater use of human capital. Similarly, the decline in housing investment over the past decade is dragging the numbers down. In addition, there are problems in the statistics on fixed investments that make it difficult to get a clear picture of developments. However, the large current account surplus, a record high of 8.8% of GDP in the third quarter of 2004 and 8.3% overall in the first three quarters, indicates that there may be cause for concern about investment developments. This reflects the fact that Swedish companies invest more abroad than in Sweden," Bergstrf6m said. "The replacement of traditional capital with IT capital seems to have given Sweden a respite from the negative effects on productivity of the weak capital formation. The IT effect continues to be promising, but does not guarantee the sustained good productivity growth. The only long-term guarantee for this is that investments will grow in line with the economy," Bergstrf6m noted. "Going forward, we also have to face an unfavorable age structure and decline in active generations, which poses a challenge not only to public sector finances but also to potential growth. A high savings rate going forward and an improved investment climate, which stimulates more investment in our country and thus increased capital stock in the economy, are required to meet these challenges. Capital growth would then offset the reduced labor growth, the tax base would rise and the opportunities for continued financing of health and social care would increase," Bergstrom said. "The large current account surplus today means that total savings are significantly larger than investments and that we have a corresponding outflow of capital. Thus, there is considerable scope already today for increased domestic investments without increasing savings, but this presupposes that there is a willingness on the part of companies to invest within the country and, consequently, the possibility of good returns," Bergstrf6m concluded.

Title: Bright outlook for the Swedish economy
text: Bergstrf6m: Bright outlook for the Swedish economy Date 2005-11-25 Deputy Governor Villy Bergstrf6m spoke on Friday at d6rebro Byggme4starff6rening about the current economic situation. "In the previous inflation report presented in October, the Riksbank's assessment was that international growth would remain good, albeit somewhat slowing down, this year and in the coming years. Oil prices had become higher than forecast in June and were expected to be higher in the future than previously assumed. Growth in the Swedish economy seemed to have picked up again after the downturn at the beginning of the year. Household consumption was expected to continue to strengthen in the coming years, and public consumption was expected to increase, especially next year. The upturn in investment that began last year was expected to continue, although it would enter a calmer phase. Overall, the assessment was that growth would be relatively good in the Swedish economy over the next few years. Wage developments were expected to be relatively favourable and the conditions for increased growth in domestic demand and employment appeared to be favourable. The expansionary fiscal policy was also expected to contribute to increased domestic demand," Bergstrf6m began. "The new information received thereafter suggests that the international economy continues to improve. In the US, preliminary national accounts show continued good growth in the third quarter. There have also been positive economic signals from other parts of the world. The manufacturing purchasing managers' index rose in October in both the euro area and Japan. The turnaround that has taken place in Japan seems to be more stable this time, which means that the world's second largest economy is gaining momentum," Bergstrom said. "Swedish growth also seems to continue to strengthen. Exports are developing strongly and there are signs that household consumption is starting to pick up, while disposable incomes and the labour market situation are improving. Housing construction is an important growth engine and the infrastructure investments decided last year remain unchanged. Productivity has been high, which has improved Sweden's competitiveness. Together with the weak krona, it contributes to a favorable situation for the export industry. In this context, it is also important to underline that economic policy is strongly stimulating through a low repo rate and expansionary fiscal policy. This will reasonably lead to continued high demand growth in the economy going forward," Bergstrf6m continued. "The low interest rate environment has also contributed to rapid growth in lending to households and rising asset prices. We have seen a continued strong rise in the price of residential properties and the prices of commercial properties are also increasing now," Bergstrf6m added. "Let me say a few words about the recent development of the crown. As is well known, the Riksbank has no target for the krona exchange rate. Monetary policy is geared towards achieving low and stable inflation. At the same time, it is clear that the exchange rate is an important factor in inflation. If the krona were to establish itself at a weak level for a long time, it would have an impact on our inflation assessment. The krona has recently been significantly weaker than expected. However, there is currently no reason to believe that the background to this is a concern about the Swedish economic development. Therefore, there is hardly any reason to fundamentally change our assessment of the exchange rate going forward. However, this does not prevent the weak krona from having effects. Already what has happened so far affects our forecast to some extent. In addition, and this is certainly something my colleagues agree with, the longer the krona is weak, the greater the risk that it will affect future inflation. Thus, the development of the krona may in practice play a role in the design of monetary policy going forward," Bergstrf6m continued. "My assessment is - this is my personal assessment - that financial conditions are very expansionary and that it now looks like a tightening of monetary policy is needed to ensure that inflation is not allowed to pick up and threaten the 2 per cent target. I also see developments in the real estate market as reasons to soon change policy in a less expansive direction. I worry that if the trend continues, sooner or later we may have an abrupt adjustment, which would have a negative impact on general demand and employment," Bergstrf6m concluded.

Title: Wage formation in focus
text: Bergstrom: Wage formation in focus Date: 2000-02-10 Speaker: Deputy Governor Villy Bergstrom Location: Upplands Vasby municipality The picture that Sweden is in a strong economic upturn has recently been consolidated. Growth is broad-based and is expected to amount to approximately 3.5 per cent per year over the next few years. The economic upturn is taking place from a favourable situation where the imbalances that previously characterized the Swedish economy have been sharply reduced. Public debt has fallen from 80% of GDP in 1995 to around 70% in 1999. Thus, Sweden is one of the most successful countries in the EU when it comes to addressing fiscal problems. Several years of current account surpluses have also helped to reduce our country's external debt. It has now fallen to just over 20 percent of GDP from being at most around 40 percent of GDP in 1993. At the same time, inflation expectations have come down and stabilised at a low level, close to the target for monetary policy. While unemployment remains high, both employment and newly registered vacancies are now rising strongly. Thus, almost all variables point in a positive direction and in the coming years it is likely that the remaining imbalances will be further reduced. The outlook for the Swedish economy thus looks better than it has been for a very long time and the conditions for sustainable and stable growth thus seem to be very favourable. There are therefore good reasons to assume that the first boom of the 2000s will not give birth to inflationary impulses in the Swedish economy in the same way as during the booms of the 1970s and 80s. But even so, we must not forget that the current recessionary regime has not been fully tested in a boom. This applies not least to wage formation, which I will come back to later. Challenges for monetary policy The challenge for the Riksbank is to balance monetary policy so that the economic upturn does not break prematurely, but so that demand does not rise so much that inflation also picks up. If the economy is in balance and long-term inflation expectations are low, it can be hoped that monetary policy geared towards an inflation target will lead to a stabilisation in output growth on its long-term growth path. Inflationary pressures vary with the business cycle, but as demand increases in line with capacity growth in the economy, inflation stabilises at a low level. When there are spare resources, the central bank keeps interest rates so low that the economy is stimulated, and when resource utilization is high, interest rates are kept at such a high level that overheating of the economy and rising inflation are avoided. Raising and lowering interest rates will thus also indirectly be a means of dampening cyclical fluctuations and stabilising output and employment. On average, over a business cycle, monetary policy in a balanced economy needs neither to stimulate nor dampen growth and inflation. The real interest rate should then be at its long-term equilibrium level. Setting a level for it cannot be done because it varies over time. But a very rough rule of thumb, according to some theories of optimality, is that it is close to long-term real GDP growth. On long term, it is reasonable to assume that the real interest rate is internationally determined. In both Germany and the United States, short-term real interest rates have averaged around 3.5 percent since 1982, which with inflation expectations of 2 percent would mean nominal interest rates around 5.5 percent. Resource utilisation in the Swedish economy has been low for a long period and the repo rate has therefore been at such a low level that the economy has been stimulated. Even after last week's repo rate hike from 3.25 to 3.75 percent, monetary policy seems to be stimulating the economy. One difficulty with the monetary policy trade-offs in practice is to determine at a given stage how much demand can be allowed to rise without exceeding the inflation target. This may be particularly true in economies where the low-inflation regime is relatively new and not in all parts tested. As monetary policy affects inflation with lags, monetary policy decisions must be based on projections of inflationary pressures going forward. Decisions on austerity may need to be made before there are any visible signs of inflation. One risk that must be taken into account is that if a rate hike comes too late or is too small, for example due to miscalculations of the strength of inflation impulses, inflation expectations may also rise. The consequences could be that the painstakingly achieved credibility of the low-inflation economy deteriorates. It could take much greater and longer-term austerity measures to get inflation back in place than if inflation were stopped in time. Wage formation in focus Monetary policy is based on forecasts of inflation over one to two years' time. The forecasts are based, among other things, on assessments of the development of import prices, profits and wage costs. Demand pressure in Sweden and internationally are important determinants and the economy is currently very strong. There are many indications that the Swedish economy has largely adapted to a low-inflation regime. But, as I said earlier, it is still impossible to ignore the fact that the processes of price and wage formation have not yet been tested in such a strong economic upturn as the one we now seem to be in. In the coming years, the focus will be on wage formation. When wage agreements for some 2.3 million workers are to be renegotiated this year and next year, the functioning of the labour market will be seriously put to the test. Nominal wage cost increases must, in the long term, be kept within the space limited by productivity growth and the 2% inflation target. Higher wage cost increases than this initially lead either to reduced profit shares for companies or to higher inflation. In the short term, profit shares may indeed fluctuate, but in the slightly longer term, profit growth must be in line with that in the rest of the world. Temporarily, low import price increases may also create some scope for higher wage cost increases without exceeding the inflation target. But sooner or later, too high wage costs will lead to subdued growth, either because the Riksbank is forced to counteract higher inflationary pressures with higher interest rates or because the willingness to invest in Sweden is dampened in the face of the prospect of profit margins being squeezed. Challenges for wage formation The Swedish labour market has previously tended to generate wage wage spirals. For example, it has been difficult to change relative wages without generating compensatory wage increases. The fact that the upcoming negotiations are taking place at a time when demand for labour is strong increases the risk of a repeat of the pattern. Since 1997, employment has increased by almost 150 000 people. With the growth that is in the Riksbank's assessment, the demand for labour will continue to rise in the coming years. One sign of this is that newly registered vacancies increased in number throughout the autumn of last year. In some industries and regions, there are indications that the workforce is becoming scarce. At the same time, however, it is important to bear in mind that there is a very long way to go before the shortage figures shown in the late 1980s. Another challenge for wage formation is that public sector employees will be first out on the plane in the salary negotiations. This spring, contracts for about 280,000 people in the health and education sector expire. Teachers and healthcare professionals are groups that have clearly fallen behind in their salary development and where the consequences have been that shortcomings have arisen. Take, for example, a teacher of science subjects such as mathematics and physics. The student who passes an academic education in these subjects probably also has the conditions to pass a master's degree in engineering. However, the pay gap between these occupational categories is very large, both in terms of starting salaries and development opportunities. A teacher's final salary can come up slightly over SEK 20,000 a month, while there is no ceiling for a good civil engineer. With such pay differences, it is no wonder that there is a great shortage of certain categories of teachers and that it is difficult to attract young people to such an education. The fact that many nurses leave the public sector in Sweden to instead practice their professions in, for example, Sweden. Norway and Denmark have also contributed to shortages in healthcare. The Swedish labour market has not only had problems dealing with wage imbalances between different professions. It has also found it difficult to address regional imbalances in the same occupational category through the adjustment of relative wages. Labour shortages, for example, have mainly affected metropolitan areas. Lower living costs and higher living standards in rural areas at the same wage have probably contributed to this. For example, the housing costs for a secondary school teacher in Falun are significantly lower than for the same category in Stockholm. With more flexible wage formation, labour market imbalances could probably be reduced. Low inflation expectations dampen wage growth The starting point for the upcoming salary negotiations is thus not unproblematic. But while there are concerns, there is also much to suggest that the wage and price formation process has changed. The most important change since the 1970s and 80s is probably the change in the monetary policy target and the support and credibility of the inflation target. I am convinced that the Riksbank's inflation target is understood and accepted by trade unionists, ombudsmen and federal leaders. Knowledge of the inflation target and the role of monetary policy has penetrated society in a completely different way than the norm of fixed exchange rates. The fixed-rate regime basically demanded that wage cost increases be adapted to the outside world so that employment would not suffer. However, when wages steadily rose more than in competitor countries, recurrent devaluations saved employment. This probably contributed to reducing the adjustment pressure on the Swedish labour market. The fact that activity in the Swedish economy was high, especially in the second half of the 1980s, also played an important role in the fact that the shortcomings in wage formation were not addressed. The realisation that wage increases that are too high quite quickly leading to a slowdown in growth and unemployment rising with a monetary policy geared towards an inflation target seems to have made its mark in public opinion. If the Riksbank deems wage cost increases to drive inflation above target, the Riksbank will raise interest rates and demand will slow down. In the short term, while wage cost increases may be offset by lower profit shares, squeezed profit margins reduce willingness to invest and growth slows down. Strong real wage growth over the period of low inflation is likely to have increased awareness of the value of price stability. Over the past four-year period, despite low nominal wage increases, real wages have risen on average by almost 4% per year. This should be compared with the fact that, on average, real wages increased only half a per cent during the period of hyperinflation between 1975 and 1995, despite nominal wage increases in those years amounting to an average of 8%. These developments clearly show that high nominal wage increases are not positively linked to real wage developments. High credibility of monetary policy objectives has led to a downward shift in inflation expectations. And stable inflation expectations in themselves reduce the risk that wage negotiations will lead to higher wage increases than there is room for. Stable inflation expectations reduce uncertainty for the parties about what a nominal wage requirement means for real wages. A sign that the low-inflation economy has taken hold in the Swedish economy is the result of the calculations reported in the Riksbank's inflation report of October 1999. They show that there is now a different exchange ratio between the capacity utilisation rate in the economy and the inflation it gives rise to. According to the same calculations, an increase in demand does not lead to price increases to the same extent as before. Competitive pressures increase cost awareness? Increased competition in globalised markets could also contribute to low inflation. Globalised goods markets with strong competition should reduce companies' ability to compensate for high wage costs with price increases. At the same time, the highly globalized capital market is likely to make it more difficult for companies to squeeze profit margins even in the short term. One conclusion is that firms' resistance to wage cost increases that cannot be borne by productivity growth may have increased. Another change in the Swedish labour market is the trend towards increases in short-term employment. e.g. in the form of project employment and temporary positions. Particularly evident are developments in the expanding services sector. The share of temporary contracts in total has increased from 9% to about 14% of the total number of employees between 1990 and 1999. The trend may have been reinforced by the tough labour market situation during these years, but many believe that the trend will continue. New compensation methods are also spreading. Bonus wages, profit sharing and a 13th month salary are elements of wage formation that increase flexibility in the labor market. Increased cost awareness as a result of intensified competition may be a factor driving this development. Trends towards fixed-term contracts and variable remuneration for work are not only a good thing. For individuals and households, security, predictability of income development and the possibility of long-term planning, for example, to have children and buy a house are reduced. Changes in the forms of wage formation Although there is a broad understanding of the consequences of excessive wage cost increases for the entire collective of wage earners, it can sometimes be rational for NGOs to demand high wage increases. Excessive wage increases can lead to high costs to the national economy in the form of increased unemployment. However, the individual organisation can, at least in the short term, gain from its actions. It could be the start of a wage spiral. Among other things, in order to reduce the risk of such behaviours occurring, various changes in the forms of wage formation have been implemented and planned. The most important thing is the so-called'Green Paper '. The industrial agreement concluded between 20 organizations in the labor market; 12 from SAF and 8 from LO, TCO and SACO. The agreement thus affects 20% of the workforce and consists, among other things, of an agreement regulating the negotiation procedures. The agreement stipulates that negotiations shall begin three months before the expiry of the existing agreement. There is a broad consensus among the social partners that wage formation is facilitated if new agreements are concluded before the old ones expire. The Industry Committee, which is a joint group, appoints a group of persons to act as impartial chairmen to enter into the negotiations. These have a range of powers, including postponing strikes for 14 days. The construction of the agreement should reasonably mean that the risk of industrial action is significantly reduced. The industrial agreement has been likened to the Saltsjobad agreement of 1938, i.e. the agreement that began the long peace process on the Swedish labor market. According to many assessors improve the industrial agreement's ability to cope with wage demands and relative adjustments within the economy's overall wage space. The flexibility of wage formation is estimated to have increased and the negotiating climate has improved. With the stated aim of promoting wage formation compatible with social economic balance, the government presented a bill in December last year that included proposals to establish a new authority, the Mediation Institute. The idea is to reduce the risk of different groups in the labor market in competition with each other driving up wage increases in a way that ultimately creates worse outcomes for everyone. Measures aimed at concluding new contracts before the end of the previous contract period are included in the proposal. Another important task for the institute is proposed to be to increase knowledge and information about wage formation. The bill also contains proposals for rules that aim to reduce the risk of conflicts breaking out and that make the path to conflict slower. However, the rules must be dispositive, which means that they only enter into force if contractual solutions are not reached. The construction should stimulate the conclusion of agreements similar to the Industrial Agreement. Institutional changes have also been made for government employees that may act as a drag on wage formation. The changes aim, among other things, to avoid the state sector becoming a wage leader in the wage round. The so-called framework budget process generally makes it more difficult to exceed budgeted costs in the state. The appropriation standard for wage costs is designed in such a way that the wage development of the export industry should be decisive. The changes were only introduced in 1997, which means that their effectiveness has not yet been evaluated. Finally In summary, there are therefore concerns about wage formation in the coming years. The negotiations are taking place in an economy in strong growth at the same time as there is a need for wage increases in the shortage professions that have lagged behind. But there have also been changes in the Swedish labor market that make it possible to look with some confidence at the development. Above all, this applies to the support and understanding of the inflation target and the low inflation expectations that have been established. But institutional changes in the forms of wage formation that have been implemented or planned also work in a positive direction. Finally, globalisation and competition may have increased companies' cost awareness. In the Riksbank's inflation report from December last year, the improved demand situation was assessed even without accentuated wage spirals to have an effect on wage increases during the forecast period. The rate of wage growth was estimated at 4-4.5% in 2000 and 2001, which means that real wages continue to increase historically at a high rate. My intention here is not to give a different assessment of wage developments in the future. But the functioning of the labour market will be tested in the coming years and there are reasons to follow developments there closely. The Riksbank's Executive Board's decision on 3 February to raise the repo rate by 0.50 percentage point from 3.25 to 3.75 per cent means that monetary policy is now being conducted in a somewhat less expansionary direction. The decision was based on the assessments presented in the Riksbank's inflation report from December last year and the economic indicators received since then. The picture of a strong economic upturn is confirmed and most of the evidence suggests that the growth outlook has improved. The rate hike is simply a normal feature of the current economic picture. As available resources are gradually used, there are reasons to expect rising inflationary pressures, which reduces the scope for expansionary monetary policy. The assessments underlying the current monetary policy assume that wage formation has largely been adapted to a low-inflation economy. However, the risk picture is that the demands for relative adjustments may lead to higher wage increases. Flexibiliteten i lnebildningen bedms ha kat och frhandlingsklimatet frbttrats. Tanken r att minska risken fr att olika grupper p arbetsmarknaden i konkurrens med varandra driver upp lnekningarna p ett stt som i slutndan skapar smre utfall fr alla. tgrder som syftar till att nya avtal sluts innan fregende avtalsperiod lper ut ingr i frslaget. Propositionen innehller ocks frslag om regler som syftar till att minska risken fr att konflikter bryter ut och som gr vgen till konflikt trgare. Reglerna skall dock vara dispositiva, vilket innebr att de enbart trder i kraft om avtalslsningar inte ns. Frndringarna syftar bl.a. till att undvika att den statliga sektorn blir lneledande i avtalsrrelsen. Den s.k. rambudgetprocessen gr det generellt sett svrare att verskrida budgeterade kostnader i staten. Anslagsnormen fr lnekostnaderna r konstruerad s att exportindustrins lneutveckling skall vara bestmmande. Frndringarna infrdes frst 1997 vilket innebr att det nnu inte gtt att utvrdera effektiviteten i dessa. Avslutningsvis Sammanfattningsvis finns allts orosmoment nr det gller lnebildningen under kommande r. Frhandlingarna sker i en ekonomi i stark tillvxt samtidigt som det finns behov fr lnekningar i bristyrken som slpat efter. Men det har ocks skett frndringar p den svenska arbetsmarknaden som gr att man kan se med viss tillfrsikt p utvecklingen. Framfrallt gller det uppslutningen och frstelsen fr inflationsmlet och de lga inflationsfrvntningar som etablerats. Men ven institutionella frndringar i formerna fr lnebildningen som genomfrts eller planeras verkar i positiv riktning. Slutligen kan globaliseringen och konkurrensen ha kat fretagens kostnadsmedvetande. I Riksbankens inflationsrapport frn december frra ret bedmdes det frbttrade efterfrgelget ven utan accentuerade lnespiraler f effekt p lnekningarna under prognosperioden. Lnekningstakten bedmdes uppg till 4-4,5 procent 2000 och 2001, vilket innebr att reallnerna fortstter att ka historiskt sett i hg takt. Min avsikt r hr inte att ge en annan bedmning av lneutvecklingen framver. Men arbetsmarknadens funktionsstt kommer att prvas under kommande r och det finns skl att noga flja utvecklingen dr. Riksbankens direktions beslut frn den 3 februari att hja reporntan med 0,50 procentenhet frn 3,25 till 3,75 procent innebr att penningpolitiken nu frs i en ngot mindre expansiv inriktning. Beslutet grundades p de bedmningar som redovisades i Riksbankens inflationsrapport frn december frra ret samt de konjunkturindikatorer som inkommit sedan dess. Bilden av en stark konjunkturuppgng bekrftas och det mesta talar fr att tillvxtutsikterna har frbttrats. Rntehjningen r helt enkelt ett normalt inslag i nuvarande konjunkturbild. Nr de lediga resurserna successivt tas i ansprk finns det skl att rkna med ett stigande inflationstryck, vilket minskar utrymmet fr en expansiv penningpolitik. Bedmningarna som ligger till grund fr den aktuella penningpolitiken utgr ifrn att lnebildningen i stort anpassats till en lginflationsekonomi. I riskbilden ligger dock att kraven p relativanpassningar kan leda till hgre lnekningar.
