Title: The limits of wage formation at different stages
text: Bergstrom: The limits of wage formation at different stages Date: 1999-09-29 Speaker: Deputy Governor Villy Bergstrom Location: LO-SNS conference Bonnier Conference Center Wage formation always takes place under restrictions. Productivity development and international price rises set the long-term framework. Restrictions sometimes only strike when major imbalances have developed. They take the form of various institutional arrangements. This century presents many examples and from these we can learn lessons. The gold standard was valid from 1873 to 1931 with a break during and after The First World War. Wage-setting surges led to the loss of gold reserves through current account deficits and led to austerity policies and unemployment. There was hardly any corresponding automaticity in the opposite situation. The gold standard therefore had a slant on unemployment and it became too expensive to maintain in countries such as Britain and Sweden, which abandoned the system and coped with the depression of the 1930s better than the United States, which held on to gold. The Bretton Woods system that characterized the post-war period until the early 1970s was basically gold-based, as the dollar was redeemable against gold at a fixed rate and the currencies of the participating countries were in a fixed-byte relationship to the dollar. The difference from the older gold standard was that capital movements were regulated and that in the post-war period there was an international supervisory body that set out rules for credit to deficit countries and rules for exchange rate adjustments. These rules put needy countries under strict supervision by the IMF. Wage formation thus had to take into account the fixed exchange rate and the equilibrium of the current account. There were automatics, which triggered sanctions if wages pulled away so that competitiveness deteriorated fundamentally with structural current account deficits as a result. But even the Bretton Woods system had a punch side. There were no corresponding sanctions against countries that, through restrictive policies and persistent unemployment, accumulated current account surpluses, although Keynes wanted such restrictions at the Bretton Woods conference. The arrangements for international cooperation, the Gold Standard and the Bretton Woods system, were aimed at price stability, as a means of achieving full employment in the slightly longer term. The stabilization of prices was also successful until the collapse of the Bretton Woods system in the early 1970s. In the background is the notion that low inflation and stability in general  public finances and foreign trade in balance or in surplus - lead to maximum sustainable economic growth and full employment. For those who believe that politicians always act disinterestedly, rationally and long-term there was nothing problematic about the dissolution of international restrictions in the early 1970s. Surely it would be fine to shape economic policy for stable prices and full employment under full, national freedom of action! But it became chaotic, not least in Sweden. At first, the crown was unilaterally tied to the D-mark zone. This was unsustainable due to the difference in inflation rates between Sweden and then West Germany. In 1977, Sweden switched to stabilizing the currency against a basket of trade-weighted currencies. It didn't get any easier. In 1991, we formally moved to stabilisation against the ECO, a basket limited to the MEMBER STATES of the EU. During this period, we were not bound by any international treaties. We decided all by ourselves, under a self-declared restriction on fixed exchange rates. It didn't last. Sweden devalued five times between 1976 and 1982, then the krona depreciated by about 10 percent between 1985 and 1987, through the double weight of the dollar in the "currency basket". Thus, things did not go well in the "free period" from the early 1970s to the mid-1990s. From 1975 to 1995, the hourly wage for industrial workers rose by 7 percent per year, but wages fell in these 20 years by SEK 12/hour, measured in the last year's monetary value. How, then, is it to assess the stabilization policy environment to which we now belong? What are the similarities and differences from past experiences? The fact that the exchange rate is floating and that the Riksbank has an inflation target is one thing. The inflation target has replaced the fixed exchange rate, as a guideline for the social partners, for companies' pricing policy, rent setting and more. But how should we view the international ties compared to previous relationships? The Stability Pact that we outside EMU are also honouring is similar to the Bretton Woods system. It has a bias in the sense that there are sanctions against countries that run into budget deficits greater than 3% of GDP. There are no sanctions against countries that tighten up, and that way creates budget surpluses. The system is designed to promote growth and employment through price stability and sound public finances. This has been the case with all international stabilisation policy pacts and agreements, implicit as the Gold Standard and explicitly such as the Bretton Woods system. The notion, as I said, is that this favours rapid, sustainable growth and high employment. The question is, will the Stability and West Pact sometimes become a real 'pact of instability'? On two occasions, Sweden has incurred budget deficits of over 10 percent of GDP. Many of the EU countries have on several occasions had significantly larger deficits in their public finances than 3% of GDP. Already in the spring, the joints of the Stability Pact creaked when Italy was granted a departure from its stability plan by the EU. A strict adherence to 3% would come at the cost of rising unemployment and real decline in GDP. Therefore, for exceptional situations, there is a special procedure in which exceptions to the 3% limit can be granted. Will the current system be permanent, the free movement of capital, the inflation target and the Stability Pact? Hardly in all its constituent parts. I have already asked questions about the EU's Stability Pact. Capital movements have triggered currency crises almost every year in the 1990s, from the Nordic countries and the UK in 1992 to Brazil this year. It is innocent people -- poor peasants, workers and middle-class wage earners -- who are forced to pay for governments' mismanagement and the frivolity of banks. The international order around capital movements is not complete. Stabilization policy regimes have often lasted a couple of decades. During that time, the reality has time to change so that that regime turns out to cause problems. The periods associated with the free movement of capital, the gold standard of 1873-1931 and the current regime in the 1990s have been and are so far associated with mass unemployment and widening income inequality. The exceptions are employment in the UK and the US. The question is whether these undesirable conditions are in the nature of the regime or whether they are transitory after a period of adaptation? I would like to see further comparative studies of economic development before and after liberalisation. Deregulation took place at various times in the UK, the US, Germany and Sweden. But the timings are easily identifiable; in Sweden at the end of the 1980s. How did GDP, unemployment, inflation, the distribution of income and wealth develop before and after deregulation? Already a decade after the dominance of norm policy, when price stability was strongly emphasized, in order to bring down high inflation, central bank policies can now be formulated as "flexible inflation targeting", which means that capacity utilisation is in one way or another factored into the banks' target functions. There may not be much difference in practice, but central bank policies are now described in a way that also takes into account employment and capacity utilisation in general. Nevertheless, it is price stability, which is the overarching objective and responsibility of central banks. We are now facing the first really serious test in Sweden of the success of low-inflation policy. I do not believe for a moment that we should fail at the inflation target. It will not give way. But I'm worried about the consequences of maintaining the inflation target. Will unemployment continue to fall? Major imbalances have developed in the labour market. I can point to a blatant example. Only a few training places were requested to become science teachers and mathematics teachers in the school system. There are many other areas with similar imbalances in the public sector. After all, people who pass higher education in science and mathematics can become civil engineers or natural scientists and go to industry. The teaching profession provides 14,000  16,000 in starting salary. The industry offers much more and much better development opportunities, at least for the skilled. Can such imbalances be corrected without triggering a compensatory spiral and wage inflation? Failing this, it can cost us dearly. The fact is that the credibility of a low-inflation economy is very easily lost, but it can only be regained very slowly. Therefore, the Riksbank is concerned about the confidence that has been achieved. The credit rating agency Moody's puts a question mark on the functioning of the labour market. The same applies to the IMF and the OECD. They want to see changes in unemployment insurance and in social security laws, changes that would be perceived by most wage earners as deteriorations, at any rate. The problem is that the labour market can never be fully a market. It is also a social institution, with norms and rules that have moral roots. Each trade union has on its program solidarity and equalization between its members. Therefore, there is a conflict between the labor market as a forum for market clearance and the labor market as a social institution with moral rules and social norms. During the crisis years of the 1990s, the government was criticized for the clean-up of public finances, because austerity policies created mass unemployment. But Keynesianism had lost credibility. And that was a reality. With free movement of capital and public finances with large deficits, an expansion of expenditure would only bring higher interest rates while austerity, admittedly at first created unemployment, would eventually pay off by stimulating demand from falling interest rates, as we have actually experienced in recent times. But anti-Keynesianism seems to have bitten into people's minds. One cannot explain the bizarreness of cutting taxes and increasing government spending simply because the budget shows a surplus in another way. The surpluses are the result of boom. It is the real economy  the socio-economic balance  that should determine the levels of expenditure and taxation, not the budgetary surplus. Perhaps we should interpret what is now happening as a deliberate reversal of Gunnar Myrdal's slogan from the 1940s: "High taxes and low interest rates" to "Slightly lower taxes and slightly higher interest rates"?

Title: The Riksbank affects future inflation, not today's
text: Bergstrf6m: The Riksbank influences future inflation, not today's Date 2005-04-05 Deputy Governor Villy Bergstrf6m spoke today at Landshypotek in Ge4vle-Dala about what guides monetary policy. "Recently, we have had high GDP growth, while employment has developed weakly and inflation has been low. At the same time, house prices have continued to rise sharply, as has credit growth. It is not surprising that there will then be a debate on monetary policy. The discussion has gone both ways; on the one hand, there are those who have considered monetary policy to be "too little" expansionary and that employment has thus been held back unnecessarily, and on the other hand, there are those who have warned that it has been "too" expansionary and thus fueled asset prices too much. Something that surprises me, however, is that the criticism of the Riksbank, that interest rates are not low enough, is often based on today's inflation and not on the assessments of future inflation," Bergstrf6m began. "It is therefore important to clarify that today's inflation does not guide what the interest rate should be today. However, it is important in that it is the starting value for the 1-2-year forecast that we make over inflation and which guides our decisions on interest rates," Bergstrf6m said. "When you follow the debate, you can sometimes get the impression that there is an overconfidence about what the Riksbank can actually do with monetary policy, especially in the short term. Hypothetically, it might be possible to influence inflation in the coming months, but in that case very large changes in interest rates would be required. It would probably have other, less desirable, effects in other parts of the economy, such as large throws in production. In addition, it would result in an even greater effect on inflation over the 1-2 year term, since it is in this time perspective that a change in interest rates is expected to have the greatest effect. Then it wants us to believe that inflation in that perspective will deviate sharply from the target," Bergstrom said. "That's not the situation today. Although we see continued low inflation in 2005 and 2006, it is expected to be in line with the target towards the end of the forecast horizon - the horizon that thus guides monetary policy today. This follows from the fact that domestic inflation is expected to rise in line with the economic upturn and reduced spare resources. Similarly, we assume that the factors that have led to falling prices of imported goods over the past year will gradually subside over the forecast period, although we believe in continued low imported inflation," Bergstrf6m reported. "Moreover, the key drivers of today's low inflation, i.e. rapid productivity growth and low imported inflation, are factors that monetary policy largely ignores. These are supply factors that in themselves act as a stimulus for growth - a growth that is already high and also exceeds what is considered to be sustainable in the long term. To then pursue a more expansionary monetary policy to drive up domestic prices would be risky and could result in domestic inflation that could be difficult to stop if the economy continues to develop strong and resource utilization is rising. This could further fuel house price growth and credit expansion, and lead to large fluctuations in private demand going forward," Bergstrom said. "Other factors that have contributed to some extent to low inflation are the increased competition in the retail sector, which has led to a fall in food prices, and the removal of EU import quotas for clothing and textiles. Let me make it clear here that such changes, particularly the fall in food prices but also, to some extent, the removal of import quotas, involve, at least in part, price level adjustments that are of a transitory nature. However, it is difficult to determine how long such adjustments will continue, but in the Inflation Report we assessed that they will not affect inflation rates to the same extent as they do now in the long term," Bergstrf6m said. "Our latest assessment thus points to inflation in line with the target towards the end of the forecast period. If we were to end up in a situation of a declining economy and a deteriorating labour market, that assessment may obviously need to be reconsidered. Likewise if the economy picks up unexpected momentum. As always, the direction of monetary policy going forward depends on the new information that will be received about economic development abroad and in Sweden, and how the Riksbank values the inflation picture," Bergstrf6m concluded.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Bergstrm: Riksbanken pverkar den framtida inflationen, inte dagens Datum 2005-04-05 Vice riksbankschef Villy Bergstrm talade idag p Landshypotek i Gvle-Dala om vad som vgleder penningpolitiken. Den senaste tiden har vi haft en hg BNP-tillvxt samtidigt som sysselsttningen utvecklats svagt och inflationen varit lg. Ngot som dock frvnar mig r att kritiken mot Riksbanken, att rntan inte r tillrckligt lg, ofta grundar sig p dagens inflation och inte p bedmningarna om den framtida inflationen, inledde Bergstrm. Det r drfr viktigt att klargra att dagens inflation inte r vgledande fr vad rntan ska vara idag. Den r dock viktig stillvida att den utgr startvrdet fr den prognos p 1-2 rs sikt som vi gr ver inflationen och som r vgledande i vra beslut om rntan, menade Bergstrm. Nr man fljer debatten kan man ibland f uppfattningen att det finns en vertro om vad Riksbanken faktiskt kan gra med penningpolitiken srskilt p kort sikt. Rent hypotetiskt skulle det kanske g att pverka inflationen de nrmaste mnaderna men i s fall skulle det krvas mycket stora rntefrndringar. Dessutom skulle det resultera i en nnu strre effekt p inflationen p 1-2 rs sikt eftersom det r i det tidsperspektivet som en frndring av rntan bedms f strst effekt. D vill det till att vi tror att inflationen i det perspektivet kommer att avvika kraftigt frn mlet, sade Bergstrm. S r inte situationen i dag. Vi ser visserligen en fortsatt lg inflation under 2005 och 2006, men den bedms vara i linje med mlet mot slutet av prognoshorisonten  den horisont som allts r vgledande fr penningpolitiken idag. Det fljer av att den inhemska inflationen vntas stiga i takt med konjunkturuppgngen och minskade lediga resurser. Likas antar vi att de faktorer som lett till fallande priser p importerade varor under det senaste ret gradvis kommer att avta under prognosperioden, ven om vi tror p en fortsatt lg importerad inflation, redogjorde Bergstrm. De viktiga drivkrafterna bakom dagens lga inflation, det vill sga den snabba produktivitetstillvxten och den lga importerade inflationen, r dessutom faktorer som penningpolitiken till stor del inte rr p. Det r utbudsfaktorer som i sig verkar stimulerande p tillvxten  en tillvxt som redan r hg och dessutom verstiger vad som bedms vara lngsiktigt hllbart. Att d fra en mer expansiv penningpolitik fr att driva upp de inhemska priserna skulle vara riskfyllt och kunna resultera i en inhemsk inflation som kan bli svr att stoppa om konjunkturen fortstter utvecklas starkt och resursutnyttjandet stiger. Det skulle kunna sp p husprisutvecklingen och kreditexpansionen ytterligare, och leda till stora svngningar i den privata efterfrgan framver, sade Bergstrm. Andra faktorer som i viss mn har bidragit till den lga inflationen r den kade konkurrensen i detaljhandeln som har medfrt sjunkande livsmedelspriser, och borttagandet av EU:s importkvoter p klder och textilier. Lt mig hr klargra att sdana frndringar, framfrallt sjunkande livsmedelspriser men i viss mn ocks borttagandet av importkvoter, tminstone delvis innebr prisnivanpassningar som r av vergende karaktr. Det r dock svrt att avgra hur lnge sdana anpassningar fortgr, men i inflationsrapporten gjorde vi bedmningen att de inte lngsiktigt kommer att pverka inflationstakten i samma utstrckning som nu, sade Bergstrm. Vr senaste bedmning pekar allts p en inflation i linje med mlet mot slutet av prognosperioden. Om vi skulle hamna i ett lge med vikande konjunktur och en frsmrad arbetsmarknad kan den bedmningen sjlvklart behva omprvas. Likas om ekonomin tar ovntad fart. Precis som alltid beror penningpolitikens inriktning framver p den nya information som inkommer om den ekonomiska utvecklingen utomlands och i Sverige, och hur Riksbanken vrderar inflationsbilden, avslutade Bergstrm. Title: What does it take for us to be the best again?
text: Bergstrom: What does it take for us to be the best again? Date 2004-03-24 Deputy Governor Villy Bergstrom spoke in Tierp about the role of capital formation in economic growth "A country's long-term growth capacity is determined by the growth of labour and capital, as well as technological development. Thus, in order to increase long-term growth, measures that affect these factors are required. In the discussion about Sweden's growth, the population development in the future and the high level of sick leave have been in focus. Weak labour force growth poses both a financing problem for the public sector and resource shortages for the care of an ageing population. An equally large but neglected problem is the weak capital formation in our country (the new addition to the capital working in production in the form of machinery, buildings and facilities). The problem applies both in the short and in the long term. The fact that investments are not getting started slows down the recovery in the economy, but it is worse that Sweden has had weak capital formation since the mid-1970s," Bergstrom began. "After Swedish productivity growth (growth in production per hour worked or person) has been one of the fastest in the world for 100 years, the pace slowed down from the mid-1970s. From being one of the world's richest countries, Sweden became a relatively poor industrial country. An important reason was that the proportion of our available resources invested in capital formation then fell from about 15 percent of available resources to 5. Since then, capital formation has never scratched itself. This means that the pace of technological renewal of business and the rest of the economy is being held back, as well as investments in the country's infrastructure. Title: BIS Annual General Meeting
text: BIS Annual General Meeting Datum: 1999-06-07 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Backstrom Plats: Basel The following are excerpts from the speech delivered by Urban Backstrom, Chairman of the Board of Directors and President of the Bank for International Settlements, to the Annual General Meeting held in Basel today, 7 June 1999. At this point I should like to take a look at the global economy and consider some of the policy issues we face. There is now a much greater spirit of optimism about world economic prospects than was the case only a few months ago when we were all anxiously waiting to see what the fallout from the Brazilian crisis might be. It was not thought implausible that Brazilian inflation would get out of control, that Latin America would experience a renewed flight of capital and that the devaluation of the real would spark another round of devaluations, perhaps even extending back to Asia. With the memory of the repercussions of the Russian crisis and the near failure of Long-Term Capital Management all too fresh, the possible impact of such events on overextended global financial markets was another source of great concern. In the event, none of these fears have materialised. The Brazilian situation itself appears to have stabilised, with the impact so far on other Latin American countries contained. Both the IMF and the OECD are now forecasting global growth of about 2% in 1999 and further acceleration into the new millennium. The United States is expected to see an orderly slowdown, Europe to pick up speed, South-East Asia and Latin America to recover convincingly, and output in Japan to cease to fall. Asset markets already seem to be counting on such an outcome. Equity markets have risen worldwide, rebounding to record levels in the United States and Europe. Capital inflows into Asia, including Japan, have supported sharp increases in share prices, and a number of Latin American sovereign borrowers have been able to tap international bond markets within months of the Brazilian devaluation. Credit and liquidity spreads in many markets have also fallen sharply, albeit not back to the excessively low levels seen this time last year. However, these favourable developments should not lead us to conclude that the danger has passed. Indeed, the principal risk at this point is that the sense of urgency in the need both to manage current problems and to prevent the emergence of new ones will be lost. This would be irresponsible since there remain some evident threats to international financial and economic stability and, perhaps even more importantly, there may well be vulnerabilities that are not so evident. Recall that the scale of the Mexican crisis in 1994 was foreseen by very few. In South-East Asia the onset, duration and scope of the recession were all missed by the forecasting community. At this meeting last year, no one had anticipated the extent of the turmoil in financial markets that would be generated by the Russian devaluation and moratorium. The way in which rising credit spreads led to losses by highly leveraged investors, liquidity shortages and the virtual drying-up of some markets was generally not anticipated. Let us be honest with ourselves: the track record shows that there are many things that we do not understand and cannot predict. It would be highly imprudent simply to assume that all will be well. If many unexpected problems have surfaced over the last few years, many expected problems have failed to materialise. Whether this means the fears were not justified in the first place, or rather that problems have continued to build under the surface, remains to be seen. Perhaps the greatest of the unrealised fears has been that the US economy would slow down sharply before spending elsewhere had recovered sufficiently to support the global economy. This has not come about, in large part because of the continued strength of consumer spending in the United States. But the coincidence of declining private saving rates and a widening current account deficit is a matter of continuing concern. If investors became less willing to hold the rapidly expanding external debt of the United States, a falling dollar might increase nascent inflationary pressures in the United States, even triggering a hard landing. Fortunately, this has not happened, though the sharp rise in the yen in the third quarter of last year and last month's CPI statistics provide illustrations of how quickly the unexpected can arise. Another fear, again related to current trade imbalances, has been that of rising protectionism. While such pressures have been kept under control to date given continued growth in most of the industrial world, the challenge of maintaining an open trading system would surely increase were unemployment to begin rising again. Another concern has been that equity markets, particularly in the United States but also elsewhere in the industrial world, might fall back rapidly and in a disorderly manner. With personal saving rates now near zero in many of the countries with highly valued stock markets, a marked decline could well herald lower spending and growth. For some years now, many analysts have questioned whether the expected growth of profit rates implicit in equity prices has not been unrealistically high. At the same time, others have asserted that technological progress and corporate restructuring provide the foundation for a new economic environment that will support significantly higher profit growth in future. The evidence to date on the validity of this assertion is scanty. In the meantime, it is prudent not to ignore an abundance of evidence that markets are prone to overshoot on both the upside and the downside. The expected acceleration in the growth of global demand reflects the recent easing of monetary policy in most industrial countries and many emerging market economies. This easing, including that following the autumn crisis in financial markets, has been made possible by continuing disinflationary trends arising in part from high levels of excess industrial capacity. Moreover, the loans made earlier on to finance this expansion of capacity, in Asia in particular, still weigh on the health of the international financial system and have provided a further rationale for monetary easing in many countries. The recent experience of Japan reminds us, however, that the efficacy of monetary policy may be limited by the zero nominal interest rate constraint, particularly if prices are already falling and this is expected to continue. Concerns that an associated decline in the exchange rate might serve to export deflation to others may be a further impediment to policy activism. Nor are these the only constraints on the use of accommodative monetary policy. What also seems to have been reasonably well established by the events of recent years is that such policies can themselves contribute to turbulence in financial markets. Easy and low-cost financing over an extended period may drive up the price of financial assets, even at times when the rates of return on the underlying real assets are declining. This is what happened in Japan in the late 1980s and in SouthEast Asia subsequently, and may help explain the sharp rebound in equity prices in the last few quarters. Periods of monetary accommodation may also lead to a more cavalier attitude to risk-taking on the part of lenders. Such tendencies are accentuated by competitive pressures to maintain or increase rates of return on capital. However, the build-up of excessive leverage sets the stage for the type of market turbulence seen in the wake of the Russian moratorium when investor sentiment suddenly reverses. If there are limitations to the use of monetary policy in some circumstances, then other policies might have to be relied upon more heavily. Policies of microeconomic reform remain the top priority to spur non-inflationary growth. Given that the overhang of excess capacity will hold back investment in many sectors for years, it also becomes more important to deregulate and open profit opportunities in other sectors. If such opportunities could be augmented by more favourable labour market policies, which might themselves eventually build confidence by creating jobs, the potential for a significant strengthening of medium-term economic prospects would surely be enhanced. These microeconomic reforms could, in countries where medium-term fiscal consolidation is sufficiently advanced, also be supported by the countercyclical use of fiscal policy. Given the costs and the difficulties faced in managing the successive crises experienced over the last few years, it is not surprising that considerable attention has been paid to how future crises might be avoided. One obvious insight is that affected emerging market economies must reform their domestic financial systems. Simultaneous restructuring of the corporate and banking systems, and a clear recognition and allocation of losses, is required if profitability is to be restored and sustained. Further progress in establishing a sound legal infrastructure covering both bankruptcy procedures and effective corporate governance would also seem very high on the list of priorities. To say that the key to avoiding future crises in emerging markets must be found in domestic reforms is not to deny the international dimension of the problem. Excessive capital inflows and outflows did exacerbate domestic problems and steps should be taken to deal with the possible recurrence of such events. To begin with, the dangers inherent in adjustable peg exchange rate systems need to be clearly recognised. There should also be less hesitancy in using market-based prudential instruments to prevent the build-up of excessive external indebtedness. And finally, countries that receive capital inflows should also prepare for the day when the movement might reverse. Countries that are vulnerable in this regard should consider carefully the adequacy of their foreign exchange reserves, particularly when measured against their short-term external debt. Since large numbers of countries cannot build up their reserves by increasing their trade surpluses simultaneously, this would seem to argue for greater use of contingent lending facilities provided by the private sector. Given such arrangements, recourse to the new IMF Contingent Credit Lines would then add public sector to private sector affirmation that the domestic policies being followed by the borrowing country are sensible and sustainable. If domestic self-help is the best response, even to problems with an international dimension, part of the solution may still be found in measures to change the way in which international financial markets sometimes operate. While financial liberalisation and international financial integration bring unquestioned benefits, they can also be subject to episodes of excessive risk-taking. In recent years, there does seem to have been imprudent lending, and not just to emerging market economies but also to borrowers within the industrial world. In part this has been spurred by competitive forces. These seem unlikely to diminish as financial restructuring accelerates. However, the potential of public safety nets to distort incentives and breed complacency can also be discerned and these structures should be reevaluated. It is important that all investors are held accountable for their decisions. The international community should also ensure that all investors and lenders play their part in the resolution of any future financial crisis and, to this end, should implement, inter alia, changes to international bond covenants that would facilitate debt restructuring should this become necessary. The events of last year have also made clear that greater efforts are needed to strengthen the functioning of markets lest market processes themselves add to volatility during periods of stress. The expanded role of markets in channelling funds from surplus to deficit sectors and for managing a variety of risks is one factor making this imperative. Information asymmetries lie at the heart of market failure, and the market's way of resolving them can give rise to unpredictable outcomes. Ensuring that markets have adequate information about national economies, the strength of financial systems, aggregate positions in markets and the financial standing of counterparties is important. Equally, if not more, important is to ensure that market participants' approach to risk management reflects the full balance of costs and rewards implied in their decisions. Finally, it is also necessary to consider the micro-prudential policies that apply to individual firms in a wider setting, including the potential for unintended aggregation effects. Internal risk assessment procedures must recognise the interrelationships that exist between categories of risk before, not when, markets are under strain. The fact that markets are becoming increasingly global means that efforts to promote financial stability must also become increasingly international. One underlying theme of the many meetings held last year at the BIS and elsewhere has been the need to involve directly the emerging market countries likely to be affected by the decisions taken to promote monetary and financial stability. This reflects a very practical consideration. Implementation will be an even bigger challenge than setting international standards in the first place, and a sense of shared ownership will materially improve the chances of such implementation. Allied with other incentives for change, including surveillance by peers, the IMF and the World Bank, progress can be made if we keep insisting that progress must be made. Let me finish by noting my personal satisfaction that the BIS, and the various groups and committees which meet here, continued last year to make substantive contributions to the pursuit of both monetary and financial stability. These efforts will be taken further, with the assistance of additional input from the newly established Financial Stability Institute and the even newer Financial Stability Forum. Recent episodes of financial crisis and macroeconomic disturbance underline how much work still needs to be done. Yet there is considerable comfort in knowing that the global community is addressing these issues in a serious and systematic way.

Title: Monetary policy after corona  we need to think in new ways
text: Breman: Monetary policy after corona - we need to think in new ways "The pandemic and its economic consequences make it abundantly clear that we cannot predict what the next economic crisis will look like - either in terms of what triggers it or what kind of monetary policy response may be needed." This is what Deputy Governor Anna Breman said when she spoke today at a webinar organized by Swedbank. "This means that innovation and new thinking in monetary policy will be required for us to continue to fulfil our mission of price stability in Sweden." Date: 2021-02-23 09:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Anna Breman Location: Swedbank, digital Monetary and fiscal policy contribute in different ways So far during the coronavirus crisis, monetary and fiscal policy have managed to complement each other well without there being any formal cooperation. Monetary policy has focused partly on keeping the supply of credit going and partly on keeping interest rates low. Fiscal policy has focused on helping businesses in crisis sectors so that they are not wiped out and need to lay off staff, and on providing support to the households affected by the crisis. "With interest rates so low globally, we see that fiscal policy going forward will become increasingly important in dealing with recessions," Breman continued. "And already now we need to discuss how to create the best preparedness for new crises through good interaction between fiscal and monetary policy. We also need to examine what the boundaries of monetary policy with fiscal policy should look like." Monetary policy needs a larger toolbox This becomes particularly important when we consider how we can expand the monetary policy toolbox and thus create more room for manoeuvre to counter recessions and maintain price stability. "I think we have managed to think in new ways during the crisis, and this is not least noticeable in the new tools we have used, such as securities purchases of various kinds. And I think it's entirely possible to expand the toolbox further," Breman said. She discussed four different tools that the Riksbank has not yet used but which are flourishing in the international debate: very negative interest rates, double interest rates, yield curve control and helicopter money. If more monetary policy stimulus were needed in the short term, the tools Anna Breman envisions in the first place are negative repo rates and extended quantitative easing. "But none of the tools I've discussed today can be ruled out, provided they're legal," Breman pointed out. Flexibility required One effect of the pandemic is that it has accelerated changes in the national economy that pose both challenges and opportunities for the Riksbank. "We therefore need to constantly adapt to a changing world and develop our analysis in order to achieve the inflation target and contribute to good economic development in general," concluded Anna Breman. Title: The Riksbank is prepared to act
text: Breman hearing in the Finance Committee: The Riksbank is prepared to act Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Anna Breman will today participate in this year's first hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. There they comment on, among other things, the effects of the coronavirus on the economy. Date: 2020-03-10 09:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Anna Breman Place: Finance Committee, Swedish Parliament Anna Breman highlights the effects of the coronavirus on the economy. She points to the uncertainty that has arisen in the financial markets in the wake of the spread of the virus. The Riksbank has opportunities to stimulate the economy if the downturn were to be sharp, she says: "I feel confident that the Riksbank can act to stabilize the Swedish economy if a crisis threatens. The Riksbank's toolbox can be fully used. However, the type of measures needed is situational depends. It is important that measures are put in place where they have the greatest impact. The possibilities of counteracting a downturn in the Swedish economy also improve when several policy areas contribute." In the current situation, the Riksbank is in close contact with other authorities in Sweden, as well as with other central banks. Title: Hearing on monetary policy
text: Cecilia Skingsley on the Finance Committee. Hearing on monetary policy Date: 2015-09-24 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Skandiasalen, Swedish Parliament How is the Swedish economy doing? Why do we have negative interest rates? What can be done to curb rising household indebtedness? These are some of the questions that Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley will answer when they begin the second hearing of the year on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee on Thursday. Stefan Ingves presents the latest monetary policy decision from the beginning of September, when the Riksbank's Executive Board decided to leave the repo rate unchanged at -0.35 percent in order to provide continued necessary support for the rise in inflation. The Riksbank's expansionary monetary policy, with negative interest rates and purchases of government bonds, is an important explanation for the stable development of growth in Sweden, the fact that unemployment is falling and that there is a clear upward trend in inflation. Inflation has risen from 0.5% to 1.4% over the past year, excluding interest rate effects and volatile energy prices. But the rise in inflation may be jeopardised by developments in the rest of the world, and the Riksbank therefore remains highly prepared to act if the outlook for inflation deteriorates. At the same time, Ingves emphasizes the importance of further measures from the government, parliament and the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority to mitigate the risks of high household indebtedness. An amortisation requirement is a welcome, but not enough, step to calm down the development of the mortgage market, says Ingves. "We are behind schedule in solving these problems in Sweden, but there is an opportunity to act, there are more measures to take. If nothing more is done, there are obvious risks of very poor economic development down the line." Cecilia Skingsley discusses in her introduction the effects of digitalisation on inflation and believes that these have contributed to dampening price developments. But they are not the main explanation for the low inflation rate in recent years. The recovery in the rest of the world has been slow, the krona strengthened sharply after the financial crisis, energy prices have fallen and in the uncertain environment after the crises, it has been difficult for companies to raise prices. "But monetary policy is having an effect. Inflation is now rising from low levels. This shows that it is possible to raise inflation despite digitalisation." Skingsley also addresses discussions about whether central bank targets should be changed. She points out that in the Swedish debate, arguments have mainly been put forward for lowering the inflation target, while the international discussion is rather about whether the target should be raised. But you don't create confidence by adjusting the target to where inflation is at the moment, skingsley says. "Stable expectations about general price developments mean one less uncertainty factor for both price and wage-setters in our society."

Title: Cecilia Skingsley in Norrkping and Linkping
text: Cecilia Skingsley in Norrkoping and Linkoping Date: 2015-03-03 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Louis De Geer Concert & Congress in Norrkoping On Tuesday, Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley will visit Norrkoping and Linkoping. She talks about the economic situation and the latest interest rate decision, including at a breakfast with representatives from Norrkoping municipality and the local business community. Skingsley also makes a couple of company visits and participates in a lunch with representatives from Linkoping municipality and the business community. The Riksbank's Executive Board recently decided to lower the repo rate to -0.10 percentage points and adjust the repo rate path downwards. In addition, the Riksbank buys government bonds for SEK 10 billion. "Growth and employment are higher than in many of our neighbouring countries and we are seeing signs that low inflation has bottomed out. But the risks from the outside world have increased. Then we can't sit on our hands. We remain prepared to act if necessary to support the rise in inflation and for the favourable conditions in Sweden to continue," says Skingsley. The link contains the pictures that Skingsley shows at his presentation in Norrkoping. In connection with the spring and autumn monetary policy reports, the members of the Executive Board carry out visits to different locations in the country where they present the monetary policy decisions. The members then give lectures and meet with the business community, municipal representatives, media and universities in the locality in question.

Title: Currency arrangements between EMU and its neighbours
text: Currency arrangements between EMU and its neighbours Datum: 1996-11-22 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Backstrom Plats: The 6th Frankfurt European Banking Congress Let me start by thanking you for this invitation enabling me to elaborate somewhat on the relationship between the Ins and the Outs. Under Article 109m of the Treaty there is an obligation to treat exchange rate policy as a matter of common interest. I assume that one reason behind this provision is the creation of a single market with freedom of movement for goods, individuals, services and capital. In order to ensure the efficient functioning and development of the Single Market, it is important that real exchange rate misalignments between EUcurrencies be avoided, as well as excessive nominal exchange rate fluctuations, which could disrupt trade flows among Member States. Sound fundamentals a prerequisite A prerequisite for sustained exchange rate stability is the lasting convergence of economic fundamentals, in particular price stability. Sound fiscal and structural policies in Member States are equally essential. This means that in the absence of a convergence of fundamentals, any attempt to co-ordinate exchange rate policies is bound to be unsuccessful. Exchange rate policy co-operation cannot be a substitute for stability-oriented domestic policies. Thus, it is primarily a close co-ordination of stability-oriented domestic policies between Member States that will lead to the desired exchange rate stability. Consequently, it can be argued that membership in an exchange rate arrangement is not necessary. On the other hand, one can also take the view that if the co-ordination of domestic policies is successful and delivers exchange rate stability, then Member States might as well belong to an exchange rate arrangement. However, there is a line of reasoning that suggests that market-induced exchange rate misalignments can occur even in the absence of policy related misalignments. It has been argued that fixed parities may invite currency speculation, which could be self-fullfilling. It would then be necessary to avoid offering one-way bets by having bands that are wide enough to minimize such a risk. This has in fact been fully acknowledged - hence the existence of the wide standard fluctuation bands in the present ERM system and their proposed continuation in the new ERM2 system. The size of the standard fluctuation band in the ERM2 has still to be decided but, as I see it, the principles of continuity and equal treatment among all Member States are important arguments for maintaining the current 15 per cent. Why a need for an exchange rate system? This still leaves a fundamental question unaswered. If it is the close co-ordination of stability-oriented domestic policies between euro-area and non-euro-area Member States that leads to the desired exchange rate stability, why do we need a formal exchange rate system? This question may well be put to the other members of today's panel, but permit me to suggest three possible answers: Firstly, the ERM has, in fact, worked quite well after 1993 and has served as an external anchor for economic policies in many Member States. Such a mechanism has helped to ensure that policies are oriented towards stability. Secondly, common agreement about a central rate could help to enhance the credibility of sound, stability-oriented domestic policies by establishing a focal point for agents' expectations. Thirdly, the present ERM and the ERM2 both contain a common agreement about a central rate. This means that an ex ante joint decision exists concerning a reference rate for the conduct of domestic economic policies in Member States. Thus, this procedure gives content to the agreement that exchange rate policy shall be treated "as a matter of common interest". Stability and/or formality? Thus far I have concentrated on exchange rate stability's true foundations and on the reasons for having a formal exchange rate system such as the present ERM and a new ERM2-system. This leaves the issue of why certain countries consider the ERM membership to be compulsory prior to participation in the EMU. My starting point here is that, already at the Florence meeting, the Heads of State or of Government declared that participation in ERM2 is voluntary. There are, of course, no legal grounds for deciding otherwise. Moreover, considering that certain Member States are not participating at present, it represents a continuation of the existing order. Why, then, do certain countries consider the ERM membership to be compulsory prior to participation in the EMU? After all, the confirmation procedure in the spring of 1998 affords an opportunity to decide whether the exchange rate has been stable at a level that is acceptable to other Member States in accordance with the criteria for the establishment of a central rate in the ERM. Assume a country where all the relevant indicators signal sustainable economic stability and convergence, accompanied by an exchange rate that has been definitely stable at a level that conforms with the criteria for the establishment of a central rate in the ERM, but the currency has not been a formal participant in the ERM system. What rational ground could there then be for refusing membership in the EMU, considering that the currency is shortly to be abolished and absorbed in a monetary union? In the case of a country that is preparing to join the monetary union, the reason can hardly be that the development of the exchange rate outside the ERM might constitute a threat to the stability of that union. This leaves the argument that participation in the ERM is cited in the Maastricht Treaty. However, the exchange rate criterion is not entirely clear. Furthermore, since the Treaty was adopted the ERM has been modified. It seems unreasonable that a currency which has been a member of the ERM but has fluctuated by up to 15 per cent should be regarded as a stable currency. Surely it is exchange rate stability as such which matters, not the institutional arrangement. I am aware that on this point there is a broad majority of Member States whose opinion differs from Sweden's. But I still have difficulty in understanding the grounds for that interpretation. The last word rests with the Heads of State or of Government at their meeting in the spring of 1998. I want to make one point perfectly clear. The Swedish position does not imply that exchange rate stability lacks importance for entry to the monetary union. On the contrary, we share the opinion of all Member States as regards the importance of such stability. The difference is thus one of form rather than substance. The Swedish position is rooted in the doubts that many in my country have about exchange rate arrangements, not least in the light of our experience in the early 1990s. Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, has during this autumn, however, initiated a discussion about swedish participation in the ERM in the context of the vigorous consolidation of government finance and the low level of inflation, together with the resultant improvement in the economic policy's credibility. At the same time we have made it perfectly clear that ERM membership is not being considered at present and will require broad support in swedish society. To date, however, the reactions have been hesitant. To conclude, in the light of these remarks, my opinion is that monetary and exchange rate policy co-operation within the European Union should be sufficiently flexible to accommodate different strategies for economic convergence.

I am aware that on this point there is a broad majority of Member States whose opinion differs from Sweden's. But I still have difficulty in understanding the grounds for that interpretation. The last word rests with the Heads of State or of Government at their meeting in the spring of 1998. I want to make one point perfectly clear. The Swedish position does not imply that exchange rate stability lacks importance for entry to the monetary union. On the contrary, we share the opinion of all Member States as regards the importance of such stability. The difference is thus one of form rather than substance. The Swedish position is rooted in the doubts that many in my country have about exchange rate arrangements, not least in the light of our experience in the early 1990s. Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, has during this autumn, however, initiated a discussion about swedish participation in the ERM in the context of the vigorous consolidation of government finance and the low level of inflation, together with the resultant improvement in the economic policy's credibility. At the same time we have made it perfectly clear that ERM membership is not being considered at present and will require broad support in swedish society. To date, however, the reactions have been hesitant. To conclude, in the light of these remarks, my opinion is that monetary and exchange rate policy co-operation within the European Union should be sufficiently flexible to accommodate different strategies for economic convergence. Title: Current monetary policy
text: Current monetary policy Date: 1996-11-07 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Hearing at the Finance Committee Thank you for the invitation to publicly discuss developments in the Swedish economy and current monetary policy here in committee. My introduction today largely follows the approach that applied in the past. After that, I am prepared to answer questions. The economy is improving After the summer and during the autumn, there have been more tangible signs of an improved economy. The conditions for continued improved growth in the Swedish economy also appear to be favourable. Nevertheless, inflationary pressures over the next two years are expected to be moderate. Inflation expectations also remain low, which is an indication of confidence in economic policy. There are also many indications that the credibility of Sweden as a country with low inflation is about to be established. All in all, this means that the possibilities for inflation in line with the price stability objective are good. However, each projection is about weighing risks and probabilities. I will come back to this in a moment, but will first address some aspects of real economic developments. According to the latest GDP statistics, the Swedish economy grew faster in recent years than previously estimated. There have been upward revisions for both 1994 and 1995 and the first half of 1996. Thus, between the summer of 1993, when the trend turned upwards, and the summer of 1996, GDP rose at an annual rate of 3% on average. The economic upturn in the 1990s has thus far been faster than that which took place in the early 1980s. At the same time, inflation has been significantly lower and even below real growth rates. We have to go back to the 1960s to find periods of equivalent length when growth has been higher than inflation. There are likely to be several reasons for that. A first obvious explanation is that resource utilisation throughout the economy was lower in the 1990s when the economic upturn started compared to the 1980s. This has a dampening effect on inflation rates, while the economy can grow faster for some time as spare resources are used. However, there are underlying factors, which may be of a more lasting nature. However, it is too early to draw any definitive conclusions, but the question is whether the Swedish economy does not now have greater growth potential than in the 1970s and 1980s and whether the propensity for inflation in the broad sense has not decreased. These hypotheses are based on several interacting factors. Behind the higher growth rate in the 1990s is a tendency towards increased productivity and increased capital formation, as well as an increase in average working hours. Regardless of the period compared, productivity appears to be a number of tenths higher in the 1990s compared to the 1980s. These may seem small numbers, but if they turn out to be lasting, they quickly accumulate over time into tangible effects. The tax reform, various deregulations and changed compensation rules in the social security systems may have contributed to improving the way the Swedish economy works. Low inflation is also likely to contribute to a better functioning economy. In addition, EU membership, and the globalisation of trade in general, have increased competitive pressure. Something that also suggests that there are more lasting effects on the Swedish economy is a rapid pace of capital formation, in the form of an increase in investments, which has occurred in recent years. Gross capital formation, excluding housing construction, has reached relatively high levels. Investments in industry normally rise after a period of increase in capacity utilisation. The new pattern in the 1990s is that the upturn in investment came faster and became larger compared to what happened in the 1980s. It is also possible to discern a new development in the composition of foreign trade. During the 1990s, medical, pharmaceutical and telecommunications products have rapidly increased their combined share. Between 1990 and 1995, the pharmaceutical industry has doubled the volumes of its export deliveries while the telecommunications industry has almost quadrupled itss. Progress in 1996 has also been rapid in these areas. A new development is also that exports to Asia have increased significantly. These are, of course, important explanations for the fact that Swedish exports also performed well in 1996, despite weak development in some EU countries and despite the fact that the krona appreciated and part of the relative cost improvement that took place after the fall of the krona in the autumn of 1992 has thus been regained. These trends can be seen as signs that the Swedish economy's capacity for structural change has improved. These are all new and encouraging patterns in the Swedish economy, which may be signs of a more lastingly higher production potential. So far, these are hypotheses, but there is reason to follow developments also from the monetary policy horizon as they are important for the inflation assessment. Although growth has been strong during the economic upturn, there has been a slowdown in total output over the past year. A partial explanation for this is the development of investment in stocks, which I raised here in committee at the hearing in May. In upturn phases, production tends to rise faster than demand, something that also happened in connection with the recent upturn. The reason is that companies generally do not want to end up in a situation where they cannot deliver when demand is increasing rapidly. Gradually, the companies discover that the inventory build-up has gone too far and then begin an adaptation process. Then a reverse effect occurs, production increases more slowly than the final demand in the economy. Just such a stock adjustment came towards the end of last year and continued during the spring in Sweden. It also came somewhat earlier in some other countries that are important for Swedish exports. It is not uncommon for similar inventory adjustments to occur at this point in a business cycle. The same thing happened at about the same time in the 1970s and 1980s. Statistics Sweden's statistics also show this clearly. Total output is estimated to have grown by only 1.6 per cent in the first half of this year compared with the corresponding period last year. Production was dragged down by an adjustment in inventories amounting to 0.9% of GDP, which means that final demand actually grew by 2.5%. After all, it is by holding back production in relation to overall demand that the adjustment of stocks desired by the companies can be achieved. When companies temporarily cut back on production, lay-offs and even redundancies can take place, as also happened in 1996. The labour market has therefore, among other things, developed weakly during the current year. However, if the underlying conditions for expansion continue to be good, the production increase will start again once the inventory adjustment is completed, but there may also be a situation where underlying demand is adversely affected if, for example, a weakened labour market has repercussions on household confidence and thus has a downward impact on private consumption. It was this risk that prompted the Riksbank to work in parallel in the analysis with a weaker so-called. side options this spring, which if realized further would have dampened inflationary pressures. However, the statistics so far suggest that the risk of such a scenario seems to have subsided. The adjustment of inventories seems to be coming to an end and, although the labour market has developed weakly, private consumption appears to continue to show a stable trend improvement. This is one of the reasons why we are now assessing that a recovery in production is under way. The fact that the economy abroad also seems to be improving is another indication of this, as well as the fact that exports have held up fairly well so far during the year. Low-inflation regime on the way to establish Another key feature of the picture is that inflation expectations, in the short as well as in the slightly longer term, have fallen and more and more in line with the target. This means that households, companies and financial actors now have faith in the will and ability of Swedish economic policy to maintain low inflation. In other words, this means that confidence in Swedish economic policy has increased significantly over the past year. Confidence in the objective of price stability is not just about words, but also about deeds. The Riksbank's tighter interest rate policy between the summer of 1994 and 1995 shows that we take the price stability objective seriously, while the consolidation of public finances is proof of the political system's willingness to create the conditions for maintaining this objective in the long term. I have stressed many times here in committee that if current inflation is kept in line with the objective and long-term confidence in economic policy in general is strengthened by a move towards sound public finances, then sooner or later a tangible positive effect will have on long-term interest rates and the krona's exchange rate. It's such a so-called. confidence shock we experienced over the past year. Since the summer of 1995, the krona has strengthened by about 13 percent and the five-year housing rate has fallen by almost 4 percentage points. This has had a major one-off effect on the development of consumer prices. Import prices and interest costs for own homes have fallen sharply as a result of the positive development. This is a dominant reason why, according to the latest measurement, consumer prices have risen by only 0.2% year-on-year, which in itself is below the lower limit of the price stability objective tolerance range. Normally, however, various types of temporary price disturbances should be able to be captured by the tolerance range, given that underlying inflation is around 2 percent. Moreover, the target is not constructed in terms of individual monthly figures, but should be seen in an annual perspective. However, even in terms of 1996 as a whole, it cannot be ruled out that the lower tolerance limit may be slightly lower than. In order to analyse the currently low level of inflation in terms of the price stability objective, an assessment must be made of the trend or underlying inflation rate and how it can be expected to develop in the future. A rough purge of the temporary effects from import prices and interest costs for own homes shows an underlying increase of around 2 percent, which means that all other things being equal, registered inflation may gradually move up to that level as the temporary effects disappear from the measurements. It should be added straight away that various measures of underlying inflation are very rough, to which I shall return in a moment. Do wage increases and an upturn in consumption pose inflationary risks? Any assessment of future inflation is based on risks and probabilities. One such risk, as we have highlighted, is wage formation. In the first half of the year, wages and salaries appear to have risen by around 5 per cent in the whole economy compared with the corresponding period of the previous year, if one corrects some temporary and statistical factors. This represents an increase from the more than 3.5 percent annual rate at which wages rose in the second half of 1995. Compared to the inflation target of 2 percent, a wage increase of just over 5 percent means a real wage increase of 3 percent. This is well above the socio-economic space, given the trend in productivity development. In the long run, real wage developments that deviate from productivity developments are not consistent with the inflation target. The Riksbank currently sees no imminent risk that the wage agreements that have been reached would pose any tangible danger to inflation developments for the next two years. On the other hand, it is important that there is an adjustment in the agreements that are negotiated next. The question is how should the high wage increases be interpreted? The pessimistic interpretation is that the high wage increases will continue in the future. This would mean that unemployment will remain at a high level, unless a major change in the structure of the labour market is brought about which makes it work significantly better. The pessimistic interpretation suggests that wage growth in addition to the agreements increased in 1996, despite the weak labour market situation. The main hypothesis that the Riksbank is working on is somewhat more optimistic, which does not exclude the need for an improvement in the functioning of the labor market. Wage outcomes may have been influenced by the fact that the credibility of low-inflation policies was not established when the agreements were concluded. The wage round in the spring of 1995 was marked by the inflation expectations that prevailed at the time and which were up to 4 percent per year. The situation in the spring of 1995 was also marked by a rapid increase in export demand and a very favourable profit situation in the foreigncompetitive sector. If this hypothesis is reasonable, we can expect a gradual slowdown in the rate of wage growth as the current agreement expires. Next time, however, the negotiations will not be coordinated in time in the same way as last time. Already at the end of 1996, a couple of agreements expire. Admittedly, there have been statements from representatives of the workers' side, which, if properly reproduced, are very remarkable. Let me quote (from Finanstidningen on 14 October 1996):  The fact that inflation today is low has little bearing on our wage bid and  There is no direct link between our upcoming wage bid and the number of unemployed. It is possible that the statements should be seen in the light of the tactical approach to the forthcoming negotiations and, if so, can be written on this account. However, if the statements reflect a view of wage formation that is representative of the workers' side, it is clear that the labour market suffers from greater problems in terms of the rules of the game, which in that case must be addressed in the context of economic policy as a whole. For the time being, the Riksbank is sticking to its main hypothesis, i.e. that we will have a gradual adjustment of wage increases in the future. But there is every reason to follow closely the negotiations that are about to begin. Another risk could be if there is a significantly faster upturn in private consumption than the one that the Riksbank and most other analysts expect. It is not excluded that consumption may grow more rapidly in view of the improvement in household finances in recent years and the fact that consumption has developed weakly over several years. Gradually, a need arises to renew permanent durable capital goods. In relation to other countries, for example, the average age of the Swedish car fleet is high. However, experience from other countries shows that the pass-through to inflation of a rapid rise in consumption depends on several different factors, not least the degree of slack. At the present stage, therefore, a more substantial increase in consumption does not in itself have to lead to rapid price increases. Reduced propensity to inflation? Against these factors, which may indicate that there are some inflation risks, are primarily the signs, which I talked about earlier, that the propensity to inflation in a broad sense seems to have decreased in the Swedish economy. During the autumn, there has been additional information pointing in this direction. Although the current very low inflation is mainly due to temporary factors, the whole decline cannot be attributed to it. Some, albeit limited, part of the decline in inflation appears to be of a more lasting nature. I spoke earlier about the fact that it is not entirely possible to accurately clear the impact of various temporary factors on inflation. The Riksbank's overall assessment is that underlying inflation is now somewhere between 1.5 and 2 per cent. If the propensity to inflation turns out to be lower than what is built into the Riksbank's assessments of future inflation, it could affect our inflation forecast in a favourable direction. However, more information and time are needed to be able to draw conclusions about this. Monetary policy There was a major adjustment of the repo rate in 1996. Since the start of the cuts, the repo rate has been adjusted down from 8.91 to currently 4.6 per cent, i.e. an almost halving of the level of the repo rate. However, this should be seen in the light of the favourable inflation outlook and also in the light of the strengthening of the krona. The repo rate has been lowered in small but continuous steps. A pattern has formed in the reductions. It has been important for the Riksbank to continuously receive confirmation of our analysis in the incoming statistics and also to feel that market players have shared our analysis. Ultimately, it is confidence in economic policy that determines the degree of room for manoeuvre for the Riksbank. In connection with the reduction of the interest rate corridor and the repo rate on 24 October, it was declared that the pattern of the regular cuts ceases. To clearly show this, a fixed repo rate of 4.60 percent was decided, which is valid for four weeks. At the same time, the comments highlighted that we do not want a strong focus on the repo rate that will be set immediately thereafter. The reason for our action is that although we see some limited scope for further lowering the repo rate, the picture is not entirely clear. We need time to analyze and follow the incoming statistics. The conclusion of the assessments made may also be an unchanged repo rate.
