Title: Current monetary policy
text: Current monetary policy Date: 1996-05-09 Speaker: Governor Urban Be4ckstrf6m Location: Finance Committee hearing Thank you for the invitation to the committee to discuss developments in the Swedish economy and current monetary policy. Better conditions for sustainable growth 1995 was also a good year for the Swedish economy (Chart 1). GDP grew by 3 per cent and output grew by as much as 9 per cent in manufacturing. It is also positive that investments continued to increase by over 10 percent last year, as well as that Sweden's overall business with the rest of the world gave a surplus of just over 2 percent of GDP. The general government deficit also continued to decline. Employment increased by 60,000 people. However, unemployment remains at a high level. Since the low point at the beginning of 1994, employment has increased by 100,000 people, which means that only 20 percent of the previous reduction of just over 500,000 jobs has been recovered. However, the picture is slightly different in terms of the number of hours worked, where almost half the decline has been recorded, see Figure 1. Average working hours have thus increased. A continued improvement in the economy with increased employment requires sustainable growth, which in turn requires low inflation and confidence in Swedish economic policy in general. The previous situation, with uncertainty about economic policy, meant that the krona was weak and long-term interest rates high. This made it difficult for the economy to enter a trajectory of balanced and sustainable economic growth. It is true that since the turnaround in the second quarter of 1993, GDP has grown at an annual rate of 2.7%. The contribution to this growth came to three-quarters from the industrial sector, which makes up only about. 20 percent of the economy. This meant a structural change in the Swedish economy and a build-up of relatively large current account surpluses, but spare capacity in the industrial sector was quickly taken up and inflationary tensions therefore arose at an early stage in the upswing. Producer prices rose, cost awareness slowed down and wage formation difficulties arose. The notion spread that inflation would rise again and the higher expected inflation was consequently on the verge of being fulfilled. The Riksbank therefore raised its key interest rates between August 1994 and July 1995 in order to safeguard its inflation target. The alternative would have meant higher inflation, which would have had a negative impact on future growth and employment. Inflationary tendencies in the industrial sector have now slowed down. Inflation has shifted to a path of around 2 percent. During this spring, the increase in consumer prices has even fallen to 1.7%. Inflation is now the lowest in over 35 years, which is a success for economic policy. The fall in interest rates and the strengthening of the krona since last summer are an indication that Swedish economic policy has gained increased confidence in a more lasting direction on price stability. However, we must not forget that development has benefited from stable international financial markets. Chart 2 shows the evolution of the long-term interest rate differential with Germany and the krona since 1994. The fundamental conditions ahead for sustainable, balanced and non-inflationary growth have thus improved. The benefits of keeping inflation under control have become clear over the past six months. In connection with previous international slowdown phases, the Swedish economy has often found itself in a situation of high and rising inflation. It has tended to amplify the downturns in the economy in the 1970s and 1980s. Low inflation has now provided a better starting point for the future. During the spring, the Riksbank has been able to lower its repo rate at a relatively rapid pace. The nominal policy rate has come down to the lowest levels since the early 1970s. Chart 3 shows the evolution of the repo rate and the short and long-term interest rates since 1994. During the spring, it has sometimes been emphasized that the Riksbank would have acted too late when it came to lowering the repo rate. At the same time, none of the more prominent analysts of the Swedish economy predicted inflation in line with the target for 1996 and 1997 in late autumn last year. On the part of the Riksbank, it has been important now, as before, to stick to the inflation target. It was only when we saw that conditions had changed that we began to ease interest rate policy. The repo rate does not automatically control market interest rates with different maturities. The possibility of influencing the structure of interest rates - and, above all, interest rates on securities with longer maturities - is based on the existence of confidence in economic policy. A premature reduction in the repo rate would have created ambiguity about the long-term direction of monetary policy, not least given that Sweden has an unfavourable inflationary history. Such action by the Riksbank could have led to higher long-term interest rates and a weaker exchange rate this spring or at a later stage. Nor should we be led to believe that fine-tuned economic policies make it possible to eliminate cyclical fluctuations or to influence quarterly fluctuations in growth. Nor can it be ignored that Sweden is a small open economy, with a great dependence on developments in the outside world. On the other hand, policies aimed at keeping inflation under control can help to mitigate fluctuations in the economy. The greater the confidence in budget and monetary policy, the more confident households and companies feel about the future and the greater freedom of action the Riksbank has in the short term. Favourable inflation outlook The rate of increase in consumer prices fell to 2 per cent in January and to 1.7 per cent in February and March. A breakdown of the CPI statistics shows that it was mainly the prices of goods imported and the cost of interest on own homes that contributed to the falling inflation rate at the beginning of 1996. Although domestically generated price developments (as we have tried to measure them) have fallen slightly in 1996, they have remained broadly stable since 1992, when the downward shift in inflation began, see Chart 4. The increase in the 1993 chart is probably due to the fact that the entire import price effect resulting from the depreciation of the krona could not be distinguished. Domestically generated price developments have also been temporarily affected by increased indirect taxes and the tapering of subsidies as a result of fiscal consolidation. This means that domestically generated inflation, measured in this way, has been trend-wise for several years around 2 percent. For inflation to move, upwards or downwards, from this two per cent level, it is necessary either to increase or decrease inflation expectations or to bring resource utilisation in the economy below or rising above the long-term sustainable level or through a combination of the two. Let me first turn to the role of inflation expectations. In general, it can be said that the longer inflation has developed in line with the target, the greater the likelihood that more and more of the economy's players will have confidence that this will continue to apply in the future. Expected inflation is ultimately about confidence in economic policy and its consistency. The completion of the consolidation programme is therefore of the utmost importance. Wage formation also plays a role. Lower wage increases also increase the conditions for reconciling low inflation with a decline in unemployment. Of course, the design of monetary policy also has an impact on the picture of expectations in the economy. After all, inflation is ultimately a monetary issue. With regard to the development of demand in the economy, activity appears to have developed weakly in the first quarter of 1996. Several economic analysts have also revised down their forecasts for 1996. The changed view of the outlook for the current year has been relatively rapid. This has been due to, among other things, declining international demand. As recently as December, for example, the united states were counting the The NIER with growth of around 2% this year and next, and with a gradual increase in inflation to the upper end of the tolerance range surrounding the inflation target over the course of 1997. Roughly speaking, one can speak of two options for development in the future. A main alternative where activity in the Swedish economy gradually starts to increase again over the course of 1996 and a side option where the recovery process becomes more protracted and perhaps weaker. Let me discuss these two options. In the main option, the continued favourable development in the US and the upturn in the Japanese economy contribute to a gradual strengthening of activity in Europe. As a result of low inflation in Europe, monetary policy has eased. This, together with lower long-term interest rates, has a stimulating effect on the economies in our immediate area. Stronger growth in Europe and in the world economy as a whole benefits Swedish export companies. Investments in inventories account for a not insignificant part of the economic fluctuations. Figure 5 shows the evolution of GDP and final demand. In upturn phases, production tends to rise faster than demand, which also happened in connection with the recent upturn. The reason is that companies generally do not want to end up in a situation where they cannot deliver when demand is increasing rapidly. Conversely, overstocking occurs when demand is dampened. The subsequent adjustment of stocks weakens production beyond final demand. The development of information technology has meant that companies have made material handling more efficient. There is often talk of Just-in-Time, which means that inputs are delivered exactly when they are needed in production. Nevertheless, it is not uncommon for there to be greater negative as well as positive bearing contributions to the development of total production over time. An improved international economy can reduce the contractive effect of the inventory cycle on the economy that one would normally otherwise expect at this stage of the business cycle. Corresponding periods of inventory adjustments at about the same time in the economic cycle also occurred in both the 1970s and 1980s. The underlying conditions for continued expansion in business in Sweden are otherwise favorable, with continued good profitability and extensive investment activity. Even in the case of private consumption, there may be conditions for a cautious recovery. Real household income can be expected to increase in 1996 and 1997, despite budgetary consolidation. Even their balance sheets are stronger than they have been for many years. There should also be a pent-up need to renew durable capital goods. Households have become more positive about the development of their own economy if account is taken of the methodological change that EU harmonisation has meant for Statistics Sweden's survey. The balance figures, which hovered around zero in the autumn of last year, have become more positive after the turn of the year, according to the old method. It turns out that people over the age of 64, who are now also included in the sample, are more pessimistic in their responses than people aged between 16 and 64, who made up the old sample. Turnover in retail trade developed slightly in the period January to February compared with the corresponding period last year, but increased slightly compared with the last months of last year. On the other hand, car sales appear to be weak. Thus, there are some signs of some improvement in the outlook of households and the development of private consumption. However, it is too early to draw any more definite conclusions from this information. However, as always in the case of slowdown phases, there is no lack of risk factors for a weaker development. Therefore, one could speak of a side option. A weaker European economy leads to a weaker export trend and a greater adjustment of inventories. This, in turn, could have repercussions on the domestic economy if the labour market is negatively affected and household confidence weakens. Moreover, it cannot be ruled out that wage increases provoke rationalisation in domestically oriented sectors and affect unemployment. Against this background, what assessment can be made of the inflation outlook in 1996 and 1997? Demand-side inflation risks should be assessed as limited. This is also true in the main option. Indications of some increase in potential growth rates compared to the 1970s and 1980s as well as some signs of a decline in the propensity to inflation in the economy are behind this conclusion. However, a further adjustment of wage formation is necessary in a medium-term perspective. In the side option, the demand-side inflation risks should be less than in the main option. Given low inflation expectations and confidence in economic policy, the conditions thus remain good for inflation in line with the target in the coming years. The way forward monetary policy In general, it can be said that monetary policy can have a neutral, expansionary or contractual approach. A neutral monetary policy is appropriate as expected inflation is low, capacity utilisation is normal and, consequently, the likelihood of meeting the inflation target in the future is good. A contractive policy is appropriate as inflation risks accelerating, while a certain expansionary orientation is possible if the expected inflation is low and resource utilisation in the economy is low or falling, as the probability then increases that the inflation target will be undercut. Determining what is a neutral, contractive or expan-sive monetary policy is not straightforward. For a small open economy, of the Swedish type, it is important to look at both the interest rate and the exchange rate when assessing the overall monetary conditions. Provided that the krona's exchange rate is in the process of adjusting to its equilibrium level, it should at present be possible to describe monetary conditions in Sweden as broadly neutral. The short-term Treasury bill rate is currently in the range of 6 to 6.5 percent. It varies a bit depending on maturities and whether you use simple or effective annual interest. Inflation in the last twelve-month period was just under 2 per cent. This would roughly estimate the short-term real market rate at around 4.5%. The experience of the last 15 years shows that such a level of short-term real market interest rates is slightly above the historically international average level. In Germany and the UNITED STATES, for example, the average since the early 1980s and until today has been around 4 percent. However, the corresponding average in Sweden has been slightly higher, just over 4.5 percent, which is probably due to difficulties with confidence in the low-inflation regime that the fixed exchange rate policy required. A G-10 study has shown that the real interest rate on bonds in the industrial world has increased by about one percentage point from 3 to about 4 percent since the 1960s. An important reason is a reduction in global savings due to public deficit problems in many industrialised countries. Another reason is that the abolition of administrative regulations meant an international adjustment from the artificially low levels that the previous regulations gave rise to. For example, negative real interest rates were not uncommon in the 1970s. Thus, it is difficult to calculate historical average real interest rates over longer periods of time. The development of the average real interest rate in the future depends, among other things, on confidence in the economic policies of different countries and the global balance between savings and investment. This means that the historically measured average does not necessarily have to be what will continue to apply in the future. As a result of central banks' monetary policy, the short-term real interest rate tends to fluctuate around its average, see Chart 6. The U.S. real interest rate was between 6 and 7 percent in the first half of the 1980s. At times, the levels were even higher. In Germany, too, real interest rates were high at the start of the 1980s, but then fell. In the late 1980s, monetary policy tightened. In the US, the real interest rate came up to 5 percent and in Germany to 6 percent. As inflationary pressures eased in the early 1990s, these countries again pursued a lighter monetary policy. In the US, the short-term real interest rate bottomed out around 0 percent, which was a very low level, and was raised starting in the spring of 1994 to around 3 percent, where it is now located. In Germany, the short-term real interest rate has been reduced from the end of 1992 to around 2%. As I stressed earlier, it is important also to look at the development of the exchange rate when analysing the overall monetary conditions. It turns out that countries that have had stronger exchange rate developments often have lower short-term real interest rates than countries with a weaker exchange rate. This is one of several explanations for the fact that continental European countries, for example, now have lower short-term real interest rates than other countries. Germany's real effective exchange rate, for example, has appreciated relatively strongly in recent years. What conclusions can be drawn about monetary policy going forward in Sweden in the light of this discussion and of the Riksbank's view of the inflation outlook? Regardless of which of the two real economic alternatives will prove to be the most likely in the future, the Riksbank believes that there may still be some room for cuts in the repo rate. However, the degree of space will depend on the materialisation of the real economic option, the resulting inflation outlook and confidence in economic policy. The Riksbank will therefore closely monitor developments.

Title: Current monetary policy
text: Current monetary policy Date: 1997-05-15 Speaker: Governor Urban Be4ckstrf6m Location: Finance Committee Thank you for the invitation to discuss developments in the Swedish economy and current monetary policy here in committee. In my introduction today, I will mainly touch on the following five areas, see Figure 1: The Swedish economy is showing new patterns, which may be signs of a better functioning economy, a persistently higher production potential and a lower propensity for inflation. The improvement in the Swedish economy continued in 1996. Although an adjustment in inventories temporarily reduced total production, final demand was kept up well. Most indications are now that growth is once again on the verge of picking up. The recovery in employment is slow, despite the fact that total output has recovered from the fall in the early 1990s and is now at a higher level than in the previous peak year of 1990. It's an indication that a lot of unemployment is structural - not cyclical. We still have higher long-term interest rates compared to other countries in continental Europe and the krona has weakened in recent months. These are signs that confidence in Swedish economic policy in general must continue to improve. The Riksbank currently sees no need to change the repo rate. With last year's repo rate cuts in combination with the krona's development, the recovery in the economy is supported. With the information available today, inflation seems to be under control. Improved economy and low inflation Overall, growth since the turnaround in the summer of 1993 has been higher than we were used to in the inflation years of the 1970s and 1980s. The upturn in industrial output has been the largest since the early 1960s. At the same time, inflation has been the lowest in decades. It is likely that the low inflation itself has contributed to a better functioning economy. Growth and demand in the economy are perceived as more sustainable, which, together with the fact that price signals become clearer, makes it easier for households and companies to plan and make decisions. Tax reform, various deregulations and changes in social security systems have also improved the functioning of the economy. EU membership and the globalisation of trade in general have increased competitive pressure. The results manifest themselves in the form of a higher rate of capital formation and a structural transformation of the economy. The product composition of foreign trade has received more of high-tech elements and inroads are being made in fast-growing markets. In 1996, total final demand increased by 2.1%. During the second half of the year, there was an acceleration and the rate of increase was 2.6 percent, compared with the corresponding period a year earlier. The contribution to total final demand was as great from domestic demand as from foreign trade. This means that the two-pronged character that the Swedish economy has shown in recent years slowed down last year. However, GDP did not grow at the same rate as total final demand, which was due to companies choosing to reduce their inventories. GDP - which reflects total output - rose by only 1.1% in 1996. As a result, resource utilization in the economy declined. In addition, inflation expectations declined. This markedly improved the inflation outlook for 1997 and 1998, which was the reason why the Riksbank lowered its repo rate by almost 5 percentage points. In connection with the Finance Committee's hearings in May and November, I discussed the ongoing inventory adjustment. It is not uncommon for companies to trim their inventories at this stage of the economic cycle. The same thing happened at about the same time in the 1970s and 1980s. This is due to the fact that companies normally produce more than what is demanded in upturn phases. The reason is that companies do not want to end up in situations where they cannot deliver when demand is increasing rapidly. Gradually, they discover that the inventory build-up has gone too far and then begin an adaptation process. Then a reverse effect occurs, production increases more slowly than the final demand in the economy. An inventory adjustment can in some cases be the beginning of a deeper economic downturn. This can happen, for example, if the adjustment of inventories is extensive and has spill-over effects to private consumption or if it has negative repercussions on the labour market and on households' confidence in the future. The Riksbank was therefore vigilant about the risk of a weaker development in private consumption during the spring and summer of last year. If this had happened, the inflation outlook would have been further dampened. However, private consumption continued to grow during the summer and also strengthened slightly in the autumn. As the adjustment of inventories in the Swedish economy slows down, demand will again lead to a gradual increase in production. Most indications are that growth is now well on its way to rising. Over the course of 1996, inflation rates slowed down, see Chart 1. The starting point for the ongoing growth phase in the Swedish economy is thus more favorable than in a very long time. However, the moderation in consumer prices was significantly strengthened by the Riksbank's interest rate cuts, as they contributed to a fall in interest costs for homeowners. Monetary policy should not, of course, react to a temporary decline or rise in inflation that is due to the Riksbank's own interest rate changes, whether it is about interest rate cuts or interest rate hikes. It would be like chasing your own tail. Normally, the tolerance range of the price stability objective should be sufficient to absorb temporary effects. However, the drop in interest rates last year was large, as many factors fell into place. The weak price development so far in 1997 is also mainly due to last year's interest rate cuts. However, the methodological change that Statistics Sweden announced at the beginning of May means that the decline in interest costs for own homes has previously been exaggerated in the calculations. However, these changes do not affect the Riksbank's analysis of underlying inflation. Continued high unemployment Although the Swedish economy seems to be working better on many levels, however, it does not yet seem to apply to the labour market. Despite favourable developments for the economy as a whole, unemployment remains at a high level and employment has largely stagnated. Figure 2 shows what might be called the employment gap. The graph shows that total output recovered from the fall in the early 1990s and is now at a higher level than in the previous peak year of 1990. Yet employment, measured by the number of people, remains at a very low level - the lowest since 1974. This suggests that a lot of unemployment is structural in the sense that it risks staying at a high level even if the economy improves, unless the structure of the economy changes. Estimating structural unemployment is no easy task. An independent assessor such as the OECD concluded in the latest Sweden report that structural unemployment is between 6 and 7 percent, expressed as open unemployment. Other economists have come to roughly the same conclusion, or possibly to a slightly lower level. Most of the evidence suggests that structural unemployment has risen, although it is not possible to be sure of the exact level. Structural unemployment cannot be reduced by traditional demand policy, whether monetary or fiscal. An expansionary economic policy - which seeks to drive demand that is not compatible with what the economy can sustainably produce - would, over time, even risk exacerbating the situation in the labour market. Inflation would increase, the economy would function worse and setbacks would occur. It is not only in Sweden that unemployment is high. This is something that characterises virtually the entire EU area. Moreover, European unemployment has remained at a high level for much of the 1980s. In the U.S., on the other hand, unemployment has hovered around 6 percent over the past 25 years without showing an upward trend. The direct cause of the differences between the EU and the US is that employment has increased significantly faster on the other side of the Atlantic. In the US, employment has risen by just over 60% over the past 25 years, while the corresponding figure for the EU is just under 15%. However, there are positive examples in Europe. The Netherlands is one of the few European countries that has managed to reverse the employment curve from the mid-1980s. After a long period of stagnation, employment has risen by 25% since the mid-1980s. Unemployment in the Netherlands has largely halved from 12% to just over 6% in 10 years. It is important to note that there has not been much difference in GDP growth between the US, the EU and the Netherlands, see Figure 3. Nevertheless, employment developments have been markedly different. Thus, it is not a higher demand due to a more expansionary monetary and fiscal policy that can explain the fact that so many new jobs have been created in the United States or during the last ten years also in the Netherlands. The labour market, like the economy at large, is characterised by rapid transformation. Technological development is rapid and manual work is being replaced by machines. The number of people employed in industry is decreasing, or at best stagnating in developed countries. Recently, the same trend is also visible in new industrialized countries that have come a long way in development. In addition, competition from countries with significantly lower wage levels is increasing. This is a development that places great demands on the labour market and wage formation to work well. Although good real wage growth is desirable in the long term, it is a fact that low average real wage growth seems to slow down the process of eliminating existing jobs and tends to stimulate the creation of new jobs. Average real wages in the US have increased by 15% overall since 1970, while they have risen by as much as 60% in the EU, see Figures 4 and 5. The trend in employment, as I have just said, has been reversed; A 60 percent increase in the U.S. versus 15 percent in Europe. The deceleration of real wage growth also appears to be an important factor in the creation of new jobs in the Netherlands, as do some other changes. In the U.S., increased wage dispersion has contributed to a rapidly emerging private services sector. A particular problem in the European labour market is that it does not appear that an increase in unemployment will lead to wage demands being held back. One possible explanation could be that the unemployed in practice have a very limited influence in wage negotiations. Instead of a restrained rate of wage growth with lower costs for companies and the possibility of an increased number of employees, wage increases remain high and unemployment high. We have been able to take note of statements from representatives of the social partners that indicate that in Sweden, too, it is increased real wages that are given priority rather than increased employment. Weak employment growth and persistent unemployment are signs of a poorly functioning labour market, and these problems, in turn, are mainly due to wage formation - because price formation is the central market mechanism. However one looks at the causes of high unemployment, the functioning of the labour market plays an important role in reversing the trend. Room for confidence improvement Chart 6 shows interest rate developments in recent years. Long-term interest rates fell by 1.75 percentage points in 1996, causing the interest margin vis-e0-vis Germany to shrink from 250 to 90 basis points. Short-term interest rates fell even more - from just under 9 percent down to under 4 percent. This decline was mainly an expression of the cuts in the repo rate implemented by the Riksbank. Last year, the repo rate came down to 4.1 percent, which is the lowest level of the policy rate since the early 1960s. The krona's share price was largely unchanged for the year as a whole. All in all, this meant a tangible easing of monetary policy. It is clear that many pieces need to be put in place if it is to be possible to implement such rate cuts. During the beginning of 1997, the repo rate remained unchanged, but at the same time the krona has weakened by between 4 and 5 percent, Chart 7. As a result, the economy has been further stimulated. But given that it will take time for monetary policy to take full effect, it is likely that a lot of the results of the development of interest rates and the krona are still ahead of us. The weakening of the krona and the higher long-term interest rate compared to Germany and the rest of continental Europe, see Chart 8, say something about confidence in economic policy in general. Looking at the longer term, financial market conditions can be seen as a gauge of this confidence. These are signs that Swedish decision-makers must continue to convince various actors in Sweden and in the rest of the world of the will and ability to pursue a stability-oriented economic policy in the long term. Even if public finances develop in the right direction and may even, if things go well, show a surplus in a few years' time, the structure of fiscal policy must also take into account demand developments. An improvement in government finances due to favourable cyclical developments does not allow for fiscally expansionary measures. I can understand if my comments in this area can be perceived as premature, given the low inflation in recent years and in the light of the favourable inflation assessments generally made for 1997 and 1998. But in the economic policy of the next few years, we sow the seeds of the economic development that we will see at the beginning of the next century. Experience shows that stable economic development with low inflation pays better dividends than economic policy stimulus that comes at the wrong stage. The way forward monetary policy In the latest inflation report published by the Riksbank in March, GDP growth was estimated to be 2 and 3 per cent, respectively, for 1997 and 1998. Furthermore, it was stressed that no more significant capacity constraints should arise during the period. Given that households and firms continue to expect continued low inflation, domestic underlying inflation (as measured by the Consumer Price Index) was assessed development adjusted for temporary effects on inflation) will be between 1.5 and 2 per cent in one to two years with unchanged monetary policy. Developments in the economy so far seem to essentially confirm the picture presented in the latest Inflation Report. Various forward-looking indicators suggest that the Swedish economy is once again facing a period of increased output growth. At the same time, most indications are continued low price rises this year and next, which is the period that we are looking at today. The repo rate was last lowered in December last year. Since then, we have often said that monetary policy is well balanced. This is still true. The Riksbank currently sees no need to change the repo rate.

Efterhand som lageranpassningen i svensk ekonomi avtar kommer efterfrgan ter att leda till en successivt kad produktion. Det mesta tyder p att tillvxten nu r p god vg att stiga. Under loppet av 1996 dmpades inflationstakten, se diagram 1. Utgngslget fr den pgende tillvxtfasen i svensk ekonomi r drmed gynnsammare n p mycket lnge. Dmpningen av konsumentpriserna frstrktes dock ptagligt av Riksbankens rntesnkningar, genom att de bidrog till att rntekostnaderna sjnk fr egnahemsgare. Penningpolitiken br sjlvfallet inte reagera p en tillfllig nedgng eller uppgng i inflationen som beror p Riksbankens egna rntefrndringar, vare sig det handlar om rntesnkningar eller rntehjningar. Det vore som att jaga sin egen svans. Normalt br prisstabilitetsmlets toleransintervall rcka till fr att kunna absorbera temporra effekter. Rntenedgngen frra ret blev dock stor, till fljd av att mnga faktorer fll p plats. Den svaga prisutvecklingen hittills under 1997 beror ocks i huvudsak p att frra rets rntesnkningar. Den metodfrndring som SCB aviserade i brjan av maj innebr dock att nedgngen i rntekostnaderna fr egna hem tidigare verdrivits i berkningarna. Dessa ndringar pverkar dock inte Riksbankens analys av den underliggande inflationen. Fortsatt hg arbetslshet ven om svensk ekonomi tycks fungera bttre p mnga plan frefaller det dock nnu inte glla arbetsmarknaden. Trots en gynnsam utveckling fr ekonomin i stort ligger arbetslsheten kvar p en hg niv och sysselsttningen har i stort sett stagnerat. Diagram 2 visar vad man skulle kunna kalla sysselsttningsgapet. Diagrammet visar att totalproduktionen terhmtat fallet frn nedgngen i brjan av 1990-talet och nu ligger p en hgre niv n vid det tidigare toppret 1990. nd ligger sysselsttningen, mtt i antalet personer, kvar p en mycket lg niv - den lgsta sedan 1974. Det antyder att en hel del av arbetslsheten r strukturell i den meningen att den riskerar att stanna p en hg niv ven om konjunkturen frbttras, svitt inte ekonomins struktur ndras. Att skatta den strukturella arbetslsheten r ingen enkel uppgift. En oberoende bedmare som OECD kom i den senaste Sverigerapporten fram till att den strukturella arbetslsheten ligger mellan 6 och 7 procent, uttryckt som ppen arbetslshet. En strukturell arbetslshet kan inte reduceras med traditionell efterfrgepolitik, vare sig det gller penning- eller finanspolitik. Den europeiska arbetslsheten har dessutom legat p en hg niv under en stor del av 1980-talet. I USA har dremot arbetslsheten pendlat kring 6 procent under de senaste 25 ren utan att visa ngon trend uppt. Den direkta orsaken till skillnaderna mellan EU och USA r att sysselsttningen kat vsentligt snabbare p andra sidan Atlanten. I USA har sysselsttningen stigit med drygt 60 procent under de senaste dryga 25 ren, medan motsvarande siffra fr EU r knappt 15 procent. Det finns dock positiva exempel i Europa. Nederlnderna r ett av f europeiska lnder som lyckats vnda sysselsttningskurvan frn mitten av 1980-talet. Efter en lng tids stagnation har sysselsttningen stigit med 25 procent sedan mitten av 1980-talet. Arbetslsheten har i Nederlnderna i stort sett halverats frn 12 till drygt 6 procent p 10 r. Det r viktigt att konstatera att det inte rtt ngon strre skillnad i BNP-tillvxt mellan USA, EU och Nederlnderna, se diagram 3. nd har sysselsttningsutvecklingen varit markant annorlunda. Det r sledes inte en hgre efterfrgan beroende p en mer expansiv penning- och finanspolitik som kan frklara att det skapats s mnga nya jobb i USA eller under den senaste tiorsperioden ven i Nederlnderna. Dessutom kar konkurrensen frn lnder med betydligt lgre lneniv. De genomsnittliga reallnerna har i USA totalt sett kat med 15 procent sedan 1970, medan de stigit med hela 60 procent i EU, se diagram 4 och 5. Utvecklingen fr sysselsttningen, har som jag nyss sade, varit den omvnda; 60 procents kning i USA mot 15 procent i Europa. Uppbromsningen av reallneutvecklingen tycks ocks vara en viktig faktor bakom tillkomsten av nya jobb i Nederlnderna, liksom ven en del andra frndringar. I USA har en kad lnespridning bidragit till en snabbt framvxande privat tjnstesektor. Ett srskilt problem p den europeiska arbetsmarknaden r att det inte verkar som om en kning av arbetslsheten leder till att lnekraven hlls tillbaka. En mjlig frklaring kan vara att de arbetslsa i praktiken har ett mycket begrnsat inflytande i lnefrhandlingarna. Istllet fr en terhllen lnekningstakt med lgre kostnader fr fretagen och mjligheten till ett kat antal anstllda, frblir lnekningarna hga och arbetslsheten hg. Vi har kunnat ta del av uttalanden frn representanter fr arbetsmarknadens parter som tyder p att det ocks i Sverige snarare r kade reallner som prioriteras n kad sysselsttning. En svag sysselsttningsutveckling och en varaktig arbetslshet r tecken p en dligt fungerande arbetsmarknad och dessa problem har i sin tur sin grund framfr allt i lnebildningen - eftersom just prisbildningen r den centrala marknadsmekanismen. Hur man n ser p orsakerna till den hga arbetslsheten spelar arbetsmarknadens funktionsstt en viktig roll fr mjligheterna att vnda utvecklingen. Utrymme fr frtroendefrbttring Diagram 6 visar rnteutvecklingen under senare r. Den lnga rntan fll med 1,75 procentenheter under 1996, vilket ledde till att rntemarginalen gentemot Tyskland krympte ihop frn 250 till 90 rntepunkter. De korta rntorna fll nnu mer - frn strax under 9 procent ned till under 4 procent. Denna nedgng var frmst ett uttryck fr de snkningar av reporntan som Riksbanken genomfrde. Reporntan kom under frra ret ned till 4,1 procent, vilket r den lgsta nivn p styrrntan sedan brjan av 1960-talet. Kronans kurs var i stort sett ofrndrad fr ret som helhet. Sammantaget innebar detta en ptaglig lttnad av penningpolitiken. Det r uppenbart att mnga bitar mste komma p plats fr att det skall vara mjligt att genomfra sdana rntesnkningar. Under inledningen av 1997 har reporntan hllits ofrndrad, men samtidigt har kronan frsvagats med mellan 4 och 5 procent, diagram 7. Drmed har ekonomin stimulerats ytterligare. Men tanke p att det tar tid innan penningpolitiken fr full effekt r det sannolikt att en hel del av resultaten av rntans och kronans utveckling nnu ligger framfr oss. Frsvagningen av kronan och den hgre lnga rntan jmfrt med Tyskland och vriga kontinentaleuropa, se diagram 8, sger ngonting om frtroendet fr den ekonomiska politiken i stort. Sett i ett lngre perspektiv kan frhllandena p de finansiella marknaderna ses som en mtare p detta frtroende. Detta r tecken p att svenska beslutsfattare mste fortstta att vertyga olika aktrer i Sverige och i omvrlden om viljan och frmgan att lngsiktigt bedriva en stabilitetsinriktad ekonomisk politik. ven om statsfinanserna utvecklas i rtt riktning och rentav kan, om utvecklingen gr vl, komma att visa verskott om ngra r s mste finanspolitikens upplggning ta hnsyn ocks till efterfrgeutvecklingen. En frbttring av statsfinanserna som beror p en gynnsam konjunkturutveckling ger inte utrymme fr finanspolitiskt expansiva tgrder. Jag kan frst om mina kommentarer p detta omrde kan upplevas komma i frtid, med tanke p den lga inflationen under senare r och mot bakgrund av de gynnsamma inflationsbedmningar som allmnt grs fr 1997 och 1998. Men i de nrmaste rens ekonomiska politik sr vi fret till den ekonomiska utveckling som vi kommer att se i brjan av nsta sekel. Erfarenheten visar att en stabil ekonomisk utveckling med lg inflation ger bttre utdelning n ekonomisk-politiska stimulanstgrder som kommer i fel fas. Olika framtblickande indikatorer talar fr att den svenska ekonomin ter str infr en period av kad produktionstillvxt. Samtidigt tyder det mesta p fortsatt lga prisstegringar i r och nsta r, vilket r den period som vi idag verblickar. Reporntan snktes senast i december frra ret. Title: The Swedish economy
text: The Swedish economy Date: 1997-05-14 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Be4ckstrf6m Location: Ske5nska sparbanksff6reningen Let me start by thanking you for the invitation to come to Ske5ne and talk about the Swedish economy. I intend to paint with slightly broader brushstrokes to give perspective to developments in our country in recent years, but I will also comment in conclusion on current monetary policy. Positive development in recent years Much is positive in the Swedish economy. In my opinion, there is a clear possibility that in future we will be able to avoid the economic problems that have recurred several times in recent decades and which, in the early 1990s, led to a deep crisis. Since the summer of 1993, GDP growth has been about 2.8% annual, which is significantly higher than the average growth rate we have been accustomed to over the past 25 years. Similarly, the surpluses in our business with foreign countries are larger than in a very long time, which means that we amortize the external debt. Investment has remained at a favourable level and government deficits have gradually decreased. Inflation has not been so low for decades. An important reason for this is that the Riksbank has lowered the repo rate and that this has reduced housing interest rates, which in turn has a temporary dampening effect on inflation. Although the underlying price development is not as low as the actual KPIs figures suggest, inflation appears to be under control. If we in Sweden continue to pursue a disciplined fiscal and monetary policy and also otherwise build confidence in economic policy, most of the evidence suggests that growth will gradually strengthen without inflation picking up. We now have good opportunities to reconnect with the tradition of price stability that existed before the 1970s and 1980s in Sweden. Tradition of stability 1830 marked the beginning of a long period of price stability. Then the Riksdag decided that Sweden should switch to the silver standard, after a period of high inflation. After the silver standard, gold came to play a prominent role from 1863. During the following more than 100 years, Sweden, with shorter interruptions, mainly caused by the First and Second World Wars, had the value of the currency tied to gold. This was also true under the so-called Bretton Woods system until the early 1970s. Formally, the value of the krona was pegged to that of the US dollar, but its value, in turn, was based on the development of the price of gold. From 1830 until 1960, annual inflation averaged just under 2 percent. With the exception of war periods and the 1970s and 80s, price stability has been the rule for the past 100 years or so. There is therefore good reason to speak of a Swedish tradition. The fact that the stable value of money has not been an obstacle to economic development is illustrated by the fact that Sweden from the mid-1800s until the end of the 1960s was among the countries in the world that grew the fastest. Rather, the low inflation and stability it represented should have contributed to the favourable development. Not least the decades after the Second World War were characterized by high growth, low inflation, a balance in business with foreign countries and a belief in the future that led to a gradual expansion of the Swedish economy. It was a favorable period with stable and good economic development and with rising living standards. The crisis of the 1990s and its roots After the collapse of the Bretton Woods system in the early 1970s, it proved difficult to establish a fixed exchange rate regime with a corresponding statute. There was no longer a clear "anchor" for economic policy as a whole or for wage formation. Devaluation cycles followed each other, fiscal policy was expansionary, wage formation worked poorly, structural problems built up and the deregulation of the financial sector made the problems obvious. Swedish growth weakened during the 1970s and 1980s in relation to developments in other countries. Nevertheless, the economy overheated, which, together with the expansion of public activities, temporarily held back unemployment. The development was not sustainable. An inflationary and speculative bubble cannot be as big as it gets. Sooner or later it cracks. Similarly, the scope for additional publicly funded employment was limited. Towards the end of the 1980s, the Swedish economy was in need of structural changes. The development led to a deep crisis in the early 1990s. Over three years, output decreased by around 5 per cent. The open unemployment rate rose to nearly 9 percent. At the same time, general government finances weakened and the budget deficit peaked at just over 12 per cent of GDP. We also experienced severe problems in the banking sector. The downturn was far deeper than anyone imagined, largely as a result of the fact that imbalances in the economy had to build up for so long and that the changes coincided with weak international development. Reorienting economic policy The 1970s and 1980s are an illustration of how an inflationary period leads to an uncertain and unstable economic environment. Inflation often also leads to a speculative climate and to short-term economic thinking. Step by step, in this way, long-term production conditions deteriorate. High and rising inflation is due to households and firms becoming accustomed to ever-rising prices, as well as underlying tensions between demand and the productive capacity of the economy. Such a development requires measures to avoid setbacks in economic development. If economic policy reacts too late to various warning signs - as was the case in the second half of the 1980s - tensions have time to become high and negative repercussions on growth and employment threaten. This is the grim experience we have experienced after the longest inflationary period in Swedish history since the 1830s. An economic policy geared towards low and stable inflation cannot prevent cyclical fluctuations. On the other hand, such a policy can contribute to a more sustainable development. Experience also suggests that production will increase over time, as a more stable environment facilitates the financial planning of households and businesses and stimulates productive investment. It was against this background, among other things, that Swedish economic policy was changed in the shift between the 1980s and 1990s. The focus on price stability has gradually gained broad support in Swedish society and among political parties in the Swedish Parliament. 60 percent of Swedes think it is right to have 2 percent inflation as a target for monetary policy, while only 12 percent are negative. The Riksdag has stated that there is general support for the value of price stability and that such a focus provides the conditions for growth and employment. The government has explicitly supported the Riksbank's target of 2 per cent inflation. However, the severe economic problems at the start of the 1990s, memories of the inflationary years and the large budget deficits made it difficult to quickly establish credibility for the new economic policy line. This has been shown from time to time, among other things, in the form of turbulence in the interest rate and currency markets and excessive wage increases. Developments in the financial markets can, in the slightly longer term, be seen as a gauge of the confidence that exists in the will and ability to pursue a consistent and stability-oriented economic policy. Experience from other countries shows that it takes time and effort to build confidence in a low-inflation regime. Keeping inflation low and the state's finances in order is a process that never ends if the aim is to have low interest rates and a stable currency, which in the long run is a prerequisite for growth and employment. Decisive policies deliver results After the crown began to float in the fall of 1992, it weakened significantly. The depreciation, as is usually said when the exchange rate is variable, gave a strong demand impulse to primarily the export-oriented sectors of our country. The result was not long in coming. For a couple of years, we had one of the strongest upturns in the industrial economy that Sweden has experienced since the early 1960s. Short-term and long-term market interest rates fell, which contributed to other parts of Swedish business being able to increase their production as well. However, this happened to a much lesser extent than in the sectors that benefited from the weak krona. The economy was divided into two parts, but the growth figures overall were probably stronger than many noted. Credit losses declined and the banking sector emerged from the crisis. In the first half of 1994, there was growing concern that the old pattern would once again make itself felt. Fiscal consolidation was insufficient. Inflationary tendencies began to emerge. Would the economic upturn once again be allowed to result in an inflation bubble? In other words, would we have a repeat and a continuation of what regularly happened in the 1970s and 1980s, with the risk of subsequent setbacks for growth and employment? During the summer of 1994, more and more people began to expect rising inflation again. The long-term interest rate rose in the spring from just below 7 to almost 12 percent and the krona's share price continued to weaken as a confirmation of inflation uncertainty. The pass-through of increases in import prices at the consumer price level began to increase. In addition, inflationary pressures in industry became more pronounced. Cost awareness waned and the likelihood of a difficult collective bargaining process increased. (Something that we also got when agreements were signed in the spring of 1995 at a far too high level). In other words, more and more elements of the patterns of the 1970s and 1980s could be discerned. In this situation, a passive economic policy would have confirmed the fears and could have meant a continuation in the old rut. Economic policy was thus at a crossroads. It was either a question of confirming past patterns or of consistently pursuing a stability-oriented policy and breaking with the old experience. The government, the Riksdag and the Riksbank chose to show determination. Central government finances were cleaned up and monetary policy tightened. This gradually increased the likelihood that the old pattern would not be repeated. Inflation remained at a low level and confidence increased step by step that this would also be the case for a long time to come. It is the stronger government finances and the break with the history of inflation, which have been behind the lower market interest rates in recent years. The starting point for the future is therefore different and better now compared to the corresponding phases of the economic cycle in the 1970s and 1980s. The interest rate policy of recent years is a clear illustration of how monetary policy works with a price stability objective under a floating exchange rate regime. The more negative inflation forecasts generally made in mid-1994 meant that it was necessary to start a period of increases in the key interest rate. The sooner monetary policy reacts, the less interest rates need to be raised. Now that the inflation outlook has improved, the repo rate has been lowered. In simple terms, the reasons for the easing of interest rate policy in 1996 were the favourable outlook for inflation in the future. Continuous falls in inflation expectations as well as subdued demand conditions gradually improved the inflation outlook for 1997 and 1998. The repo rate was lowered from 8.91% to 4.1% in 1996. This is the lowest level of the policy rate in over 30 years. If the price stability objective is met, there is a basis for stable and sustainable growth and employment. If there is confidence in low inflation policy, there is also room for monetary policy to contribute in the short term to supporting the recovery in the Swedish economy. Conclusion My message here today has been essentially positive. There are many good signs in the Swedish economy. Step by step, we are returning to the low-inflation regime that for so long was characteristic of the development of our country and which formed a stable base for growth and employment. However, we have not reached the final destination. For example, we still have higher long-term interest rates compared to the countries of continental Europe and the krona has weakened in recent months. This continues to place high demands on discipline in economic policy. There is one circumstance that is less bright in the development of recent years. This is the continuing high unemployment rate. The recovery in employment has so far been very slow, despite a rather favourable economic climate in recent years. Most of the evidence suggests that structural unemployment has arisen, which means that unemployment risks remaining high even if the economy improves, unless nothing is done. This, in turn, is a sign of a poorly functioning labour market, which is partly due to wage formation - because price formation is the central market mechanism. If a large proportion of unemployment is structural, measures should be aimed precisely at bringing down structural unemployment. However, it is something that is beyond the reach of demand policy, i.e. monetary and fiscal policy. What monetary policy can do is to try to keep low and stable inflation and thus indirectly contribute to stable growth. The Swedish economy seems to be once again facing a period of increased growth. By all accounts, there are also spare resources in the economy, which means that there should be no decisive capacity constraints in the near future. Moreover, if households and firms continue to expect low inflation when making their economic decisions, most indications are that price rises will remain low in 1997 and 1998, which is the period we are currently looking at. The repo rate was last lowered in December last year. Since then, we have often said that monetary policy is well balanced. It's the same message I have today. Developments in the economy seem to mainly confirm the picture that the Riksbank presented in the latest Inflation Report. Thus, we currently see no need to change the repo rate.

Samtidigt frsvagades de offentliga finanserna och budgetunderskottet uppgick till som mest drygt 12 procent av BNP. Vi fick ocks uppleva svra problem i banksektorn. Nedgngen kom att bli lngt djupare n vad ngon frestllt sig, mycket till fljd av att obalanserna i ekonomin ftt byggas upp under s lng tid och att frndringarna sammanfll med en svag internationell utveckling. En hg och stigande inflation beror p att hushll och fretag har vant sig vid stndigt stigande priser samt p underliggande spnningar mellan efterfrgan och ekonomins produktionsfrmga. Erfarenheten talar ven fr att produktionen ver tiden blir hgre, eftersom en stabilare milj underlttar hushllens och fretagens ekonomiska planering och stimulerar produktiva investeringar. Det var bl.a. mot denna bakgrund som svensk ekonomisk politik lades om i skiftet mellan 1980- och 1990-talen. Inriktningen p prisstabilitet har efter hand ftt ett brett std i det svenska samhllet och bland politiska partier i Sveriges riksdag. 60 procent av svenskarna tycker att det r riktigt att ha 2 procents inflation som ml fr penningpolitiken, medan bara 12 procent r negativa. Regeringen har uttryckligen stllt sig bakom Riksbankens ml om 2 procents inflation. De svra ekonomiska problemen vid 1990-talets inledning, minnen frn inflationsren och de stora budgetunderskotten gjorde det dock svrt att snabbt skapa trovrdighet fr den nya ekonomisk-politiska linjen. Det har frn tid till annan visat sig bl.a. i form av turbulens p rnte- och valutamarknaderna och fr hga lnekningar. Utvecklingen p de finansiella marknaderna kan p lite lngre sikt ses som en mtare p den tilltro som finns till viljan och frmgan att fra en konsistent och stabilitetsorienterad ekonomisk politik. Erfarenheter frn andra lnder visar att det tar tid och krver ett mdosamt arbete fr att skapa tilltro till en lginflationsregim. Arbetet med att hlla inflationen lg och statens finanser i ordning r en process som aldrig tar slut om strvan r att ha lga rntor och en stabil valuta, vilket i det lnga loppet r en frutsttning fr tillvxt och sysselsttning. Beslutsam politik ger resultat Efter det att kronan brjade flyta hsten 1992 frsvagades den ptagligt. Deprecieringen, som man brukar sga nr vxelkursen r rrlig, gav en stark efterfrgeimpuls till i frsta hand de exportorienterade sektorerna i vrt land. Resultatet lt inte vnta p sig. Vi fick under ett par r en av de starkaste uppgngarna i industrikonjunkturen som Sverige har upplevt sedan brjan av 1960talet. Under sommaren 1994 brjade fler och fler ter rkna med en stigande inflation. Den lnga rntan steg under vren frn strax under 7 till nstan 12 procent och kronans kurs fortsatte att frsvagas som en bekrftelse p inflationsoskerheten. Genomslaget av hjda importpriser i konsumentprisledet brjade ka. Till detta kom att inflationstrycket inom industrin blev tydligare. Kostnadsmedvetandet avtog och sannolikheten kade fr en svr avtalsrrelse. (Ngot som vi ocks fick nr avtal tecknades under vren 1995 p en alldeles fr hg niv). Fler och fler inslag i 1970och 1980-talens mnster kunde med andra ord sknjas. En passiv ekonomisk politik hade i den situationen bekrftat farhgorna och kunnat innebra en fortsttning i de gamla hjulspren. Den ekonomiska politiken stod drmed infr ett vgval. Det handlade antingen om att bekrfta tidigare mnster eller att konsekvent fullflja en stabilitetsinriktad politik och bryta med de gamla erfarenheterna. Regeringen, riksdagen och Riksbanken valde att visa beslutsamhet. Statsfinanserna sanerades och penningpolitiken blev stramare. Drmed kade sannolikheten successivt fr att det gamla mnstret inte skulle komma att upprepas. Utgngslget infr framtiden r drfr annorlunda och bttre nu jmfrt med motsvarande faser i konjunkturen p 1970- och 1980-talen. De senaste rens rntepolitik r en tydlig illustration p hur penningpolitiken fungerar med ett prisstabilitetsml under en flytande vxelkursregim. Det r den lgsta nivn p styrrntan p ver 30 r. Uppfylls prisstabilitetsmlet finns en bas fr stabil och varaktig tillvxt och sysselsttning. Finns det en tilltro till lginflationspolitiken finns det ocks utrymme fr penningpolitiken att kortsiktigt bidra till att stdja terhmtningen i svensk ekonomi. Avslutning Mitt budskap hr idag har i huvudsak varit positivt. Det finns mnga goda tecken i svensk ekonomi. Vi har dock inte kommit nda fram till slutmlet. Fortfarande har vi t.ex. hgre lnga rntor jmfrt med lnderna i kontinentaleuropa och kronan har under de senaste mnaderna frsvagats. Det stller fortsatt hga krav p disciplin i den ekonomiska politiken. Det finns en omstndighet som r mindre ljus i de senaste rens utveckling. Det r den fortsatt hga arbetslsheten. terhmtningen i sysselsttning har hittills gtt mycket lngsamt trots en ganska gynnsam konjunktur de senaste ren. Det mesta talar fr att det har uppkommit en strukturell arbetslshet, vilket innebr att arbetslsheten riskerar att frbli hg ven om konjunkturen frbttras, svitt ingenting grs. Det r i sin tur ett tecken p en dligt fungerande arbetsmarknad, som bl.a. har sin grund i lnebildningen - eftersom just prisbildningen r den centrala marknadsmekanismen. Om en stor del av arbetslsheten r strukturell br tgrder inriktas just p att f ned den strukturella arbetslsheten. Det r dock ngot som ligger utom rckhll fr efterfrgepolitiken, dvs penning- och finanspolitiken. Vad penningpolitiken kan gra r att ska hlla en lg och stabil inflation och drmed indirekt bidra ocks till en stabil tillvxt. Den svenska ekonomin tycks ter st infr en period av kad tillvxt. Av allt att dma finns det ocks lediga resurser i ekonomin, vilket gr att det inte br uppkomma ngra avgrande kapacitetsrestriktioner inom den nrmaste framtiden. Om dessutom hushll och fretag fortstter att rkna med en lg inflation nr de fattar sina ekonomiska beslut tyder det mesta p att prisstegringarna kommer att vara fortsatt lga under 1997 och 1998, vilket r den period som vi idag verblickar.
