Title: Electronic money from a central bank perspective
text: Electronic money from a central bank perspective Date: 1998-03-04 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Stockholm Thank you for the opportunity to come here and speak. What I wanted to tell you about is how we as the Riksbank view the phenomenon of electronic money, an area that is closely linked to the overall topic of this conference. What we are seeing today, and for some time now, is a rapid electronization of payment traffic in its broad sense  this takes many forms and e-money is one of the expressions of this, and perhaps the most spectacular. There are slightly different ways of defining e-money, but the definition I intend to apply here is the one formulated in the public inquiry into e-money that recently published a first report, namely as electronic recordings of values that can be used as a general payment instrument, without being in an individualised account. This covers both "money" on chip cards and on hard drives, so-called network money. When paying using a credit card number over the internet, however, this is not an example of electronic money, but a method of making basically traditional account payments, but in a new way. Calling cards and the like are also not to be seen as electronic money - they can rather be seen about electronic tokens. The concrete example of electronic money that we have in Sweden today is the so-called "electronic money". The cash card, which is under introduction in several places of the country. From the Riksbank's side, we believe  perhaps contrary to popular belief  that electronic money is fundamentally a good thing: properly designed, this contributes to increased speed, efficiency and security in payment traffic. But the medal also has a flip side. Payment systems of various kinds are about building and developing infrastructure. Infrastructures are often sensitive to disruptions of various kinds and the effects of disruptions are often spread in an unforeseeable and unwieldy way. Moreover, infrastructures are characterized by certain production-economic features; typically, these are large initial investments and high fixed costs, as well as low, or very low, marginal costs. All this places special demands on risk management, legal arrangements, competitive conditions and more. These are issues that are not easily solved by the market itself, and this is basically why almost all central banks, including the Riksbank, have a general mandate to, as it is called in the Riksbank Act, work for a "safe and efficient payment system". The situation today on the e-money front can, briefly summarized, be said to be that there is a lot going on in many parts of the world, but that the broad impact is still waiting. This may take some time yet; what it is all about is reaching the so-called critical mass, when enough people have accepted and started using this new payment technology. Once that point has been passed, on the other hand, it can go a lot quickly. How quickly one reaches this critical point depends on many things; product design, infrastructure deployment, pricing philosophy and the extent to which producers and users are able to cooperate. All this is largely connected, and it can well be said that the Swedish experiences  at least as they are reflected in the media  have unfortunately been quite mixed here. Anyway: the e-money begins to leave the pilot stage and enter the regular service offering. In parallel with this, intensive work is underway in many places  including Sweden  by the authorities to consider whether and how this should be regulated and how the legislation should be adapted. In the world of international central banks, this issue has been in the picture for quite some time; however, it was well seen by most people to begin with as a kind of science fiction without much practical relevance. But a few years ago, things really took off, both within the G-10 cooperation and within the EU circle, when it was seen that things were really starting to happen. Since then, systematic reviews have been made of the issues that are important to central banks. A great deal has been clarified and a common view is beginning to emerge, although there are still clear differences in attitudes on certain issues, perhaps especially on the issue of the right of publication. What kind of money is it about ? How, then, should one view the phenomenon ? What kind of an animal are we talking about ? Is it cash or is it account money or neither ? I think it can be said a little carelessly that there is somewhere in between: some solutions are closer to cash, others closer to account funds. The similarity with cash lies in the fact that the transactions can be made basically anonymously and without any check against any account, i.e. "off-line". In such systems where the values can circulate from user to user without going back to the issuer after each turn, the cash similarity becomes even greater - however, this does not apply to the Swedish cash system. The differences with cash are, in the same way as for money in a bank account, partly that the value is not guaranteed by the state and the Riksbank, and thus can be lost if the issuer goes bankrupt, and partly that they are not, as banknotes and coins, so-called legal means of payment, i.e. a means of payment that everyone is legally obliged to accept. In general, it can well be said that the degree of anonymity and transferability in practice determines whether it most resembles cash or money on account. It can be said that e-money is something new in the sense that it is definitely something more than just an electronization of an existing service or product. At the same time, it can also be said that it is "old" in the sense that it is basically about traditional functions and routines. In other words: it's a new way of combining and packaging different traditional routines and services. Central banks and e-money As I said, the work started in earnest 2-3 years ago, first within the framework of the G-10 cooperation, where a rapid and comprehensive problem inventory was carried out in the spring of 1996. The summary of the results was also published, focusing on a number of core issues: effects on seigniorage, i.e. the effects on central bank income effects on monetary policy effects on financial stability and the supervisory requirements legal issues technical security issues As far as the first point is concerned, it is of course the case that the issuance of banknotes is traditionally a core task for all central banks. This gives us interest income  i.e. what is sometimes called the seigniorage. One possible knee-jerk reaction from central banks could, of course, be to safeguard this unique and monopolised source of revenue and to discourage the introduction of a competing means of payment. However, those central banks that feel this way  and we do not belong to that  can take comfort in the fact that the analyses carried out showed that there are not very likely to be any major effects on the seignorate, at least not for the foreseeable future, and to the extent that the effects would be more tangible, it is nevertheless possible to deal with the financing problems that could then arise for the central banks. In addition, it can be added that the problem is anything but new  after all, notes and coins have long been facing competition from other payment instruments, without this in any way threatening our ability to carry out our tasks. An indication of this is the fact that the value of all banknotes in circulation in relation to GDP has steadily declined throughout the post-war period: Even when it comes to monetary policy, it cannot be argued that the problems would be particularly difficult: the ability of central banks to conduct monetary policy does not depend on the issue of banknotes. Some practical complications could, of course, arise, including statistical in nature. Some changes in monetary policy techniques could also be necessary. But there is nothing shaky about this; we've weathered those kinds of changes before. Is regulation needed ? For the central banks, it is the third point I mentioned, i.e. the stablite issues, that come into focus when it comes to e-money. In a broader sense, this may also include paragraphs four and five, i.e. the legal and technical arrangements. I was therefore going to dwell on this a bit. In general, then, it can be stated that payment intermediation and money management of traditional means have been considered to involve major societal protection interests. The requirements for financial, administrative, technical and legal stability have been set high. Therefore, to ensure that an adequate standard is maintained, the bulk of financial services production has been considered to require regulation and supervision. The question then is whether the same should apply to e-money. First of all, it should be said that these questions become interesting only to the extent that systems are developed in which the money or units of value can be used for several purposes and among several recipients, i.e. an open system. It is then that you establish an infrastructure, an intermediary system or network that many people can use and benefit from, but which can also cause major and often difficult-to-understand problems for many if something goes wrong - for example, if a publisher goes bankrupt or if technical security does not measure up. The risks exist both for the individual users (consumers) and for the stability of the financial system. These two aspects usually interact with each other. The classic example of a financial crisis is a bank failure, in which both depositors/consumers lose money, and the functioning of the overall payment system is threatened by the knock-on effects that occur for other financial institutions. Typically, these so-called systemic risks are rarely clarified and thus manageable for the individual actors. Now, it is hardly likely that disruptions in an e-money system or in a traditional credit card or giro system would lead to a total breakdown in the payment system as a whole. Nevertheless, there is a "systemic problem", but of a different kind. What can happen is that poorly designed and incompetent or frivolously managed systems can lead to extensive trust problems that drag similar systems with them and technologies, which in turn can lead to a gradual erosion of the functioning of the payment system. One consequence could be a return to the cash economy, which would be a very costly "flight to quality" from a socio-economic point of view. From this point of view, moreover, the issuing of notes and coins by the Central Bank can be seen as a last-ditch safety net for an even bigger and even more devastating step backwards: a return to the barter economy. For that safety net to work, in turn, confidence is required that money can retain its value  price stability is therefore something that is important from this perspective as well. In short, there is a public interest in the systems being technically secure and financially and legally sound. What, then, does it take to achieve this ? What detailed requirements should be placed on the institutional arrangements, especially who should be allowed to be the publisher, has in recent years been the subject of a lively international discussion, in both EU cooperation  both the European Commission and the EMI  and the G-10 cooperation. As far as European cooperation is concerned, the EMI, the European Monetary Institute, which includes the EU's central banks, adopted in 1994 the position that the payment power of prepaid cards is to be regarded as a means of deposit and that the right of issue should therefore be limited to credit institutions, i.e. in practice banks, something that has since been enshrined in law in most continental European countries. Over the past year, the EMI has been working on a review and follow-up to this recommendation. Within the framework of the European Commission, a draft directive is currently being discussed, which includes a comprehensive regulation of the right to issue, etc. A decision on this is to be expected sometime in the summer. The basic attitude to regulation is still different from country to country to central bank. In terms of a standard, it can be said that the central banks on the continent have a more restrictive attitude than the Nordic central banks, as well as the Bank of England. The UNITED STATES and Canada represent the other opposite, where they did not want to see any special regulation at all. In the Swedish investigation that has recently been published, the starting point is that a issuer should be under the supervision of the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority, but does not necessarily have to be a bank. Another important issue for trust and stability concerns technical security. According to several observers, chip technology today is very safe and difficult to enforce. But unlike "regular" counterfeiting, if encryption is successfully broken, electronic money that is completely identical to the "genuine" ones is possible, while the source of the counterfeit is difficult to trace and lead to evidence. In other words, technical integrity must be very high to avoid the risk of "trust collapses" in the systems. To this end, it seems necessary for the systems to be auditable so that the transactions made can be monitored, which makes it possible to see reasonably quickly whether false values have entered the system. But the fact remains: the financial incentives for intrusion will be significant, and it will stimulate criminal creativity. Even with advanced technical protections, these risks can never be ignored. Finally, there is reason to point out the international dimension in terms of the requirements to be imposed on financial strength, legal arrangements and technical security. For several reasons, it is important that we do not build up the systems and on the basis of standards that deviate from those of other countries. The analysis and regulatory work that is now underway with regard to electronic money is thus to a very large extent a work in international cooperation, and here, as I said, the Riksbank is active. Here there is particular reason to point to the emergence of network-based systems which, by their very nature, are cross-border and global; Regulations that are limited to Sweden -- but also to the EU -- risk in this perspective becoming a powerful blow in the air. The Riksbank and e-money So what does the Riksbank intend to do? As I have well indicated quite clearly, we do not intend to discourage the development of electronic money - on the contrary, technological and structural innovation is fundamentally positive, here as in other areas. There are risks and problems that need to be addressed, but the opportunities for increased speed, efficiency and safety are great and it is important that they are taken advantage of. On the other hand, it is precisely for this reason that it is important to establish a solid basis for development, otherwise the setbacks can be difficult and costly both for companies and society and for technology as such. It is in this perspective that one should see the discussion around what type and what degree of regulation and supervision we may need. We will therefore follow developments closely. However, we are not seeking an operational role in this area. We believe that it is the market that should play the main role, here as in the case of other payment services, and, for that matter, in the case of financial services in general. This does not prevent efforts from being needed to make the market function rationally  given the production economic characteristics of such activities, which I touched on at the beginning, there are risks of undesirable effects in terms of price formation and competition. Here, of course, other authorities than the Riksbank also have a role to play, such as the Swedish Competition Authority. After all, as I have said, issuing notes and coins is a time-honoured core task for all central banks. At the same time, it is also a source of revenue for central banks and, indirectly, the state  the so-called seigniorage. As I said, we are not particularly concerned about this. First of all, notes and coins have long been subject to competition from cheques, giro payments and credit cards, which has contributed to a large halving of the value of banknotes in circulation as a percentage of GDP in the post-war period. In this perspective, the introduction of electronic money will not be quite so dramatic, as was clear from the diagram I showed earlier. Moreover, we do not believe that we will have a "cashless society", even in the long term - historically it has worked so that new means of payment have not eliminated but added to existing technologies and systems. There will always be room for notes and coins, albeit to a lesser extent than today. Last but not least, it is actually the case that our task in society is to promote stability and efficiency in the payment system, not to maximize our own fixed income. We are therefore keen to contribute to making the payment system more efficient and, to the extent that we see concerns here, it is rather the risk that development will be too slow than that it will be too fast; not least from an international competitiveness perspective, it is important that Swedish banks and other players are at the forefront when it comes to technical development and the ability to produce new technology  this applies not least to the payment area. If we can take a catalyzed and driving role here, we would like to do this, and we are currently planning a discussion with the "payment market" parties to identify what problems and development obstacles may exist and, if so, what can be done about them. This may concern questions about regulatory needs, about pricing and availability, about cooperation on the producer side and between producers and users, about the role of the Riksbank, the role of other authorities and so on. We think there may be a need for such a forum to get a situational determination  then we will see how we proceed. Part of a larger process So far, I have focused on electronic money as an individual phenomenon. Finally, with regard to the theme of this conference, electronic commerce, I would like to air some general reflections on the broader context of electronic money. The emergence of e-money is something that largely coincides with  and is partly conditioned by  the advent of internet commerce and the need for payment technologies adapted to this. This applies not only to e-money in the sense I have been talking about today, but also to the new forms of account-based payment intermediation  now, of course, secure systems for credit card-based online payments are beginning to emerge. The rapid development of the possibilities to order electronically and to pay electronically thus reinforce each other. The rapid growth of the number of people with access to the networks at the same time creates the necessary base for acceptance and profitability of the business. To this can be added one more factor: if less than one year, a large number of European countries will have introduced a new, single currency  the euro. This means, among many other things, that price comparisons between different countries will be much easier  even for those of us who are at least initially outside EMU; if nothing else, we'll get a dozen less currencies to keep track of. Another aspect of the introduction of the euro that is of interest in this context is, of course, that for a period of about three years there will be no euro in the form of notes and coins, which will provide interesting opportunities for the electronic handling of euro payments, both in the form of electronic euros and in the form of account-based payments. Without losing ourselves in too much speculation about the rapid and exciting development that we are on the threshold of, I think it is nevertheless daring to make the assessment that all this together will mean the rapid growth of electronic commerce and electronic payments, while at the same time a truly internationalised retail market is taking shape, with all that this entails in terms of increased competition and price pressure for the benefit of consumers. The Riksbank basically has two tasks that we have been given the Riksdag's mandate to handle. One is monetary policy, which is to be conducted with price stability as the overriding objective. The ultimate purpose of this is to create the conditions for long-term high and stable economic growth. The second is to promote a "secure and efficient payment system". Developments in the electronicisation of the payment system are a very tangible example of the importance of a well-functioning payment system for the general economic development. In other words, both of the Riksbank's main tasks are ultimately about one and the same thing: promoting good economic development. In conclusion, I would like to say the following: the ongoing electronisation of the payment system - of which electronic money is a part - offers an important potential for streamlining payment processing, in the long run probably also of many neighbouring activities. There is considerable socio-economic interest in this potential being exploited, and the Riksbank, for its part, wants to contribute appropriately to this. However, if this potential is to be fully realised, systems must be - and perceived by users as - technically secure and legally and financially sound. To ensure this, some regulation and supervision of the business is required, and efforts may also be required to promote the proper functioning of the market. Another important prerequisite for exploiting the opportunities is that there is international harmonisation of standards, etc., but also in terms of regulation. Here it does not work with its own Swedish models, but EU solutions are not enough either. What is required and what we must work towards are agreements at global level.

Vad jag tnkte bertta om r hur vi frn Riksbankens sida ser p fenomenet elektroniska pengar, ett omrde som ju hnger nra samman med det vergripande mnet fr den hr konferensen. Det vi ser idag, och sen en tid tillbaka, r ju en snabb elektronisering av betalningstrafiken i dess breda mening  detta tar sig mnga former och e-pengar ett av uttrycken fr detta, och kanske det mest spektakulra. Det finns lite olika stt att definiera e-pengar, men den definition jag tnker tillmpa hr r den som formulerats i den offentliga utredning om e-pengar som nyligen publicerat en frsta rapport, nmligen som elektroniska registreringar av vrden som kan anvndas som ett allmnt betalningsinstrument, utan att finnas p ett individualiserat konto. Detta tcker svl pengar p chip-kort som p hrddisk, s.k. ntverkspengar. Nr man betalar med hjlp av ett kontokortsnummer ver internet r detta dremot inte ett exempel p elektroniska pengar, utan en metod att gra i grunden traditionella kontobetalningar, fast p ett nytt stt. Telefonkort och liknande r inte heller att se som elektroniska pengar - de kan snarast ses om elektroniska poletter. Det konkreta exemplet p elektroniska pengar som vi har i Sverige idag r det s.k. Cash-kortet, som r under introduktion p flera platser i landet. Frn Riksbankens sida anser vi  kanske tvrtemot vad mnga tror  att elektroniska pengar i grunden r ngot bra: rtt utformat bidrar detta till kad snabbhet, effektivitet och skerhet i betalningstrafiken. Men medaljen har ocks en baksida. Betalningssystem av olika slag handlar om att bygga upp och utveckla infrastruktur. Infrastrukturer r ofta knsliga fr strningar av olika slag och effekterna av strningar sprids ofta p ett svrfrutsgbart och svrhanterligt stt. Vidare knnetecknas infrastrukturer av vissa produktionsekonomiska srdrag; typiskt sett handlar det om stora initiala investeringar och hga fasta kostnader, samt lga, eller mycket lga, marginalkostnader. Allt detta stller speciella krav p riskhantering, juridiska arrangemang, konkurrensvillkor med mera. Det hr r frgor som inte utan vidare lses av marknaden sjlv, och det r i grunden drfr som nstan alla centralbanker, inklusive Riksbanken, har ett generellt mandat att, som det heter i Riksbankslagen, verka fr ett skert och effektivt betalningsvsende. Lget idag p e-pengafronten kan, kort sammanfattat, sgas vara att det r mycket p gng p mnga hll i vrlden, men att det breda genomslaget nnu lter vnta p sig. Detta kan drja nnu en tid; vad det handlar r framfr allt att n den s.k. kritiska massan, nr tillrckligt mnga accepterat och brjat anvnda denna nya betalningsteknik. Har den punkten vl passerats, kan det  andra sidan g mycket fort. Hur snabbt man nr denna kritiska punkt beror p mnga saker; produktutformning, utbyggnad av infrastruktur, p prissttningsfilosofi och p i vad mn producenter och anvndare frmr samarbeta. Allt detta hnger ihop till stor del, och man kan vl konstatera att de svenska erfarenheterna  i varje fall s som de avspeglas i media  tyvrr varit rtt blandade hr. Hur som helst: e-pengarna brjar lmna pilotstadiet och komma in i det reguljra tjnsteutbudet. Parallellt med detta pgr ett p mnga hll  Sverige inberknat  intensivt arbete frn myndighetshll med att vervga om och hur detta skall regleras och hur lagstiftningen skall anpassas. I den internationella centralbanksvrlden har den hr frgan funnits med i bilden ganska lnge; dock sgs den vl av de flesta till att brja med som en slags sciencefiction utan strre praktisk relevans. Men fr ngra r sen tog det fart p allvar, bde inom G-10-samarbetet och inom EU-kretsen, nr man sg att det verkligen brjade hnda saker. Sen dess har systematiska genomgngar gjorts av de frgor som har betydelse fr centralbankerna. En hel del har klarats ut och en gemensam syn brjar komma fram, ven om det fortfarande finns klara attitydskillnader i vissa frgor, kanske framfr allt kring frgan om utgivningsrtten. Vad fr slags pengar handlar det om ? Hur ska man d se p freteelsen ? Vad r det fr ett djur vi pratar om ? r det kontanter eller r det kontopengar eller ingetdera ? Jag tror man lite slarvigt kan sga att det ligger nnstans dremellan: vissa lsningar ligger nrmare kontanter, andra nrmare kontomedel. Likheten med kontanter ligger i att transaktionerna kan gras i princip anonymt och utan ngon kontroll mot ngot konto, d v s off-line. Hos sdana system dr vrdena kan cirkulera frn anvndare till anvndare utan att efter varje vnda g tillbaka till utgivaren blir kontantlikheten nnu strre - detta gller dock inte det svenska cash-systemet. Skillnaderna mot kontanter r, p samma stt som fr pengar p ett bankkonto, dels att vrdet inte garanteras av staten och Riksbanken, och allts kan frloras om utgivaren gr i konkurs, dels att de inte som sedlar och mynt r s.k. legala betalningsmedel, d v s ett betalningsmedel som alla enligt lag r skyldiga att acceptera. Allmnt kan man vl sga att graden av anonymitet och verfrbarhet i praktiken avgr om det mest liknar kontanter eller pengar p konto. Man kan sga att e-pengar r ngonting nytt i den meningen att det definitivt r ngot mera n bara en elektronisering av en befintlig tjnst eller produkt. Samtidigt kan man ocks sga att det r gammalt i s mtto att det i grunden handlar om traditionella funktioner och rutiner. Med andra ord: det r ett nytt stt att kombinera och frpacka olika traditionella rutiner och tjnster. Centralbankerna och e-pengarna Arbetet kom, som sagt, igng p allvar fr 2-3 r sen, frst inom G-10-samarbetets ram, dr en snabb och omfattande probleminventering genomfrdes vren 1996. Sammanfattningen av resultaten publicerades ocks, och fokuserades p ett antal krnfrgor: effekter p seignioraget, dvs. effekterna p centralbankernas inkomster effekter fr penningpolitiken effekter p den finansiella stabiliteten och vilka krav som br stllas p tillsyn legala frgor frgor kring teknisk skerhet Vad gller den frsta punkten, r det ju s att sedelutgivning av hvd r en krnuppgift fr alla centralbanker. Detta ger oss rnteintkter  dvs. det som ibland kallas seignioraget. En tnkbar ryggmrgsreaktion frn centralbankshll skulle naturligtvis kunna vara att sl vakt om denna unika och monopoliserade intktsklla och motverka introduktionen av ett konkurrerande betalningsmedel. De centralbanker som till ventyrs knner s  och dit hr inte vi  kan dock hmta trst i att de analyser som gjordes visade att det inte r srskilt sannolikt att det uppstr ngra strre effekter p seignoraget, i varje fall inte under verskdlig tid, och i den mn effekterna skulle bli mer ptagliga gr det likvl att hantera de finansieringsproblem som d kunde uppkomma fr centralbankerna. Dessutom kan det tillggas att problemstllningen r allt annat n ny  sedlar och mynt har ju sedan lnge mtt konkurrens av andra betalningsinstrument, utan att detta p ngot stt hotat vra mjligheter att skta vra uppgifter. En indikation p detta r det faktum att vrdet av samtliga utelpande sedlar i relation till BNP stadigt minskat under hela efterkrigstiden : Inte heller nr det gller penningpolitiken kan man hvda att problemen skulle bli srskilt besvrliga: centralbankernas frmga att bedriva penningpolitik hnger inte p sedelutgivningen. Vissa praktiska komplikationer skulle frsts kunna uppst, bland annat av statistisk art. Vissa frndringar i de penningpolitiska teknikerna skulle ocks kunna bli ndvndiga. Men det r inget omskakande i detta; vi har klarat den sortens frndringar frr. Behvs reglering ? Fr centralbankerna r det den tredje punkten jag nmnde, allts stablitetsfrgorna, som kommer i fokus nr det gller e-pengar. I vidare mening kan detta innefatta ven punkterna fyra och fem, d v s de legala och tekniska arrangemangen. Jag tnkte drfr uppehlla mig en del kring detta. Allmnt kan man d konstatera att betalningsfrmedling och penninghantering av hvd har ansetts innefatta stora samhlleliga skyddsintressen. Kraven p finansiell, administrativ, teknisk och juridisk stabilitet har stllts hgt. Fr att skerstlla att en tillrcklig standard hlls har drfr huvuddelen av den finansiella tjnsteproduktionen ansetts krva reglering och tillsyn. Frgan r d om detsamma ska glla fr e-pengar. Frst ska sgas att de hr frgorna blir intressanta bara i den mn man utvecklar system dr pengarna eller vrdeenheterna kan anvndas fr flera ndaml och hos flera mottagare, dvs. ett ppet system. Det r d som man etablerar en infrastruktur, ett frmedlingsystem eller ntverk som mnga kan utnyttja och dra nytta av, men som ocks kan stlla till stora och ofta svrverskdliga problem fr mnga om ngot gr p tok - till exempel om en utgivare gr i konkurs eller om den tekniska skerheten inte hller mttet. Riskerna finns bde fr dom enskilda anvndarna (konsumenterna) som fr stabiliteten i det finansiella systemet. Dom hr tv aspekterna vxelverkar oftast med varandra. Det klassiska exemplet p finansiell kris r en bankkonkurs, dr bde insttarna/konsumenterna frlorar pengar, och det samlade betalningssystemets funktionsfrmga hotas genom de kedjeeffekter som uppstr fr andra finansiella institut. Det typiska r att dessa s.k. systemrisker sllan r tydliggjorda och drmed hanterbara fr de enskilda aktrerna. Nu r det knappast troligt att strningar i ett e-pengasystem eller i ett traditionellt kontokorts- eller girosystem, skulle leda till ett totalt sammanbrott i betalningssystemet i stort. Likafullt finns det ett "systemproblem", men av ett annat slag. Det som kan hnda r att dligt utformade och inkompetent eller oserist sktta system kan leda till omfattande frtroendeproblem som drar med sig liknande system och tekniker, vilket i sin tur kan leda till en stegvis erodering av betalningssystemets funktionsfrmga. En konsekvens kan bli en tergng till kontantekonomin, vilket skulle vara en samhllsekonomiskt mycket kostsam flight to quality. I det perspektivet kan man fr vrigt se centralbankens utgivning av sedlar och mynt som ett sista skyddsnt fr ett nnu strre och nnu mer frdande steg bakt: en tergng till bytesekonomin. Fr att det skyddsntet skall fungera krvs i sin tur ett frtroende fr att pengarna kan behlla sitt vrde  prisstabilitet r drfr ngot som r viktigt ocks ur det hr perspektivet. Det finns kort sagt ett samhllsintresse att systemen r tekniskt skra och finansiellt och juridiskt sunda. Vad krvs d fr att uppn detta ? Vilka nrmare krav som br stllas p de institutionella arrangemangen, frmst d vem som ska f vara utgivare har under senare r varit freml fr en livlig internationell diskussion, inom bde EU-samarbetet  svl EU-kommissionen som EMI  och G-10-samarbetet. Vad gller det europeiska samarbetet antog EMI, det Europeiska Monetra Institutet dr EUs centralbanker ingr, r 1994 stndpunkten att betalkraft p frbetalda kort r att betrakta som inlningsmedel och att utgivningsrtten drfr skall begrnsas till "credit institutions", d.v.s. i praktiken banker, ngot som man sedemera lagfst i flertalet kontinentaleuropeiska lnder. Inom EMI har man det senaste ret arbetat med en versyn och uppfljning av denna rekommendation. Inom EU-kommissionens ram diskuteras fr nrvarande ett utkast till direktiv dr en vergripande reglering av utgivningsrtt m.m. ingr. Beslut om detta r att vnta ngon gng framemot sommaren. Grundattityden till reglering r fortfarande skiftande mellan olika lnder och olika centralbanker. Lite schablonmssigt kan man sga att centralbankerna p kontinenten har en mer restriktiv attityd n de nordiska centralbankerna, liksom Bank of England. USA och Canada representerar den andra motpolen, dr man inte velat se ngon srskild reglering verhuvudtaget. I den svenska utredning som nyligen publicerats r utgngspunkten att en utgivare skall st under finansinspektionens tillsyn, men inte ndvndigtvis mste vara bank. En annan viktig frga fr frtroendet och stabiliteten gller den tekniska skerheten. Enligt flera bedmare r chip-tekniken idag mycket sker och svrforcerad. Men till skillnad frn vanlig falskmyntning gr det  om man lyckas bryta krypteringen  att producera elektroniska pengar som r helt identiska med de kta, samtidigt som kllan till frfalskningen r svr att spra och leda i bevis. Med andra ord mste den tekniska integriteten vara mycket hg fr att undvika risken fr frtroendekollapser i systemen. Till den ndan frefaller det ndvndigt att systemen r reviderbara s att man kan flja de transaktioner som gjorts, vilket gr det mjligt att ngorlunda snabbt se om falska vrden kommit in i systemet. Men faktum kvarstr: de ekonomiska incitamenten till intrng kommer att vara betydande, och det kommer att stimulera den brottsliga kreativiteten. ven med avancerade tekniska skydd kan dessa risker aldrig negligeras. Till sist finns anledning att peka p de internationella dimensionen nr det gller vilka krav som ska stllas p finansiell styrka, juridiska arrangemang och teknisk skerhet. Av flera skl r det viktigt att vi inte bygger upp systemen och utifrn normer som avviker frn andra lnders. Det analys- och normgivningsarbete som nu pgr nr det gller elektroniska pengar r allts i mycket hg grad ett arbete i internationell samverkan, och hr r Riksbanken som sagt aktiv. Hr finns det srskild anledning att peka p framvxten av de ntverksbaserade system som till hela sin karaktr r grnsverskridande och globala; regleringar som begrnsar sig till Sverige -- men ven till EU -- riskerar i det perspektivet att bli ett kraftfullt slag i luften. Riksbanken och e-pengarna Vad tnker d Riksbanken gra ? Som jag vl har antytt ganska klart har vi inte fr avsikt att motverka utvecklingen av elektroniska pengar - tvrtom r teknisk och strukturell frnyelse ngot i grunden positivt, hr som p andra omrden. Det finns risker och problem som mste hanteras, men mjligheterna till kad snabbhet, effektivitet och skerhet r stora och det r angelget att de tas tillvara.  andra sidan r det just drfr viktigt att stadkomma en stabil grund fr utvecklingen, annars kan bakslagen bli besvrliga och kostsamma bde fr fretagen och samhllet och fr tekniken som sdan. Det r i det perspektivet man ska se diskussionen kring vilken typ och vilken grad av reglering och vervakning vi kan behva. Vi kommer allts att flja utvecklingen uppmrksamt. Dremot efterstrvar vi inte en operativ roll p det hr omrdet. Vi menar att det r marknaden som ska spela huvudrollen, hr som nr det gller andra betaltjnster, och, fr den delen, nr det gller finansiella tjnster i stort. Det hindrar inte att insatser kan behvas fr att f marknaden att fungera p ett rationellt stt  med tanke p dom produktionsekonomiska srdrag som finns i sn hr verksamhet, och som jag berrde inledningsvis, finns risker fr onskade effekter nr det gller prisbildning och konkurrens. Hr har naturligtvis ven andra myndigheter n Riksbanken en roll att spela, exempelvis Konkurrensverket. Att ge ut sedlar och mynt utgr ju, som jag nmnt, en hvdvunnen krnuppgift fr alla centralbanker. Samtidigt r det ocks en klla till intkter fr centralbankerna och, indirekt, staten  det s.k. seignioraget. Som jag sa r vi inte srskilt bekymrade ver det hr. Det r ju frst och frmst s att sedlar och mynt sedan lnge utsatts fr konkurrens frn checkar, girobetalningar och kontokort, vilket bidragit till att vrdet av utelpande sedlar som andel av BNP i stort sett halverats under efterkrigstiden. Introduktionen av elektroniska pengar blir i det perspektivet inte fullt s dramatiskt, som ju framgick av det diagram jag visade tidigare. Dessutom tror vi inte att vi kommer att f ngot "kontantlst samhlle", inte ens p lng sikt - historiskt har det fungerat s att nya betalningsmedel inte eliminerat utan adderats till befintliga tekniker och system. Det kommer alltid att finnas plats fr sedlar och mynt, om n i mindre utstrckning n i dag. Sist men inte minst r det faktiskt s att vr uppgift i samhllet r att verka fr stabilitet och effektivitet i betalningssystemet, inte att maximera vra egna rnteinkomster. Vi r allts angelgna att bidra till att effektivisera betalningssystemet, och i den mn vi ser bekymmer hr r det snarare risken att utvecklingen gr fr sakta n att den gr fr fort; inte minst i ett internationellt konkurrenskraftsperspektiv r det angelget att svenska banker och andra aktrer ligger i framkant nr det gller teknisk utveckling och frmga att produktionsstta ny teknik  detta gller inte minst betalningsomrdet. Kan vi inta en katalyserade och pdrivande roll hr vill vi grna gra detta, och vi planerar fr nrvarande en diskussion med betalmarknadens parter fr att identifiera vilka problem och utvecklingshinder som kan finnas och vad som i s fall kan gras t dem. Det kan glla frgor om regleringsbehov, om prissttning och tillgnglighet, om samarbete p producentsidan och mellan producenter och anvndare, om Riksbankens roll, andra myndigheters roll och s vidare. Vi tror att det kan finnas behov av ett sdant forum fr att f en lgesbestmning  sen fr vi se hur vi gr vidare. En del av en strre process S hr lngt har jag uppehllit mig vid elektroniska pengar som s.a.s. enskilt fenomen. Bland annat med tanke p den hr konferensens tema, den elektroniska handeln, tnkte jag avslutningsvis lufta ngra allmnna reflektioner kring det bredare sammanhang som elektroniska pengar ingr i. Framvxten av e-pengar r ju ngot som i mycket sammanfaller med  och delvis betingas av  tillkomsten av internethandeln och behoven av betaltekniker anpassade till detta. Det gller i och fr sig inte bara e-pengar i den mening jag talat om idag, utan ocks de nya formerna fr kontobaserad betalningsfrmedling  nu brjar ju skra system fr kontokortsbaserade betalningar ver ntet att komma fram. Den snabba utvecklingen av mjligheterna att bestlla elektroniskt och att betala elektroniskt frstrker allts varandra. Den snabba tillvxten av antalet mnniskor med tillgng till ntverken skapar samtidigt den ndvndiga basen fr acceptans och lnsamhet i verksamheten. Till detta kan lggas ytterligare en faktor: om mindre n ett r kommer ett stort antal europeiska lnder att ha infrt en ny, gemensam valuta  euron. Detta innebr, bland mycket annat, att prisjmfrelser mellan olika lnder blir mycket enklare  ven fr oss som tminstone till en brjan str utanfr EMU; om inte annat fr vi ju ett tiotal valutor mindre att hlla reda p. En annan aspekt p euro-introduktionen som r av intresse i det hr sammanhanget r ju att det under en period p cirka tre r inte kommer att finnas euro i form av sedlar och mynt, ngot som kommer att innebra intressanta mjligheter fr elektronisk hantering av eurobetalningar, bde i form av elektroniska euros och i form av kontobaserade betalningar. Utan att frlora sig i alltfr vidlyftiga spekulationer kring den snabba och spnnande utveckling som vi str p trskeln till, tror jag nd man vgar gra den bedmningen att allt detta sammantaget kommer att innebra en snabb tillvxt av den elektroniska handeln och de elektroniska betalningarna, samtidigt som en verkligt internationaliserad detaljhandelsmarknad tar form, med allt vad detta innebr i form av kad konkurrens och prispress till gagn fr konsumenterna. Riksbanken har ju i grunden tv uppgifter som vi ftt Riksdagens mandat att skta. Den ena r penningpolitiken, som skall fras med prisstabilitet som verordnat ml. Det yttersta syftet med detta r att skapa frutsttningar fr en lngsiktigt hg och stabil ekonomisk tillvxt. Den andra r att verka fr ett skert och effektivt betalningsvsende. Utvecklingen nr det gller elektroniseringen av betalningsvsendet utgr ett mycket handgripligt exempel p vilken betydelse ett vlfungerande betalningssystem har fr den allmnna ekonomiska utvecklingen. Med andra ord handlar bgge Riksbankens huvuduppgifter i slutndan om en och samma sak: att frmja en god ekonomisk utveckling. Sammanfattningsvis skulle jag vilja sga fljande: Den fortgende elektroniseringen av betalningsvsendet - dr de elektroniska pengarna r en del - innebr en viktig potential fr effektivisering av betalningshanteringen, i frlngningen sannolikt ocks av mnga angrnsande verksamheter. Det finns ett betydande samhllsekonomiskt intresse att denna potential tas tillvara, och Riksbanken vill fr sin del p lmpligt stt medverka till detta. Om denna potential skall kunna frverkligas fullt ut krvs dock att systemen r - och av anvndarna uppfattas som - tekniskt skra och juridiskt och finansiellt sunda. Fr att skerstlla detta krvs viss reglering och tillsyn av verksamheten, och det kan ocks krvas insatser fr att frmja en vl fungerande marknad. En annan viktig frutsttning fr att mjligheterna skall kunna utnyttjas r att det sker en internationell harmonisering av standarder etc., men ocks nr det gller reglering. Hr fungerar det inte med egna svenska modeller, men det rcker inte heller med EU-lsningar. Vad som krvs och vad vi mste arbeta fr r verenskommelser p global niv. Title: EMU and central banks
text: EMU and central banks Date: 1997-08-22 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Swedish Bankers' Association Mr President, first of all I would like to begin by thanking you for being able to come here and talk about EMU and what will happen in europe's central banks at the beginning of 1999. 1 January 1999 is likely to be the starting point for one of the most extensive projects undertaken in Europe in the economic field. A number of countries will replace their national currencies with the euro and they will have a single monetary and exchange rate policy. EMU is a project that includes many different dimensions. Firstly, EMU is a political project in the sense that the introduction of a single currency requires political decisions. EMU is also on the political agenda in many countries for a variety of reasons. Secondly, EMU is a macroeconomic project in that the convergence criteria describe what should apply vis-a-vis the macroeconomic developments of potential participating countries. Much of the discussion, not least in the press, has also concentrated on which countries may meet the macroeconomic criteria for participation in EMU. Thirdly, EMU is about establishing a new financial infrastructure in Europe. Conducting a European monetary policy requires standardised rules and a uniform transaction system. EMU is thus also another step on the way to establishing the internal market. 1 January 1999 will be the end of most of the very extensive preparatory work carried out for the implementation of the project. Many areas of work are already beginning to be completed and in several cases only systems remain to be tested. After 1999, however, it will take another couple of years for the entire changeover to be completed, not least for the introduction of euro notes and coins. By the beginning of 2002 at the latest, everything should be ready. In my speech, I will outline EMU and the various components of monetary union, with an emphasis on institutional and technical aspects. This will also include how the future European Central Bank cooperation will be managed and operated. Finally, I will also mention something about how the various financial markets may be affected by EMU. Swedish EMU membership 1999 or not There are many indications that Sweden will not participate from the start, on 1 January 1999. A final decision will be given by the Swedish Parliament, probably in December this year. A decision not to participate from the start does not mean that we in the financial sector can ignore EMU and carry on as before as if nothing has happened. The creation of the single market and the creation of EMU are events that fundamentally affect the operating conditions of the financial sector in all countries of the Europe, regardless of whether you are in EMU from the beginning or not. This means that there is every reason to continue to actively monitor what is happening and to adapt different activities to the commercial requirements being shaped by the emerging new financial infrastructure in Europe. Preparing in Sweden For some years now, the Riksbank has been working on practical preparations for EU membership. We have had the starting point of being ready if the Riksdag were to come to the conclusion that Sweden should join in 1999. Although Sweden is now likely to be outside EMU at the start, the realization of the currency union will still mean changes for Sweden. The Swedish financial sector has realised this and has prepared to cope with this new competitive situation. In other words, it will be prepared to offer euro services to those customers who so wish at the start of monetary union. This will require parallel systems for transactions in sek and in euros, which means increased costs. In addition to macroeconomic requirements and technical preparations, the Maastricht Treaty also requires countries to make their central banks independent. In Sweden, five parliamentary parties have reached an agreement to make the Riksbank more independent. The objective of safeguarding price stability is enshrined in law. The Governor of the Riksbank, like the other 5 members of the new Executive Board, cannot normally be removed from office during his six-year term of office. It is the Executive Board that independently formulates monetary policy. The function of the Riksbank's council will in future be controlling. The council has 11 members and 11 deputies. How the Riksbank and the financial sector will adapt to a situation where Sweden may be outside the currency union will be discussed in more detail in a report that the Riksbank will compile during the autumn in collaboration with the financial sector. The different parts of monetary union The structure of monetary union can be likened to a building: the Maastricht Treaty is the foundation on which the entire EMU building rests. The Treaty contains the principles for the whole project. The next level is the building blocks, of which the building consists. So what are these? Single currency A very important building block is, of course, a single European currency. The euro will be introduced as a separate currency on 1 January 1999, but euro notes and coins will not be introduced until the end of 2001 or the beginning of 2002 in the countries then joining the Union. For some time, no more than 6 months, the national currency unit and the euro will be used in parallel. Each country will decide on the timetable for the exchange of notes and coins. For practical reasons, the Riksbank hopes that the exchange can take place faster than six months, if and once Sweden has joined the currency union. Monetary policy A single currency presupposes a single monetary policy and it is the European Central Bank, the ECB, that will be responsible for it. Once the countries participating in monetary union are determined, which is scheduled for April/May 1998, the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) will be established. This includes the ECB and the national central banks. The ECB will have three decision-making bodies: the Governing Council, the Executive Board and the General Council. The Governing Council will be composed of the governors of the central banks whose countries are members of the monetary union. Each central bank governor has in principle one vote, i.e. no country formally has more decision-making influence than the others. It is important to note, however, that they must take decisions on the basis of objective objectives relating to the whole of monetary union and not on the basis of national interests. In the Council, the ECB's the Executive Board and the President of the ECB to be included. The governing council's primary task is to shape monetary policy. The Executive Board then ensures that the decisions are implemented and shall consist of 5 members and the President of the ECB. Members shall be chosen from among persons, as it is called, "whose authority and professional experience in the financial sector are widely known". They are added in 8 years and the time cannot be extended. The long term of office is intended to strengthen the ECB's independence. The General Council is composed of all governors of the central banks of the EU. The Council will exist as long as there are countries that are not part of monetary union. Its task will be to prepare participation for those countries that are outside. The countries that are outside will be involved in the work, but not decided, on a lot of issues that they will be affected by on the day they enter monetary union. The General Affairs Council, on the other hand, will have no influence on monetary policy in EMU. However, the Governing Council will be informed of the Governing Council's decisions. However, this right of information does not apply to the decisions of the Executive Board. The influence of outside countries will be relatively small, the rights few and the obligations many, as these countries will have to follow in practice the policies of the ECB but without being able to influence it. The ECB's objective will be price stability. The instruments that the ECB will use to achieve its objective are not yet fully defined. This will be decided by the ECB as soon as it is formed in 1998. In all likelihood, this is likely to be mainly open market operations, but also standing loan facilities and possibly also reserve requirements. Only those countries that will be involved from the outset will be able to influence what policies are to be pursued and with what instruments. The final decisions on the technical design of monetary policy are taken once the ECB is formed. For Sweden, if we join, there will be no change in the monetary policy objective, since monetary policy in Sweden is already governed by a price stability objective. The establishment of the ECB and the ESCB also technically requires something akin to extensive central bank merger work. The ECB shall be constituted in a legal sense, endowed with its own funds and foreign reserves, etc. All national central banks (NCBs) will be shareholders in the ECB, while the earning capacity of individual central banks will be affected by the creation of the ECB. This means, among other things, that the question of how the profits generated by the right to issue banknotes today generate at national level must be dealt with, when we have a single currency and a single monetary policy. The ECB's capital will amount to EUR 5 billion and Sweden's ownership will correspond to just under 3% of this, approximately EUR 145 million, which today corresponds to approximately SEK 1.2 billion. The ECB's foreign reserve assets shall not exceed EUR 50 billion. If/when Sweden joins the currency union, Sweden will provide funds corresponding to its ownership in the ECB. Even the return will be paid back in relation to that percentage. Valutapolitiken Monetary union also means that monetary policy towards countries outside the euro area becomes common. The ECB will be responsible for the implementation of this single monetary policy. Should the euro have a fixed rate against the currencies of third countries, the Council of Ministers will decide on the design of the system. If, on the other hand, the euro becomes mobile, which is the most likely thing, the Council of Ministers may draw up general guidelines for monetary policy. However, these guidelines must not conflict with the ECB's price stability objective. For those EU countries that are not part of the monetary union, a fixed exchange rate system ERM II will instead be established, thereby replacing the current ERM system. ERM II will essentially function as the current one. Participation is voluntary, but even if a country chooses to remain outside, its monetary policy must nevertheless be conducted in the interests of the Community. The reason is to prevent countries outside EMU from depreciations gain undue competitive advantage. The June 1997 European Council laid down the main features of the new exchange rate system. This means, among other things, that central rates should be set against the euro and not, as at present, against all participating currencies. The participating currencies are allowed to fluctuate by /- 15% around the central rates. The decision on the central rates will involve the ECB and the finance ministers of the euro area countries, as well as the governors and ministers of the countries participating in ERM II. Betalningssystemet Another important building block of the EMU building is the secure functioning of the payment and monetary policy infrastructure within the euro area. It must be possible to influence interest rates in all countries at the same time. This will be possible through the new European single payment system, TARGET. The national banking systems for large payments will be interconnected in this common network. All participants in the national systems - in Sweden's case the RIX system - will be included. TARGET will also be able to be used for commercial payments, which does not mean, however, that the central bank will have a monopoly on payments within EMU. Banks are free to use other avenues, such as correspondent banks. The cost of using the system as well as the speed and security will control how much banks and companies will use the system. TARGET's pricing policy will be based on the principle of full cost recovery. The system will be available to the central banks of all EU countries, regardless of whether they are members of the Union or not. However, it is still uncertain whether countries outside the Union will be allowed to participate on an equal footing with the others. This may include, for example, restrictions on borrowing in euros during the day in order to fend off fluctuations in payment flows. The justification for such restrictions is the risk that intraday credit could shift to over-night lending, thereby affecting aggregate euro liquidity and interest rates. From the Swedish side, however, we believe that this risk is not an actual problem. This issue will not be decided conclusively until the European Central Bank is in place. Collateral A single payment system and a single monetary policy presuppose that it is possible to carry out monetary policy operations in securities issued in different countries. These securities must also be available as collateral for loans made by central banks of countries other than those in which the paper is issued or deposited. There will be two categories of collateral that may be used in monetary policy operations, Tier one and Tier two. The tier one list contains collateral that meets uniform eligibility criteria for the entire monetary union. The tier two list consists of collateral that is of particular importance to national financial markets and where the requirements are set by the national central bank. Both types of assets can be used as collateral in monetary policy operations with the exception of outright purchases, "outright" transactions. For these transactions, only Tier one paper is normally approved. Both Tier one and two papers can be used as collateral for cross-border transactions within the monetary union. However, papers where the issuer is established outside the euro area and which are included in a Tier Two list may be excluded from this possibility. There is a discussion in the EU about whether mortgage bonds should be approved as Tier One paper. Sweden is pushing the line that this should be the case. The issue is not yet settled. "Legal system" If I continue my analogy between EMU and a building, one could compare the legal detail structure of EMU with the building's plumbing system: something that runs through all parts of a building and is necessary for its functionality. You don't think much about it until the day it starts to malfunction. Monetary union would not be able to function without a legal structure, which must be a "watertight system". Otherwise, chaos will arise for those who live in the house. There must be a legal framework for the euro to be used. This is regulated, among other things, in the two euro regulations. The first of these regulations stipulates that the euro must legally be the currency of the Union from day one, thus replacing the national currencies as from 1 January 1999. Furthermore, it is included that the change of currency to the euro should not be the basis for termination of contracts, i.e. contract continuity should apply. The second regulation regulates issues relating in particular to transitional issues for the period 1999-2002, in order to allow for the rapid introduction of the euro. This includes, for example, that no one should be prevented from using the euro, but neither should anyone be forced to do so during this transitional period. Furthermore, it is envisaged that the countries joining the monetary union will carry out all new issues in euro-denominated government securities. If a Member State also wants to convert its outstanding debt stock into euros, it may take appropriate measures itself. All private economic operators should be able to choose when they want to switch to the euro during the transitional period or at the end of the euro. In addition, legal rules are being prepared on, among other things, collateral, securities systems, payment systems and monetary and exchange rate policy operations. What happens 1/1 1999 within the ECB and central banks? The first thing that happens is that exchange rates are fixed and the euro becomes an independent currency. From this point on, national currencies become mere national expressions of the euro. The single monetary policy in euro is starting to be pursued through TARGET. The NCBs will act as the "extended arms" of the ECB in the implementation of monetary policy. For the banks and financial institutions that currently participate in central bank monetary policy operations, the changes will not be very large. However, the overnight market will be significantly larger and potential counterparties will be located across Europe. The merger process I mentioned earlier is to be carried out. The national central banks have transferred foreign reserve funds to the ECB so that it can conduct monetary policy vis-a-vis third countries on the first day of monetary union How the foreign exchange interventions will take place, we do not know anything about today. Either it can be decentralised through the national central banks on behalf of the ECB or centralised in Frankfurt. The NCBs shall provide the ESCB on an ongoing basis with statistical and analytical material to ensure that the ECB is able to carry out its tasks. ... and central banks whose countries are outside? The national central banks will retain responsibility for national monetary and exchange rate policy. If the country is a member of ERM II, the currency will be pegged directly to the euro and not, as in the current system of a network of exchange rates between the constituent currencies. The risk of tensions will probably be somewhat less than in the current system because convergence is better between countries now than before in the 90s. Countries which are outside monetary union and do not participate in the ERM II exchange rate mechanism are not, however, allowed to pursue a fully autonomous monetary policy. It must conduct a monetary policy in the common interest of the Eu ropean Union, as this is mentioned in the Maastricht Treaty. The difference from how the Riksbank works in practice today will not formally be so great. The RIX system will continue to work in sek, but there will also be a parallel system in euros. The Swedish financial sector will be able to make fast and secure payments through TARGET. Reporting requirements for the financial sector for statistical needs will remain, in principle to the extent that If Sweden were a member from 1999. What are the consequences of EMU for the financial sector and securities markets in Europe? Major structural changes are taking place in the financial system in Europe. These are due, among other things, to technological innovations, changing government regulations and globalization. The formation of EMU intensifies and accelerates this process of transformation. Monetary union is likely to bring interest rates between the countries of Europe closer together. This is due to the fact that there will be economic convergence between the countries and that there will be a common anti-inflationary monetary policy. The single monetary policy and the disappearance of exchange rate risks will mean that the remaining interest rate differentials between sovereign debt will mainly reflect other types of market assessments. It is also conceivable that there will be an increased scope for borrowers other than the state and housing institutions. Most likely, a more differentiated range of securities will come. Financial products will change, some will disappear, for example, currency, forward and options products in the currencies that turn into euros. With the creation of EMU, a single European monetary and capital market will be created, which will be both larger and more liquid than any of the existing national markets. This is likely to mean increasing competition between the institutions active in the money and capital markets. Borrowers will find it easier to get hold of attractive financing via, among other things, the bond market. Competition between institutions in EMU countries will increase, among other things, as they lose the advantage of their own home country currencies. Instead, institutions are allowed to share their new "home currency" with a large number of European competitors. It will therefore be important for financial institutions to be present in the single markets at an early stage so as not to risk losing customers. This ratio will also apply to Swedish financial companies if Sweden is excluded. Some of the companies' activities may then move abroad to subsidiaries and branches that already exist in the future EMU countries. Here, among other things, the upcoming design of the TARGET system plays a role. Well-developed European markets across national borders may emerge for different types of bonds, such as corporate, residential and municipal bonds. This can be partly explained by the fact that investors want to spread their risks by diversifying their portfolios to several countries. In this way, the risk of loss can be limited if asymmetric shocks occur in any country. The Swedish market will be affected even if Sweden is not part of EMU from the beginning. EMU will mean fewer restrictions for investors when it comes to cross-border trade and this will also apply to Sweden regardless of membership. Together with government bonds, mortgage bonds dominate the Swedish bond market. Within Europe, Sweden is around 4th place in terms of amount in terms of outstanding mortgage bonds. Investments in Swedish mortgage bonds are highly concentrated in Sweden. However, foreign lenders have increasingly targeted the Swedish bond market over the past year. However you twist and turn the numbers, the Swedish financial sector is quite small in a European perspective. Customers of the financial sector may demand euro services such as euro savings accounts and euro pension accounts. It may also be relevant for customers who wish to borrow in euros. Swedish financial institutions have expressed concern that they may find themselves in a worse competitive position compared to European banks that will have their deposit base in euros. Vardepappersmarknad The stock exchanges in Europe have announced that securities trading will switch to euros, in the countries that are involved from the beginning. The transition will also take place through a so-called Big Bang, i.e. that virtually all trade in one fell swoop will move from national currency to the euro, on 1/1 1999. The assessment is that the stock market will become larger and that one or a few dominant markets will form for the most traded European shares. If Sweden is excluded, it is likely that trading in some shares on the Stockholm Stock Exchange will switch to euros in any case. This change is probably necessary in order to offer a continued competitive marketplace. Foreign customers account for a third of the trading on the Stockholm Stock Exchange and Swedish investors trade on foreign exchanges of the same order of magnitude. The securities industry therefore estimates that there will be a high demand in euros for the most traded shares right from the start, even if Sweden does not join from 1999. Summary The final sprint in the EMU work has begun. Sweden is a qualified candidate if we wish to join in 1999, which at present, however, seems highly uncertain. Monetary union will have major consequences for all EU countries, regardless of whether they are in the currency union or not. What can exclusion mean for Sweden as a country? The need for inflation control and budgetary rigour remains, the degrees of freedom do not increase. We are losing influence by not being able to participate in shaping the operations of EMU in the initial, formative, stage. There is also a risk of a loss of influence in other European negotiations as well, because we are not part of the 'inner circle'. Consequences for the financial system On the one hand, Swedish banks, the stock exchange, VPC, etc. and companies must be prepared to introduce euro services and euro accounting if the market so requires. The duplication of sek/euro work entails additional costs and competitive disadvantages vis-a-vis EMU banks. Swedish financial institutions face a challenge not to be left behind in structural change if it is concentrated in EMU Europe. The reason is that they work in a smaller market (Sweden) than others, who work in the broad euro market and who will participate in the single monetary policy, etc. Swedish banks participate in TARGET as well as others, but there may be some disadvantages depending on the design. On the other hand, Swedish banks are likely to have more foreign exchange trading than if Sweden is part of EMU, and Swedish financial institutions and markets can implement the euro changes at a slower pace and thus benefit from the experiences of others. This also applies to the Riksbank and government agencies, such as the Swedish National Debt Office, the Swedish National Tax Agency. There is a certain risk that Swedish financial institutions may be marginalized and end up outside the focus of the changes. Strong measures are needed to counteract this - active strategies on the part of financial institutions and an economic policy that means that Sweden is an attractive country for foreign investment. In any case, the authorities, the financial system and the Riksbank must constantly regard EMU as a reality that affects us even if we are outside. The Riksbank's emu work will therefore not slow down even if the Riksdag this autumn decides that Sweden should remain outside. Continued EMU work is ultimately a consequence of EU membership and it will therefore continue to be important to follow the development of the EMU project. Otherwise, Sweden will miss the opportunity to participate in the discussions ahead of the decisions that will govern much of the european countries' economic future. For the Riksbank, it is essential that Sweden's interests are safeguarded, even in the event of exclusion. It is important that, as far as possible, we are involved in the peaceful revolution into which europe's economy is about to enter.
