Title: Erik Theden: Committee on Finance hearing on the Riksbank's operations and monetary policy
text: Erik Thedeen: Committee on Finance hearing on the Riksbank's operations and monetary policy On Tuesday, the entire Executive Board took part in an open hearing at the Committee on Finance about the Riksbank's operations and current monetary policy. This was the first time that the Riksdag had invited board members to a hearing on the Riksbank's overarching operations and the 2022 Annual Report. Date: 14/03/2023 09:00 Speaker: Governor Erik Thedeen Place: The Committee on Finance Published 14/03/2023 Governor Erik Thedeen began the hearing by summarising the past year and noted that a great deal has happened at the Riksbank and abroad that has had an impact on operations: "Last year, we saw inflation starting to rise sharply and interest rates have risen rapidly. Raising the policy rate was necessary to safeguard the inflation target, but at the same time, rising interest rates caused the market value of the Riksbank's asset holdings to fall. This unrealised decrease in value has in turn had a negative impact on the Riksbank's financial result and, just like many other central banks around the world, we will report a significant loss for 2022. However, this does not affect the Riksbank's ability to carry out its tasks. In the longer run, however, the Riksbank's capital needs to increase to ensure the bank's financial independence. In addition, a new Riksbank Act has come into force and the bank has new management." Erik Thedeen also noted that digital developments in the payment market are proceeding at a rapid pace. At the same time, the Riksbank saw a temporary increase in the demand for cash following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "It is clear that the demand for cash increases in times of crisis, but it is important to remember that if it is to be possible to use cash in a crisis, we must also be able to use it in normal times. We consider that it must always be possible to at least purchase vital goods and services with cash. As a result of the new Riksbank Act, we have been given increased responsibility for cash management and during the year we have prepared the ground for the opening of new banknote depots. The Riksbank has also launched a new service for instant payments, RIX-INST, and work on an e-krona continues. Digital central bank currencies (CBDC) have become a major issue internationally during the year and Sweden is seen as a pioneer. We are active in various international partnerships linked to both CBDC and international payments". The second part of the hearing focused on current monetary policy. Erik Thedeen began by summarising the decision from February and noted that inflation is still far too high and that monetary policy needs to act to bring inflation back to 2 per cent within a reasonable period of time. He also commented on the ongoing bank problems in the United States. "We are following developments in the financial markets, and we currently consider there to be no risk to financial stability in Sweden. Among other aspects, Swedish banks are subject to stricter regulatory requirements than the agents in the US that have encountered problems. Direct exposure to these agents is also limited among Swedish banks. At the same time, it is not unusual for turbulence in foreign capital markets to spill over into Sweden. We are therefore closely monitoring the situation and, as always, we are prepared to take action in the event of a rapid change". Deputy Governor Aino Bunge then went on to talk about what the new Riksbank Act means for monetary policy. Among other things, a clause has been added under which the Riksbank shall contribute to a balanced development of output and employment without disregarding the price stability target. "Although this can be seen as an adjustment to existing practice, it probably affects how the public and elected representatives view monetary policy and how it is evaluated. We therefore need to be clearer in our communication with both our assessment of the real economy and how we consider it our monetary policy decisions". Aino Bunge also said that it is important to acquire a broad picture based on incoming data and forecasts for the economy and employment, but stressed that it is essential to bring down the high inflation in order to avoid even greater problems for the economy further ahead.

Title: Erik Theden: Committee on Finance hearing on monetary policy
text: Erik Thedeen: Committee on Finance hearing on monetary policy Things are going in the right direction, inflation is falling, but price pressure remains too high in the economy. That was the message from the Executive Board when they took part in this year's second hearing at the Riksdag Committee on Finance on current monetary policy on Tuesday. Governor Erik Thedeen and First Deputy Governor Anna Breman began by making presentations prior to the hearing. Date: 17/10/2023 09:00 Speaker: Governor Erik Thedeen Place: The Committee on Finance Published 17/10/2023 We need to ensure that we regain purchasing power Erik Thedeen summarised the motives behind the current monetary policy. He emphasised that the strong upturn in inflation last year was due to both global supply shocks and strong demand in the Swedish economy. The supply disruptions resulted in large increases in costs for companies. The unexpectedly strong demand associated with the recovery after the pandemic allowed companies to pass these costs on to consumer prices to a greater extent than normal. And the price increases spread widely throughout the economy. In addition, the weak krona has contributed to the upturn in inflation. "When inflation rises sharply, it is important that monetary policy reacts to avoid the economy being stuck in a situation where high inflation begins to appear normal. The fact that the Riksbank has gradually raised the policy rate is dampening inflationary pressures in the economy/' said MrThedeen. "We can see that the interest rate increases are having an effect. Inflation is falling and that is welcome. But the fall in CPIF inflation is also largely due to a sharp fall in electricity prices. Underlying inflation, which usually provides good guidance on where inflation is heading, is still too high." ErikThedeen, governor. The Executive Board's forecast from the interest rate decision in September indicates that the policy rate may need to be raised somewhat further. As before, Mr Thedeen pointed out that new information and how it affects the outlook for the economy and inflation determine the monetary policy stance. "In tough times, the economic policy frameworks are challenged. We understand that it is noticeable when interest rates rise. But the cost of a permanently too high inflation rate is significantly higher. We need to ensure that we regain purchasing power," concluded ErikThedeen. Good conditions for inflation to fall - but considerable uncertainty Anna Breman also welcomed the fall in inflation. "Inflation is on the way down. But we need a broad fall in inflation to achieve sustainably low and stable inflation." She said that there are good conditions for inflation to continue falling. Producer prices have fallen sharply, the social partners have shown responsibility and inflation expectations are stable. "But we need additional scope for potential setbacks, and it will be important to analyse how new information affects the outlook for the economy and inflation." Ms Breman highlighted three areas that she believes will be important to follow: household consumption and saving, labour market developments and companies' pricing behaviour. "What determines the direction of monetary policy at future meetings will be our overall assessment of where inflation is heading. Monetary policy needs to be clearly contractionary for a period to come for us to return to sustainably low and stable inflation. This is important, because it enables increasing real wages, competitive companies and increased welfare."

Title: Theden: The Riksbank needs to restore its capital
text: Thedeen: The Riksbank needs to restore its capital Today, Governor Erik Thedeen visited the Riksdag Committee on Finance to present an analysis of the Riksbank's financial position, earnings capacity and long-term capital requirements. "The preliminary results of the analysis indicate that the Riksbank needs to have its equity restored to at least the basic level stated in the Sveriges Riksbank Act of SEK 40 billion. As per the end of September 2023, a restoration to the basic level would entail a capital injection of almost SEK 80 billion. The Riksbank also needs prospects for additional earnings/ said Mr Thedeen. Date: 24/10/2023 11:00 Speaker: Governor Erik Thedeen Place: Committee on Finance Published 24/10/2023 Earlier securities purchases have resulted in losses In the annual accounts for the financial year 2022, the Riksbank reported a loss of just over SEK 80 billion. As a result of the loss, the Riksbank's equity was negative, SEK -18 billion. "The loss and negative equity are due to the sharp rise in interest rates in 2022. This has led to a fall in the value of the bonds purchased by the Riksbank during the period 2015-2021 to maintain confidence in the inflation target, Erik Thedeen, governor. secure the credit supply during the coronavirus pandemic and contribute to good economic development," said MrThedeen. When the value of the Riksbank's holdings of bonds decreases, it leads to unrealised losses that burden the Riksbank's result and equity. "A negative equity does not affect the Riksbank's ability to conduct monetary policy in the short term. But to maintain confidence in an independent monetary policy in the long term, it is necessary that the Riksbank is financially independent, that is, has sufficient equity and earnings to cover its costs," continued MrThedeen. The Riksbank's asset purchases took place in a situation of international stress, when the major central banks around the world were making extensive asset purchases. New Sveriges Riksbank Act requires capital injections in the event of insufficient equity The new Sveriges Riksbank Act, which applies from this year, contains provisions that the Riksbank's equity should have a target level of SEK 60 billion and a basic level of SEK 40 billion. The Act also stipulates that the Riksbank shall submit a petition to the Riksdag (Swedish Parliament) to restore equity if it falls below a minimum level of SEK 20 billion. The Riksbank has made an analysis of the bank's financial position, earnings capacity and long-term capital requirements. At the meeting with the Riksdag Committee on Finance, Erik Thedeen presented the preliminary results of the analysis and the measures taken to reduce the risks on the balance sheet. The analysis shows that, despite the measures taken, the Riksbank needs to have its equity restored to at least the basic level of SEK 40 billion, and also an opportunity for additional earnings. The Riksbank will now continue to work on the petition to the Riksdag and the possibility of additional earnings. "When the Riksbank's Annual Report for 2023 is completed in February 2024, the Executive Board of the Riksbank intends to make a decision on a petition that includes a request for capital injections and possibly also proposals for additional earnings capacity. The size of the capital injection in the petition will be based on the Riksbank's equity and reported results for 2023. The intention is to submit the petition to Parliament in March 2024," concluded MrThedeen.

Title: Theden: Property companies need to reduce debts
text: Thedeen: Property companies need to reduce debts Many property companies have had problems since the Riksbank started raising the policy rate and now they need to reduce their debts, both to strengthen their balance sheets and to increase confidence among those who buy their shares and bonds. "The fact that the Riksbank recently decided to hold the policy rate unchanged at 4 per cent should not be interpreted as meaning that inflation risks have disappeared and that interest rates will fall rapidly." This was what Governor Erik Thedeen said when he spoke on Friday about his views on developments in the commercial property sector at Moody's property conference at the Grand Hotel in Stockholm. Date: 01/12/2023 09:55 Speaker: Governor Erik Thedeen Place: Moody's property conference Published 01/12/2023 Good times increased risk-taking among property companies During the years of low interest rates and very good access to finance, many commercial property companies increased their borrowing substantially, expanded their property portfolios too quickly and took on major financial risks. When inflation then increased and the Riksbank began to raise the policy rate, many property companies came under pressure as their financing costs increased and property values began to fall. Debt reduction is good for financial stability Although the companies have different conditions for dealing with the challenges, the property sector's sensitivity to interest rates and its close connection to the banking system can upset financial stability. The property companies therefore need to take more measures and more extensive ones to reduce their debts. Both new issues of shares and divestment of property are needed to a greater degree. "If this strengthens their balance sheets, the companies will have greater freedom to take a more offensive approach," Mr Thedeen pointed out. It can also lead to a strengthening of confidence among investors who buy property companies' shares and bonds. The tight monetary policy also justifies lower risk-taking The fact that the Riksbank recently decided to hold the policy rate unchanged at 4 per cent should not be interpreted as meaning that inflation risks have disappeared and that interest rates will fall rapidly. "Monetary policy needs to remain contractionary and the Riksbank is prepared to raise the policy rate further if inflation prospects deteriorate," explained Mr Thedeen. Real estate companies therefore need to look at their risk-taking in a long-term perspective, fix the interest rates on their loans and borrow at longer maturities. This would also improve the conditions for the bond market to remain an important source of funding for both property and other companies. "There is also a need for long-term structural changes in the bond market with higher transparency, better risk awareness and a broader investor base than before," concluded Erik Thedeen.

Title: The role of the euro in housing finance
text: The role of the euro in housing finance Date: 1998-08-27 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Location: ByggBo conference for the 2000s First of all, I would like to thank you for being able to come here and talk about EMU and housing finance. I wanted to start by showing some trends for how Swedish housing finance has developed in recent years. Then I want to try to put Swedish housing finance in a European context and discuss how Swedish housing institutions and the system for housing finance that they represent compare to their European competitors. With this description, I hope to be able to give a picture of where we stand today, ahead of EMU getting underway in 1999. I will then describe what consequences EMU can have for housing finance. My focus will then be on trends that are particularly important for the market for mortgage bonds. I will also say something about how EMU can affect banking in general, and real estate lending more specifically. I would already like to point out something that is important to consider when Sweden is not a member of EMU from the start. This is that the introduction of the euro is only one step, in itself a very important step, in the development towards creating a common market in Europe. Integration between the countries' markets has been going on for a long time and it is not over with the formation of EMU. Financial firms and markets are comparatively advanced in the integration process. Although Sweden did not introduce the euro in 1999, Swedish companies and markets are part of the ongoing integration. The increased competition and integration between markets that EMU is expected to contribute to affects Sweden, despite the exclusion. The impact on Swedish financial firms will in many cases be no different than on their euro area competitors. Trends in Swedish housing finance I will dwell on Swedish housing institutions when discussing Swedish housing finance, as these account for the vast majority of private housing finance. As the figure shows, housing institutions' lending has decreased overall over the past five years. On closer inspection, however, it is lending to financial institutions that has decreased. Since such loans are not part of the core business of housing institutions and the margins on this lending are normally low, this is hardly a major problem. In terms of core business, lending to households and non-financial corporations or what is commonly referred to as lending to the general public, lending has remained relatively stable in the latter part of the 1990s. Lending to households has increased slightly, while lending to non-financial corporations has decreased. The decrease in lending to companies can be explained by the low level of housing construction. If new construction starts to increase from today's low levels and property prices continue to rise, there is reason to believe that lending may increase in the coming years. This, of course, is what most people here in the room are hoping for. For my part, I will mostly focus on trying to assess whether such a development is justified on the basis of what is a stable long-term development, or whether there is a risk that lending bubbles similar to those that arose in the late 80s are about to arise. Analyses of lending growth in banks and housing institutions are an important part of the Riksbank's work to promote a stable financial system. [Figure 1] As is well known, housing institutions finance themselves primarily by issuing housing certificates and mortgage bonds. These securities constitute approx. 70 per cent of housing institutions' funding. The market for residential securities is by far the dominant market for fixed income securities issued by Swedish private institutions. The outstanding stock of residential securities amounts to approx. SEK 730 billion and it is more than 13 times the total stock of fixed income securities issued by other private institutions in Sweden. It is today a couple of hundred million less than the volume of government securities. However, this will decrease as the state redeems part of the AP Fund's holdings of government securities and after this the stock of residential securities will be substantially larger. In 1997, other types of financing became more important in housing institutions. Housing institutions finance themselves more through other financial institutions, especially Swedish banks and housing institutions. The independence of housing institutions is based on the fact that their own financing is achieved through the issuance of bonds, bonds that are primarily bought by various institutional investors. If the interdependence between Swedish banks and housing institutions increases, the risk of financial problems in one company spreading to others increases. This risk is usually referred to as systemic risk. Trying to reduce this is important in order to strengthen the stability of the financial system. [Figure 2] Swedish housing finance in a European perspective There are many different ways in Europe to finance housing. Borrowing money against a pledge in the property is for us the obvious way to finance the vast majority of the cost of building or buying a property. Lending against mortgages in real estate occurs in all EU countries, but they have very different scopes in relation to other economic activities. Lending against mortgages in real estate amounts to 65 percent of GDP in Denmark, while the corresponding figure is only 6 percent in Greece. Sweden is relatively high at 51 percent, compared to the EU average of 36 percent. [Figure 3] Even when housing is financed through loans against mortgages in real estate, this can be done in many different ways. The Swedish system of special housing institutions that specialize in providing bottom loans and that finance this lending by issuing bonds or certificates is just a variant. In several countries, lending for housing takes place through the usual banking system. The countries where housing institutions similar to the Swedish ones have a significant role in the market are Denmark and Germany. The market for mortgage bonds is larger in nominal terms in both these countries, but it is only in Denmark that housing institutions are as dominant as in Sweden, seen in relation to the size of the country. In Sweden, housing institutions account for about half of all lending from financial companies. [Figure 4] In some countries, housing finance has special support from the state. In France, for example, there is an institution set up by the state which finances mortgages granted by banks by issuing bonds. Housing finance is often characterized by a specific national structure, where it is not uncommon for institutions that have some support from the state. We have seen comparatively little European competition in the form of lending institutions trying to enter new national markets in Europe in terms of the market for credit relating to residential immovable property, at least in relation to developments in competition in other parts of the financial market. This is the case despite the fact that mortgages, at least to consumers, is a relatively standardized product, which normally means that the entry barriers are lower for new entrants. Institutional differences, both regulatory and traditional, may be a contributing factor to the fact that cross-border competition has not been widely observed in European mortgage markets. Helping to reduce the institutional disparities arising from the special treatment of different types of institutional solutions by authorities in European countries should be a main task in improving competition within the EU, after EMU has started. Current issues regarding housing finance I would like to dwell here somewhat on an issue that has been relevant in relation to Swedish housing finance over the past year  the proposal to introduce so-called gold-edged bonds in Sweden. The proposal was presented by a government inquiry in the second half of 1997. One of the main arguments in the study was that it would contribute to the harmonisation of the markets for mortgage bonds in Europe. My view is that they would rather counteract the real integration of European mortgage markets. The proposal provided for rather far-reaching detailed regulation by the authorities of the activities of housing institutions. The wording of an EU directive on which the proposal was based was not intended as an attempt at harmonisation and was unclearly worded. The result of so-called harmonisation based on this directive is that the national authorities will fill the detailed regulation with different content, at least the existing systems that comply with the directives differ significantly. This creates differences between the housing institutions of different countries that can lead to barriers to competition. In my opinion, it is better if the authorities were content with the rules necessary to maintain financial stability and refrain from unnecessary detailed regulation. As a result, different institutional variants have to be tested against each other and a competitive situation arises between different countries' systems, where the system that in the long run can best achieve cheap housing financing is likely to dominate the market over time. I see no reason why Swedish housing institutions will not stand up well in this competition between institutional forms. A competing institutional form of housing finance that has been much discussed in recent years is securitization. Securitisation means that banks or other companies remove assets, primarily loans, from their balance sheets and finance them by issuing bonds. Real estate loans have proven suitable for securitisation and this form of financing may become increasingly important in a European mortgage market characterised by fierce competition. In the past, it has mainly been in the United States that securitization has occurred to some great extent. In 1997, securitisations were made outside the UNITED STATES of assets roughly equivalent to the value of Sweden's GDP. There is reason for Swedish authorities to consider what securitisation means for the risks in the financial system and whether it causes any special legislative need. European settlement financing efficiency In this context, there is reason to try in some way to compare the housing finance of different countries. However, comparisons are made more difficult by the fact that there are many national specificities in terms of European housing finance systems. I have made an attempt here to give some sort of indication of the effectiveness of the various systems by comparing how the interest rates on mortgages in different countries relate to the government rates in one's own country. The intention is to show what home loans cost in relation to the general interest rate situation in the country. By showing the spread between interest rates on housing loans and government borrowing rates with the same maturity, it is at least possible to eliminate the differences due to currencies and the differences resulting from the traditional use of different interest durations for housing loans in different countries. Nevertheless, the comparison necessarily becomes uncertain, taking into account, inter alia, that the conditions may differ for the loans on which the interest rates are based. [Figure 5] The picture shows that Dutch and German mortgage rates are at about the same level as swedish ones. Norwegian and Belgian mortgage rates are more expensive. In this comparison, Swedish housing financing thus looks competitive. A more liquid and efficient securities market I would now like to go into a little more about what effects EMU may have on the European securities market. Since Swedish housing institutions will be able to issue their bonds in this market, this development will be significant for Swedish housing financing. Like any asset, bonds have an element of liquidity aspects in pricing. The degree of liquidity in a bond is usually measured in how easy it is to convert it into cash. Investors who invest in bonds therefore usually demand a liquidity premium equal to the cost required to convert a bond into cash. It follows, of course, that borrowing costs will be relatively high for borrowers who finance themselves through bonds issued in markets where liquidity is low. The introduction of the single currency will create a larger and more liquid bond market for potential investors. The conversion of bonds denominated in a number of different local currencies into euro-denominated bonds will create a common bond market of impressive size. This market is likely to be characterized by good liquidity and efficient pricing, which, in combination with tougher competition in the credit market, can, among other things, lead to lower borrowing costs. In general, monetary union - because a counter-inflationary monetary policy is the common foundation - will lead to the convergence of interest rates in the high-interest and low-interest rate countries. This also suggests that the currency risk premium on bonds issued in different countries will disappear completely, since in EMU there is only one currency. What will remain, even after the transition process is fully completed, is above all credit risks and legal risks associated with different types of securities. As currency risk disappears and investment decisions will be more about credit risks, there is much to suggest that well-developed European markets may form across national borders for different types of bonds such as corporate, residential and municipal bonds. This is likely to be accompanied by an interest on the part of investors in spreading their risks by diversifying their portfolios to several countries in order to limit loss risks in the event of asymmetric shocks in any country. The tighter budgetary discipline in European states is likely to lead to a reduction in the outstanding stock of the sovereign debt of the various countries. This means that there is an increased need for safe, liquid bonds for investors. Swedish mortgage bonds have the potential to provide such an alternative. In order to fully become part of the single European securities market, residential institutions are likely to be required to issue bonds in euro. As long as lending is predominantly in Swedish kronor, a currency risk arises in the housing institutions if the borrowing is to be made in euros. This risk will exist unless Swedish borrowers start taking out loans in euros instead of in kronor. However, it does not seem likely that this would happen on a larger scale. Swedish mortgage bonds denominated in SEK will certainly also be positively affected if a common European securities market develops. As I mentioned earlier, European investors will be more focused on trading bonds that are not issued by states. Currency risk does not then have to be an insurmountable obstacle. Although there are few who deny that securities markets within EMU will be large and efficient, harmonisation may, however, be delayed as a result of different tax, accounting and investment rules in different countries. However, competitive pressures are likely to result in these differences being erased relatively quickly to the extent that they hamper the competitiveness of individual markets. Harmonisation of market structures within EMU However, in order for this positive development that can be associated with a larger and more efficient capital market to be possible, a well-developed financial infrastructure is required where transactions can be settled safely and efficiently. The infrastructure allows buyers and sellers to meet in an easy way. The infrastructure comprises a number of interconnected parts that are interdependent in different ways. From a Swedish perspective, it is of course important that the Swedish market appears attractive in comparison with competitors, especially as the Swedish market appears relatively small in a European perspective. The market must have a high level of liquidity and a well-functioning infrastructure. The Swedish market must appear easily accessible and efficient. If it is technically difficult and expensive to exploit the Swedish market, it is quite easy for both foreign and Swedish players to find an alternative market or for foreign investors to find substitutes for Swedish investments in their portfolios. If you look at the four central infrastructure systems in the Swedish market, the Stock Exchange, OM, VPC and RIX, they are each relatively well ahead in an international perspective. What is important in my opinion is to improve the integration between the systems. A technical integration of the entire transaction chain - closing, clearing, settlement and account keeping - would simplify access to the Swedish market and thus strengthen its competitiveness and also contribute to a welcome risk reduction in the financial system. High security is a competitive factor in itself. Of course, successful integration is not just about "connecting" some technical systems. It also deals with regulatory systems, access issues and supervisory aspects where the basic aim is to ensure good and transparent risk management. With regard to the possibilities for the interconnection of computer systems and regulations between different countries, I would also like to mention the unique legal conditions that exist to link the financial infrastructures of the Nordic countries. One obstacle that is often encountered in international interconnections of this type is that the regulations surrounding financial trade in different countries are based on different civil law grounds. The fact that the Nordic countries' regulations are based on equal civil law bases opens up great opportunities to link the securities markets and thus create a market that can be competitive in terms of size and depth even in a future EMU. The integration of the Nordic financial infrastructures could thus serve as a model for other regions within the EU. Of course, we at the Riksbank would like to contribute to such integration being carried out. Not least as a small country, it is important that we actively work for openness and free trade. It is a good Swedish trade policy tradition that we should apply here as well. I will mention two, partly interrelated areas, where we in the Riksbank have been active. One concerns central banks' lending against collateral in foreign securities and the other concerns the future EU payment system TARGET. The issue of "foreign collateral" has been discussed both in a Nordic context and in eu circles; in the latter case, it is obviously necessary from an EMU perspective to be able to use paper that exists in one part of the Union, say Germany, to get credit in, for example, the French Central Bank. Apart from the purely technical problems of such management, which of course exist in considerable proportions, it is difficult, in my view, to see any fundamental problems of principle with such arrangements - with or without monetary union. Nevertheless, this has been considered very problematic in some quarters. With regard to the arrangements within EMU, for example, the papers must, as an absolute minimum requirement, be issued within the EEA. The question one can then ask is what is interesting when taking collateral for a loan. Surely this must be the creditworthiness of the issuer, rather than in which country he happens to have his estates or where he has chosen to carry out an issue. But such an approach, we have noticed, often meets with intense resistance. With regard to the TARGET system, the ECB has decided that while banks in the NON-EMU EU countries will be allowed to participate in the system, access to intraday credit in the system will be restricted. Since intraday credit from central banks is the "lubricant" for payment flows in this type of system, this will in that case make it more difficult and expensive for the Swedish banks to use the system. The official argument for this is that intrdagskredit to "outs" could in some situations complicate monetary policy within EMU. For our part, it seems to us that we have been able to show that this argument is not tenable - firstly, such monetary policy effects are unlikely, secondly, they are perfectly manageable should they arise after all. Nevertheless, this has been maintained, which amounts to a defacto protectionism which is deplorable. If our analysis of the monetary policy aspects of intraday credit holds, then from this point of view there is really no fundamental reason to restrict foreign participation in a national payment system. As I mentioned earlier, I also do not see any fundamental problem with using securities from different countries and in different currencies as collateral for such credits. As an example of the Riksbank's openness in this matter, we have chosen to accept, for example, Finnish government securities as collateral when granting credit in the RIX system. It is only to be regretted that this openness has so far not prompted any corresponding action on the part of our Finnish colleagues. Increased competition between lenders It is also likely that EMU will affect not only the financial markets but also the conditions for conducting traditional banking, such as lending for housing finance. The process of liberalisation and internationalisation we have been engaged in over the last decade is a global phenomenon rather than a European one. Nevertheless, it is clear that integration within the EU in general and EMU in particular accentuate these trends. Trends point to a continued rapid development of the financial markets, with new instruments, industry slippage and concentration of certain specialist functions. Competitive pressures in traditional banking are likely to continue to intensify at the same time as long-term demand for financial services increases and customers , whether we are talking about companies, municipalities or households - are becoming increasingly demanding. The number of "full-service" banks has already decreased while increasing their size. The trend of traditional bank deposits and lending decreases, while supply and demand for market-based instruments increases, is expected to continue. As a result of these trends, profitability in lending on the Swedish market has recently declined. With regard to housing finance, it can be stated that lending in this segment is particularly exposed to fierce competition and accompanying price pressure. This is most likely due to the fact that the specialist knowledge of the large banks about the credit situation of borrowers here is a less significant competitive advantage due to the fact that lending is carried out against collateral, the value of which can be determined using relatively objective criteria. A traditional bank's established customer contacts, local knowledge and thus an office network in the traditional sense, are thus of less importance. This makes the entry barriers for companies wanting to enter the market is relatively low, which also manifests itself in a relatively large number of players in the mortgage market. It is likely that EMU and technological development will work together to reinforce these trends further, by increasing access to customers, as well as market transparency, and the single currency facilitating price comparisons between operators from different countries. It is therefore to be expected that the mortgage market will be one of the consumer markets in the financial field most affected by EMU. With these final words, I would like to thank you for me.

Title: Five years of price stability objectives
text: Five years of price stability objective Date: 1998-02-18 Speaker: Governor Urban Be4ckstrf6m Location: Nationalekonomiska Ff6reningen Thank you for the invitation to come to the National Economic Association for the fourth time and discuss monetary policy. Over the years that have passed, I have in turn discussed "Price stability and monetary policy" (1995), "The Riksbank and monetary policy" (1996) and "Monetary policy and unemployment" (1997). The notice of today's negotiations in the Association is entitled "Five years of inflation target". It has been five years since the Riksbank's council took the decision on 14 January 1993 to direct monetary policy in our country towards a stated inflation target. The decision meant that the change in the consumer price index from 1995 onwards would be limited to 2% with a tolerance range of plus/minus 1 percentage point. For 1993 and 1994, monetary policy would focus on preventing an upturn in underlying inflation rates. The Riksbank's council made the decision under quite a lot of time pressure. Time for deeper analysis was limited. The fixed exchange rate regime had been forced to be abandoned on 19 November 1992. Although it can be said that the decision was prescient and that the new regime has essentially worked well so far, there are grounds for touching on some aspects of the monetary policy set-up after five years. In my talk this evening, I intend to address the following questions: how is the inflation target constructed? Is there any reason to change the wording of the target? How should monetary policy be conducted in order to achieve this objective? To what extent can and should the Riksbank take into account real factors such as growth and employment? Why is transparency and clarity important for monetary policy? Has the inflation target been met? Next, I will briefly look back at the monetary policy pursued to finally summarise and look to the future. The inflation target has deep historical roots Focusing monetary policy on low inflation, or price stability, is not a new idea. In fact, it was already discussed by the well-known Swedish economist Knut Wicksell. Perhaps the particularly interesting thing for us this evening about that discussion was that it was conducted here in the Economic Association and it was conducted 100 years ago. More specifically, it was on April 14, 1898, that Wicksell gave a talk on "The Importance of Money Interest for Commodity Prices." He suggested that monetary policy should focus on price stability. The speech was based on a work published in German, but the lecture in the Economics Association was the first time he presented his ideas to a Swedish audience. Wicksell began his speech with the following words: "Many words are not needed to prove that the exchange value of money or, which is the same, only from the opposite side, the general level of the commodity price is maintained at such a fixed and immutable height. After all, money is and is becoming for every day more and more the gauge of all values, the basis of all wealth juices: all goods are exchanged for money, and not only this, but we produce only to exchange and exchange for moneys. What, then, could be more difficult than that what constitutes the yardstick of all else remains immutable in size?" Wicksell continued, pointing out that it was "fairly certain, that all interests would best be in agreement, if the equal for the value was kept as meticulously unchanging as the equal for measure, goal, and value." Wicksell's important point, which is also taken into account in today's inflation target, was that it is equally important to avoid both inflation and deflation. Over time, his views came to play a central role in economic research and in monetary policy in many ways, including in Sweden. Just over thirty years later, when Sweden was forced to leave the gold standard in September 1931, the Swedish government and the Riksbank declared that the goal of monetary policy would be to "preserve the domestic purchasing power of the Swedish krona with available means". With this step, the Riksbank became the first central bank to openly make price stabilization the norm for monetary policy. Against this background, it can be said that the Riksbank's decision in January 1993 to introduce an inflation target rested on a solid Swedish tradition. That inflation in Sweden was about. 2 percent on average per year between 1830 and 1970 further reinforces that conclusion. I do not think that replacing the word inflation target with price stability objective can be said to distort the language, given measurement errors and other things that the consumer price index may contain. I also think that the word price stability objective has a better connotation and more clearly shows what today's objective is really about. It is not a question of achieving a certain rate of inflation, but rather of avoiding both inflation and deflation, i.e. achieving and maintaining price stability. I shall therefore in future use the term price stability objective instead of inflation target. Sweden is not alone in using an explicit price stability objective. This is also the case in, for example, New Zealand, Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom. But even in the vast majority of other industrialised countries, monetary policy is now geared towards price stability, even if it is done with the help of so-called . intermediate or intermediate objectives such as fixed exchange rates or monetary targets. In particular, a growing consensus in three areas has led to an increasing number of countries now focusing their monetary policies on long-term price stability. Firstly, it has come to the realisation that there does not appear to be a stable long-term exchange ratio between inflation and real factors such as output and employment. Monetary policy can only influence the level of inflation in the long term. Secondly, most agree that, to the extent that monetary policy has any bearing on real quantities at all, the correlation seems to be that price stability itself can make a positive contribution to long-term productivity growth. Thirdly, it is considered that too short-term economic policy tends to lead to higher inflation in the trend. At first glance, monetary policy on the basis of a price stability objective seems relatively simple. It is basically a question of regulating the amount of final means of payment, using the policy rate, so that it remains at a 'moderate' level in relation to the value of the country's production. But the inflation process is complicated and the effects of monetary policy on the economy operate with long and variable lags. The Central Bank thus has only indirect control over inflation. It raises a lot of questions about the practical construction of the price stability objective. The design of the price stability objective Starting When choosing a target variable, a measure that covers as much as possible of price formation in the economy should be used. The measure should thus be related to the welfare of individuals and households and be well known. It should further be published regularly with little backlog and not revised too often. This suggests that the consumer price index or any variant of it is preferable to other available measures, such as the GDP deflator or the producer price index. However, monetary policy measures have limited scope to immediately counteract temporary price movements resulting from disturbances of various kinds, such as sudden changes in the exchange rate, indirect taxes and subsidies, commodity prices, etc. Drastic monetary policy measures would possibly have an effect, but at the same time they would destabilise the real economy. It is therefore undesirable to counteract the direct effects of such disturbances, unless they affect inflation expectations and thus have a more lasting impact on the domestic price formation process. Nor is it reasonable for monetary policy to seek to counteract the impact of interest rates on, for example, consumer prices. In that case, it would mean that monetary policy would, so to speak, chase its own tail. Viewed over an entire business cycle, the effects of interest rates on measured inflation cancel each other out. Thus, an ideal target variable should reflect the long-term and trend inflation process, but not necessarily temporary price movements. However, it is difficult to separate temporary price movements from more sustained inflationary impulses in different measures. Therefore, it can be difficult to know in advance which measure, which in retrospect, turns out to be the most appropriate. A further aspect of the choice of target variable is that it should also allow for opportunities for international price comparisons. Why KPI? The Riksbank originally chose the Consumer Price Index (CPI) as its target variable. I have already established that the CPI, or some variation on this measure, is preferable to other already available price indices. The public would not recognize themselves if a measure of the underlying inflation rate were chosen instead, as it requires special calculations to separate out temporary price movements. On the other hand, it is important to analyze different measures of underlying inflation in inflation reports, etc., in order to deepen the understanding and knowledge of temporary effects in the inflation process. Steps in this direction were taken in the December Inflation Report when a special section on the temporary effects was introduced and by publishing a special chart for the forecast for one of the various measures of underlying inflation, which the Riksbank is working on. As I said, it is the long-term and trend inflation process that should be at the forefront when monetary policy is set up. Nor is there any reason at present to switch to the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), the aim of which is to become an internationally comparable measure of inflation. The harmonisation work has not been completed. The short history of the HICP also means that it is fairly unknown and has only been used to a limited extent as a measure of inflation so far. Why 2%? In 1993, the Riksbank chose a price stability target of 2 per cent. There is no scientific evidence that precisely 2% - and not, for example, 1.5% or 2.5% - is the most appropriate level for a price stability objective. However, not choosing a target lower than 2% can be justified by the following reasons. First, there are many indications that inflation as measured by the CPI overestimates actual inflation in a number of countries. Secondly, a price stability objective that is too low can cause problems if nominal wages are sluggish downwards, as is probably the case. Adjustments following economic disruptions are then made unnecessarily through reduced employment, as this is the only way to reduce the overall wage bill if inflation is permanently non-existent. Not choosing a price stability objective above 2% is linked to: inflation is harmful to the economy the higher it gets. In addition, the countries of Europe are striving for an inflation rate at that level. In addition, there is a growing consensus among economists as to what approximate level of inflation it is reasonable to aim for. The well-known economist and now deputy head of the International Monetary Fund Stanley Fischer has summed up the prevailing view as follows: "These arguments point to a target inflation rate in the 1 to 3 percent range; more specifically, they suggest that inflation should be targeted at about 2 percent, to stay within a range of 1 to 3 percent per year." Toleransintervall An important characteristic of a target variable is its controllability. A high level of controllability means that monetary policy can be designed so that the deviation of the target variable from the target is small. Controllability is determined by the occurrence and extent of different types of disturbances and the ability of monetary policy to counteract these disturbances. The degree of controllability should determine the width of the tolerance range. Here, the person formulating tolerance ranges is faced with a difficult trade-off. On the one hand, a wide range of tolerances means that monetary policy can be conducted with great flexibility. Temporary inflation impulses can easily be let through without the central bank having to explain this in detail. Other types of disruptions that more permanently affect inflation upwards or downwards do not need to trigger rapid and strong reactions. There is, however, another side, which weighs heavily, especially when it comes to establishing confidence in the low-inflation regime, and which speaks in the other direction. A wide tolerance range can be perceived as the central bank attaching little importance to achieving its goal. As a result, inflation expectations may set themselves at a higher level than desirable. The costs of maintaining long-term price stability will be greater in terms of growth and employment when expectations deviate from the target. A high degree of flexibility in monetary policy in the short term is generally perceived as a positive thing. The central bank does not have to act so "strictly" with the key interest rate. But paradoxically, over time, this flexibility may force a higher policy rate than otherwise as a result of the public building expectations into its behavior of higher inflation than that pursued by the central bank. There are currently no strong arguments in favour of changing the tolerance limit. The undercutting of the tolerance limit that has occurred in recent years has essentially been the result of temporary effects. The period of price stability objectives has been too short to draw firm conclusions on the verifiability of the target variable. However, it is important to clarify that the tolerance range indicates the range within which the target variable is normally expected to move and that its purpose is to indicate how controllable the target variable is. Nevertheless, it cannot be ruled out that inflation may still fall outside the range. In such cases, it is particularly important that the Riksbank clearly declares its view of the causes and how inflation should be brought back to its target. How should the evaluation take place? One issue related to the choice of width of the tolerance range is the length of the period of time over which the achievement of the objectives is to be evaluated ex post. The Riksbank has previously said that this should be done in an "annual perspective". One way to increase the likelihood of goal achievement is to extend the time period over which the goal achievement is to be evaluated. It is easier to keep average inflation close to the price stability objective over, for example, a two-year period than over a one- year period mainly because temporary disturbances are evened out. However, one disadvantage of extending the evaluation period is that the role of the price stability objective as an "anchor" for inflation expectations may decrease. Extending the evaluation horizon thus has similar advantages and disadvantages as widening the width of the tolerance range. The conclusion is that the evaluation of the price stability objective should continue to take place in a slightly longer, "annual" perspective. However, there is reason to clarify this concept. The evaluation need not be limited to calendar years. One possibility is to advance the horizon so that the evaluation always concerns a continuous moving average of the twelve-month figures over the last twelve months, regardless of whether these constitute a calendar year or not. The inflation reports should be used to evaluate the monetary policy pursued on an ongoing basis. Charts highlighting how well the target has been achieved will be published. At the same time, the previous developments and the degree of achievement of goals will be commented on in particular. This should provide a good basis for the monetary policy discussion. Is the real economy taken into account? The fact that the Central Bank is being given the task of striving for low inflation should not be understood as meaning that this is the only and ultimate objective of the entire economic policy. The reason why the Central Bank is given this task is that low inflation is a means of achieving the broader and more general objectives of economic policy as a whole. Monetary policy pursued on the basis of a price stability objective is sometimes criticised for not taking into account real variables such as growth and employment. Fundamentally, however, it is wrong to say that monetary policy ignores the real economy even if it has price stability as its objective. A policy guided by a price stability objective takes indirect account of growth and resource utilisation in the economy in a number of ways. A clear example of this is that the policy aims to achieve the 2% target. This means that avoiding inflation is as important as it is avoiding deflation. Since it is usually resource utilisation in the economy that controls the underlying inflation process, this means that monetary policy almost automatically seeks to avoid resource utilisation falling to low levels, as well as rising in a way that risks inflation picking up. Over time, the conditions are thus normally created for the economy to be able to expand along its long-term growth trajectory. The choice of the steering horizon is also important for the development of resource utilisation in the economy and the degree of variation in growth or demand in the short term. The steering horizon is a forward-looking concept that relates to the long-term orientation of monetary policy to achieve the price stability objective. A too short steering horizon means that substantial changes in the policy rate may be required to reach the target. These sharp changes in interest rates could result in undesirably large variations in growth and employment and risk making monetary policy appear too jerky. On the other hand, while an excessively long steering horizon may lead to greater short-term stability in growth and employment, inflation may vary more. This, in turn, could weaken confidence in low-inflation policy and lead to the policy rate being higher over time than is otherwise necessary. Although there is no long-term exchange relationship between the level of inflation rates, on the one hand, and growth and employment, on the other, it is quite clear that there is a choice between the variation in inflation and the variation in developments in the real economy. The very concept of a steering horizon is an expression of consideration for real factors such as growth and employment. Seeking to achieve the price stability objective on a fairly short horizon requires sharp changes in interest rates and rapid shifts in monetary policy. There are several reasons for choosing a longer horizon instead and taking a gradual adaptation of Monetary policy. Against this background, the Riksbank has chosen a steering horizon that is one to two years ahead. In line with this, we analyse the inflation outlook in the inflation reports essentially in the same perspective. In the event of a sharp supply shock in the form of, for example, a large-scale rise in international crude oil prices, it could also be necessary to extend the steering horizon. Even a financial disruption somewhere in the world could have the effect of temporarily putting inflation outside the tolerance range. Then, however, the Riksbank must clearly justify how and in what term inflation can be expected to return to its target. Otherwise, there is a risk that inflation expectations and the inflation process will be affected. An open Riksbank is important A major advantage of a monetary policy geared towards a clearly defined price stability objective is that it can be combined with openness regarding the Riksbank's actions. It becomes relatively clear how the policy works, which should facilitate efforts to get the public to support the goal. Market participants can get a clear picture of what governs the Riksbank's actions. The price stability objective is a means of stabilising expectations of the conduct of monetary policy. Therefore, transparency is important in order to make monetary policy work effectively. A lack of transparency and clarity makes it more difficult for inflation expectations to adjust to the target. This, in turn, can make it more difficult to achieve high and stable growth. Against this background, the Riksbank has worked for greater transparency in recent years. Some of the work is conducted internally. The better the basis for analysis of the policy, the easier it will be to formulate, justify and explain the policy. That is why the Riksbank invests resources in research and advanced investigative work. But the Riksbank also works in various ways with external activities aimed at increasing transparency and knowledge of the bank and its policies. This has been expressed, among other things, in the form of participation in open committee hearings in the Riksdag, inflation reports, speeches, articles, discussions and various forms of seminars and publication of expert memoranda. The work has gradually created greater insight into how monetary policy works among both market participants and the wider public. The surveys that the Riksbank continuously commissions show, gratifyingly, that the Swedish people support for the price stability objective is very good and that a majority on the whole supports the monetary policy stance. The demands for transparency will increase even more in the future. This is linked to the Riksbank's increased independence. Five political parties want to legislate on the price stability objective and increase the Riksbank's independence. However, the latter is something that in the general discussion is sometimes misinterpreted by talking about the Riksbank becoming "independent". The Riksbank will continue to be the central bank of the kingdom, an authority under the Riksdag. Increased independence and clear delegation to the Riksbank place high demands on the possibility of transparency and evaluation of the bank's operations. The structure of monetary policy must be seen as legitimate. This means that the process towards greater transparency should continue to evolve as far as is reasonable and possible. For example, there are grounds for considering whether the minutes of the meetings of the new Executive Board should not be open, even if with a certain time lag. It is an arrangement that already exists in a slightly different way in the US and in the UK and that, at least so far, seems to be working well. Whether such a system should be enshrined in law or tested by the new Executive Board is a question that the Riksbank's principal, the Riksdag, has to decide on. Has the goal been met? An additional advantage of an explicit price stability objective is that the monetary policy pursued can be evaluated. The evaluation should therefore be carried out in a slightly longer, "annual perspective". One possibility is to make use of averages of rolling twelve-month CPI figures, see Chart 1. In addition, this chart provides a measure of "underlying inflation", calculated in the same way. Chart 1 shows that underlying inflation fell gradually over the course of 1993 and 1994, in line with the target set by the council for those years. Since the target formally came into force in 1995, inflation, as measured by the CPI, has averaged 1.5%. The outcome during these three years is thus relatively close to the target and well within the tolerance range. However, inflation, measured as a rolling average, fell below the lower tolerance threshold in 1997. It can therefore be said that the Riksbank did not meet its price stability objective during this year. At the same time, it is important to recognise that the deviation from the target is almost exclusively linked to the existence of clearly identifiable temporary effects. This is evident from the evolution of underlying inflation. This is also evidenced by the fact that, as expected, actual inflation has risen rather rapidly in recent times as the temporary effects have gradually begun to disappear from the twelve-month figures. Actual inflation has thus moved closer to the underlying one. There has been a discussion about whether the Riksbank acts symmetrically or not. In other words, is it as important to avoid exceeding the target as it is to be undercut? The answer to that question is a categorical yes. The Riksbank aims to achieve inflation at 2 per cent. Nothing more and nothing less. Since it is easy to evaluate monetary policy, it is in practice impossible for the Riksbank to be asymmetrical in the long run in its view of the price stability objective. If so, it would be revealed afterwards. After only three years of price stability objective policy, it is, of course, too early to finally evaluate the policy. However, when the impact of temporary effects is taken into account, it is difficult to push home the thesis that the Riksbank would have acted asymmetrically. Chart 1: Actual and underlying inflation in an "annual perspective" 1993-1997 Running average of rolling twelve-month figures (see word file) Note: The chart shows one of several measures of underlying inflation that the Riksbank is working on. The definition in this measure is CPI excluding indirect taxes and subsidies, interest costs for own homes and prices of goods and services that are mainly imported. It is usually called domestic underlying inflation, UNDINH. In this context, the idea of accounting for UNDINH as a measure of underlying inflation is not to elevate its role or that the measure would always be the best measure of underlying inflation. The reason for using a measure that corrects the prices of imported goods is that the krona's share price fluctuations have mainly been due to rapid changes in confidence in budget consolidation. One problem with the measure, however, is that more long-term structural effects stemming from trade are eliminated. Developments in 1996 and 1997 show that inflation, as measured by the CPI, can sometimes deviate from the target and even fall outside the tolerance range. The important thing then is that the Riksbank gives an explanation for what happened. In such a situation, we must make it likely that inflation will gradually return to 2%. If it is temporary effects that are behind the deviation, the Riksbank should show this. Normally, as I have said before, it should not affect the monetary policy pursued unless inflation expectations are affected. If a deviation from the target - and the tolerance range - is due to more lasting effects, the policy rate should be used to steer inflation back to the target, within the time period in which monetary policy operates. Perspectives on monetary policy in recent years In the five years since the price stability objective was decided, the primary task of monetary policy has been to establish credibility for the price stability objective and for the new regime. The degree of credibility of the price stability objective depends on what to the public's confidence that inflation rates will be permanently around the target. Lack of credibility takes various forms. Firstly, monetary policy must be tighter than would otherwise be necessary, and resource utilisation in the economy consequently lower, in order to counter the inflationary impulses caused by high inflation expectations. Secondly, a lack of credibility means that the scope for stabilising real factors such as production is limited. Attempts in this direction may be perceived as the central bank placing less emphasis on the price stability objective in a medium- and long-term perspective. This, in turn, can further weaken credibility, drive up long-term interest rates, have a negative impact in contract negotiations, etc. If the central bank nevertheless chooses to ignore credibility problems and pursues an expansionary monetary policy that leads to exceeding the target, it will be even more difficult in the future to overcome inflation expectations. In view of the real economic costs of a lack of credibility, it is essential that inflation expectations are brought into line with the price stability objective as quickly as possible. Figure 2 shows inflation and inflation expectations of workers' organisations in recent years. In 1995, they projected an inflation rate of up to 4% per annum for the next five years. Expectations for other groups showed similar results. Since then, inflation expectations have gradually moved more in line with the target and credibility has consequently increased. Of course, it is not possible to draw precise conclusions about the level of inflation expectations on the basis of surveys. At the same time, there are plenty of other indications to support the view that inflation expectations were high at first and then gradually approaching the target. The trend in long-term interest rates and implicit forward rates relative to other countries is two such. The higher outcomes of the 1995 wage round and the start of the negotiations that are now being conducted with slightly lower outcomes are yet another, etc. In recent years, it has been necessary to focus policy on gradually strengthening the credibility of the new regime. It has been a task for monetary policy, but also, of course, for economic policy in general. Confidence in the work on the adjustment of central government finances has had a decisive impact on the conditions for monetary policy at various stages. The five-party agreement on the Riksbank's future position has also been important. Figure 2: Inflation and inflation expectations of workers' organisations (See word file) The lack of credibility at the beginning of the period made it necessary to conduct a tight monetary policy. It was important that demand growth was moderate, with the aim of raising resource utilisation in the economy at a leisurely pace. In the event of a faster upturn, inflation expectations of around 4% could have led to price stability objectives being exceeded. The period of lack of credibility would then probably have been longer than it actually was, with a negative impact on interest rates and long-term expansion in the economy. Summary In conclusion, I think that the regime with price stability objectives and variable exchange rate has worked well so far. There is also no reason today to rephrase the case in any respect. In 1993 and 1994, the underlying inflation rate fell, which was in line with the objective set by the council. Since the target formally came into force, inflation, as measured by the CPI, has averaged 1.5 percent per year. The outcome is thus relatively close to the target and well within the tolerance range. However, inflation fell below the lower tolerance point, mainly in 1997. It can thus be said that the Riksbank thus did not meet the target during this period. At the same time, it is important to realize that the deviation is almost exclusively related to clearly identifiable temporary effects. In the five years since the setting of the price stability objective, the primary task of monetary policy has been to give credibility to the price stability objective. In Europe, for example, the formation of monetary union is currently underway, which Sweden has chosen to remain outside for the time being.
