Title: Financial Crises the Swedish experience
text: Financial Crises: the Swedish experience Datum: 1998-11-07 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Backstrom Plats: The Trilateral Commission Thank you for the invitation to talk about financial crises in general and the Swedish experience in particular. What is a financial crisis? Financial crises and their subset, banking crises, have become worldwide phenomena during the 1990s. Up until a few years ago, views on financial crises were split into two polar campsthose associated with monetarists versus a more eclectic view. Monetarists have linked financial crises with bank panics. They stress the importance of banking panics because they view them as a major source of contractions in the money supply which, in turn, have led to severe contractions in aggregate economic activity. Monetarists do not view as real financial crises events in which there is no potential for a banking panic and a resulting sharp decline in the money supply, despite a sharp decline in asset prises. An opposite, but more traditional, view defines what constitutes a real financial crises in much broader terms. In this view, financial crises either involve sharp declines in asset prices, failures of both large financial and non-financial firms, deflation or disinflation, disruptions in foreign exchange markets, or some combination of all of these. The problem with the monetarist view of financial crises is that it is extremely narrow, focusing exclusively on bank panics and their affect on the money supply. At the same time, the more traditional definition is too broad and imprecise. However, in recent years, the asymmetric information analysis which has been applied in order to understand the structure of the financial system and the rationale for bank regulation has also been used to develop a theory of banking and financial crises. To understand this analysis we must look at what banks do. The business concept is based largely on the banks' ability to reduce the uncertainty about borrowers and their chances of meeting commitments. Sound borrowers must first be distinguished from others, followed by continuous monitoring of well-founded credit assessments. The problem is that a borrower usually has better information about the potential returns and risks associated with his planned investment projects than does the lender. Asymmetric information creates problems in the financial system in two basic ways: before and after the transaction has been executed. In order to do a proper job of screening good borrowers from bad, banks need a stable environment in the economy and in financial markets. Any negative effects of the existence of asymmetric information can also be limited by the banks requiring collateral for the loans they do provide. If banks cease to be able to reduce the uncertainty associated with the lending process and improve, or make up for, the asymmetric information, then they may refrain from providing credits. In such a situation banks may simply no longer be in a position to distinguish between good and bad borrowers and therefore could stop lending at all. This cuts off the economy's supply of liquidity and hits lending to consumers and investors as well as to other banks. A contraction of the credit supply a credit cruncharises and may have contagious effects on the real economy, in that consumers and firms can no longer obtain the credits their plans require. GDP falls and unemployment rises. This analysis suggests that, in order to define a financial crisis we should look for events in the economy that make the screening process difficult for banks. Such events could be sharp declines or surges in asset prices, sharp swings in market interest rates and major failures of non-financial institutions. But of course, not all declines in asset prices or increases in interest rates constitute real financial crises. We need additional information to help detect a situation where banks have difficulties in distinguishing between good and bad borrowers and therefore have a tendency to cut down their lending activities. One such signal is the spread between interest rates for low and high-quality borrowers. In a situation where banks experience difficulties in distinguishing between good and bad borrowers, one should expect a rise in interest rates to borrowers about whom it is genuinely difficult to obtain reliable information. This is precisely what we have seen in various segments of financial markets this autumn, not least the rate spreads between sovereign debt in industrial countries and in emerging markets. But many other spreads between interest rates for high and low-quality borrowers have also been rising and that has been a source of serious concern for policy makers all over the world. Spreads were also high during the Swedish crisis in the early 1990s. While the current high spreads seem to be exaggerated, I should like to point out that the earlier spreads may have been too low, not reflecting actual risk. The Swedish crisis - what happened? Let me now turn to the Swedish crisis in the early 1990s. The economic problems in Sweden should be seen in their historical context. For several reasons, economic growth in Sweden had been relatively weak ever since the beginning of the 1970s. Following the collapse of the Bretton Woods system, the creation of a stable macroeconomic environment turned out to be difficult. Wage formation functioned badly, fiscal policy was unduly weak and in addition structural problems were gradually making more and more of an impact. Credit market deregulation during the first half of the 1980s, necessary in itself, meant that monetary conditions became more expansionary. This coincided, moreover, with an already rising level of economic activity and relatively high inflation expectations. In the absence of a more restrictive economic policy to parry all this, the freer credit market led to a rapidly growing stock of private sector debt, of which a large part was short-term debt in foreign currency channelled through the banking system. Real aggregate asset prices increased substantially. A speculative bubble was generated. Step by step the Swedish economy became increasingly vulnerable to shocks. During 1990 matters came to a head. Competitiveness had been eroded by the relatively high inflation in the late 1980s, resulting in an overvalued currency. This caused exports to weaken and meant that the fixed exchange rate policy began to be questioned, leading to periods with relatively high nominal interest rates. Asset prices began to fall and economic activity turned downwards. A tidal wave of bankruptcies was a heavy blow to the banking sector. Various spreads between interest rates for low and high-quality borrowers had been rising. Accordingly, signs of a real financial crises were emerging. Management of the crisis When a serious financial crisis threatens to develop it is important both to avoid a widespread failure of banks and to bring about a macroeconomic stabilisation. The two are interdependent. A collapse of much of the banking system would aggravate the macroeconomic situation, just as failure to stabilise the economy would accentuate the banking crisis. Accordingly, this requires both macroeconomic measures and measures to maintain the banking system's solvency and liquidity in order to prevent large segments of the banking system from failing on account of acute financing problems. In September 1992 the Government and the Opposition jointly announced a general guarantee for the obligations of the whole of the banking system. This broad political consensus was, I believe, of vital importance and made the prompt handling of the financial crisis possible. The bank guarantee provided protection from losses for all creditors except shareholders. The Government's mandate from Parliament was not restricted to a specific sum and its hands were also very free in other respects. This necessitated close co-operation with the political opposition in the actual management of the banking problems. The decision was of course troublesome and far-reaching. Besides involving difficult considerations having to do, for example, with the cost to the public sector, it raised such questions as the risk of moral hazard. However, the political system concluded that in the event of widespread failures in the banking system, the Swedish economy would suffer major repercussions. There was simply no choice. One way of limiting moral hazard problems was to engage in tough negotiations with the banks that needed support and to enforce the principle that losses were to be covered in the first place with the capital provided by shareholders. A separate authority, the Bank Support Authority, was set up to administer the bank guarantee and manage the banks that landed in a crisis and faced problems with solvency, though the crucial decisions about the provision of support were ultimately a matter for the Government. It was up to the central bank to supply liquidity on a relatively large scale at normal interest and repayment terms but not to solve problems of bank solvency. Collateral was not required for the loans to banks, neither intraday nor overnight. The banking system was free to obtain unlimited liquidity by drawing on its accounts with the central bank. The bank guarantee meant that the solvency of the central bank was not at risk. In order to offset the loss of credit lines in foreign currency to Swedish banks, during the height of the crisis the Riksbank also lent large amounts in foreign currency. Thus, the central bank assumed the role of provider of liquidity, not only in domestic currency but also in foreign currency. Banks applying for support had their assets valued by the Bank Support Authority, using uniform criteria. The banks were then divided into categories, depending on whether they were judged to have only temporary problems as opposed to no prospect of becoming viable. Knowledge of the appropriate procedures was built up by degrees, not least with the assistance of people with experience of banking problems in other countries. The Swedish Bank Support Authority chose to disclose expected loan losses and to assign realistic values to real estate and other assets. This method was consistent with other basic principles for the bank support, such as the need to restore confidence. Since the acute crisis had been triggered by difficulties in obtaining international finance, great pains were taken to give a transparent picture of how the crisis was being managed so as to gain the confidence of Sweden's creditors. This applied both to the account of the magnitude of the banking problems and to the content of the bank guarantee. Various informative projects were arranged for this purpose throughout the world. In Sweden, too, considerable efforts were made to legitimise the measures and their costs. The banking problems did arouse a lively debate in Swedish society but the work could still be done in broad political consensus, which was a great advantage. The bank guarantee was terminated in 1996 and replaced with a deposit guarantee that is financed entirely by the banks. With regard to macroeconomic policy, the following could be said. In the early stage of the crisis, the automatic stabilisers in the government budget probably helped to lessen the contraction of GDP. This meant that business profits and household disposable income were sustained relatively well. But it also entailed, after a while, a massive increase in the budget deficit and this in turn generated new problems, which of course had to be tackled when the acute crisis was over. Furthermore, monetary conditions were given a stimulatory turn. That also helped to stabilise both the economy and the banking system. Lower market rates eased the fall in asset prices, lightened the burden of servicing private sector debt and mitigated the negative impact on the financial system. Rescuing the banking sector was necessary to avoid a collapse of the real economy. But it was also necessary to stabilise the economy directly through macroeconomic measures. Similarities with other countries experiencing financial crises There are several aspects of the build-up to the crisis in the Swedish case that are worth highlighting and that were similar to the situation in Southeast Asian countries. Current-account deficits had been financed with short-term loans mediated via the banking system in connection with rapidly growing credit. Weakening economic activity, falling asset prices and rising lending losses eroded confidence in the banking system and spread uncertainty among foreign creditors. This resulted in tendencies towards a shortage of foreign liquidity in the banking system, capital outflows and downward pressure on exchange rates. The lender of last resort mechanism depends on the ability of the central bank to provide sufficient liquidity to the banks. However, when the liquidity needs are in foreign currency, the central bank may be unable to fulfil its role as lender of last resort due to a lack of adequate foreign reserves. This could lead to the threat of an outright default for the whole banking system and a severe financial crises. The Swedish central bank managed to provide the banking system with liquidity in foreign currency. This was not the case to the same extent in Southeast Asia. Thus, the crisis developed differently in those countries. They had to turn to the International Monetary Found for assistance. One important factor that stimulates short-term capital inflow is a fixed exchange rate regime. Both Sweden and the countries in Southeast Asia had fixed exchange rate regimes at the time of the build-up to the crisis. Fixed exchange rate regimes mean that the central bank seemingly absorbs the risks of exchange rate movements on behalf of the investors, which tends to encourage capital inflows, especially with short-term maturity. But should the currency have to depreciate, large credit losses will affect the banks. Conclusions Allow me now to summarise what I consider to be the most important lessons of a financial crisis: 1. Prevent the conditions for a financial crisis The primary conclusion from the experience of financial crisis is, of course, that various steps should be taken to ensure that the conditions for a financial crisis do not arise. Fundamentally, this is a matter of conducting a credible economic policy focused on price stability. This provides the prerequisites for a monetary policy reaction to excessive increases in asset prices and credit stocks that would be liable to boost inflation and avoids the type of speculative climate that paves the way to a financial crisis. In this respect a floating exchange rate regime is helpful in that it gives monetary policy an active roll. In contrast to a fixed exchange rate regime, it does not encourage the inflow of short-term and volatile capital by the central bank absorbing the exchange rate risk. Looking back, it can be said that if various indicators that commonly form the background to a financial crisis had been followed systematically, then incipient problems could have been detected early on. That in turn could have influenced the conduct of economic policy so that Sweden's financial crisis was contained or even prevented. In Sweden's case the supervisory authority was not prepared for the new environment that emerged after credit market deregulation. The lesson from this is that much must be required of a supervisor operating in an environment characterised by deregulated markets. 2. If a financial crisis does occur In a sense all major financial crises are unique and therefore difficult to avoid or prepare for. Once a crisis is about to develop, however, there are some important lessons to learn concerning its handling. If an economy is hit by a financial crisis, the first important step is to maintain liquidity in the banking system and prevent the banking system from collapsing. For the management of Sweden's banking crisis, the political consensus was of major importance for the payment system's credibility among the Swedish public as well as among the banking system's creditors throughout the world. The prompt and transparent handling of banking sector problems is also important. The terms for recapitalisation should be such as to avoid moral hazard problems. It is important both to avoid a widespread failure of banks and to bring about macroeconomic stabilisation. The two are interdependent. The collapse of much of the banking system would aggravate the macroeconomic weaknesses, just as failure to stabilise the economy would accentuate the banking crisis.

Title: Financial markets and EMU
text: Financial markets and EMU Datum: 1997-10-21 Talare: Vice riksbankschef Stefan Ingves Plats: IBC i Stockholm Today, I will not go into any detail about our payment system and the measures being taken to adapt it to Target. That would be a rather time-consuming task. Moreover, these issues and facts are quite well documented in papers published both by the EMI and by ourselves. Concerning the RIX-system, I might add that we will shortly be publishing a booklet describing the system. Instead, I will focus on some structural developments in the financial sector in the light of the EMU. Economic integration within the EU is, in a sense, a two-sided matter: First, we have the EMU, which may be described as integration on the"macro"-level; second we have integration on the "micro" level, expressed in terms of the "single market". Of course, these two sides are interrelated; for example, EMU might well be interpreted as an important further step to a true "single market". Still, they represent somewhat different angles in approaching the European economy. Looking at the financial markets in Sweden and elsewhere in Europe and their development in recent years as well as what is likely in the years to come, it is not easy to tell to what extent changes have been and will be driven primarily by the "single market", or by the preparations for the EMU or, for that matter, by factors which are "global" rather than specific for Europe. However, I think it is fair to say that the implementation of the single market has been the most important factor, at least so far, behind the restructuring of the financial markets that we have witnessed in recent years. But I believe that the preparations for the EMU and the creation of various financial infrastructures to support the EMU such as the Target system - is playing and will play an increasingly important role as a driving force for structural change. When the EMU is in place, this completion of the Single Market is likely to boost the restructuring process even further. In Sweden, we are, as most of you know, in the midst of a restructuring of the banking sector. We have seen mergers between Swedish banks, between Swedish banks and foreign banks, between banks and mortgage institutions and between banks and insurance firms. Part of these activities can of course be seen as an aftermath of the banking crisis of the early '90s, but it is obvious that the "European perspective" in general and the EMU in particular is an important explanation behind the steps being taken. This motive has also, in most cases, been stated explicitly by the banks involved. The same process is taking place in other European countries as well, and also in other parts of the financial sector. e.g. in the case of stockexchanges and derivatives exchanges. The latter phenomenon has been observed in for example Germany, Holland and Finland. In my view, there are good reasons for the measures being taken - the EMU will lead to important changes in the business environment for European financial institutions. It is also important to note that the introduction of the Euro will affect the Swedish financial market profoundly, despite the fact that Sweden will not participate in the euro area from the start - being "out" does not mean "status-quo". The effects will be different in some respects due to the "out"- situation, but I believe the overriding structural tendencies will be largely the same among "outs" and "ins". The EMU and structural change At present, capital markets in Europe are fragmented. Domestic banks and insurance companies dominate in most countries and Sweden is no exception. The background is not just the existence of different currencies but probably still more the tendency for customers to stick to the banks they know, together with the banks' accumulated fund of knowledge about credit risks and local markets. The arguments in favour of a national base for operations will continue to apply for quite a long time after the introduction of the common currency, especially in the "retail" sector. However, in the case of corporate services - particularly for large companies - there is reason to believe that the effects may be fairly large quite soon. Over time countries with the single currency can be expected to become increasingly integrated. Since a common currency affects the very core of a financial system, this will naturally be particularly marked in the financial sector. Therefore, the large, intergrated, more transparent and more competitive european financial market we will see in the future will certainly promote a continuation of the financial markets' rapid development. This means new instruments, cross-fertilisation and a concentration of some specialist functions. It also means that competition in traditional banking is likely to be even more intense, accompanied by rising long-term demand for financial services and increasingly sophisticated customers, be they firms, local authorities or households. Full-service banks have already become fewer but larger. No doubt one can also expect a continued growth of niche banks and other financial enterprises that concentrate on a small selection of services or outlets. The downward tendency in traditional bank lending and deposits is likely to continue, accompanied by an increased supply and demand for market-based instruments. There is also reason to assume that some of the financial markets' products will be dropped and new ones introduced. These developments have been clearly evident here in Sweden over the last few years, in parallel with the considerable improvement of profitability and competetive strength within the Swedish banking sector. Today, the Swedish banks are performing very well by international standards. Taking profitability and costefficiency, to mention two examples, Swedish banks hold a top position in a European context. On account of economic convergence and a single anti-inflationary monetary policy, the monetary union will cause interest rates in high- and low-rate countries to converge. The absence of an exchange risk premium inside the euro area will also contribute to this. What will remain after the changeover process has been completed, is mainly liquidity and credit risks. With no exchange risk and a tendency for investment decisions to focus more on credit risk, it seems likely that welldeveloped and integrated European markets will be established for various types of bonds, e.g. corporate bonds and municipal bonds. Another contributory factor here is that investors will probably be interested in spreading risk by diversifying portfolios across more countries. As an "out"-country, there is a risk of not being part of this process. Therefore, our challenge will be to manage our economic policy in a way that promotes such high confidence in the market that,for example, investments in assets denominated in kronor will be regarded as attractive, not "risky". If so, we might still be part of this process, in spite of being "out". In other words, staying outside the EMU leaves no room for lax policies. Such policies will harm us not only in macroeconomic terms, but in structural terms as well. Changing the infrastructures As to the infrastructure, the institutes mainly affected are, for securities, the Stockholm Stock Exchange, OM and the VPC, while for the handling of money and payments they are the banks and the Riksbank. The fundamental practical problem for us as an "out" country, is that we have to prepare for a doubling of infrastructures in many different aspects, this will involve extra costs and thus give rise to potential problems of competition. The Swedish banks, the Stockholm Stock Exchange, the VPC and others are working actively today to seek solutions that are flexible and cost-efficient to handle this in the best possible way, but there are of course no cost-less solutions to be found. This also concerns the Riksbank, where we will have to manage two RTGS-systems - one for kronor and one for Euro, where the latter will be linked to Target. Concerning the Target, we also run a risk of de-facto discrimination i terms of a more or less restricted access to intraday liquidity i euro. Apart from this issue, I would say that in general, our payment system is fairly easy to adapt to the Target-environment, mainly because we have worked in a RTGS-concept longer than most other European central banks. However, and coming back to structural changes, it is interesting to note that the Target-project has served as a catalyst for a number of changes in the Swedish payment system. This applies to operational issues as well as policy issues. To a certain extent it also includes the technical integration from RIX towards the banks and towards the VPC. The technical integration between RIX and the banks - based on SWIFT-communication - will probably lead to a lot more payment transactions being processed in a real-time, gross mode, and in a way that is cost-efficient. In my view, this is a good example of how changes in the financial infrastructure may kick off further changes. Concerning the payments area, it should also be noted that efforts are being made to create networks on a private basis - the EBA-clearing is perhaps the most wellknown example, but there are also a number of other initiatives, for example the newly announced cooperation between a number of European banks, named "TransEuropean banking Services". As a central banker, I do not see this as some kind of unwanted competition with Target - instead, we welcome such initiatives. Target will not, and shall not, be a monopoly in the field of cross-border payments. On the securities' side there are also interesting moves towards integration, linking the different European depositories and clearing-houses together in a common network - I expect Mr Reveman from the VPC will give you more information about this later today. As I mentioned earlier, similar things are happening among e.g. the stock-exchanges in Europe. In other words, we see moves towards integration and standardisation covering the entire trading process; trade, clearing and settlement. All these changes in the infrastructure will give us all new playing fields and sometimes new roles to play. In this way it also will promote further structural change.

Title: Financial globalization
text: Financial globalization Date: 1998-03-05 Speaker: Governor Urban Be4ckstrf6m Location: Gf6teborg International Business Convention Thank you for the invitation to speak here in Gothenburg about financial globalisation. As a result of changes in communication and information technologies and the new risk management instruments and methods they have enabled, the financial system is much more comprehensive and efficient today than ever before. What we do not yet know for sure, but strongly suspect, is that the rapid financial development and its internationalization is a necessary and logical consequence of an ongoing and rapid general economic development that creates a need for new financial solutions for business and households. Economic growth in the world is facilitated by financial developments, which, however, at the same time entail increased risks. The interdependence of markets and market participants has increased significantly, both within and beyond national borders. A disturbance in a market segment or in a country can now quickly spread throughout the world economy. We have also seen financial crises develop in recent years, as a result of too rapid credit expansion in some countries, often in combination with strongly inflated prices for various types of assets such as shares and real estate. In my speech today, I will touch on some aspects of the development of the financial system and the demands it places on various decision-makers in both the private and public sectors of our economy. A financial revolution First of all, it is important to point out that the financial system has not developed for its own sake. Its purpose is to facilitate the production of and trade in goods and services. Nor is it a new creation. People have been engaged in financial transactions since the dawn of history. It is told that credits were used systematically in agriculture and in other contexts already about 3000 f.Kr. in Mesopotamia. But it was not until the 1100s that banks began to be established in Genoa, Florence and Venice, where they flourished for several centuries. Issuance of securities similar to the modern form also originated in the Italian city-states of the later Middle Ages. In Sweden, what we now call the Riksbank was founded in 1668. A few years before that, banknotes were issued in our country. These were receipts for metals deposited. The receipts - or banknotes - were used to trade with. Nor are organized exchanges for futures trading and trading other financial derivatives anything new. Similar contracts were widely traded on the Amsterdam Securities Exchange in the 1600s. The historical perspective shows that financial activities such as lending, investing in securities and other forms of financial contracts are in fact: something very old. Since the mid-1980s, the pace of financial development has accelerated significantly. It is probably no exaggeration to say that the past decade has seen the beginning of a revolutionary process of change and transformation with consequences that can still only be partially discerned. We cannot know for sure, but most of the evidence suggests that we will see a substantially larger financial system well into the 2000s. Deregulation, globalisation, advances in information technology and new methods of risk assessment and risk management have all helped to set in motion a dynamic process in which financial markets, institutions and instruments interact. As an example of the increased international financial flows, the outstanding volume of total international bond borrowing amounted to the equivalent of SEK 1,800 billion in 1980. By 1995, it had increased to SEK 18,000 billion. the outstanding volume of derivative contracts (nominal values) amounted to the equivalent of SEK 12,000 billion in 1985. In 1995, the corresponding figure was SEK 216,000 billion. the outstanding volume of the international assets of G-10 banks in 1980 amounted to the equivalent of SEK 8,000 billion. The amount in 1995 was approximately SEK 40,000 billion. The figures are just a few examples of the dramatic developments that have taken place in the international financial markets over the last ten to fifteen years. For Sweden, the turnover of kronor against foreign exchange in 1997 was just over eight times higher than in 1986, while both GDP at current prices and foreign trade only doubled. Daily turnover on the Swedish foreign exchange market in 1997 amounted to SEK 100 billion. Transactions directly linked to foreign trade accounted for only 5% of turnover. This gives a hint of the financial performance over the past decade. Globalisation takes different forms. Credit is being channelled from countries with savings surpluses to those with deficits, direct and portfolio investments are being financed, banks and financial institutions from one part of the world are establishing themselves in other parts, trading in financial instruments and derivatives is widening and deepening, etc. New role for banks The role of banks is changing. Banking is traditionally about taking deposits from the public and converting this short-term savings into lending with longer maturities to firms and households. This transformation of maturities is a very important function for the economy. Banks also often have long-term relationships with their customers. This gives them an information advantage, which increases the conditions for safer lending. However, this traditional role of banks has increasingly changed. Competition for savers' money is growing, and new forms of credit are emerging on the lending side. The information advantage is being nipped at the edge of the increased transparency brought about by the existence of financial markets. It is clear that traditional banking is under pressure from many quarters, and banks are trying to adapt to the new situation. In all likelihood, we will see continued structural changes to the banking systems and other changes over the next five to ten years. Smaller banks form larger entities both within the country and across national borders. At the same time, smaller and more specialized players are emerging and gaining ground. These are two parallel paths of development that may seem incompatible. But larger units are required for costly investments to pay off itself. At the same time, it is well known that knowledge development and innovations are often given a better breeding ground in smaller units. Competition for savings comes from many quarters. In Sweden, specialized players such as niche banks can offer slightly higher deposit rates because they run the business with often low costs. Even food and gasoline retailers now offer favorable savings instruments that attract customers. Furthermore, people increasingly prefer to invest in securities, either directly or indirectly through various forms of mutual funds. Demographic factors are often behind the development of savings. In the West, a large proportion of the population is found within the age group 45 to 60 years. These are people who often have good incomes and who want to save to ensure an income they can live on after retirement. These savers are looking for medium to long-term investments that offer a higher return than regular bank accounts. In addition, cross-border financial investment is increasing. People are increasingly investing their long-term savings in securities issued in other countries. In Sweden, this development goes hand in hand with increased holdings by foreign investors of financial instruments issued in our country. When it comes to lending, an increasing share takes place through the securities market. So far, this has mainly been done by companies financing their borrowings through issues directly on the securities market, e.g. through so-called commercial paper. With the exception of the US and, to some extent, the UK, the form of indirect 'securitisation', whereby banks grant loans and then resell them to special financial firms which then in turn issue securities against the loan capital, has not yet taken off. One reason for this may be temporary legal and regulatory barriers, and it is possible that in the future we in Europe will see an increase similar to that in the US of this form of 'securitisation'. The development of savings, and even more so lending, is stimulated by the use of derivatives. With derivatives, it is possible to hedge against risks by separating them and pricing them separately. Investors and borrowers can create exactly the combination of risk they prefer. Banks themselves can also control the risks in their portfolios by using derivatives. This does not mean that they strive for total risk elimination. Risk-taking is an essential part of banks' business operations. But the risks they take should be well calculated and controlled by bank management. In the future, it is also conceivable that different types of derivative products will help an entrepreneur to eliminate common business risks that have nothing to do with his core business. Already today, many companies protect themselves against currency and interest rate risks. We must also not forget the range of different types of insurance such as theft, fire and accident insurance, which are basically derivative products. Banks have already reacted in various ways to the rapid development. The new technologies have made it possible to offer a wide range of traditional banking services without having a large branch network in the form of offices. This has lowered the threshold for entry into the banking market and has a cost reduction, since a bank with only a few branches or a business concept based on the telephone or the Internet has a competitive advantage in certain, more standardised market segments. In Sweden, we see that the traditional banks have reacted to this by starting to offer their own "telephone" or "Internet" services. This has attracted a large number of customers in a very short time. If one moves in the opposite direction, some tendencies may favor large banks. The fixed costs, for example in the form of branch networks but also in the form of the sophisticated computer systems required to manage a global business required to become a truly international bank, are enormous. A development that has gained momentum in recent times is called "outsourcing". Financial products are becoming increasingly sophisticated and their design and production is increasingly dependent on expertise available outside the banks. Some academics point out that in the future banks may become a kind of broker with a number of independent companies attached to them that act as subcontractors and that specialize in various financial services. Banks can make money from providing these services by having a well-known and respected brand name and a large customer base. In and of themselves, banks can also themselves be specialists in some - but hardly all - financial operations. Academia is not alone in this perspective. The described phenomenon is relatively common in the real economy. Many large groups are associated with strong competition, extreme specialization, dependence on subcontractors and brand development. The development of the financial system can be seen as a spiral of innovation, where organised markets and intermediaries such as banks both compete with and complement each other. Financial markets tend to be effective institutional alternatives to banks, when products have standardised terms and prices are therefore favourable. Banks are more suitable for tailor-made products with relatively smaller volumes. As products such as futures, options, swaps and loans converted into securities are standardised and moved from banks to markets, trading in these new markets is expanding. The success of these trading markets and these standardised products, in turn, stimulates banks to create new markets and products. There is no indication that the pressure and pace of the very rapid change in the financial system will diminish in the foreseeable future. On the contrary, the pace of development seems to be accelerating. The step to the third stage of EMU will probably accentuate this. A stable environment Transformation and development processes have not always been completely painless, either in the real economy or in the financial sector, throughout history. From time to time, it has been shown that a completely stable development has been difficult to achieve. There are many episodes in the past that can easily be identified as financial crises. One example is the so-called tulip hysteria in Holland in the 1600s where, via financial speculation, hugely inflated prices for tulip bulbs suddenly plummeted. Other examples are the so-called "South Sea Bubble" of 1720, the crisis of the East India Company in 1772, the collapse of the railroad boom in the United States in 1846, the periods of banking panic in the United States in 1873, 1893 and 1907 and of course the Black Thursday in October 1929, as well as the worldwide bank collapse in subsequent years. Events today also bring with them problems and difficulties. The past decade has seen banking crises in a number of countries as well as examples of abrupt corrections in stock prices, interest rates and currencies. This has been the case in Sweden in the early 1990s, in Mexico a few years ago and in the current crisis in several countries in Asia. The countries that have financial problems in Asia show several fundamental similarities with developments both in Mexico and in Sweden. A common feature is that during a boom, there is a development in the financial area that entails a sharp increase in vulnerability. Rapid credit expansion, inflated asset values and current account deficits with consequent foreign borrowing as a consequence are some elements of this process. Sooner or later, the boom slows down and asset prices start to fall. Heavily indebted companies and households are in difficulty and banks suffer credit losses. Foreign creditors are pulling their ears and a currency crisis is further exacerbating the problems in the banking system. The internationalisation and transformation of the financial sector puts national and international authorities in a new and more complex situation. It can be said that the greater efficiency of global markets also causes mistakes to be made on through the entire financial system vastly faster than a hundred years ago. It is against this background that one should see the International Monetary Fund's (IMF's) efforts in the Asian crisis, as well as Sweden's contribution in this context. In some sense, all major financial crises are unique, and therefore it is difficult to prepare for them or avoid them. But important steps can be taken to ensure that conditions that pave the way for a financial crisis do not arise. As we have seen, serious financial problems can be triggered either directly in the banking system or via loss of international confidence with a currency crisis as a result. Basically, it is about pursuing a credible economic policy geared towards price stability. This provides the conditions for a wise monetary policy response to excessive increases in the price of various assets and increased lending that could lead to inflation and create the kind of speculation that paves the way for a financial crisis. Economic policy therefore focuses in many countries on low inflation. Sound public finances make the general economic environment more stable, which also benefits the stability of the financial system. The speed with which changes affect the financial markets makes disruption inevitable. However, the economic consequences of these disruptions will be less severe if they are not further exacerbated by financial instability resulting from variations in inflation rates. But supervisors of the financial system still face challenges. International cooperation between different authorities is extremely important, especially as problems in one country now tend to spread to other countries at a greater speed than before. One conclusion from this is that traditional regulations are still needed, but they need to be better adapted to the current situation. Financial operations have simply become so multifaceted that the traditional forms of control are no longer suitable for all situations. There is therefore a tendency to place greater responsibility for the implementation of internal and joint controls on market participants themselves. This can be arranged, for example, by requiring detailed and transparent accounting so that different actors can obtain a clear picture of a bank's financial position and risk status. For example, the lack of clear and transparent accounting rules may have exacerbated the problems in Asian countries. Centralbankernas roll Developments in the financial field are of interest to central banks because they affect their two primary responsibilities - monetary policy and the payment system. In some countries, the responsibility for the control of financial institutions lies with certain special authorities, such as in Sweden, where the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority has this role. However, it is important that central banks have the resources to independently assess the various institutions, not least in situations where the central bank, in its role as "lender of last resort", may be forced to consider liquidity support. Monetary policy is implemented through the financial system. Problems in the financial sector therefore affect the ability to effectively implement monetary policy. Banks also have a central role as the channel through which all liquidity in the economy passes. It is therefore important that the financial position of banks is stable and that they operate efficiently and reliably. Otherwise, the flow of payments may be disrupted. If the problems become so great that they pose a risk to the stability of the entire system, it is incumbent on central banks to consider liquidity support. Central banks often also have a direct and operational role in the payment system by providing a system for executing payments of large amounts. These systems are the hub of the payment system in that it handles payments between banks. Through the Riksbank's so-called RIX system, several hundred billion kronor flow daily. Conclusion In conclusion, it can be said that the financial system is undergoing a rapid change and development. The Industrial Revolution is usually considered to have begun in the 1800s in Sweden. Perhaps future historians will cite the late 1900s as the prelude to the financial revolution. This will require a great deal from different authorities. The state and the Central Bank play a fundamental role in supporting the infrastructure of the financial system in a broader sense. At the same time, rapid developments are a major challenge for all those holding different positions in the financial system in order to avoid financial disruptions with the attendant potential risks of more or less serious consequences for activity in the real economy. We in the Riksbank are focusing on the problems and concerns that may arise as a result of this rapid and far-reaching development. Other actors in the financial system should do the same. The financial revolution presents us with challenges that we must address, but it is also a revolution that, by all accounts, will be of great benefit to the future growth of the world economy.

Det beskrivna fenomenet r relativt vanligt frekommande i den reala ekonomin. Mnga stora koncerner frknippas med stark konkurrens, extrem specialisering, beroende av underleverantrer och utveckling av varumrken. Det finansiella systemets utveckling kan ses som en innovationsspiral, dr organiserade marknader och mellanhnder som banker bde konkurrerar med och kompletterar varandra. Finansiella marknader tenderar att vara effektiva institutionella alternativ till banker, nr produkterna har standardiserade villkor och priserna drfr blir frmnliga. Banker r mera lmpade fr skrddarsydda produkter med relativt sett mindre volymer. I takt med att produkter som terminer, optioner, swappar och ln omvandlade till vrdepapper standardiseras och flyttas frn banker till marknader, expanderar handeln p dessa nya marknader. Framgngen fr dessa tradingmarknader och dessa standardiserade produkter stimulerar i sin tur bankerna till att skapa nya marknader och produkter. Det finns ingenting som tyder p att trycket frn och tempot i den mycket snabba frndringen av det finansiella systemet kommer att minska inom verskdlig tid. Tvrtom verkar utvecklingstakten att accelerera. Steget till EMU:s tredje steg kommer frmodligen att accentuera detta. En stabil milj Omvandlings- och utvecklingsprocesser har inte alltid varit helt smrtfria, varken i den reala ekonomin eller i den finansiella sektorn, under historiens lopp. Frn tid till annan har det visat sig att en helt igenom stabil utveckling varit svr att stadkomma. Det finns mnga episoder i det frgngna som ltt kan identifieras som finansiella kriser. Ett exempel r den s.k. tulpanhysterin i Holland p 1600-talet dr de via finansiell spekulation enormt uppdrivna priserna p tulpanlkar pltsligt rasade. Andra exempel r den s.k. "South Sea Bubble" 1720, Ostindiska Kompaniets kris 1772, jrnvgsboomens kollaps i USA 1846, perioderna med bankpanik i USA 1873, 1893 och 1907 och naturligtvis den svarta torsdagen i oktober 1929, liksom den vrldsomspnnande bankkollapsen de pfljande ren. Hndelseutvecklingen idag fr ocks den med sig problem och svrigheter. Det gngna decenniet har sett bankkriser i ett flertal lnder liksom exempel p abrupta korrigeringar i aktiekurser, rntor och valutor. Detta har varit fallet i Sverige i brjan av 1990-talet, i Mexiko fr ngra r sedan och i den nu pgende krisen i flera lnder i Asien. De lnder som har finansiella problem i Asien uppvisar flera grundlggande likheter med utvecklingen svl i Mexiko som i Sverige. Ett gemensamt drag r att det under en hgkonjunktur sker en utveckling p det finansiella omrdet som innebr en kraftigt kad srbarhet. Snabb kreditexpansion, uppdrivna tillgngsvrden och bytesbalansunderskott med tfljande utlandsupplning som konsekvens r ngra element i denna process. Frr eller senare mattas hgkonjunkturen och tillgngspriserna brjar falla. Kraftigt skuldsatta fretag och hushll rkar i svrigheter och bankerna drabbas av kreditfrluster. Utlndska kreditgivare drar ronen t sig och en valutakris frvrrar ytterligare problemen i banksystemet. Internationaliseringen och omvandlingen av den finansiella sektorn frstter nationella och internationella myndigheter i en ny och mer komplex situation. Man kan sga att de globala marknadernas strre effektivitet ocks gr att misstag frs vidare genom hela det finansiella systemet oerhrt mycket snabbare n fr hundra r sedan. Det r mot den bakgrunden man skall se Internationella Valutafondens (IMF:s) insatser i Asienkrisen, liksom Sveriges bidrag i detta sammanhang. I viss bemrkelse r alla strre finansiella kriser unika, och drfr r det svrt att frbereda sig fr dem eller undvika dem. Men viktiga tgrder kan vidtas fr att se till att frhllanden som bddar fr en finansiell kris inte uppstr. Som vi har sett kan allvarliga finansiella problem utlsas antingen direkt i banksystemet eller via frlust av internationellt frtroende med valutakris som fljd. I grund och botten handlar det om att driva en trovrdig ekonomisk politik inriktad p prisstabilitet. Detta ger frutsttningar fr en klok penningpolitisk reaktion p verdrivna hjningar av priset p olika tillgngar och kad kreditgivning som skulle kunna leda till inflation och skapa den typ av spekulation som banar vg fr en finansiell kris. Den ekonomiska politiken inriktar sig drfr i mnga lnder p lg inflation. Sunda statsfinanser gr den allmnna ekonomiska miljn stabilare, vilket ocks gynnar stabiliteten i det finansiella systemet. Den snabbhet, med vilken frndringar pverkar de finansiella marknaderna gr att strningar blir oundvikliga. De ekonomiska konsekvenserna av dessa strningar kommer dock att bli mindre allvarliga om de inte ytterligare frvrras genom sdan finansiell instabilitet som fljer av variationer i inflationstakten. Men vervakare av det finansiella systemet str nd infr utmaningar. Internationell samverkan mellan olika myndigheter r ytterst viktig, srskilt som problem i ett land numera med strre hastighet n tidigare tenderar sprida sig till andra lnder. En slutsats av detta r att traditionella freskrifter fortfarande behvs, men de mste anpassas bttre till den nu rdande situationen. Finansiella operationer har helt enkelt blivit s mngfacetterade att de traditionella formerna fr kontroll inte lngre lmpar sig fr alla situationer. Det finns drfr en tendens att lgga ett strre ansvar fr genomfrandet av interna och gemensamma kontroller p marknadsaktrerna sjlva. Detta kan t.ex. ordnas genom att krva detaljerad och ppen redovisning s att olika aktrer kan skaffa sig en klar bild av en banks finansiella stllning och riskstatus. Bristen p tydliga och transparenta redovisningsregler kan exempelvis ha frvrrat problemen i de asiatiska lnderna. Centralbankernas roll Hndelseutvecklingen p det finansiella omrdet r av intresse fr centralbankerna drfr att den pverkar deras tv primra ansvarsomrden - penningpolitiken och betalningssystemet. I en del lnder ligger ansvaret fr kontrollen av finansinstituten hos vissa speciella myndigheter, som exempelvis i Sverige dr Finansinspektionen har den rollen. Det r emellertid viktigt att centralbanker har resurser fr en oberoende bedmning av de olika instituten, inte minst i situationer nr centralbanken i sin roll som "lender of last resort" kan bli tvungen att vervga likviditetsstd. Penningpolitiken implementeras via det finansiella systemet. Problem i finanssektorn pverkar drfr mjligheterna att p ett effektivt stt genomfra penningpolitiken. Bankerna har ocks en central roll som den kanal genom vilken all likviditet i ekonomin passerar. Drfr r det viktigt att bankernas ekonomiska stllning r stabil, och att de driver verksamheten p ett effektivt och tillfrlitligt stt. Annars kan betalningsfldet stras. Om problemen blir s stora att de utgr en risk fr hela systemets stabilitet ligger det centralbankerna att vervga likviditetsstd. Centralbanker har ofta ocks en direkt och operativ roll i betalningssystemet genom att de tillhandahller ett system fr verkstllande av betalningar av stora belopp. Dessa system r navet i betalningssystemet genom att det skter betalningar mellan bankerna. Genom Riksbankens s.k. RIX-system flyter dagligen flera hundra miljarder kronor. Avslutning Sammanfattningsvis kan sgas att det finansiella systemet undergr en snabb frndring och utveckling. Den industriella revolutionen anses vanligen ha inletts p 1800-talet i Sverige. Kanske kommer framtida historiker att ange det sena 1900-talet som inledningen till den finansiella revolutionen. Detta kommer att krva tskilligt av olika myndigheter. Staten och centralbanken spelar en grundlggande roll nr det gller stdet till det finansiella systemets infrastruktur i bredare mening. Samtidigt r den snabba utvecklingen en stor utmaning till alla dem som har olika befattningar i det finansiella systemet fr att man skall undvika finansiella strningar med tfljande potentiella risker fr mer eller mindre allvarliga fljder fr aktiviteten i realekonomin. Vi i Riksbanken inriktar oss p de problem och bekymmer som kan uppst till fljd av denna snabba och lngtgende utveckling. Andra aktrer i det finansiella systemet br gra detsamma. Den finansiella revolution stller oss infr utmaningar som vi mste ta itu med, men det r ocks en revolution som av allt att dma kommer att vara till stor nytta fr den framtida tillvxten i vrldsekonomin. Title: Financial Infrastructure  Where are we going and why?
text: Financial Infrastructure - Where are we going and why? Date: 1997-06-09 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Annual Meeting of the Stockholm Chamber of Commerce 1 Introduction Mr President, first of all let me thank you for having the opportunity to participate today and give my view on developments in the financial sector. I will talk about various issues that in one way or another concern the development of the financial infrastructure in Sweden. In a very recent essay by Prof Michael Brennan, he argues, freely interpreted, that information is the industry of the financial industry and that the systems used to process the information, accomplish business and re-disseminated information represent the digestive system of the financial sector that converts information into energy, business and profit. Since everyone has had a nutritious and tasty lunch, it is perhaps not entirely wrong to spend a moment thinking about the financial sector's digestive system. Changes in the Swedish financial market are by no means new. Over the past ten years or so, I myself have witnessed the first futures transactions in government bonds carried out, the options market has been introduced and grown very strongly, the share certificates have been abolished, floor trading on the stock exchange has disappeared, the entire stock market regulatory framework has changed radically and further rule changes are underway. Since the deregulations in Sweden came late, it has been a matter of catching up over the past decade. We have done that too, but nothing lasts forever. Today's discussion is about how we can continue to manage a good development. In the following, I will mainly touch on the issues addressed in my report Views on the Swedish financial sector's infrastructure. 2 Why a well-developed financial sector ? In the social debate, concepts that have to do with the "market" are often value-laden and there are different questions about whether it is good or less good with a well-developed financial sector in an economy. Let me be clear on this point. In my opinion, the financial markets produce services that are of great use in a modern well-functioning market economy. The products produced by the financial sector enable businesses and households to convert savings into investments while at the same time being able to deal effectively with economic uncertainties. With a little sloppy language, it is said that it is about packaging and distributing risk and return. Financial products and services serve as lubricants in the economy. Efficient financial markets help to reduce costs and reduce risks in the production of goods and services. A well-functioning financial sector thereby promotes growth and employment. With an approach like this, does it matter where the financial activity takes place? Is it good if the transactions take place in Sweden, can they not as easily take place abroad? In a technical sense, nowadays financial transactions can take place almost anywhere in the world. For example, how do you define where a transaction takes place on the Internet and does it matter? Financial transactions are not just about technology. It is equally about information, contacts between people and building knowledge about financial theology. I think it is of value to a country to s a s have these functions at home even though in a technical sense everything can be done elsewhere. I believe, for example, that a country with a liquid domestic venture capital market is probably in a better position when it comes to the supply of capital to business than countries in the absence of one. A viable financial market has important spin-off effects on employment and production in related industries, for example in the IT industry. Sweden is at the forefront of technological development and has a good level of education in the financial field. Maintaining and developing competence in the financial field is, in my opinion, valuable for the economic development of the country. It is this approach that has guided me when I have come to work with issues concerning the Swedish financial sector's infrastructure during the winter and spring. 3 Today's financial market What forces, then, affect the development of the financial sector today? One can always discuss how to describe a changing world. Here I use some factors as they have been listed in the aforementioned essay by Brennan. Globalisation For a long time, there has been a strong trend towards increased free trade in both goods and services. The freedom of establishment and trade in financial services within the EU is for Sweden a step on the way to increasingly internationalized financial markets. Competition in both financial products and transaction technology itself is increasing. Yield differentials will eventually even out and more and more people can take advantage of the diversification opportunities brought about by globalisation. Regelharmonisering In addition to the free trade trend, there has been an increasingly far-reaching harmonisation of rules in recent years, at least between developed countries. Historically, all nation-states have created regulations that contain a lot of specifically national arrangements. In parallel, in line with the increase in free trade in financial services, very intensive regulatory harmonisation work is under way. This work gradually leads to the fact that accentuated national peculiarities tend to disappear, i.e. the rules of the game are becoming increasingly uniform worldwide. This international standardisation facilitates trade in financial services while increasing the possibilities of competition. Regulatory harmonisation also raises the difficult question of how we are to develop an effective regulatory framework, both in competition with others and in cooperation with others. Technology Technological developments are making it increasingly easy to create and distribute financial services. This leads to lower barriers to entry, which in turn increases competition. Globalisation, regulatory harmonisation and technological development all point in the same direction. It is becoming easier to produce and distribute financial services and it is becoming less and less meaningful to maintain national specificities in the highly restrictive direction. Financial services have long been nationally defined and entirely locally produced. The trend points towards trade in services which, in this area, will be increasingly reminiscent of international trade in goods. In short, the trend points in the direction of increasing competition. Position of the Swedish financial sector If the perspective broadens a little beyond Kungstradgarden, there are many ways to describe how the Swedish financial sector relates to it in other countries. Here I confine myself to the EU and the comparisons in no way have the ambition to be complete or necessarily the most appropriate in describing the the position of the Swedish financial sector in Europe. However, they highlight in a fairly clear way how we relate to other markets. If you rank the total balance sheet total of credit institutions, we come in tenth place in the EU and our balance sheet total is about one tenth of the balance sheet total in Germany. Among the stock exchanges, we are in seventh place in terms of turnover, with a turnover that is about eight times greater in London. On the derivatives side, we are in fourth place after the UK, Germany and France. In terms of fund wealth in mutual funds, we are in ninth place with a fund wealth sixteen times greater in France. When it comes to issues of debt securities, we are in sixth place with an issue volume just over four times larger in Germany. With this kind of rankings, the picture is quite unambiguous. Financial markets have historically, except in a few large financial centers, been nationally defined and tied to the size of one's own economy. Given the size of the Swedish economy, we are, as the figures show, somewhere in the middle of an EU order but in most cases far below the large countries. An exception is the derivatives market, which shows that product development can pay off. In a Europe with free movement of capital and freedom of establishment, this means that there will always be competitors or potential competitors operating in a market larger than our own. This approach also concludes that the competitive picture and views on competition issues will be completely different depending on whether a strictly national or a European perspective is taken. Given the trends that I have outlined above, it is in my opinion a European or, by extension, a global perspective that one should have when discussing developments in the Swedish financial sector. This approach in no way excludes our own Swedish solutions, but one must be aware that the operating conditions for the foreseeable future will be completely different from the closed and "home-made" world that we have worked so hard to get away from over the past decade. 4 Verksamhetsforutsattningar The financial market is an important part of the national economy and, if developed, can contribute to strengthening the Swedish economy. If we have not been able to face up to competition, there is a risk that the trading of financial instruments will seek other markets. In the event of a falling turnover, the fixed cost of maintaining trading systems, etc. must be distributed among fewer transactions, costs increase and trade becomes more difficult. Such a development can then also have a negative impact on the supply of capital. Such a development is not desirable, on my basis. In order for a relatively small market such as the Swedish market to be able to hold its own, it must appear attractive in comparison with its competitors. The market must have a high level of liquidity and a well-functioning infrastructure. In order for the securities market to function, there must be an infrastructure that makes it easy for buyers and sellers to meet. This infrastructure comprises a number of interconnected parts that are interdependent in different ways. The methods, regulations and capital stock required to manage information, matching of transactions, transfer of ownership and registration and payment constitute in a broad sense what one might call the financial infrastructure. With today's technological developments, this infrastructure largely consists of computer systems of various types. The development of the financial infrastructure is therefore today very much about computer systems, who has access to the systems, how they communicate with each other and who owns them. The computer systems are then combined with the legal regulations to define the financial products and the transaction chain. When creating financial products in this world, four factors are of decisive importance meaning. - the costs of carrying out financial transactions shall not exceed those of competing marketplaces, - there must be no or as few obstacles as possible to an operator's access to the market place, This applies to different types of actors as well as between countries. -The choice of transaction technology throughout the transaction chain must be of high international standard and based on international standards. - Knowledge of financial products, product development and financial regulations must maintain a high international level. The Swedish market must simply appear to be easily accessible and efficient. If it is technically difficult and expensive to exploit the Swedish market, it is quite easy for both foreign and Swedish players to find an alternative market or for foreign investors to find substitutes for Swedish investments in their portfolios. 5 Some current issues During the past winter, I have presented my views on the development of the financial infrastructure on the part of the Ministry of Finance. The views I have come up with have their starting points to a large extent in the development picture that I have sketched above. With some regrouping and merging, it can be said that I have had views on technical issues, legal issues, ownership issues and knowledge issues. The work has since continued during the spring, among other things, on the state side, where some of these issues are addressed partly in the memorandum Strengthened supervision of stock exchanges (Ds 1997: 40) and in the Budget Bill (1996/97: 150). Technical Assessed separately in an international perspective, the four central infrastructure systems in the Swedish market, the Stock Exchange, OM, VPC and RIX, are relatively well ahead. In view of international developments, it is, in my opinion, necessary to review the technical integration between the systems in order to ensure a positive development of the Swedish financial market. Integration of the entire transaction chain - clearance, clearing, settlement and account keeping - would simplify access to the Swedish market and thus strengthen its competitiveness and also contribute to a welcome risk reduction in the financial system. High security both operationally and risk-wise is a competitive factor in itself. The trend is increasingly towards real-time transactions, which is something that affects the entire transaction chain. This, in turn, requires technical cooperation in order to be realised. On a technical level, I also think it is important to find ways of dematerialising securities so that we no longer need manual securities management (mvps). It would also be valuable to conduct a benchmark study to position the Swedish market in relation to other markets. Discussions are also under way on how to deal with all these issues. Law The Ministry of Finance has just recently in a memorandum made a number of proposals in the area of the stock exchange. I am not going to discuss all the proposals here, but only to draw your attention to two of the proposals. Firstly, a proposal is now being put forward on how to deal with disciplinary matters when carrying out stock exchange activities. This is an issue that has been discussed a lot and that did not come to be regulated the last time the stock exchange legislation was redone. For my part, I think it is good that the issue is being dealt with and that there is now a concrete proposal for how disciplinary issues should be regulated. Secondly, it is proposed that it should be possible to have direct access on a stock exchange, i.e. if you meet certain requirements, you do not need to be a securities institution to trade on the stock exchange. It is a question that can arouse strong emotions but nevertheless I think it is good that we now have a bill that allows direct access. With today's technology and the developments that are underway, direct success seems to me to be a reasonable measure. If you do not absolutely have to act through intermediaries, you create a system that clarifies the added value that intermediaries must create in order for that transaction channel to be chosen. In my report, I suggested that the VPC's monopoly on account keeping under the Stock Account Act should be removed. In my opinion, the law we have today should be replaced but a new law that is not company-specific but general in terms of rules for account keeping. In this area, the law needs to be changed much in the same way as happened with stock exchange legislation in the early 90s. This spring's budget proposal addresses, among other things, ownership issues concerning VPC. In connection with these discussions, it is important to run a legislative project in parallel that takes care of the legislative changes that need to be made. agarfragor In my previous memo, I noted that it is difficult to find any objections in principle to a possible merger of the Stock Exchange and OM. In my opinion, there is no reason today to change that approach. Stakeholders in the Swedish financial market have justified demands that a possibly redesigned marketplace be constructed so that integrity, neutrality and transparency are achieved. The final design of a new marketplace is part of the negotiations between the parties. Just as in other business contexts, this is a question of financial conditions, choice of company structures, ownership diversification, influence issues, etc. The budget bill's positions on ownership in VPC and an extra dividend of SEK 500 million from Securum make it possible for the state to participate in the discussions in a more active way than otherwise, which is something we are also prepared to do. It is currently too early to say what a solution should look like. There are many different interests to be heard in the process now before us. I note with satisfaction that the budget bill also makes it possible to actively start working on issues relating to the VPC in addition to the legislative process I mentioned above. VPC currently has securities worth around SEK 4000 billion registered in its systems. Consequently, we are talking here about a very substantial part of the Swedish financial infrastructure, among other things, a large part of the Swedish state debt is registered in the system. This means that it is both in the interest of the state, as a major player in the financial sector, and for many others to ensure that the company develops well. Research Financial products are all about packaging technology. It is important to pre-paper and distribute different patterns of return and risk. Many of the new packaging, the new financial products, are far from trivial. In order for us to create good conditions for skills development in the financial area, a knowledge base is needed both in the industry but also in the state sector so that regulations and supervision are developed in an effective way. I therefore believe that it is important that we think through what research resources on financial issues are needed in the country. 6 Summary Today, I wanted to point out in general terms where the development is heading and what it means for us in the financial sector. Here with special emphasis on some key elements of the financial infrastructure. Going forward, we will live in a fully open financial system with increasing competition. There is no single miracle cure that guarantees that we will do well in that world, but there are many different measures and long-term gnawing that together give us good conditions to cope with the future in a good way. This spring's work on the public side can be seen as a way to rake in the manege. It is now a question of continuing to work in a constructive way. References - M.J Brennan, Developments in the Financial Sector - Enhanced Oversight of Stock Exchanges, Ds 1997:40 - 1997 Spring Economic Bill

En sdan utveckling kan d ocks pverka kapitalfrsrjningen negativt. En sdan utveckling r inte, med mina utgngspunkter, nskvrd. Fr att en relativt liten marknad som den svenska skall kunna hvda sig mste den framst som attraktiv i jmfrelse med konkurrenterna. Marknaden skall ha en hg likviditet och en vl fungerande infrastruktur. Fr att vrdepappersmarknaden skall kunna fungera mste det finnas en en infrastruktur som p ett enkelt stt gr det mjligt fr kpare och sljare att mtas. Denna infrastruktur omfattar ett antal sammanlnkade delar som p olika stt r beroende av varandra. Med dagens tekniska utveckling bestr denna infrastruktur i hg utstrckning av datasystem av olika slag. Utvecklingen av den finansiella infrastrukturen handlar drfr idag mycket om datasystem, vem som har tilltrde till systemen, hur de kommunicerar med varandra och vem som ger dem. De synpunkter jag kommit fram till har sina utgngspunkter i hg grad i den utvecklingsbild som jag har skissat ovan. Med dagens teknologi och den utveckling som pgr frefaller direktacces enlig min mening vara en rimlig tgrd. Hur en lsning skall se ut r det idag fr tidigt att uttala sig om. Det r mnga olika intressen som skall komma till tals i den process som vi nu har framfr oss. Jag noterar med tillfredstllelse att budgetpropositionen ocks gr det mjligt att p ett aktivt stt brja arbeta med frgor rrande VPC utver den lagstiftningsprocess som jag nmnde ovan. VPC har idag vrdepapper till ett vrde av omkring 4000 miljarder registrerade i sina system. Det hr innebr att det ligger svl i statens intresse, som en stor aktr inom den finansiella sektorn, som fr mnga andra att se till att bolaget utvecklas vl. Title: Hearing on monetary policy
text: Floden in the Finance Committee. Hearing on monetary policy Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Martin Floden visited the Riksdag's Finance Committee today for the second hearing of the year on monetary policy. Date: 2017-09-28 09:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Location: Skandiasalen, Riksdagen, Stockholm Ingves began by describing the Riksbank's work to ensure the role of the inflation target as an anchor for price and wage formation in Sweden: "We have acted vigorously with monetary policy. After a long time with inflation below target, we are now back to 2 percent and we have a good economy in Sweden. In order for inflation to remain close to the target also in the future, we need to have a continued expansionary monetary policy". When economic development is strong, it is often warned of overheating. But it's hard to see any clear signs of that right now, Martin Floden said in his introduction: "Prices and wages are only increasing moderately, households are saving a lot and we have a current account surplus." On the other hand, both Floden and Ingves are concerned about developments in the housing market and household indebtedness. Debt has been rising for a long time, and did so even when interest rates were higher. The Riksbank believes that a combination of measures in different policy areas is needed to address these problems and achieve long-term sustainable development in the Swedish economy. text: Flode9n: The Riksbank and monetary policy Date: 2015-05-27 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Flode9n Location: Swedish-Finnish Folk High School, Haparanda "It is important that inflation rises towards the 2 per cent target. He talks there about the economic situation and the latest interest rate decision, including at a breakfast with representatives from the banks in the region. Flode9n also makes two company visits and gives a lecture at the Swedish-Finnish Folk High School in Haparanda. In Lulee5, he meets, among others, the County Administrative Board. At the same time, Martin Flode9n points out that the low interest rate environment can lead to excessive risk-taking both in the housing market and in the financial markets. Measures to reduce risks are urgently needed. He is therefore positive that the government and the alliance are trying to bring about a law that allows the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority to introduce the amortization requirement. text: Floden: Large maturity imbalances in the Swedish mortgage market  what do we want the market to look like? "Swedish banks finance mortgages by issuing bonds with significantly shorter maturities than the repayment period of the loans. This maturity imbalance has strengthened in recent decades and it is larger in Sweden compared to most other countries. I think it is important that we discuss the risks posed by this development and whether we are satisfied with how the mortgage market works," says Deputy Governor Martin Floden. Date: 2017-04-04 07:30 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Location: Swedish House of Finance, Stockholm Major Swedish banks finance mortgages by issuing covered bonds. The average maturity of these bonds is about three years. This means that major Swedish banks have a smaller share of financing with a longer maturity than many of their European counterparts. At the same time, the average repayment period on a mortgage in Sweden today is almost 80 years. This creates large maturity imbalances in the Swedish mortgage market. In the Riksbank study "The structural liquidity risks of the major Swedish banks", the Riksbank and the authors of the report have presented proposals for various measures that could reduce liquidity risks. The study can be used as a starting point for a continued discussion of the maturity imbalances in the Swedish mortgage market. RELATED CONTENT Presentationsbilder (pdf 495,9 kB) Updated 2018-01-04
