Title: Monetary policy needs to be sustainable
text: Floden hearing in the Finance Committee: Monetary policy needs to be sustainable The Swedish economy has recovered quickly in the pandemic, supported by extensive economic policy measures. This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves said in his introduction when he and Deputy Governor Martin Floden today participated in this year's second hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. Date: 2021-10-19 09:30 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Place: Finance Committee, Swedish Parliament Floden also focused on inflation in its introduction. "In light of inflation having been below 2 per cent for many years, it is welcome that it has now risen. This can help ensure that inflation expectations are not too low and strengthen confidence in the inflation target," floden said. "Inflationary pressures are not very strong, suggesting that the upturn is transitory. But I think the risks of inflation being higher than in our forecast have increased. We need to continuously monitor how the high energy and producer prices affect other prices, inflation expectations and wages", Floden concluded. Title: Preparing for EMU and the issue of the ERM
text: Preparing for EMU and the erm issue Date: 1996-09-19 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Nordbanken's Capital Markets Day Introduction nder this coming weekend, the Finance Ministers and Governors of the European Union will meet in Dublin, Ireland, for a so-called. informal ECOFIN meeting. Although no formal decisions are taken at this type of semi-annual meeting, it will mean that further steps will be taken to prepare for the creation of a European Monetary Union on 1 January 1999. The issues that will be dealt with in Dublin, expressed in EU jargon, include the so-called Stability Pact and the issue of Ins and Outs. These questions concern how discipline in the various countries' fiscal policy can be maintained even after EMU has been formed and how the countries' monetary and exchange rate policies within and outside EMU can be coordinated. In Sweden, the discussion about Sweden's future relationship with EMU is currently underway. The question is whether Sweden will strive to be part of the first group of countries to form EMU or whether the political process will lead to us waiting. It will not be until autumn 1997 that the Riksdag will take a position. In the meantime, the Riksbank is actively participating in the preparations that must be made for the Riksdag to have a real choice. Sweden and EMU The idea of closer economic and monetary cooperation between the Member States of the European Union is far from new. Increased cooperation in the monetary field has been seen as one of the prerequisites for greater integration in Europe ever since European cooperation began in the 1950s. Already in the Treaty of Rome of 1957 one can find wordings on economic policy coordination. Although these wordings were rather vague, not least in light of the then stable economic environment. During the late 1960s, conditions changed. Changes in various currency parities within Europe led to an elaborate of the so-called The Werner plan on the initiative of France and Germany. Presented in 1970, the plan proposed the introduction of economic and monetary union in three stages. It was unanimously adopted by the finance ministers of the ECOFIN Council in March 1971, but the plan was overturned by the ensuing turbulence associated with the collapse of the Bretton Woods system and the oil crisis. However, one idea lingered. It was the currency snake that can be said to be the predecessor of the current ERM system. The idea of closer cooperation came to the fore again towards the end of the 1980s and the principles that now form the basis of EMU and the Maastricht Treaty were drawn up by the Delors Committee. Throughout history, Sweden has participated and been inspired by various international arrangements in the field of monetary and exchange rate policy. These include the gold standard, the Scandinavian Monetary Union and the Bretton Woods system. For almost a hundred years, the krona was directly or indirectly tied to gold, and for longer than that, inflation averaged at what is now called a "good European level". What has characterized many of us is the 1970s and 1980s, but it is the longest inflationary period in modern history and is really a parenthesis in our tradition. From 1870 until the first years of the 1970s, Sweden had an economic growth rate that was among the highest in the world. It shows that low inflation and stability in the economy have not been an obstacle to high and stable growth and employment. On the contrary, low inflation is, by all accounts, one of several important prerequisites for emerging prosperity. EMU is the new project of the late 1900s for international monetary and monetary policy cooperation in our immediate area. It is not free from risks and difficulties, but also brings tangible benefits and opportunities. The Swedish discussion seems to be mostly concerned with the difficulties of the project and less with its possibilities. In its own way, this is surprising because it so clearly connects to the Swedish monetary policy tradition. The discussion about EMU in Sweden should be less about the question of whether a monetary union should be formed in Europe or not and instead more about how we view Swedish participation in the event that many countries in Europe join EMU. That is the most likely thing today. It is important that, in the debate, we also clearly and clearly consider the costs of exclusion. For its part, the Riksbank council has come to the conclusion that ""there are predominant advantages to a Swedish accession to a European Monetary Union""." Preparing for EMU The timetable is now getting tight. Nevertheless, preparations within the various EU institutions are progressing according to plan. As early as spring 1998, the Heads of State or Government of the EU countries will decide which countries will be involved from the outset. Soon after, the European Central Bank is formed. Emu will start on 1 January 1999. Exchange rates are fixed and the European Central Bank takes over monetary policy. By January 2002 at the latest, euro notes and coins will be issued. In order to keep preparations together in the field of central banks, the European and Monetary Institute (EMI) in Frankfurt, which is the forerunner of the new central bank, is running a large number of projects in several areas. According to the latest list, 89 different projects are being worked on in the run-up to EMU at the same time. Other projects have already been completed and some will certainly be added later. Much must be fully discussed and decided already this year, other things can wait further. The areas concerned are the formulation of monetary policy, the coordination of payment systems, the design of banknotes, the collection of statistics, etc. The Riksbank and its staff participate in everything from expert bodies and subcommittees to the Deputy Committee and the Council of the EMI. The Riksbank has also taken the initiative for practical preparatory work within Sweden. An overall consultation group for the financial sector has been formed under the leadership of the Riksbank. In this, various high-level representatives on the state side participate. It consults on the arrangements for the changeover to a single currency with the Bankers' Association and various groupings of non-association financial institutions, insurance companies, securities institutions and clearing and settlement institutions. This consultation group organises and follows the work of a number of underlying working groups. Sweden's economy and convergence In recent years, imbalances have been reduced and the conditions for stability have increased in the Swedish economy. Growth has averaged an annual rate of 2.5% since the turnaround in mid-1993. The current account shows relatively large surpluses. The financial crisis is overcome. In addition, public deficits are gradually decreasing and that most of the evidence today is in favour of a deficit of no more than 3% in 1997 and a balance in 1998. The inflation ceiling is now also low, while inflation expectations have been decelerated. In the financial markets, too, there has been a reassessment of Swedish economic policy. The krona has strengthened and interest rates have fallen. The situation has thus improved markedly. However, the picture is not bright in all respects. Unemployment and public debt are high, although the latter is expected to decline as a share of GDP, and wage formation has not yet been adjusted to a low-inflation world. All in all, this means that there have been improvements in several areas of the Swedish economy. In many ways, the picture of the Swedish economy has thus changed significantly. Sweden also has good opportunities to meet the entry requirements to EMU already when the Union is formed. The current situation in the Swedish economy is characterized by the fact that demand and activity have apparently begun to recover after the economic slowdown that began towards the end of last year. In the first half of this year, both investment and foreign trade made relatively large contributions to economic growth. Some growth in private consumption was balanced by a corresponding decrease in public consumption. Increased confidence in economic policy, which has been reflected in reduced inflation expectations, has led to a stronger krona and lower interest rates, which will allow for more balanced growth over the next few years. All in all, this should mean that the outlook is good for inflation to be in line with the inflation target over the next few years. "Ins and Outs" och vaxelkurskriteriet The question of 'Ins and Outs' is about the relationship between the countries that join EMU from the start and those that, for various reasons, end up without-for. Following the previous informal ECOFIN meeting in Verona last spring, a report was prepared by the ECOFIN Council for the meeting of Heads of State or Government in Florence. The report outlines some basic elements of the exchange rate arrangement: The euro becomes anchor Central rates are set in a common procedure with finance ministers, the European Central Bank (ECB) and other central banks Central rates are monitored and, if necessary, subject to change at the initiative of interested parties, including the ECB At the margins, compulsory intervention shall be taken, but both the ECB and the outside central banks should be able to suspend support if their own price stability is threatened Broad bands should be the standard model; but closer links and cooperation can be developed on a voluntary basis. Since the Florence meeting, discussions continued on how the exchange rate arrangement should be designed. The discussions over the coming weekend will build on the basic features I have just mentioned. The ECOFIN Council is expected to report later to the Meeting of Heads of State or Government in Dublin in December, when a political agreement will be reached on the system for ensuring exchange rate stability between ins and outs. On the Swedish side, we have consistently emphasised that fundamental economic convergence is a basic prerequisite for stable exchange rate developments. Participation in an exchange rate arrangement cannot replace this. Each EU country should be able to choose independently the form in which monetary stability is achieved. An inflation target of the Swedish model is an expression of a level of ambition as high an ambition for stability-oriented economic policy as that which must characterise a country with a fixed exchange rate target. Sweden has also been given a hearing for voluntary participation in the exchange rate arrangement. In order to strengthen the credibility of alternative forms of able to provide the same economic stability, we have underlined the importance of effective supervision by the ECB and the ECOFIN Council in the area of monetary and fiscal policy respectively. Another but related issue concerns the exchange rate criterion. Different interpretations of the Treaty texts are made here. A number of countries, which are central to the process of building monetary union, believe that membership of the ERM should be compulsory for two years before participation in EMU. Others, including Sweden, have argued that it is the stability of the exchange rate itself that is the decisive factor and not the membership itself. The discussion on the exchange rate criterion may well continue, but the final answer to the question of how it should be interpreted will only come when the Heads of State or Government deal with the issue in the spring of 1998. For the time being, therefore, the Swedish interpretation remains firm. Sweden and the ERM The Swedish view of the exchange rate criterion does not prevent the conditions for Swedish ERM accession from being analysed and discussed. A decision on Swedish ERM participation must have support in Swedish society. It is therefore important to have an open discussion both about ERM membership itself and about the forms of it. Swedish ERM entry could be seen as a general confirmation of the improved conditions for stability that have arisen and also further demonstrate our willingness to pursue a stability-oriented economic policy in the long term. It is important to firmly show this will in the event of imminent EMU membership, but perhaps even more important if Sweden chooses to wait with EMU. After all, it is the long-term credibility of this ambition that leads to market interest rates at a lastingly good European level. The ERM could act as support in this regard and would also increase the Riksdag's freedom of action to make decisions in the autumn of 1997, whether it be to enter EMU in the first round or to wait. The Riksbank has previously emphasized that inflation expectations have been too high and that the imbalances in the Swedish economy have been so large that an ERM accession would hardly be perceived as credible. The lesson that Sweden has learned from the currency turbulence in the autumn of 1992 is that the path to a stable currency goes beyond a credible stability-oriented economic policy in general - not just through declarations of a fixed exchange rate. In recent years, as I pointed out earlier, imbalances have been reduced and the conditions for stability have increased in the Swedish economy, although the adjustment has not yet been completed. Further developments in the right direction will allow for the actualisation of ERM accession, although it is still unclear when it would be appropriate from an economic point of view. Experience with the floating exchange rate regime and the inflation target has so far been good. Economic policy has concentrated on achieving domestic monetary stability. A good result of this is reflected in a stable exchange rate. It is a reverse order compared to whether the exchange rate is the target, which is supposed to lead to the same rate of inflation as in the countries against which the krona is pegged. But the ultimate target inflation around 2 percent  is the same. We should look for an idea of whether an inflation target can be reconciled with ERM membership. With such an arrangement, deviations from the set central rate, which shows more permanent ten-denser and which risks affecting inflation, would be met with paring changes in interest rates, upwards as well as downwards where appropriate. This would not be done to defend a certain level of exchange rate, but to ensure that our Swedish inflation target is achieved. This objective corresponds to the good European level in force within the ERM countries. Such an order is not so different from how it works even today. Exchange rate developments are an important indicator of confidence in the economy politics and on inflationary pressures in a small open economy. Low inflation and good confidence in economic policy provide stability in the exchange rate, and it should be possible to establish such stability also within the framework of ERM participation with the help of the Swedish inflation target. One question that is debatable is whether there may be a conflict between the inflation target and ERM membership. The risk of such a move should be low as long as confidence in economic policy continues to improve and given the current framework for ERM cooperation. However, the inflation target should, as at present, be the overriding target of monetary policy. It would also be consistent with the monetary policy guidelines that apply within the EU and the principles that are now also relevant in the context of the discussion on 'Ins and Outs'. I would like to make it clear that erm participation is not on the agenda now. On the other hand, it is both appropriate and desirable that we begin a more in-depth discussion of this issue. This is especially true as the imbalances in the Swedish economy have been reduced and the conditions for stability have increased. Conclusion It is probably a not too bold guess to say that this coming weekend's meeting of EU finance ministers and central bank governors will mean that further steps are being taken on the road to a European Monetary Union. The closer to the moment of truth that the process progresses, the more intense the preparation will be, as well as the discussion of the various details of the project. So far, the preparatory work seems to be going according to plan and most indications are that EMU will be established on 1 January 1999. There may be a smaller group of countries that are included in the first round, but it cannot be ruled out that it will be a larger group. All this means that the Swedish discussion should focus on less discussing the project as such and instead focus on the question of how Sweden should relate to a situation when a number of countries in Europe enter EMU. What are the risks and opportunities of joining and being excluded? Personally, I find it difficult to see that Sweden will in the long run remain outside if a monetary union is formed in Europe consisting of several countries.

Title: Preparing for a European Monetary Union (EMU)
text: Preparing for European Monetary Union (EMU) Date: 1996-04-11 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Visby Within the European Union, preparations are now under way to probably the biggest monetary reform ever in history. Although there are rules in the Maastricht Treaty on how the Union is to be formed in practice, the decision is ultimately political. The discussion about EMU has been going in waves since the early 1970s. My assessment is that the political momentum of the EMU process is strong. The ambition to form EMU is a reality, although of course we should not underestimate the various difficulties that arise the closer the strategic times get. Preparatory work is focused on the start of the Union in 1999. The European Council in Madrid last December confirmed this. In the coming weekend, EU finance ministers and central bank governors will meet again to continue the preparatory work. The question of whether Sweden should participate in EMU is also a political one. The Riksdag will decide on Sweden's participation in 1997. The foundations of a European monetary union The discussion about the pros and cons of monetary union has really only just begun in our country. We will see many posts on this issue in the future. For its part, the Riksbank council has come to the conclusion that there are predominant advantages to Swedish accession to a European monetary union. Let me briefly elaborate on the reasoning on how monetary union can be viewed and its implications for economic policy. The overriding objective of the single monetary policy in EMU is price stability. It is sometimes argued that this very thing makes participation in the Union a serious risk. However, inflation is not a recipe for success for growth, employment and prosperity. The economic performance of countries that, with inflation, have sought to achieve short-term benefits in terms of growth and employment is disappointing. In a medium-term perspective, such countries have had a worse development in almost all areas of the economy. It is these experiences that are the reason why the countries of Europe have come to emphasise that a stability-oriented economic policy is a prerequisite for high and stable economic growth and employment. It is the same approach that guides Swedish economic policy. A focus on price stability is a crucial prerequisite for favourable economic development regardless of how we choose to approach EMU. This is illustrated not least by our history. The first half of the 1800s marked the beginning of a long period of price stability in our country. From 1830 until basically 1960, annual average inflation was just under 2 percent on average. With the exception of war periods and the 1970s and 1980s, price stability over the last few years has been 100 years been the rule. There is therefore reason to speak of a Swedish tradition. The repercussions on the Swedish economy after the overstimulation and inflation of the 1970s and 1980s are illustrative. This contributed to Sweden experiencing the deepest downturn in the economy since the 1930s in the early 1990s. In the old days, precious metals played an important role in securing confidence in the value of money. In 1830, the Riksdag decided that Sweden should switch to the silver standard, after a period of high inflation. It was a type of fixed exchange rate because the Swedish currency was pegged to the silver. After the silver standard, gold came to play a prominent role from 1863. During the next 100 years, Sweden had the value of the currency tied to gold with shorter interruptions, mainly caused by the First and Second World Wars. This was also true under the so-called Bretton-Woods system between 1951 and 1973. Formally, the value of the crown was pegged to that of the US dollar, but its value was based on the development of the price of gold. The fact that the stable monetary value, and the fixed exchange rate, did not constitute an obstacle to economic development is illustrated by the fact that Sweden from the mid-1800s until the end of the 1960s showed the almost fastest growing economy in the world. Rather, the low inflation and stability of the economy it represented should have contributed to the favourable development. However, the experience of the 1970s and 80s shows that it is not enough to advertise a fixed exchange rate to achieve credibility and stability. It also requires that the policy as a whole is consistent with this objective, including a high degree of fiscal discipline. This is all the more true in the 1990s against the background of the globalised capital market. One could call monetary union the ultimate form of fixed exchange rate. This means that the advantages associated with a fixed exchange rate for a small open economy of the Swedish type in terms of stability and favorable growth conditions also exist in a monetary union. Common objection to EMU In the Swedish debate, it is mainly an objection that has been discussed. It is that in monetary union, the possibility of changing the exchange rate in order to facilitate the adjustment of the economy in the context of external disturbances affecting the countries of the Union in different ways disappears. What, then, is the likelihood of such serious disturbances affecting the Member States of a monetary union in different ways? Studies have indicated that most EU countries, including Sweden, form a relatively homogeneous area with a well-diversified industrial structure. This suggests that the risk of disparate external disturbances is thus relatively small. But although these risks can thus be designated as small, of course, it cannot be ruled out that in the future such disturbances of a completely unpredictable nature will occur. If there is a disturbance that affects the countries of monetary union in different ways, demands are made on the adaptability of the economy. It must be possible to shift labour and other resources to new activities or to change labour costs so that the activities can continue. In the debate on EMU, it is often argued that Europe's labour markets are so special and so poorly integrated that disruptions suffered by a country within EMU will lead to persistently high unemployment. However, it is doubtful what role adjustable exchange rates can play in reducing the importance of such rigidities, as experience has clearly shown in the 170s and 1980s. A better approach is to consider what can be done to increase the flexibility of labour markets in EU countries. This is where the crux of the problem lies. If the labour market is judged to have difficulties in adapting to new conditions, this is an issue that cannot be solved by devaluations. Rather, it is a question of improving the functioning of the labour market. Adjustable exchange rates are therefore not a means of achieving high and stable employment. Many countries have found it difficult to overcome unemployment even during periods when exchange rates have changed. Sweden has as famously devalued the krona on numerous occasions since the 1970s, yet unemployment has risen trend-wise with every recession since then. It must also be borne in mind that fiscal policy remains the means of redressing imbalances at national level. However, preserving freedom of action from fiscal policy requires a high degree of budgetary discipline and strong public finances. On this point, too, it cannot be argued that participation in EMU tightens up the requirements. The starting point for Sweden is such that, in any case, high demands will be placed on budgetary discipline. " " """Ins and Outs""" Well in advance of the introduction of EMU, a solution must be found regarding the rules for those countries that are part of the EU but which, for various reasons, end up outside EMU. The relationship between the so-called. ""Ins and Outs""" will be discussed this weekend, among other things, when EU finance ministers and central bank governors meet in Italy. It is reasonable to create a successor to the current exchange rate cooperation, the ERM. However, it should be possible for a country to be able to direct its economic policy directly towards an inflation target, of the type that Sweden currently has. We base this position on the fact that price stability is the overarching objective of monetary policy. In the long run, it is also the degree of convergence in the area of inflation that forms the basis for exchange rate stability. It is important for a country to achieve a fundamental stability of the currency and of the economy before entering monetary union. This stability may need to be confirmed by participation in exchange rate cooperation for a period prior to entry. This applies both before the formation of EMU and later when the Union is in operation. The lesson that Sweden has learned from the currency turbulence in the autumn of 1992 is that the road to a stable currency goes beyond a stability-oriented economic policy in general - not with only declarations of a fixed exchange rate. A future participation in the ERM for Sweden is that Sweden must have achieved good stability in the economy, as well as that the krona's rate is correctly valued and so stable that we do not have to expect tensions and high interest rates in relation to the stronger currencies within the cooperation. The road to EMU Let me now set out the basic steps on the road to monetary union. In the spring of 1998, the EU will decide which countries will be included in EMU from its inception. According to the requirements set out, these countries must meet a number of so-called convergence criteria. Emu will start on the first of January 1999. Then all the currencies of the Member States are pegged against each other by fixed and irrevocable exchange rates, and the euro begins to be used for various purposes, such as monetary policy. By 2002 at the latest, notes and coins will be issued in the new currency, the euro. They are used for a few months in parallel with the other currencies, but from 1 July 2002 at the latest the national currencies will be withdrawn and only the euro may be used in the Member States. Let us assume that Sweden joins EMU from 1 January 1999. In what way will this be noticeable for Sweden and what preparations need to be made? The most tangible, of course, is the transition to a new currency. Although the krona is our national currency until 2002, we will increasingly have to adapt to the use of the euro. For example, the new currency will be used in the accounts of many companies and authorities long before it is available in the form of notes and coins. One aim of the gradual changeover to the euro is to: that people should gradually get used to the new currency and gain confidence in it. A first important step is, of course, for the authorities in the Member States themselves to clearly demonstrate that they are behind the currency. Therefore, the new government loans that governments - in our case, the National Debt Office - take up new ones will be denominated in euros. The Riksbank will conduct its operations within the framework of the single monetary policy in the currency union. A special payment system for euro transactions is launched in order to be able to quickly transfer large amounts of capital throughout the currency area. Banks will have an increased stream of payments expressed in euros, and this may spread rapidly across the money and foreign exchange markets. For those who place money in euro loans, the change is not so great. Until 2002, interest and amortisation will be paid in euro, which can be converted into sek at a fixed rate and then euro at the same value. It is certainly that, by the year 2002, investors will also have the opportunity to be paid directly in kronor without the detour via euros, if they so wish. A further step in the transition to the new currency is that banks will probably already from 1999 re-record all their transactions and customers' loans and account balances both in kronor and in euros at the fixed conversion rate. It is not excluded that, as a bank customer, you will notice this in the form of bank statements with ""double data""" - in crowns and in euros. As early as January 1999, the exchange rates of the EMU countries will therefore be fixed against each other. It provides benefits for individuals, companies and also for the state. The risk of losing money on exchange rate changes between the EMU countries ceases. This reduces business costs and should mean increased opportunities for international business within Europe. By the beginning of 2002 at the latest, the new euro banknotes and coins will be issued. The design of these, incidentally, has just started. The proposals for banknote motifs presented so far contain various European historical styles, for example in architecture and art. An alternative proposal is abstract patterns. In the autumn of 1996, we will see the image proposals. It has not yet been decided whether the banknotes should be completely the same in all countries or whether each country should have a "national element". In that case, it would be a small piece of the banknote where the individual country could insert an image typical of the country where the banknote was issued. The idea is that such a banknote would be more easily accepted by its own population. However, there are problems with printing banknotes with different images in different countries. It will be more expensive and many banknotes will be used in countries other than where they were originally issued. But it's not just the currencies that are affected. Monetary policy will also be organised in a different way. A single European Central Bank will be established before 1999. It is placed in Frankfurt. The national central banks will remain, but some of our tasks will be transferred to the single central bank. From there, monetary policy will then be guided. Conclusion As I said at the beginning, the European Union is preparing for probably the biggest monetary reform ever in history. The work has entered an intensive stage. The question of the formation of EMU is ultimately a political decision. My assessment is that the political momentum of the EMU process is strong and that the ambition in the EU countries to form EMU is a reality. The Riksbank participates in various ways in the preparatory work. One can, of course, ask why the Riksbank is already putting so much energy into preparing Sweden's participation in EMU when the Riksdag makes a decision only in 1997. My answer is the following: There are three passages that must be cleared before Sweden can join EMU. One is that the Riksdag says yes, the other is that we meet the convergence criteria and the third is that we are also otherwise well prepared. If the latter two points are not fulfilled, there is no room for manoeuvre required by the parliamentary reading.

Sdana lnder har i ett medelfristigt perspektiv haft en smre utveckling p snart sagt alla ekonomiska omrden. Det r samma synstt som vgleder svensk ekonomisk politik. En inriktning p prisstabilitet r en avgrande frutsttning fr en gynnsam ekonomisk utveckling oberoende av hur vi vljer att frhlla oss till EMU. Erfarenheten frn 1970- och 80-talen visar dock att det inte rcker att annonsera en fast vxelkurs fr att uppn trovrdighet och stabilitet. Det krvs ocks att politiken som helhet r konsistent med detta ml, inklusive en hg grad av finanspolitisk disciplin. Detta gller i n hgre grad p 1990-talet mot bakgrund av den globaliserade kapitalmarknaden. Man skulle kunna kalla en monetr union fr den yttersta formen av fast vxelkurs. Det innebr att de frdelar som en fast vxelkurs r frknippad med fr en liten ppen ekonomi av Sveriges typ i form av stabilitet och gynnsamma tillvxtbetingelser ocks finns i en monetr union. Vanlig invndning mot EMU I den svenska debatten r det frmst en invndning som diskuterats. Hur stor r d sannolikheten fr att det ska uppst sdana allvarliga strningar som pverkar medlemslnderna i en monetr union p olika stt? Studier har pekat p att de flesta EU-lnderna, inklusive Sverige, bildar ett relativt homogent omrde med en vl diversifierad industristruktur. Det tyder p att risken fr olikartade yttre strningar drmed r relativt liten. Men ven om dessa risker sledes kan betecknas som sm, kan det naturligtvis inte uteslutas att det i framtiden uppstr sdana strningar av helt ofrutsgbar karaktr. Om det uppstr en strning som trffar lnderna inom den monetra unionen p olika stt, stlls krav p ekonomins anpassningsfrmga. Det mste g att flytta arbetskraft och andra resurser till nya verksamheter eller att ndra arbetskraftskostnaderna s att verksamheterna kan drivas vidare. I diskussionen om EMU hvdas ofta att Europas arbetsmarknader r s speciella och s dligt integrerade att strningar som drabbar ett land inom EMU kommer att leda till varaktigt hg arbetslshet. Det r dock tveksamt vilken roll justerbara vxelkurser kan spela fr att minska betydelsen av sdana stelheter, vilket erfarenheterna klart har visat under 170- och 1980-talen. Ett bttre angreppsstt r att fundera p vad som i s fall kan gras fr att ka flexibiliteten p arbetsmarknaderna i EU-lnderna. Det r hr krnan i problemet ligger. Om arbetsmarknaden bedms ha svrigheter att anpassa sig till nya frhllanden, r det en frga som inte kan lsas med devalveringar. D handlar det snarare om att frbttra arbetsmarknadens funktionsstt. Justerbara vxelkurser r sledes inte ett medel att stadkomma en hg och stabil sysselsttning. Mnga lnder har haft svrt att komma tillrtta med arbetslsheten ven under perioder d vxelkurserna ndrats. Sverige har som bekant devalverat kronan vid ett flertal tillfllen sedan 1970-talet, nd har arbetslsheten stigit trendmssigt vid varje lgkonjunktur sedan dess. Man mste ocks komma ihg att finanspolitiken finns kvar som medel fr att p nationell niv komma tillrtta med obalanser. Bevarad handlingsfrihet frn finanspolitiken krver dock en hg grad av budgetdisciplin och starka statsfinanser. Inte heller p den hr punkten kan det hvdas att kraven skrps av ett deltagande i EMU. Utgngslget fr svensk del r sdant att under alla omstndigheter kommer att stllas hga krav p budgetdisciplin. " " """Ins and Outs""" I god tid fre infrandet av EMU mste en lsning skapas betrffande reglerna fr de lnder som r med i EU men som av olika skl hamnar utanfr EMU. Frhllandet mellan de sk. """Ins and Outs""" kommer bl.a. att diskuteras denna helg nr EU:s finansministrar och centralbankschefer mts i Italien. Det r rimligt att skapa en efterfljare till det nuvarande vxelkurssamarbetet, ERM. Det br dock vara mjligt fr ett land att kunna inrikta sin ekonomiska politik direkt mot ett inflationsml, av den typ som Sverige fr nrvarande har. Vi bygger denna stndpunkt p att prisstabilitet r det vergripande mlet fr penningpolitiken. I lngden r det ocks graden av konvergens p inflationsomrdet som utgr grunden fr stabilitet i vxelkursen. Det r viktigt fr ett land att uppn en grundlggande stabilitet av valutan och i ekonomin innan ett intrde i den monetra unionen. Denna stabilitet kan behva bekrftas genom ett deltagande i vxelkurssamarbetet under en period innan intrde sker. Detta gller bde infr bildandet av EMU och senare nr unionen r i funktion. Den lrdom som Sverige har dragit frn valutaturbulensen hsten 1992 r att vgen till en stabil valuta gr ver en stabilitetsinriktad ekonomisk politik i stort - inte med enbart deklarationer om en fast vxelkurs. Ett framtida deltagande i ERM fr svensk del handlar om att Sverige mste ha uppntt god stabilitet i ekonomin, liksom att kronans kurs r rtt vrderad och s stabil att vi inte behver rkna med spnningar och hga rntor i frhllande till de starkare valutorna inom samarbetet. Vgen till EMU Lt mig nu ange sjlva grundstegen p vgen mot den monetra unionen. Under vren 1998 beslutas i EU vilka lnder som ska ing i EMU frn dess start. Enligt de krav som stlls upp ska dessa lnder uppfylla ett antal s kallade konvergenskriterier. Den frsta januari 1999 startar EMU. D binds alla medlemslndernas valutor mot varandra med fasta och oterkalleliga vxelkurser, och euron brjar anvndas fr olika ndaml, t.ex. i penningpolitiken. Senast r 2002 brjar man ge ut sedlar och mynt i den nya valutan, euro. De anvnds under ngra mnader parallellt med de andra valutorna, men senast frn den 1 juli 2002 dras de nationella valutorna in och endast euro fr anvndas i medlemslnderna. Lt oss anta att Sverige gr med i EMU frn 1 januari 1999. P vilket stt kommer detta att mrkas fr Sverige och vilka frberedelser behver gras? Det mest ptagliga r frsts vergngen till en ny valuta. ven om kronan r vr nationella valuta nda fram till r 2002 s kommer vi allt mer att behva anpassa oss till anvndningen av euro. Den nya valutan kommer t.ex. att anvndas i redovisningen hos mnga fretag och myndigheter lngt innan den finns ute i form av sedlar och mynt. Ett syfte med att vergngen till euro kommer att ske gradvis r att man successivt ska vnja sig vid den nya valutan och f frtroende fr den. Ett frsta viktigt steg r givetvis att myndigheterna i medlemsstaterna sjlva p ett tydligt stt visar att de str bakom valutan. Drfr kommer de nya statsln som regeringarna - i vrt fall Riksgldskontoret - tar upp nya att anges i euro. Riksbanken kommer att genomfra sina operationer inom ramen fr den gemensamma penningpolitiken i valutaunionen. Ett srskilt betalningssystem fr eurotransaktioner startar fr att snabbt kunna verfra stora kapitalbelopp inom hela valutaomrdet. Bankerna kommer att f en kad strm av betalningar uttryckta i euro, och detta kan f snabb spridning ver penning- och valutamarknaderna. Fr dem som placerar pengar i euroln r frndringen inte s stor. Rntor och amorteringar betalas fram till r 2002 i euro som kan omrknas i kronor efter en fast kurs och drefter euro till samma vrde. Skert kommer placerarna fram till r 2002 ocks att f en mjlighet att f betalt direkt i kronor utan omvgen via euro, om de s skulle nska. Ett ytterligare steg i vergngen till den nya valutan r att bankerna troligen redan frn 1999 kommer att re-dovisa alla sina transaktioner och kundernas ln och kontotillgodohavanden bde i kronor och i euro till den fasta omrkningskursen. Det r inte uteslutet att man som bankkund kommer att mrka detta i form av kontoutdrag med """dubbla uppgifter""" - i kronor och i euro. Redan frn januari 1999 kommer allts EMU-lndernas vxelkurser att vara lsta mot varandra. Det ger frdelar fr privatpersoner, fretag och ven fr staten. Risken att frlora pengar p vxelkursfrndringar mellan EMU-lnderna upphr. Det minskar fretagens kostnader och br innebra kade mjligheter till internationella affrer inom Europa. Senast i brjan av 2002 kommer det nya eurosedlarna och mynten att utges. Utformningen av dessa har fr vrigt just startat. De frslag till sedelmotiv som hittills framlagts innehller olika europeiska historiska stilarter exempelvis inom arkitektur och konst. Ett alternativt frslag r abstrakta mnster. Till hsten 1996 kommer vi att f se bildfrslagen. Det har nnu inte avgjorts om sedlarna ska vara helt lika i alla lnder eller om varje land ska ha ett "nationellt inslag". Det skulle i s fall rra sig om en liten bit av sedeln dr det enskilda landet kunde lgga in en bild som var typiskt fr det land dr sedeln utgavs. Tanken r att en sdan sedel lttare skulle accepteras av den egna befolkningen. Det finns dock problem med att trycka sedlar med olika bilder i olika lnder. Det blir dyrare och mnga sedlar kommer att anvndas i andra lnder n dr de ursprungligen utgivits. Men det r inte bara valutorna som pverkas. Penningpolitiken kommer ocks att organiseras p ett annat stt. Redan fre 1999 kommer en gemensam europeisk centralbank att upprttas. Den placeras i Frankfurt. De nationella centralbankerna kommer att finnas kvar men en del av vra arbetsuppgifter kommer att verfras till den gemensamma centralbanken. Drifrn kommer sedan penningpolitiken att styras. Avslutning Inom den europeiska unionen frbereds, som jag sa inledningsvis, den frmodligen strsta valutareformen ngonsin i historien. Arbetet har gtt in i ett intensivt skede. Frgan om EMU:s bildande r sist och slutligen ett politiskt beslut. Min bedmning r att EMU-processens politiska momentum r starkt och att ambitionen i EU-lnderna att bilda EMU r en realitet. Riksbanken deltar p olika stt i frberedelsearbetet. Man kan naturligtvis stlla sig frgan varfr Riksbanken redan nu lgger ner s mycket energi p att frbereda Sveriges deltagande i EMU nr riksdagen fattar beslut frst 1997. Mitt svar r fljande: Det finns tre passager som mste klaras innan Sverige kan komma med i EMU. Den ena r att riksdagen sger ja, den andra r att vi uppfyller konvergenskraven och den tredje r att vi ven i vrigt r vl frberedda. Title: Future structure of the Swedish securities market
text: Future structure of the Swedish securities market Date: 1997-11-13 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Bank and Finance-97 1. The New World There are many and important things that have happened in the financial markets over the last fifteen years. In a fairly short time, we have gone from a highly regulated and distinctly national market to a liberalised market with rapidly growing international competition. Moreover, this has gone hand in hand with rapid technological development. During these years, I myself have been involved in seeing the first futures transactions in government bonds carried out, seen the options market introduced and grow, seen the share certificates abolished and floor trading on the stock exchange disappear. Furthermore, large parts of the financial regulatory framework have been radically changed. Since the deregulations in Sweden came relatively late in an international perspective, it has been quite a lot about catching up over the past decade. So have we, but nothing lasts forever. Today's discussion is about how we can continue to manage good development. Today we have free trade in the financial field, basically the same kind as we have had for the manufacturing industry for a long time. The benefits are also fundamentally the same - more of specialization, increased efficiency, and ultimately increased prosperity. The same goes for the price of this - big and rapid changes that can sometimes be painful or at least confusing for many. In this context, it might be worth pointing out that the financial sector is a 'nourishing' and not 'draining' sector of the national economy, although I know full well that there may be some who think otherwise, at least outside this room. In any economy that has abandoned barter as the dominant form of economic exchange, the financial system plays a central role. It can be said that the financial system has three main tasks: to provide payment services, to convert savings into investment, and to enable households and businesses to cope with economic uncertainty and risk. The financial system acts as a lubricant for the entire economy. With a well-functioning financial system, we get lower costs and less risks in the production of goods and services. This promotes growth and employment. Similarly, a disruption in the functioning of the financial system can have negative consequences for the entire national economy. Crises in the financial system can contribute to socio-economic development entering a vicious circle of falling output, rising unemployment and deflation. I think it is important to state and communicate this - the latter we have well, if we are to be self-critical, not always so good at in the financial sector, and the task, of course, did not get any easier during the financial crisis and its aftermath. In any case, the lack of awareness of the role and importance of the financial sector is a problem and we ourselves have a responsibility here. Not everything is straightforward and not everything can be explained in ten seconds, but most of it can still be described in an understandable way if you put in a little effort, and it is important that we all do this in different contexts. My thesis is that the most fundamental change that has happened in the financial markets is that free trade has now reached this part of the economy as well. How, then, do we deal with such a situation? Sweden is a small country and a small economy and we cannot be the best at everything. Here, as in industry, we need to see what we are good at and develop this. The next question - and where we on the government side come into the picture is whether there are obstacles to such a development that we can remove or at least reduce. Put another way: How should we best rake the manegen ? Financial markets have historically been mainly nationally defined and linked to the size of one's own economy. Given the size of the Swedish economy, we are somewhere in the middle of an EU ranking but in most cases far below the large countries - stock market turnover is about eight times greater in London than in Stockholm, issues of fixed income securities are four times larger in Germany than in Sweden, to take two examples. An exception to the pattern is the derivatives market, where we are in fourth place in the EU, which shows that product development can pay off. In a Europe with free movement of capital and freedom of establishment, this means that there will always be competitors or potential competitors operating in a market larger than our own. This approach also concludes that the competitive picture and views on competition issues will be completely different depending on whether a national or a European perspective is taken. Given the trends that I have alluded to, it is, in my opinion, a European or, by extension, a global perspective that should be taken into account when discussing developments in the Swedish financial sector. This approach in no way excludes our own Swedish solutions, but one must be aware that the operating conditions in the future will be completely different than in the closed and "home-made" world in which we have lived in the past. 2. Review the infrastructure! A first question to ask is, of course, whether it matters where the financial activity takes place. Is it good if the transactions take place in Sweden, can they not as easily take place abroad? After all, in a technical sense, financial transactions can now take place almost anywhere in the world. For example, how do you define where a transaction takes place on the Internet and does it matter ? Financial transactions are not just about technology. It is also about information, contacts between people and building knowledge about financial theology. I think it is valuable for a country to have these functions at home, even if the concrete operations in a technical sense can be carried out elsewhere. I believe that a country with a liquid domestic venture capital market is in a better position to supply capital to business than countries in the absence of one, to take one example. A viable financial market also has spin-off effects on employment and production in related industries, for example in the IT industry. Sweden is at the forefront of technological development, and has a developed tradition and a good level of education in the financial field. This also gives us a platform for the future. In short: maintaining and developing skills in the financial field is, in my opinion, valuable for the country's economic development. How, then, are we to take advantage of the potential we have ? In order for a relatively small market like the Swedish market to be able to assert itself, it must: appear attractive in comparison with competitors. The market must have a high level of liquidity and a well-functioning infrastructure. In order for the securities market to function, there must be an infrastructure that makes it easy for buyers and sellers to meet. This infrastructure comprises a number of interconnected parts that are interdependent in different ways. The methods, regulations and capital stock required to manage information, matching of transactions, transfer of ownership and registration and payment constitute in a broad sense what one might call the financial infrastructure. With today's technological developments, this infrastructure largely consists of computer systems of various types. The development of the financial infrastructure is therefore today very much about computer systems, who has access to the systems, how they communicate with each other, how the services are priced and who owns the systems. The computer systems are then combined with the legal regulations to define the financial products and the transaction chain. When creating financial products in this world, four factors are of crucial importance. The costs of carrying out financial transactions shall not exceed those of competing marketplaces. There shall be no or as few obstacles as possible to an operator's access to the market place. This applies to different types of actors as well as between countries. The choice of transaction technology throughout the transaction chain must be of high international standard and based on international standards. Knowledge of financial products, product development and financial regulations must be of a high international level. The Swedish market must simply appear to be easily accessible and efficient. If it is technically difficult and expensive to exploit the Swedish market, it is quite easy for both foreign and Swedish players to find an alternative market or for foreign investors to find substitutes for Swedish investments in their portfolios. Assessed separately in an international perspective, the four central infrastructure systems in the Swedish market, the Stock Exchange, OM, VPC and RIX, are relatively well ahead. In view of international developments, it is, in my opinion, necessary to review the technical integration between the systems in order to ensure a positive development of the Swedish financial market. Integration of the entire transaction chain - clearance, clearing, settlement and account keeping - would simplify access to the Swedish market and thus strengthen its competitiveness and also contribute to a welcome risk reduction in the financial system. High security both operationally and risk-wise is a competitive factor in itself. The trend is increasingly towards real-time transactions, which is something that affects the entire transaction chain. This, in turn, requires technical cooperation in order to be realised. On a technical level, I also think it is important to find ways of completing dematerialisation on the securities side so that we no longer need manual securities management (MVPS). Of course, successful integration is not just about "connecting" some technical systems. It also deals with regulatory systems, access issues and supervisory aspects where the basic aim is to ensure good and transparent risk management. This is far from straightforward, but it is important that the discussion takes place - we ourselves discuss these kinds of issues, among other things, in terms of how to more closely integrate our RIX system with VPC. A few months ago, the Ministry of Finance came up with a number of proposals in the area of the stock exchange, including proposing that it should be possible to have direct access on an exchange, i.e. if you meet certain requirements, you do not need to be a securities institution to trade on the stock exchange on your own account. It is an issue that has aroused some strong feelings, but nevertheless I think it is good that we now have the discussion on the table. With today's technology and the development that is going on seem to me to be reasonable. In addition, I believe it can contribute to a better and clearer price formation for this type of financial services. If you do not absolutely have to act through intermediaries, you create a system that clarifies the added value that intermediaries must create in order for that transaction channel to be chosen. 3. Promote free trade! Not least as a small country, it is important that we actively work for free trade. It is a good Swedish trade policy tradition that we should apply here as well. I will mention two, partly interrelated areas, where we as the Riksbank have been active. One concerns central banks' lending against collateral in foreign securities and the other concerns the future EU payment system TARGET. The issue of "foreign collateral" has been discussed both in a Nordic context and in eu circles; in the latter case, it is obviously necessary from an EMU perspective to be able to use papers that exist in a part of the Union, say Germany, in order to obtain credit in, for example, the French Central Bank. Apart from the purely technical problems of such management, which of course exist in considerable proportions, it is difficult, in my view, to see any fundamental problems of principle with such arrangements - with or without monetary union. Nevertheless, this has been considered very problematic in some quarters. With regard to the arrangements within EMU, for example, the papers must, as an absolute minimum requirement, be issued within the EEA. The question one can then ask is what is interesting when taking collateral for a loan. Surely this must be the creditworthiness of the issuer, rather than in which country he happens to have his estates or where he has chosen to carry out an issue. But such an approach, we have noticed, often meets with intense resistance. With regard to the TARGET system, the Council of EMI has decided that banks in the EU countries outside EMU will be allowed to participate in the system, but that preparations should be made for the fact that access to so-called intraday stages of the system may be restricted or absent altogether. Since intraday credit from central banks is the "lubricant" for payment flows in this type of system, this will in that case make it more difficult and expensive for the Swedish banks to use the system. The official argument for this is that intrdagskredit to "outs" could in some situations complicate monetary policy within EMU. For our part, it seems to us that we have been able to show that this argument is not tenable - firstly, such monetary policy effects are unlikely, secondly, they are perfectly manageable should they arise after all. Nevertheless, we have held on to this, leaving it to the future ECB to decide definitively. In any case, if you go on the restriction line, this amounts to a de facto protectionism that there is every reason to deplore. If our analysis of the monetary policy aspects of intraday credit holds, then from this point of view there is really no fundamental reason to restrict foreign participation in a national payment system. As I mentioned earlier, I also do not see any fundamental problem with using securities from different countries and in different currencies as collateral for such credits. If we add this together, it is difficult to see any fundamental obstacles to linking payment systems around the world and where payments in any currency could, in principle, also be settled anywhere. Let me say right here that this may indeed seem like a far-reaching conclusion based on a sketchy analysis, but these are nevertheless questions that should be raised and analysed in the future. If we had such a thing, it would, of course, mean an improvement in the security and efficiency of the global financial system. Of course, it would also involve great technical and legal difficulties to implement such a thing to build Target within the EU circle has been quite complicated. In other words, this is definitely not something that is done on a coffee break, but I still think it is worth holding out as a vision, a first prerequisite for starting to move in that direction is that you know where you want to go, and it may require that you get rid of some previous ballast. 4. Effects of EMU The process of liberalisation and internationalisation we have been engaged in over the last decade is a global phenomenon rather than a European one. Nevertheless, it is clear that integration within the EU in general and EMU in particular has put additional carbon on the fire. Trends point to a continued rapid development of the financial markets, with new instruments, industry slippage and concentration of certain specialist functions. Competitive pressures in traditional banking are likely to continue to intensify at the same time as long-term demand for financial services increases and customers , whether we are talking about companies, municipalities or households - are becoming increasingly demanding. The number of "full-service" banks has already decreased while increasing their size. It is also likely that there will be continued growth of niche banks or financial companies focused on just a few services or distribution channels. The trend of traditional bank deposits and lending decreases, while supply and demand for market-based instruments increases, is expected to continue. However, some other likely developments are more directly linked to EMU. Major markets and new instruments Firstly, it is about the creation of a larger and more uniform market area. Today, we have about 9 million potential investors in Sweden. There are a total of just over 370 million in the EU. In addition, investors from other countries in Europe and from the rest of the world can be expected to seek out this new large market. A larger market normally leads, through rising competition, to lower costs and increased liquidity. Monetary union thus gives borrowers a larger market to operate in. There will also be more investors and as the currency risk disappears, it will be cheaper for them to diversify their portfolios. In short, in one fell swoop, we will have a much larger and much more liquid European capital market, which, both in size and in nature, may gradually become more and more similar to the American one. Secondly, there is reason to assume that some products on the financial markets will disappear while new ones are coming into being. Examples of products that may disappear are e.g. intra-European currency futures and intra-European currency swaps. At the same time, new products can be created, such as euro options, euro futures, euro area stock indices, etc. However, language difficulties, cultural differences and differences in market structure and conventions mean that the arguments for nationally based activities will persist even quite long after EMU has been formed. This applies in particular to the financial 'retail trade' vis-e0-vis households. In the long term, however, the constituent countries and markets will grow ever closer together here too. If we look at the institutional structure, it is clear that the EMU effects have already begun to work - we see stock market mergers a little everywhere in Europe, here at home the banking structure is changing. In part, this is to be seen as a positioning for what is to come, and this has also been confirmed in most cases by the companies involved. Credit risk is increasing in importance In general, monetary union - because an inflation-fighting monetary policy is the common foundation - will lead to the convergence of interest rates in the high-interest and low-interest rate countries. This also suggests that the currency risk premium will disappear completely, since there is only one currency in EMU. What will remain, even after the transition process is fully completed, is above all liquidity and credit risks. As currency risk disappears and investment decisions will be more about credit risks, there is much to suggest that well-developed European markets may form across national borders for different types of bonds such as corporate, residential and municipal bonds. This is likely to be accompanied by an interest on the part of investors in spreading their risks by diversifying their portfolios to several countries in order to limit loss risks in the event of asymmetric shocks in any country. Consequences for the Swedish securities market What, then, will be the likely consequences for the Swedish market, especially in view of the fact that Sweden will at least initially remain outside EMU? Of course, we cannot know this with any certainty. However, it is likely that Swedish investors will turn to a fairly large extent against the liquid euro market. All other things being equal, this would mean that investments in Sweden would then decrease. The same effect can also occur on the part of foreign investors - here there is a risk that Swedish companies will not benefit from a likely "wave of diversification" against such assets where the currency risk previously constituted a restriction. If Sweden later steps in, there is a risk that the portfolio adjustment has mainly already been implemented - and also in a "one-sided" way. Against this background, the challenge for us in Sweden will be to pursue an economic policy that maintains and strengthens confidence in the Swedish economy and that makes investments in Swedish assets not appear risky but attractive. If so, we can still benefit from this process, despite an "out-position". This confirms once again that exclusion leaves no room for inflationary policies. Fixed income market The Swedish money and bond market is already highly internationalised. If you look at how the Riksbank's so-called. Primary dealers and the extent to which they trade with foreign counterparties, it can be noted that this has increased rapidly in recent years. The share of foreign counterparts increased from 5% to 25% between 1992 and the beginning of 1997. At the same time as the degree of internationalization is high and growing, it is clear that Swedish companies still have a significant competitive advantage in the Swedish market. It has established channels between a wide range of players and thorough knowledge of the market and of the Swedish economy. This advantage would, of course, gradually disappear upon entry into EMU. Today, the most liquid part of European fixed income trading is conducted in twenty futures contracts, and mainly in London. In the US market, there are three contracts that support the corresponding market. In the long run, it is reasonable that we will approach the American situation. Here it is also likely that we will see a concentration of the institutions that dominate the market. Here, Swedish institutions have a general disadvantage in terms of size. On the other hand, the opportunity to make good local/national credit assessments and valuations will be of great importance in the light of the likely emerging European markets for corporate, municipal bonds and the like. Stock market The Swedish stock market is also already highly internationalized - today foreign players account for about a third of the trade. The fact that In 1993 Sweden was the first country in the world to allow remote participation has naturally contributed to this. Admittedly, it was a while before the first foreign participant joined, but today twelve out of forty-five exchange members are such remote members. The qualities a successful Swedish stock exchange must have - inside or outside EMU - are good transparency, low transaction costs, competent members and a generally high level of professionalism. In my opinion, the Stockholm Stock Exchange is competitive in this respect. To be competitive in an "out" scenario, it will be necessary for the stock exchange to set prices in several different currencies, of which the euro will be one. Together with VPC, they are also working on solutions to handle clearing and settlement in both sek and euros, as well as perhaps also other currencies. The "multi-currency environment" will, of course, affect all players in the market to a greater or lesser degree. As I said earlier, this will entail costs that some of our competitors avoid, but at the same time there may also be a positive side to this, namely that it puts the focus on the importance of creating rational infrastructure solutions. 5. Conclusions In conclusion, I would like to say the following: the transformation of the financial markets from a regulated and closed environment to an environment of market management and international competition has been beneficial not only for the financial market itself, but also for the national economy as a whole. Of course, this does not mean that it has been problem-free, but structural change processes are never problem-free. For Sweden, it is important in international contexts to defend and advance the positions of free trade in the financial market area, in the same way as we do with the manufacturing industry. Sweden is not and is unlikely to become a globally leading marketplace. But we do not need to allow ourselves to be marginalised, let alone eliminated. It requires us to take note of and develop what we are good at. This includes, not least, offering an infrastructure of the highest class both in terms of efficiency and stability. The achievement of EMU will further reinforce several of the developments that have characterised the financial markets in recent years. When it comes to the infrastructure side, life is somewhat complicated for us in Sweden, since we will at least initially be outside EMU. This means that we must, to a large extent, build up dual infrastructures. This will cost. However, hopefully it can still be turned into something positive in the sense that it helps to put the focus on the construction of the financial infrastructure. Let's hope that this can free up a lot of creative thinking that results in the solutions both getting better and coming about faster than would otherwise have been the case!
