Drtill kom frn Sverige tecken p att varuexporten och industriproduktionen kade mindre n vntat och att arbetsmarknaden nnu inte vnt uppt p ett tydligt stt. Mot den hr bakgrunden betonade vi att vi avsg att noga flja om de tendenser till uppbromsning i konjunkturen som noterats var tillflliga eller mer bestende", sade Heikensten. "Svl i samband med inflationsrapporten som vid vrt senaste penningpolitiska mte i april valde Riksbanken som bekant att lmna reporntan ofrndrad p 2 procent. Besluten var inte sjlvklara, ven om vi var eniga i Riksbankens ledning. ven om inflationen i slutet av den tvrsperiod vi verblickade bedmdes bli i linje med mlet rknade vi med att den dessfrinnan hela tiden skulle vara lgre n Riksbankens ml p 2 procent, delvis beroende p effekter av olika typer av s kallade utbudsfaktorer. Samtidigt rknade vi dock med  fr vrigt i likhet med i stort sett alla andra bedmare  att tillvxten de nrmaste ren skulle bli hgre n den ekonomin lngsiktigt kunde antas klara av utan att inflationen tar fart. Frgan var drmed hur meningsfullt det skulle vara att ytterligare sp p efterfrgan, srskilt som vi var en bra bit in i konjunkturuppgngen. Till bilden hrde ocks den hga tillvxten i hushllens upplning i kombination med stigande huspriser. ven om inget av dessa argument var fr sig rckte fr att avst frn att snka rntan talade de sammantaget som vi sg det fr en viss frsiktighet", menade Heikensten. "Kanske finns det skl att i detta sammanhang ngot utveckla den diskussion som har frts om den snabba kreditexpansionen och husprisernas utveckling. Riksbanken oroar sig inte fr huspriserna i sig. Inte heller oroar vi oss fr banksystemet i sin helhet, ven om skuldniverna kat och en del 80-talsliknande inslag brjat dyka upp. Jag tnker till exempel p kvllstidningarnas lpsedlar och de alltmer upptrappade kampanjerna fr att f hushllen att lna mer. Vad vi inte helt kan bortse ifrn r vad som kan komma att ske med den allmnna efterfrgan och sysselsttningen framver om frhllandena ndras och hushllen vill minska sin skuldsttning. Risken r att detta framtvingar en abrupt anpassning av efterfrgan. Att detta inte enbart handlar om teoretiska spekulationer skdliggrs av utvecklingen i Nederlnderna under senare r, men ocks av den oro som idag finns ven i exempelvis Frenta staterna, Storbritannien och Australien", fortsatte Heikensten. "Nr inflationen r s lg som den varit i Sverige p senare tid r det ltt att glmma hur sambanden mellan konjunkturen och inflationen normalt brukar se ut. Det som hnt i Frenta staterna och p senare tid ven i Storbritannien kan d tjna som pminnelse om att det vanliga sambandet fortfarande verkar glla. Det senaste ret har den amerikanska inflationstakten stigit gradvis och det verkar till stor del kunna frklaras p traditionellt vis av att fretagens arbetskraftskostnader har kat allt snabbare i takt med att produktivitetstillvxten dmpats och resursutnyttjandet kat", pminde Heikensten. "Hur ska man d se p den ekonomiska utvecklingen och inflationen de nrmaste ren? Vrldsekonomin vxer fortsatt relativt stabilt och f bedmare rknar med annat n att denna utveckling ska fortstta, ven om det naturligtvis finns risker inte minst till fljd av de sparandeobalanser som byggts upp. En grundlggande drivkraft bakom uppgngen r den p mnga hll stimulerande ekonomiska politiken. Fretagens balansrkningar r nu ocks efter ngra r med lga rntor generellt sett starka samtidigt som vinstlget r gott. ven i Sverige finns det mnga faktorer som talar fr fortsatt god tillvxt. Svl finans- som penningpolitiken r expansiv och kommer antagligen att s frbli nnu en tid. Med nominella lnekningar runt 3,5 procent och dagens lga inflation blir reallneutvecklingen god. Sammantaget bidrar detta till att hushllen kan vntas f en god inkomstutveckling. Ocks fretagens situation r god, med starka balansrkningar och goda vinster. Ytterligare std till efterfrgan ger den fr nrvarande frhllandevis lgt vrderade vxelkursen. Riskerna fr en svagare utveckling fr svensk del sammanhnger antagligen frmst med den fortsatt svaga arbetsmarknaden", sa Heikensten. "Jmfrt med den bedmning vi gjorde i mars finns det skl att se ngot mindre optimistiskt p den internationella utvecklingen. Det handlar frmst om att utvecklingen i euroomrdet verkar bli ngot svagare n vad vi rknade med i inflationsrapporten. Nr det gller Sverige fortstter tillvxten av allt att dma att vara relativt god. En vridning frefaller nu som vntat ske mot inhemsk efterfrgan. Nyinkommande siffror ver arbetsmarknaden har dock fortsatt att vara ngot svagare n vntat, ven om tecken finns p en stabilisering. Tillsammans med den ngot svagare internationella bilden frefaller detta idag motivera en mer dmpad svensk produktionstillvxt, frmst under innevarande r, n vad vi rknade med i inflationsrapporten", sa Heikensten. "Lt mig runda av med ett par reflektioner om det aktuella beslutslget nr det gller penningpolitiken. Som vanligt gller det fr oss i Riksbankens ledning att ta stllning till den information vi har och att frska gra en s bra bedmning som mjligt. Sammantaget synes mig, som jag var inne p tidigare, hittills inkommen statistik tala fr att konjunkturen kan bli ngot svagare n vi rknade med i mars. Till detta kommer enligt min uppfattning att oskerheten om konjunkturen bde i Sverige och utomlands kat ngot. Men det handlar inte om ngon dramatisk frndring", sade Heikensten. "Fr egen del har jag vid upprepade tillfllen under vren understrukit betydelsen av att inte lsa fast sig i ngon position. Det gller att ocks framver hlla alla drrar ppna. Title: The economic picture stands out in broad terms
text: Heikensten: The economic picture is broadly stable Date 2005-04-04 At a meeting at the County Administrative Board in Lulea, Riksbank Governor Lars Heikensten spoke about the current monetary policy. "In the general debate on monetary policy, one can easily get the impression that interest rates in Sweden are too high and hamper economic activity and are the main explanation for the weak employment development. It is therefore worth pointing out at the outset that interest rates in nominal terms are at a record low. We have to go back to the 60s and 70s to find equally low short-term interest rates. Even measured in real terms, i.e. nominal interest rates minus inflation, interest rates are among the lowest we have seen in 20 years. Monetary policy is thus significantly expansionary. The picture also includes that the Riksbank has communicated that there is no rush to raise the repo rate. Together with new information on economic developments in recent months, this has contributed to a fall in long-term market interest rates and to a slightly weaker exchange rate, changes that also stimulate the economy," Heikensten began. "The expansionary policy has had tangible results. Households have been increasing their borrowing for a long time, and there are now also signs of larger corporate borrowing. Investments and construction are growing, and consumption also looks set to increase stably," Heikensten said. "The Riksbank last published its view on the inflation and economic outlook for the next few years on 15 March. Our assessment was that economic growth in the world had peaked, but that it can nevertheless be expected to remain good. The world economy thus continues to improve, although of course, as always, there are risks. The picture for Sweden was expected to be similar, with slightly lower production growth this year than last year. But growth is still expected to be around three percent per year, which is higher than the economy is expected to be able to handle in the long term. The composition of demand was expected to be significantly different from last year. In front of us, we saw reduced contributions from foreign trade and increasing from primarily investment, but also from household consumption. With developments along these lines, where domestic demand is expected to pick up, there were reasons to expect employment to start to pick up as well. Despite the continued strong economic development, we expected inflation to be low, albeit rising. Underlying this assessment were assumptions of high domestic productivity growth and low global inflation. Added to this were a number of factors of a more special nature, such as increased competition in the grocery trade and the abolition of import quotas for textile products," Heikensten explained. "As many of you probably know, we left the repo rate unchanged at 2 percent even though inflation was estimated to be below the 2 percent inflation target for much of the next two-year period. As is so often the case, it was not an obvious decision. Therefore, it is also quite natural that there is some discussion, especially now that there is a lively political debate in society about employment and unemployment," Heikensten said. "It wasn't one factor but a combination of several that explained the decision. Among other things, we asked ourselves how meaningful it would be to try to push up general demand further beyond the level we believe is sustainable in this situation, well into the economic upturn. The already low interest rates and an ample supply of liquidity also suggest that the effects of a lower policy rate would be smaller than usual. In particular, this can be expected to apply if households and firms see through that a possible interest rate cut may have to be reversed within not too long, a thought that is hardly far-fetched when the global interest rate trend has now turned upwards. Moreover, the low rate of price increase is currently linked to factors that have little to do with demand developments and whose durability is uncertain. Further fuelling demand may then have its risks. The picture also includes the increase in household debt combined with rapidly rising house prices. The problem with this is primarily not what it might mean for the banks. Rather, it is about what may happen to general demand in the future if conditions change. While perhaps none of these arguments individually would have been sufficient, I think they collectively speak for a degree of caution," Heikensten said. "Since we made our assessment, there have been signs that the expansion in the export industry has slowed. Among other things, the statistics on foreign trade and the latest business cycle barometer indicate that the industrial economy is entering a calmer phase. At the same time, the same barometer suggests that the domestically oriented sectors, such as construction, large parts of trade and the private service industry, are now facing increasingly strong demand. There are also other signals that sales growth in the retail sector is stable and that Swedish households have become more optimistic about the future. In summary, the economic picture we have drawn, with a stable upturn and a turn towards domestic demand, seems to be holding up well. Possibly the latest information suggests that the slowdown in the export-oriented parts of the industry may be somewhat more marked than expected. At the same time, as in the past, there are other risks that affect the conditions for monetary policy," Heikensten said. "In situations when the waves of discussion are running high, it is natural to develop arguments for the position you have taken yourself. The logic of public debate also tends to be such that one is nailed to a certain position regardless of what happens next. It therefore feels extra important in situations such as the current one to emphasize something we from the Riksbank's side always tend to emphasize: we are constantly open and continuously test the new information that comes in. In the Finance Committee a couple of weeks ago, I emphasized that all the claims that the Riksbank had closed doors to both one or the other actions in the future were, as usual, misleading. This also applies today," Heikensten concluded.

Drfr r det ocks ganska naturligt att det diskuteras en del, srskilt nr det nu frs en livlig politisk debatt i samhllet om sysselsttningen och arbetslsheten", sa Heikensten. Title: Competition, trade and inflation
text: Heikensten: Competition, Trade and Inflation Date: 1999-10-25 Speaker: Deputy Governor Lars Heikensten Location: orebro Byggmastareforening What is wrong with prices in Sweden? In the first place, this may seem like a strange question to ask at a time when prices are generally stable. Despite the fact that growth has been high for a number of years, price increases have been moderate. Admittedly, the Riksbank estimated in its October inflation report that inflation would rise somewhat in the coming years as a result of the broad economic upturn. But there was no drama in the price development in the assessment. Nevertheless, I would argue that there is a fundamental problem with prices in Sweden. The problem is not the rate of price increase, but the price situation. Let me give a few examples: why should Swedish consumers pay almost twice as much for a bottle of all-purpose cleaners as the Danes, or almost three times as much as the Dutch do? And how is it that Swedish travellers pay two thirds more for their air tickets than travellers in the rest of the EU pay for the same route? The gap between prices in Sweden and the rest of Europe is evident in the study of price levels in the EU countries published by the European Commission this year. (1) The study shows that the Swedish price for a basket of consumer goods is 27 percent above the price of the same basket in the EU, as much as 44 percent above the price in the UK and no less than 59 percent above the price level in the UNITED STATES. Sweden, together with Denmark and Germany, is one of the EU's most expensive countries. Figure 1. Relative price level in 1996 These are conditions that affect the prosperity of us Swedes. Roughly speaking, each percent drop in the price level corresponds to an extra SEK 2000 for a normal household. This shows that if the high prices in Sweden are due to some mismatch that over time can be corrected, it can provide great wealth gains for several years. Since the Swedish price situation is particularly high for e.g. food or housing, which constitutes a larger share of the consumption basket for the low-paid, a price correction would also particularly benefit the most deprived in society. For me, as a member of the Riksbank's management, there is another reason to raise this issue. After all, the Riksbank's task is to protect the value of money; in practice, to meet the target of 2% inflation. All factors that affect the price development thus affect the conditions for our work. Improved competition can put downward pressure on prices. Admittedly, these are likely to be essentially one-off effects on inflation. But if these break through gradually over a fairly long period, it will make it easier for the Riksbank to contain inflationary pressures. Against this background, I intend to discuss today some factors that affect the price level in Sweden. I will give you an example of a sector that has not worked so well from the point of view of competition, which is close to your heart. However, I will also mention good examples of liberalisations carried out in recent years. My intention is in addition, to highlight the importance of free trade. Finally, I shall comment in a little more detail on the importance of competition for inflation and thus for monetary policy. What are the price differences due to? An obvious explanation for the deviations in consumer prices is the Swedish VAT rate of 25 percent. This level is higher than in most other EU countries, although not in all of them. Our higher VAT is linked to the tax system we have in Sweden, but at the bottom is of course our relatively high public expenditure. These have to finance in one way or another and if VAT were reduced, we would have to raise other taxes that would probably affect our relative price level. VAT is not sufficient to explain the discrepancies. Adjusted for VAT differences, the price level in Sweden is still 10-15 percent higher than the average price level in the EU and 15-20 percent above the price level in the US. Added to vat is the relatively high Swedish labour costs, not least in service industries such as retail trade. Since we in Sweden have less wage dispersion than in many other countries, we usually have higher wages for traditionally low-paid professions, although wages for these groups have also fallen relative to Europe in recent decades. Moreover, labour costs are greatly affected by taxes on labour; Employers' contributions, for example, are among the highest in the EU. It is also likely that Sweden, as a sparsely populated country on the outskirts of Europe, will suffer from higher transport costs. These factors probably go quite a long way as an explanation for the price differences, but the picture also includes the competitive conditions in the Swedish economy. Parts of the Swedish economy have long been fiercely competitive. Not least, we in Sweden have a long tradition of free trade, which has meant that most of the goods production has been subject to clear international price pressure. In these areas, too, price differences are not normally so great. But in parallel, there are other markets in Sweden where competition is in practice low. Some of these markets are ones that consumers come into contact with on a daily basis. A few large players dominate the market and their market power allows them to maintain a higher price level. The fact that Sweden in particular is characterized by a lack of competition can to some extent be explained by geographical and cultural factors. We are, as I have just mentioned, a sparsely populated country and a small language and cultural area, where there may be natural reasons why there are few companies competing in some markets. But the lack of competition often seems to be linked to regulations and systems that the government and parliament have built up. It has sometimes been a question of pure legislative monopolies, but often administrative rules and laws that have erected such high barriers that new players have not been able to break in. In a number of other cases, it can be argued that the authorities have not acted forcefully enough to maintain competition, but have allowed one or more operators to abuse their dominant position. A classic example is the establishment rules for new stores that have contributed to an internationally high concentration in the retail sector in Sweden. The concentration, in turn, has probably contributed to the high prices of food and groceries. At the same time, the situation in the retail sector demonstrates the difficulties of competition policy. In the early 80s, the establishment rules were abolished after a long discussion, but these reappeared again in the early 90s in partly new forms. Figure 2. Food price levels in 1996. One possible effect of poor competition is high profit margins. The statistics for the food industry support this. Profits in this industry are not only higher than in other parts of the business world, in addition, the difference is increasing. Profit levels also seem to be quite insensitive to changes in the economy, which may seem a bit strange. It should be stressed that weak competition can also manifest itself in poor efficiency in production. With low competition, rationalization pressure decreases; productivity in the sector will thus be lower than it would otherwise be. An example: the construction sector In this company, it is natural to take a closer look at the competitive situation and price developments in the housing and construction sector. Housing costs make up a very large part of household consumption; a third of the CPI basket. Construction and building material prices in Sweden are higher than in most EU countries and in the US. According to Eurostat data, Swedish building prices were 27% above the average construction prices in the EU in 1996. Only in Denmark it is more expensive to build houses. For example, apartment doors cost about 60 percent more in Sweden than in Finland and Germany. Figure 3. Building material costs compared to CPI. The relatively high price level of housing in Sweden is partly due to high quality requirements. However, there is hardly any doubt that the system used to subsidize housing construction in Sweden has also been a significant culprit in the drama. The motives of producers for holding back the development of costs were in the system that previously prevailed too weak Over the past 5-10 years, there have been significant changes that make construction in this regard today work better. A discussion is now taking place in the media about changing the policy again in light of some problems in the construction and residential area. It is extremely important that any changes that may be made do not again reduce competition and drive up the prices of accommodation. Although the subsidy system has changed, concentration problems remain. According to the Construction Cost Delegation, foreign competition is low. According to a 1996 study by the Swedish National Board of Trade, the Swedish Competition Authority and Nutek, the Swedish construction market is dominated by four companies that together have just over 60 percent of the market. Even the building materials industry is concentrated and only to a limited extent exposed to foreign competition. For example, the study shows that one cement manufacturer has a market share of 95 percent, while two manufacturers of asphalt account for 75 percent of the asphalt market. Geographical and regional factors are likely to come into play, as the transportation of building materials is expensive and cumbersome. The Swedish Competition Authority's reports also indicate that the regulations restrict competition within the EU's internal market. The question is whether the diversity of standards and type-approval in different countries, with the difficulty of getting building materials approved in EU countries other than their own, does not restrict competition. In the construction sector, there have been many examples of how poor competition can create inefficiencies. There is reason to believe that this has also had an impact on wage formation. During the 80s, strong wage-driving impulses spread from the construction sector to other parts of the economy. The latest contracts in the construction industry of around 3 per cent per annum exceed the average wage agreements for the whole economy. History also shows that wage slippage has been significant in this sector. The question is whether the lack of competitive pressure means that it is still easier to demand wage increases in addition to productivity growth in the construction industry in particular, than, for example, in the highly competitive export-oriented engineering industry? Some other examples: electricity and telecommunications Thus, in Sweden, there are examples of markets where competition is incomplete. But today there are also good examples of what can be achieved if you dare to open up and create competition. In recent years, deregulations have been carried out in Sweden in markets such as formerly considered natural monopolies and where bad competition was seen as a necessary evil. This mainly concerns telecoms and energy. Competing players have been allowed in and managed to establish themselves in these markets helped both by legislative and regulatory changes and by new technology. Developments in the Swedish electricity market are a good example of the fact that deregulation must be carried out consistently and that even simple administrative obstacles can be enough to prevent competition. Despite the fact that the market has been liberalised since 1996, the requirement for expensive electricity meters has acted as an effective barrier to competition with household customers. Now that the electricity meter requirement has been abolished this year, even though the process is only in its infancy, we can already see a real downward pressure on prices for households as well. A family with a normal-sized electrically heated villa can reduce their electricity bill by as much as SEK 1500 per year. A similar development has taken place in the field of telecommunications. As the telephone market gradually opened up to competition in the 90s, long-distance calls pushed prices by competition. But at the same time, Telia's tariffs rose on local calls. With the new ability to choose the operator, lower call costs are expected overall. We already see that competitors offer up to 50 percent lower tariffs for Swedish calls. In these areas, Sweden is also below the price level in other industrialized countries. According to oecd calculations, we are 41% below the OECD average price level for telecommunications and 58% below the average price level for electricity distribution. Since the calculations were made, prices have fallen further. Liberalisation contributes further to this fundamentally positive image. Of course, not all deregulation is easy. They must be carried out thoughtfully and sometimes gradually. Not least, it is important that consumers are given real opportunities to compare prices and products. The fact that it is not always easy shows the deregulation of taxis. In the field of aviation, the price effects of the implemented changes have not been as desired. Here, producers appear to have found new ways of restricting competition. The fact that deregulation in various dimensions has an impact on inflation is well illustrated by developments in recent years and at present. In the inflation report, which was a few weeks old, the Riksbank estimated that the deregulations and liberalizations implemented in recent years will together reduce CPI inflation by 0.2-0.3 percentage points this year and next year and by slightly less in 2001. This year, the liberalisation of the electricity market in particular is expected to contribute to lower inflation. Next year, however, the changes in the telecommunications market and agricultural reform in the context of Agenda 2000 are also expected to dampen consumer prices to the same extent as the liberalisation of electricity. Effects of deregulation - contribution to the CPI. The importance of free trade Before I discuss the effects of increased competition on the Riksbank's work and inflation, let me digress a little about free trade and its importance. Free trade is perhaps the most important prerequisite for bringing about good competition, pushing down prices and creating high prosperity in a small open economy like Sweden. Today, imports also account for almost 40 percent of GDP and the share has been steadily increasing. Through a free trade-friendly policy, Sweden has actually been able to achieve low prices compared to the EU average for a number of goods, such as clothes, shoes and consumer electronics. With participation in the EU's internal market, price competition has increased further in Sweden. At the same time, Swedish companies that are otherwise active in the EU area are subject to tougher competitive pressure. Since almost 70 percent of Sweden's total trade goes to the EU area, the effects of this are central. EMU contributes to a further increase in competition. When the prices of goods within the monetary union can be quickly and casually compared in the same currency, the euro, so facilitates it is for consumers to make their purchases in the countries where prices are lowest. It also affects companies' pricing strategies and exposes other costs such as taxes that affect prices. All in all, this means that prices are being squeezed further. Price drops as high as 10-15 percent have been mentioned, but all studies are associated with very great uncertainty. The fact that there is scope for strengthening price competition within the EU is shown by the fact that price differences between different countries within the EU are still as high as around 16% on average. Although the differences have narrowed by about 6 percentage points over the past ten years, the differences are still 40 percent higher than they are between different states and regions in the United States. However, in order to both reduce price differentials and generally squeeze price levels within the EU, increased competition within the EU alone is not enough. At least as much competition from the outside world is required. Several studies show that competition from outside the EU could contribute to a more uniform and lower price level. According to a study by the OECD, developments within the EU have moved rapidly towards increased free trade from the end of the 80s until 1993, with falling trade barriers and an increased share of imports in consumption in the EU. Since then, however, progress has stagnated and the number of attempts to restrict competition by means of anti-dumping procedures has increased. On the contrary, the US, which was previously less open than the EU as a whole, is now more open than the EU and has a larger share of imports relative to GDP, 18%, compared with just under 13% for the EU. Particularly disappointing is the fact that imports of less high-tech goods are lower in the EU than in the US. It is disappointing because it is a sign that the production of countries with less developed industries - including many of our neighbours in Eastern Europe - is being held back by the barriers to trade that exist. It is precisely these countries that we should give a chance as they try to recover from a number of decades lost economically. But it is also disappointing because, in areas of this kind in particular, consumers could often get significantly lower prices if trade were freer. In a few months' time, a new free trade round within the WTO will begin with pressure on the EU and other participants to further reduce trade barriers and open up markets for agricultural products, among other things. However, success in the WTO is not a foregone conclusion. We see that the negotiations sometimes encounter temporary setbacks right now with the notorious "banana war" and the "hormone beef war" between the US and the EU, where the US is now imposing punitive tariffs on European goods. Another setback for free trade is the EU's halt to parallel imports from a non-EU country, according to the so-called Silhouette ruling. Parallel imports are a way for importers to avoid the price discrimination used by branded producers to charge the highest possible prices in each country. The Swedish Competition Authority shows in a study that 60 percent of Swedish parallel imports come from countries outside the EU and that this type of import has pushed down prices by 10-30 percent for goods such as car parts, clothes, shoes and medicines. A decision to re-authorise parallel imports would thus be of considerable benefit to consumers. The Swedish Competition Authority believes that this would mean as much as 0.4 percentage points on the CPI, or about SEK 1000 per household in Sweden. It is clear from this discussion that the EU has not always shown itself to be at its best in the area of trade policy. Since the EU countries pursue a common trade policy towards the outside world, it is important that we in Sweden clearly pursue as free trade-friendly a policy as possible within the Community. Competition and inflation The debate on the importance of competition for inflation has intensified in recent years. Not least, the US Federal Reserve Governor Alan Greenspan has contributed to this, as he reasoned about the fact that inflation in the US has been low for several years despite high capacity utilisation. It is not surprising that this problem has also been put on the agenda in Sweden. We were able to state earlier that the Swedish inflation rate is currently affected by deregulation both in Sweden and internationally. The fact that the Riksbank is working on an inflation target also contributes to an increased focus in the debate on price developments. As I mentioned earlier, trade in the world has increased as a result of tariffs and tariffs being reduced. Within individual countries, important sectors have also been liberalised. In addition, there are also the effects of lower transport costs and the emergence of a number of new countries in which efficient production has been possible at low costs. A special dimension to this is given to the new information technology: it opens up, among other things, the possibility of quickly comparing different prices via the Internet without physically moving to the different shops. Therefore, already today, lower prices are noted online. One example is the price of CDs, which are up to 20 percent cheaper in Swedish internal stores than in the retail trade. According to HUI, online stores in the United States are another 10-20 percent cheaper. Taken together, these are factors that are likely to have intensified competitive pressures in large parts of the economies of developed countries. Other expressions of the same process are the rapid changes taking place in the ownership and corporate structure in many sectors. The question then is how increased competition affects inflation. It can be illustrated with a concrete example. Let me take the trade in used cars, although I might as well have exemplified with books or any other commodity. The Internet etc. is said to have led to a number of Swedes starting to buy used cars in, among other places. Germany because the prices there are lower. A first obvious effect of this is that it becomes more difficult to charge equally high prices for this type of car in Sweden. The price level is thus falling. In the next stage, we can imagine that car dealers are trying to counteract the negative effect on profitability by rationalizing their own operations. Productivity in the motor vehicle trade is increasing. If this work is carried out successfully enough, perhaps profit margins can be maintained. Another possibility is that, in the next wage movement, the car dealerships do not grant as high wage increases as they would otherwise have done or that when they buy the cars they pay less, etc. Thus, when a market is opened up to competition in this way, it can have both direct and indirect price and wage effects. It can also lead to a shift in productivity. In essence, however, it's all about one-off effects; the price level falls and/or the productivity level rises. But a process of this kind - with increased competition - can still affect overall inflation as measured by some index such as the CPI for many years if the process takes effect gradually in different parts of the economy. Perhaps, just in case, I should say that effects also on the development of productivity cannot be ruled out. Increased competition could conceivably lead to slightly higher potential growth. However, the empirical support for this would have happened is small. What does this mean for the Riksbank and monetary policy? Perhaps it could be put that we are currently being helped in our efforts to keep inflation down by, among other things, new technology, deregulation and reduced trade barriers. They do not play a decisive role in inflation in the long term, but they are also not entirely insignificant. If this type of one-off effect is a recurring feature of the price picture, we should take them into account when conducting monetary policy; in the same way that the Riksbank, for example, in the 70s and 80s - if monetary policy had then worked with inflation targets - would have had to take into account the increased taxes. Should there be arguments that competition has increased the potential growth rate, this should of course also be taken into account. On this point, however, there are reasons to be much more sceptical. Let me conclude by emphasising that the comments I have made here on the importance of well-functioning competition - primarily for the development of prosperity - are not intended to be a contribution to the current discussion on the repo rate. In the inflation report from the beginning of October, we took into account the effects we had been able to identify of increased competition, etc. The conclusion reached by the Riksbank in connection with the publication of the inflation report - that the repo rate will have to be raised if nothing unforeseen happens - thus applies. Footnote (1) The nera consultancy firm for the European Commission in the context of the Cardiff II process, publicerad bl. a. I European Economy, Nr. 1 1999, Supplement A, Economic trends.

Grovt rknat motsvarar varje procents nedgng i prisnivn 2000 kronor extra fr ett normalhushll. Det visar att om de hga priserna i Sverige beror p ngot missfrhllande som med tiden gr att rtta till, s kan det ge stora vlstndsvinster under flera r. Fr mig som medlem av Riksbankens ledning finns det ytterligare ett skl att ta upp denna frga. Riksbankens uppgift r ju att vrna penningvrdet; i praktiken att uppfylla mlet om 2 procents inflation. Alla faktorer som pverkar prisutvecklingen pverkar drmed frutsttningarna fr vrt arbete. En frbttrad konkurrens kan stadkomma en press nedt p priserna. Mot den hr bakgrunden tnker jag idag diskutera ngra faktorer som pverkar prisnivn i Sverige. Arbetskraftskostnaderna pverkas dessutom i hg grad av skatter p arbete; arbetsgivaravgifterna r t.ex. bland de hgsta inom EU. Troligt r ocks att Sverige som ett glest befolkat land i Europas utkant drabbas av hgre transportkostnader. Ett exempel: byggsektorn I det hr sllskapet r det naturligt att titta nrmare p konkurrenssituationen och prisutvecklingen inom bostads- och byggsektorn. Geografiska och regionala faktorer spelar sannolikt in, eftersom transporter av byggmaterial r dyra och besvrliga. Konkurrensverkets rapporter tyder ocks p att regleringarna begrnsar konkurrensen inom EU:s inre marknad. Frgan r om inte mngfalden standarder och typgodknnande i olika lnder, med svrigheten att f byggmaterial godknt i andra EU-lnder n det egna, begrnsar konkurrensen. Inom byggsektorn har det funnits mnga exempel p att dlig konkurrens kan skapa ineffektivitet. Det finns skl att tro att detta ocks terverkat p lnebildningen. Under 80-talet spred sig starka lnedrivande impulser frn byggsektorn till andra delar av ekonomin. De senaste avtalen inom byggbranschen p omkring 3 procent per r verskrider de genomsnittliga lneavtalen fr hela ekonomin. Historien visar ocks att lneglidningen varit betydande inom denna sektor. Frgan r om bristen p konkurrenstryck gr att det fortfarande r lttare att stlla krav p lnekningar utver produktivitetskningen inom just byggbranschen, n till exempel inom den hrt konkurrensutsatta exportorienterade verkstadsindustrin? Ngra andra exempel: el och tele Det finns allts i Sverige exempel p marknader dr konkurrensen r ofullstndig. Frmst gller det telekom och energi. Konkurrerande aktrer har slppts in och lyckats etablera sig p dessa marknader hjlpta bde av lag- och regleringsndringar och av ny teknologi. Frihandel r den kanske viktigaste frutsttningen fr att f till stnd en god konkurrens, pressa priserna och skapa ett hgt vlstnd i en liten ppen ekonomi som Sverige. Importen utgr idag ocks nstan 40 procent av BNP och andelen har kat stadigt. Genom en frihandelsvnlig politik har Sverige faktiskt kunnat uppn lga priser jmfrt med EU-genomsnittet p en rad varor, som klder, skor och hemelektronik. I och med deltagandet i EU:s inre marknad har priskonkurrensen kat ytterligare i Sverige. Samtidigt utstts de svenska fretag som r aktiva inom EU-omrdet i vrigt fr en hrdare konkurrenspress. Eftersom nstan 70 procent av Sveriges totala handel gr till EU-omrdet r effekterna av detta centrala. EMU bidrar till att konkurrensen kar ytterligare. Nr priserna p varor inom valutaunionen snabbt och ledigt kan jmfras i samma valuta, euron, s underlttar det fr konsumenterna att gra sina inkp i de lnder dr priserna r som lgst. Det pverkar ocks fretagens prissttningsstrategier och blottlgger andra kostnader t.ex. skatter som pverka priserna. Sammantaget medfr det att priserna pressas ytterligare. S hga prisfall som 10-15 procent har nmnts, men alla studier r frknippade med mycket stora oskerhet. Att det finns utrymme fr att strka priskonkurrensen inom EU framgr av att prisskillnaderna mellan olika lnder inom EU alltjmt r s hga som omkring 16 procent i snitt. Visserligen har skillnaderna minskat med cirka 6 procentenheter under de senaste tio ren men skillnaderna r nd 40 procent hgre n vad de r mellan olika delstater och regioner i USA. Fr att bde minska prisskillnaderna och allmnt pressa prisniverna inom EU rcker det dock inte med skrpt konkurrens bara inom EU. I minst lika hg grad krvs konkurrens frn omvrlden. Flera studier visar att just konkurrens frn lnder utanfr EU skulle kunna bidra till en mer enhetlig och lgre prisniv. Enligt en studie frn OECD har utvecklingen inom EU snabbt rrt sig mot kad frihandel frn 80-talets slut och fram till 1993, med fallande handelshinder och kad andel import i konsumtionen i EU. Sedan dessa har dock utvecklingen stagnerat och antalet frsk att med anti-dumpingfrfaranden begrnsa konkurrensen har kat. USA som tidigare var mindre ppet n EU som helhet r nu tvrtom mer ppet n EU och har en strre andel import relativt BNP, 18 procent, att jmfra med knappa 13 procent fr EU. Srskilt nedslende r att importen av mindre hgteknologiska varor r lgre i EU n i USA. Det r nedslende drfr att det r ett tecken p att produktionen frn lnder med mindre utvecklad industri - dribland mnga av vra grannar i steuropa - hlls tillbaka av de handelshinder som finns. Just dessa lnder borde vi ge en chans nr de nu frsker terhmta sig efter ett antal, i ekonomiskt hnseende, tappade decennier. Men det r ocks nedslende drfr att konsumenterna just p omrden av detta slag ofta skulle kunna f rejlt lgre priser om handeln vore friare. Eftersom EU-lnderna fr en gemensam handelspolitik gentemot omvrlden r det viktigt att vi i Sverige tydligt driver en s frihandelsvnlig politik som mjligt inom gemenskapen. Konkurrens och inflation Diskussionen om konkurrensens betydelse fr inflationen har intensifierats under senare r. Inte minst har den amerikanska centralbankschefen Alan Greenspan bidragit till detta, d han resonerat kring det faktum att inflationen i USA har varit lg under flera r trots ett hgt kapacitetsutnyttjande. Det r inte frvnande att denna problematik kommit p dagordningen ocks i Sverige. Vi kunde ju tidigare konstatera att den svenska inflationstakten just nu pverkas av avregleringar svl i Sverige som internationellt. Det faktum att Riksbanken arbetar med ett inflationsml bidrar ocks till en kad fokusering i debatten p prisutvecklingen. Som jag var inne p tidigare har handeln i vrlden kat till fljd av att tullar etc. snkts. Inom enskilda lnder har ocks viktiga sektorer avreglerats. Till detta kommer ocks bl.a. effekterna av lgre transportkostnader och framvxten av ett antal nya lnder inom vilka en effektiv produktion har kunnat ske till lga kostnader. En srskild dimension till detta ger den nya informationsteknologin: Den ppnar bl.a. mjligheter att via Internet snabbt jmfra olika priser utan att frflytta sig fysiskt till de olika butikerna. Redan idag noteras drfr lgre priser p ntet. Ett exempel r priset p CD-skivor, som r upp till 20 procent billigare i svenska internbutiker n ute i handeln. Enligt HUI r ntbutiker i USA ytterligare 10-20 procent billigare. Sammantaget r det hr faktorer som sannolikt skrpt konkurrenstrycket i stora delar av industrilndernas ekonomier. Andra uttryck fr samma process r de snabba frndringar som sker i gar- och fretagsstrukturen i mnga sektorer. Frgan r d hur kad konkurrens pverkar inflationen. Det kan skdliggras med ett konkret exempel. Lt mig ta handeln med begagnade bilar, ven om jag lika vl kunde ha exemplifierat med bcker eller ngon annan vara. Internet mm. sgs ha medfrt att ett antal svenskar brjat kpa begagnade bilar i bl.a. Tyskland eftersom priserna dr r lgre. En frsta sjlvklar effekt av detta r att det blir svrare att ta ut lika hga priser p denna typ av bilar i Sverige. Prisnivn faller allts. I nsta led kan vi tnka oss att bilhandlarna frsker motverka den negativa effekten p lnsamheten genom att rationalisera den egna verksamheten. Produktiviteten i bilhandeln kar. Bedrivs detta arbete tillrckligt framgngsrikt kanske vinstmarginalerna kan upprtthllas. Ytterligare en mjlighet r att bilhandeln i nsta lnerrelse inte beviljar lika hga lnekningar som de annars skulle ha gjort eller att de nr de kper in bilarna betalar mindre osv. Nr en marknad p det hr sttet ppnas upp fr konkurrens kan det allts f bde direkta och indirekta pris- och lneeffekter. Det kan ocks leda till ett skift i produktiviteten. I huvudsak handlar det dock om engngseffekter; prisnivn faller och/eller produktivitetsnivn stiger. Men en process av det hr slaget - med kad konkurrens  kan nd pverka den sammantagna inflationen mtt med ngot index som t.ex. KPI under mnga r om processen slr igenom gradvis i olika delar av ekonomin. Kanske ska jag fr skerhets skull sga att effekter ocks p produktivitetens utveckling inte kan uteslutas. En skrpt konkurrens skulle kunna tnkas medfra en ngot hgre potentiell tillvxt. Det empiriska stdet fr detta skulle ha skett r dock litet. Vad betyder d detta fr Riksbanken och penningpolitiken? Kanske kan man uttrycka det som att vi fr nrvarande fr hjlp i vr strvan att hlla nere inflationen av bl.a. ny teknologi, avregleringar och minskade handelshinder. De spelar ingen avgrande roll fr inflationen p sikt, men de r inte heller helt betydelselsa. Om den hr typen av engngseffekter utgr ett terkommande inslag i prisbilden br vi ta hnsyn till dem nr vi bedriver penningpolitik; p samma vis som Riksbanken t.ex. under 70- och 80-talen - om penningpolitiken d arbetat med inflationsml - skulle varit tvungen att beakta de kade skatterna. Om det skulle finnas argument fr att konkurrensen kat den potentiella tillvxttakten, br detta naturligtvis ocks beaktas. P den hr punkten finns det dock skl att vara betydligt mer skeptisk. Lt mig avslutningsvis understryka att de synpunkter jag hr framfrt om vikten av en vl fungerande konkurrens - i frsta hand fr vlstndsutvecklingen - inte r avsedda att vara ett inlgg i den aktuella diskussionen om reporntan. I inflationsrapporten frn brjan av oktober beaktade vi de effekter vi kunnat identifiera av kad konkurrens etc. Den slutsats Riksbanken drog i samband med publiceringen av inflationsrapporten - att reporntan kommer att behva hjas om inget ofrutsett intrffar - gller allts. Title: Low inflation, but the picture still stands in broad strokes
text: Heikensten: Low inflation, but the picture still stands in broad strokes Date 2005-01-21 Riksbank Governor Lars Heikensten spoke at a meeting in Sala about the current economic situation and monetary policy. "At the beginning of December last year, the Riksbank last published its view of the future economic outlook in the world around us and in Sweden. Our assessment at the time was that global GDP growth had peaked. However, growth was still expected to be good and international resource utilisation will thus increase in the future. By and large, this picture stands. It is possible that there is reason to be somewhat less optimistic about the euro area as newly emerged statistics show a fragmented picture of economic developments there. In the US, on the other hand, economic development appears to remain strong. The natural disaster that has occurred around the Indian Ocean is a great tragedy that has hit an awful lot of people hard. In this perspective, the macroeconomic impact of what has happened is certainly not the essential thing. Nevertheless, in a speech such as this, there may be reason to note that the effects in macroeconomic terms are not considered to be so great even for the majority of the affected countries," Heikensten began. "In Sweden, the euro area and the US, long-term interest rates remain very low in a historical perspective. The krona has weakened slightly against both the euro and the dollar recently. However, developments in the financial markets are broadly in line with the assessment in the previous Inflation Report and my view of future financial conditions is therefore essentially the same as in December," Heikensten said. "In Sweden, GDP growth was high last year. In December, the Riksbank's assessment was that growth would slow somewhat this year and next year, but despite this, resource utilisation was expected to continue to rise in the future. So far, growth has been supported by, among other things, a strong export economy, but domestic demand has been assumed to contribute more and more in the future. All in all, I do not think that newly received statistics will cause any major change in this view of the future economic outlook. Labour market developments have been broadly in line with the assessment made in December. Demand for labour remains low, but a continued strengthening of the economy is expected to lead to an increase in employment and a fall in unemployment," Heikensten said. "Inflation stood at 0.4 percent and 0.8 percent, respectively, according to the CPI and UND1X, respectively. This was lower than our assessment in December and a consequence of lower than expected imported inflation. Even earlier, the Riksbank expected low inflation to be well below its target for 2005. It was not until the end of the current projection horizon for monetary policy that inflation was expected to increase and be in line with the inflation target, driven by continued good demand developments and higher resource utilisation. The question now is whether there is reason to change the assessment of the inflation forecast over a couple of years' time as a result of the new information received since December. My first cautious assessment so far is that it doesn't to any great extent, although shorter-term projections may need to adjusted slightly," Heikensten noted. "On the other hand, I see reasons to try to somewhat nuance the discussion about economic development and its consequences for monetary policy. Let me point out that the structure of monetary policy has never been as mechanical as it sometimes seems to have been perceived. In fact, last year offers good examples of trade-offs that may be relevant. The minutes of the Executive Board's meetings show, for example, that households' rapidly growing debt burden and housing price developments have been included in the discussion. In my opinion, there may sometimes be a case for considering risks in this area when deciding on the repo rate. Another question that may need to be considered, and which was discussed a bit in the late 1990s, is how to deal with the fact that the now low inflation is largely due to weak performance in the prices of imported goods. Attempts to counter this fully by driving up domestic prices may have their risks in the long run. If the international price picture changes, excessive domestic price pressures may turn out to have been established. It is also worth mentioning that several of the inflation projections made last year could in principle have justified an even lower interest rate environment, as the forecasts indicated that inflation would remain below target for almost the entire next two-year period. However, the reason why I did not advocate further or greater interest rate cuts was not only due to the fact that inflation was expected to be in line with the target for just two years, but also, among other things, because demand developed strongly. That it is reasonable to take some account also of real economic developments, both because it says something about inflation in the longer term but also because stable real economic development is important in itself, the Riksbank has previously explained. This can be seen, among other things, from the clarification made by the Executive Board in 1999," Heikensten pointed out. "At the monetary policy meeting next week, we will start by setting a new assessment for inflation. As usual, this will be of crucial importance when deciding on the repo rate. Issues of the kind I have just touched on may also play a certain role in the discussion", Heikensten concluded.

I brjan av december frra ret publicerade Riksbanken senast sin syn p de framtida konjunkturutsikterna i vr omvrld och i Sverige. Vr bedmning d var att den globala BNP-tillvxten hade kulminerat. Efterfrgan p arbetskraft r alltjmt lg, men en fortsatt frstrkning av konjunkturen vntas medfra att sysselsttningen kar och arbetslsheten sjunker, sa Heikensten. Inflationen uppgick i december till 0,4 procent respektive 0,8 procent enligt KPI och UND1X. Detta var lgre n vad som lg i vr bedmning i december och en fljd av att den importerade inflationen blev lgre n vntat. Redan tidigare rknade Riksbanken med en lg inflation tydligt under mlet fr 2005. Frst i slutet av den fr penningpolitiken nu aktuella prognosperioden bedmdes inflationen ka och bli i linje med inflationsmlet, tillfljd av en fortsatt god efterfrgeutveckling och ett hgre resursutnyttjande. Frgan r nu om det finns anledning att ndra bedmningen av inflationsprognosen p ett par rs sikt till fljd av den nya information som inkommit sedan i december. Min frsta frsiktiga bedmning s hr lngt r att det inte gr det i ngon strre utstrckning, ven om prognoserna p kortare sikt kan behva justeras ngot, konstaterade Heikensten. Dremot ser jag skl att ngot frska nyansera diskussionen om den ekonomiska utvecklingen och dess konsekvenser fr penningpolitiken. Lt mig pongtera att upplggningen av penningpolitiken aldrig varit s mekanisk som den ibland frefaller ha uppfattats. Fjolret erbjuder i sjlva verket bra exempel p avvgningar som kan vara aktuella. Av protokollen frn direktionens sammantrden framgr t.ex. att hushllens snabbvxande skuldbrda och prisutvecklingen p bostder har funnits med i diskussionen. Risker p detta omrde kan det enligt min uppfattning ibland finnas skl att vga in nr beslut fattas om reporntan. En annan frga man kan behva fundera p, och som diskuterades en del i slutet av 1990-talet, r hur man ska hantera det faktum att den nu lga inflationen till stor del beror p att priserna p importerade varor utvecklats svagt. Frsk att motverka detta fullt ut genom att driva upp de inhemska priserna kan ha sina risker p sikt. Om den internationella prisbilden ndras kan ett alltfr hgt inhemskt pristryck visa sig ha etablerats. Mjligen frtjnar det ocks att nmnas att flera av de inflationsbedmningar som gjordes under fjolret i princip hade kunnat motivera ett nnu lgre rntelge eftersom prognoserna tydde p att inflationen skulle komma att ligga under mlet under nstan hela den nrmaste tvrsperioden. Att jag nd inte frordade ytterligare eller strre rntesnkningar berodde inte enbart p att inflationen vntades vara i linje med mlet p just tv rs sikt, utan ven bl.a. p att efterfrgan utvecklades starkt. Att det r rimligt att ta viss hnsyn ven till den realekonomiska utvecklingen, bde fr att den sger ngot om inflationen p lngre sikt men ocks fr att en stabil real ekonomisk utveckling r viktig i sig, har Riksbanken frklarat tidigare. Det framgr bl.a. av frtydligandet som direktionen gjorde 1999, pongterade Heikensten. Vid det penningpolitiska sammantrdet nsta vecka kommer vi att brja med att lgga fast en ny bedmning fr inflationen. Denna kommer som vanligt att vara av avgrande betydelse nr beslut tas om reporntan. Title: Minor changes in the inflation picture
text: Heikensten: Minor changes in the inflation picture Date 2004-11-30 At a meeting organized by Handelsbanken in Gothenburg, Riksbank Governor Lars Heikensten spoke about the current economic situation and monetary policy. "The Riksbank published its latest assessment of the economy and inflation in mid-October. Since then, there have been a couple of things that warrant a certain nuance in the view of developments ahead. Most important is the rapid fall in the dollar in recent times and the signs of weaker development in the euro area," Heikensten began. "In recent years, the dollar has gradually weakened against both the euro and the Swedish krona. Lately, development has accelerated. The dollar is today weaker against the krona than it has been since 1996 and against the euro than it has been at any time since its introduction in 1999. It seems that it is mainly an increased focus on the large deficit in the US current account that has driven this development. In general, there are good reasons not to rush off and revise long-term assessments solely as a result of rapid movements in the market. However, most analysts today seem to expect a continued weakening of the dollar. However, some revision of the krona's development in trade-weighted terms over the next few years seems reasonable," Heikensten continued. "With regard to real developments in the euro area, there have been some less positive signals since mid-October, including a more than expected slowdown in growth in the third quarter. This development is likely to be linked to the high oil price and the strong euro. As oil prices can be expected to be slightly higher and the euro stronger going forward than assumed in the previous inflation report, GDP growth in the euro area can be expected to be weaker next year as well," Heikensten said. "Against this background; what is my overall view of the future economic outlook? In October, it was assumed that the global economy would continue to strengthen this year as well as in 2005 and 2006. In the OECD area, there was growth this year of about 3.5 percent. Over the next two years, we expected slightly lower growth, averaging 2.8 percent. There are therefore grounds for a certain downward adjustment here. However, my assessment is still that the global economy will continue to strengthen in the future. This is partly due to the fact that real interest rates are still very low, despite the fact that key interest rates have been raised in some countries," Heikensten said. "Over the past year, the Riksbank has had a positive view of the Swedish economy. Despite this, we have gradually had to adjust our growth forecasts upwards, including in October. In recent quarters, the Swedish economy has grown faster than is usually considered sustainable in the long term. Nevertheless, inflation has not yet picked up, which can be largely explained by good productivity developments and by low import prices. In October, Swedish growth was estimated to be around 3.5 per cent this year and just over 3 per cent in 2005 and 2006. In general, I stand by this assessment, although a somewhat weaker development in the outside world and a stronger krona are likely means that growth going forward may need to be adjusted down slightly," Heikensten said. "Swedish unemployment and employment have mainly developed in line with the assessment in the previous Inflation Report. The labour market is thus relatively weak despite a clear increase in the number of hours worked. In the previous report, the continued good growth was estimated to contribute to an increase in employment and a fall in unemployment over the course of next year. There is no reason to change that assessment at this time," Heikensten said. "So what does this mean for inflation? In the previous Inflation Report, we assessed that rising domestic and international capacity utilisation and cost pressures would lead inflation to rise and approach the 2% target over the course of 2006. The risks of higher inflation, for example as a result of higher oil prices or lower productivity growth, were assessed to be as great as the risks of lower inflation. My view now is that this assessment essentially still stands. We have come a little further into the economic upturn. That in itself tends to result in higher inflation at the end of the forecast horizon. At the same time, however, slightly weaker growth and the consequent lower resource utilisation should have some dampening effect on inflation. Possibly there are also reasons to value the risks somewhat differently. For example, a more dramatic fall in the dollar could slow growth more significantly. However, my assessment is that given the information available today, it is reasonable to believe that inflation in a couple of years' time will be in line with the target," Heikensten said. "Let me conclude by saying that the most likely thing - despite the small slowdown tendencies that have existed recently and the turmoil that today characterizes mainly the foreign exchange market - is that we will eventually have to expect a higher repo rate. The reason is that growth in the coming years is expected to continue at a pace that is higher than the economy can handle in the long term. Sooner or later, the Riksbank will be forced to intervene to ensure inflation in line with its target and a long-term stable development in the Swedish economy. When it may be relevant, however, remains to be assessed", Heikensten concluded.
