Title: Monetary policy in a low inflation environment: some reflections by a policy maker
text: Heikensten: Monetary policy in a low inflation environment: some reflections by a policy maker Datum: 2000-11-03 Talare: Forste vice riksbankschef Lars Heikensten Plats: ECB's first conference: Why Price Stability? Frankfurt, Germany I should like to begin by thanking the European Central Bank for arranging a conference of this kind, with many interesting and penetrating contributions to both the theory and practice of monetary policy. I am also grateful for the opportunity to comment on Jose Vinals (JVs) paper. JV has presented a very broad and stimulating paper that illustrates his good knowledge of the academic literature in this field. In a way, that makes commenting on his contribution difficult. I have carefully to select what I want to consider. In another way it makes things easier. I can talk about essentially anything I have been working on in recent years and still be able to relate it to JVs paper. I shall be discussing some of JVs arguments, mainly as someone who in recent years has been involved in the development of Swedish monetary policys intellectual framework and who is now also one of those who sets the interest rate. This I believe will amount to a natural division of labour between me and my codiscussant. What I have to say refers above all to three of the issues JV considers. The first concerns the effectiveness of monetary policy in a low-inflation environment. The second is the significance for monetary policy of various disturbances or shocks. The third issue is monetary policy and financial stability. I shall then conclude by looking briefly at some general issues that touch on what JV deals with when he discusses the importance of securing the transition to low inflation, as well as when he concludes with respect to the conduct of monetary policy in practice. Those of you who know me can no doubt anticipate what is coming  a call for transparency and clarity in analytical frameworks and processes, internally as well as externally. Low inflation and the effectiveness of monetary policy So, in section 3 JV discusses the effectiveness of monetary policy in a world with low inflation. He follows three tracks, of which the first two at least have attracted a good deal of attention in the literature. They are the zero bound on nominal interest rates and output-inflation trade-offs: the role of wage and price rigidities in a low-inflation environment. The zero bound on nominal interest rates The first problem with a downward limit for the nominal interest rate arises when the price trend is negative. Since nominal interest rates cannot be below zero, there is a limit to how far down real interest rates can be pushed. While the consequences of landing in such a situation could indeed be serious, it seems to me that the question has been accorded undue weight in the academic literature. There are two main reasons why I consider that the zero bound on nominal interest rates should not be a particularly important practical matter for monetary policy. My main ground for this standpoint is that I believe that today we know a great deal about the issue and how we should behave to avoid ending up in a deflationary spiral. First, central banks can act so that inflation expectations are stabilised at a level above zero. This can be aided by clearly targeting a specific rate symmetrically. I can mention in passing that a couple of years ago in Sweden we did in fact have falling prices. It might perhaps interest you to see the concurrent development of inflation expectations (Chart 1). The chart shows that the rate of inflation expected by economic agents (in this case the money market) remained stable even during that episode. Indeed, expectations have been in line with the target for several years now, regardless of what the current rate of inflation has been. As I see it, that demonstrates the value of having a distinct target for inflation. Second, deflationary spirals have a tendency to go together with problems in the financial sector. By introducing systems that reduce the risk of imbalances accumulating and of banks finding themselves in difficulties, the risk that financial problems will contributed to a deflation build-up can be reduced. A good deal remains to be done here in many countries, including the construction of systems whereby prompt, resolute action can be taken when a crisis looms. The latter, moreover, is a matter that increasingly has to be handled internationally, which adds to the complications. Output-inflation tradeoffs: the role of wage and price rigidities The other problem JV considers in connection with the effectiveness of monetary policy is the role of price and wage rigidities. The potential problems is, as pointed out by Akerlof et al (1996), that wage rigidities in combination with low inflation may prevent a necessary downward adjustment of real wages and thus lead to higher unemployment. To me, the performance of the U.S. economy in the 1990s is in itself a strong refutation of the conclusion that low inflation (below 3 per cent in the case of the United States) would lead to permanently higher unemployment. There are also more fundamental reasons for questioning their analysis, which presupposes that wage-earners do not understand the effects of inflation, particularly when this is low. That I simply do not believe. Since the inception of a low-inflation regime in Sweden, the behaviour of wage negotiators has clearly changed. When they formulate wage demands, the labour unions now start explicitly from the 2 per cent inflation target. Our inflation reports are sufficiently detailed for the negotiating parties to be able to insert whatever wage increases they want and read off the approximate consequences for inflation. To take an example, in our October Report, adding 1 percentage point to the average rate of wage increases would lift the rate of inflation at the end of the forecast period by about half of a percentage point. On the basis of this, the negotiating parties can form a fairly clear picture of how we would react with the repo rate. Here, too, I would like to beat the drum for targeting a specific rate. An interval of 0-2 per cent can, after all, be taken to imply that inflation will average around both 2 and 1 per cent. This may not seem all that important at first sight. But if settlements are based on 1 per cent inflation and the outcome turns out to be 2 per cent, roughly half of the anticipated real wage improvement will have been lost, given the reasonable assumption that productivity growth is 2 per cent. That naturally risks leading to unnecessary misunderstandings. To conclude my comments on the section about monetary policys effectiveness, I can say that I agree with what I perceive to be JVs main tenets. The objections to a policy commitment to low inflation are not as weighty as is sometimes suggested in the academic literature. Perhaps they have also become somewhat less important over time in that wage formation has been adapted in many places and we now know more about how to avoid a zero interest rate trap. It is important on both counts that inflation expectations are firmly anchored, which in our case seems to have been facilitated by targeting a specific rate symmetrically. Different sources of macroeconomic fluctuations In the following section JV raises some issues to do with whether monetary policy is now easier to conduct than it used to be. One notion is that with a low-inflation regime established, the transmission mechanism is easier to understand. Another is that conducting monetary policy has become easier now that fiscal policy is more oriented to stability. In a sense I would agree with JV that these changes presumably have made our work easier. Still, I should like to draw attention to another consequence. In a world where demand shocks  not infrequently caused by an unduly expansionary fiscal policy  were the central banks main problem, what mattered was taking vigorous action when the situation called for it. This is still the case, of course, but on the whole the job of central bankers it is now less a question of flexing muscles and more of our analytical potential and our ability to communicate our deliberations. That does not necessarily make our work easier in every respect. Supply shocks, as we have known for a long time, entail difficult monetary policy decisions. Matters are not made easier by inflation being low or by inflation expectations being locked at a lower level in many countries. But we must  as JV points out  take a stand on whether the changes we seem to see are temporary rather than permanent and whether they reflect new technology or belong to the cost-push category. We must also consider in what ways and how quickly any supply-side changes are likely to affect demand. The recent difficulty in predicting the course of events is evident from my next two charts (Chart 3). They show the mean errors in a number of analysts forecasts of GDP and inflation in the U.S. and Swedish economies in the period 19912000. In the United States, GDP has been consistently underestimated, while inflation has been overestimated. The picture in Sweden is broadly the same. The charts witness to a negative correlation between the forecasting errors for GDP growth and inflation. This underscores the increased importance of supply shocks in recent years, at least in these two countries. It also meant that growth has exceeded expectations without causing inflation to take off. Highlighting the implications directly in terms of monetary policy  which is what JV does in a Taylor rule framework  is of course important. However, one also has to think about them in terms of the structural relationships that drive the economy. Let me illustrate this by using the framework we have chosen for our discussions in the Inflation Reports. This framework basically entails structuring the assessment around a simple open-economy model for inflation in which inflation is broadly determined by the output gap, import prices and inflation expectations. At this point I should perhaps stress that I am not presenting this example to try your patience with a lengthy account of what has happened in my country up in the North. My purpose is to illustrate how one can reason in terms of an inflation targeting model and to demonstrate that this framework provides a good structure for identifying, analysing and communicating the changes taking places in our economies. Let me take the starting point in the forecast we published in spring 1999 (Chart 3). Obviously we counted on inflation moving up gradually as activity strengthened and the output gap closed. The domestic price rise was expected to be countered, however, by a calculated import price fall due to, among other things, an appreciation of the krona. How have things turned out? Quite differently from what we anticipated. Import prices have risen, mainly on account of higher oil prices, while domestic inflation has moved up considerably less than expected even though growth has been strong. The crucial issue is, of course, to understand this development in terms of the economys way of functioning. At a broad level, one may identify two possible sources: The time paths of the factors explaining inflation have changed. Structural shifts can have occurred in the relationships that generate inflation. It seems fairly obvious that the first source possesses some explanatory power. I have already touched on the changes in the wage formation system. Another possibility is that the output gap was larger initially than we counted on. Judgements in this respect have been complicated, of course, by the fact that unemployment shot up from 23 per cent around 1990 to 810 per cent some years later. This hypothesis of a larger gap also seems to be supported by regular measurements of capacity utilisation which point in that direction. Our revised measurements of the unemployment gap yield the same picture (Chart 4). Productivity growth is another potential candidate and here the question of permanent versus transitory shifts becomes particularly important. Concerning the second source  structural shifts in the relationships generating inflation  it is so far difficult to find firm empirical evidence in any country. However, some preliminary evidence from several countries does suggest that there have been shifts in the pass-through mechanism of import prices. In Sweden we have indications that the coefficient in front of the output gap has changed (Chart 5). Such a shift may for example be related to the better functioning of the labour market or to other structural reforms, not least in the early 1990s, beginning to pay off. Before turning to the next issue  financial stability and monetary policy  let me stress that these issues are extremely complicated. Personally, I believe the structural changes may have been even larger than confirmed to date. One important underlying change in many countries is of course the move to low inflation. In the Swedish case I believe we have also seen effects from the regime shifts on productivity. Also it is striking how major supply shocks in recent years, like the Asian crisis and now the rising oil prices, so far have not had major effects on underlying inflation or inflation expectations. Financial stability and monetary policy Having discussed the importance for monetary policy of different types of shock, JV moves on to an analysis of matters connected with financial stability. The issues he raises are how a central bank can use the information contained in asset prices and whether there are grounds for letting monetary policy be influenced by the risks inherent in financial imbalances even if there is no immediate threat to the goal of price stability. Against the background of the growing importance of the financial sector in our economies and of the financial markets becoming global, it is hardly surprising that the academic literature in this field is expanding rapidly. In the most recent years the discussion has been fuelled by the long boom in the United States and the accompanying increases in credit and asset prices. One batch of questions concerns central bank policy. Should, for example, asset prices be included in the price indexes that central banks aim to stabilise? With the aid of the literature, JVs answer is no and I agree. There are fundamental theoretical arguments against it. Also, I agree it is likely that an index which includes asset prices will fluctuate widely. That could necessitate large interest rate adjustments. It is hardly controversial to assert that asset prices should be taken into account when monetary policy is formulated if they form a part of the inflation process. There is reason to believe that an increase in household wealth affects consumption and thereby demand in general and the price trend. Share price increases may perhaps affect the corporate investment propensity in a similar fashion, for example via Tobins q. There are also potential effects from the financial accelerator. But much remains to be done, theoretically as well as empirically, when it comes to understanding the nature of these relationships. There is considerably less agreement in the literature as to whether central banks should try to influence the path of asset prices in connection with a risk of growing financial imbalances. One is immediately faced by the difficulty of determining whether an asset market is in fact over-valued. And if one does decide to intervene, how is the bubble to be deflated in an orderly manner? Just mentioning these two problems often leads those concerned with central banking to conclude that intervention is not advisable. JV comes to a similar conclusion and adds that motivating interest rate hikes externally would be extremely difficult in the absence of a threat to price stability. My position is somewhat different. The arguments should at least be placed in a wider context. In addition to the objective of price stability, as the central bank of Sweden the Riksbank is responsible by law for the payment system and financial stability. Without prejudice to these aims, we should, moreover, support economic policys other goals, such as high growth and employment. This means, for example, that we should take pains to avoid unnecessary fluctuations in output and employment. So if we see what we believe to be mounting financial imbalances and judge that in time they will jeopardise a stable economic development, I consider that in principle, at least, there is a case for acting with the repo rate even if we do not perceive a direct threat to the inflation target. Whether this may lead, as claimed by Cecchetti et al. (2000), to less risk of bubbles is another matter that does not materially affect my argument. Another issue is of course how likely this scenario is, given that we work with a forward-looking price stability oriented framework and financial imbalances normally have affects on inflation in the longer run. Also I should stress that financial instability is normally created, not so much by rising asset prices in themselves as by a credit build-up which is too rapid. The Riksbank has made it clear that there could be situations in which we would need to act even if there is no immediate threat to our inflation target. We would then have clearly to motivate why the decision was taken. In that we so recently experienced a profound financial crisis not least through the bursting of an asset price bubble, I do believe that in those circumstances we would get broad acceptance for action. I want to add that JVs reasoning assumes that the repo rate is the only means available to the central bank, which does not need to be the case. For some time now we have, for example, been publishing reports on financial stability in the Swedish economy twice a year. In these reports, any risks we identify are highlighted with a view to getting them corrected. On the basis of our assessments, we are also in a position to propose rule changes and legislative amendments as a means of reducing the risk of financial problems in the economy. Concluding remarks In an early section, JV discusses the transition to price stability in the western world and whether this new policy commitment to stability has come to stay. This is an issue that needs to be considered. I am old enough to know that policy regimes come and go fairly quickly. Ten years ago there were hardly any academic economists in Sweden who advocated a flexible exchange rate. Today it is recommended by almost everyone. The question is, what will be the position in ten years time? Future prospects for a stability-oriented policy are likely to depend at least in part on how we as central bankers succeed in maintaining and improving confidence in monetary policy. About this issue JV has little to say. He only notes that the greatest risk lies in a continuation of high unemployment, making it important to ensure that further labour market reforms are undertaken in Europe. While I agree about that risk, I am not content to leave the question there. Those of us who work in central banks ought perhaps to deal less with matters that are beyond our control and concentrate more on matters to do with our own actions and how we communicate them. That in itself would, I believe, help to gain greater support for our work. In other contexts I and many others have stressed the importance of clarity and transparency to afford good opportunities for assessments and exacting accountability. This in turn is important for the legitimacy of our institutions and for monetary policys credibility. Also, clarity and transparency are important in the new economic policy context in the EU. Central banks have distinctive rules from governments and social partners. The better the actors understand each other, the greater the opportunities for trust and for a successful policy mix. However, I would like to stress a different aspect here: the importance of clarity and transparency for the central banks internal work and decision-making. In that we work with a precise policy target and publish our forecasts in Inflation Reports, in which we systematically attempt to weigh up all the relevant information about future price tendencies, we have been forced to tighten up our internal analysis. The publication of Financial Stability Reports has had the same consequences. Some years later, moreover, we adopted a rule of action with a specific target horizon and a clarification of our approach to transitory effects. All this means that almost every time a new policy decision is at hand, we have to assess any new information in the light of the analytical framework we have built up. This is a very beneficial process. Recently, for instance, we have been wrestling with just the question of how to handle the development of asset prices and the risks of shocks beyond our target horizon. Partly as a result of these deliberations, we are now thinking of publishing a discussion about the development of inflation in a somewhat longer perspective. In the light of many years work both in the vicinity of decision-making in economic policy and now as a member of the Riksbanks executive board, it seems to me that in work of this kind, perhaps the most important thing to do is build up clear processes whereby a foundation for decisions based on sound economic analysis is produced systematically and then subjected to as broad a scrutiny as possible. One will then at least have provided conditions for consistent and wise decisions. That in turn is fundamental for a central banks credibility and will in the end, I believe, contribute to safeguarding the stability-oriented policy. Thank you. Title: Some aspects of financial development
text: Heikensten: Some aspects of financial development Date 2004-04-20 Riksbank Governor Lars Heikensten spoke today at Bryggaren in Vastervik at a seminar organized by Sparbanksstiftelsen Tjustbygden. In the speech, in addition to inflation developments in the future, Heikensten touched on some financial aspects "In this year's first inflation report, which was presented a couple of weeks ago, the Riksbank noted that the recovery in the world economy has become increasingly evident over the past six months. In Sweden, too, the economic upturn has come a long way with rising export demand, continued optimism among companies and households and good consumption development. Over the next few years, we expected average output growth of just over 2 1/2 percent. The Swedish economy would thus gradually approach full capacity utilisation. Against this background, rising price pressures are natural. Nevertheless, we estimated that inflation, according to UND1X, would fall below target in the next few years. High productivity combined with a weak labour market and low imported inflation were expected to dampen the rise in prices. This assessment was the reason why we lowered the repo rate by 0.5 percentage points. Newly received statistics both internationally and in Sweden largely confirm the picture we outlined in the Inflation Report," he said. "We currently have very low interest rates in the bond market, especially in light of the economic picture we and most others see ahead of us. Low actual and expected inflation and thus also low key interest rates are of course an important explanation. But there are also other reasons that have contributed to interest rates being unusually depressed. One contributing factor is that Asian central banks have bought US Government securities extensively to prevent an appreciation of their own currency. The differences between interest rates on U.S. Treasuries and more bad debts on other countries or on companies have also been significantly pushed down, stimulated by good availability of liquidity worldwide. As the global upturn consolidates and investment increases, interest rates will return to higher, more normal levels," according to Heikensten. "The low interest rate environment, combined with an improved earnings outlook, has also meant that share prices have risen on a broad front worldwide over the past year. To some extent, it is still about cost reductions, but there are many indications that companies have recently also increased their sales. The stock market's valuation suggests that stocks are generally somewhat highly valued compared to the average over the past decade. At the same time, it is not uncommon to have valuations above the historical average at the beginning of an economic upturn. Again, it is mainly the IT/telecom sectors that are pulling up the stock valuation. Prices that go up quickly can just as quickly go down if the forecasts are not met, I think it may be good to remind yourself of that when bursting headlines again promise quick cuts on the stock market. It is fundamental factors such as growth and profit prospects going forward that determine the sustainability of development," Heikensten noted. "The low interest rate environment has also contributed to a relatively sharp increase in household debt and single-family house prices in many countries. There is a discussion on whether development is sustainable and whether there is a risk of excessive debt in Economy. Swedish households' debt as a share of disposable income is approaching the levels prevailing in the early 1990s. But at the same time, the low interest rates mean that households' interest costs as a share of income have largely halved since then and are now at a historically low level. Nor when we look at households' balance sheets as a whole, i.e. household debt in relation to total wealth (financial assets and real estate), the development is not dramatic. The share of consumption in GDP has also not changed, suggesting that the rapid build-up of debt has been widely used to finance various assets, mainly housing. We have no concerns at present about the payment system as a result of these developments. For the household sector as a whole, too, development should not pose any great difficulties. But for individual households, there can be problems when interest rates start to rise especially if property prices were to fall at the same time. Here, then, it is important that households themselves watch out. It is also something banks and housing institutions have every reason to follow closely. Some companies are already carrying out rigorous sensitivity assessments and testing their customers' ability to pay even for higher interest rates. I think that's wise," Heikensten said. "All in all, I can state that neither financial developments nor recent real economic statistics since the previous monetary policy meeting have changed the picture in any significant way. The economy is strengthening at the same time as inflationary pressures are expected to rise gradually. Over a couple of years, inflation after the interest rate cut we have implemented is expected to be roughly in line with the target," Heikensten concluded.

Title: Openness and clarity in monetary policy - Swedish experiences
text: Heikensten: Openness and clarity in monetary policy - Swedish experiences Date: 2000-03-20 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Lars Heikensten Location: Customer meeting SEB, Stockholm Let me begin by thanking you for the invitation to come here and talk about transparency and clarity in monetary policy. This has been a topical topic in the Swedish debate in recent times, partly in light of the Riksbank's new Executive Board. It is also something that is very much discussed internationally, not least in the discussion about the new European Central Bank, the ECB. There are many issues to highlight that have to do with transparency and clarity in monetary policy. Today, I will mainly dwell on some of the issues that the changes in the Riksbank over the past year have raised. But before I get into this, I will say something about the fundamental arguments for transparency and briefly describe how I perceive monetary policy to have evolved in some of these respects before the new Executive Board took office. 1. Transparency, clarity and accountability In the international debate on monetary policy, there is often talk about the importance of transparency and accountability. These concepts are not entirely easy to translate into Swedish. "Transparency" becomes transparency in direct translation, which reasonably means both transparency and clarity. Accountability, on the other hand, is about the possibility of demanding accountability, more specifically that those responsible for policy and policy objectives can be identified. In practice, this presupposes transparency about the processes leading to decisions. Are transparency and clarity, as well as the possibility of demanding accountability, important prerequisites for a well-functioning monetary policy? Yes, most people would probably answer, but when you specify the meaning of the question, there is not the same consensus either in the Swedish or international debate. The differing views are probably due to the fact that national traditions vary in terms of openness in society at large, but also because the view of how accountability can be demanded and democratic control maintained can differ both between countries and between individuals. It is also about what approach one has to the financial markets and how well different ways of conducting monetary policy have been shown to work in the past in different environments. Let me highlight the arguments for openness that are common in the economic debate, but also comment on what has guided me in my work over the years in the Riksbank. Perhaps I should underline that there are strong links between the various arguments. Credibility The main argument for transparency and clarity is usually that it can help to: establish credibility for monetary policy. In the academic literature, it has mainly been emphasized that it will be easier to continuously follow, understand and evaluate the actions of central banks. It will thus also be possible to ensure that the considerations taken are not undue and that the policy is conducted in what is usually called a time-consistent manner. This argument is particularly important for a central bank that, like the Riksbank, built up confidence in a new regime during the 1990s. By being clear and open in communication, a central bank can find a shortcut to the credibility that otherwise requires a long history of good results. Legitimacy One aspect that is rarely highlighted in the economic discussion, but which in my opinion is crucial, is that it is hardly possible in the long run to conduct monetary policy in a way that is credible in the usual sense if there is no broader support for the policy. A successful monetary policy requires understanding and support in society at large. In this respect, too, the results of the policy and its professional conduct are, of course, central. Formulating clear goals and working methods, in order to bind up and facilitate evaluation and questioning can be a way to create understanding, support and respect. The requirements for "accountability" seem particularly reasonable for institutions that have gained a lot of power, as is the case today for central banks in Europe. Added to this is the fact that the citizens of a democracy should be able to demand transparency from monetary policy in the same way as from any other policy, as Alan Blinder  former deputy governor of the Federal Reserve  has pointed out. Forutsebarhet There are also good reasons to believe that a more transparent and clear interest rate policy works better in a technical sense. If different actors in the economy - in the financial markets, in companies and among households - can more easily predict the structure of monetary policy going forward and adapt to this, the fluctuations in interest rates and other market prices should be able to be smaller. This should be reflected in more stable developments in the real economy. My British colleague, Mervyn King, has put it this idea as saying that politics should be conducted in such a way that it is so predictable that it becomes boring. Thus, according to him, there is no point whatsoever in surprising the markets. My impression is that this is a view that has gained increased support in central bank circles in recent years, but that it is by no means fully accepted everywhere. Efficiency in the organization Finally, I would like to emphasise that transparency and accountability are essential from the point of view of the internal life and efficiency of organisations. This is especially true in institutions which, like central banks, have monopolies and, moreover, have often traditionally been closed. Clear goals and the ambition to both publish the basis for the decisions and to justify the policy in a convincing way increase the focus of the work and sharpen the analysis. It also opens up for a broader monetary policy discussion in society, which in turn can be constructively born back into the central bank. Perhaps it will be less convenient to work in a central bank, but for the results I think it is good. 2. State of play of the new Executive Board In many ways, the starting point was good for the new Executive Board to take office in January 1999. Inflation was low and growth had started considerably after the crises in the early 90s. This development, in turn, would not have been possible without extensive fiscal consolidation and would have been well supported by strong international developments with low inflation. A lot had also happened in the area of monetary policy and the ambition had been to conduct the policy in an open and clear way. Let me briefly say something about the results with regard to the various aspects of transparency that I have just outlined  credibility, legitimacy, predictability and efficiency in the organisation. Inflation expectations, as measured in surveys, showed that credibility had increased. They were parked around the target 2 percent in the longer term. (Figure 1) The same picture showed the pricing in the market. The implicit ten-year forward rate was now almost on par with, for example, the German one from having been several percentage points above three to four years earlier. (Figure 2). Although the krona had weakened sharply in the turbulence following the Asian crisis in the autumn of 1998, but in a slightly longer perspective it had still stabilised significantly. There were also clear indications that inflation targeting policy had received increased support in society. Surveys showed that the understanding of our work had gradually increased and that about 60 percent thought we were doing a good job. (See Table 1) This is also the impression one got from what was written in the media, although this is of course more difficult to substantiate. Perhaps it can also be said that the fact that the Riksbank was given legal independence was a recognition of the success of the inflation targeting policy, although the decisive factor behind this decision was EU membership and the international consensus that developed regarding the value of having independent central banks. This view is clearly stated in the Maastricht Treaty. Even in terms of communication with the market, the general picture was that the development has gone in the right direction. The Riksbank's actions were well understood. If you compare the actual repo rate with the market forecasted, you see a high degree of consistency. (Figure 3) Naturally, the accuracy is worse in the longer term, but this is mainly due to the fact that inflation perspectives have had time to change as a result of unforeseen events. On a few occasions, however, there had been criticism of the communication, mainly when the Riksbank had changed policy. Perhaps the best example of this is the discussion in June 1998, when we lowered the repo rate in a situation where many had expected the opposite until just a few weeks earlier. But there were also problems in connection with the increase in the autumn of 1997. I also stressed at the outset the value of openness to internal assessments and of inviting outside assessors to a mutual, evolving discussion. The results in this area are not so easy to assess. The evaluations we carry out on an ongoing basis do not show that the forecasts have clearly improved. However, each situation offers its forecasting problems and it is not easy to evaluate in retrospect which ones were the most difficult. However, it is clear that we have had a lot of help from external economists from the universities and the market in developing analytical frameworks and forecasting methodology and that a dialogue with our critics has stimulated us to move forward and deepen as we can. However, we had an obvious problem with the clarity of the policy, which there were reasons to remedy before the new Executive Board took office. It was about how our target was formulated and how temporary deviations from the target were handled in monetary policy. The Riksbank had been grappling with this issue ever since the inflation target was introduced in 1993, but there was still a great deal of confusion on this point. Our target was formulated in terms of inflation as measured by the change in the consumer price index. The Riksbank was therefore naturally criticized during the years when CPI inflation undercut its target. But some confusion arose as the policy in practice, with good reason, disregarded temporary effects. We had tried to explain this again, but the issue is difficult and we obviously had not got our message across about the structure of monetary policy. There was therefore a case for changing the target formulation or in some other way clarifying the policy. A proposal on what these clarifications might look like was drawn up at the end of autumn 1998 and adopted in its main features by the Executive Board at the beginning of February 1999. Another problem was that inflation, as measured by the CPI, had fallen below the target level over a succession of years - even after taking into account the temporary effects. We were therefore accused of conducting politics in an asymmetrical manner. It is true that there were many explanations for the low inflation, including rapid changes in the rest of the world that were hardly possible to predict. Perhaps it is also so difficult to make inflation forecasts that over time we have to count on deviations of this magnitude. Nevertheless, there were, of course, reasons for the Riksbank to try to become better at assessing inflation under the new Executive Board. However, the urgent and most important task we faced was to adapt the monetary policy decision-making process and communication to the new situation of six members of the Executive Board. An important starting point for the preparatory work we did in the autumn of 1998 was for members to take the monetary policy decisions jointly, but under individual responsibility. This individual responsibility was not, in itself, stated in the legislation in any other way than that each was elected on his own merits. However, we ourselves judged that, in light of this, it was important that the individual efforts and decisions could be evaluated, for example, before re-election. In several other countries, there were experiences with similar decision-making structures and against this background, extensive contacts were made with colleagues abroad. I myself visited, among other things, the United States. The Bank of England's equivalent of our Executive Board in terms of monetary policy decisions - the Monetary Policy Committee. I also had extensive contacts with colleagues in the Bundesbank, whose executive board is in many ways similar to that of the Swedish Riksbank and who also has a long experience in this area. On the basis of these contacts, our own experiences  and on the basis of the academic literature available in the field  we were able to draw up proposals for, among other things, the preparation process in the Bank, the working methods in the Management Committee and signalling. Whatever the members of the new Executive Board would be, it was important that these foundations were in place in good time so that the new Executive Board could quickly become effective in its work. 3. The internal preparation process The proposal drawn up in autumn 1998 was for the Executive Board to discuss monetary policy at pre-scheduled meetings 8-10 times a year. It was considered valuable both for the market and for internal work to have a fixed schedule for the monetary policy meetings. We chose to meet on monetary policy less frequently than the decision-makers do in, for example, The Netherlands. Bank of England and ECB. The reason was that new relevant information does not come in so often that meetings needed to be held at more frequent intervals. In this way, we could also have time to produce well-prepared documentation for each meeting. Of course, we can meet at short notice and take a decision if the situation so requires. The staff was proposed to continue to play a strong role in the new preparation process. The assessments on which the Executive Board's discussions would be based would continue to be prepared by the services which had had this task until then. In order to secure the best and most comprehensive evidence possible, all assessments and monetary policy bases would also be discussed in the monetary policy preparation group, which includes experts from different parts of the bank. The preparation procedure has been developed and clarified during the past year. According to the cycle we follow today for the inflation reports, the main issues that are considered to be important in the next report are normally discussed as early as shortly after the previous decision meeting. A reconciliation of a synopsis that may contain ideas on in-depth analyses and themes for the next report is normally reconciled in the Executive Board after a few more weeks. The Economic Department then produces a complete assessment of the economy and inflation, which is presented together with alternative trajectories for the economy and calculation examples showing the sensitivity of the results to various key variables. On the basis of this evidence, the Executive Board discusses inflation perspectives and sets out its views. The Economic Department then prepares a draft Inflation Report based on the Executive Board's picture. This is discussed and put into practice a week before the report is published so that it can be printed. One day before the publication of the report, the Executive Board meets for a monetary policy meeting where a formal decision is taken on the report, while at the same time discussing the implications for monetary policy. Of course, other preparation schemes would be possible and there are also differences between us and our colleagues in other central banks. However, most have chosen, like us, to work with fixed meeting schedules and to give their staffs the task of producing coherent data and forecasts. However, the Bank of England has opted for a slightly different approach. Their Monetary Policy Committee receives a very comprehensive review of new statistics and of the staff's various assessments, but they do not receive a coherent forecast. They have chosen to put this together themselves, among other things, so as not to risk being too guided in their thinking by the staff, from what I understand. Their way of working is probably also linked to the fact that, unlike, among other things, they have to work. The Boards of Governors of the Riksbank and the ECB work exclusively with monetary policy and that their members are appointed against this background, with a uniquely high level of economic-technical competence. For my part, I think it is important to put the staff in a strong position. Only then can a high level of competence be maintained in the long run and continuity of work ensured. It is hardly by engaging in the details of the assessments that the members of the Executive Board can make the best contribution to monetary policy. However, the Executive Board should highlight other perspectives and broaden the analysis. For that kind of discussion, coherent assessments with alternative scenarios are a good starting point. From time to time, suggestions arise to make the role of the staff even more clear. This could be done, for example, by publishing the staff's own assessments. However, it is not as obvious a solution as it might seem at first. My main objection is that it risks driving a wedge between staff and the Executive Board. What happens when there are clear deviations in the assessments and how does this affect the view of the Riksbank? Should the staff go out and defend their positions? Who will then produce the basis for the replies of the members of the Executive Board, etc.? Another question is who the staff or staffs are in practice and why these particular people should be given a position in the debate? A very complex issue, which has recently been somewhat highlighted in the academic debate, and which has clear relevance to our work is how an inflation assessment is made by a group. The logic of individual responsibility that can be evaluated suggests rather that each of the members of the Executive Board should draw up its own inflation forecast, just as each one votes on the interest rate. But this falls on its own unreasonableness. After all, not everyone can have their own staffs and we ourselves would probably not each be able to make better complete assessments of any of us than the one that our employees' combined efforts lead to. In addition, it is certainly an advantage if the Executive Board can communicate a reasonably cohesive majority view rather than a number of different images. How the trade-off should be made, however, is far from obvious. One possibility would be to let the Inflation Report reflect the majority view, but include boxes describing any minority views. A step further would be to point out the dissenting opinions that exist in each sub-area. However, we have so far allowed the Inflation Report to reflect the majority view and minority views have been presented in the minutes, which will be published some time thereafter. But for those who want to be part of the majority, this normally requires a willingness to compromise, since our main scenario is structured as a fairly detailed coherent picture where, in individual terms, one can of course have different opinions. 4. The work and decisions of the Executive Board In view of the fact that the members of the Executive Board would be elected on an individual mandate, we chose to have minutes of discussion from our monetary policy discussions. The idea was thus to make it easier primarily for those who have the task of evaluating and appointing us. At the same time, it goes without saying that minutes from the meetings also meant that information that previously did not exist about the conversations and discussions that had taken place within the Riksbank would now be available to outside observers. With the evaluation perspective, it became important to show how each member of the Executive Board voted. We felt that, in addition, it would be useful to have a relatively detailed discussion protocol, but never really considered a protocol from which it would be clear exactly what each one had said, as we felt that this could put a damper on the discussion. When the new Executive Board's decision-making model was published, it was subjected to some criticism. Concern was expressed that the real discussions would take place elsewhere than at the recorded meetings, in order to maintain the facade of unity and get a unified message out. Recently, however, the pendulum has swung and now the criticism has instead been about the board becoming a discussion club at Brunkebergstorg that is constantly divided. A similar debate followed the Bank of England's change of system, but after some time the forms were accepted and it has increasingly been perceived as natural for different views to occur in the Monetary Policy Committee from time to time. Of course, it is not easy to find good forms for the discussion right away. We have had to search our way and the structure of the meetings has varied somewhat over time. The best way to have a good discussion is to start from good and comprehensive data. But it is not enough with this, it is also important to conduct an open and straightforward discussion in a prestige-free way where different thoughts are tested against each other. Here there are risks with an open process and with many people present in the room, which it is important for everyone on the executive board to be vigilant about. How we communicate outwardly is important in this context, as it can also have effects on the future internal discussion. Against this background, we have chosen to avoid publicly reviewing each other and the positions we have taken. Instead, we are mainly concentrating on a discussion of the inflation perspectives ahead. Debates between us could easily escalate and have an impact on our internal work as well. The latter would also be problematic for the reason that we should not only manage monetary policy but also jointly manage a relatively large organisation. The media has periodically given the impression that we constantly have different views and that the executive board is made up of clearly identifiable hawks and pigeons. Although, of course, there are some differences between us in background, values and also attitudes towards monetary policy, this is a false picture. The deviations in perception have been relatively small and mainly reflect different assessments of the concrete macroeconomic situation. As long as we all insist that policy should focus on inflation of 2%, there is no room for allowing their possible pigeon or hawk attitudes to have such a say. That would, of course, mean advocating a policy whereby the target was systematically missed one way or the other. As for the repo rate, the deviation in view so far has been at most 25 basis points. The number of reservations has also been lower than it has been on average in the Bank of England's monetary policy committee. Personally, I believe that, in the end, we must decide on the question of individual responsibility and protocol. If you do not want to go back to a more closed order - with the consequences this would have for the Riksbank's position in the public debate, etc., and if you choose to have members who are individually responsible for policy, you probably have to reckon with the fact that from time to time there are different views in the Executive Board and dissonances in the message. Monetary policy is not an exact science, although with a clear inflation target we have set the framework for policy. In the long term, I also believe that there will be some good things to come out of the discussion that has taken place. It makes it clear that monetary policy involves difficult assessment issues, which one may think a little differently about and this in itself can be valuable for understanding the work we are set to do. Collective decision-making can also reduce the obsession with a decision-maker. Although the discussion so far has rather led to an increased personal fixation, it does not have to be the effect in the long run. Instead, the institution may come forward more clearly. 5. Monetary policy signalling In the preparatory work in the autumn of 1998, it was proposed that the inflation reports should continue to play a central role in the Riksbank's communication. We also proposed that a press release or communique be published in conjunction with the monetary policy meetings. This would give a direct account of how the executive board majority viewed inflation perspectives and justify any decision to change the interest rate. We expected that minutes of the monetary policy meetings could be ready a few weeks after the meetings were held. These, too, would provide information on how we viewed inflationary perspectives and policies. Reports the press releases and minutes would thus form the backbone of joint communication. Taken together, these joint documents provide much more detailed and regular information about the Riksbank's considerations than has been the case in the past. The inflation reports present the Executive Board's views on inflation over the next few years. They thus lay the foundations for our monetary policy action. For those who are interested in forming an idea of what interest rate developments may be like in the long term, they should be the central source. The work on the reports has also continued to develop and they now contain more information than before against which new incoming information can be continuously set. On the other hand, the reports no longer discuss the structure of monetary policy. Instead, these arguments are reflected in the press releases following the monetary policy meetings and in the minutes. The minutes also contain information that was not previously available on individual positions and on issues discussed in the Executive Board without them being reflected in the reports or in the press releases. The minutes are thus important not least to evaluate what may happen at the next meeting. Given that the members of the Executive Board have individual responsibility for policy, it was natural to suggest that everyone should be able to give speeches or otherwise communicate their views on monetary policy issues. The rules of the game thus changed a bit for those who followed the Riksbank. Previously, in practice, only the Governor of the Riksbank and myself spoke on behalf of the Riksbank on monetary policy issues. We did so only after having reconciled with each other and, of course, also, in terms of the main features of politics, with the then council. The Riksbank thus effectively spoke with one vote against now six votes. The speeches are now the responsibility of each individual member unless explicitly stated otherwise, which has so far only happened in connection with the Governor of the Riksbank giving speeches to the Finance Committee twice a year. Our experience with the new system is, on the whole, a good one. It is hardly possible to prove that this has led to the policy becoming significantly more unclear, although some criticisms along these lines have been made from time to time. One possibility to highlight the issue is to re-compare the actual repo rate with market participants' repo rate expectations three months earlier. (Figure 4) Clear deviations are really only visible at one point, during the summer and early autumn; expectations of a tightening of monetary policy were then built into market pricing, even though the Riksbank had not signaled such a thing. One possible explanation is that several forecasters revised up their growth assessments both internationally and in Sweden because the effects of the Asian crisis were not expected to have as extensive effects as had first been feared. The short-term interest rate level then rose both globally and in Sweden. Another reason for the dissonances that arose between the Riksbank's actions and some market analysts at the beginning of the autumn was probably that the board's majority chose to take the time that the inflation assessment allowed and to justify the upcoming need for a rate hike in detail and broadly in Swedish society. The purpose of this was to build support for the policy, but this may of course have surprised some observers who had not taken this aspect into account and who had seen the need for an increase early on. We have also tried to highlight whether the signalling has been unambiguous and consistent in the sense that the same future monetary policy stance is signalled by everyone on the Executive Board and whether the repo rate has changed in accordance with the signals sent. If we compare the signals in speeches, minutes and inflation reports with the repo rate and the expected repo rate in three months' time during the period January 1995 to December 1999, we can see that the members of the Executive Board appear to have given a clear picture of monetary policy (Chart 5). This means that our new way of working means that it is impossible to clearly signal where the interest rate is heading. Not really. If we want, we can ensure that a joint statement is made. It is also possible for individual members to send out signals if they think they can predict the future decisions of the Executive Board. However, the latter is fraught with a risk because at each meeting the Executive Board is sovereign and can take any decision. Let me conclude by emphasising something that may seem obvious, but which, judging by the debate, is often forgotten. We cannot be clearer than the situation allows. When there is great uncertainty, it is not possible for us on the Executive Board to point out with a steady hand where monetary policy is heading. 6. Summary and conclusions After the crisis in the early 1990s, the development of the Swedish economy has been positive. Growth has been high while inflation has been low. Many factors have contributed to this. One, of course, is the high degree of spare resources that existed after the crisis. But the relatively good international environment with growth and low inflation has also contributed, as has the extensive clean-up of the state budget. Significant measures to improve the structure of the economy have also come into play, many implemented in the shift between the 1980s and 90s. However, there are good reasons to also highlight the shift in monetary policy. From January 1993, the policy was based on an explicit price stability objective for the policy, which was initially controversial. Gradually, support for the policy has increased in line with its good results. Last year, new legislation was put to bed, which in part can perhaps be said to be proof of this. Transparency and clarity have probably contributed to the increase in support. The combination of a symmetrical target, published forecasts and the application of the rule of action that interest rates are normally raised in the event of inflation above the target and vice versa have been important elements of policy. In these respects, I believe that the approach we have chosen may be worth considering for other central banks as well. What we have done has likely been  contributed to credibility without having to wait for a long history with good results. An example of this is the fall in interest rates in the autumn of 1998, which we were able to justify clearly by revising our forecasts and thus avoiding a debate of the kind that then affected Europe.  made anchoring the new monetary policy regime in Swedish society easier. The ambition has been that the same simple pedagogy can be applied on the couch in a morning program on TV, at a working-class municipality in Skelleftea and at a seminar at Stockholm University. - facilitated policy interpretation and made it easier for market participants and others to predict policy;  contributed to a goal orientation of the internal work and opened up for a meaningful and developing dialogue with critics outside the house. But these positive results do not exclude problems in the application of the policy. There has been uncertainty about how we handle temporary effects. We have also undercut the target, partly as a result of forecasting errors. However, the Swedish experience does not suggest that a central bank should refrain from openly publishing its assessments simply because there are risks of forecasting or assessment mistakes. Within the Riksbank, we continue to work hard to develop our analysis framework and become increasingly open and clearer. Gradually, for example, we should be able to increase our own understanding of the relationships that govern inflation and thus also be able to communicate more clearly how the inflation picture is emerging. In addition to transparency, anchoring the policy requires accountability. By tying policy itself to a clear goal that can be evaluated, the Riksbank has facilitated evaluation and accountability beyond what laws and regulations themselves have required. I think this is a reasonable ambition for an institution that has gained as much power as the Riksbank in particular has gained. The forms of decision-making and communication changed with the new Executive Board. Minutes are now published from our meetings mainly to make it easier to demand accountability. At the same time, this means that the bank has become more transparent, which has been debated, among other things, because there has been concern that the internal discussion could suffer and that the bank as an institution could be damaged. I myself can to some extent understand this concern and it is important to handle the new situation with care. At the same time, it should be remembered that the new forms probably settle down after some time and then contribute to a more nuanced discussion of the considerations we have to make. In this regard, in any case, it is too early to make any evaluation. Nor can we draw any firm conclusions about what the Swedish experience may mean for other central banks. Moreover, in terms of accountability and anchoring policy, political traditions, institutional frameworks and monetary policy experience in other countries play a crucial role.
