Title: Monetary policy in Sweden and the United States
text: Heikensten: Monetary policy in Sweden and the UNITED STATES Date: 2005-10-14 Speaker: Governor Lars Heikensten Location: Lund University Thank you for the invitation to Lund University. I look forward to discussing with you the structure of monetary policy. It's not very often that I have this opportunity in an academic context like this. When we have worked over the past ten years to develop monetary policy in Sweden, we have often had reason to look outside our own country, to make comparisons and try to learn from how other countries have gone about it. Of course, monetary policy in the United States has been one of the most important benchmarks. In the debate in Sweden, it has also been common to refer to American politics on the theme that everything would have been better if we had acted like them. Against this background, I think it might be interesting to discuss our policies compared to theirs. For me, the question has also been particularly relevant since I returned from the so-called Jackson Hole symposium in the United States, which this year honored the soon-to-be outgoing US Federal Reserve Governor Alan Greenspan. Broad consensus on basic principles It is important to begin by emphasizing that the differences that exist between Swedish and US monetary policy  or, incidentally, that of any other comparable country  do not apply to the more general principles of how monetary policy should be conducted. There is today considerable international agreement on these. What is crucial is that monetary policy is conducted in such a way that the credibility that inflation will remain low is not shaken  that, as is usually put, the nominal anchor of the economy does not let go. It is clear, however, that this is not a mechanical process. Because the world is complex and unexpected events occur all the time, every decision-making moment is unique. Monetary policy must therefore necessarily be, in part, what is usually called discretionary; decisions are made on a case-by-case basis and depend on the circumstances prevailing at the moment. It is a question of considering the consequences for inflation in each situation, but also including in the picture what the effects on the economy in general will be  to simply conduct a wise stabilization of inflation. Sometimes extraordinary events also occur, the final consequences of which are difficult to overview and work into traditional analyzes and forecasts. The terrorist attacks in the United States on 11 September 2001 are an example of such an event. In connection with these, many central banks around the world lowered their interest rates quickly. The forceful action can be interpreted as a kind of "insurance" against a really weak outcome. Alan Greenspan, has expressed it on a number of occasions that monetary policy is very much about quantifying and managing various risks. The following quote ties in with this and gives a good picture of how Greenspan sees the task of monetary policy and which also fits well with my own view: "This [] framework emphasizes understanding as much as possible the many sources of risk and uncertainty that policymakers face, quantifying those risks when possible, and assessing the costs associated with each of the risks." (1) Differences and similarities in the layout I am quite convinced that most central banks would describe the general principles of their policies in much the way I have done here. However, this does not mean that there are no differences between countries in terms of the details of how monetary policy is structured. Let me address some aspects of the specific structure of Swedish and American monetary policy where we differ, but also those where there are similarities. Inflationsmalet Perhaps the most obvious difference concerns the goal of the policy. Unlike the US, Sweden has a numerical target for inflation. Although the Federal Reserve, like the Riksbank, has price stability as its goal, it has chosen not to specify what level of inflation it is aiming for. In the United States, a policy shift took place around 1980, when the Federal Reserve under central bank governor Paul Volcker managed to bring inflation down from high, sometimes double-digit levels. At this time, inflation targeting did not occur anywhere, even in the academic literature. The only more concrete experience was our own experiment with a price stability objective in Sweden in the 1930s, based on Knut Wicksell's price standard, but of course it was little known outside Sweden. Volcker referred in his argument to monetarist ideas, but in practice pursued politics in a pragmatic if harsh way. This policy and the one that has subsequently been pursued have succeeded in convincing economic operators that inflation will remain at a low level, without having formulated an explicit target for the rate of price increase. One could see the policy shift in the US as a different way of giving the economy a nominal anchor than with the numerical target we have used, although in the American case it could be said to be an implicit rather than an explicit commitment. There is little doubt that both the strategy with an explicit inflation target and the US solution have been successful and that both today enjoy great confidence. Against this background, it is interesting  and perhaps also less well known here at home  that there is still a debate in the US about whether there can be gains in taking a further step and introducing an explicit target for inflation. (2) One argument in the US debate has been that the introduction of an explicit inflation target would help to increase the clarity of monetary policy. This may involve making policies more predictable in advance for economic actors. But it can also be about making decisions easier to evaluate afterwards. Another argument has been that an inflation target would help to better anchor inflation expectations. (3) The better anchored these are, the less likely there is that, for example, a sudden increase in costs will have spillover effects and the more expansionary monetary policy can be allowed to be in such a situation. Therefore, by further strengthening the credibility that inflation will be kept low, the introduction of an inflation target  which may possibly seem paradoxical  can increase rather than limit the room for manoeuvre of monetary policy. A further argument has been that an inflation target would help to focus the policy debate on what monetary policy can actually achieve in the long term  controlling inflation  rather than what it cannot achieve  to raise growth and employment on a lasting basis. The arguments against have primarily been about the fact that the current regime has worked well. Other arguments are essentially political and not entirely easy for a non-American to value. They have to do with the risks of appearing too focused on inflation, as an "inflation nutter", to use an expression borrowed from my British colleague Mervyn King. Some also have concerns that a discussion of the case would raise other issues in Congress that they don't want on the table. But the main argument still seems to be "if it ain't broke, don't fix it". I have probably also said that it is likely that if some form of inflation targeting policy had been invented and used in the US as early as the late 1970s, that policy would have enjoyed as much confidence as today's. Malformuleringen Another difference concerns how the Riksbank's and the Federal Reserve's assignments are formulated in the underlying legal text. The Federal Reserve has a so-called "dual mandate" which means that monetary policy should strive for both "maximum employment" and "stable prices". In Sweden and many other countries with inflation targets, the legal text has primarily focused on inflation. Objectives for employment or output are either not specified or subordinate to the objective of price stability  one usually speaks of a so-called lexicographical order of the objectives, in which any objectives of the real economy are to be met provided that the objective of price stability is not threatened. The differences in the way central bank tasks are formulated have largely historical explanations. During the 1990s, many countries received new central bank legislation. This has been characterized by the practical experiences and theoretical insights that emerged during the 1970s and 80s. It then became clearer to everyone that it was not possible with monetary policy to increase production and employment in a country in the long term. What central banks could do, however, was to ensure price stability. In this way, a foundation could also be laid for otherwise good economic development. Added to this was increased decision-making autonomy, also motivated by practical experience mainly in Germany, and theoretical insights that the design of the institutional framework is central to the ability to keep inflation at a low level. (4) By placing the emphasis on inflation in the legislation, a clear signal was sent that policies would focus much more decisively than in the past on keeping inflation low and stable. My view is that, not least in Sweden, there was also a concern that generally formulated goals in terms of the real economy would be interpreted precisely as meaning that monetary policy was also responsible for the longer-term development of, for example, employment, which it is thus not able to do. In this context, it is also worth noting that in the preparatory work for the new Swedish regulatory framework for monetary policy that entered into force in 1999, the assessment was made that it was understood that the Riksbank, as an authority under the Riksdag, has the task of supporting the general economic policy established by the Riksdag  to the extent that this does not conflict with the price stability objective. This obligation, it was argued, therefore did not need to be specifically stated in law. (5) Developments in the United States have followed somewhat different trajectories. The Federal Reserve's "dual mandate" was added by an amendment to the Federal Reserve Act of 1977. The policy change carried out around 1980, which marked the starting point for the credible low-inflation policy pursued since then, could take place within the framework of the current monetary policy framework with dual objectives. The fact that this was possible is probably due to a combination of factors, which I have already mentioned in part. This is partly due to the fact that inflation was increasingly perceived as the most acute problem. It is probably also partly because the Federal Reserve at that time had a leadership that had the determination to tackle the inflation problem, even though the downshift in inflation would very likely mean a sharp increase in unemployment over a period of time. It can perhaps also be said that it reflects that the American goal formulation leaves quite a lot of room for the Federal Reserve to make its own interpretations of what priorities need to be set. Monetary policy in practice What practical implications do the differences have in the different goal formulations? One reason to ask this question is that from time to time in the Swedish debate the American solution of a "dual mandate", which must take into account both employment and inflation, has been highlighted as an example. The discussion was particularly intense in connection with the development of the new regulations for the Riksbank that came into force in 1999, but similar ideas have emerged in the debate in recent years as well. However, the fact that the Riksbank's regulations do not say anything about real economic objectives does not mean that real economic developments are not taken into account. The Riksbank is pursuing what has been called a flexible rather than a strict inflation targeting policy. Thus, the focus is not only on stabilizing inflation, but the policy is flexible in the sense that other considerations are also taken into account. How we reason in the Riksbank in these respects is shown by a clarification that we made at the beginning of 1999. (6) This clarification states that we set monetary policy so that some deviations from the inflation target are accepted while normally striving to bring inflation back to the target within a period of two years. This can be justified both by the fact that we are not able to control inflation precisely in the short term and the need to have flexibility  to be able to take into account other than inflation, such as the stability of the real economy. At the same time, it is important that this flexibility does not diminish the credibility of the inflation target over time, but that it can fulfil its function as a "nominal anchor". The two-year horizon can be interpreted as a restriction on how much consideration can normally be given to targets other than fixed monetary value, a restriction that the Riksbank itself  like the specified inflation target  has imposed in order to create credibility for its policy aimed at price stability. My use of the word 'normal' is because, in certain cases and circumstances, situations may arise in which flexibility must be allowed to be greater in order for the overall economic outcome to be acceptable. In extreme cases, the deviations from the inflation target may be so large that it is not actually possible to return inflation within the usual two-year time horizon. The rate at which it is possible and desirable to return inflation to target after a deviation is generally dependent on the magnitude of the disruptions the economy is experiencing and the nature of the disruptions. Therefore, during periods, such as when major supply-side disruptions occur, inflation may deviate for more than two years from the two per cent target. The notion that the differences are small in practice is also indirectly supported by the debate that is taking place in the United States and that I touched on earlier. It has been argued that the Federal Reserve has gradually begun to pursue a policy that could essentially be described as an implicit inflation targeting policy. (7) The proponents of this view argue that a benefit from taking a further step and introducing inflation targeting policies even in a purely formal sense  in addition to those I mentioned earlier  is that it would be a way of ensuring that the same balanced policies pursued under Alan Greenspan will continue to be pursued in the future. In other words, it would essentially just mean a codification and institutionalisation of the current policy that would make it less 'person-dependent'. The differences between the Swedish and american goal formulations are thus, as I understand it, significantly greater on paper than in practice. As I see it, it is basically about two different ways of describing the same type of policy rather than about the fact that there are crucial differences in policy as such. (8) Mervyn King has put this in a slightly different way when he argues that the flexible inflation targeting policy is "generic" and includes other ways of conducting monetary policy as special cases. (9) Transparency and communication In terms of the degree of transparency and communication, on the other hand, there are clear differences between monetary policy in Sweden and the United States. Internationally, especially in the latter part of the 1990s, the Riksbank has been at the forefront among central banks when it comes to transparency. For the Federal Reserve, the opposite is true, at least when compared to other industrialized countries. For example, it was actually as recently as 1994 that the Federal Reserve began by publishing its interest rate decisions immediately after they were made. But also within the Federal Reserve, a lot of steps have been taken to increase transparency and clarity. Since 1994, there has been a gradual shift to more substantial press releases, which provide a justification for interest rate decisions. Since 2002, individual votes and any reservations to the decision have been published. From 2005 onwards, the minutes will be published with a shorter backlog than before  now they are published three weeks after the monetary policy meeting. However, in scientific studies that try to map the degree of openness, the Riksbank ranks among the foremost and regularly a bit higher than the US Federal Reserve. (10) What can be said about the differences in how politics is described in Sweden and the UNITED STATES? I would like to make the following rough interpretation. In the case of the United States, one could say, somewhat simplistically, that monetary policy is presented and communicated in a way that is quite close to the textbook model's description of a monetary policy with a "dual mandate"; the policy rate should be set in such a way that the expected developments in inflation and the real economy together "look good". This rather general way of describing policy and its consequences gives the Federal Reserve a great deal of "leeway". The flip side of the coin is that politics can sometimes be perceived as unclear  it can be difficult to see exactly what it is striving to achieve. This problem would probably be even worse if politics had not been so closely linked in recent years to an individual whose communication had been the "law" of the market. Put another way; with a group of decision-makers who also communicate their own approaches to the policy rate, the value from a communication point of view of a clear analytical framework is probably even greater than in a system dominated by an individual decision-maker. In Sweden, the description and communication of monetary policy has the advantage that it can take the inflation target as a starting point. The decisions on the policy rate can be explained and justified in terms of the fact that they ultimately aim to bring inflation around the target. At the same time, as I have mentioned, there is scope to take account of real economic developments by allowing inflation to temporarily deviate from the target. Central to this is that the approach with inflation targets forces us in such situations to present clear and good arguments for our actions  we need to explain why we have chosen to deviate from the target and in what time perspective we intend to try to bring inflation back. Apart from what this means for communication, it has been a useful process that forces a more considered approach than would have resulted from a less cohesive procedure, at least that is my conviction. All in all, I think this is an arrangement that has worked well. The clarity and statute that the inflation target has meant has probably also been an important explanation for why we in Sweden have managed to avoid the "personal fixation" that characterized monetary policy in the United States. Neither Urban Backstrom's resignation a few years ago nor the decision I myself recently took have given rise to any serious speculation that the basic monetary policy strategy would change in the future. At the same time, it should be said that not everyone agrees that inflation targeting policies have made it easier to understand and interpret the structure of monetary policy. For example, there is a more general criticism at international level that an explicit inflation target makes central banks' communication more difficult to understand and murky about other considerations besides those relating specifically to inflation developments. (11) The task facing the Riksbank, as I see it, is to further clarify the principles formulated in 1999. The discussion over the past two years shows that, despite the clarification, monetary policy is often evaluated in a mechanical way, solely on the basis of what the outcome has been for the CPI and UND1X. (12) This may be a reasonable starting point for a discussion, but the discussion should be taken further and also be about: how the outcome of the policy relates to the considerations taken into account for various more temporary price fluctuations such as the rises in electricity prices in 2002-2003. Real and financial developments should also be taken into account in the contexts in which they have influenced policies. Exactly how this should be done is something the Riksbank and those who evaluate us have reason to think about. Work on this focus is now also underway in the Riksbank. At the same time, I do not see that this work will lead to any fundamental changes to the monetary policy strategy. Rather, it is about creating greater clarity about how we work to further facilitate the understanding and predictability of the policy and at the same time enable a more effective and efficient evaluation. Summary and concluding reflections Let me now briefly summarise what I have said and make a couple of final reflections. There is currently a broad consensus on the basic principles that should characterise a well-designed monetary policy. Crucial in this context is that policy is conducted in such a way that the credibility of inflation remaining low and stable is not shaken. However, the fact that there is considerable agreement on the more general principles does not prevent differences between countries as regards the details of policy-making. Differences between the US and Sweden exist when it comes to the goal formulation, both because there are no inflation targets in the US and because the balance between low and stable inflation and real stability is described in a different way. When it comes to transparency, despite several steps towards increased openness, the Federal Reserve has recently not come as far as the Riksbank. Nevertheless, the similarities in the application of the policy are, in my view, considerable; in both cases, it is a question of having long-term price stability as a benchmark and of balancing this ambition primarily against real stability, but also against other risks, such as threats to financial stability. The difficult task that we face in the Riksbank, and we probably share it with the Federal Reserve, is to make it clearer how we handle these trade-offs. The misunderstandings that have sometimes occurred have generally had to do with this. The task is not simple mainly because the world rarely repeats itself. Every situation tends to look a little different. Nor is there any other central bank, to my knowledge, that has set itself the task of trying to set out a clear strategy on how to make these trade-offs and how, against this background, it wants to be evaluated. Personally, I see this work as the next major challenge for the Riksbank in the area of monetary policy. Thanks. Footnotes: 1) Greenspan, A. text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Heikensten: Penningpolitiken i Sverige och USA Datum: 2005-10-14 Talare: Riksbankschef Lars Heikensten Plats: Lunds universitet Tack fr inbjudan till Lunds universitet. Jag ser fram emot att tillsammans med er diskutera penningpolitikens upplggning. Det r inte s ofta jag har denna mjlighet i ett akademiskt sammanhang som detta. Nr vi under de senaste dryga tio ren har arbetat med att utveckla penningpolitiken i Sverige har vi ofta haft anledning att blicka utanfr vrt eget land, fr att gra jmfrelser och frska lra av hur andra lnder gtt tillvga. Naturligtvis har d penningpolitiken i Frenta Staterna varit en av de viktigaste jmfrelsenormerna. I debatten i Sverige har det ocks varit vanligt med referenser till den amerikanska politiken p temat att allt skulle ha varit bttre om vi agerat som dem. Mot den hr bakgrunden tror jag att det kan vara intressant att diskutera vr politik jmfrt med deras. Fr mig har ocks frgestllningen varit srskilt relevant sedan jag kom hem frn det s kallade Jackson Hole-symposiet i USA, som detta r hedrade den snart avgende amerikanske centralbankschefen Alan Greenspan. Bred samsyn om grundlggande principer Det r inledningsvis viktigt att understryka att de skillnader som finns mellan den svenska och den amerikanska penningpolitiken  eller fr vrigt den i ngot annat jmfrbart land  inte gller de mer allmnna principerna fr hur penningpolitik br bedrivas. Om dessa rder det idag en betydande internationell enighet. Det som r avgrande r att penningpolitiken bedrivs p ett sdant stt att trovrdigheten fr att inflationen kommer att frbli lg inte rubbas  att, som det brukar uttryckas, ekonomins nominella ankare inte slpper. Klart r dock att det inte handlar om ngon mekanisk process. Eftersom vrlden r komplex och det hela tiden intrffar ovntade hndelser r varje beslutstillflle unikt. Penningpolitiken mste drfr med ndvndighet till en del vara vad man brukar kalla diskretionr; besluten fattas frn fall till fall och r beroende av de just fr stunden rdande omstndigheterna. Det handlar om att i varje situation beakta konsekvenserna fr inflationen, men att ocks i bilden ha med vad effekterna p ekonomin i vrigt blir  att helt enkelt bedriva en klok stabilisering av inflationen. Ibland intrffar ocks extraordinra hndelser, vars slutliga konsekvenser r svra att verblicka och arbeta in i traditionella analyser och prognoser. Terrordden i USA den 11 september 2001 r ett exempel p en sdan hndelse. I samband med dessa snkte mnga centralbanker vrlden ver sina rntor snabbt. Det kraftfulla agerandet kan tolkas som en sorts "frskring" mot ett riktigt svagt utfall. Alan Greenspan, har vid ett antal tillfllen uttryckt det som att penningpolitik i hg grad handlar om att kvantifiera och hantera olika risker. Fljande citat anknyter till detta och ger en bra bild av hur Greenspan ser p penningpolitikens uppgift och som ocks stmmer vl med min egen uppfattning: "This [] framework emphasizes understanding as much as possible the many sources of risk and uncertainty that policymakers face, quantifying those risks when possible, and assessing the costs associated with each of the risks."(1) Skillnader och likheter i upplggningen Jag r tmligen vertygad om att de flesta centralbanker skulle beskriva de allmnna principerna fr sin politik p ungefr det stt jag har gjort hr. Detta innebr dock inte att det inte finns skillnader mellan lnder nr det gller detaljerna fr hur penningpolitiken lggs upp. Lt mig ta upp ngra aspekter p den specifika upplggningen av den svenska och den amerikanska penningpolitiken dr vi skiljer oss t men ven sdana dr det finns likheter. Inflationsmlet Den kanske mest uppenbara skillnaden gller mlet fr politiken. Sverige har till skillnad frn USA ett siffersatt ml fr inflationen. Federal Reserve har visserligen liksom Riksbanken prisstabilitet som ml men vilken niv p inflationen som man siktar p har man valt att inte specificera. I USA genomfrdes en politikomlggning omkring 1980, d Federal Reserve under centralbankschefen Paul Volcker lyckades bringa ner inflationen frn hga, tidvis tvsiffriga niver. Vid denna tidpunkt frekom inte inflationsmlsstyrning ngonstans, inte ens i den akademiska litteraturen. Den enda mer konkreta erfarenheten var vrt eget experiment med ett prisstabilitetsml i Sverige p 1930-talet, baserat p Knut Wicksells prisnorm, men det var frsts fga knt utanfr Sverige. Volcker refererade i sin argumentation till monetaristiska tankegngar, men bedrev i praktiken politiken p ett pragmatiskt om n hrt vis. Genom denna politik och den som senare har frts har man lyckats vertyga de ekonomiska aktrerna om att inflationen kommer att hllas p en lg niv, utan att man frdenskull formulerat ngot explicit ml fr priskningstakten. Man skulle kunna se politikomlggningen i USA som ett annat stt att ge ekonomin ett nominellt ankare n med det siffersatta ml vi anvnt, ven om det i det amerikanska fallet kan sgas handla om ett implicit snarare n ett explicit tagande. Det rder knappast ngon tvekan om att svl strategin med ett explicit inflationsml som den amerikanska lsningen har varit framgngsrika och att bda idag tnjuter stort frtroende. Mot den bakgrunden r det intressant  och kanske ocks mindre knt hr hemma  att det i USA nd frs en debatt om huruvida det kan finnas vinster med att ta ett ytterligare steg och infra ett explicit ml fr inflationen.(2) Ett argument i den amerikanska debatten har varit att infrandet av ett explicit inflationsml skulle bidra till att ka tydligheten i penningpolitiken. Det kan dels handla om att gra politiken i frvg mer frutsgbar fr ekonomins aktrer. Men det kan ocks handla om att gra besluten lttare att utvrdera i efterhand. Ett annat argument har varit att ett inflationsml skulle bidra till att nnu bttre frankra inflationsfrvntningarna.(3) Ju bttre frankrade dessa r desto mindre r risken fr att till exempel en pltslig kostnadskning ska f spridningseffekter och desto mer expansiv kan penningpolitiken i ett sdant lge tilltas vara. Genom att ytterligare strka trovrdigheten fr att inflationen kommer att hllas lg kan drfr infrandet av ett inflationsml  vilket mjligen kan tyckas paradoxalt  snarare ka n begrnsa penningpolitikens manverutrymme. Ytterligare ett argument har varit att ett inflationsml skulle bidra till att fokusera den politiska debatten p vad penningpolitiken p lng sikt faktiskt kan stadkomma  att kontrollera inflationen  snarare n vad den inte kan stadkomma  att varaktigt hja tillvxten och sysselsttningen. Argumenten emot har i frsta hand handlat om att den nuvarande regimen fungerat bra. Andra argument r i huvudsak politiska och inte alldeles enkla fr en ickeamerikan att vrdera. De har att gra med riskerna fr att framst som alltfr fokuserad p inflationen, som en "inflation nutter", fr att anvnda ett uttrycksstt lnat frn min brittiska kollega Mervyn King. En del hyser ocks oro fr att en diskussion om mlet skulle vcka andra frgor i kongressen som man inte vill ha upp p bordet. Men huvudargumentet verkar nd vara "if it aint broke, dont fix it". Drmed har jag antagligen ocks sagt att det r troligt att om ngon form av inflationsmlspolitik hade uppfunnits och anvnts i USA redan i slutet av 1970-talet s hade den politiken tnjutit ett lika hgt frtroende som dagens. Mlformuleringen En annan skillnad gller hur Riksbankens respektive Federal Reserves uppdrag r formulerat i den bakomliggande lagtexten. Federal Reserve har ett s kallat "dualt mandat" som innebr att penningpolitiken ska strva efter svl "maximal sysselsttning" som "stabila priser". I Sverige och mnga andra lnder med inflationsml har lagtexten i frsta hand fokuserat p inflationen. Ml fr sysselsttning eller produktion r endera inte specificerat eller underordnat mlet om prisstabilitet  man brukar tala om en s kallad lexikografisk ordning av mlen, dr eventuella ml fr realekonomin ska uppfyllas givet att mlet om prisstabilitet inte r hotat. Skillnaderna nr det gller hur centralbankernas uppgifter formulerats har till stor del historiska frklaringar. Mnga lnder har under 1990-talet ftt en ny centralbankslagstiftning. Denna har prglats av de praktiska erfarenheter och teoretiska insikter som vxte fram under frmst 1970- och 80-talen. Det blev d tydligare fr alla att det inte gick att med penningpolitik lngsiktigt hja produktion och sysselsttning i ett land. Vad centralbanker dremot kunde gra var att skra prisstabilitet. P s vis kunde ocks en grund lggas fr en i vrigt god ekonomisk utveckling. Till detta kom en kad sjlvstndighet i beslutsfattandet, ocks den motiverad av praktiska erfarenheter frmst i Tyskland, och teoretiska insikter om att utformningen av det institutionella ramverket r av central betydelse fr mjligheterna att hlla inflationen p en lg niv.(4) Genom att i lagstiftningen lgga tyngdpunkten p inflationen skickades en tydlig signal om att politiken p ett betydligt mer beslutsamt stt n tidigare skulle inriktas p att hlla inflationen lg och stabil. Min bild r att det inte minst i Sverige ocks fanns en oro fr att allmnt formulerade ml nr det gller realekonomin skulle komma att tolkas just som att penningpolitiken ansvarade ven fr den mer lngsiktiga utvecklingen av till exempel sysselsttningen, vilket den allts inte har mjlighet att gra. Det r i sammanhanget ocks vrt att notera att det i frarbetena till det nya svenska regelverk fr penningpolitiken som trdde i kraft 1999 gjordes bedmningen att det var underfrsttt att Riksbanken, i egenskap av en myndighet under riksdagen, har som uppgift att stdja den allmnna ekonomiska politik som riksdagen lagt fast  i den mn detta inte strider mot prisstabilitetsmlet. Denna skyldighet, menade man, behvde drfr inte srskilt anges i lag.(5) Utvecklingen i USA har fljt delvis annorlunda banor. Federal Reserves "duala mandat" tillkom genom ett tillgg till Federal Reserve Act 1977. Den politikomlggning som genomfrdes omkring 1980 och som innebar startpunkten fr den trovrdiga lginflationspolitik som bedrivits sedan dess kunde ske inom ramen fr det rdande penningpolitiska regelverket med dubbla ml. Att detta var mjligt beror frmodligen p en kombination av faktorer, som jag redan delvis varit inne p. Det handlar dels om att inflationen alltmer brjade upplevas som det mest akuta problemet. Det handlar frmodligen ocks till en del om att Federal Reserve vid den tiden hade en ledning som hade beslutsamhet nog att tackla inflationsproblemet, trots att nedvxlingen av inflationen med stor sannolikhet skulle komma att innebra kraftigt kad arbetslshet under en period. Man kan mhnda ocks sga att det avspeglar att den amerikanska mlformuleringen lmnar ett ganska stort utrymme fr Federal Reserve att gra egna tolkningar av vilka prioriteringar som behver gras. Penningpolitiken i praktiken Vilka praktiska implikationer har d skillnaderna i de olika mlformuleringarna? Ett skl att stlla sig denna frga r att man frn och till i den svenska debatten lyft fram den amerikanska lsningen med ett "dualt mandat", dr hnsyn ska tas bde till sysselsttning och inflation, som ett fredme. Diskussionen var srskilt intensiv i samband med framtagandet av det nya regelverk fr Riksbanken som trdde i kraft 1999, men liknande tankegngar har framskymtat i debatten ven under senare r. Det faktum att det i Riksbankens regelverk inte sgs ngot om realekonomiska ml innebr emellertid inte att hnsyn inte tas till den realekonomiska utvecklingen. Riksbanken bedriver vad som har kallats en flexibel snarare n en strikt inflationsmlspolitik. Fokus ligger allts inte enbart p att stabilisera inflationen utan politiken r flexibel i meningen att ven andra hnsyn tas. Hur vi resonerar i Riksbanken i dessa avseenden framgr av ett frtydligande som vi i gjorde i brjan av 1999.(6) I detta frtydligande sgs att vi lgger upp penningpolitiken s att vissa avvikelser frn inflationsmlet accepteras samtidigt som vi normalt strvar efter att fra tillbaka inflationen till mlet inom en tidsperiod av tv r. Detta kan motiveras bde av att vi inte har mjlighet att kontrollera inflationen exakt p kort sikt och behovet av att ha flexibilitet  att kunna ta hnsyn till annat n inflationen, till exempel stabiliteten i den reala ekonomin. Samtidigt r det viktigt att denna flexibilitet inte minskar trovrdigheten fr inflationsmlet p sikt utan att det kan fylla sin funktion som "nominellt ankare". Tvrshorisonten kan tolkas som en restriktion p hur stor hnsyn som normalt kan tas till andra ml n fast penningvrde, en restriktion som Riksbanken sjlv  i likhet med det preciserade inflationsmlet  lagt p sig fr att skapa trovrdighet fr sin politik inriktad mot prisstabilitet. Att jag anvnder ordet normalt beror p att det i vissa fall och under vissa omstndigheter kan uppst lgen d flexibiliteten mste tilltas vara strre fr att det sammantagna ekonomiska utfallet ska bli acceptabelt. I extremfall kan avvikelserna frn inflationsmlet bli s pass stora att det faktiskt inte r mjligt att terfra inflationen inom det vanliga tvriga tidsperspektivet. Den takt med vilken det r mjligt och nskvrt att terfra inflationen till mlet efter en avvikelse r allmnt sett beroende av storleken p de strningar ekonomin trffas av samt av vilken typ strningarna r. Under perioder, till exempel nr stora strningar p ekonomins utbudssida intrffar, r det drfr mjligt att inflationen avviker en lngre tid n tv r frn tvprocentsmlet. Uppfattningen att skillnaderna i praktiken r sm fr ocks indirekt std av den debatt som frs i USA och som jag tidigare berrde. Dr har det hvdats att Federal Reserve gradvis har brjat fra en politik som i allt vsentligt skulle kunna beskrivas som en implicit inflationsmlspolitik.(7) Fresprkarna fr denna syn menar att en vinst med att ta ytterligare ett steg och infra inflationsmlspolitik ven i ren formell mening  utver de jag tidigare nmnde  r att det skulle vara ett stt att frskra sig om att samma vlavvgda politik som bedrivits under Alan Greenspan kommer att bedrivas ven i framtiden. Det skulle med andra ord i allt vsentligt bara innebra en kodifiering och institutionalisering av den nuvarande politiken som skulle gra den mindre "personberoende". Skillnaderna mellan den svenska och den amerikanska mlformuleringen r allts som jag uppfattar det vsentligt strre p pappret n i praktiken. Som jag ser det handlar det i grunden om tv olika stt att beskriva samma typ av politik snarare n om att det finns avgrande skillnader i politiken som sdan.(8) Mervyn King har formulerat detta p ett lite annorlunda vis nr han hvdat att den flexibla inflationsmlspolitiken r "generisk" och inrymmer andra stt att bedriva penningpolitik som specialfall.(9) ppenhet och kommunikation Nr det gller graden av ppenhet och kommunikation finns det dremot tydliga skillnader mellan penningpolitiken i Sverige och USA. Riksbanken har internationellt sett srskilt under senare delen av 1990-talet gtt i brschen bland centralbankerna nr det gller ppenhet. Fr Federal Reserves del gller snarast motsatsen, tminstone om man jmfr med andra industrialiserade lnder. Som exempel kan nmnas att det faktiskt var s sent som 1994 som Federal Reserve brjade med att offentliggra sina rntebeslut omedelbart efter att de fattats. Men ocks inom Federal Reserve har en hel del steg tagits fr att ka ppenheten och tydligheten. Efter 1994 har det skett en gradvis vergng till mer substantiella pressmeddelanden, som ger en motivering till rntebesluten. Sedan 2002 offentliggrs individuella rster och eventuella reservationer mot beslutet. Frn och med 2005 publiceras protokollen med kortare efterslpning n tidigare  nu offentliggrs de tre veckor efter det penningpolitiska mtet. I vetenskapliga studier som frsker kartlgga graden av ppenhet hamnar dock Riksbanken bland de frmsta och regelmssigt en bit hgre n den amerikanska centralbanken.(10) Vad kan man d sga om skillnaderna i hur politiken beskrivs i Sverige respektive USA? Jag skulle vilja gra fljande grova tolkning. Nr det gller USA skulle man lite frenklat kunna sga att penningpolitiken framstlls och kommuniceras p ett stt som ligger ganska nra lroboksmodellens beskrivning av en penningpolitik med ett "dualt mandat"; styrrntan ska sttas p ett sdant stt att den vntade utvecklingen av inflationen och realekonomin sammantaget "ser bra ut". Detta tmligen generella stt att beskriva politiken och dess konsekvenser ger Federal Reserve ett stort "spelutrymme". Baksidan av myntet r att politiken ibland kan uppfattas som otydlig  det kan vara svrt att se exakt vad den strvar efter att uppn. n vrre skulle detta problem antagligen vara om inte politiken under senare r varit s nra kopplad till en enskild person vars kommunikation varit marknadens "lag". Annorlunda uttryckt; med en grupp beslutsfattare som ocks kommunicerar egna frhllningsstt till styrrntan r vrdet frn kommunikationssynpunkt av en tydlig analytisk ram antagligen nnu strre n i ett system dominerat av en enskild beslutsfattare. I Sverige har beskrivningen och kommunikationen av penningpolitiken frdelen att den kan ta inflationsmlet som utgngspunkt. Besluten om styrrntan kan frklaras och motiveras i termer av att de i slutnden syftar till att f inflationen att hamna kring mlet. Samtidigt finns, som jag varit inne p, utrymme att beakta den realekonomiska utvecklingen genom att inflationen tillflligt kan tilltas avvika frn mlet. Centralt i sammanhanget r att upplggningen med inflationsml tvingar oss att i sdana lgen redovisa tydliga och goda argument fr vrt agerande  vi behver frklara varfr vi valt att avvika frn mlet och i vilket tidsperspektiv vi avser att frska fra tillbaka inflationen. Title: Monetary Policy and Academics
text: Heikensten: Monetary policy and academics Date: 2005-10-28 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Lars Heikensten Place: Keynote lecture, Faculty of Social Sciences, Umea University Let me start by underlining how happy and grateful I am to have been appointed honorary doctor at Umea University and to stand here and speak to you today. I intend to talk about a subject that I think might fit quite well in an environment like this, namely the link between academic research and practical monetary policy. It's also a topic that's close at hand for me. I imagine that one of the reasons why Umea University wanted to give me this award is precisely that for more than 20 years now I have contributed to creating a bridge between the academies and the institutions in the country  primarily the Ministry of Finance and the Riksbank  where economic policy is designed. There is little doubt that the research conducted in the academic world has had a major, and in some respects perhaps even decisive, importance for how monetary policy today is structured in Sweden and many other countries. At the same time, it is equally clear that practical policy has sometimes in turn been one step ahead and given important impulses and ideas to academic research. So it has been a mutual exchange. I think it is fair to say that there are few areas in the social sciences where the interaction between academics and practitioners has been  and still is  as intense and fruitful as in monetary policy. A look back It may be appropriate to start with a brief look back at the economic development in Sweden in recent decades. As you all remember, our country suffered a deep economic crisis in the early 1990s. This crisis had several specific causes, but on a more general level could be described as a dramatic end to almost twenty years of stabilization policy problems in the Swedish economy. During the 1970s and 80s, the policies pursued tended to become too expansive for various reasons. This created an environment where it proved difficult to keep price and wage increases at a reasonable level. The fixed exchange rate policy did not, as intended, lead to inflation in Sweden being on a par with that of our most important trading partners. Instead, price and wage developments repeatedly clashed with the fixed exchange rate  we ended up in cost crises. These cost crises were temporarily "solved" by devaluations of the krona, but the fundamental problem  the too rapid trend increase in domestic prices and wages  remained in the background all the time. In this way, the economy came to be characterized by "devaluation cycles" with alternating sharp decelerations and sharp stimulus measures. The failed stabilization policy was, in my opinion, an important reason why the Swedish economy developed weakly, both compared with previous periods and in relation to other countries. After the fixed exchange rate system had finally had to be abandoned in November 1992, in the wake of yet another cost crisis and after an inconclusive struggle to defend the krona and break the negative trend, it was obvious that something quite drastic needed to be done to put the Swedish economy on a better track. The solution was a stabilization policy regime change, in which both monetary and fiscal policy tasks were fundamentally redefined. Fiscal policy, which in the past had often been too expansionary and contributed to high inflation, would now instead be subject to demands for long-term stability and sustainability in public finances. Monetary policy, for its part, took on a much more central and active role than it had had in the past. Now that the krona was allowed to continue to float, the main task of monetary policy was to work more directly to keep inflation at a low and stable level, mainly by influencing the demand situation in the economy with changes in interest rates. This data was interpreted by the Riksbank as meaning that the increase in the consumer price index would be two per cent per annum. Thus, in 1993, Sweden became one of the first countries to introduce a so-called inflation targeting policy. Since then, this way of setting up monetary policy has gained in popularity and is today applied by some twenty central banks worldwide. Looking back at developments over the last ten years, it is difficult to come to any conclusion other than that the new regime has worked well. Sweden is no longer a high-inflation economy with recurring cost crises, high interest rates, unstable economic development and modest real wage increases. Instead, inflation has been low, growth in the economy higher and more stable than in the 1970s and 80s, and real wage developments significantly more favourable (Chart 1). Employment trends have not been as good, but it is nevertheless worth pointing out that the situation today is significantly better than it was in the mid-1990s. At the time, assessments were common to suggest that unemployment would be stuck around 8 percent. The role of academic research The introduction of an explicit target for inflation What role, then, has academic research played in the way monetary policy is designed today and thus also, in part, in the favourable economic development of the last decade? Let me start by saying something about the idea of allowing monetary policy to be guided by a specific, numerical target for inflation. As I have just mentioned, Sweden was one of the first countries to introduce inflation targeting policies. First out, more specifically in 1990, was New Zealand, which, like Sweden, had long struggled with problems of high trend inflation and otherwise poor economic development. (2) The idea of setting a numerical target for inflation seems quite natural today, but was actually at this time almost revolutionary. For countries with variable exchange rates, during the 1980s it was instead common to use different measures of the money supply to control inflation, supported by the academic literature. But it proved increasingly difficult to find stable useful methods for this, or as a former Canadian central bank governor put it: "It was not we who abandoned the money supply, it was the one who abandoned us". Another common system, as I have already mentioned, was to keep the exchange rate fixed in order to stabilise inflation. Thus, although monetary policy in many countries was already tasked at this time with keeping inflation low and stable, no direct and clearly figured target for inflation had hitherto been specified. A side note that may be interesting in this context is that Sweden actually applied what could be described as a form of inflation targeting policy as early as a period in the 1930s. After the fixed exchange rate had been abandoned in the autumn of 1931, the Riksbank and the government declared that the goal of the Riksbank would be to stabilize the price level, that is, an inflation target of zero percent if you will. Sveriges Riksbank thus became, by all accounts, the first central bank in the world to clearly advertise price stabilization as the norm for its policy at floating exchange rates. (3) The inspiration for the price stabilization norm came from works done much earlier, in the late 1800s, by Knut Wicksell, who today stands out as our country's perhaps foremost economist of all time. However, the experience of the Swedish price stabilization standard was far back in time in 1990 and should hardly have played any role  or even been known  in New Zealand's decision to introduce inflation targeting policies. As reported, the decisive effort to introduce an explicit inflation target for monetary policy was made by far-sighted officials at New Zealand's Treasury and central bank. There was no current academic research to lean on, but you had to, so to speak, launch the new regime more or less "on chance" and simply see how well it worked in practice. The concept of an explicit inflation target for monetary policy can thus  at least in its modern guise  be said to have originated not in academia but in the hands of practicing economists. An illustration of the fact that academic research initially played a more limited role can be obtained if, in one of the most well-known databases of scientific publications in economics, you search for the concept of "inflation targeting"  the English term for inflation targeting policy  and count the number of hits for each year (Figure 2). It is then found that it did not appear to be until the mid-1990s, that is, about five years after it had been introduced into practice, that inflation targeting policy began to attract somewhat more extensive interest in academic research. To my knowledge, the first international conference on inflation targeting policy with the participation of both academic researchers and central bank representatives took place in Milan in 1994. (4) From the mid-1990s, however, academic interest increased rapidly. The importance of independent central banks Thus, while research may not be said to have played a decisive role in the introduction of a specific inflation target, it has played an all the more important role in shaping inflation targeting policy in another key respect, namely how the institutional framework should be designed to deliver the best possible results. To illustrate this, let me return for a moment to the Swedish development during the 1970s and 80s. As I noted earlier, the main problem was that Swedish prices and wages tended to increase at too fast a pace. It is worth stressing that this development was not due to a lack of insight into the problems or ambition  at least on paper  to try to remedy them. On a number of occasions, the government stressed the importance of bringing inflation under control. For example, the report "Crisis plan for Sweden" presented by the government in October 1982 states: "After the effects of devaluation have taken effect, inflation must be pushed down and stabilised at a low level. Both the demand and cost development in the Swedish economy must be adapted to this". (5) Similarly, the 1985 SNS report, The Road to a More Stable Sweden, states that: "Today we are faced with an important choice between basically two different approaches to economic policy. One option is a continued accommodative [...] regime. The second is a [...] price stabilization policy [...] [where a] low and constant inflation [...] [is] the central prerequisite for a balanced economic development in Sweden with high employment and growth". (6) Why, then, despite all the pledges, did it not succeed in breaking the unfavourable trend? The answer is likely given largely by the research on the economic the so-called time inconsistency problem of politics, which was one of the reasons why Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott were awarded the Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel in 2004. (7) This research focused on the fact that difficulties in issuing binding pledges in stabilisation policies can make it difficult to keep inflation down. The basic problem is that the short-term motives of economic policymakers may conflict with the long-term ambition to keep inflation at a low level. This makes it difficult to convince economic actors that the policy will remain firm, that is, be consistent over time  hence the term time inconsistency problem. Suppose that the government declares that inflation will be kept at a certain low level in the future and that the actors in the economy initially actually believe that this will also be the case. Inflation expectations in society will then adapt to the low inflation. However, once inflation expectations have been adjusted, there may be reasons for economic policymakers to deviate from the set long-term inflation standard for various reasons. For example, a temporary reduction in unemployment, achieved by stimulating the economy and releasing inflation, may be perceived as politically advantageous, even if the benefits are not lasting. At the same time, the costs of higher inflation are not perceived as so serious because inflation in the initial situation is low. It is easy to imagine that the temptation to pursue such a policy can be especially strong in certain situations, for example, on the eve of an election. However, as economic actors recognise that there is such a constant temptation for economic policymakers with an ambitious employment target, they will align their inflation expectations from the outset with this fact rather than with the declared inflation target. Price and wage setting will thus in practice be based on higher inflation than the target set. The best thing the government thinks it can do in this situation is to pursue an accommodative policy that meets the high inflation expectations. The end result is that inflation ends up at a higher level than that which society strives for in the long term  there is a so-called inflation bias  without production and employment ultimately being higher. This seems to be a pretty good description of what happened in Sweden and many other countries during the 1970s and 80s. The repeated pledges that inflation would be kept low were simply not perceived as credible. Excessively high wage increases were not perceived as so severe by wage earners and employers; it was expected that the exchange rate would be adjusted downwards if employment was threatened. In other words, inflation expectations came to align in advance with an expected economic policy pattern in which high price and wage increases were accommodated by devaluations. It can be said, then, that what was missing was enough convincing arrangements to back up the ambitions to keep inflation low that apparently existed anyway. Academic research subsequently generated several more or less realistic theoretical solutions to address the time inconsistency problem and the inflation bias it gives rise to. (8) However, many of these solutions were based on the assumption that the temptation to stimulate the economy in order to achieve short-term benefits exists not only for a government but also for a central bank, regardless of whether it has been given a clear mandate and freedom to act independently. I do not think that this is a really accurate description of reality, as I think practical experience has shown. It seems to me, therefore, that, at least in some of the research, it was underestimated for some time what delegating monetary policy to an independent central bank can achieve in terms of tackling the problem of excessive inflation. Alan Blinder, a well-known American economist and for some time also vice-president of the US Federal Reserve, seems to share this view. He has argued that during his time in the Federal Reserve, he never felt there was any temptation to stimulate the economy at the expense of inflationary ambitions in order to achieve short-term benefits in the form of temporarily higher employment and output. There was simply an awareness of the costs of such a policy. (9) The same applies to: the ten years of monetary policy with inflation targets that I can see in Sweden. Behind the successful policy lies a change in the behaviour of central banks. The realisation has spread that monetary policy cannot permanently raise the level of employment and that attempts in this direction will only lead to higher inflation. Employment problems must instead be tackled through improvements in the functioning of the labour market. The fact that monetary policy cannot permanently improve employment or raise output is one of the key insights to which theoretical and empirical academic research has contributed, and it is supported by the practical experience of monetary policy in several countries over more than a decade. It is, after all, quite natural that it is far easier for an independent central bank to resist the temptation to pursue an excessively expansionary policy than for a government that has to make decisions on an ongoing basis under the pressure of key groups of voters. When this temptation no longer exists, the actors in the economy trust that inflation will be kept low and thus the inflation bias will also disappear. My interpretation, then, is that the problem is very much political and that it is the very delegation of monetary policy to an independent central bank, together with the realisation that monetary policy cannot raise employment permanently, that has been the key to the solution. In line with this, monetary policy research now no longer assumes that central banks have any tendency to overstimulate the economy. But while some of the research may have underestimated the benefits of an independent central bank undoubtedly, the fact remains that Kydland and Prescott's original contributions have had great practical significance. The realisation that inflation can become unnecessarily high if there is no opportunity to make it credible to economic actors that the announced low inflation policy will remain firm over time can be said to have been the starting point for the institutional reforms regarding the position of the central bank that have been implemented in many countries since the early 1990s. In Sweden, monetary policy was in practice conducted independently from at least the mid-1990s. The regulations themselves were amended on 1 January 1999 in such a way that the Riksbank's position was also formally strengthened, for example by replacing the previously directly politically elected Riksbank's board by an executive board with full-time members, who will independently take the monetary policy decisions. At the same time, it was stipulated that the objective of the Riksbank's operations should be to maintain a fixed monetary value. Further developments in inflation targeting policies What, then, can be said about the further development of inflation targeting policy that has taken place over the last ten to fifteen years? There is no doubt that the Riksbank's monetary policy strategy has gradually been developed and modified during the period of its inflation target. In other words, we do not think, act and communicate in the same way today as we did when the inflation targeting regime was new. The driving force for the changes has partly been practical experiences, both in Sweden and in other countries that conduct politics in a similar way and with which we in many different international contexts have an exchange. But academic research has also been of great importance. This is, moreover, increasingly taking place in the central banking world (Chart 3). If one were to try to summarize on a more general level what the research has meant for the development of inflation targeting policy, one could say that it has largely been about it helping to systematize and discipline thinking within central banks on various issues  it has, so to speak, made the basis of policy more stable. A good example of this type of work and of fruitful interaction between researchers and the central bank world is the early work on inflation targeting policy made by the Riksbank's advisor Lars Svensson, where the balance between inflation stability and real stability is formalized and clarified. (10) They helped to make it clearer to us in the Riksbank what inflation targeting is all about. They also helped us start publishing our forecasts and make policy clearer by communicating a principle of how target deviations would be handled; we normally said we had the ambition to bring inflation back to target within two years when a deviation occurred. (11) Research on inflation targeting policies has also long emphasized the importance of openness and clarity, or transparency as it is commonly called in these contexts. Not too long ago, it was traditional for central bank actions and actions to be surrounded with a considerable amount of mystery and secrecy, as in Sweden. There are both political and economic reasons why a high level of transparency is desirable. (12) The political reason is simply that transparency and clarity are important for the evaluation and exercise of democratic control. This is, of course, a requirement that should be possible for all public services to be imposed. But when it comes to monetary policy, this is especially important in light of the autonomy central banks have today. The economic reasons are of different nature. One is related precisely to the time consistency problem I spoke about earlier. By making clear openly and clearly the principles we follow in our decision-making, and also presenting our evidence, we make it possible for anyone who so wishes to follow our policies and see if we live up to our principles. So we tie ourselves to the mast, so to speak. This was a strategy the Riksbank deliberately embarked on in 1996 and in the following years, when there was as yet no legislation on independence to fall back on, and it worked very well in general. Even today, however, this way of working is of great value. A recent example is the Riksbank's decision in June to cut interest rates. Surely this would have been questioned by some observers, and described as the result of political pressure, had it not been for the fact that it was so easy to see the basis for the decision. With the clear principles we follow, it was clear that the new information received about a weaker economy almost automatically led to the conclusion that a reduction was justified. The ability to control the economy is also likely to increase the more transparent the central bank is. Both theory and empiricism suggest that long-term interest rates, exchange rates and conditions in other financial markets have as much impact on how monetary policy affects the economy  what is usually called the transmission mechanism  as the short-term interest rates that the central bank can more directly control. Long-term interest rates and other financial asset prices, in turn, reflect the expectations of economic actors about future short-term interest rates as well as how uncertain they are about future developments. The clearer the central bank is about what it does and why, and how it sees the future, the easier it will be for economic actors to get an idea of how short-term interest rates will develop. This increases the central bank's ability to influence interest rates in the slightly longer term and get them better in line with what it considers desirable. It can be put that monetary policy will thus be more effective. Thus, inflation targeting policies are now  almost necessarily  pursued with a high degree of transparency and clarity. During the latter part of the 1990s, the Riksbank was at the forefront of this development and usually ranks high in international comparisons of monetary policy transparency (Chart 4). (13) It may also be worth mentioning the research in both financial economics and econometrics. It has been of great practical importance, in particular by providing new tools for the analysis and forecasting activities carried out within central banks. Among other things, this means that research has developed methods for extracting important information for monetary policy from price formation in financial markets. The development here has been quite dramatic and the decision-making basis we in the Riksbank have when it comes to interpreting developments in different markets is today completely different from what was the case about ten years ago. For example, from the yield curve, i.e. the interest rate on investments with different maturities, we can, through different methods, estimate what monetary policy market participants expect in the future or via option pricing, form an idea of how the market views uncertainty. Another area where research in recent years has been quite extensive is that central banks have to deal with the fact that their decisions are made under uncertainty. (14) A central theme of this research is that it is not only the projections as such  the expected outcome  that play a role in the monetary policy to be pursued, but also the uncertainties and risks associated with these projections. One line of research has revolved around so-called Bayesian methods, which in short can be said to be a technique for formally incorporating estimated subjective probabilities of different possible outcomes into the analysis. Another part of the research has focused on so-called robust policy, which, somewhat simplified, means a policy where the central thing is to avoid really bad outcomes. It is then often a matter of acting preventively when extraordinary events occur as a kind of "insurance" against a really weak development. The Riksbank's actions in the autumn of 1998 could be seen as an example of this. We then saw a small but still clear risk that, as a result of the then serious disruptions in the financial system, the economy could go into a downturn and therefore implemented a couple of interest rate cuts in fairly quick succession. It turned out in retrospect, when the situation had cleared up, that the fears were exaggerated and that it would not have been necessary to reduce interest rates. But we did not know this at the time of the decision and the rate cut was a way to guard against a really bad outcome. The lower interest rate meant an "unnecessary" stimulus to the real economy, but this could be corrected with a slightly tighter monetary policy later on. The research in this area can to some extent be said to be positive in the sense that it describes how central banks tend to behave in practice and tries to find theoretical arguments for this. But at the same time, it has helped formalize and structure thinking within central banks regarding how monetary policy should best be conducted under uncertainty. It has also clearly put its finger on the fact that the management of various risks is a particularly important element of monetary policy. Another, slightly more specific example of the practical influence of research  incidentally, a fairly topical one for the Riksbank  concerns the assumption for the future development of the key interest rate that we base our forecasts on. With few exceptions, it has been the practice of central banks with inflation targets to base, or condition, forecasts on the assumption that the policy rate will remain constant over the forecast period. One reason for making this assumption was that it was perceived to facilitate monetary policy communication by clearly showing when there may be reason to change the interest rate  if the forecasted inflation deviates from the target at unchanged policy rate, this is usually a sign that the current interest rate is wrong. However, there are also some disadvantages to the assumption of unchanged policy rates, as pointed out not least in academic research. (15) This makes it difficult, for example, both to evaluate in retrospect the accuracy of the central bank's forecasts and to compare them with those of other forecasters. Other analysts usually base their forecasts on the key interest rate path that the central bank is expected to follow, and in practice it is quite unusual for the repo rate to be kept unchanged for as long as is usually the case, at least two years. If the policy rate has changed during the period, it is rather strange whether the central bank's forecasts hit the right one. On a more general level, it can also be noted that the assumption of unchanged policy rates may in some situations be so unrealistic that it may be difficult to make consistent and meaningful forecasts. This is an issue that for the Riksbank has become increasingly important as knowledge has increased and its analytical capacity has improved. Therefore, like some other central banks, such as those in Norway and the UK, we have now chosen to start from the interest rate development expected by the market. However, the discussion will hardly end here. Within the research community, for example, there is an ongoing discussion about whether it would not be even better if the interest rate path is completely "endogenized", that is, for the central bank to more explicitly determine and advertise the trajectory for the future policy rate that it deems optimal given today's information and the central bank's goals. Finally, I hope that today you have a picture of the close links that exist between academic research and practical monetary policy. These connections have sometimes meant that research has influenced practitioners and sometimes that the influences have gone the other way, from practical politics to research. The emphasis in my speech has been slightly more on the first of these channels than on the second, reflecting that I am a practitioner who has been able to benefit from the insights of academics. But there is no doubt that the problems faced by central banks and the practical experience they do have also been, and still are, an important source of inspiration for academic research.
