Title: Implementing the regulatory reform agenda - the pitfall of myopia
text: Implementing the regulatory reform agenda - the pitfall of myopia The subject of this conference is indeed very timely  six years after the out-break of the financial crisis, there has been substantial progress in the post-crisis regulatory reform agenda, with a number of important milestones reached. Therefore, now is a good time to take a step back and ask how the different bits and pieces of the regulatory framework fit together. And, more specifically  have the vulnerabilities revealed in the crisis been ad-equately addressed? Are additional adjustments still necessary? Or, conversely, have we gone too far and created a regulatory Frankensteins monster that no-one has full control over and that stifles lending and econom-ic growth? This latter view is one that I sometimes hear when meeting representatives of the banking industry. The feeling seems to be that we are overwhelming the financial system with a regulation tsunami with too many reforms being im-plemented too soon. This will lead to unacceptable consequences in the form of higher funding costs, reductions in market liquidity with market-makers pull-ing out of markets, collateral shortages; and many banking activities simply disappearing, or moving to the so called shadow banking sector. And indeed  the financial crisis has led to a comprehensive response from regulators and policymakers across the world. Compared to the pre-crisis era, international banks will face: - substantially higher capital requirements, - higher demands on the quality of capital, - a leverage ratio, - an international liquidity framework, with both short-term and structur-al liquidity requirements (I am proud to note that the Basel Committee, less than a week ago, published the final standard for the net stable funding ratio, NSFR), and - a regulatory framework for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). When you add to this ongoing work related to reducing RWA variability and disclosure, you end up with a pretty impressive list  a list that represents an unprecedented leap forward in terms of global banking regulation. So then, how do I see this? Do I claim to know how all these new rules will play out together? Am I confi-dent that there will be no inconsistencies and contradictions? No, definitely not. We have every reason to be humble in this respect. Monitoring and as-sessing the effects of reforms will therefore be imperative. Will the reforms be costly for banks in the short term? Yes, they will. Will banks have to adjust their activities? Yes, a return to pre-crisis banking be-haviour is neither appropriate nor viable. Do I therefore think that regulation has gone too far and that parts should be undone? No, not at all. In this presentation I will try to explain why I think this is so. I will also speak about what is still lacking and the regulatory challenges we face ahead. Why we shouldnt back-track on regulation There are several reasons why I dont think the regulatory agenda has gone too far. First of all, my experience is that important regulatory and structural re-forms are all too often hindered by myopia. People tend to focus on costs and pains in the short run, leaving aside the longer term gains that reforms aim to achieve. The perceived short-term costs are simply much easier to sell politically, com-pared to the abstract benefits of lowering the risk of crises. This is especially so, since the benefits may accrue only to future generations  a group that has dif-ficulties making its voice heard in todays policy debate. This time has been no exception: for years, people shied away from necessary actions to strengthen the financial system. When the crisis hit, perceptions changed, providing a window of opportunity for regulatory reforms that were long overdue. However, we must not begin to close this window and lose sight of why we are undertaking these reforms. Let me start with a reminder of the regulatory framework before the crisis. Both Basel I and II included a risk-weighted capital adequacy framework. However, for the last 20 years banks balance sheets ballooned, while their equity failed to take off. For example, from 1993 to 2008 the total assets of a sample of what we call global systemically important banks saw a twelve-fold increase (increas-ing from 2.6 trillion to just over 30 trillion). But the capital funding these as-sets only increased seven-fold, (from 125 billion to 890 billion). Put different-ly, the average risk weight declined from 70% to below 40%. The problem was that this reduction did not represent a genuine reduction in risk in the banking system. To take an even more concrete example from my own country: during the past twenty years or so, the risk weights for retail mortgages in the major Swedish banks have decreased from 50% to 35% with the adoption of Basel II (from Ba-sel I) and further, to about 6% when banks themselves were allowed to model risk weights. In equity terms, this means that instead of SEK 17,000 of their own equity to fund a mortgage of 1 million, banks models implied that SEK 1,200 was enough.1 In retrospect, it is clear that the decrease in risk weights did not reflect actual risks and banks therefore needed more capital. 1 The figure SEK 17,000 1,000,000*50%*3.4%, where 3.4% is the implied minimum core Tier 1 capital requirement under Basel I. The risk-weight for mortgages was 50% during this period. Under Basel II the implied minimum core Tier 1 capital requirement fell from 3.4% to 2% of risk-weighted assets, and was 2% in 2011-2012 when banks internal average risk weights for mortgages was 6%. SEK 1,200 SEK 1,000,000*6%*2%. For more information see Sveriges Riksbank (2013) Financial Stability Report 2013:2, November, pp 21-24. Furthermore, although it is a historical fact that banks problems often start in the form of liquidity constraints, there were no global liquidity regulations for banks prior to the crisis. This meant that banks could rely heavily on very short-term market funding to finance highly illiquid and long-term assets. This worked fine during the Great Moderation, but unfortunately with the collapse of Lehman Brothers another old truism suddenly came to life: markets func-tion the worst when you need them the most. Against this background, it is quite embarrassing that so few could see the cri-sis coming. From a regulatory point of view, all the ingredients were there, or rather they were lacking. And this is the first point I want to make  the regula-tory framework was unsatisfactory and becoming more so the more complex the financial system became. Then, turning to my second point, which is: The costs of financial crises are huge. This is true in general, but especially so for the recent one. For example, according to a recent study by IMF economists, in a sample of countries repre-senting just over 50% of world GDP, the total amount of government recapital-isation, asset purchases and guarantees during the period 20072011 amount-ed to nearly 5 trillion. This is equivalent to 16% of the GDP of these econo-mies, or nearly 5,000 per citizen.2 2 Calculations of costs are based on L Laeven and F Valencia (2013) using data from the banking crisis database and calculations of the BIS and the Riksbank. 3 L Laeven and F Valencia (2013) Systemic Banking Crises Database, IMF Economic Review 61(2), 225-270, IMF. Output losses are computed as the cumulative sum of the differences between actual and trend real GDP over the crisis period in relation to pre-crisis GDP. 4 Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) (2010) An assessment of the long-term economic impact of the new regulatory framework, August. The loss of output referred to represents the median cumulative discounted output loss reported by a number of academic studies assessed in the study, measured over the period from the peak to the end of the crisis. The output loss does not include per-manent losses in GDP, ie where the GDP trend does not recover to the pre-crisis level. But, this is only a lower bound of the cost of the crisis. If we also include the impact on GDP and the loss of production relative to its pre-crisis trend, the costs rise. This has been showed by several studies, including the one just men-tioned by IMF economists, which estimates that banking crises that occurred between 1970 and 2000 are resulting in output losses of more than 20% on average if we look at all countries, and more than 30% of GDP in advanced economies.3 These results are in line with the BIS finding that the median dis-counted cumulative loss of output over the course of a crisis in the same peri-od was about 19% of pre-crisis GDP.4 Now, the question of exactly how much regulation leads to the optimal out-come in terms of long-term growth is, of course, debatable. But let me under-line that ambitious attempts have been made by the BIS, but also the OECD and others, to assess the net effect of recent regulatory reform measures, and the results generally point in one direction: that the net effect of reforms is positive. In addition, let me also underline that the Basel Committee has not been blind and deaf to the worries expressed by the industry about excessive regulation. Many adjustments have been made, not least when it comes to the new liquidi-ty regulation. It is also standard procedure that new regulations are subject to industry consultation and in many cases additional discussions also take place with the industry itself, as well as with investors, to avoid unintended conse-quences. In this context, however, let me remind us all that the reactions we get from the banking industry are sometimes slightly biased, if I dare say so. A telling example is the lobbying effort during the design of the Basel II framework. As part of that work, in 2003 the Committee consulted on a new securitisation framework, which, with the benefit of hindsight, turned out to be very weak. Yet the comments from the industry on the proposed securitisation framework were in general quite alarming. Allow me to quote just a couple of the replies to the consultation proposal that the Committee received (all of which are publicly available):  One bank wrote: The prescribed risk weightings for securitisation ex-posure(s)result in excessive risk weights compared to the economic risks of securitisation tranches, particularly for retail and mortgage portfolios.  This particular bank happened to incur 24.7 billion in losses from CDOs during the crisis.5 5 The bank stating this was Merrill Lynch. Source: The Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, January 2011.  Another bank wrote: If adopted, the current proposal for securitisation will materially impair the ability of banks to distribute risk from their own balance sheets into the capital markets.  This bank incurred USD 13 billion losses in Q1 2008 and USD19 billion in writedowns on real estate and related structured credit positions.13 billion losses in Q1 2008 and USD19 billion in writedowns on real estate and related structured credit positions.13 billion losses in Q1 2008 and USD19 billion in writedowns on real estate and related structured credit positions. 6 Source: Shareholder Report on UBS Write-Downs. 7 By end-2014 it is expected that all jurisdictions with G-SIBs will have been assessed, in addition to some others (total 17 countries). By 2016, all Basel Committee member jurisdictions are expected to have gone through the assessement of their capital framework. Let me emphazise that there is nothing special with these two examples. I can assure you that there are many more similar examples to quote  the message being that the proposed reforms were overly restrictive, would damage the market and reduce activity. This illustrates that we need perspective when as-sessing the feasibility of reforms. To sum up so far: yes, there has been a strong regulatory reaction to the crisis, but as I see it, this is appropriate, given - the pre-crisis regulatory framework, - the costs crises give rise to, and - the efforts that the Basel Committee has made to mitigate risks of un-intended consequences, The problem is that myopic observers tend to forget these aspects. Are we there yet? What are the remaining challenges? I would now like to change perspective slightly and ask, are we there yet? Have our efforts done the trick, or are there still challenges to be tackled? Well, from a Basel Committee perspective I am pleased to be able to say that the Basel III framework is now agreed  in principle. This is a major achieve-ment that all participating parties should be proud of. If I widen the scope, be-yond the Basel III framework, and look at other parts of the reform agenda, it is obvious that the work on ending the too big to fail problem has been diffi-cult, and that some work still remains to be done. However, the reason we have not yet reached our goal is not lack of effort, but simply that the resolution of very large, cross-border banks is not easy. The main remaining issue here concerns how to ensure that global systemically im-portant banks have sufficient capacity to absorb losses in resolution, without having to ask tax-payers to foot the bill. This work goes under the name of T-LAC, or total loss absorbing capacity. I find it reasonable to believe that there will be an agreement on a consultative document to be published in the con-text of the G20 summit in Brisbane. So, viewed against the broad regulatory reform agenda put in place as a reac-tion to the crisis, it is fair to say that we are indeed seeing some light at the end of the tunnel. The main pieces are starting to come in place. Unfortunately, concluding the post crisis reform agenda does not mean that we can lie down, relax and declare mission accomplished. We need to look close-ly at the regulatory framework, remind ourselves of the reasons we put these measures in place, and ask whether they are delivering the right outcomes. And here I would like to focus on the interlinked issues of implementation and cali-bration. Let me start with some reflections on implementation. For some time now, the Basel Committee has engaged in the process of moni-toring and assessing how members implement what has been agreed by the Committee. The assessment work is carried out on a jurisdictional as well as on a thematic basis. In the jurisdictional assessment we look at how Committee members have im-plemented the Basel standard  determining whether or not it is a fair reflec-tion of the Basel III requirements. After an assessment has been thoroughly de-bated in the Committee, the final assessment becomes public.7 7 By end-2014 it is expected that all jurisdictions with G-SIBs will have been assessed, in addition to some others (total 17 countries). By 2016, all Basel Committee member jurisdictions are expected to have gone through the assessement of their capital framework. The assessments, and the publication of the results, have proved to be a pow-erful tool. To date, more than 200 adjustments have been made by member jurisdictions in response to findings raised by the assessment teams. In addi-tion, the process has also generated a positive feedback loop, meaning that the lessons learnt from assessments are used to improve and clarify the standards. So far, the assessments have concentrated on the capital framework, but from 2015 onwards the scope of this work will widen further to include the imple-mentation of the liquidity coverage ratio and the SIB-requirements. However, for the new, stricter requirements to bring the benefits we are aiming for, it is important that they be properly reflected, not only in national legisla-tion, but also at the level of individual banks. To use an analogy of car safety, if we are now providing banks with air bags, in the form of higher capital re-quirements, it is important that those airbags are actually activated in case of an accident. For this to happen, the sensors need to be functioning and well-calibrated. For banks, this means that risk weights need to signal appropriately the risks that individual banks actually face. This aspect is captured in the Committees thematic assessments. To put it simply, in these assessments we examined whether the banks risk-weighted assets could be trusted. The results showed that banks risk-weighted assets differ to an extent that goes well beyond what can be explained by business models and historical experiences. If we just take the banking-book results, two banks with exactly the same assets could report capital ratios that differ by as much as 4 percentage points. The potential for differences this wide, particularly as they are derived from on-ly a part of a banks business, weakens confidence in the measurement of bank capital. Of course, this was not a total surprise. It was a reflection of what I mentioned earlier: that internally-modelled risk weights lead to capital not keeping pace with asset expansion. This has undermined the confidence in banks and the credibility of the concept of banks internally-modelled risk weights. Ensuring consistency in the implementation of risk-based capital standards will therefore be a key factor in restoring confidence in banks. The Committee is thus assessing bank capital ratios with a view to ensuring that they appropriately reflect the risks that banks face. There should be truth in advertising for the regulatory ratios that banks present. To achieve this, the regulatory framework needs to deliver readily comprehensible and comparable outcomes. In my view, these assessments, both the jurisdictional and the the-matic that compares risk-weighted assets, are absolutely vital for achieving our goals. This will be an important focus for the Committee in the coming years. I would now like to take a step further and focus on the link between imple-mentation and how the system should be calibrated. Because my view is that there are a number of trade-offs at play here, which need to be taken into ac-count. For instance, if we dont implement the necessary changes and succeed in properly restoring the credibility of risk-weighted capital ratios, a more im-portant role will have to be played by other parts of the regulatory system, such as the leverage ratio. For now, our working hypothesis is a regulatory min-imum leverage ratio of 3%, but to me this is more of a place-holder. What the final outcome should be will depend on the calibration of the whole regulatory framework, in which the risk weights and leverage ratio are important pieces. An important element in this calibration will be transparency  the more trans-parent banks are with methods and models to calculate risk weights, the better it will be for the credibility of the system as such. If we widen the perspective further, I think there is also an interesting issue of calibration linked to the concept of going-concern capital requirements on the one hand, and gone-concern capital requirements on the other. When we dis-cuss appropriate levels of TLAC we should keep in mind that the less we strengthen the credibility of the system for going concern capital requirements, the higher banks gone-concern capacity to absorb losses will have to be. Concluding remarks So, to wrap up: I see no reason to pull the brake on regulatory reforms. We must not lose sight of the long-term benefits of limiting the costs to society that financial crises cause. And, although a lot has been achieved, challenges still remain  especially when it comes to implementation, implementation monitoring and calibration of the whole framework. As I said earlier, I do not know with full certainty how all the different parts of the reforms will play out together. This further under-lines the necessity to constantly monitor what is happening, very much in line with what the organisers of this conference are doing. And as financial systems have an amazing ability to reinvent themselves, regulatory reform is a never-ending task. Therefore, we need forums such as this conference to evaluate where we are, and where we should be going  hopefully, then, we wont have to make regulatory leaps quite as far as we were forced to this time.

Title: Low interest rate supports the rise in inflation
text: Ingves: Low interest rates support the rise in inflation Date: 2015-03-18 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Bank & Finance Outlook, Berns Salonger, Stockholm "Last month we made an unusual decision - to lower the repo rate to a historically low -0.10 percent and to buy government bonds for SEK 10 billion." This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves says when he participates in the Bank & Finans Outlook on Wednesday morning. "We are showing in action that we are supporting the rise in inflation. The measures we have taken - and which we can extend if necessary - are an insurance policy against the risk of lower inflation and inflation expectations". But Ingves also points to the risks of having a low interest rate situation for a long time. As house prices and household debt continue to rise, this threatens both real economic developments and financial stability. "It is urgent to slow down debt growth. There are several possible measures to address the problems that complement already introduced measures, such as lowering the interest deduction, expanding the mortgage ceiling with a so-called debt ratio cap, limiting the share of mortgages at variable interest rates, expanding housing taxation and generally working for a better functioning housing market", emphasizes Ingves. "The risks have been increasing for a long time. Now debt is showing signs of picking up faster again. It is extremely important that the discussion on how we manage the risks of household debt continues - and that other policy areas deal with them", concludes Ingves. Title: Towards a more stable banking system
text: Ingves: Towards a more stable banking system Date: 2014-10-03 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Location: SNS/SIFR Finanspanel, Stockholm Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves will participate in SNS and SIFS's finance panel on Friday morning to talk about the new Basel III regulations and about the challenges that the Basel Committee has ahead of it. The regulations aim to enable the banking system both in Sweden and in the rest of the world to be able to prevent and manage risks better, while continuing to fulfil its basic functions. As Chairman of the Basel Committee, Ingves is leading the work to design the new global regulatory framework for banks (Basel III). It has now been more than seven years since the financial crisis began. It is time to sum up what has been done and look ahead to the challenges ahead. "Going forward, the Basel Committee will place increasing emphasis on monitoring and evaluating the application of the acquis. But there is also more to be done to strengthen it," says Ingves. According to him, one of the biggest challenges ahead is to ensure a comparable and credible application of the regulatory framework worldwide; it is necessary for the rules to have the intended effect. According to Ingves, there are specific circumstances in Sweden, special structural vulnerabilities, which constitute good reasons for placing higher demands on the major Swedish banks than the minimum requirements in the Basel III regulations. This is linked to the fact that the big banks are closely linked and depend on market financing. And although the big banks today have high capital ratios, they have little equity in relation to the total assets. Title: Resilience to cyber-attacks must be further strengthened
text: Ingves: Resilience to cyberattacks needs to be further strengthened Today, the Riksbank, in collaboration with the other Nordic central banks, is organizing a conference on cybersecurity in the financial sector. This is the third in a series of annual cyber conferences organised by the Nordic central banks. Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Martin Floden will participate. Date: 2019-11-28 09:00 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Location: IVA Conference Center, Stockholm This year's conference begins with a discussion of the governance and organizational challenges posed by cyber risks. It will then discuss a number of concrete initiatives to improve cyber risk resilience in the financial sector. Stefan Ingves will give a keynote speech and representatives from both the private and public sectors will speak, including deputy central bank governors from the Nordic central banks participating in panel debates. "Resilience to cyberattacks needs to be further strengthened. However, it is not enough to strengthen the resilience of individual companies. To strengthen the resilience of the financial system as a whole, we need to work together more." This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves said during his opening speech. Title: Monetary policy with inflation target
text: Ingves: Monetary policy with inflation targeting Date 2008-02-21 Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves spoke today at LO in Stockholm. Ingves discussed inflation targeting policy on a more general level, but also presented the economic assessment in connection with the Riksbank's latest interest rate decision. "The Riksbank is pursuing what is called a flexible inflation targeting policy. We are trying, first of all, to stabilise inflation around the two per cent target, but to the extent that there is room for that, we also attach some importance to ensuring that output and employment do not fluctuate too much. More concretely, this means that we are trying to find a path for the repo rate that means that the forecast for inflation will be close to the target within a reasonable time horizon, while at the same time the real economy develops in a way that is sustainable in the long term," Ingves began. "For the policy to work well, it is crucial that confidence in it is high. One sign of this is that inflation expectations are firmly anchored around the target. If they were to rise sharply, as in the 1970s and 1980s, we might have to wage the costly battle of bringing inflation down yet again. And the fact that inflation expectations have risen recently, even in a few years' time, was one of the pieces of the puzzle behind our interest rate decision this February," Ingves continued. "At our monetary policy meeting just over a week ago, we in the Riksbank's Executive Board decided to raise the repo rate to 4.25 percent. We expect the repo rate to remain around that level over the next year. According to our forecast, this contributes to inflation falling back and ending up around the target of 2 percent over a couple of years' time, while production and employment develop in a balanced way," stefan Ingves noted. "We based our decision on a combination of many factors. Different forces counteract each other. Inflation rose rapidly in 2007 and will continue to be high over the next year. Inflation expectations have also risen and cost pressures are high. The economy in Sweden is still good and the labour market is strong. Although GDP growth is slowing and employment is growing more slowly this year, the use of the economy's resources will be higher than normal. On the other hand, we see that the risk of a weaker development in the world economy has increased. There is great uncertainty about the outlook for economic development in the US and its impact on the rest of the world, and developments in the financial markets have continued to be characterized by turmoil and turbulence," Ingves continued. "So quite a lot has happened, both things that can drive up inflation and things that can dampen it. But overall, the indicators for future inflation ahead of the decision were in line with our forecast in December. When we weighed in all the factors, we landed largely in the same view of the development of the repo rate as we did then. But it is important to remember that there is great uncertainty about the future economic and inflation outlook. It may be worth repeating that the path of interest rates is a forecast and not a promise. And future interest rate decisions will of course be affected by new information of importance for the Swedish inflation and economic outlook," Ingves continued. "The Riksbank received criticism in connection with the latest interest rate decision. Most of the criticism was that the raise we implemented surprised most observers. Of course, we need to think about this. We're always wondering if there's anything we can do better. Of course, we want our policies to be clear and predictable," Ingves concluded.

Title: Monetary policy and macroprudential policy in a globalised world
text: Ingves: Monetary policy and macroprudential policy in a globalised world Date: 2014-05-28 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Stockholm School of Economics, Stockholm The financial crisis has shown that a new way of thinking is needed in the interaction between monetary policy and the supervision and regulation of the financial markets both at home and in the outside world. We simply need to make greater joint efforts to avoid future financial imbalances. Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves pointed this out when he spoke at the School of Business, Economics and Law on Wednesday. Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves summarizes his speech The Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority has been given the main responsibility for the new policy area macroprudential policy that has emerged after the financial crisis. But since the policy areas need to interact, close cooperation between the authorities is required, Ingves said. In the Swedish debate, however, there is not much discussion about the need to coordinate macroprudential policy and monetary policy - nor about the fact that monetary policy may need to be used in certain situations to counteract financial imbalances. Here it seems rather that it is assumed from the outset that macroprudential policy and monetary policy have no significant points of contact, but can be conducted more or less independently of each other without any problems. In today's complicated world, according to Ingves, it is not possible to have such watertight bulkheads. "If monetary policy is to cope well with its tasks in the future, macroprudential policy must function well - but the reverse is also true," Ingves said. We also need to work together on concrete measures that can solve the problems we see today. "My hope is that the discussions in the newly formed Financial Stability Council will lead to the decisions that need to be made also really being made, even though it will probably be politically quite uncomfortable decisions from time to time. Household debt - the biggest domestic risk Ingves pointed to an obvious problem that we have to deal with today: the indebtedness of Swedish households. The debt ratio has roughly doubled in twenty years and this is not sustainable development. We can hardly overcome this problem without it being felt by individual households and entailing costs for the economy as a whole. Ingves showed with some very simple calculation examples that of the measures now being discussed - the countercyclical capital buffer, the mortgage cap, the interest deduction and the amortization requirement - amortization requirements have the greatest effect on households' incentives to take out loans. "The natural thing would be to set requirements for amortisation. The stock of existing home loans would then decrease. It would also give households stronger incentives to rein in borrowing. Such a requirement would be reasonable - and something that is seen elsewhere in the world as a matter of course. But Ingves stressed that other efforts are also needed to tackle household debt. We need to deal with the poorly functioning housing market and the lack of housing that has pushed up prices and thus debt. The supply of housing needs to increase. Ingves pointed out that it is important to act as soon as possible. If indebtedness and house prices continue to rise, they will gradually reach levels that pose even greater risks and an economy that becomes even more sensitive to disruptions. Ingves concluded by stating that the need for cooperation between policy areas is a given, while it is uncertain exactly what an appropriate policy mix should look like. "But we cannot delay all concrete measures while waiting for the research to give us answers. To that, the risks are too high. Title: The repo-rate path and monetary policy
text: Ingves: Interest rate path and monetary policy Date 2007-03-14 Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves spoke today at a meeting with representatives of the local business community in Kf6ping. Ingves presented the Riksbank's view of the economic situation. He also discussed the reasons for presenting the Riksbank's own assessment of how the repo rate will develop in the new monetary policy report in the future. "The Swedish economy is doing well. Inflation is low at the same time as the economy is developing strongly, both in Sweden and in the world around us. The economy is expected to grow at a good pace this year as employment rises and consumption increases rapidly. Our assessment is that growth will slow somewhat in the coming years. The international economy will then enter a calmer phase at the same time as the rapid increase in productivity will slow down," Ingves began. "Over the next six months, we estimate that inflation will temporarily fall. The reason is mainly lower energy prices. After that, we expect prices in the economy to start rising faster. One reason is the more subdued growth in productivity. Wages are also expected to increase faster as employment rises. But the upturn in inflation we see ahead of us is still relatively moderate. This is due to continued favorable supply conditions. On the one hand, productivity growth is expected to be relatively high despite slowing down, and on the other hand, the supply of labour is likely to increase more than in previous economic upturns. We also expect continued international price pressure to keep down the price increases of imported goods," Ingves continued. "In order to keep inflation close to the target over a couple of years' time and to contribute to balanced real economic development, the repo rate needs to be raised. When we met on the Executive Board on 14 February, we therefore decided to raise the repo rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.25%. As we believe that inflationary pressures will be relatively limited, we expect to have to raise interest rates only moderately going forward," Ingves said. Ingves then went on to explain why the Riksbank has now begun to publish its own assessment of the future repo rate. "We have chosen to present our own assessment of how the repo rate will develop. The explanation for that is basically simple. The most important reason is that we want to be as clear and transparent as possible about the interest rate development we consider to be the most appropriate going forward, given the information we have today. It will then be easier for, for example, households planning their personal finances to form an idea of where the interest rate is heading," Ingves noted. "But it is important to be clear that the path for the repo rate presented in the monetary policy report is a forecast and not a promise. The Riksbank cannot pledge to follow the path that has been published regardless of what happens in the economy. New information can change the financial picture. Then we need to rethink how the repo rate should be set in the future. But that is hardly a reason to refrain from stating as clearly as possible what we today believe will happen. It would be much as if SMHI would refrain from publishing five-day forecasts just because conditions may change in the meantime. I also believe that today there is a broad understanding both among the public and among market players that monetary policy must be adapted when conditions change," Ingves continued. "When we published our monetary policy report a month ago, we found that the revisions since the December monetary policy meeting overall had little impact on the inflation forecast. We therefore saw no reason why the repo rate should need to be raised faster than what was then in the cards. Some had expected slightly stronger interest rate hikes in the coming years and were therefore surprised. The fact that forecasters make different assessments, especially in the slightly longer term, is not in itself particularly remarkable - it is part of the nature of things when dealing with economic forecasts. I can only state that the Riksbank has made the best assessment we think we can make," Ingves concluded.

Title: Resolving Cross-Border Banks-Lessons from the Nordic and European Banking Crises
text: Resolving Cross-Border Banks: Lessons from the Nordic and European Banking Crises Keynote speech at the Conference on Cross-Border Banking and Regulatory Reforms Stefan Ingves, Chairman of the Basel Committee and Governor of Sveriges Riksbank Mauritius, February 2, 2017 Good morning. I am honored to deliver a key note address today at this joint IMF/BCBS conference on the topic of Making Finance Work for Africa. In the early 1990s, Sweden experienced a massive banking crisis. To make things worse, the Swedish economy was at the same time hit by a combined currency, macroeconomic and fiscal crisis. In those days, the cross-border element of the Swedish banking system was still very limited, except on the funding side, and the crisis was essentially home-made and domestic in nature. As we all know, the financial sector has gone through considerable globalization and cross- border integration since then. This is true also for the Swedish banking system. In the mid- 1990s, the remaining Swedish banks  restructured and revitalized after the crisis  began to expand their activities rather aggressively outside the Swedish borders, primarily in other Nordic and Baltic countries. When the Global Financial Crisis hit the world with full force in 2008, Swedish banks had roughly half of their combined assets abroad and nearly half of their total profits came from business outside Sweden. In little more than a decade, the Swedish banking system roughly quadrupled in size compared to the early nineties, to somewhere in the region of four times the Swedish Gross Domestic Product when the global financial crisis broke out. Of course, cross-border integration is not necessarily a bad thing. It is likely to enhance competition, and thus benefit households and enterprises with lower financing costs and a larger supply of financial services. This is something that tends to favor economic growth and well-fare in general. However, as the Swedish banks expanded their activities abroad, it became increasingly evident that this cross-border integration would also pose a number of challenges to financial stability. In particular it could significantly complicate management of future financial crises. Typically, financial crisis management requires the involvement of a number of authorities, such as central banks, supervisors, resolution agencies, deposit insurance agencies and finance ministries, depending somewhat on how financial stability work is organized and how responsibilities are distributed. In general, coordination of the actions of these authorities is challenging enough in a purely domestic crisis. In a cross-border crisis, where you essentially have to multiply these authorities by the number of countries involved, the sheer quantity of authorities makes coordination very difficult. Add to this any number of legal complications, such as confidentiality legislation that restricts information-sharing between authorities in different countries. Of course, also differences in language, culture, and, in particular, views on what or who deserves to be protected, can add further to all of these complications. However, probably the greatest complication of all, is that conflicts of national interests could lead to political bargaining games that risk hi-jacking the resolution process altogether, or could lead to destructive ring-fencing that would crush any prospect of an overall beneficial outcome. Ill come back to this later. Because of all these foreseen complications, Swedish authorities took several initiatives, from the early 2000s and onwards, to put in place arrangements, such as cross-border MoUs and various working groups, to enhance cross-border cooperation in the Nordic-Baltic region. In the fall of 2007, an extensive Nordic-Baltic crisis exercise was carried out, with participants from the central banks, supervisory authorities and finance ministries in the five Nordic countries and from the central banks in the Baltic countries, all-in-all eighteen authorities. The cooperation efforts in the Nordic-Baltic region continues to develop to this day. A new MoU between authorities in the Nordic and Baltic countries was set up in 2010, and is now being revised again. And an MoU between the Central Banks in the Nordic and Baltic countries was signed as recently as in December 2016. A special forum  the Nordic-Baltic Stability Group  was formed in 2011 to address crisis management and other financial stability concerns and includes representatives from all relevant authorities in the Nordic-Baltic Region. Under the umbrella of this group, a relatively detailed formula for sharing the financial burdens of a cross-border crisis, was developed. Some of these multilateral arrangements are now either being complemented or replaced by other arrangements as a result of the European Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive, which I will come back to later. To be perfectly honest, a lot of the efforts to foster cooperation in the Nordic-Baltic region has so far not amounted to much in terms of ex ante binding agreements. MoUs of this kind are notoriously fuzzy, and are also often easily ignored. As a consequence, no burden-sharing discussions held among the Ministries of Finance involved have so far resulted in any real ex ante commitments. Nevertheless, in my opinion, the efforts undertaken have great value in other respects. They have brought authorities in different countries together and made them more aware of the risks with cross-border banking. A shared terminology on financial stability concerns and challenges has developed, which makes it easier to talk about them. Valuable networks have been established, which has made personal contacts and communication swifter and easier. In my opinion, it was a great advantage to have had a lot of the crisis management discussions before the crisis, and we even had a chance to carry out a comprehensive crisis exercise before it erupted with full force. As I touched upon earlier, conflicts of national interests can be particularly destructive. When taxpayers in one country risk ending up bailing out the citizens of another country, or when the citizens of one country perceives that theyve been unfairly treated by others, bilateral relations can become tense. In the worst case, such things could stir up old wounds. During the global financial crisis we saw several examples of cross-border banking crises leading to some rather heated quarrels between countries. Some of you probably remember the diplomatic dispute that arose after the failure of the large Icelandic banks in October 2008, when the Icelandic deposit insurance fund was unable to make good on its guarantees to over 300 000 primarily British and Dutch depositors, who had placed their savings in IceSave, a branch of the Icelandic bank Landsbanki. When attempts were made by the British government to freeze Landsbankis assets in the UK using anti- terrorist legislation, massive demonstrations broke out in Reykjavik in protest of this. Another example from the same period is Fortis. It was a then Belgium-based financial conglomerate, which had recently become a global player after having embarked on a joint acquisition of the Dutch mega bank ABN AMRO. After running into difficulties in financing its part of the ABN AMRO deal, Fortis was brutally broken up and divided along national lines among the Benelux countries. Feelings were upset in all camps, and the Dutch-Belgian relations were frosty for quite some time, as I recall it. Of course, there have been many other instances where bilateral discussions have become heated as a result of crises involving cross-border banks. Admittedly, some difficult discussions also took place between Sweden and some of its Nordic and Baltic neighbors during the global financial crisis, regarding swap agreements and other matters. (During that period, Swedish authorities were very concerned about the Swedish banks exposures in the Baltic countries and the risk of contagion back to the Swedish banking system. Ironically, today, the authorities in the Baltic countries have expressed similar concerns about the Swedish banks domestic activities, in particular the rapid expansion of mortgage lending, and the risk of contagion back to the Baltic subsidiaries and branches.) This is where I think the IMF deserves a lot of credit. Besides being able to bring its expertise, let alone its financial muscles, to the table, the Fund often also plays an important role as a neutral third party in such sensitive bilateral talks. It will typically be easier for an impartial technocratic body like the IMF to impose conditionality on a country than it would be for an individual country without being accused of catering to national interests. In the end it is probably better that any patriotic indignation is directed towards the IMF rather than towards a neighboring country. The new resolution framework that is now being implemented on a large scale around the world  in Europe this is happening via the implementation of the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive  is based on the premise that home and host countries largely can agree ex ante on how a failing cross-border bank would be resolved. Detailed resolution plans are being developed within the context of so-called resolution colleges. In principle, the new framework is supposed to ensure that banks can be resolved in an orderly way, without jeopardizing financial stability, at the same time as shareholders and unprotected creditors  rather than the taxpayers  will shoulder the losses. The key instrument that is meant to achieve this is the bail- in tool, which lets the unprotected creditors of a near-failing bank have their claims written down and/or converted into shares, after the original shareholders have been wiped out. There is, however, still a lot of uncertainty surrounding bail-in. For example, there is still a lot of wavering regarding exactly what and whose instruments should be bailed-in. This is still a cause for some concern. The preparations for a bail-out of Monte dei Paschi and possibly other banks that are now taking place in Italy adds further to this uncertainty, in particular about the available policy choice between bail-in and the application of precautionary capital support by the state. Until the stage for bail-in has been more thoroughly prepared, the jury is still out on how it will be applied in practice, especially on a larger scale. Some of the challenges Ive discussed concerning cross-border banking can be greatly affected by changes in the way banking groups are organizing themselves. The Swedish Banking Group Nordea, which is on the Financial Stability Boards list of Global Systemically Important Banks, has recently (2 January) carried out a transformation from a subsidiary structure to a branch structure. This means that large parts of Nordeas foreign banking operations, which were previously conducted via separate foreign subsidiaries, are now instead being conducted through branches of a Swedish company. Such a change gives Swedish authorities a much more pronounced responsibility for both supervision and crisis management regarding the companys operations abroad. One positive aspect of this is that some of the coordination problems I just discussed can be reduced, as the decision power over such things becomes more concentrated and less scattered among different authorities. On the other hand, a cross-border branchification of this kind, will considerably increase the undertakings of the Home country, which in the case of Nordea happens to be the Kingdom of Sweden. Such undertakings include possible liquidity support from the Swedish Central Bank and potential public crisis management measures, such as precautionary capital injections, should such measures be deemed relevant. Notably, the Homelands Central Bank may need to provide liquidity support  not only in its domestic currency  but also in foreign currencies, something which might prove challenging in some crisis scenarios (in particular if swap markets are dysfunctional at the time). In my opinion, the branchification of a cross-border banking group should therefore be met with stricter requirements on the bank to maintain liquidity buffers in all relevant currencies. The expanded undertaking should also trigger a discussion about the relevant size and composition of the Central Banks foreign exchange reserves, and a discussion about possible swap agreements among central banks. A branchification also implies an extended responsibility for the Home countrys supervisor to include also supervision of the banks foreign activities. It is therefore important that the supervisor is granted the proper resources to fulfil this greater task. Finally, let me share with you some of the general lessons Ive learned over the years, dealing with various crises around the world. Lesson 1: A hole in the balance sheet never goes away just because you choose to ignore it. Someone always has to fill it, whether it be bailed-in creditors or someone else. Lesson 2: Restoring confidence is key. Eliminating suspicions about any remaining losses lurking under the surface is crucial in this respect. It takes a great deal of determination to provide credible valuations, and above all, transparency about what you are doing. Valuation efforts that do not seem serious or simply too optimistic are counterproductive. They send the signal that you are either in denial or trying to hide something. Markets hate this kind of uncertainty, and will only postpone the recovery. Lesson 3: Act quickly. It is typically better to just rip off the band-aid than to let problems drag on, allowing them to accumulate. Lesson 4: Functions, not stakeholders, are the important thing. Upholding critical functions is the main goal, not protecting the wealth of bankers or others. Lesson 5: If state support is still necessary in the end, make sure taxpayers get an upside. Dont just socialize the losses. In summary, Lesson 6: Go out and get the lemons, squeeze them, and start to plant new ones! Thank you!

Title: Sound government finances and low inflation  the road to success!
text: Ingves: Healthy public finances and low inflation  the road to success! Date 2006-09-27 Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves today gave a speech at the Swedish Embassy in Helsinki on the theme of Finnish and Swedish economic policy. Stefan Ingves did not touch on current monetary policy in his presentation. "In the early 1990s, both Sweden and Finland were hit by a deep economic crisis. However, the difficult situation was the starting point for successful stabilization policy regime changes that contributed to low inflation and sound government finances. These are important factors behind the favourable economic development in Sweden and Finland in recent years," Ingves began. "The Finnish and Swedish economies have many common denominators, including in terms of economic policy before the crisis years. In the post-war period up to the 1980s, monetary policy was conducted under the protection of regulated financial markets and with various variants of fixed exchange rate targets. However, the overall economic policy was not consistent with exchange rate commitments. As a result, stabilization policies in both countries came to be characterized by devaluation cycles to deal with high inflation and recurring cost crises," Ingves said. "When the financial markets were then gradually deregulated in the 1980s, the conditions for both economic policy and the private sector changed radically. High inflation rates and the design of tax rules contributed in the latter part of the 1980s to very low real interest rates after tax, which in connection with deregulation resulted in a sharp expansion of credit. The current economic boom was boosted by lending growth, which contributed to rapidly rising asset prices, investment and consumption. Monetary policy was tied to defending the exchange rate, and when fiscal policy was not tightened sufficiently, the economy overheated. High inflation and high cost pressures eroded the competitiveness and credibility of fixed exchange rates," Ingves continued. "The economy turned around the beginning of the 1990s. When monetary policy in Germany tightened after the reunification of the former East and West Germany, high real interest rates were spread within Europe via the fixed exchange rate system, the ERM. The situation became more difficult and speculation against several currencies, including the Finnish markka and the krona, contributed in the autumn of 1992 to Finland and Sweden, after protracted defence of exchange rates, allowing their currencies to float. The rising real interest rates, which were partly a result of the exchange rate defense, worsened the domestic situation. GDP fell while unemployment and budget deficits increased rapidly. Asset prices plummeted and both countries were hit by banking crises," Ingves said. "The economic crisis helped to seriously raise awareness of the need for reform. It required an economic policy capable of breaking the trend of the 1970s and 80s and compatible with the free movement of capital across borders. In both Finland and Sweden, broad support had emerged for a policy of price stability and orderly government finances as the basis for more long-term stable economic development. Against this background, stabilisation policy regime changes were enforced. Government finances were cleaned up and fiscal policy was given a clear regulatory framework, in Sweden, among other things, a new framework was introduced. expenditure ceilings and surplus targets. Central banks were given a stated mission to keep inflation low and stable and increased independence to give credibility to the policy," Ingves continued. "When it comes to monetary policy, however, we chose different paths. While Sweden decided to let the crown continue to float, the land was connected to the ERM. Finland has been part of the European Monetary Union since 1999. In this way, we were given slightly different conditions for pursuing stabilization policy. The Riksbank is adjusting its key interest rate on the basis of forecasts for Swedish inflation and economic development in general. The European Central Bank, the ECB, formulates its monetary policy with regard to developments throughout the euro area and thus does not take separate account of developments in individual Member States. In the event of country-specific economic disruptions, fiscal policy is therefore required to shoulder a heavier stabilization policy burden in Finland compared to Sweden," Ingves noted. "Despite different currency policy choices, economic development has in practice not differed much between countries. Our starting positions in the early 1990s were quite similar and we had to take much the same type of measures after the crisis. Finland and Sweden are two small, open economies and in today's globalised economy with free movement of capital, a national stabilization policy and sound public finances are required regardless of whether the economy is part of a currency union or not. I think an important lesson is that a functioning economic policy framework around the set goals is needed for the policy to succeed," Ingves continued. "In my opinion, the stabilization policy regimes that Finland and Sweden have had since the mid-1990s have largely worked well and been crucial to the countries' success. Today, we have significantly more stable economic conditions with healthy government finances, low inflation and a number of years of good growth and rapid productivity development behind us. However, unemployment remains relatively high in both Finland and Sweden, although we are far from the record levels in the early 1990s. However, the long-term solution to this problem lies largely beyond what can be affected by central banks and stabilization policy," Ingves concluded.

Den samlade ekonomiska politiken var dock inte frenlig med vxelkurstagandena. Det ledde till att stabiliseringspolitiken i de bda lnderna kom att prglas av devalveringscykler fr att hantera hg inflation och terkommande kostnadskriser, sade Ingves. Penningpolitiken var bunden till att frsvara vxelkursen och d finanspolitiken inte stramades t tillrckligt verhettades ekonomin. Nr penningpolitiken i Tyskland stramades t efter terfreningen mellan fre detta st- och Vsttyskland spreds hga realrntor inom Europa via det fasta vxelkurssystemet, ERM. Situationen frsvrades och spekulation mot flera valutor, dribland den finska marken och kronan, bidrog under hsten 1992 till att Finland och Sverige efter utdragna frsvar av vxelkurserna lt sina valutor flyta. Tillgngspriserna rasade och bda lnderna drabbades av bankkriser, sade Ingves. Den ekonomiska krisen bidrog till att p allvar skapa insikt om behovet av reformer. Det krvdes en ekonomisk politik som kunde bryta 1970- och 80-talens utveckling och som var frenlig med fria kapitalrrelser ver grnserna. Bde i Finland och Sverige hade det vuxit fram ett brett std fr en politik med prisstabilitet och ordnade statsfinanser som grund fr en mer lngsiktig stabil ekonomisk utveckling. Nr det gller valutapolitiken valde vi dock olika vgar. Medan Sverige bestmde sig fr att lta kronan fortstta flyta, anslts marken till ERM. Finland ingr sedan 1999 i den europeiska valutaunionen. Title: Hearing in the Finance Committee: The Riksbank is prepared to act
text: Ingve's hearing in the Finance Committee: The Riksbank is prepared to act Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Anna Breman will today participate in this year's first hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. There they comment on, among other things, the effects of the coronavirus on the economy. Date: 2020-03-10 09:00 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Finance Committee, Swedish Parliament The spread of the virus will inevitably have negative effects on economic activity. But how large and long-lasting the effects will be is still too early to say. "In order to avoid the destruction of viable businesses during this period, the overall economic policy may need to provide support to affected sectors as well as access to credit and liquidity. The financial sector and banks also need to be prepared to contribute in such a situation," says Stefan Ingves. The Riksbank can act in various ways to mitigate the negative effects the virus has on the economy. The high level of uncertainty can mean that liquidity does not flow to where it is most needed. There is then a risk that the financial system will lose its ability to maintain credit that companies need to be able to run their business. "Our assessment right now is that maintaining the liquidity supply is central. This may involve more generous terms for loans to banks and/or direct purchases of securities. The Riksbank's previous government bond purchases have led to plenty of liquidity in the system. In this uncertain situation, it is important that it remains so. The Executive Board's assessment is therefore that the Riksbank's balance sheet should at least not decrease in the coming year. We do not currently see a lower interest rate as the most important measure," says Ingves. Title: Hearing in the Finance Committee: A combination of measures most effective to support the economy
text: Ingve's hearing in the Finance Committee: A combination of measures most effective in supporting the economy Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Henry Ohlsson today participated in this year's second hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. There, they commented on, among other things, the measures the Riksbank has put in place to mitigate the economic consequences of the corona pandemic. Date: 2020-10-20 10:00 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Finance Committee, Swedish Parliament The economy has begun to recover from the sharp fall in the spring. "But we're far from solid ground. The recovery can be both protracted and volatile and is greatly affected by how the spread of infection develops", Stefan Ingves pointed out in his introduction to the hearing. He showed how the combination of measures that the Riksbank has put in place since the beginning of the crisis  with asset purchases and offers of liquidity  has been effective in calming financial markets and contributing to interest rates for households and companies kept low in the crisis. In this uncertain situation, it is important that this remains the case, as low interest rates create the conditions for the recovery and inflation developments. "Without the Riksbank's measures, the crisis would probably have become even worse for households and companies, not least unemployment could have been higher," Ingves said. But in order to deal with such a severe shock to the world economy, it is important to harness the power of the entire economic policy, Ingves stressed, highlighting how fiscal policy compared to monetary policy can provide more accurate support to affected sectors. Title: Hearing in the Finance Committee on monetary policy
text: Ingves: Hearing in the Finance Committee on monetary policy Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Per Jansson today visited the Riksdag's Finance Committee for the second hearing of the year on current monetary policy. Date: 2019-09-24 09:30 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Finance Committee, Swedish Parliament Stefan Ingves began the hearing by justifying the Riksbank's latest monetary policy decision, in which the repo rate was left unchanged at -0.25 percent: "With the support of the Riksbank's negative interest rate and bond purchases, we in Sweden have had good economic development and inflation in line with the target for several years. At our monetary policy meeting in September, we noted that the overall development had turned out as expected. The economy is entering a calmer phase, both in Sweden and in the rest of the world, but Swedish resource utilisation remains quite high. Therefore, we thought it appropriate to maintain the monetary policy stance in the near term and the forecast to raise interest rates from this very low level sometime towards the end of the year or early next year," Ingves explained. At the same time, he pointed out that the Riksbank sees the weaker sentiment and the low interest rate situation in the rest of the world. The Executive Board therefore concluded at the monetary policy meeting that interest rates are likely to be raised at a very slow pace going forward. "In this way, we continue to support the economy and inflation developments in Sweden," Ingves said. Title: Hearing in the Finance Committee on monetary policy 2018
text: Ingves: Hearing in the Finance Committee on monetary policy 2018 On Thursday, the entire Executive Board of the Riksbank participated in an open hearing in the Finance Committee on the report Report on Monetary Policy 2018. The report is one of the basis for the Finance Committee's annual evaluation of monetary policy. Date: 2019-05-02 10:00 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Place: First Chamber Hall, Parliament, Stockholm Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves began the hearing by summarizing the report. Robert Bergqvist and Anna Seim provided comments on the report and the design of monetary policy. First Deputy Governor Kerstin af Jochnick then commented on the discussion before the committee members asked questions. Ingves emphasized that the goal fulfillment has been good in recent years. CPIF inflation was at 2 percent in both 2017 and 2018. At the same time, the economy has been strong and the employment rate the highest in over twenty years. In 2018, however, energy prices contributed relatively much to CPIF inflation and there were question marks about the strength of inflationary pressures during the year. But the conditions were good for inflation to remain around the target and in December the Riksbank raised the repo rate for the first time since 2011, from 0.5 to -0.25 percent. For a number of years, the Riksbank has pursued a very expansionary monetary policy to secure confidence in its inflation target. The negative repo rate and purchases of Swedish government bonds have had an effect on other interest rates in the economy. This has contributed to both inflation and inflation expectations  following a negative trend up to 2014/2015  rising to 2%. The Riksbank's forecasts for 20162017 captured the development of CPIF inflation and the economy in general in a relatively good way. On the other hand, the krona has become weaker than expected and in the debate, the responsibility of monetary policy for the krona's development has come into focus. Ingves noted that it is important to clarify that the starting point for monetary policy is that Sweden has an inflation target, not an exchange rate target. Title: Hearing in the Finance Committee: Monetary policy needs to be sustainable
text: Ingve's hearing in the Finance Committee: Monetary policy needs to be sustainable The Swedish economy has recovered quickly in the pandemic, supported by extensive economic policy measures. This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves said in his introduction when he and Deputy Governor Martin Floden today participated in this year's second hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. Date: 2021-10-19 09:30 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Finance Committee, Swedish Parliament "We are now moving from a very rapid recovery to more normal growth rates," Ingves said. The rapid recovery and sharply rising energy prices have meant that inflation has risen rapidly in some parts of the world, including Sweden. But well into next year, it is expected to fall back again. "Underlying inflation is moderate, indicating CPIF inflation close to the target over time. But that assumes monetary policy remains expansionary," Ingves said. "As long as we don't see signs of sustained rising inflation rates, or inflation expectations turning upwards in a worrying way, we should tread carefully in making monetary policy less expansionary." Title: Hearing in the Finance Committee: Monetary policy supports the recovery and inflation
text: Ingve's hearing in the Finance Committee: Monetary policy supports recovery and inflation The Swedish economy has withstood the second wave of the spread of infection relatively well, supported by extensive economic policy measures. This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves said in his introduction when he and Deputy Governor Per Jansson today participated in the first hearing of the year on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. Date: 2021-03-16 10:00 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Finance Committee, Swedish Parliament At the same time, Ingves pointed out that the recovery that has now begun is twofold. Several service industries, which employ many young people and foreign-born people, are still hard hit. The uncertainty is great and the development ahead is dependent not least on how the vaccinations go. However, unlike in many other crises, GDP is expected to eventually return to pre-pandemic levels. This is partly due to the different nature of this crisis, but also to the fact that the crisis has been met with major economic policy measures. "The various measures that the Riksbank and other central banks have been able to put in place have meant that we have managed to avoid the health crisis developing into a financial crisis," Ingves pointed out. The supply of credit has worked and interest rates to households and companies have been kept low. "Without the measures, the crisis would have become even worse for households and businesses, not least unemployment would have been higher. But uncertainty remains high and expansionary monetary policy is still needed to facilitate the recovery and contribute to inflation rising towards its target," Ingves said. Title: Hearing on financial stability
text: Ingves: Hearing on financial stability Date: 2018-01-23 09:30 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Riksdagen, Andrakammarsalen "High debt makes the economy vulnerable and it is important that we slow down that development." This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves said when he visited the Riksdag's Finance Committee today for this year's hearing on financial stability and macroprudential policy. Ingves began his presentation on the current situation by pointing to household indebtedness as the main risk to financial stability. He also highlighted that financial crises are often preceded by high and rapidly rising debt. Experience shows that the downturns in the economy tend to become deeper and more protracted if they coincide with a financial crisis. Ingves highlighted the Riksbank's responsibility to have a holistic view of the functioning of the payment market, a role that the Riksbank has had for 350 years. According to Ingves, one way to meet the challenges posed by developments in the payment market, including a sharply declining demand for cash, could be for the Riksbank to issue a digital central bank money - an e-krona. Title: Challenges related to the design and implementation of macroprudential regulation
text: Ingves: Challenges in the design and implementation of macroprudential regulation Date: 2011-01-17 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Location: BOK-BIS conference, Seoul, Korea Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves gave a speech on Tuesday in Seoul Korea at a conference organized by the Bank of Korea and the Bank for International Settlements, BIS. In his speech, he underscored the need for countries to develop and establish effective macroprudential frameworks covering the entire financial system and discussed some of the key challenges for the design and implementation of this supervision. Despite the relatively strong recovery in the Swedish economy after the financial crisis, there are a number of potential vulnerabilities in the Swedish financial system. In particular, growth in house prices and household indebtedness are unsustainable in the long term. The fact that problems are under construction is even clearer from an international perspective. This applies not least to the difficulties that euro area countries with weak public finances have recently had with their issuance of government bonds. The governance structure must be effective in three overarching respects: it must ensure that the macro-prudential decision-making process (the 'macro-prudential authority'): (i) has a clear mandate, (ii) has access to the information and analytical capacity needed to design the regulation, and (iii) has sufficient tools at its disposal to fulfil its mandate. He also discussed methods for modeling how macroprudential policy and monetary policy interact, but they are still not sufficiently developed to produce any result that could have any practical application. Therefore, a number of unanswered questions/ambiguities are likely to remain when macroprudential regulation is put into effect. Fortunately, however, this is nothing new for policymakers. "In any case, this is an exciting and, I think, potentially very fruitful area of research for the future. It is also encouraging to see that eminent researchers are paying increasing attention to issues related to financial stability. I therefore have high hopes that in the future we will see mutually beneficial cooperation between academics and policymakers." Read the full speech in the pdf file.

text: Ingves: Hearing in the Finance Committee on monetary policy 2017 On Thursday, the entire Executive Board of the Riksbank will participate for the first time in an open hearing in the Finance Committee on the report Report on Monetary Policy 2017. Title: The economic situation and monetary policy
text: Jansson: The economic situation and monetary policy Date: 2014-10-06 Speaker: Deputy Governor per Jansson Location: Statistics Sweden's Business Cycle Seminar, Stockholm Deputy Governor Per Jansson will participate on Monday in Statistics Sweden's Economic Seminar "The economy and low inflation". He talks there about how it is of the highest priority to get inflation to rise. In his presentation, Jansson shows that inflation towards the end of 2013 and the beginning of 2014 was lower than both the Riksbank and other analysts expected and that the Riksbank reacted to the development by repeatedly lowering both the repo rate and the forecast for the repo rate. "It is important that everyone should be able to trust that the inflation target will fulfil its role as nominal anchor in price and wage formation," says Jansson. At the seminar, Jansson also touches on the monetary policy of recent years more generally and believes that many who have commented on monetary policy exaggerated the importance that the risks of household debt have had for interest rate setting. Monetary policy has consistently been very expansionary, which has contributed to Sweden coping with the crisis much better than many other countries. Title: Hearing on monetary policy
text: Jansson in the Finance Committee. Hearing on monetary policy Date: 2016-09-27 Speaker: Deputy Governor per Jansson Location: Skandiasalen, Swedish Parliament Monetary policy has contributed to strengthening Sweden's economy. This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Per Jansson say when they participate today in this year's second hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. Stefan Ingves begins the hearing by stating that monetary policy works well and provides support for the Swedish economy. The economy is strengthening and inflation is rising. At the same time, he points out the Swedish economy's great dependence on the world around us. The global economic recovery remains fraught with uncertainty, while monetary policy is generally very expansionary. "The low interest rate situation in the rest of the world spills over onto us and is something that Swedish monetary policy must relate to," says Ingves, mentioning in this context the importance of the exchange rate for inflation developments. As before, Ingves also highlights the problems in the Swedish housing market in his introduction. "Interest rates now need to be low to defend the inflation target. At the same time, household debt continues to increase and this is not sustainable in the long run. In this respect, we in Sweden live dangerously", says Ingves. In order for us to have stable economic development also in the longer term, measures from other policy areas are therefore needed that limit the growth in household debt, Ingves concludes. In his introduction, Per Jansson recalls the situation at the beginning of 2015. The low inflation then left a mark on inflation expectations, which fell further and further from the target. At the same time, there was a risk that the low interest rates in the rest of the world would mean that the krona would strengthen sharply, which would not only have weakened the chances of raising inflation but also weakened the competitiveness of Swedish exports. "The risks in the spring of 2015 when the ECB started its major asset purchases are underestimated by many, it was a dangerous situation," says Jansson. The Riksbank's monetary policy, with a negative repo rate and purchases of government bonds, has contributed to the situation now looking better. But the inflation picture needs to be even better for us to feel safe, he concludes.

Title: The economic situation
text: Jansson in Jonkoping: The economic situation Date: 2015-02-19 Speaker: Deputy Governor per Jansson Location: Jonkoping University On Thursday, Deputy Governor Per Jansson will visit Jonkoping. He talks about the economic situation and the latest interest rate decision, including at a breakfast arranged by the Chamber of Commerce and at Jonkoping University. Jansson also makes a company visit and participates in a lunch with representatives from the local business community. The Riksbank's Executive Board recently decided to lower the repo rate to -0.10 percent and adjust the repo rate path downwards. In addition, the Riksbank will buy government bonds for SEK 10 billion. "It has become more uncertain in the world around us and this increases the risk that inflation in Sweden will not rise fast enough. By making monetary policy more expansionary, we are supporting the rise in inflation. We are also prepared to be able to quickly do more if necessary for inflation to rise towards the target," says Jansson. In his presentation, Jansson also points out that the inflation target has contributed to significant stability in Swedish wage formation since the late 90s, in sharp contrast to the 70s and 80s when wage formation created large imbalances in the form of highly variable and averagely too high nominal wage increases. "Deviating from the inflation target in wage formation is a dangerous way to go," says Jansson. In connection with the spring and autumn monetary policy reports, the members of the Executive Board carry out visits to different locations in the country where they present the monetary policy decisions. The members then give lectures and meet with the business community, municipal representatives, media and universities in the locality in question.
