Title: Flodn: Monetary policy will bring inflation back to target
text: Floden: Monetary policy will bring inflation back to target "The Riksbank's monetary policy obviously cannot affect the high international commodity and shipping prices and it is unavoidable that near-term inflation will remain high. But our monetary policy can ensure that inflation does not remain persistently high". These were the words of Deputy Governor Martin Floden when he spoke at Dagens Industrie Risk and Return conference in Stockholm. Date: 06/04/2022 09:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Place: DI Risk and Return, Grand Hotel Stockholm Published 06/04/2022 In his speech, Floden discussed what monetary policy can achieve in this situation and described the three channels through which it can operate: the exchange rate; expectations and confidence in the inflation target; and economic activity. "To understand the appropriate timing and strength of our monetary policy response, we need to consider how robust inflation expectations and wage formation currently are and how economic activity will be affected by recent developments," Floden said. "In the coming weeks I will analyze and discuss with my colleagues the precise implications of all this for our monetary policy. There will also be new information and data releases to process in the three weeks prior to our next policy meeting. I want to emphasize that we therefore have not yet concluded what the monetary policy decision will be. It is, however, already evident that we must reassess and substantially adjust our plan for monetary policy. This means that we must raise the policy rate much earlier than we planned in February," Floden concluded.

Title: Martin Flodn: Monetary policy aimed at bringing inflation back to target
text: Martin Floden: Monetary policy aimed at bringing inflation back to target Inflation has been higher than expected over the summer. It is clear that we will need to continue to raise the policy rate in the near term in order for inflation to fall. These were the words of Deputy Governor Martin Floden, speaking at DNB in Stockholm today on the economic situation after the summer. Date: 24/08/2022 12:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Place: DNB Bank Published 24/08/2022 There is high pressure in the economy: the labour market is strong and manufacturing companies remain optimistic about the situation in the future. But the high inflation and rising interest rates are worrying Swedish households. "After a very strong year, we expect a slowdown in the economy. So far, forecasts have indicated a soft landing in the economy. However, it is difficult to assess how much the economy needs to slow down in order for the high inflation to return to target. The development of the economy may thus be weaker," said Floden. Over the summer, inflation has been quite a lot higher than the Riksbank expected in its forecasts. At the same time, the prices of several international input goods, such as commodities and petrol, have begun to fall. This is because monetary policy measures around the world have begun to restrain demand and supply problems have begun to decline. "But energy prices in Europe will entail major challenges this winter," said Floden. "Inflation is problematically high. Monetary policy is aimed at ensuring that inflation returns to the target. "In June, our assessment was that raising the policy rate more in the short term would reduce the risk of high inflation in the longer term and thereby also reduce the need for greater monetary policy tightening further ahead. Developments over the summer underline the need to continue to act decisively so that inflation returns to the target of 2 per cent. But exactly how much the policy rate needs to be raised is something we will return to on 20 September when our next monetary policy decision is published," concluded Floden.

Title: Flodn: Inflationary pressures are far too high
text: Floden: Inflationary pressures are far too high "Inflationary pressures have been subdued but are still too high/ said Martin Floden, speaking today at FinansKompetensCentrum in Gothenburg. Date: 18/10/2023 10:30 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Place: The School of Business, Economics and Law at the University of Gothenburg Published 18/10/2023 CPIF Inflation fell from 4.7 per cent in August to 4.0 per cent in September. Inflation is thus moving in the right direction, but the rapid decline is largely driven by energy prices being considerably lower than last year. When energy prices are excluded, inflation was 6.9 per cent in September. Even looking at high-frequency price movements, such as changes in the last month or in the past three months, the rate of increase for goods and services is high, observed Mr Floden. "In September, for example, the price of international travel and fruit and vegetables increased significantly faster than our forecast. Although these are product groups where price movements are often large and may be due to temporary factors, they are also product groups that have a large import element. The weak krona is not helping the fight against inflation. We have previously pointed out that the krona may have a greater impact than usual on prices at a time when inflation is high. Perhaps it is such an impact that we are beginning to see in the inflation figures for September." Martin Floden, deputy governor. "Inflation is moving in the right direction, but there is still some way to go before we can say that inflationary pressures have normalised. Given this, it is becoming increasingly clear that monetary policy needs to remain contractionary for quite some time to come."

Title: Martin Flodn visits Vsters
text: Martin Floden visits Vasteras Date: 2015-10-07 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Location: Vasteras "We see that monetary policy is having an effect as the economy strengthens and inflation is on the way up. The Riksbank's interest rate cuts are an important explanation for the swedish economy's well development. We will continue to pursue expansionary monetary policy to ensure that inflation continues to rise towards our target." This is what Deputy Governor Martin Floden said when he visited Vasteras on Wednesday. He talks about the economic situation and the latest interest rate decision, including at a seminar at SEB and a lecture at Malardalen University. Floden also points out that the inflation target is good for the Swedish economy because it guides price and wage formation and thus creates stability and predictability. He also believes that confidence in monetary policy and monetary value is hardly created by changing the target as soon as it becomes difficult to achieve it. When it comes to the risks that build up with the low interest rate situation, Floden points out that the Riksbank has for several years been calling for measures in other policy areas. These are fundamental reforms in the housing market aimed at achieving a better balance between supply and demand and mitigating the upturn in household debt through so-called macroprudential measures. Floden also points out that higher inflation is needed for interest rates to rise permanently. The link contains the pictures that Martin Floden shows at his presentation at SEB. In connection with the spring and autumn monetary policy reports, the members of the Executive Board carry out visits to different locations in the country where they present the monetary policy decisions. The members then give lectures and meet with the business community, municipal representatives, media and universities in the locality in question.

Title: Hearing on monetary policy
text: Martin Floden in the Finance Committee. Hearing on monetary policy Date: 2016-02-23 Speaker: Deputy Governor Martin Floden Location: Skandiasalen, Swedish Parliament On Tuesday, Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Martin Floden will participate in this year's first hearing on monetary policy in the Riksdag's Finance Committee. Ingves presents the background to the decision to lower the repo rate to -0.50 percent. He notes that although the Riksbank's very expansionary monetary policy has contributed to a strengthening of the economy, a fall in unemployment and a trend increase in inflation since the beginning of 2014, inflation is now expected to be lower in 2016 compared with previous forecasts. A longer period of low inflation increases the risk that confidence in the inflation target will weaken and that inflation will not rise towards the target as expected. Uncertainty about global developments in the rest of the world also remains high, with low inflation and several central banks pursuing a more expansionary monetary policy with the aim of stimulating the economy and raising inflation. "We have to choose between acting now or waiting for more information. In my opinion, it is better to be proactive because it is much more difficult to deal with increased monetary stimulus in the rest of the world afterwards". At the same time, Ingves points to the risks posed by the low interest rate environment. "Reforms are urgently needed to improve the situation in the housing market and to reduce household incentives to go into debt. Without them, there are obvious risks of very poor socio-economic development later on," Ingves warns. Floden discusses in his introduction the factors that have been decisive for his monetary policy stances over the past year or so. Inflation has long been below target, which, together with falling inflation expectations, risked damaging confidence in the inflation target. In addition, monetary policy in the rest of the world has become increasingly expansionary, and we have seen a downward trend in real interest rates in recent decades. "With lower interest rates in the rest of the world, the Swedish key interest rate must also be low; otherwise, growth and employment will be hampered and inflation will be too low," floden says. But as the Swedish economy now continues to strengthen and resource utilisation in the economy rises and will approach a strained level in the coming year, this suggests that inflation will continue to rise. This was an important reason why Floden expressed reservations about the recent decision to lower the repo rate. "I also think we are approaching the limit at which the pass-through of monetary policy weakens. Therefore, I think it is better to wait with further reductions", floden points out. Drfr tycker jag att det r bttre att avvakta med ytterligare snkningar", framhller Flodn. I lnken bredvid finns bilderna som Flodn visar i finansutskottet. Title: Modelling credit risk
text: Modelling credit risk Datum: 1999-06-10 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Backstrom Plats: Inledningsanforande pa ett seminarium arrangerat av Sveriges Riksbank och Finansinspektionen When this seminar on modelling credit risk was being planned, we wondered just how interested people would be in what might be regarded as simply a narrow niche of the financial sector. So we are glad to see so many of you here today. We are presumably not alone in seeing this topic as important. I shall be opening the seminar by explaining why I consider the modelling of credit risk to be, not a narrow concern but, on the contrary, a major component of modern financial operations. First let me take you back a number of years. In my early encounters with banking theory, one of the basic questions for meas no doubt for many of youwas what makes banks so special. A simple answer is that banks borrow short and lend long, a strategy that is founded on what banks know about their borrowers future ability to pay. The banks long-term customer relationships, involving deposits, lending and payment transactions, gave them a unique advantage in this respect. Compared with other institutions, they were in a better position to conduct lending operations. In recent years, however, there have been many developments which prompt the question whether that is still the case. Extensive deregulation has enabled banks to broaden their operations at the same time as other institutions have had opportunities of moving into traditional banking markets. Now that a Swedish banking permit is no longer tied to the criterion of need, new types of banks have been established with customer relationships that are not necessarily as clear as those of the traditional banks. These developments, together with the accelerating pace of technological innovations, have fundamentally altered the financial markets. For a number of years now, currency and interest rate contracts are being actively traded over a range of maturities and the prices are updated in real time. The market for interest-bearing securities is attracting more and more issuers. Whereas previously this was primarily a market for government borrowing, it has been opened by degrees to financial enterprises and now also to a growing extent to non-financial companies. One consequence of this is the emergence of rating companies, mainly engaged in assessing the creditworthiness of players wishing to borrow directly in the market. The credit assessments that banks used to make are now undertaken by independent raters. Another interesting point is that these ratings are paid for by the companies that apply for them. Instead of being absorbed by banks in the process of providing credit, the cost is carried directly by the borrower. The securities that are issued will be priced by the market in the light of the rating companys assessment. It is therefore no exaggeration to say that the banks have lost their earlier advantage as regards information about borrowers who are in a position to raise funds directly in the securities market. A similar conclusion applies to the market for consumer borrowing, though developments here have been somewhat different. Consumer credits and house mortgage loans have become increasingly standardised. With a large stock of customers, the provision of credit can be based on much the same lines as insurance. The calculation of default risks in bank loan portfolios has much in common with how insurance companies manage the risk of accidents and damage. Under these circumstances it is hardly surprising that credit risk assessments have become more sophisticated. The examples I mentioned make it natural to adapt the assessments so that they are appropriate for a particular category of borrower. It is then important that we and other authorities follow these developments and keep ourselves up to date. Banks and authorities have been a little hesitant about using credit risk models in certain cases because this might be seen as an excessively mechanical approach to the provision of credit and risk assessments. One of the problems discussed in connection with the reform of the capital adequacy standards is that the models are only applicable to certain categories of borrower, usually those with a credit rating. In my opinion it should not be considered a drawback that banks use certain models for one type of credit and other models for other types, for instance credit scoring for standardised consumer credits. Moreover, it is perfectly possible to combine the models with more traditional credit assessments, using unique information, in the case of loans to small and medium-sized firms. These developments in the financial sector have gone hand in hand with technical advances that permit a very high rate of innovations. One highly significant innovation in this field is credit derivatives, which make it possible to separate the provision of credit from the credit risk. A bank wishing to establish a long customer relationship can advance credit and then, by selling the associated risk to some other investor, still refrain from taking a risk it prefers to avoid. At the same time, someone with no experience of credit operations and the associated information about counterparties can still take credit risks as a means of altering the level of risk in their total portfolio. There is a similar trend in securitisation, which in very simple terms can be described as selling credit items in the form of securities. In that credits can be securitised and marketed, while exposure to credit risk can be adjusted by trading in credit derivatives, it can be said that in certain respects credit risk resembles market risk. Exposures can be altered very quickly and market prices can be used to manage the aggregate risk with the aid of models. For those of us who represent public authorities, it is then more difficult to monitor the risk positions of financial institutions by analysing their statistical reports. Even the monthly data that are presented to the authorities can be difficult to penetrate. In Sweden as well as internationally, these consequences have been recognised in the construction of the capital adequacy standards for market risks by admitting the use of Value-at-Risk models. But the approach to credit risk remains more traditional: each credit is considered separately and capital requirements are set for broad institutional categories. The accelerating pace of changes concerning credit risk makes it important to pay more attention to the management of these risks as well. Oversight and supervision of financial system stability can no longer be practised solely with analyses of a quantitative nature. That work must be augmented with more qualitative assessments of risk management in individual institutions. This has in fact been highlighted in a very satisfactory way in the recent report from the Bank Law Committee. This, then, is the background to the decision by the Riksbank and the Financial Supervisory Authority to arrange a seminar on the modelling of credit risk. It is our hope that this will generate a broader discussion in Swedens financial market concerning these models and their purely practical applications for the banks. This is, of course, an important way for us to improve our knowledge in the field but it is no less important that we thereby demonstrate the Riksbanks interest in following developments. Any shortcomings will need to be identified and overcome so that full use can be made of the positive effects. Another consequence is that in its own work on analysing systemic stability, the Riksbank will be paying increased attention to risk management in the major banks as a complement to the present analysis.

Title: Some reflections on financial crises
text: Some reflections on financial crises Date: 1998-01-14 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Place: Aktiespararnas Pejlingtraff One issue that is hotly debated among various observers is what impact the problems in Asian countries will have on developments in the rest of the world. I am thinking of the short time available here tonight touching on some aspects of the subject of financial crises that have to do with that issue. At the same time, it must be remembered that there are also other factors that affect demand and price development. The countries that have financial problems in Asia show several fundamental similarities with developments in Mexico a couple of years ago, as well as with the Swedish crisis at the beginning of 199. What they have in common is that a boom has coincided with the build-up of financial vulnerability. Rapid credit expansion, inflated asset prices and current account deficits, resulting in foreign borrowing, are some of the factors behind the problems. Sooner or later, the boom slows down and asset prices start to fall. Leveraged households and businesses start a consolidation process. A period of weak economic development is generally inevitable and the more asset prices have been driven up and lending has risen in the period before, the more difficult the subsequent adjustment process will be. An important aspect that has a major impact on the course of the economy is the impact of the crisis on confidence in the financial system and its ability to perform its functions in the national economy. I am thinking of the ability of banks to operate a well-functioning payment system and to supply the economy with credit. If these two functions are adversely affected, adjustment problems can develop into a real financial crisis with wider macroeconomic repercussions and with consequent greater spillovers to other countries. Banking is traditionally about taking deposits from the public and converting this short-term savings into lending with longer maturities to firms and households. This transformation of maturities usually contributes positively to the national economy. But borrowing short-term and lending long-term means that banks have a so-called. mismatch in its balance sheet. It is a business idea that has its risks. In addition, banks operate with a relatively large leverage effect, since the solidity of the balance sheet is usually significantly lower than in other companies. If the public experiences uncertainty about a bank's position and withdraws its money, the bank relies on being able to obtain liquidity elsewhere. Otherwise, it will be forced to suspend payments and ultimately go bankrupt. In such a situation, the bank can no longer contribute to the payment system of the economy and broker credit. If this happens in an individual bank, the national economy does not have to be negatively affected, but if it is an entire banking system, economic activity risks being seriously weakened. The Central Bank can, in extreme situations, exercise its classic "lender of last resort" function. It is about providing liquidity when the stability of the financial sys-temet is endangered. More severe repercussions on the national economy can thus be avoided and, if the fundamental problems that triggered the crisis are addressed, the situation in the banking system and in the economy will stabilise. Gradually, the crisis is moving towards its solution. However, the Central Bank normally provides only domestic currency. If a country has a deficit vis-a-vis the rest of the world and export earnings are below the cost of imports, it must borrow foreign currency to cover the difference. If this borrowing is short-term, substantial and channelled through the banking system into long-term financing projects, vulnerability increases. If the banks in the country in question have problems renewing borrowing abroad, the usual "lender of last resort" function does not exist. In such a situation, a financial crisis may arise and even coincide with a currency crisis. This is what happened in Sweden. The same thing characterises the situation in several of the Asian countries. Current account deficits have been financed by short-term borrowing and channelled through the banking system in the context of rapid credit expansion. A weaker economy, falling asset prices and increased credit losses have affected confidence in the banking system and foreign lenders have become uncertain. The result has been tendencies towards a lack of foreign liquidity in the banking system, outflows of capital and currencies have come under pressure. Sweden succeeded in building confidence in the handling of the banking problems by taking strong measures in broad political agreement and reporting the problems openly. The economy gradually stabilised, although a great deal of aftercare was required, for example in the form of a fiscal adjustment. Sweden's way of dealing with the crisis allowed the state to borrow abroad even during the most intense stage of the crisis. Therefore, Sweden never had to turn to the International Monetary Fund for help with foreign liquidity. In several of the countries in Asia, the situation has become different. The international community, headed by the Monetary Fund, has contributed foreign liquidity in various forms at the request of the country in question. The private banks have also been involved in the work, which is almost self-evident since it is the same banks that have exposures in these countries. In return, demands have been made that countries take measures in such a way that confidence can be restored. The basic problems must therefore be addressed. Liquidity support measures alone are not enough. These requirements include the orderly dismantling of insolvent banks, making the accounting of problems more transparent, reducing current account deficits, consolidating public finances so that the costs of restoring the financial sector can be covered, and targeting monetary policy so that international liquidity does not flow out of the country. One cannot expect a painless adaptation, which is free from difficult decisions. When a country gets into this kind of problem, it is inevitable that there will be consequences for growth in the short term. This can have spillover effects to other countries as well. The weakening of currencies also affects trade flows and thus economic activity in other countries. What is important, however, is that the financial crisis can be lifted and the macroeconomy stabilised. It is about increasing confidence in economic policy and in the ability of economic policy-makers to deal resolutely with the problems. Otherwise, the economic impact on the countries concerned will be greater. This is particularly the case if the payment system and credit intermediation are adversely affected. It is therefore quite clear that developments in Asia will have some effect on economic activity in the world as a whole. So far, it looks set to be slightly larger than previously assessed. However, the degree of impact will depend on how the problems are addressed. How the crisis is handled and how quickly international confidence can be restored thus determines how the problems in Asia will affect development in other parts of the world, including Sweden. The current fluctuations in asset prices, such as in the currencies of the countries concerned and in the international stock exchanges and bond markets are, by all accounts, a reflection of variations in the assessment of different probabilities of how the crises in each country will be handled. Sooner or later, the problems in Asian countries will subside. Basically, these are economies with favourable production potential. If not before, it is high time to seriously ask a number of questions. How could things go like this, not only for the Asian countries that are now in trouble, but also for those countries that were previously in a similar situation? What can be done to prevent similar problems in the future? If problems arise, how should they be dealt with in the best way? It is in itself a discussion that has already begun in various international contexts, but which must be given a comprehensive content.

Title: More expansionary monetary policy to increase inflation towards target
text: af Jochnick: More expansionary monetary policy for inflation to rise towards the target Date: 2015-02-13 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Kerstin af Jochnick Location: Morgan Stanley, London On Friday, First Deputy Governor Kerstin af Jochnick will be in London where she will, among other things, give a presentation at Morgan Stanley. af Jochnick talks about the latest interest rate decision and explains that although there are signs that underlying inflation has bottomed out, the outside world is uncertain and this increases the risk that inflation will not rise fast enough. Therefore, monetary policy needs to be expansionary. At the last monetary policy meeting, the Executive Board decided to lower the repo rate by 0.10 percentage points and adjust the path of interest rates downwards. In addition, the Riksbank will buy government bonds for SEK 10 billion. af Jochnick points out that these measures - as well as the readiness to be able to do more quickly if necessary - underline that the Riksbank safeguards the role of the inflation target as a nominal anchor for price and wage formation. In connection with the monetary policy reports, the members of the Executive Board carry out visits to various locations in Sweden and abroad to present the conclusions of the monetary policy decisions. The members then give lectures and depending on the occasion they meet financial market participants, the business community, municipal representatives, media and / or higher education institutions on the plastic in question. Title: New currency in Europe
text: New currency in Europe Date: 1998-10-20 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Stockholm Chamber of Commerce seminar There are now 73 days left until a new currency is introduced in Europe, the euro. As is well known, it is not in the whole of Europe that this happens, but in eleven countries, but for Sweden there are eleven important countries with which we have almost half of our foreign trade and with which we have extensive financial relations. This provides an important reason for us in Sweden to monitor what happens within this bloc of countries when they get a common currency. As is well known, Sweden could also have been in the same position as the eleven, if the right conditions had existed. It is not a theme for this seminar, but the consequences for Sweden of EMU are undeniably affected by the fact that the possibility for Sweden to later join the euro area is still open. As a prelude to this seminar, it may be useful to recapitulate what has happened so far to establish the euro area and what it looks like at present. When the EU Heads of State or Government decided on 1 May which countries will adopt the euro when it is created on 1 January 1999, it hardly came as a surprise. But just a few months earlier, the discussion had been in full swing as to whether all eleven countries would actually qualify. The reason for this discussion was the different backgrounds that the countries had in terms of economic policy stability and the question marks that this could raise in the future for the overall stability of the future monetary union. The discussion therefore revolved a lot around how the convergence criteria provided for by the Maastricht Treaty would be interpreted and applied by the Heads of State or Government. In retrospect, it may well be noted that the flexibility afforded by the wording of the Treaty was also used in the decision. The 60% debt ratio was set more as a long-term balance target than as an entry requirement, exchange rate stability came to be assessed in more general terms than in relation to the duration of two of the countries' participation in the exchange rate mechanism, etc. Even if the flexibility of the Treaty was used, it is nevertheless important to note that the entire EMU process has resulted in a much stronger culture of stability within the EU than has been the case in the past. The emphasis on price stability and public finances that evolve in line with the economy's resilience has gained a foothold as economic policy guiding principles and will create entirely new conditions for economic development in the EU going forward. Thus, a look back at past sins in economic policy does not necessarily give the best forecast for the future. Like every country and currency area, the euro area will, of course, also be subjected to pressures of various kinds. It remains to establish a short-term interest rate level that is the same across the area, and inflationary pressures are not equally restrained in all countries. This requires continued adjustment in view of the start of the third stage of EMU. Furthermore, the ongoing financial turmoil in the world has so far had relatively little impact on EU countries, but we have not yet seen the final bill. Depending on how the further development turns out, it cannot be ruled out that some EMU countries will suffer more than others. And, of course, the euro area must show resilience to a weaker economic situation - whether the reason comes from outside the world or through weaker internal demand - and cope with its balancing act between good employment and fiscal balance. It is reasonable to assume that Sweden would have been judged to meet the convergence criteria if we had shown the political readiness to participate in the euro area from the start. In its Convergence Report, the EC Commission found that we had met three out of four convergence criteria. On the other hand, the Commission blamed us for the fact that we had never participated in the EU's exchange rate cooperation and that we had not fully adapted the central bank legislation in time to participate in the European System of Central Banks. Without prejudging how our exchange rate stability will be assessed when Sweden is to be examined next time, it can still be concluded that the obstacles to Swedish participation in the euro area are affordable if Sweden registers as an applicant in the future. The fact remains, however, that we will not participate from the outset and that we thus have a period ahead of us in which eleven of our comrades in eu circles are moving ahead with their monetary integration, while the krona continues to be an independent currency with its own exchange rate and its own monetary policy. We have seen recently that this gives rise to some uncertainty in the foreign exchange market, despite the fact that the underlying economic fundamentals have hardly changed. The currencies in the future euro area, on the other hand, have remained very stable among themselves and have remained close to the rates announced as final lock-in rates in May. Preparations for the European Central Bank (ECB) have progressed since then. Initially, a six-member Executive Board was appointed, chaired by former EMI Director Wim Duisenberg. All the candidates for the posts of Executive Board were subjected to close scrutiny by the European Parliament, and there is no doubt that all of them meet the requirements of authority and professional experience laid down in the Treaty. Once the Executive Board was in place, the ECB could also be formally established on 1 June this year, although it will take until the end of the year before the bank assumes responsibility for monetary policy in the euro area. This train regime has come about because the COUNCIL needs to get down to business and take formally binding decisions on all the points prepared by the European Monetary Institute (EMI) during its four-year lifetime. In addition to the six members of the Executive Board, the eleven governors of the future euro area countries are taking part in this decision-making process, and the eleven national central banks concerned are preparing their integration into the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) and their roles in the division of labour that will prevail with regard to the implementation of the single monetary policy. The Riksbank is also actually part of the ESCB, but of course under different conditions than those to be included in the common policy. Our role is based on the fact that the ECB is to monitor relations between the euro area and the other EU countries. To this end, a special body, the General Council of the ECB, has been set up to examine the conditions for a later entry, just as the EMI examined this for the start of the euro area. The General Council of the ECB is thus required to assess on a regular basis the convergence paths of the Member States not participating in the euro area and ultimately to prepare for a fixing of their exchange rates as well. Particular emphasis will be placed on monitoring the formulation of monetary policy and on promoting alignment with the instruments and procedures used in the euro area. This contributes to the stability of relations during the period when the countries are outside the euro area and, of course, makes it easier for them to join later. The General Affairs Council shall also monitor the functioning of the new exchange rate mechanism ERM2 for the participating countries. Then, within the ESCB, there are certain functions which are common to all EU countries and which require close cooperation between all central banks. I am thinking primarily of the single payment system TARGET (to which I will return in a moment) but also of other essential functions and systems. For example, the ECB is responsible for collecting statistics on developments in the financial sector, and the Riksbank has to a large extent already introduced the reporting requirements for Swedish banks that will apply in the euro area. The ECB also has an important role to play in commenting on the various legislative and regulatory proposals prepared by individual countries or the Commission for financial activities. This work is likely to lead to all European central banks looking fairly similar in the long run in a technical sense. Within the ESCB, thirteen different committees have been set up to involve the national central banks in the coordinated preparation of the ECB's activities. Such committees also existed within the EMI, but some new areas of the committees' activities have been added, such as international relations, as well as information on the ECB and the decisions taken by the bank. Both of these areas illustrate the new role created by the ECB becoming a real central bank. The ECB has already taken command of most of the committees formed and has become much more proactive in the negotiation process than the EMI ever had the potential to be. At the time, the EMI prepared extensively all issues relevant to the ECB's activities but did not have a mandate to bind the ECB and therefore prepared alternative proposals for arrangements on a number of points. When these have subsequently ended up on the table of the Governing Council, it has become possible to move forward and also take decisions. The Executive Board of the ECB is responsible for the day-to-day operations of the ECB and consequently submits its own proposals for decisions by the Governing Council of the Highest Body. Decisions are usually announced in the form of press releases from the ECB and at press conferences with Mr Duisenberg. Documentation is published on the detailed content of decisions made, primarily when they concern counterparties in the financial sector. The issue of the ECB's transparency has been the subject of considerable attention, as there are not such clear rules in the Treaty on this point. In addition, there are very different traditions in eu countries about how important it is for the central bank to report its decisions and the basis for them. The discussion has, of course, primarily concerned the presentation of the monetary policy that the ECB is set to conduct; After all, this activity has not yet started, but the Bank will set the tone for its transparency already through the information provided on the decisions taken on an ongoing basis. For those interested, there is a wealth of material from the ECB, which, among other things, has recently described the instruments and procedures to be used within the framework of the monetary policy framework. Among the decisions taken so far by the Governing Council on monetary policy governance, an important position concerns the use of reserve requirements, i.e. provisions requiring banks to keep a certain part of their debt obligations in accounts in the system of central banks. The ESCB provides for a market rate and reserve requirements are designed in such a way that they can help stabilise bank demand for liquidity from central banks. Otherwise, the monetary policy steering system of the ESCB has great similarities with the one the Riksbank applies today, with regular repos being the main means of controlling liquidity in the economy so that the desired level of interest rates is established. An issue on which the Governing Council has only recently decided concerns the monetary policy strategy, i.e. how monetary policy should be designed to ensure that the objective of price stability is achieved. To begin with, the ECB has defined price stability as the increase of less than 2% per year by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP); this objective is to be achieved over the medium term and in individual years inflation rates may thus deviate slightly from there. The ECB considers that money growth plays an important role in the inflation process and will set out a specific reference value for which money supply growth can be considered consistent with the price stability objective. The actual increase will then be continuously evaluated in relation to this reference value, but without the ECB seeking to correct individual deviations. With the formation of the euro area, it will prove difficult to draw conclusions about inflationary pressures on the basis of only a few individual factors. In particular, the demand for money may be strongly influenced by the shift from national money markets to a single euro money market. A broad analysis of the inflation outlook in the euro area on the basis of a wide range of economic and financial indicators will therefore play a central role in the ECB's monetary policy strategy. All in all, there are many similarities with the strategy applied by the Riksbank. One difference, however, lies in the fact that the ECB does not intend to publish its own inflation forecast, as it is feared that it may become self-fulfilling in situations where the forecast suggests that the target will be exceeded. At the Riksbank, we have found that useful to talk about inflationary pressures in such forecasting terms, because it makes the conclusions for monetary policy clearer. We will see how the ECB will present its considerations once it gets started on conducting its monetary policy in practice. The ECB will also have direct operational responsibility for monetary policy towards the rest of the world. This will have a slightly different meaning than for most individual EU countries today, as the euro area will not have as much foreign trade in relative terms. For example, the need for foreign exchange reserves will not be as great, and it is not foreseeable that the evolution of the euro exchange rate against the dollar will have such an impact on the ECB's monetary policy. In concrete terms, monetary policy will be through the central bank cooperation established to manage the new exchange rate mechanism ERM2, which pegs the currencies of the noneuro area EU member states to the euro through a central rate with specified fluctuation bands around it. The ECB has reached agreements with the central banks of the non-member countries on how this is to be done in practice. The Riksbank has signed this agreement without the krona being included in exchange rate cooperation. Sweden's exclusion in relation to the euro area naturally means that the Riksbank will no longer participate in the further preparations for the ECB's policy activities in this area. This is a new situation, both because the Riksbank has been on board ever since Sweden's membership of the EU became clear and because we must now focus on our relationship with the ESCB in a situation outside the common monetary policy. A very tangible illustration of both these conditions is the development of the TARGET issue. Since 1995, it has been clear that all central banks in the EU would participate in the construction of the single payment system TARGET. At the time, of course, it was not known how many countries would adopt the single currency, but it was agreed that there was an intrinsic value in constructing a payment system that could increase the speed and security of payment transfers within the EU. Such a system should be based on the fact that each payment is settled in real time, i.e. without netting with payments in the opposite direction. Each central bank would set up such a gross settlement system and all the systems would be linked together to enable transfers in euro between countries. The liquidity required to make payments in this way would be provided by central banks in the form of secured credit; any net deficits made at the end of each day would be covered primarily by loans on the market or by borrowings in central banks at an interest rate above the market level. The Governing Council has now decided that central banks outside the euro area will not receive credit during the day with the other central banks. For example, the Riksbank may also not readily grant credit in euros to banks that wish to make euro payments without having their own balances on hand. Such credit may only be granted if the Riksbank has first deposited a corresponding amount with any central bank within the euro area. Moreover, this amount is capped at EUR 1 billion. In order for the Riksbank to be able to process such a payment as is to be made to a bank within the euro area, the Swedish bank must, of course, provide security to the Riksbank. But such collateral  such as Swedish government securities  must be accepted by the ECB, even though it is we and not the ECB or any other central bank that bears the credit risk. The ECB's rationale for the restrictions is that there is a risk that credit taken up in one day will not have time to be settled before the end of the day, and lending outside the euro area may thus have an undesirable impact on the Union's monetary policy. The specific collateral requirements are justified by the desire to limit the risk of obtaining collateral of insufficient value in relation to the credit agreed. The Council's decision thus means that the conditions for banks outside the euro area to use Target will be clearly worse. Either these banks run the risk that such payments take time to be made because there is no liquidity or collateral available for the purpose, or they even run the risk that the payments cannot be made at all during the intended date. However, the Swedish banks do not, of course, have to suspend all payment traffic to the euro area only as a result of the restrictions on using Target via Sweden and the Riksbank. After all, the big banks have offices in the euro area and can obtain central bank credit directly there, and they can borrow eligible collateral from other parties that do not use them at the moment. One option for banks is, of course, also to borrow euros on the market, although this will not be free. Furthermore, you can, for example, use the so-called EBA clearing, of which all four major Swedish banks will be members. It will also continue to be possible to use the traditional method of foreign payments via correspondent banking - which, however, takes a number of days to complete, whereas in TARGET it is a matter of minutes and seconds. Of course, there will be passable payment routes for us as well  but Swedish banks and Swedish companies are unfortunately forced to submit to various restrictive traffic rules on the new "highway" that is now about to be inaugurated. The end result is likely to be that banks in Sweden and the other countries outside the euro area will not use Target to the extent that would otherwise be possible. This, in turn, should make the TARGET system as a whole less attractive and competitive. Banks and other players in the euro area are also negatively affected by the fact that payments from EU countries outside the euro area are made more difficult and delayed. As a result, the idea behind TARGET is also in danger of being wasted, namely to ensure that payments within the EU are carried out quickly, safely and cheaply. It is a powerful argument in the financial integration of the EU and has little to do with the ECB's monetary policy. The risk that credits during the day do not have time to be settled can be managed through various fees and other procedures. Our views on this part are not unknown to the ECB, but it has not proved possible to avoid the divergent treatment of the Governing Council's decisions. Who knows whether the situation would have been different if the outside central banks had participated in the final decision of the Governing Council, but now we were at least deprived of the opportunity to speak on our behalf at the time of the decision. We must also look for other solutions to minimise the damage to Swedish banks that are unable to obtain the euro liquidity that mobilises the collateral needed in the euro area. Despite the somewhat gloomy outcome of the TARGET issue and our limited influence on decision-making within the ECB, it should not be forgotten that there are areas of EU cooperation in which Sweden continues to participate as a full party. The framework for what Member States can allow themselves has become clearer, for example in the Stability Pact's rules on public finances. And several mechanisms have been strengthened to increase the effectiveness of EU surveillance of member states, for example by more clearly stating their economic policy intentions. This activity is of great importance to Sweden as a small and heavily foreign-dependent economy. The successes we have had in stabilising public finances and establishing a credible inflation target have made us a respected member of the club. It also gives us the opportunity to argue with greater weight for a continued stability orientation in other countries insofar as this is threatened by shortcomings in economic policy. The Swedish preparations for the establishment of EMU in 73 days' time have shown considerable realism. A few months ago, we had a debate about the marginalisation of the krona, i.e. that the krona would be squeezed out by the euro as a transaction currency in a variety of contexts. The Riksbank never saw this as a real opportunity in a situation where our own economic policy direction was so similar to that of the euro area. We simply did not see any particularly strong incentives for widespread euro use in Sweden. Only in individual areas could the euro be expected to have a certain use, but even then it would be mostly at the expense of other foreign currencies rather than of the krona. I also believe that the demand to start using euros was overestimated in many places; one of the latest indicators is that quite a few listed companies now seem interested in starting to list their shares in euros instead of in kronor. Shortly, the government will launch an information initiative on the euro and the euro area with a special focus on households and small businesses. It is a welcome initiative, which I hope will develop into a greater interest among the public in order to lead, in due course and in democratically orderly fashion, to us feeling mature enough to sort out our future approach to EMU. Advocacy must be based on facts and factual analysis of the consequences. Whatever path Sweden takes on this issue, we can never shield ourselves from the uncertainty that lies in the fact that the future is unknown. However, the uncertainty about Sweden's future relationship with EMU does not make matters any easier. This is especially true for those in the private sector who have to take a stand on the commercial importance of the euro, notwithstanding the political turmoil on this issue.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Ny valuta i Europa Datum: 1998-10-20 Talare: Vice riksbankschef Stefan Ingves Plats: Stockholms handelskammares seminarium Nu r det 73 dagar kvar tills en ny valuta infrs i Europa, euron. Som bekant r det inte i hela Europa som det sker utan i elva lnder, men fr svenskt vidkommande r det elva viktiga lnder som vi har nrmare hlften av vr utrikeshandel med och som vi har omfattande finansiella relationer till. Det ger ett viktigt skl fr oss i Sverige att bevaka vad som sker inom detta block av lnder nr de fr en gemensam valuta. Som bekant hade Sverige ocks kunnat befinna sig i samma lge som de elva, om de rtta frutsttningarna hade frelegat. Det r inte ett tema fr det hr seminariet, men konsekvenserna fr Sverige av EMU pverkas onekligen av att mjligheten fr Sverige att senare ansluta sig till euro-omrdet fortfarande str ppen. Som inledning p detta seminarium kan det vara lmpligt att rekapitulera vad som skett hittills fr att upprtta euro-omrdet och hur det ser ut i nulget. Nr EU:s statsoch regeringschefer den 1 maj beslutade vilka lnder som skall infra euron nr den skapas den 1 januari 1999, kom det knappast som en verraskning. Men bara ngra mnader tidigare hade diskussionen varit i full gng om alla de elva lnderna verkligen skulle kvalificera sig. Sklet till den diskussionen var den olika bakgrund som lnderna hade nr det gller ekonomisk-politisk stabilitet och de frgetecken som detta kunde ge upphov till framver fr den vergripande stabiliteten i den kommande valutaunionen. Diskussionen cirklade drfr mycket kring hur de konvergenskrav som Maastricht-frdraget freskriver skulle komma att tolkas och tillmpas av stats- och regeringscheferna. I efterhand kan man vl konstatera att den flexibilitet som formuleringarna i frdraget ger mjlighet till ocks kom att utnyttjas vid beslutet. 60% skuldkvot sattes mera upp som ett lngsiktigt balansml n som intrdeskrav, vxelkursstabiliteten kom att bedmas i mera allmnna termer n i frhllande till hur lnge tv av lnderna deltagit i vxelkursmekanismen osv. ven om man gjorde bruk av flexibiliteten i frdraget, r det dock viktigt att konstatera att hela EMU-processen resulterat i en betydligt starkare stabilitetskultur inom EU n vad som tidigare varit fallet. Betoningen av prisstabilitet och offentliga finanser som utvecklas i takt med vad ekonomin tl har vunnit fotfste som ekonomisk-politiska rttesnren och kommer att skapa helt nya frutsttningar fr den ekonomiska utvecklingen i EU framver. En tillbakablick p gngna frsyndelser i den ekonomiska politiken ger allts inte ndvndigtvis den bsta prognosen fr framtiden. Som varje land och valutaomrde kommer naturligtvis ven euro-omrdet att utsttas fr pfrestningar av olika slag. Det terstr att etablera en kortfristig rnteniv som r likadan ver hela omrdet, och inflationstrycket r inte lika tillbakahllet i alla lnder. Detta stller krav p fortsatt anpassning infr starten av den tredje etappen av EMU. Vidare har den pgende finansiella oron i vrlden hittills haft frhllandevis sm effekter p EU-lnderna, men vi har nnu inte sett slutnotan. Beroende p hur den fortsatta utvecklingen blir kan det inte uteslutas att vissa EMU-lnder kommer att drabbas mer n andra. Och sjlvfallet mste euroomrdet visa motstndskraft mot ett smre konjunkturlge - oavsett om orsaken kommer utifrn vrlden eller genom en svagare intern efterfrgan - och klara sin balansakt mellan god sysselsttning och statsfinansiell balans. Det r rimligt att anta att Sverige hade bedmts klara konvergenskraven om vi hade visat den politiska beredskapen att delta i euro-omrdet frn starten. EGkommissionen konstaterade i sin konvergensrapport att vi uppfyllt tre av fyra konvergenskrav. Dremot lade Kommissionen oss till last att vi aldrig deltagit i EU:s vxelkurssamarbete och att vi inte i tid anpassat riksbankslagstiftningen fullt ut till ett deltagande i det europeiska centralbankssystemet. Utan att fregripa hur vr vxelkursstabilitet kommer att bedmas nr Sverige skall granskas nsta gng kan man nd dra slutsatsen att hindren fr ett svenskt deltagande i euro-omrdet r verkomliga om Sverige anmler sig som skande framver. Faktum kvarstr nd att vi inte kommer att delta frn starten och att vi allts har en period framfr oss d elva av vra kamrater i EU-kretsen gr vidare med sin monetra integration, medan kronan fortstter att vara en sjlvstndig valuta med egen vxelkurs och egen penningpolitik. Vi har kunnat se den senaste tiden att detta ger upphov till en viss oskerhet p valutamarknaden, trots att underliggande ekonomiska grundfrutsttningar knappast har ndrats. Valutorna inom det blivande euro-omrdet har dremot hllit sig mycket stabila inbrdes och legat nra de kurser som frannonserades som slutliga lsningskurser i maj. Frberedelserna fr Europeiska centralbanken (ECB) har gtt vidare sedan dess. Till att brja med utsgs en direktion av sex ledamter med den tidigare EMI-chefen Wim Duisenberg som ordfrande. Alla kandidaterna till direktionsposterna utsattes fr en ingende granskning av Europaparlamentet, och det rder ingen tvekan om att samtliga uppfyller de krav p auktoritet och yrkeserfarenhet som frdraget stller upp. Nr vl direktionen kom p plats kunde ECB ocks upprttas formellt den 1 juni i r, ven om det allts drjer till rsskiftet innan banken vertar ansvaret fr penningpolitiken i euro-omrdet. Denna tgordning har kommit till drfr att ECBrdet behver komma igng och fatta formellt bindande beslut p alla de punkter som Europeiska monetra institutet (EMI) frberedde under sin fyraochetthalvtriga livstid. Frutom de sex direktionsledamterna deltar de elva centralbankscheferna frn de blivande euro-lnderna i detta beslutsfattande, och de elva berrda nationella centralbankerna frbereder sin integration i Europeiska centralbankssystemet (ECBS) och sina roller i den arbetsfrdelning som kommer att rda betrffande genomfrandet av den gemensamma penningpolitiken. ven Riksbanken r faktiskt en del av ECBS, men naturligtvis under andra villkor n fr dem som skall inordnas i den gemensamma politiken. Vr roll grundas p det frhllandet att ECB skall vervaka relationerna mellan euro-omrdet och de vriga EU-lnderna. Drfr har det inrttats ett srskilt organ, ECB:s allmnna rd, med uppgift att granska frutsttningarna fr ett senare intrde, p samma stt som EMI granskade detta infr starten av euro-omrdet. ECB:s allmnna rd skall allts terkommande bedma konvergensutvecklingen i de medlemslnder som inte deltar i euro-omrdet och ytterst frbereda en lsning ven av deras vxelkurser. En srskild tonvikt skall lggas p att flja utformningen av penningpolitiken och frmja en anpassning till de instrument och frfaranden som anvnds inom euro-omrdet. Detta bidrar till en stabilitet i relationerna under den tid som lnderna str utanfr euro-omrdet och underlttar naturligtvis fr dem att intrda senare. Allmnna rdet skall ocks vervaka hur den nya vxelkursmekanismen ERM2 fungerar fr de lnder som deltar dr. Sedan finns det inom ECBS vissa funktioner som r gemensamma fr alla EU-lnder och som franleder ett nra samarbete mellan alla centralbanker. Jag tnker i frsta hand p det gemensamma betalningssystemet Target (som jag strax skall terkomma till) men ven p andra vsentliga funktioner och system. ECB r t.ex. ansvarig fr insamlandet av statistik om utvecklingen i den finansiella sektorn, och Riksbanken har i stor utstrckning redan infrt de rapporteringskrav fr svenska bankerna som kommer att glla inom euro-omrdet. ECB har ocks en viktig roll i att kommentera de olika frslag till lagstiftning och andra regelverk som enskilda lnder eller Kommissionen utarbetar fr finansiell verksamhet. Detta arbete leder sannolikt till att alla europeiska centralbanker p sikt kommer att se ganska likadana ut i teknisk mening. Inom ECBS har det inrttats tretton olika kommitter fr att involvera de nationella centralbankerna i en samordnad beredning av ECB:s verksamhet. Sdana kommitter fanns ven inom EMI, men det har tillkommit ngra nya omrden fr kommitternas verksamhet, t.ex. internationella relationer samt information om ECB och de beslut som banken fattar. Bda dessa omrden illustrerar den nya roll som tillkommit i och med att ECB blir en riktig centralbank. ECB har redan tagit kommandot i flertalet av de bildade kommitterna och blivit mycket mer drivande i frhandlingsprocessen n vad EMI ngonsin hade frutsttningar att vara. EMI frberedde p sin tid utfrligt alla frgor av relevans fr ECB:s verksamhet men hade inte mandat att binda ECB utan utarbetade drfr alternativa frslag till upplgg p ett antal punkter. Nr dessa sedermera hamnat p ECB-rdets bord, har det blivit mjligt att g vidare och ocks fatta beslut. ECB:s direktion har ansvar fr bankens lpande verksamhet och lgger fljdriktigt fram egna frslag till beslut frn det hgsta organet ECB-rdet. Besluten tillknnages vanligen i form av pressmeddelanden frn ECB och vid presskonferenser med Duisenberg. Dokumentation publiceras om detaljinnehllet i fattade beslut, i frsta hand nr de berr motparter i den finansiella sektorn. Frgan om ECB:s ppenhet har varit freml fr betydande uppmrksamhet, eftersom det inte finns s tydliga regler i frdraget p denna punkt. Dessutom finns det mycket olika traditioner i EU-lnderna om hur viktigt det r att centralbanken redovisar sina beslut och grunderna fr dem. Diskussionen har naturligtvis i frsta hand gllt redovisningen av den penningpolitik som ECB r satt att fra; denna verksamhet har ju nnu inte kommit igng, men banken kommer att stta tonen fr sin ppenhet redan genom den information som ges om de beslut som fattas fortlpande. Fr den intresserade finns det ett rikhaltigt material frn ECB, som bl.a. nyligen beskrivit vilka instrument och frfaranden som skall anvndas inom ramen fr det penningpolitiska styrsystemet. Bland de beslut som ECB-rdet hittills tagit om den penningpolitiska styrningen gller ett viktigt stllningstagande anvndningen av kassakrav, dvs. freskrifter om att banker mste hlla en viss del av sina skuldtaganden p konto i centralbankssystemet. I ECBS skall dessa medel ges en marknadsmssig rnta och kassakraven r konstruerade s, att de kan bidra till att stabilisera bankernas efterfrgan p likviditet frn centralbankerna. I vrigt har det penningpolitiska styrsystemet fr ECBS stora likheter med det som Riksbanken tillmpar idag, med regelbundna repor som det frmsta medlet att styra likviditeten i ekonomin s att den nskade rntenivn etableras. En frga som ECB-rdet frst nyligen fattat beslut om rr den penningpolitiska strategin, dvs. hur penningpolitiken skall utformas fr att se till att mlet om prisstabilitet uppns. Till att brja med har ECB definierat prisstabilitet som att det harmoniserade konsumentprisindexet inom EU (HIKP) kar med mindre n 2 procent per r; detta ml skall uppns p medellng sikt och enstaka r kan inflationstakten allts avvika ngot drifrn. ECB anser att penningmngdens tillvxt spelar en viktig roll fr inflationsprocessen och kommer att ange ett srskilt s.k. referensvrde fr vilken tillvxt i penningmngden som kan anses frenlig med prisstabilitetsmlet. Den faktiska kningen kommer sedan att lpande utvrderas i frhllande till detta referensvrde men utan att ECB efterstrvar att korrigera enskilda avvikelser. I och med att euro-omrdet bildas kommer det att visa sig svrt att dra slutsatser om inflationstrycket p basis av endast ett ftal enskilda faktorer. Srskilt efterfrgan p pengar kan komma att pverkas starkt av vergngen frn nationella penningmarknader till en enhetlig euro-penningmarknad. En bred analys av inflationsutsikterna i euro-omrdet utifrn en mngd ekonomiska och finansiella indikatorer kommer drfr att spela en central roll fr ECB:s penningpolitiska strategi. Sammantaget finns det allts mnga likheter med den strategi som Riksbanken tillmpar. En skillnad ligger dock i att ECB inte avser att publicera en egen inflationsprognos, drfr att man befarar att den kan bli sjlvuppfyllande i lgen d prognosen antyder att mlet kommer att verskridas. P Riksbanken har vi funnit det anvndbart att tala om inflationstrycket i sdana prognostermer, drfr att det gr slutsatserna fr penningpolitiken tydligare. Vi fr se hur ECB kommer att presentera sina vervganden nr banken vl kommer igng med att bedriva sin penningpolitik i praktiken. ECB fr vidare ett direkt operativt ansvar fr valutapolitiken mot omvrlden. Detta kommer att f en ngot annan innebrd n fr de flesta enskilda EU-lnderna idag, eftersom euro-omrdet inte kommer att ha lika omfattande utrikeshandel relativt sett. Behovet av valutareserver kommer t.ex. inte att bli lika stort, och man kan inte frutse att euro-kursens utveckling mot dollarn kommer att f s stor betydelse fr ECB:s penningpolitik. Mest konkret kommer valutapolitiken att bli genom det centralbankssamarbete som etableras fr att frvalta den nya vxelkursmekanismen ERM2, som knyter valutorna i EU-lnderna utanfr euro-omrdet till euron genom en centralkurs med preciserade fluktuationsband runt omkring. ECB har trffat avtal med centralbankerna i de utanfrstende lnderna om hur detta i praktiken skall sktas. Riksbanken har undertecknat detta avtal utan att kronan fr den skull kommer att ing i vxelkurssamarbetet. Sveriges utanfrskap i frhllande till euro-omrdet innebr naturligtvis att Riksbanken inte lngre deltar i de fortsatta frberedelserna nr det gller ECB:s politikverksamhet i detta omrde. Detta r en ny situation, bde drfr att Riksbanken varit med p tget nda sedan Sveriges medlemskap i EU blev klart och drfr att vi nu mste inrikta oss p vr relation till ECBS i ett lge utanfr den gemensamma penningpolitiken. En mycket ptaglig illustration till bda dessa frhllanden r utvecklingen av Target-frgan. Alltsedan 1995 har det sttt klart att alla centralbanker i EU skulle delta i uppbyggnaden av det gemensamma betalningssystemet Target. D visste man frsts inte hur mnga lnder som skulle komma att infra den gemensamma valutan, men man var verens om att det lg ett egenvrde i att konstruera ett betalningssystem som kunde ka snabbheten och skerheten i betalningsfrmedlingen inom EU. Ett sdant system borde bygga p att varje betalning avvecklas i realtid, dvs. utan nettning med betalningar i motsatt riktning. Varje centralbank skulle bygga upp ett sdant bruttoavvecklingssystem och alla systemen skulle lnkas samman fr att mjliggra verfringar i euro mellan lnderna. Den likviditet som krvs fr att genomfra betalningar p detta stt skulle tillfras av centralbankerna i form av kredit mot skerhet; eventuella nettounderskott nr alla betalningar genomfrts vid slutet av varje dag skulle i frsta hand tckas med ln p marknaden eller genom upplning i centralbankerna till en rnta ver marknadsnivn. ECB-rdet har nu beslutat att centralbankerna utanfr euro-omrdet inte skall f kredit under dagen hos vriga centralbanker. T.ex. Riksbanken fr inte heller utan vidare ge kredit i euro till banker som nskar genomfra euro-betalningar utan att ha egna tillgodohavanden till hands. Sdan kredit fr bara ges om Riksbanken frst deponerat ett motsvarande belopp i ngon centralbank inom euro-omrdet. Detta belopp r dessutom maximerat till 1 miljard euro. Fr att Riksbanken skall kunna frmedla en sdan betalning som skall till en bank inom euro-omrdet, mste den svenska banken givetvis stlla skerhet till Riksbanken. Men sdana skerheter  exempelvis svenska statspapper - mste vara accepterade av ECB, trots att det r vi och inte ECB eller ngon annan centralbank som br kreditrisken. ECB:s motiv fr begrnsningarna r att det finns en risk fr att krediter som tas upp under en dag inte hinner avvecklas fre dagens slut och kreditgivning utanfr euroomrdet kan drmed pverka unionens penningpolitik p ett onskat stt. De srskilda kraven p skerheterna motiveras med att man vill begrnsa risken att f skerheter med otillrckligt vrde i frhllande till den kredit som avtalats. ECBrdets beslut innebr allts att det blir klart smre villkor fr banker utanfr euroomrdet att utnyttja Target. Antingen riskerar dessa banker att sdana betalningar tar tid att genomfra drfr att det inte finns likviditet eller skerheter tillgngliga fr ndamlet, eller ocks riskerar de rent av att betalningarna ver huvud taget inte kan genomfras under den dag som var avsett. De svenska bankerna behver dock naturligtvis inte instlla all betalningstrafik till euro-omrdet bara till fljd av begrnsningarna nr det gller att anvnda Target via Sverige och Riksbanken. Storbankerna har ju verksamhetsstllen inne i euroomrdet och kan skaffa sig centralbankskredit direkt dr, och de kan lna godtagbara skerheter frn andra parter som inte har anvndning fr dem just fr stunden. Ett alternativ fr bankerna r naturligtvis ocks att lna upp euro p marknaden, ven om detta inte kommer att vara gratis. Vidare kan man exempelvis utnyttja den s.k. EBA-clearingen, dr alla de fyra svenska storbankerna kommer att vara medlemmar. ven i fortsttningen kommer det ocks att vara mjligt att anvnda den traditionella metoden fr utlandsbetalningar via korrespondentbank - som dock tar ett antal dagar att genomfra, medan det i Target handlar om minuter och sekunder. Visst kommer det att finnas framkomliga betalningsvgar ven fr oss  men svenska banker och svenska fretag tvingas tyvrr underkasta sig olika begrnsande trafikregler p den nya motorvg som nu snart ska invigas. Slutresultatet blir troligen att banker i Sverige och de andra lnderna utanfr euroomrdet inte kommer att utnyttja Target i den utstrckning som annars vore mjlig. Detta torde i sin tur innebra att Target-systemet som helhet blir mindre attraktivt och konkurrenskraftigt. ven banker och andra aktrer inom euro-omrdet pverkas negativt av att betalningar frn EU-lnder utanfr euro-omrdet frsvras och frdrjs. Drmed riskerar ocks tanken bakom Target att frspillas, nmligen att se till att betalningar inom EU utfrs snabbt, skert och billigt. Det r ett kraftfullt argument i den finansiella integrationen i EU och har inte s mycket med ECB:s penningpolitik att gra. Risken fr att krediter under dagen inte hinner avvecklas kan hanteras genom olika avgifter och andra frfaranden. Vra synpunkter i denna del r inte oknda fr ECB, men det har inte visat sig mjligt att undvika den olikartade behandling som ECB-rdets beslut innebr. Vem vet om situationen hade varit annorlunda om de utanfrstende centralbankerna hade deltagit i det slutliga beslutet i ECB-rdet, men nu var vi i vart fall bervade mjligheten att fra vr talan vid beslutstillfllet. Vi fr ocks ska andra lsningar fr att minimera skadeverkningarna fr de svenska banker som inte kan skaffa den euro-likviditet som mobiliserar de skerheter som behvs inom euro-omrdet. Trots det lite dystra utfallet av Target-frgan och vrt begrnsade inflytande p beslutsfattandet inom ECB skall man inte glmma bort att det finns omrden inom EU-samarbetet dr Sverige fortstter att delta som en fullvrdig part. I takt med den kade tonvikten p konvergensutvecklingen inom EU och den kade interdependensen mellan lnderna som en fljd av den fortgende ekonomiska integrationen har behovet av ekonomisk-politisk samordning ocks hamnat mer i blickpunkten. Ramarna fr vad medlemslnderna kan tillta sig har blivit tydligare, t.ex. i stabilitetspaktens regler fr de offentliga finanserna. Och flera mekanismer har frstrkts fr att ka effektiviteten i EU:s vervakning av medlemslnderna, t.ex. genom en klarare redovisning av lndernas ekonomisk-politiska intentioner. Denna verksamhet r av stor vikt fr Sverige som liten och starkt utlandsberoende ekonomi. De framgngar som vi haft nr det gller stabiliseringen av de offentliga finanserna och etableringen av ett trovrdigt inflationsml har gjort oss till en respekterad medlem av klubben. Det ger oss ocks mjligheter att med strre tyngd argumentera fr en fortsatt stabilitetsinriktning i andra lnder i den mn denna hotas av brister i den ekonomiska politiken. De svenska frberedelserna fr att EMU upprttas om 73 dagar har givit prov p en betydande realism. Vi hade fr ngra mnader sedan en debatt om kronans marginalisering, dvs. att kronan skulle komma att trngas ut av euron som transaktionsvaluta i en mngd olika sammanhang. Riksbanken sg aldrig detta som en reell mjlighet i ett lge dr vr egen ekonomisk-politiska inriktning var s snarlik euro-omrdets. Vi sg helt enkelt inga srskilt starka incitament fr en utbredd euroanvndning i Sverige. Bara p enskilda omrden kunde man frvnta sig att euron skulle f en viss anvndning, men vens skulle det mest ske p bekostnad av andra utlndska valutor snarare n av kronan. Jag tror ocks att efterfrgan p att brja anvnda euro verskattades p mnga hll; en av de senaste indikatorerna r att ganska f brsbolag nu synes intresserade av att brja lta notera sina aktier i euro i stllet fr i kronor. Inom kort initierar regeringen en informationssatsning om euron och euro-omrdet med srskild inriktning p hushll och smfretag. Det r ett vlkommet initiativ, som jag hoppas skall utvecklas till ett strre intresse hos allmnheten fr att i sinom tid och i demokratiskt ordnade former leda fram till att vi knner oss mogna att reda ut vrt kommande frhllningsstt till EMU. Opinionsbildningen mste bygga p fakta och saklig analys av konsekvenserna. Vilken vg Sverige n tar i denna frga kan vi aldrig avskrma oss frn den oskerhet som ligger i att framtiden r oknd. Oskerheten om Sveriges framtida relation till EMU gr dock inte saken lttare. Det gller srskilt fr dem i den privata sektorn som mste ta stllning till eurons kommersiella betydelse, oaktat de politiska turerna i denna frga. Title: American mortgage crisis and financial turbulence
text: Nyberg: American mortgage crisis and financial turbulence Date 2008-02-04 Lars Nyberg gives his picture of recent developments in the financial markets. Nyberg also gives his view on the monetary policy decision-making situation when he speaks today before the Board of Directors in Stockholm. "Over the past six months, the development has been turbulent in the international financial markets. The problems started in the rather limited US market for borrowers with poorer credit ratings, the so-called subprime market. A large part of the mortgages in this market have been repackaged in various so-called structured products and sold on to investors around the world. When borrowers had trouble paying their credits, it became difficult to value products with these loans as the underlying asset. At the same time, there was great uncertainty about which players were sitting on the actual risks." So says Deputy Governor Lars Nyberg, who today speaks before the Board of Directors in Stockholm. "So what we're experiencing now extends far beyond the crisis in the U.S. mortgage market. It has taken a number of different forms. Investors are now demanding substantially higher compensation for risk. It has become both more expensive and more difficult to borrow in the market, especially for financial companies. During the autumn, there were also major disturbances in the interbank market. Several central banks have chosen to intervene to provide that market with liquidity injections. The short-term financing market in particular seems to have recovered somewhat since December, but far from completely." "Another effect is that a number of large and well-established banks have been forced to write down the value of subprime-related assets that they directly or indirectly own. The write-downs are so far up to over 130 billion. This has led to several large financial groups needing new capital. In several cases, this has been possible through the addition of public funds and other investors from Asia and the Middle East." "While pressure has eased somewhat in some submarkets, there has been renewed international concern. This concern has largely been about the large insurance companies, known as monolines, that specialize in insuring bonds. Those who buy the companies' insurance are, for example, municipalities and states that have a poorer credit rating. With the insurance, their bond loan gets the highest credit rating and can be sold at better interest rates. However, the recent unrest has now caused problems for monolines as well as they have exposures to the subprime sector in various ways. Some of the companies have already had their credit ratings lowered, and there are risks of further cuts." "When monolines get worse credit ratings, this also affects the bonds they insured. They also have their credit ratings lowered. However, many institutions that buy such bonds have investment rules that only allow investments in papers with the highest credit rating. They are then forced to sell their holdings. Because monolines insuring bonds for at least USD 2000 billion, this can have significant effects on the market. It could also put additional strain on bank liquidity." "At the same time, the U.S. economic downturn has taken hold, partly as a result of falling real estate prices. The concern that this will exacerbate the financial crisis is obvious. And of course, the financial crisis could also amplify the economic downturn." "In Sweden, we have not been directly affected by the crisis because the Swedish banks have not been significantly involved in subprime-related products. But their financing costs have increased, hitting customers in the form of higher interest rates. In this way, the turmoil in the financial markets has already led to a monetary policy tightening." "We are receiving some criticism for not commenting on economic developments and how we view the monetary policy situation at this time. I understand that criticism. At the same time, the situation is the most difficult to assess during my time at the Riksbank. For this reason, the monetary policy trade-offs we have to make are unusually complicated." "On the one hand, there is a risk that the crisis will be both longer and deeper than we previously thought. The sharp cuts in the key interest rate made by the US Federal Reserve, and the statements that have followed them, undoubtedly indicate a strong concern on their part. How a deepening crisis affects the world in general and Sweden in particular is difficult to determine. But the turmoil in the markets is significant here too, which is reflected in monetary policy expectations. Hopefully, the markets are too pessimistic in assessing economic developments. But it is still too early to say, as I see it." "On the other hand, the economy in Sweden is still good, resource utilisation in some places strained and inflation over the next year is well above the inflation target of two percent. In addition, inflation expectations have risen, both in the short and slightly longer term. And Swedish monetary policy can only be conducted on the basis of Swedish conditions. This suggests that the Riksbank needs to raise its key interest rate at about the pace discussed at the end of last year." "The Swedish economic trend thus suggests that interest rates should be raised, the international concern that it is best to wait. In a week and a half we will have a monetary policy meeting. There are six of us on the Executive Board and everyone is now thinking best, based on their experience and analysis, about how that balance should be struck."
