Nyberg ger ocks sin syn p det penningpolitiska beslutslget nr han idag talar infr Styrelsekollegiet i Stockholm. Det senaste halvret har utvecklingen varit turbulent p de internationella finansiella marknaderna. Problemen startade p den ganska begrnsade amerikanska marknaden fr lntagare med smre kreditvrdighet, den s kallade subprimemarknaden. En stor del av bolnen p denna marknad har paketerats om i olika s kallade strukturerade produkter och slts vidare till investerare vrlden ver. Nr lntagarna fick problem med att betala sina krediter blev det svrt att vrdera produkter med dessa ln som underliggande tillgng. Samtidigt uppstod stor oskerhet om vilka aktrer som satt p de faktiska riskerna. Det sger vice riksbankschef Lars Nyberg, som idag talar infr Styrelsekollegiet i Stockholm. Det vi upplever nu strcker sig allts lngt utanfr krisen p den amerikanska bolnemarknaden. Det har tagit sig en rad olika uttryck. Investerarna krver nu vsentligt hgre kompensation fr risk. Det har blivit bde dyrare och svrare att lna p marknaden, srskilt fr finansiella fretag. Under hsten uppkom ocks kraftiga strningar p interbankmarknaden. Flera centralbanker har valt att ingripa fr att frse den marknaden med tillskott av likviditet. Just marknaden fr kort finansiering tycks ha terhmtat sig ngot sedan december, men lngt ifrn helt. En annan effekt r att en rad stora och vl etablerade banker har tvingats skriva ned vrdet p subprime-relaterade tillgngar som de direkt eller indirekt ger. Nedskrivningarna r s hr lngt uppe i ver 130 miljarder dollar. Det har lett till att flera stora finanskoncerner behver nytt kapital. I flera fall har detta kunnat ske genom tillskott av offentliga fonder och andra investerare frn Asien och Mellanstern. Samtidigt som trycket har lttat ngot p vissa delmarknader har det uppsttt en frnyad internationell oro. Denna oro har i mngt och mycket handlat om de stora frskringsbolag, s kallade monolines, som r specialiserade p att frskra obligationsln. De som kper bolagens frskringar r exempelvis kommuner och delstater som har en smre kreditvrdighet. Med frskringen fr deras obligationsln hgsta kreditbetyg och kan sljas till bttre rntor. Men den senaste tidens oro har nu orsakat problem ocks fr monolines eftersom de p olika stt har exponeringar mot subprime-sektorn. Ngra av bolagen har redan ftt sina kreditbetyg snkta, och det finns risker fr ytterligare snkningar. Nr monolines fr smre kreditbetyg drabbar detta ocks de obligationer de frskrat. De fr ocks kreditbetygen snkta. Mnga institutioner som kper sdana obligationer har emellertid placeringsregler som bara tillter investeringar i papper med hgsta kreditbetyg. De tvingas d slja sina innehav. Eftersom monolines frskrar obligationer fr minst 2000 miljarder USD kan detta ge betydande effekter p marknaden. Det kan ocks innebra ytterligare pfrestningar p likviditeten i bankerna. Samtidigt har den amerikanska konjunkturnedgngen ftt ordentligt fste, delvis som en fljd av fallande fastighetspriser. Oron fr att detta ska frvrra den finansiella krisen r uppenbar. Och naturligtvis kan den finansiella krisen ocks frstrka konjunkturnedgngen. I Sverige har vi inte direkt drabbats av krisen eftersom de svenska bankerna inte i ngon nmnvrd utstrckning varit engagerade i subprime-relaterade produkter. Men deras finansieringskostnader har kat, vilket drabbat kunderna i form av hgre rntor. P det sttet har oron p de finansiella marknaderna redan lett till en penningpolitisk tstramning. Vi fr en del kritik fr att vi i detta lge inte kommenterar den ekonomiska utvecklingen och hur vi ser p det penningpolitiska lget. Jag har frstelse fr den kritiken. Samtidigt r situationen den mest svrbedmda jag upplevt under min tid i Riksbanken. De penningpolitiska avvgningar vi har att gra r av den anledningen ovanligt komplicerade.  ena sidan finns det en risk att krisen blir bde lngre och djupare n vad vi tidigare har trott. De kraftiga snkningar av styrrntan som den amerikanska centralbanken gjort, och de uttalanden som fljt dessa, tyder utan tvekan p en stark oro frn deras sida. Hur en djupnande kris pverkar vrlden i vrigt och Sverige i synnerhet r svrt att avgra. Men oron p marknaderna r betydande ven hr, vilket speglas i de penningpolitiska frvntningarna. Frhoppningsvis r marknaderna alltfr pessimistiska i bedmningen av den ekonomiska utvecklingen. Men det r, som jag ser det, nnu fr tidigt att sga.  andra sidan r konjunkturen i Sverige fortfarande god, resursutnyttjandet p sina hll anstrngt och inflationen under det nrmaste ret p vg upp en bra bit ver inflationsmlet p tv procent. Dessutom har inflationsfrvntningarna stigit, bde p kort och p lite lngre sikt. Och den svenska penningpolitiken kan bara fras utifrn svenska frutsttningar. Detta talar fr att Riksbanken behver hja styrrntan ungefr i den takt som diskuterades i slutet p frra ret. Den svenska konjunkturutvecklingen talar allts fr att rntan br hjas, den internationella oron fr att det r bst att avvakta. Om en och en halv vecka har vi penningpolitiskt mte. Vi r sex ledamter i direktionen och alla funderar nu utifrn sina erfarenheter och analyser som bst p hur den avvgningen br ske. Title: Construction and monetary policy
text: Nyberg: Construction and monetary policy Date: 2000-02-17 Speaker: Deputy Governor Lars Heikensten Location: Fastighetsforum 2000 To begin with, I would like to thank you for the invitation to come here today and discuss such an important topic as construction and monetary policy. After all, construction is by its nature such that it often takes on the role of an accordion in the course of the business cycle. In the boom times, demand seems insatiable, customers want fast delivery even though construction inevitably requires time, bottlenecks arise in production, it is difficult to find labor and prices rise. In the recessions, it's just the opposite. The demand for new buildings is rapidly waning as vacant premises appear on the market and the shortage of labor is replaced by unemployment. Construction is undoubtedly a business that has a lot to gain from calm and stable growth in the economy. Monetary policy for stable and long-term growth The Riksdag's task to the Riksbank is, of course, to maintain a fixed monetary value. But it is difficult to keep the value of money fixed if the economy runs between periods of strong overheating with shortages of both goods and labor, when inflationary pressures are high, and periods of weak demand, high unemployment and low inflationary pressures. Therefore, it is important to conduct monetary policy in such a way that the development of output and employment is disturbed as little as possible. However, monetary policy has the peculiarity that it does not affect the economy immediately. When the Riksbank changes the repo rate, this will have an effect on production and employment with a significant backlog. This is certainly easy to see for those who are involved in construction, where the planning times are naturally long. Effects on inflation cannot be expected until after one to two years. In order to be able to contribute to stabilizing economic activity, the Riksbank must therefore act in very good time; if you wait until an overheating is a fact, it is already too late. Now, as is well known, it is difficult to know exactly what the reality will be in two years' time. All decisions must be based on forecasts of economic development, and forecasts can be wrong. In addition, there is a constant stream of new data that causes the forecasts to change. Gradual adjustments to the repo rate as a result of the availability of new information are therefore a natural part of a monetary policy that is fundamentally aimed at a stable development of output and employment. During the 1970s and 1980s, Sweden lived through a number of economic cycles where the development was anything but calm and stable. However, after the crisis of the early 1990s and the transition from a fixed exchange rate to an inflation target, growth of around three per cent per annum and rising employment have been reconciled with low inflation. During this time, the interest rate has adjusted both upwards and downwards. When the Riksbank in stages raises interest rates in the way that has happened in recent months, it is thus by no means in order to break a positive economic trend. The aim is to help ensure that the period of good growth can be extended without us ending up in a overheated situation, which may require far stronger measures to address. Not least for construction, this should be a strong interest. Development of construction After the crisis in the real estate market in the early 1990s, construction, as is well known, suffered a very sharp decline. Vacant premises were available in most parts of the country and property prices were largely halved. In most places, buying existing properties was significantly cheaper than building new ones. Last year, however, there was a clear turnaround. Prices of apartment buildings in metropolitan areas rose by over 20 per cent in the first half of the year alone. Prices of single-family homes are now at a higher level than before the fall in the early 1990s. In Stockholm, prices of detached houses have risen by 33% over the past two years and by 15% between November 1999 and January this year alone. However, it should be stressed that the price increases mainly concern the metropolitan regions. Price developments in the rest of the country are subdued. This is an important difference from the 1980s when we saw sharp price increases across the country. The ratio between what an existing house costs and what it costs to build a new one is usually a useful indicator of what may happen to construction. If the ratio is equal to one, the cost of building a new house is equal to buying an existing one. The higher the quota, the more profitable it will be to build new. According to recent statistics, the quota is now a bit above one in all metropolitan areas, in the hottest municipalities in the Stockholm area such as Lidingo, Danderyd and Sundbyberg almost two. Malmo and Gothenburg show values of about 1.2. In all these areas, we can thus expect strong demand for new construction. In places such as Gullspang, Hagfors and Kramfors, on the other hand, the quota remains around 0.3. There, an existing house costs only 30 percent of what it costs to build a new one. One of the reasons why property prices have risen recently is certainly the historically low nominal interest rates. Interest costs have not felt as daunting as in previous economic upturns for developers or for households that have to make room in the monthly budget. More than 70 percent of new lending from mortgage institutions today also takes place at variable interest rates, which can perhaps be interpreted as borrowers gaining increased confidence that the Riksbank's inflation target will be met. Another reason for the rising prices is certainly that demand in metropolitan areas has increased very quickly and that it is difficult to adapt construction to a desired level in a short time. The shortage of construction workers in big cities points in that direction. From the industry's point of view, it is of course positive that demand and prices are rising, although the development could be more even in both time and space. From the Riksbank's point of view, there is an element of concern. Will the shortage of construction workers in big cities drive sharp wage increases and, if so, will these have spillover effects in other sectors of the economy? And will the rapid increase in demand bring about shortages in other parts of the construction industry? These are issues that there is reason to follow closely over the next year. Expansionary monetary policy remains On the third of February, the Riksbank decided to raise its repo rate from 3.25 to 3.75 per cent, i.e. by half a percentage point. The decision was presented and justified in the usual way in a press release on the fourth of February. How the Executive Board reasoned more closely at its meeting will be clear from the Minutes, which will be published on 22 February, and I will not prejudge what is said there. Instead, let me touch on a few factors that are important for future development. To begin with, there is reason to recall that the Riksbank, through the latest interest rate decision, hardly stepped on the brakes, but rather eased the throttle. Monetary policy remains essentially expansionary. Even with a level at 3.75%, real interest rates are so low that they are likely to contribute to an expansion of activity in the economy. If you look at the repo rate reduced by household inflation expectations, this is below two percent, which is low in a historical comparison. Moreover, the real interest rate measured in this way has been falling for a longer period until the last interest rate decision. In both Germany and the United States, short-term real interest rates have averaged around 3.5 percent since the early 1980s. With inflation expectations of two percent, this would mean nominal interest rates of about 5.5 percent. The U.S. federal funds rate has also fluctuated between 4.5 and 6 percent since 1994. During that period, the U.S. has experienced the longest boom of the postwar period without inflation picking up. However, comparisons with other countries should be made with some caution. Demand pressure in relation to production capacity has been high in the US economy, while in Sweden during the 1990s we had significant spare capacity. It is also worth recalling that the repo rate has actually been reduced from 4.40 per cent to a minimum of 2.90 per cent over the past two years, i.e. by one and a half percentage points. The reductions took place against the background of the crises in Asia and Russia, but also against the background of concerns that European economic development was weak. As recently as April last year, there was general talk of the risk of deflation in the world economy. If the positive US growth trend had been broken in this situation, it could  as was then assessed  lead to too weak international demand growth. Now it didn't turn out that way. The US economy continued to grow and developments in Europe were significantly better than most expected. Therefore, in last year's last inflation report, the Riksbank stated that international development remained strong and also synchronized in the sense that most important countries in the world economy are showing increasing growth. One factor that will be at the centre of interest in the coming months is, of course, developments in the labour market. This is not only true in the construction sector. This spring, agreements for 280,000 employees in health care and schools will be negotiated. The negotiations take place in a strong-growth economy where bottlenecks are beginning to appear in certain areas and the bargaining power of those who want to be paid more is rising. At the same time, the negotiations are taking place in an environment where understanding of the inflation target has increased and where inflation expectations are low. Over the past four years, despite small nominal wage increases, real wages have been able to rise by almost four per cent per year. Whether this experience is sufficient to allow contracts to be concluded at a level compatible with a stable monetary value remains to be seen. Rising asset prices Swedish economic development at the end of last year was characterized, among other things, by rapidly rising asset prices. I have already mentioned property prices, but even more striking is, of course, the development of the stock market. During the second half of 1999, the stock index rose by just over 40 percent and from the turn of the year until mid-February this year, prices have increased by about 15 percent. The Stockholm stock exchange is now the highest valued in Europe with a P/E ratio of about 40. In essence, as is well known, the development is controlled by the internet and telecom companies. Eriksson has a P/E ratio of 80. The performance of the Swedish (and Finnish) stock exchanges has closely followed the US IT dominated NASDAQ stock exchange. Stock markets in the rest of Europe have shown a much calmer development. It is not only the prices that have risen, but also the trading volumes. Banks and stockbrokers made record profits in last year's final quarter. It is also interesting that private individuals sharply increased their share of turnover. Households sold Swedish listed shares for SEK 2 billion in the second quarter of last year and bought for almost SEK 13 billion in the third. The figure for the fourth quarter has not yet been published, but it is likely to be significantly higher. The average number of trades per day on the O-list, where most of the IT companies are listed, rose from about 6000 in the first quarter of 1999 to 24000 in December. In January of this year, more than 29000 trades were made per day. There is, of course, every reason to consider what the consequences of this development might be in the short term. Experience shows that wealth growth usually helps to increase consumption, but we have never before been able to study the effects of such a large increase in such a short period of time. To what extent will households realise the share gains and use them for consumption purposes? Thus, following the development of consumption over the next few months will be of great interest. However, it does not seem unreasonable to assume that some of the increased demand for residential properties that we have seen in metropolitan areas  and the subsequent price rises  could be attributed to the stock market upturn. The increase in financial asset values does not appear to have been used to pay off loans. On the contrary, bank lending to households increased by just over 9% in 1999 and growth was particularly high in the last quarter. In addition, liquidity in the form of notes and coins increased by as much as 12% from December 1998 to December 1999. Both of these conditions can provide the basis for rising private consumption and thus raise demand pressures in the economy. Of course, there is also a risk factor in the rapid stock market development. More and more analysts point out that the prices of many of the IT companies are very difficult to justify for those who calculate the companies' expected earnings development. It is easy to understand such an approach. "Hopes and faith in the future are nice, but sanity and balance may be needed too" an editorial the other day read. There is also reason to ask whether the increasing number of private investors entering the market really understands the risks that exist. It is worth noting that a number of major owners have recently taken the opportunity to take home part of their profits. A correction of the prices on the Stockholm Stock Exchange under so-called "orderly arrangements" would hardly have any serious effects on economic development. Nor should the functioning of the financial system be affected. We are a long way from the situation that prevailed when property prices fell in the early 1990s. A large part of the share price gains are still unrealized and the shareholdings are only to a small extent leveraged. Banks and brokers have apparently been cautious in their lending with shares as collateral. Possibly in recent months, stocks have increasingly been bought with collateral in real estate, but this is hardly a problem for banks as long as property prices do not fall drastically. Growth and inflation One issue that has come into strong focus over the past year is the relationship between growth and inflation. A common view is that the Swedish economy can withstand long-term growth of between 2 and 2.5 percent without this leading to overheating and thus tendencies towards rising inflation, which the Riksbank must fend off with increases in the repo rate. In the US, the corresponding figure has been estimated at between 3 and 3.5 percent. How is it that the U.S. economy can grow faster than the Swedish economy without this driving up inflation? And can't this "new economy" also come to Sweden? To these questions there are as yet no unequivocal answers. What can be seen is that productivity growth in the US has been high for much of the 1990s. This, in turn, has helped to ensure that demand has been able to grow and be satisfied without bottlenecks in production and a shortage of labour leading to rising prices. But behind the increase in productivity is a sharp increase in investment, especially in high-tech areas. American companies have almost doubled their investments in the 1990s. Capital per employee in industry has also increased very significantly. In Sweden, despite the IT boom on the stock exchange, we have not yet seen much of this development. Although productivity has grown half a percentage point faster in the 1990s than in the 1980s, according to available statistics, investment is still well below the US level. However, after the deep crisis in Sweden in the early 1990s, it was a long way to full capacity utilization, which should not be forgotten when comparing. Perhaps we will follow american developments during the economic upturn we are now seeing ahead of us. It would not be unnatural because the technology is also available to Swedish companies and Sweden undoubtedly has a high IT maturity. The high level of activity and the many newly formed companies in high-tech fields can be signs that something is about to happen. But it takes time to increase the capital stock in industry and thus give rise to rising productivity and, as yet, very little is visible in the investment figures for the economy as a whole. Possibly, however, the agg government of the investment figures hides some of the truth. Now we are not alone in eagerly scouting for signs of a "new economy". We are joined by most of the countries in Europe and they have not progressed any further. Perhaps we in Europe have less flexibility than in the USA, especially in the labour market, and therefore more difficult to take advantage of the new technology. In that case, it may delay, but hardly prevent in the long run, an increase in the level of investment and productivity. Conclusion It appears that construction is emerging from a long period of low activity and into a substantially better construction economy. For the construction industry, this is, of course, a positive development. However, one danger lies in the imbalances that appear to be occurring between the metropolitan regions and the rest of the country. Another danger lies in the bottlenecks that easily appear when demand increases rapidly without resources being created at a corresponding rate. In part, this reflects the eternal dilemma of construction because construction must adapt the log of real estate to that demanded in society. It will be easy so that the log is too large and then no construction is needed or the log is too small and then the demand for construction becomes greater than the available resources. Words like just right and balance are often more difficult to apply to construction than to other activities in the economy. However, the special conditions of construction make stable economic development particularly valuable. In its efforts to keep the value of money constant, the Riksbank is also working for stable economic growth where periods of strong acceleration or strong deceleration can be avoided. If the economy continues to develop as expected, this probably means rising interest rates for some time to come. At the same time, after the increase in early February, we felt that we had done what was then needed to secure inflation in line with the target for one to two years. Now we get to evaluate the new information that is coming. The next time the Executive Board will take a position on the repo rate will be in connection with the publication of the Inflation Report on 23 March.

Title: After the crisis
text: Nyberg: After the crisis Date: 2010-02-05 Speaker: Deputy Governor Lars Nyberg Location: Samfunnsf8konomforeningen, Oslo, Norway Deputy Governor Lars Nyberg spoke on Friday about his view of how the rules governing the financial sector need to be changed as a result of the crisis. Summary The regulation of the financial system is an issue that becomes front-page news in every financial crisis. The crisis we have recently gone through is, of course, no exception. All sorts of recipes have been launched to create a more stable financial system, some more appetizing than others. However, one view that the vast majority share is that the rules of the game need to be tightened. The question is only how much and in what way. Lars Nyberg argued that the reform work is not so much about inventing a new recipe for financial stability. Rather, it's about adding more of already existing ingredients. The crisis is largely explained by the fact that there were too few of three things: There was too little capital. There was too little liquidity. And there was far too little focus on the overall and system-wide risks that had been building up in the global financial system for some time. In the future, more of these scarce goods will be required. Nyberg also argued that it is important that we are vigilant that the regulatory reforms that follow the crisis do not impair the financial system's ability to fulfill its socially beneficial functions. What the reform work is fundamentally about is finding a reasonable socio-economic balance between the financial system's risk and return. Read the full speech in the pdf file.

Title: Financing of deposit insurance  a central banker's perspective
text: Nyberg: Financing of deposit insurance  a central banker's perspective Datum: 2005-09-15 Talare: Vice riksbankschef Lars Nyberg Plats: Sveriges riksbank OBS: Talet publiceras endast pa engelska Introduction Some of you may be wondering why on earth a central banker would have an opinion on the financing of deposit insurance. But to the extent that central banks are concerned with financial stability, there is actually an important reason for the central bank to take an interest in the overall design of deposit insurance. Deposit insurance and financial stability In the EU as in most other developed economies in the world, deposit insurance is seen primarily as a form of consumer protection. Bank failures are few and far between and bank crises involving the entire system are something that most of us have only read about or heard about at a conference. Under these generally stable circumstances, the role of deposit insurance is limited to reimbursing the relatively few customers who are unfortunate enough to have deposits in the (always) very small banks that once in a while have to be closed down. When large banks show signs of being in serious trouble, on the other hand, authorities are often very keen to avoid an outright insolvency and a subsequent failure. Instead, the authorities usual procedure is to support the ailing bank  through injections of liquidity or capital  while at the same time enforcing some kind of restructuring, including replacing the management, merging the weak bank with a stronger competitor, raising capital through the sale of non-core operations, etc. Hence, deposit insurance payouts for large bank failures or systemic banking crises are practically unheard of. But it was not always like this. At the time when deposit insurance was introduced in the United States in 1933, the main purpose was to restore public confidence in the nations banking system. It was created in response to the thousands of bank failures that occurred in the 1920s and early 1930s, culminating in a national bank holiday in 1933. In essence, the federal deposit insurance was motivated by financial stability concerns  to stop the bank runs and enable the banking system to start functioning normally again. More recently, many emerging economies in Latin America and Asia have had similar experiences  to avoid a complete breakdown of or to restore the confidence in the banking system, authorities have had to convince the public that their deposits will not be lost. In other words, even though in todays Europe deposit insurance in 99 per cent of the cases is about consumer protection, ultimately, it is also an important building block in the safety net underpinning the stability of the financial system. The nature of deposit insurance Given that society seems to want deposit insurance, we need to think about how it should be organised and who should pay for it. Because someone will  there is no free lunch. I will now try to give you some tentative answers to these questions. I should also say that these ideas are not the unique intellectual property of the Riksbank but are very much in line with the recommendations given this spring by a Swedish government committee on reforming the deposit insurance system. Today, deposit insurance in the EU is provided either by cooperatives where the member banks insure each other or, more frequently, by a government authority. In many cases, there is a fund in place and a scheme for how surviving banks would pay for failing banks. In this sense, deposit insurance systems in the EU often have both public and private characteristics. When small banks fail, the funds in place or the cooperative arrangements can be expected to be adequate. In the case of a really large bank going bankrupt or even a system-wide banking crisis, however, there is no doubt that the ultimate guarantor is the state, that is, the tax payers  either by supporting the deposit insurance system or, more likely, by saving the banks from failure through injections of capital or liquidity. Still, we should always ask ourselves if the market could not solve this on its own without public interference. After all, insurance companies sell insurance against various other forms of low probability-high impact events like terrorist attacks and earthquakes. Why couldnt insurance companies also sell insurance protecting depositors against bank failures? Well, beyond political considerations such as depositors also being voters, in the end, it boils down to the fact that the state cannot avoid responsibility for the payment system. Since the market understands that the state has a very strong interest in the functioning of the payment system, it is almost impossible for the state to convince the market that it wouldnt  in one way or another  protect depositors. Thus, if deposit insurance  whatever the institutional arrangements  ultimately rests on a state guarantee, where the risk is borne by the tax payers, it seems sensible that tax payers should be made aware of this. This speaks in favour of an explicit state guarantee that clearly shows the distribution of responsibilities, risks and costs. Which then brings us to the next question: what is a reasonable price for the tax payers to demand from the banks for providing them with deposit insurance? The financing of deposit insurance As a starting point, it is important to recognise that deposit insurance has a value for banks, since it lowers their funding cost. And we have already concluded that it implies a (potential) cost for the state. Even if we have rejected the idea of private deposit insurance, it is useful to think about how the market, in that case, would have priced this insurance. The market would have charged a premium, which size would depend on the amount covered, the length of the insurance period and the probability of the bank failing. Personally, I think that the principles of private insurance, with some exceptions, should also be applied in the design of a public deposit insurance system. This would have mainly two implications. First and most importantly, the premiums that banks pay should be risk-based, meaning that a high-risk bank should pay a higher fee than a safe bank. This provides the banks with sound incentives for risk management and reduces some of the moral hazard inherent in all guarantees. But risk-based premiums are also economically sound from the tax-payers perspective, since a higher risk bank is more likely to go bankrupt and therefore more likely to make use of the insurance. While I am a strong proponent of risk-based premiums, it is important to admit that, in practice, it can be quite difficult to calculate the risk of a bank. I will not here go into the details and pros and cons of various models and approaches. But I would like to make some general points regarding risk calculation. To begin with, I strongly argue for a simple approach which is easy for the banks to understand and predict. The value added from developing something very complex but scientifically more precise is likely to be very marginal. Second, I would advocate authorities to make use of the risk and capital assessment that is anyway conducted by the supervisor. With the implementation of Basel II considerable resources will be invested in developing this supervisory assessment and it seems a pity to develop a parallel system. Also, with two different systems authorities run the risk of sending contradicting signals. Finally, even if premiums should be risk-based, this does not imply that they should be market-based. The state insurer differs from a private insurer in at least two fundamental ways. As we are all painfully aware, the state can raise taxes. Hence, the state cannot default in the same way as a private insurer and therefore does not need to compensate itself by charging a risk premium. The only thing that really matters to the state insurer is the expected loss for each bank. That there is high uncertainty around such expectations is not a problem for the state, as long as the expectation is correct in the long-run. In addition, the state does not need to make a profit but should, as already noted, only be concerned with covering its expected long-run cost. Thus, the risk-based premiums will be lower when charged by the state than when charged by a private insurer. Second, banks should pay their premiums in advance (or ex ante). The most important reason for this is that otherwise it is not possible to have risk-based premiums. But there are also some other good reasons for this. Paying in advance means that the premium payments are smoothed over time whether there has been a failure or not. In contrast, only paying once a failure or crisis has occurred means that banks have to increase payments when the banking system might already be in a fragile state. Alternatively, it might prove difficult in practice for the authorities to recoup all the costs of an insurance payout in the aftermath of a crisis. Finally, in some sense ex ante payment of premiums is also fairer since it implies that all banks  even the ones which will later fail  pay for the insurance. If premiums are paid ex post the remaining banks will have to pay for the failures of their competitors. What to do with the premium income? The state may use the premium income in two ways. Either it can use it to build up a deposit insurance fund ready to be used in the event of a payout case, or it can let the premium income flow into the states coffers just like any other government fee or tax. Given the long-term and potentially large liabilities of deposit insurance, however, it is probably advisable that the premiums do not flow directly into the state budget to be freely spent by the current government. Therefore, the Swedish deposit insurance committee proposed that the premium income would flow into a separate account where it can only be used to fund the government deficit. This will mean that in good times, premium income from the banks will contribute positively to the states finances by decreasing the borrowing need, while in bad times when banks fail, the state will have to increase borrowing in order to fund eventual insurance payouts. In all the ex ante paid systems that I am aware of there is also a fund. A fund may be practical since the deposit insurance authority then can manage minor cases of payouts without having to borrow money from the government. But it is difficult to see why this would be enough to motivate the setting up of a fund. In the event of major failures the government would be involved in any case. And having a fund in place also entails costs, in terms of fund management. If we do not believe that the government-appointed fund manager can systematically beat the market, which we dont, there is really no strong case for having a fund. Cross-border aspects in the EU In the EU at present, there are more deposit insurance models than there are member states, since some countries have more than one system. These systems differ in all possible aspects: scope and amount of the cover, whether premiums are paid ex ante or ex post and whether there is a fund in place and, if so, how large it is. Up to now, EU banks have conducted cross-border retail banking almost exclusively in subsidiaries as opposed to branches. In the few and relatively minor cases of retail banking being run in a branch, the differences in level and scope have been handled by the possibility of topping-up. However, as cross-border retail banking has continued  albeit slowly  to grow in importance, the interest in deposit insurance has recently been rising. The sources for this rising interest are, however, quite different. On the one hand, in the perspective of the banking sector and the Commission, deposit insurance may be both a potential barrier to further integration and a threat to the level playing field. Some large EU banks, of which one has its headquarters just 200 metres from here, have expressed discontent with the current regime on mainly two accounts. Firstly, the existence of funds and the link between the size of the fund and the level of the fees give rise to competitive effects when entering and exiting different systems. This may discourage transformation to branches and  since branches may be a more cost-efficient way to run foreign retail operations  create an additional barrier to cross-border consolidation. Let me give you an example. When a large bank exits one system, that system might become over-funded leading the authorities to lower fees for the banks competitors which remain in the system. At the same time, the large bank joins (or adds more deposits to) another system, which means that this system might become under-funded, leading the authorities to raise the fees. The net effect is that the bank ends up with a higher total cost for deposit insurance, while some of its competitors get a lower cost. Secondly and most obviously, different levels of fees threaten the level playing field between banks competing for the same deposits. Topping-up only works in one way: it allows the foreign bank that enters to get the same level of insurance as the host country banks. However, when the entering bank has a better or cheaper insurance than the host country banks, there is no way for the host country banks to compensate for this. Hence, backed with generous or cheap deposit insurance from their home system, some banks have a distinct advantage to expand into other EU countries. I believe that this criticism should be taken seriously and I welcome the review of the directive that the Commission is currently undertaking. At the same time, I would not overemphasize the competitive and level playing field aspects of deposit insurance. They are important in principle, but in practice and relative to, for example, national differences in capital regulation they are rather marginal. The perspective on deposit insurance of some national regulators and central banks, on the other hand, has been quite different and focussed on the burden sharing between home and host countries. What are the wider implications of tax payers in one country insuring substantial amounts of deposits in another country? It has been noted that it may be politically very difficult to make payouts from one country to another in the aftermath of a large bank failure. It could also be questioned if it is reasonable that, after a large bank failure, the authorities in the host country just refer its depositors to the home country authorities, without taking any responsibility. And, of course, there is always the question of whether the failure of some large cross-border EU banks will be too big to manage for a single EU member state. Conclusion Both kinds of cross-border aspects  level playing field as well as burden sharing  are indeed tricky. Still, I would like to note that if we all agreed to charge risk-based ex ante fees and scrap the funds, we would take a major step towards solving many, but not all, of these problems. The competitive effects from exiting and entering systems would be significantly reduced. Banks would pay premiums depending on their own risk and the amount of insurance received. There would still be a need for topping-up, as there would still be differences in the level and scope between systems, but at least the banks covered by a more generous insurance would have to pay a higher premium. Regarding the burden-sharing concerns, one could still doubt the capacity of an individual small country to deal with a large cross-border bank failure, but at least the countrys tax payers would be aware of the liability and compensated for the expected cost. That's what one might call killing two birds with one stone  better national systems that would at the same time work better on the EU level. Thank you.

Title: The financial crisis - developments in recent months and some lessons learned
text: Nyberg: The financial crisis - developments in recent months and some lessons learned Date 2008-05-21 Since mid-March, there are signs that tensions in the credit market have eased somewhat. In the interbank market, significant problems remain, but even there there are some positive trends. This is stated by Deputy Governor Lars Nyberg when he speaks today before the EU club in Stockholm. "There are indications that the strained conditions in international credit markets have eased. The powerful rescue of U.S. investment bank Bear Stearns in mid-March appears to have been one of several contributing factors to the return of confidence among investors. The fact that several institutions, in connection with the quarterly reporting during April and May, openly reported their losses has created a better overview of where the problems are. Large banks have also found it easier to access both borrowed and equity." "The fact that the concern among investors in the credit market has decreased can be seen in various ways, including through the pricing of credit protection. This is most clearly visible in the so-called CDS premiums, which reflect the market's valuation of credit risk at institutions and companies. They have dropped significantly since the end of March. The cost for companies to finance themselves through the capital market has also decreased slightly recently. Investors appear a little more risk-averse than before and the availability of capital has increased. Stock markets have also recovered.". "In the interbank market, the market where banks borrow from each other, interest rates are still abnormally high on many maturities. The so-called ted spread, the difference between the three-month interbank rate and the corresponding Treasury bill, is still three times as high as normal both in the US and in Europe. But in the U.S., for example, ted spreads have dropped significantly in recent weeks. In Europe, too, they have declined slightly, mainly in the UK." "It is still too early to conclude that the crisis is over. But there are signs that suggest we may have the worst behind us. However, there may be setbacks. The outlook for the economy is uncertain, especially in the US, where the real estate market has not yet bottomed out. Should the economic slowdown become stronger than expected, the financial system may be further tested. The market also remains vulnerable to rumors. It cannot be ruled out that new credit losses will emerge that will at least temporarily shake market confidence." "Iceland has been the subject of failing confidence in the international market. Following a request from the Icelandic central bank, Sedlabanki, the central banks of Sweden, Norway and Denmark last week entered into swap agreements with them. The agreements entitle Sedlabanked to receive euros against Icelandic kroner should such a need arise. These agreements are aimed at building trust and this is how the market has perceived them. Sedlabanked will also strengthen its resources in other ways. At the same time, the Icelandic government has announced its intention to implement long-term structural reforms aimed at strengthening economic stability in the country." "For Sweden, we have mainly been able to regard the crisis as spectators. Interest rates have also risen here primarily as a consequence of international banks increasing their demand for kronor, which they then exchanged for dollars or euros. That demand has now slowed and the shortest interbank rates (tomorrow-next) have normalized. Unlike in many other countries, the Swedish fixed income market has, throughout the course of the crisis, functioned without intervention from the central bank. You will hear more about our assessment of Swedish financial stability on 3 June, when we publish this spring's stability report." "What are the lessons to be learned from a crisis like this? Some things can already be said about this, although the final evaluation will have to be put on hold until we have perspective on what has happened. For private operators, it is undoubtedly the case that greater transparency about what is on the balance sheet counteracts uncertainty and mistrust. It is also important that banks keep enough capital to cover their risks. For authorities, the regulation and supervision of liquidity risk is currently a priority issue that is addressed in many countries and international organisations, including the Financial Stability Forum (SYL) and the Basel Committee. The SYL has recently published a report in which the G7 countries call, among other things, for faster and more transparent reporting by financial companies and stricter requirements for credit rating agencies. It also advocates more powerful arrangements for dealing with financial crises".

Title: The financial sector and the new economy
text: Nyberg: The financial sector and the new economy Date: 2000-11-28 Speaker: Deputy Governor Lars Nyberg Location: Financial Administrative Forum To begin with, I would like to thank you for the opportunity to discuss the new economy here at the Financial Administrative Forum. As can be seen from the headlines of today's speeches, the pace of change in the financial sector remains high. These are new products, new markets, new distribution technologies, new administrative systems. Sometimes also about a completely new business logic. Does this mean that the "new economy" has reached the financial sector? My belief is that it did quite a long time ago, long before it became fashionable to give talks about it. In the financial sector, the new economy is already middle-aged. That's what I was going to talk about today. Driving forces behind the new economy It is not always so crystal clear in the debate what is new in the "new economy". First of all, let me broaden the discussion from the financial sector to the economy as a whole. At such an overall level, the 'new' often refers simply to an increase in the growth potential of the economy as a result of faster productivity growth. Productivity is thus a central concept in the discussion of the new economy. It's productivity growth that has lifted the U.S. economy to grow by an average of 3.2 percent a year over a ten-year period without hitting the capacity ceiling and driving up inflation. And it is productivity that is a key factor when we discuss whether the new economy has come to Sweden. There are also good reasons to expect an increase in productivity, because a lot has happened in the last ten years. There are three main factors that tend to be highlighted in this context, namely macroeconomic stability, microeconomic reforms and technological progress. Macroeconomic stability is a prerequisite for long-term investment decisions and stable growth. When we in Sweden in the early 1990s focused our policy on low inflation, we left behind a long period where price and wage spirals were followed by devaluations and where growth has been lower than among our competitor countries. A credible inflation target is currently seen as a prerequisite for macroeconomic stability. After the crisis, a purposeful clean-up of the state budget also followed. One may have different opinions on individual elements of that process, but there is no doubt that it restored Sweden's credibility financially. The successful handling of the crisis in the Swedish banking system also contributed to this. Microeconomic reforms such as the liberalisation of the financial, telecommunications and electricity markets and the progressive liberalisation of trade have increased competition in the economy and forced businesses to become increasingly efficient. In addition, not least in the early 1990s, important growth-enhancing changes were made to the tax and transfer systems. Technological advances, especially the rapid development in IT, have received a lot of media attention. The advent of the internet, advances in telecoms, and increasingly better computers and programs have enabled more efficient communication and information management, which in turn has resulted in a more efficient use of resources. Has productivity increased? It would therefore not be unreasonable if the statistics were to show an increase in productivity in the Swedish economy in the same way as it has done in the United States. Now, as is well known, it is not so easy to measure productivity fairly. Productivity basically measures the value of production in sek per person employed, e.g. how many cars or how much volume of services are produced per hour worked. But when the cars get better and the services get an increased content and maybe at the same time become cheaper, it is not entirely trivial to capture this development in the statistics. The rapid development in IT in recent years has accentuated this problem. Nevertheless, if one studies productivity growth, one can discern a clear increase from an average level of 1% in the period 1980-1989 to an average level of 1.8% in 1992-1999 (Figure 1). The picture is based on the very recent revisions that have come from Statistics Sweden and which have increased the estimated productivity increase by about 0.5 percentage points for the years 19971999. In the UNITED STATES, however, productivity growth according to the national accounts has been as much as 3.9 percent per year during the years 1995-1999, i.e. significantly higher than Sweden. Productivity is sometimes divided into the part resulting from the growth of capital, thereby enabling an increase in output per person employed (capital intensity) and the part resulting from the fact that both capital and labour input can be used more efficiently through technical and organisational progress, the so-called total factor productivity (TFP). In Sweden, capital intensity has remained virtually constant throughout the 1990s, which means that the capital stock has grown in line with employment, but no more (Figure 2). The whole increase in productivity could thus be attributed to improved technology. That's not the case in the U.S. There, investments in new production capacity have contributed almost 50 percent of productivity growth. This applies above all to IT-related investments, which have grown by about 40 percent per year during the second half of the 1990s. In other activities, investments have increased only moderately. Now there are signs that the Swedish figures hide some of the truth and give a somewhat too gloomy picture of the development, at least compared to the United States. Without going too deeply into the statistical technique, it can be stated that the Swedish way of adjusting, for example, the figures for investments in software for quality increases and price drops is significantly more conservative than the American one. Statistics Sweden has itself calculated that this has created a difference in GDP growth of about 0.1 percentage points per year during the period 1993-2000. No corresponding calculations have been made for investments in hardware, which amount to approximately as much as investments in software at current prices. Perhaps even more interesting is the development of total factor productivity, which, according to some calculations, is behind the entire Swedish productivity growth. It is reasonable to assume that companies that invested more in computers, networks and electronics also gained in efficiency, whether they work in the IT sector or in other industries. The financial sector offers many examples of this, which I will come back to later. However, capturing the development in statistical series for different industries is not yet possible in Sweden. In this respect, however, we are not alone, the rest of Europe has even greater problems with the statistical basis. Overall, it seems that the difference we have observed in productivity growth between the US and Sweden could actually be partly due to differences in the statistical data. From this perspective, we are perhaps closer to the new economy than we thought just six months ago. Productivity in the financial sector What does it look like in the financial sector? Has productivity increased during it last decade and if so, what expressions has this taken? First, a few words about competition. Since the mid-1980s, the financial sector has undergone perhaps greater changes than any other sector of the economy. The foundations for these changes were laid by the major deregulations of the credit and currency sectors of the 1980s. The strong financial expansion in the late 1980s delayed adaptation to a more competitive reality for a few years. After the crisis in the early 1990s, structural change took off in earnest and the Swedish banking system today, like the entire financial sector, makes a much more dynamic impression than in the mid-1980s. The liberalisation and internationalisation of securities trading has also been important in this context. Then there is technological development. In this context, let me start with a slightly longer and perhaps more personal perspective. My first job was as an intern on a board yard. I never forget the scent of freshly sawn timber, it has followed me through life and always given a feeling of desire and joy. I'll also never forget the feeling on Friday afternoon when the clerk came down from the office and seriously distributed the brown envelopes with the week's payoff. My stomach tingled with anticipation and satisfaction. The notes in hand once a week were such tangible proof that we had achieved something valuable. Nowadays, the salary is directly deposited in a bank account and information about this is delivered via a bank statement every two months. It doesn't give nearly the same tingle as the brown envelopes. But it's undeniably quite handy. In addition, we can pay our bills from home through transfers from the account and do not have to spend an hour on Saturday morning talking in the queue in front of the post office. The mail queue I miss less than the brown envelopes. It has been estimated that the productivity gain resulting from the streamlining of the payment system corresponds to at least five per cent of gross domestic product. It's an outstanding increase in productivity over a forty-year period and one that most of us enjoy. We get at least five per cent more in the pay envelopes as a result of the development of the payment system, one might say. As a metaphor, the pay envelopes have survived. Perhaps even more important things have happened in the last ten years and in a number of cases the new technologies have had a decisive impact on how and in what direction the financial sector has developed. For example, the introduction of electronic exchange trading has reduced transaction costs to a fraction. 'Straight through processing', which you will discuss here in a moment, can be seen as the next step in that productivity development. Another example is the management of financial risk. The instruments used to trade in financial risk, such as options, futures and swaps, all depend on computer technology, not only in the trading itself but for valuation and pricing. It is simply not possible to continuously value complicated derivative instruments without the help of fast computers. In a broad sense, this applies to all those innovations in financial technology that are used to "unpack" financial risks and then "pack up" them again for trading in the markets. The whole of modern portfolio management, which itself has created a basis for the expansion of trading in financial instruments, would be impossible without advanced computer support. All this, of course, is IT and it revolutionized the financial markets long before the internet had spread from universities into society. The Internet was initially expected to lead to increased competition in the financial field by facilitating easier access to the market for new entrants. These forecasts have to some extent come true, but at the same time the business opportunities for traditional players have grown dramatically. The Internet provides new distribution and marketing channels, while the growth of e-commerce is creating demand for banks' payment services. In addition, the internet has come to be a major potential source of savings as customers increasingly handle payments and other business online themselves. In a way, this development is not so surprising. After all, financial activities are information-intensive and act largely part on the collection, handling and valuation of information. Nevertheless, progress has been far faster than most predicted five years ago. Can productivity growth in the financial sector be measured? Despite all this, it is difficult to find any statistical support for the fact that productivity growth in the financial sector has been faster in recent years than in the past. The development is even worse than for the economy as a whole. In the early years of the 1990s, productivity fell as a result of the banking crisis (Figure 3). The major increase in productivity then took place during the period 1994-1997 when the banking crisis was overstuffed, competition increased and banks were able to start rationalising branch networks. In the 1990s, one third of local branches in banks disappeared (Figure 4). To a not insignificant extent, as previously pointed out, this was probably a delayed effect of the deregulations of the 1980s. However, as has been said, productivity growth in the services sector is particularly difficult to measure. In statistics, a payment service is always a payment service  the value of being able to make the payment from home in front of the computer, without paperwork, instead of taking the cash in your hand and standing in the mail queue is not so easy to capture in the statistics. A study of American banking, which takes into account quality improvements as a result of technological developments, concludes that annual productivity growth over the period 1977-1994 has been around 7%, compared with the 1.4% recorded in official statistics. Thus, there is reason to suspect that the figures underestimate productivity growth in the financial sector in the same way as in the economy as a whole. The number of employees in the banking sector has decreased only marginally in the 1990s. Thus, if productivity is to have increased, each employee must produce more or better services. They probably do too. For example, the number of payments (in the RIX system) has grown by 30% per year in the 1990s and the number of trades on the stock exchange by 40%. It is not unreasonable to assume that significantly more bank employees would have been needed to cope with these volumes if significant investments on the system side had not increased productivity  both by increasing capital intensity and by raising overall factor productivity. But, as I said, all this is difficult to show in the statistics. What does the internet mean in this context? After all, only a third of Swedish bank customers still have an internet bank and probably even fewer who use it as much as they could (Figure 5). Still, it's fast marched compared to most other countries. But it will probably take several more years before customers fully accept the new technology. This means that banks currently have to pay for two parallel infrastructures, which makes it difficult for them to realise the full potential of the investments. However, it cannot be ruled out that the markedly improved banking performance of the past year is partly a consequence of the fact that investments on the internet side are already starting to have some effect. Risks in the new economy The Riksbank has a responsibility to ensure that the Swedish payment system is secure and efficient. Since a well-functioning payment system requires a well-functioning and sound financial sector, the Riksbank has an interest in closely following developments in the financial system. The results of this analysis are presented twice a year in the financial stability report. The next report will be presented on Thursday of this week, 30 November. The high pace of change with deregulation, internationalisation, technological innovations and increasingly sophisticated financial instruments naturally affects the stability of the financial system. In the Riksbank's opinion, this impact is fundamentally positive. Liberalisation has contributed to a more efficient financial sector, which is of great importance for the efficiency and growth of the economy as a whole. Advances in IT improve information systems and risk models and reduce the risk of miscalculations and unpleasant surprises. The advent of new instruments increases the market's ability to manage financial risk. However, there are also stability risks associated with these developments. Deregulation and internationalisation bring efficiency gains precisely because the financial sector's operators are given the opportunity to compete freely and take risks. A prerequisite for this to work is then, of course, that the actors have the necessary knowledge required to correctly assess the risks in a partly new and changed market. This is not always the case, which we had reason to ponder during the Swedish banking crisis. In Sweden, forty years of regulation had depleted the knowledge of credit assessment, both in the banks and at the supervisory authority. This was a major factor behind the banking crisis, albeit not the only one. Other countries have had similar experiences. In the wake of deregulation, crises often follow. This does not mean that the reforms were ill-conceived, but it highlights the fact that the risk of miscalculations increases during the transition period when both private actors and authorities have to adapt to new conditions. In fact, the potentially increased risks associated with deregulation are just one example of a much more general phenomenon  that it is more difficult to make correct decisions during periods of rapid change as forecasts of the future become more uncertain and historical experiences and correlations less useful as a guide. History is filled with examples of how changing market conditions and technological advances lead to excessively raised expectations and wrong investment decisions. In the UNITED STATES of the 1920s, the stock market was driven by expectations of radio and car manufacturers, among others, while in 1980s Sweden it was primarily about real estate companies. The rise and fall of the telecom and IT sectors over the past year is a useful reminder of how difficult it actually is to value new companies and industries. Periods of rapid change also place high demands on the financial institutions' internal risk control systems. It is easy to believe that the eagerness to be able to quickly provide customers with new financial products means that the necessary updating and adaptation of control systems is not given the required priority. Risks arising from a lack of internal procedures, so-called operational risks, have rightly received increasing attention in recent years. One reason for this is likely to be the more or less spectacular cases of operational mishaps that have actually occurred, of which the Barings crash is the prime example. As far as rapid technological development is concerned, there is a danger that the increasingly refined analytical tools and risk models that are now being used are lulling financial institutions into a kind of false sense of security. There is no doubt that these models are a very important support for analysis and decision-making, but it is important to remember that models are only very gross simplifications of reality and must therefore be used with caution. The failure of the hedge fund LTCM in the autumn of 1998 is a serious and appalling example. LTCM had access to some of the world's foremost experts in financial risk management and had for several years shown astonishing profitability. Nevertheless, things went wrong, of course, in part due to the size of the positions, but probably also due to an excessive reliance on the risk models used. The events of autumn 1998 also give rise to another reflection. With today's highly integrated international financial markets, disruptions spread rapidly from one market to another. In addition, many instruments can be technically complex and have a risk content that is difficult to grasp. In times of uncertainty, investors tend to want to get out of such instruments and into safe papers with clear risk content and secure liquidity. We get what is usually called an escape to quality and liquidity. The international markets have so far been able to handle this well. However, we still know very little about how the process would develop in the event of a major financial crisis in any part of the world. Slutord The financial sector in Sweden was highly regulated until the mid-1980s. Thereafter it has been subject to extensive liberalisation, increased international competition and rapid technological development. In addition, a pervasive banking crisis. Although it may be difficult to demonstrate statistically, it seems to be a reasonable hypothesis that productivity has risen somewhat during this journey. Furthermore, much of the technological development is about information technology, which is natural in a sector where electronic commerce, transparency, price information, etc. are central concepts. The Internet opens up new opportunities, but IT and the "new economy" most likely came to the financial sector already many years ago. Footnote 1) The Economist, 23 september 2000

Det r helt enkelt inte mjligt att kontinuerligt vrdera komplicerade derivatinstrument utan hjlp av snabba datorer. I vid mening gller detta alla de innovationer inom den finansiella teknologin som anvnds fr att "packa upp" finansiella risker och sedan "packa ihop" dem igen fr handel p marknaderna. Hela den moderna portfljhanteringen, som i sig skapat en bas fr expansionen av handeln med finansiella instrument, vore omjlig utan avancerat datorstd. Allt detta r naturligtvis IT och den revolutionerade de finansiella marknaderna lngt innan internet hade spritt sig frn universiteten ut i samhllet. Internet frvntades till att brja med leda till kad konkurrens inom det finansiella omrdet genom att nya aktrer lttare fick tilltrde till marknaden. Dessa prognoser har till viss del slagit in, men samtidigt har affrsmjligheterna fr traditionella aktrer vuxit dramatiskt. Internet tillhandahller nya distributions- och marknadsfringskanaler samtidigt som den vxande e-handeln skapar efterfrgan p bankernas betalningstjnster. Dessutom har internet kommit att innebra en stor potentiell klla till besparingar eftersom kunderna i kad utstrckning sjlva hanterar betalningar och andra affrer p ntet. P stt och vis r denna utveckling inte s verraskande. Finansiell verksamhet r ju informationsintensiv och handlar till stor del om inhmtande, hantering och vrdering av information. Icke desto mindre har utvecklingen gtt lngt snabbare n vad de flesta frutsg fr fem r sedan. Kan man mta produktivitetskningarna i finanssektorn? Trots allt detta r det svrt att finna ngot statistiskt std fr att produktivitetstillvxten i finanssektorn skulle ha varit snabbare under de senaste ren n tidigare. Utvecklingen r t.o.m. smre n fr ekonomin totalt. Under 1990-talets frsta r fll produktiviteten till fljd av bankkrisen (bild 3). Det stora produktivitetslyftet skedde sedan under perioden 1994-1997 nr bankkrisen var verstkad, konkurrensen kade och bankerna kunde brja rationalisera i kontorsnten. Under 1990-talet frsvann en tredjedel av lokalkontoren i bankerna (bild 4). Till en icke ovsentlig del var detta som tidigare ppekats sannolikt en frdrjd verkan av 1980-talets avregleringar. Produktivitetskningar i tjnstesektorn r emellertid som sagt srskilt svra att mta. I statistiken r en betalningstjnst alltid en betalningstjnst  vrdet av att kunna gra betalningen hemifrn framfr datorn, utan pappersarbete, i stllet fr att ta kontanterna i handen och stlla sig i postkn r inte s ltt att fnga i statistiken. En studie av amerikansk bankverksamhet dr hnsyn tas till kvalitetsfrbttringar till fljd av teknisk utveckling kommer fram till att den rliga produktivitetskningen under perioden 1977-1994 legat omkring 7 procent, vilket kan jmfras med de 1,4 procent som uppmtts i den officiella statistiken. Det finns sledes skl att misstnka att siffrorna underskattar produktivitetstillvxten i finanssektorn p samma stt som i ekonomin totalt. Antalet anstllda i banksektorn har minskat endast marginellt under 1990-talet. Om produktiviteten skall ha kat mste varje anstlld allts producera fler eller bttre tjnster. Sannolikt gr de ocks det. Antalet betalningar (i RIX-systemet) har t.ex. under 1990-talet vuxit med 30 procent per r och antalet avslut p brsen med 40 procent. Det r inte orimligt att anta att det skulle behvts vsentligt fler anstllda i bankerna fr att klara dessa volymer om inte betydande investeringar p systemsidan hjt produktiviteten  bde genom att ka kapitalintensiteten och genom att hja den totala faktorproduktiviteten. Men, som sagt, allt detta r svrt att visa i statistiken. Vad betyder internet i detta sammanhang? nnu r det trots allt bara en tredjedel av de svenska bankkunderna som har en internetbank och frmodligen nnu frre som utnyttjar den i s stor utstrckning som de skulle kunna (bild 5). Det r nd snabbt marscherat jmfrt med de flesta andra lnder. Men frmodligen kommer det att ta ytterligare flera r innan kunderna fullt ut accepterar den nya tekniken. Detta innebr att bankerna fr tillfllet mste bekosta tv parallella infrastrukturer, vilket gr det svrt fr dem att realisera den fulla potentialen av investeringarna. Det kan dock inte uteslutas att det senaste rets markant frbttrade bankresultat till viss del r en fljd av att investeringarna p internetsidan redan brjar ge viss effekt. Risker i den nya ekonomin Riksbanken har ett ansvar fr att det svenska betalningssystemet r skert och effektivt. Eftersom ett vl fungerande betalningssystem krver en vl fungerande och sund finanssektor har Riksbanken ett intresse av att noga flja utvecklingen i det finansiella systemet. Resultatet av denna analys presenteras tv gnger om ret i rapporten Finansiell Stabilitet. Nsta rapport presenteras p torsdag i denna vecka, den 30 november. Den hga frndringstakten med avregleringar, internationalisering, tekniska innovationer och alltmer sofistikerade finansiella instrument pverkar naturligtvis stabiliteten i det finansiella systemet. Enligt Riksbankens mening r denna pverkan i grunden positiv. Avregleringarna har bidragit till en effektivare finanssektor, vilket r av stor vikt fr effektiviteten och tillvxten i ekonomin som helhet. Framstegen inom IT frbttrar informationssystem och riskmodeller och minskar risken fr felbedmningar och obehagliga verraskningar. Tillkomsten av nya instrument kar marknadens mjlighet att hantera finansiell risk. Det finns dock ocks stabilitetsrisker frknippade med denna utveckling. Avregleringar och internationalisering medfr effektivitetsvinster just p grund av att finanssektorns aktrer ges mjlighet att fritt konkurrera och ta risker. En frutsttning fr att detta ska fungera r d givetvis att aktrerna har den ndvndiga kunskap som krvs fr att korrekt bedma riskerna p en delvis ny och frndrad marknad. S r inte alltid fallet, vilket vi fick anledning att begrunda under den svenska bankkrisen. I Sverige hade fyrtio r av regleringar utarmat kunskaperna i kreditbedmning, bde i bankerna och hos tillsynsmyndigheten. Detta var en viktig faktor bakom bankkrisen, om n inte den enda. Andra lnder har gjort motsvarande erfarenheter. I spren av avregleringar fljer ofta kriser. Detta betyder inte att reformerna var feltnkta, men det belyser det faktum att risken fr felbedmningar kar under den vergngsperiod nr svl privata aktrer som myndigheter har att anpassa sig till nya frutsttningar. Egentligen r de eventuellt kade riskerna i samband med avregleringar bara ett exempel p ett betydligt mer generellt fenomen  att det r svrare att fatta korrekta beslut under perioder av snabb frndring eftersom framtidsprognoser blir mer oskra och historiska erfarenheter och samband mindre anvndbara som vgledning. Historien r fylld av exempel p hur frndrade marknadsfrutsttningar och tekniska framsteg leder till verdrivet uppskruvade frvntningar och felaktiga investeringsbeslut. I 1920-talets USA drevs aktiemarknaden av frvntningar p bland annat radio- och biltillverkare, medan det i 1980-talets Sverige framfrallt handlade om fastighetsbolag. Uppgng och fall inom telekom- och IT-sektorerna det senaste ret r en nyttig pminnelse om hur svrt det faktiskt r att vrdera nya fretag och branscher. Perioder av snabb frndring stller ocks hga krav p de finansiella institutionernas interna riskkontrollsystem. Det r ltt hnt att ivern att snabbt kunna tillhandahlla kunder med nya finansiella produkter gr att ndvndig uppdatering och anpassning av kontrollsystem inte ges den prioritet som krvs. Risker som uppstr till fljd av bristande interna rutiner, s kallade operativa risker, har med rtta uppmrksammats alltmer under senare r. En anledning till detta r sannolikt de mer eller mindre spektakulra fall av operativa missden som faktiskt intrffat, varav Barings-kraschen r det frmsta exemplet. Vad gller den snabba tekniska utvecklingen finns det en fara i att de allt mer frfinade analysverktyg och riskmodeller som nu anvnds invaggar finansiella institutioner i en sorts falsk trygghet. Det rder inget tvivel om att dessa modeller r ett mycket viktigt std fr analys och beslut, men det r viktigt att komma ihg att modeller enbart r mycket grova frenklingar av verkligheten och drfr mste nyttjas med frsiktighet. Fallissemanget av hedgefonden LTCM under hsten 1998 utgr ett allvarligt och frskrckande exempel. LTCM hade tillgng till ngra av vrldens frmsta experter p finansiell riskhantering och hade under flera rs tid uppvisat en hpnadsvckande lnsamhet. nd gick det fel, naturligtvis till en del beroende p positionernas storlek, men sannolikt ocks p en verdriven tillit till de riskmodeller som anvndes. Hndelserna under hsten 1998 franleder ocks en annan reflektion. Med dagens starkt integrerade internationella finansmarknader sprider sig strningar snabbt frn en marknad till en annan. Mnga instrument kan dessutom vara tekniskt komplicerade och ha ett riskinnehll som r svrt att verblicka. I tider av oskerhet tenderar placerare att vilja ut ur sdana instrument och in i skra papper med tydligt riskinnehll och sker likviditet. Vi fr vad som brukar kallas en flykt till kvalitet och likviditet. Detta har de internationella marknaderna hittills kunnat hantera vl. Hur processen skulle utvecklas vid en strre finansiell kris p ngot hll i vrlden vet vi dock nnu mycket lite om. Slutord Den finansiella sektorn i Sverige var till mitten av 1980-talet starkt reglerad. Drefter har den varit freml fr en omfattande avreglering, en kad internationell konkurrens och en snabb teknisk utveckling. Dessutom en genomgripande bankkris. ven om det kan vara svrt att pvisa statistiskt frefaller det vara en rimlig hypotes att produktiviteten stigit en del under denna resa. Mycket av den tekniska utvecklingen handlar dessutom om informationsteknologi, vilket r naturligt i en sektor dr elektronisk handel, genomlysning, prisinformation etc. r centrala begrepp. Internet ppnar nya mjligheter, men IT och "den nya ekonomin" kom sannolikt till finanssektorn redan fr mnga r sedan.
