Title: Monetary policy under financial turmoil
text: Monetary policy during financial turmoil Date: 1998-10-20 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Stora Rantedagen Thank you for the invitation to come and talk about monetary policy here on Big Interest Day. Monetary policy in Sweden, as in many other countries, is focused on achieving price stability. There are two main reasons for this. One reason relates to the contribution of monetary policy to long-term good growth. In the long term, growth in an economy is determined by factors such as the structure and use of physical capital, the development and use of the skills of the workforce, and technological developments. None of these fundamental growth factors can be directly affected by monetary policy. What monetary policy can do, however, is create certainty around the future monetary value and thus indirectly contribute to creating a good climate for growth. The second reason relates to the stability of economic development. When the economy weakens and resource utilisation in the economy falls, inflationary pressures are normally lower. This often leaves room for interest rate cuts. Similarly, there are usually reasons to tighten monetary policy after a period of rising demand if it increases faster than the expansion of the economy's capacity, as the risk of inflation then normally rises. There should be no exaggerated expectations about the possibility of fine-tuning the economy, but a focus on price stability should normally provide better stability in the real economy as well. Therefore, once the price stability objective has been established as a credible benchmark, it can be said that the evolution of inflation rates becomes a kind of temperature gauge of whether resource utilisation is high or low in the economy. However, it is a meter that is not always adequate. Temporary factors of various kinds can influence development. But the correlation between capacity utilisation and inflation is strong. According to Statistics Sweden's latest survey in September 1998, the price level was 0.5 percent lower than in the corresponding period of the previous year. However, this does not mean that the Swedish economy is experiencing deflation in the strict sense. The fact that the average price level falls can have various reasons. Some are good, some are bad for economic development. Since deflation is really a sign that demand is falling, it is important to first note that the falling price level in the Swedish economy is not mainly due to low demand. The reason for the slight fall in the price level is mainly changes in indirect taxes, lower interest rates and low import price increases. These are relative price changes that have an essentially temporary effect on inflation rates. They, in turn, lead to temporarily higher real incomes and are thus based on increased  not reduced  demand. This type of temporary price effect, whether from a positive or negative supply disruption, is not something that monetary policy should normally take into account. Domestic underlying inflation, largely determined by resource utilisation in the Swedish economy was just under 2 percent in September. This reflects the relatively favourable development of demand in the Swedish economy. In the first half of the year, GDP rose by 3 per cent, compared with the corresponding period last year. This means that the trajectory of growth of about 3 percent at an annual rate, which the Swedish economy has had since the summer of 1993, has also continued in 1998. However, this does not mean that all is peace and joy. There are dangers that may be waiting around the corner and that monetary policy must be prepared to face. We are in the midst of a global financial crisis that has changed the picture of future developments in the world economy in a short time. From a situation with expectations of interest rate hikes in, among other things, the US economy to a situation where there is instead talk of world recession and the need for more expansionary monetary policy. Representatives of the US Federal Reserve have even spoken of the financial crisis as the most serious in the post-war period and that there is a greater risk of it worsening rather than mitigating it. Let me now take a quick look back at what has happened and discuss something about what a financial crisis really means. Next, I intend to go into the various factors that the Riksbank has to take a position on when designing Swedish monetary policy. Developments in the world economy The Southeast Asian countries were long described as economic wonders and were widely referred to as the Asian Tigers. With seemingly good economic fundamentals in the form of high growth, high savings and investment ratios and public finances in good order, assets in these countries were seen as good investment objects. There was great confidence that the positive development would continue. Capital thus flowed into the countries. In just half a decade, the external debt of the Southeast Asian countries rose to almost 30% of GDP, which in itself is not a high figure. The problem was that almost two-thirds of this debt was short-term and that the inflow of capital occurred in a short period of time. Contributingly, central banks seemingly absorbed all currency risk via a fixed exchange rate policy. However, the problems were greater than the investors thought. One of these was that the banking systems were not quite ready for the extensive inflows. Foreign capital and strong domestic credit expansion had gone to investments in real estate, shares and directly in companies that did not provide the long-term high returns expected. Eventually, the bubble burst. No clear starting point to the crisis can be deduced, but when doubts finally began to take root among investors in 1997, there was a rapid awakening. Capital flows began to reverse. When the Thai baht was devalued on 2 July 1997, the reaction was even more strong. At the end of July, therefore, the same thing happened in Malaysia. Next in line was the Indonesian currency, which fell on August 14, and the Korean won collapsed on December 16, 1997. My description shows clear similarities with the Swedish crisis in the early 1990s. A central bank that seemingly absorbs currency risk can, under certain circumstances, incentivise covered short-term currency flows. In Sweden, they were called "basket loans". This, combined with a palpable domestic credit expansion, a banking system that is not ripe for a free capital market and a bubble-like economy, often forms the starting point for a financial crisis. It did so in the Swedish case and so also in Southeast Asia. The direct impact on the OECD area was generally not expected to be very large. No one therefore expected that the problems in South-East Asia would pose any real threat to growth in the rest of the world. But what no one really realized was that the crisis in Asia would deepen and spread further across the world via the financial system. In the first place, the already extensive domestic problems in Japan and Russia were further exacerbated by the Asian crisis. When, on August 17, 1998, the Russian government chose to suspend payments on the state debt in rubles, the crisis was accentuated even more and spread to other emerging markets and to the financial the system in the Western world. In a first step, the changed risk assessments meant that investors took the safe before the uncertain and chose assets in historically safe currencies such as the Deutschmark and the dollar. These currencies strengthened at the same time as bond yields fell. When other investments were liquidated to reduce future risks, or reduce the losses that had already occurred, smaller currencies such as the Swedish krona suffered despite good economic fundamentals. Other currencies such as the Canadian, New Zealand and Australian dollars, whose central banks also have inflation targets and floating exchange rates, were also hit. As concerns increased as a result of losses and problems in the financial sector, investors were also increasingly choosing increasingly liquid investments. Long-term bond yields thus came to rise. Pursuing the highest possible degree of liquidity suggests concerns about difficulties in liquidating the positions taken; simply on a concern that the market will cease to function in some respect. What is a financial crisis? What is worrying in the situation that has now arisen is whether the course  contrary to expectations  develops into a global financial crisis in its true sense. What exactly is a real financial crisis and a so-called credit crunch? To understand this, we need to look at the functioning of banks in the national economy. Commercial banks make a living borrowing short-term from the public to, in turn, lend for the long term  a strategy that may seem a little risky. The business concept is largely based on trust, but also on the banks' ability to reduce the uncertainty that exists about borrowers and their ability to fulfill their commitments. In a first step, good borrowers must be separated from the bad ones, a well-founded credit assessment must take place that is continuously followed up. The possible negative effects of the uncertainty can also be limited by the fact that the bank requires collateral for the loans granted. If banks no longer have the ability to reduce this uncertainty and improve, or compensate for, the lack of information they have at the outset, it may lead to banks refraining from providing credit. In such a situation, banks simply can no longer determine who are good and bad borrowers and in that situation refrain from all lending. The supply of liquidity in the economy is thus cut off, which affects lending to consumers and investors as well as to other banks. A credit crunch occurs, i.e. an involuntary reduction in credit lending. This can have spillover effects to the real economy as consumers and entrepreneurs no longer have access to credit to implement their decisions. GDP is falling and unemployment is rising. Long Term Capital och hedgefondernas roll Concerns that bank lending would be affected increased as hedge fund Long Term Capital Management suffered major difficulties. Losses to this fund could have spillover effects to banks in developed countries, partly via the direct exposures to this fund and partly through increased general concern about the ability of other actors to pay. This concern is reflected in the fact that the stock prices around the world for internationally operating banks have fallen more than the general price situation. Long Term Capital started operations in 1994. In the early years, the return was around 40 percent per year. The strategy was built around complicated mathematical models to identify temporary differences between different interest rates and the likelihood with which these differences could return to more normal conditions. However, the turmoil in the financial markets meant that interest rate differentials increased instead of, as the calculations indicated and as assumed, narrowing. The large number of investments made by the fund, which had previously acted as risk diversification and protection, instead led to the losses becoming greater and greater as interest rate differentials widened in almost all markets. The lesson from this seems to be that it doesn't really matter how sophisticated different models are as a basis for investment decisions; abnormally high returns can only be achieved with the help of abnormally high risk-taking. In this context, I cannot help but paraphrase Tage Danielsson's eminent monologue on probabilities: After all, before the collapse of Long Term Capital, it was extremely unlikely that what happened would actually happen. There are still those who think that what happened to Long Term Capital was so incredibly unlikely so really it probably hasn't happened. And you understand that they hesitate because according to the hedge fund's own probability calculations, such an event happens so rarely. And if what happened to Long Term Capital is really true, then the risk of it happening once more is ridiculously small. Actually, it was lucky that it happened. Because then we know that now it is almost certain that it will not happen again. The statistics on the situation in the Swedish financial system indicate that Swedish banks do not have as extensive direct risk exposure to the crisis-hit countries as banks in other countries. Exposures to hedge funds are also small. In all the misery that the banking crisis of the early 1990s brought with it, there is nevertheless the glimmer of light that Swedish banks seem to have been rather cautious about taking too much risk in recent years and also significantly improved their ability to assess risks. However, the Swedish market has also been hit by investors' general reluctance to hold riskier and illiquid assets. This can be seen in the interest rate differences with the assets in the market that are perceived as the most creditworthy, government bonds. The remuneration investors want for accepting to hold assets issued by the private sector, including banks, instead of by the state - such as the difference between so-called interest rate swaps and government bonds - has increased markedly. The ten-year swap spread is currently around 0.8 percentage points in Sweden. The same picture of increased fear of credit and illiquid investments gives the differences between interest rates on mortgage bonds and government bonds, the so-called bospread. The difference has increased by almost half a percentage point since the summer as uncertainty has increased. This can be seen as an expression of the general concern that prevails in the international financial markets and should not be overinterpreted as distrust of the future development of the Swedish economy and of the Swedish financial sector. Reconciliation to the Inflation Report In the latest inflation report, the Riksbank assumed that growth in the OECD area would be between 2 and 2.5 percent in the coming years. As a result, we once again revised down our forecast of the international economy. The main reason was that activity in Japan and the US was expected to be weaker than previously assumed. In the Japanese economy, this was mainly due to confidence problems resulting from the situation in the banking sector. In the US, the international crisis was assumed to have an impact via lower asset prices that hamper consumption and weaker net exports. However, in the euro area, strong domestic demand was expected to lead to favourable growth developments in the coming years. What is the situation now? The clouds of concern are still thick, obscuring the view of how the real economy will develop in the wake of the financial crisis. The financial crisis may have consequences for the world economy through direct effects on production and asset values. The extent to which the consequences will be determined is also the extent to which confidence of households and businesses is declining as a result of the crisis and the extent to which banks are forced to cut back on lending. In the US, household expectations are deteriorating for the third month in a row, an indicator that has previously been closely linked to developments in private consumption. Stock market performance also plays a greater role here than in European economies. Studies show that the previous share rise contributed about a quarter of the increase in consumption between 1995-98. The rise in share prices has led to a reduction in savings. If households try to restore the previously low-depressed saving rates, this could have an impact on domestic demand. In the Japanese economy, the continued management of the new bank support package will be crucial for confidence and growth. Expectations about the future economy are closely linked to how the problems in the banking sector will be addressed. The Japanese economy is a clear example of the difficulties in influencing economic development with political measures at a time when confidence in the long-term solution is low. European developments look generally positive. In the euro area, expectations have not deteriorated significantly, with the exception of a few countries. The impact of stock market development here is less than in the UNITED STATES. However, confidence could be affected if the European industrial economy were to slow down and affect labour market developments. The development of credit will be central to the growth prospects of the world economy. Central banks are aware of this and are closely monitoring the development of banks' solvency and their ability to provide credit. The US rate cut should be seen in the context of concern for both domestic demand and the development of the banking sector. Issues on which the Riksbank must take a position At the end of September, the Riksbank concluded that the repo rate would be left unchanged. This was supported by a relatively positive picture of the Swedish economy, with good growth and inflation gradually returned to the target level during the forecast period. However, the Riksbank pointed to the difficulties in assessing the inflation outlook. If the turmoil in global financial markets were to have real economic effects, this could lead to lower inflation. On the other hand, we saw risks that a permanently weaker krona - which was not due to deteriorating economic fundamentals - could lead to higher inflationary pressures. Although it is too early to make a new forecast, it can probably be stated that most things today indicate that growth in the rest of the world will be revised downwards rather than upwards. Central to this development is likely to be how confidence develops both among households and among market participants and to what extent the situation in the international banking sector has a negative impact on credit lending in different countries. The risks of a weaker world simply seem to have increased. In such a situation, it is of course not reasonable to think it would go unnoticed for the Swedish economy. The next question will be how domestic demand is affected by what is happening at international level. Judging by the latest statistics, households' expectations of the Swedish economy have become somewhat less positive. However, this does not yet seem to imply a deterioration in their expectations of their own economy. The growth rate of loans to enterprises has also slowed down slightly. Although the current trend looks rather strong for e.g. retail sales and for various indicators of private consumption, it is important to remember that the analysis must be forward-looking. The question, then, is how consumption will develop under the new circumstances. At the same time, the exchange rate has, at least so far, developed in a different direction from that on which the Inflation Report was based. The marked weakening of the krona means a strong stimulus of the Swedish economy if it becomes permanent. This is true in a regime of floating exchange rate just like in a fixed exchange rate environment. From the monetary policy horizon, it is the effect on inflation via increased output and eventually increased resource utilisation that is the most interesting, rather than the effects the weakening of the krona may have on import prices. The reason for this is that the pass-through of past import price increases at the consumer price level has been relatively moderate. This is not surprising when medium-term inflation expectations now appear to be fairly firmly anchored around the 2% target. The question that the Riksbank has to decide on is which of the two effects will dominate. If weaker international developments dominate inflation developments, there is a risk that inflation will fall below target within the one to two-year horizon relevant to monetary policy. According to the policy framework, this means a reduction in the repo rate. If the effect of a permanently weaker krona prevails, there is instead a risk that the inflation target will be exceeded. In such a situation, good demand developments and an inflation rate in line with the target can only be achieved at a higher repo rate than today's. Economic developments must therefore be weighed against the effects that the krona exchange rate may have on the inflation outlook. In this context, it may be worth recalling once again that the Riksbank has no target for the level of the exchange rate. What is important is the overall assessment of all factors affecting the inflation outlook, including the international and Swedish economic conditions and the possible stimulus from the exchange rate. Another thing is that we do not feel enthusiasm when the development of the exchange rate is characterized by sharp reversals. The conclusion of monetary policy is that we must closely monitor developments in the real economy, in the financial system and in the financial markets. For now, we are holding off on changing the repo rate, but that conclusion may need to be changed eventually when the picture clears up.

Utvecklingen i vrldsekonomin De sydostasiatiska lnderna beskrevs lnge som ekonomiska under och omnmndes allmnt som de asiatiska tigrarna. I allt det elnde som bankkrisen i brjan av 1990-talet frde med sig finns nd den ljusglimten att de svenska bankerna tycks ha varit tmligen frsiktiga med att ta fr stora risker under senare r och dessutom ptagligt frbttrat sin frmga att bedma risker. Frtroendet kan emellertid komma att pverkas om den europeiska industrikonjunkturen skulle avmattas och pverka utvecklingen p arbetsmarknaden. Utvecklingen av kreditgivningen kommer att vara central fr tillvxtutsikterna i vrldsekonomin. Riksbanken pekade emellertid p svrigheterna att bedma inflationsutsikterna. Om oroligheterna p de globala finansiella marknaderna skulle f realekonomiska effekter skulle detta kunna leda till lgre inflation.  andra sidan sg vi risker fr att en varaktigt svagare krona - som inte berodde p frsmrade ekonomiska grundfrutsttningar - skulle kunna leda till hgre inflationstryck. ven om det r fr tidigt att gra en ny prognos kan man nog konstatera att det mesta idag talar fr att tillvxten i omvrlden snarare kommer att revideras nedt n uppt. Riskerna fr en svagare omvrld frefaller helt enkelt ha kat. I en sdan situation r det naturligtvis inte rimligt att tro det skulle passera obemrkt fr den svenska ekonomins vidkommande. Nsta frga blir hur den inhemska efterfrgan pverkas av det som hnder p det internationella planet. Av den senaste statistiken att dma har hushllens frvntningar om den svenska ekonomin blivit ngot mindre positiva. Detta verkar emellertid inte nnu innebra att deras frvntningar om den egna ekonomin frsmrats. kningstakten fr utlningen till fretagen har ocks minskat ngot. ven om utvecklingen i dagslget ser tmligen stark ut fr t.ex. detaljhandeln och fr olika indikatorer p privat konsumtion, r det viktigt att komma ihg att analysen mste vara framtblickande. Frgan r allts hur konsumtionen kommer att utvecklas under de nya omstndigheterna. Samtidigt har vxelkursen, tminstone hittills, utvecklats i en annan riktning n den som inflationsrapporten byggde p. Den markanta frsvagningen av kronan innebr en kraftig stimulans av den svenska ekonomin om den blir bestende. Detta gller i en regim med flytande vxelkurs precis som i en fast vxelkursmilj. Frn penningpolitisk horisont r det effekten p inflationen via kad produktion och s smningom hjt resursutnyttjande som r den mest intressanta, snarare n de effekter kronfrsvagningen kan f p importpriserna. Sklet till detta r att genomslaget av tidigare importpriskningar i konsumentprisledet varit frhllandevis mttliga. Det r inte frvnande nr de medelfristiga inflationsfrvntningarna numera frefaller ligga tmligen fast frankrade kring mlet p 2 procent. Frgan som Riksbanken har att ta stllning till r vilken av de tv effekterna som kommer att dominera. Om den svagare internationella utvecklingen dominerar inflationsutvecklingen, finns det risk att inflationen hamnar under mlet inom den tidshorisont p ett till tv r som r relevant fr penningpolitiken. Enligt tankeramen fr politiken innebr det en snkning av reporntan. Om effekten via en varaktigt svagare krona vervger, finns istllet risken att inflationsmlet verskrids. I en sdan situation kan en god efterfrgeutveckling och en inflationstakt i linje med mlet bara uppns vid en hgre repornta n dagens. Konjunkturutvecklingen mste sledes vgas mot de effekter kronkursen kan f p inflationsutsikterna. I detta sammanhang kan det vara vrt att ter pminna om att Riksbanken inte har ngot ml fr vxelkursens niv. Det viktiga r den sammantagna bedmningen av alla faktorer som pverkar inflationsutsikterna, inklusive den internationella och svenska konjunkturen och den eventuella stimulansen frn vxelkursen. En annan sak r att vi inte knner entusiasm nr utvecklingen av vxelkursen prglas av tvra kast. Slutsatsen fr penningpolitiken blir att vi noga mste flja utvecklingen i den reala ekonomin, i det finansiella systemet och p de finansiella marknaderna. Fr tillfllet avvaktar vi med att ndra reporntan, men den slutsatsen kan behva ndras s smningom nr bilden klarnar. Title: Monetary policy
text: Monetary policy Date: 1996-03-19 Speaker: Deputy Governor Lars Heikensten Location: Stora Bonddagen in Stockholm Thank you for allowing me to come here and tell you about how the Riksbank views the conditions for monetary policy. Today I intend to talk about three things. Initially, I will briefly say something about the Riksbank's inflation target. The idea is to address some issues that have been aired in recent marketing letters and media. Next, I intend to comment on the effects on the market of the interest rate cuts we have made during the winter. Finally, on the basis of the inflation report, which is only a few weeks old, I intend to say something about monetary policy going forward. Prisstablitetsmalet The Riksbank's task is to safeguard the value of money. That is why we have a target for inflation; the increase in the consumer price index will be limited to 2 per cent. The target is surrounded by a tolerance range of - 1 percent. The purpose of this range is that it should be able to capture various unforeseen disruptions on, for example, the supply side of the economy, such as an increase in oil prices, changes in taxes and subsidies, or for that matter, pure measurement errors. The point is that it is not possible to control inflation so precisely that we end up at 2%. As monetary policy operates with a significant lag in the economy, it is not possible to focus on influencing inflation in the coming weeks or months. Instead, we must focus on inflation a little or even a few years from now. The most important tool in the work is therefore the inflation forecast. When this  with a forecast horizon of one or a few years  shows that inflation is moving down below the inflation target, there may be room to lower interest rates. Similarly, interest rates must be raised when inflation appears to rise above the target level. Unfortunately, we do not know the economy well enough to estimate future inflation using any simple model. Therefore, we work with a large number of indicators. These can be divided into two groups, those relating to demand  and supply conditions, and those that give a picture of expected inflation. It is the interaction between these two factors that determines future inflation. From one point on end, there may be a case for placing more emphasis on certain indicators than others in discussions, speeches, etc. Something special may have happened with the cyclical situation abroad, with the measured expected inflation, with the economy's propensity to inflation, etc. But of course, this does not mean that the other variables that are important for inflation have lost their importance. For example, the value of the krona seen in a slightly longer perspective will always be important for a forecast of inflation in Sweden. Let me turn to one more aspect of the inflation target. In recent months, some analysts have argued that the Riksbank now  unlike before  takes into account the economy. The idea seems to be that if we didn't let go then at least has played down the fight against inflation. However, that is not the case. The fact that the Riksbank is taking the economy into account is nothing new. It lies in the very idea of an inflation target. When the economy shows tendencies to falter, inflationary pressures also decrease. There may then be room to relax monetary policy. Lower interest rates stimulate demand and dampen the economic downturn. The reverse is true when the economy turns upwards. At the same time, the rate hikes needed to dampen inflationary pressures are holding back demand. Monetary policy thus primarily affects inflation via demand, given that inflation expectations are low. Steering with an inflation target automatically means that account is taken of, among other things, the economic picture. But we do not have a target other than 2% inflation. Governance with inflation targets also takes into account another point of view we sometimes encounter, that fiscal and monetary policy should be better coordinated. When making inflation assessments, we take into account the fiscal policy that has been put in place for the next few years. Greater savings lead in various ways  primarily by reducing domestic demand  to a better inflation picture. This increases the chances of pursuing a simpler  or alternatively less tight  monetary policy. Similarly, weaker fiscal policy requires a tighter monetary policy. In principle, a clear division of responsibilities and clear goals  rules if you like  reduce the need for ongoing coordination. This principle is also applicable to the interaction between monetary and fiscal policy. Monetary policy in winter 1996 When the Inflation Report was published a couple of weeks ago, we noted that the inflation picture has improved in recent months. The growing strength of the krona during the autumn has been particularly important for this development. It has only partially taken hold now. In addition, there has been weaker real economic development. The picture also includes that the expected inflation, as measured in surveys, etc., has gradually crept down. A confirmation of this development has been the latest inflation figures. The rate of increase in consumer prices is now at the lower end of the tolerance range. All in all, this information has led us to lower the repo rate a number of times in 1996. In addition to the need to continuously evaluate monetary policy against its effects on the real economy, it is useful to analyse its impact on financial markets. The reason for this is that interest rates and exchange rates are important elements of the transmission mechanism while providing information on the credibility of the policy. It is no easy task to determine how monetary policy in Sweden has affected interest rate and currency developments in recent months. In parallel with the reduction of the repo rate, many other things have happened. In recent years, the krona has developed relatively in parallel with the difference between long-term bond yields in Germany and Sweden. During a significant part of the period during which reductions have been implemented, the krona has developed somewhat weaker than in the autumn. The same applies to the long-term interest rate differential. This in itself is worrying and could indicate that concerns about future inflation have increased since we started to cut interest rates. However, Figure 1 does not give this impression. This shows that, on the whole, krona weakening and long-term interest rate increases have not been correlated with the Riksbank's rate cuts. In fact, quite the opposite is true. The initial effect of the cuts was on several occasions a strengthening of the krona and a decline in long-term interest rates. Rather, what has happened seems to be that Sweden has been affected by a changed mood in the international bond market. It has also spread to the foreign exchange market. Sweden has then, as in 1994 and 1995, been hit more than, for example, ""the core countries"" within the EU. In this, however, we are by no means alone. Other countries that previously had high interest rates have also been affected. However, the rises in interest rates have come at slightly different times. In Sweden's case, mainly when the so-called The Persson plan was presented in January. In the case of Italy and Spain mainly in the case of later political problems. However, compared with the situation in 1994 and 1995, the upturn in long-term interest rate differentials and currency weakening is smaller. This suggests that the situation for the Swedish economy is better. However, the conclusion is not obvious. The same pattern seems to apply to other countries with high interest rates. Either way, the level of the interest rate differential shows that we have some way to go before the financial markets have full confidence in economic policy. In conclusion. We are closely monitoring the effects of the policies we are pursuing on the market. As before, we would wish for a stronger crown. Of course, lower long-term interest rates would also be good for the Swedish economy in several ways. However, the policy we have pursued in recent months seems, if anything, to have contributed in these respects to a move in the desired direction. The inflation picture ahead Let me conclude by briefly commenting on how we view inflation over the next few years and what conclusions we draw from this for monetary policy. My starting point is then the latest Inflation Report. There, we chose to initially highlight three factors that we considered to be particularly strategic for inflation over the next few years. They were the real development and inflation propensity of the economy, as well as the value of the krona. 1. First, the real economy and the business cycle. In this respect, our assessment was that the economy as a whole can be expected to grow below its potential over the next few years. In the export sector, there have been tendencies towards bottleneck problems in the past. These are now declining as a result of slower growth internationally and a stronger krona. Investments have been high. They are likely to grow more slowly in 1996, but a further expansion of the production apparatus seems likely. The home economy is more difficult to assess. Therefore, the Inflation Report is discussed at a relatively detailed pace. The most likely, as we see it, is a certain, but subdued rise in consumption. In these parts of the economy, however, capacity utilisation is initially low. Thus, it is difficult to see any major inflation risks from the demand side of the economy over the next few years. 2. The Inflation Report also discusses the propensity for inflation in the economy. There is circumstantial evidence that this has decreased. In that case, it would not be surprising since the same was true in several other industrialized countries in the 90s. The Swedish economy has undergone major changes in recent years. There are arguments that there have been improvements in the functioning of the economy  increased competition, etc. which should have reduced the propensity for inflation. One example is what has happened in the housing sector. But in at least one other area  that of wage formation  we know that the problems have by no means been solved. Compared with the forecasts made in Sweden a few years ago, the economy's growth has become higher at the same time as inflation has become lower. This indicates  as do the falling inflation expectations  that the propensity for inflation has become less. 3. The value of the krona has strengthened significantly since last summer. This is important and contributes significantly to the fact that inflation has fallen over the past six months. As we have pointed out in various contexts, short-term changes in the value of the krona are not decisive for monetary policy. On the other hand, it is clear that the Riksbank's policy would be affected by whether the krona would become stronger or weaker more permanently. This would have an impact on the state of activity in the economy and thus on the price picture, unless countervailing measures are taken. Seen from a long-term perspective, the krona must be judged to be undervalued. As we see it, this creates the conditions for an appreciation. Whether this comes about or not depends on how confidence in economic policy and, as I have just mentioned, the international environment develops. In this context, it is important to underline that the demand for discipline in economic policy remains high. There must be no doubt that the Riksbank protects the value of money. Nor is there room for any ambiguity from the Riksdag and the government when it comes to the state's finances. The convergence programme presented by the Government last year stipulates six-monthly follow-ups of budgetary policy. It is crucial that this programme is pursued. In the Inflation Report, we concluded that the conditions for inflation in line with our target over the next few years are good. Against this background, we considered that there could be some scope for continued easing of monetary policy. This conclusion there is no need to change. That is why today we have lowered the repo rate by 25 basis points.

Penningpolitiken vintern 1996 I samband med att inflationsrapporten publicerades fr ett par veckor sedan konstaterade vi att inflationsbilden under de senaste mnaderna blivit bttre. Rnteuppgngarna har dock kommit vid lite olika tidpunkter. I Sveriges fall frmst nr den s.k. Perssonplanen presenterades i januari. I Italiens och Spaniens fall frmst vid senare politiska problem. Title: Jansson at the Riksdag Committee on Finance: We are safeguarding the inflation target
text: Jansson at the Riksdag Committee on Finance: We are safeguarding the inflation target The high inflation creates problems. It erodes purchasing power- especially for the least well-off - and makes it difficult for both households and businesses to plan their finances. Therefore, the Riksbank, which has been given the task by the Riksdag of keeping inflation low and stable, must now act to bring inflation down. Low and stable inflation provides a foundation for good economic development. This was the message from Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Per Jansson when they took part in a hearing on current monetary policy at the Riksdag Committee on Finance. Date: 20/10/2022 09:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Per Jansson Published 20/10/2022 The inflation target is worth defending Per Jansson: "We will bring inflation down to the target level- and this is a promise, not a forecast." However, he emphasized that there are better and worse paths to get there. "The best scenario would be if we can return inflation to the target with relatively cautious rate increases. This is also contained in our forecast, where the policy rate peaks at 2.5 per cent. But a lot also depends on the support for this development in price-setting and wage formation and the formulation of fiscal policy." The inflation target has contributed to a good economic development in Sweden, he continued and pointed out, among other things, that real wages have increased more than three times faster per year since the inflation target was introduced in 1995, compared with the period 1970-1994. "The inflation target is worth defending, and I hope that we will cooperate to do so."

Title: Jansson: We can see progress in the fight against inflation, although there is considerable uncertainty
text: Jansson: We can see progress in the fight against inflation, although there is considerable uncertainty "The inflation target has contributed to the fact that we have had a very good development in real wages for almost 30 years, and it also needs to be defended going forward. The economic policy framework has so far met the challenge of higher inflation well. I firmly believe that it will continue to do so and that inflation can soon return to 2 per cent." This was the message from Deputy Governor Per Jansson, speaking today at the National Mediation Institute's conference on socio-economic conditions for wage formation in Stockholm. Date: 25/10/2023 13:30 Speaker: Deputy Governor Per Jansson Place: The National Mediation Institute Published 25/10/2023 The Riksbank's increases in the policy rate affect households with mortgages in a very concrete way. The costs of inflation can be perceived as more diffuse and are more difficult to grasp. But high inflation erodes purchasing power for everyone, especially those who already have small margins, pointed out Mr Jansson. "And the most important thing is that people maintain confidence in the inflation target when setting prices and wages," he added. "If we allow inflation to remain high for a long time, we may lose confidence in the inflation target. Then it will eventually be necessary to take more severe action with Per Jansson, deputy governor. the interest rate to regain credibility. And this would entail very large real economic costs in the form of higher unemployment and lower production," said Mr Jansson, and pointed to developments in the United States in the early 1980s as a deterrent. "Safeguarding the inflation target is thus a way of taking the real economy into account, as it will provide better economic development in the long term." Inflation is now on the way down. But Mr Jansson pointed out that the main reason why CPIF inflation has fallen so much is the sharp fall in energy prices. "Disregarding energy prices, inflation is still almost 5 percentage points above the inflation target. And the inflationary pressure here and now is still too high." Mr Jansson said that conditions were essentially favourable for inflation to continue falling. The pandemic-related imbalances between supply and demand have declined and monetary policy has been tightened rapidly and firmly. According to the Riksbank's latest forecast, the policy rate may be raised somewhat further. "But the interest rate path shows that we are making progress in the fight against inflation, and that we are approaching the policy rate peak. Having said this, there is still considerable uncertainty and we need to be prepared to change our monetary policy plan at all times." Mr Jansson emphasised that the fight against inflation is being facilitated to a large extent by our economic policy frameworks. "Considerable responsibility in fiscal policy and wage formation has not prevented inflation from rising relatively much. But it should reduce the risk of inflation rising further or becoming entrenched at a high level. It is also crucial that companies' pricing behaviour returns to its previous pattern as quickly as possible. The better the interaction to bring inflation down, the less we will need to increase the interest rate."

Title: Jansson: The inflation outlook is much brighter
text: Jansson: The inflation outlook is much brighter "My view of the situation has changed considerably. I have become increasingly convinced that inflationary pressures are now actually declining." These comments were made by Deputy Governor Per Jansson when he visited Malmo today, and spoke about the Riksbank's latest policy rate decision at Handelsbanken. Date: 08/12/2023 12:30 Speaker: Deputy Governor Per Jansson Place: High Court, Malmo Published 08/12/2023 "One should be cautious about drawing far-reaching conclusions from individual monthly outcomes. But there is nevertheless no denying that the latest outcome for October contains a large number of changes in the price picture that clearly indicate that inflationary pressures are now easing/' Mr Jansson continued. According to Mr Jansson, the fact that the inflation picture is now brighter than before is also supported by the fact that companies' price plans have been adjusted downwards, that producer prices for consumer goods are not increasing as quickly and that international inflation has become lower. "The current cooling of the Swedish Per Jansson, deputy governor. economy also reduces the risks of inflation becoming entrenched at too high a level." According to Mr Jansson, the recent appreciation of the krona is another factor that reduces the risk of an unmanageable inflation trend: "While one should be cautious about assuming that the favourable development of the krona will continue, it does provide some breathing space for the time being." Mr Jansson emphasised that conducting monetary policy is always a balancing act between waiting for more inflation to be able to draw more reliable conclusions and acting reasonably promptly so as not to end up "behind the curve". "I think that there is now sufficient information for not raising the policy rate further. The fact that the policy-rate path continues to rise somewhat at the beginning of next year indicates, however, that we are fully prepared to do more if it proves necessary. Hopefully, we will not need to, although of course you never can be certain," concluded Mr Jansson.

Title: Perspectives on monetary policy
text: Perspectives on monetary policy Date: 1996-06-03 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Monetary Policy Forum For the fourth year in a row, the Riksbank, in collaboration with SNS, is organizing the Monetary Policy Forum. It has now become a tradition, which is a good thing. An open discussion of monetary policy and its conditions is essential for the Riksbank and for the economic policy debate in general. Last year's Monetary Policy Forum was held on 11 April 1995. The repo rate was then 8.34 percent, the long-term interest rate was 11.5 percent and the krona's rate was above 130 in TCW terms. The high long-term interest rate and the weak krona that we had at the time characterized my speech. I argued that this was an expression of a lack of confidence in Sweden's ability to pursue a stability-oriented economic policy. My conclusion was that, through a sustainable economic policy geared towards price stability and sound public finances, we could reverse the trend. Over the past year, confidence in economic policy has increased. The convergence programme, with its six-monthly checkpoints, has contributed to an increase in confidence in budgetary policy. The Riksbank has shown that its inflation target is serious. This, in turn, has led to the long-term interest rate falling by about 3 percentage points to around 8.50 and the krona appreciated by over 10 percent to between 114 and 116 (TCW index) compared to the situation at the time of last year's Monetary Policy Forum. In addition, it has been possible to lower the repo rate by about 2.4 percentage points to 6.50 percent from January this year. I am going to return today to the discussion on the importance of confidence in monetary policy freedom of action. The reason why I choose this theme for my speech is that we now have a perspective on past developments. Hopefully, this will allow us to better analyse and discuss the different trade-offs that monetary policy sometimes faces. When it comes to the more up-to-date monetary policy, I intend to be brief because the Riksbank will present the second inflation report of the year the day after tomorrow. What is meant by ""confidence in economic policy""" ? Let me begin by reiterating a couple of basic conditions that are relevant to my further reasoning. When representatives of the Riksbank use the expression ""confidence in economic policy"", we mean the degree of confidence of the various actors in the economy in the will and ability of economic policy to sustainably maintain price developments in line with the inflation target. It is thus about the expectations of future inflation, i.e. what inflation do the actors of the economy expect in the 1, 2, 5 or 10 year term, and how these expectations relate to the 2% inflation target. Inflation is ultimately a monetary phenomenon. In order for inflation to remain at a sustained level, regardless of whether it is at a high or low level, the involvement of the Central Bank is required. Temporary ups or downs in inflation may occur, but in the long run it is the central bank's monetary policy that determines inflation developments. Therefore, confidence in low-inflation policy - and the level of inflation expectations - is inevitably about the view of how the central bank will handle monetary policy in the future. However, the work of the Central Bank may be more or less difficult. Distrust can arise if the country has an unfavourable history in the field of inflation. The existence of budget deficits is another factor that weakens confidence in a long-term stability-oriented policy. This is not because deficits in themselves lead to inflation. The link is more indirect and concerns how such deficit and debt problems are expected to be handled. Fears can be created that the central bank, in one way or another, will be forced to accommodate the disruptions that a mutually inconsistent policy entails. The historical pattern, in terms of how inflation and budgetary policies have been handled in the past, plays an important role in shaping the perceptions of the economy's various actors about the future. A lack of confidence in a stability-oriented economic policy - and consequently higher expected inflation than the authorities say they are aiming for - takes various forms. First, inflation expectations tend to become self-fulfilling. If households and businesses expect higher inflation, it affects their actions. In the labour market, employers and wage and salary earners can conclude agreements that are not compatible with the level of inflation sought by the authorities. Employers expect to be able to charge the higher costs in the form of higher prices, while wage earners want to guard their purchasing power. The same thing happens in the goods market. Producers are raising their prices because they expect sales to increase anyway, while consumers are willing to pay because they expect to be able to compensate themselves with higher wages. Secondly, inflation expectations have an impact on pricing in the financial markets. Although prices in the new type of global financial market that has emerged over the past decade sometimes temporarily deviate from more underlying factors, they are still, in the slightly longer term, a gauge of the confidence that exists in the ability to pursue stability-oriented economic policies. If savers and investors fear that inflation will be high in the future, they build in premiums for this in bond and exchange rates. Investors simply want to guard against the perceived uncertainty. This results in high long-term interest rates and a weak currency. What are the consequences of a lack of credibility? Let us do the thought experiment that the central bank ignores any credibility problems and instead pursues its policies with the aim of achieving short-term growth stimulus. Such a policy may give the impression that the central bank's tolerance for higher inflation in the medium and longer term has increased. This, in turn, gives the impression that the concerns expressed by various actors in survey responses or in pricing in the financial markets are coming true. This could then lead to the higher expected inflation becoming self-fulfilling and then even rising further. Long-term interest rates may then be established at a high level or rise to higher levels. Attempts to increase nominal demand when inflation expectations are high risk leading to increased actual inflation rather than real growth. In order to have any effect at all on growth, in a situation where expectations are adjusted upwards, new and unexpected monetary stimulus is constantly needed. In the worst case scenario, this could mean that the price level rises without limit. Then when inflation, sooner or Later, having to adjust back to more reasonable levels, it will be even more difficult to break inflation expectations, which risks leading to weaker growth. The result of a lack of credibility is thus reduced opportunities for high and stable growth and employment. We come here to the paradox of monetary policy. It means that the more credible and successful a central bank is in the long run in keeping inflation under control, the greater the chances in the short term of also taking into account growth aspects. The reverse tends to also apply: the more importance a central bank attaches to short-term growth stimulus in relation to price stability, the worse the chances of achieving long-term favourable growth. Confidence in the ability to maintain price stability is therefore essential for stable and favourable economic developments in both the short and long term. The main question is thus how the central bank can create such confidence. What should the central bank do in case of lack of credibility? To counter a lack of credibility, a central bank can have a clear objective for policy and work to achieve it. The goal can either be defined by the Central Bank and then actively supported by the political system, which is the situation in our country, among others, or, as in some other countries, be imposed a goal by the government or parliament. It is not an end in itself to limit one's own freedom of action by means of, for example, an inflation target or, for that matter, a fixed exchange rate. Nor can it be said with certainty that just one, two or three percent inflation or just a certain given exchange rate are optimal values for contributing to the best functioning economy possible. An unambiguous objective should be seen primarily as a means of stabilising expectations of economic policy. When the actors over time also see that the central bank acts with the key interest rate so that the goal is achieved, credibility gradually increases. Paradoxically, as I pointed out earlier, it also gives us greater freedom of action for monetary policy in the short term. No one believes - once there is credibility - that monetary policy easing in the event of a cyclical downturn will result in inflation later in the business cycle being allowed to rise above target. Therefore, inflation expectations are also not affected, long-term interest rates are consequently not rising and the currency remains broadly stable. Of course, situations may arise when the mutual inconsistency of economic policy becomes so great that monetary policy and its objectives are overloaded. This happened, for example, in the autumn of 1992, when the marginal interest rate was forced up to 500% and it was still not possible to maintain the fixed exchange rate. At times, too, under the floating exchange rate regime, we have had a general discussion that monetary policy would - as has been put it - break the economy and threaten both growth and employment. With an inflation target, however, weaker growth means that demand-side inflation risks will fade and often that expected inflation will fall. This rather reduces the need for tight monetary policy. On the part of the Riksbank, it was argued - when that discussion was at its most intense last year - that as long as the sa-nization of the state's finances is continued and gradually leads to increased confidence in economic policy in general, monetary policy will not be overloaded either. What has happened in the last year? As I pointed out at the outset, the credibility of the inflation target has increased since we last year met in conjunction with the Monetary Policy Forum. Long-term interest rates have fallen and the krona has strengthened, which is a sign of that. Various surveys also show that more and more people believe that the Riksbank will meet its target in the next few years. Today, economic policy appears to be consistent in a completely different way than before. Expectations for the slightly longer term have also fallen, although there is room for further improvement. The margin against Germany, for example, is still around 200 points, which is twice as high as in our neighbouring country, Finland. When the inflation report in November last year was presented, many monetary policy debaters expected the Riksbank to start lowering its key interest rate. The information available at the time indicated that inflation in 1996 and 1997 would be slightly above the 2% target. This is also underlined by the fact that most other - not to say all others - economic analysts also did not see the conditions for the inflation target to be met. A reduction in the key interest rate could then have created the impression that the Riksbank's tolerance for inflation had increased and that the target was not seriously intended. By all accounts, the credibility of the case was strengthened in late autumn. Long-term interest rates fell from mid-November until January by just over 80 basis points and the margin against Germany by just over 50 basis points. Even the expectations as they can be deduced in various surveys indicate the same thing. In January this year, the Riksbank began lowering its repo rate. This was done in the light of a continued improvement in the inflation outlook. These were also helped by continued falling inflation expectations, a slowdown in the economy and a stronger krona. Since then, the repo rate has been lowered from 8.91 to 6.5 per cent, i.e. by just over 2.4 percentage points. It has affected the short-term interest rate to about the same extent. On the other hand, long-term interest rates remain at roughly the same levels as they did in January. In interpreting this, however, it should be borne in mind that long-term interest rates in the rest of the world have risen over the same period. On the other hand, for the first time in a long time, it has not driven up Swedish long-term interest rates. The margin against Germany has instead decreased by another 40 basis points. This is a sign that credibility has developed well even at a time when the international interest rate situation on the long side has developed unfavourably. At the same time, as I pointed out earlier, there is room for further improvement. Therefore, long-term interest rates may continue to fall further. In this context, fiscal progress towards balance remains a key factor. The reduction in the repo rate, which has taken place at a relatively rapid pace, has thus been possible without the credibility being questioned. On the contrary, it has continued to improve. There is therefore a high probability that the reduction in the repo rate will have a beneficial effect on growth in the Swedish economy in a way that would not have been the case if credibility had been unfavourably affected. The reception among market participants has been essentially good. However, I have seen in some market letters that there is speculation that it is now the economy and only the business cycle - and consequently not credibility - that governs monetary policy. In the past, the discussion was typically often about the fact that it was only credibility and the crown, but not growth, that ruled. Both of these approaches are misleading. Let me remind you once again that it is the inflation outlook that underpins monetary policy decisions. Roughly speaking, it can be said that the inflation outlook is always determined by three factors. These are the supply and demand conditions in the economy and inflation expectations. The crown comes into the picture in that it touches both of these two. A permanently weaker or stronger krona affects demand in the competitive sector and thus gives rise to changes in the so-called . the output gap. But the krona's performance is also an indicator of how inflation expectations or credibility are developing. However, it is not the krona's short-term movements in the market that matter, but more lasting changes. However, the improved credibility has meant a better environment for monetary policy. As inflation expectations stabilise around the inflation target, real economic developments become more important for the course of inflation compared to a situation where expected inflation is well above target and when the krona is severely undervalued. Conclusion Let me conclude by saying that confidence in economic policy has increased since last year's Monetary Policy Forum was held in April 1995. This has been done through a combination of increased confidence in the consolidation of government finances and by the Riksbank showing that the inflation target is taken seriously. This has been reflected, among other things, in the fact that short and long-term interest rates have fallen, the yield curve has not only gained a positive slope, but that it has also moved downwards more or less in parallel. In addition, the previous undervaluation of the krona has been reduced. Various types of surveys also indicate that inflation expectations have come down. The previous lack of credibility for Swedish economic policy in general meant that the expected inflation was too high and that the risks were real for the inflation target to be exceeded. This led to high market interest rates in the Swedish economy, a strongly undervalued krona and also a relatively high repo rate. The changes for the better that have taken place mean that the conditions for sustainable and balanced growth in the Swedish economy have increased. This relationship often comes into the background in the general discussion. The fact that the international economy is swinging up and down is not a new phenomenon, the question is instead whether the Swedish economy has the ability to fully benefit from international trade and receive dividends in the form of increased employment and rising real incomes. At the macroeconomic level, conditions have undoubtedly improved considerably over the past year. Also in terms of the structure of the economy, many measures that are moving in the right direction have been taken since the late 1980s. A discussion is now also under way on how to improve the functioning of the labour market. Given the high unemployment and wage increases in the last round of collective bargaining, it is reasonable to focus the discussion on just that. From January, the Riksbank has been able to reduce its repo rate at a relatively rapid pace without having a negative impact on confidence in monetary policy. On the contrary, inflation expectations appear to be still adjusting downwards, as shown in various surveys. The Riksbank's assessment of the inflation outlook for the coming years, which also includes an assessment of real economic developments, also indicates that we have a good chance of achieving the inflation target. Against this background, there may therefore continue to be some scope for easing monetary policy.

I januari i r brjade Riksbanken snka reporntan. Det gjordes i ljuset av fortsatt frbttrade inflationsutsikter. Till dessa bidrog fortsatt fallande inflationsfrvntningar, en uppbromsning av konjunkturen och en starkare krona. Sedan dess har reporntan snkts frn 8,91 till 6,5 procent, dvs med drygt 2,4 procentenheter. Det har pverkat den korta rntan i ungefr samma utstrckning. Sannolikheten r drfr hg att snkningen av reporntan kommer att ha en gynnsam effekt p tillvxten i svensk ekonomi p ett stt som inte skulle ha varit fallet om trovrdigheten hade pverkats ofrmnligt. Dessutom har den tidigare undervrderingen av kronan reducerats. Ocks olika typer av enktunderskningar tyder p att inflationsfrvntningarna kommit ner. Den tidigare bristande trovrdigheten fr svensk ekonomisk politik i stort innebar att den frvntade inflationen lg fr hgt och att riskerna var ptagliga fr att inflationsmlet skulle verskridas. Det ledde till hga marknadsrntor i svensk ekonomi, en starkt undervrderad krona och ven till en frhllandevis hg repornta. De frndringar till det bttre som skett innebr att frutsttningarna fr en uthllig och balanserad tillvxt i svensk ekonomi har kat. Detta frhllande kommer ofta i bakgrunden i den allmnna diskussionen. Frn januari har Riksbanken kunnat dra ner reporntan i relativt snabb takt utan att det pverkat frtroendet fr penningpolitiken i negativ riktning. Title: Perspectives on price stability policy
text: Perspectives on price stability policy Date: 1996-09-26 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Stora Rantedagen On Tuesday, the Riksbank presented its Inflation Report. This means that our view of the Swedish economy, inflation developments and interest rate policy in the coming period is fairly well known. In contrast to the more short-term analysis, I would therefore like today to devote my speech to discussing monetary policy and the fight against inflation in a somewhat broader perspective. There are further reasons to make such an overview. Today, it is exactly 65 years ago that Sweden was the first country to start focusing its monetary policy on price stability. Late on Saturday, September 26, 1931, the Riksbank and the government announced that the gold standard would be abandoned. Instead, it was replaced by an objective of price stability. This meant that the ideas that the internationally renowned Swedish economist Knut Wicksell had already launched on April 14, 1898 at a lecture in the National Economic Association came to fruition. Sweden thus became the first country to adopt an open objective for monetary policy in terms of general price developments. Knut Wicksell argued for a stable price level. This meant that neither inflation nor deflation would be allowed. Today, explicit targets for price development are public domain and something that a number of countries have embraced. The discussion on price stability is thus still relevant today, almost 100 years after Wicksell gave his talk and exactly 65 years since a price stability objective was first introduced. During the 1980s and 1990s, economic policies around the world have focused on bringing inflation down to low levels. A high degree of price stability has now been achieved in many countries. Against this background, an interesting international discussion is currently taking place among leading academics about the next steps in this process. What level of inflation should really be sought? Is it appropriate to strive for price stability in the strict sense of the word, i.e. a stable price level in which the overall price level of the economy neither rises nor falls? With such an approach, a period of inflation is also corrected with some deflation, so that over time prices really develop stably. Another possibility is to strive for 0 percent inflation, where the central bank ignores the deviations of past periods. The price level will then not be completely stable. A third is to accept a minimal inflation rate of, say, 1, 2 or 3 percent. The optimal inflation rate In recent years, a very large number of studies have been presented on the harmful effects of inflation on production and employment. The aim has been to try to define and quantify its negative impact. The results so far from these studies suggest that inflation in the range of 1 to 3 percent seems desirable. In this range, the harmful effects of inflation are minimised. There is no support for the idea that high inflation would lead to favourable output developments. Nor can one say with today's knowledge that a inflation rates of 0% would be preferable to a very low but positive inflation rate. However, the discussion on price stability continues because most of the studies that have been done have necessarily been based on data for the last few decades when inflation has been relatively high. In general, three arguments are usually used against price stability in the strict sense: the first argument is that official consumer price indices overestimate developments in the cost of living by not taking full account, inter alia, of changes in quality, the introduction of new products and substitution in favour of products whose relative prices have fallen. For the UNITED STATES, this margin of error has been estimated at around 2 percent at most and for Canada at around half a percent. The study carried out in Europe - by the Bank of England - shows an overestimation of between 0.4 and 0.8 percent. For Sweden, there has so far been no more accurate assessment of how much the consumer price index may overestimate the cost of living. The second argument is that nominal wages are stiff downwards. If inflation is zero, nominal wages are assumed to fall if real wage reductions are required in connection with transition problems in companies and industries. However, this assumes that productivity does not increase in the current part of the economy. In such a situation, a certain degree of inflation would be required for wage rigidity not to act as a disincentive to production and employment. However, this argument is not without objection because the studies are based on starting points from the inflationary economies of recent decades. In a world of low inflation, it is by no means certain, some say, that wage cuts in special cases would be impossible. It is also important to look at the entire cost of wages, i.e. also at the benefits that are paid, and not only at the hourly wage. Already today, it often occurs that various types of benefits are reduced if the company goes bad. The third argument is that the central bank cannot cut its key interest rate more than 0%. If inflation is at 0%, it is not possible to achieve a negative short-term real interest rate in the event of a severe recession. This increases the risk of deflation and falling production. Therefore, inflation should slightly exceed 0 percent. This argument, too, has not been considered unobjectionable, since the Japanese example, which has resulted in a certain fall in prices, has been dealt with with low but positive key interest rates. The Japanese economy now appears to be emerging from its recession. In addition, the exchange rate and its development should also be taken into account in the analysis, as well as fiscal policy, which means that economic policy has the tools to deal with a given situation if interest rate policy were to be characterised by a constraint. If, on the basis of current knowledge, it is not appropriate to strive for 0% inflation, where should inflation lie? Many studies have shown the harmful effects of inflation. Inflation hides the economic signals posed by changes in relative prices and creates general uncertainty about the future. That, in turn, reduces the efficiency of the economy and the development of production. Inflation also leads to an arbitrary redistribution of income and wealth. Many of the costs of inflation have long been known. This is especially true of the problems of high inflation. However, the full costs even at low or moderate inflation have been more difficult to quantify. It is only in recent years that they have been able to be caught. There are therefore good reasons to seek to achieve and maintain very low inflation. The Swedish inflation target of 2 percent seems well balanced in light of the many studies that have come out in recent years on the harmful effects of inflation and what is considered the "optimal" inflation rate. For the time being, I do not believe that we are making too much linguistic error if the swedish inflation target of 2% is used to use the concept of price stability. The Swedish inflation target, which is also surrounded by a tolerance limit, has a specific property that also originates from Knut Wicksell. It is that it is just as important to avoid undercutting as it is to exceed the target. This in turn means that in the governance of monetary policy there is implicitly built into account the development of production in the economy, which has sometimes been called for in the Swedish debate. For example, it has been said that the Riksbank has too one-sidedly focused its policy on inflation. The development of production in relation to available capacity is an important factor determining the development of inflation. If growth becomes too high, it risks leading to inflation rising and moving above the inflation target. This calls for a tighter monetary policy. Conversely, weaker growth and a large output gap mean that inflation will fall below target, correspondingly leading to a more expansionary monetary policy. In this way, we see how monetary policy with an inflation target aims to smooth out excessive fluctuations in growth so that it becomes more sustainable and ends up more in line with the expansion of production capacity and the degree of available resources in the economy. The Swedish experience Since 1992, Swedish inflation has averaged between 2 and 3%. This is in stark contrast to the approximately 8 percent per annum average in the 1970s and 1980s. Thus, inflation has been established at significantly lower levels than in the last two decades. However, the decline in inflation was long viewed by firms, households and financial actors not to be fully lasting . It was not until 1996 that inflation expectations in the slightly longer term began to move towards the inflation target. It is also only when the economy as a whole has adjusted to the fact that the decline in inflation will also be lasting that there can be reason to expect positive results from the new low-inflation regime. There are probably two reasons why it took until the beginning of 1996 for inflation expectations to be seriously affected. One is the previously weak government finances and the other is Sweden's poor resume in the area of inflation since the 1970s. Deficits in public finances create doubts about the central bank's endurance in the fight against inflation. With permanent deficits and an ever-growing government debt, the central bank is expected sooner or later to come under pressure to pursue a more expansionary monetary policy. Some of the phenomena that can occur in the context of fiscal problems and thus lingeringly high inflation expectations are that excessive wage increases create employment problems even if the economy grows. In addition, a weak exchange rate combined with high long-term interest rates tends to create a two-tier economy, which is growing slowly. In Sweden, we have also clearly seen the reverse, i.e. how improved government finances lead to falling inflation expectations, a stronger exchange rate and lower long-term interest rates. This, in turn, provides better conditions for more evenly distributed, and thus higher, growth in the future in the various subsectors of the economy. The history of inflation plays an important role in the credibility of the authorities in the field of inflation. One way of accelerating the credibility of a reorientation of economic policy is to implement structural changes that facilitate adjustment. As a result, inflation expectations can be shaped more by future factors rather than historical developments. In view of the relatively high wage increases we have in 1996, despite high levels of unemployment, measures to improve wage formation and the functioning of the labour market may support price stability policy in the slightly longer term. In the long run, there is also a clear link to growth and employment. Conclusion My main points here today are essentially going in a positive direction. They can be summarized in the following points: There is tangible support in the many studies that have come out in recent years that low inflation contributes to creating the conditions for higher production and employment. The many studies in recent years suggest that inflation around 2% strikes an appropriate balance between, on the one hand, the argument that the consumer price index slightly overestimates actual cost-of-living developments and, on the other hand, the harmful effects that can occur even at a fairly low inflation rate. What has happened in recent years is that the credibility of Sweden as a country with low inflation may now seriously be on the verge of being established. This can be supported by the continuation of firm fiscal policies and by the structural measures in the area of the labour market that may follow the current discussion. With persistently low inflation, many of the harmful effects that have characterized the Swedish economy in recent decades may subside and production and employment may grow faster. However, how long it may take before we can more clearly perceive these effects is difficult to say today.
