Title: Perspectives on the Swedish economy
text: Perspectives on the Swedish economy Date: 1999-04-13 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Malmo Borssallskap A central bank is tasked with making and distributing money and preserving its value. If the Riksbank pursues an overly expansionary monetary policy, i.e. sets the repo rate lower than is compatible with the national economic balance, the economy threatens to overheat in the long run. Demand increases and if production capacity is not sufficient, prices rise and inflation occurs. If, on the other hand, the Riksbank pursues too tight a policy, i.e. sets the repo rate too high, it could lead to falling demand and deflation. Both inflation and deflation are equally undesirable. It is against this background that the Riksdag has instructed the Riksbank to independently be responsible for the task of maintaining a fixed monetary value. We have defined it as inflation of 2%, with a tolerance up or down of 1 percentage point. Thus, it is developments in Sweden and the inflation outlook here that are at the center of the trade-offs around monetary policy, not what other central banks do or do not do with their key interest rates. There is reason to remind ourselves of this. Once a low-inflation regime is established and the public has set itself up for long-term low price rises, inflation is determined by how demand in the economy relates to production capacity. This means that a monetary policy guided by an inflation target tends in the long run to smooth out the economy's fluctuations around the long-term growth path. Since deviations affect inflation developments, the inflation target for monetary policy will mean that interest rates change to bring demand back to the long-term path. It helps to make growth more sustainable and stable. However, one should beware of having excessive expectations of the possibility of fine-tuning the economy with stabilization policies. Since high and variable inflation creates uncertainty in connection with economic decisions and therefore tends to impair long-term growth, it is reasonable to expect that low and stable inflation, if any, will improve long-term growth opportunities. Monetary policy can, by all accounts, affect the growth trajectory in an indirect way. Monetary policy, on the other hand, cannot directly affect the long-term growth path. Instead, it is determined by the growth of the population and capital stock, technological development and how efficiently the economy's resources are used in production. All these factors are beyond the direct control of the Riksbank. However, the Riksbank must have a rough idea of where the actual growth path lies so that demand in the economy, which monetary policy can influence, can be adjusted accordingly. As I have just said, deviations from this trajectory are a major cause of either inflation or deflation. A major problem, however, is that we do not have a directly readable measure of the long-term growth trajectory. For day-to-day monetary policy, we must therefore rely on various indicators and work gradually with the repo rate. Therefore, it is useful to sometimes stop and study the longer trends in terms of growth. I'm going to do that tonight. My speech is therefore entitled: Perspectives on the Swedish economy. Surprisingly low inflation and rising productivity in the 1990s Since the late 1980s, there has been a conscious effort by virtually the entire political system in our country to bring about a low inflation rate. During the 1970s and 80s, the annual inflation average was 8 percent. During the 1990s, the corresponding annual average has been around 3 percent, and from 1993 at about 2 percent. At the same time, probably all forecasters, including the Riksbank, have experienced that models based on historical correlations almost consistently overestimated the actual outcome for inflation. An important reason for this and the fact that in recent years it has been possible to reconcile a relatively high growth rate with a maintained low inflation in the Swedish economy is, of course, the overcapacity that existed and still exists in the Swedish economy after the recession in the early 1990s. However, the low inflation is not exclusively due to overcapacity. The picture also includes changes of a more structural nature that the Swedish economy has undergone. Not least, the explicit inflation target announced in January 1993 can be expected to influence price and wage formation. Economic actors are now expecting a low rate of price increase, which affects their behaviour. Other economic policy measures of a structural nature were also taken in the second half of the 1980s and 1990s. There are also many indications that international competitive pressure has intensified, for example as a result of increased opportunities to locate even relatively advanced production in countries with significantly lower wages than in the Western world. Although this is strictly speaking a series of one-off effects, increased competition can have an impact on global inflationary pressures over a long period of time. In the same direction, increased international trade, EMU and various liberalisations are working. That inflation has been low and that it is likely to continue to be so is shown in the Riksbank's latest inflation report. But let's take a closer look at the real economy to see if developments in the 1990s deviate from long-term developments. One observation that is interesting is that labour productivity has been higher in the 1990s compared to the two previous decades. Between 1974 and 1993, for example, labour productivity grew by about 1.4% per year on average. Since 1994, the corresponding figure has been around 1.9%. It can be argued that we have experienced an economic upturn since the summer of 1993 and that it is therefore not surprising that productivity is then increasing faster than the trend. But the conclusion still stands if we compare with the corresponding phase of the economic upturn in the 1980s. Labour productivity now seems to be growing about half a percentage point faster now than before. It has also been something that we in the Riksbank, together with several other analysts, have not foreseen. It may not seem like much, but half a percent more in growth every year for twenty years means a difference of a full ten percent in the level of production at the end of the period. The figure is so large that it corresponds to a significant part of the fall in the international growth league that Sweden has undergone since the beginning of the 1970s. The question is whether the lower inflation and higher labour productivity in the 1990s contain any clue about the long-term growth trajectory of the Swedish economy. Can we say that the Swedish economy can handle higher growth in the long term? If so, would it be in stark contrast to the 1970s and 1980s and would mean an increase in the potential growth rate from between 1.5% and 2% to between 2% and 2.5%, which is more in line with that of other industrialised countries? No, it is still too early to draw any more definitive conclusions, but it is still possible to make a couple of reflections that point in this direction. Growth in the post-war period Both the 1950s and 1960s were characterized by high and stable growth. The 1960s in particular appear in a historical perspective as an exceptional growth decade. GDP rose by just over 4.5 per cent on average per year. The corresponding figure for the 1950s was just under 3.5 percent per year on average. This was followed by a markedly lower growth rate. From 1970 until the early 1990s, there was a sharp deceleration. There are different interpretations of why this has happened; everything from the loss of demand during the oil crisis years of the 70s and in connection with the hangover after the "bubble economy" in the early 90s, to an emphasis on more fundamental factors such as system disruptions or lack of transformation and adaptation to changing competitive conditions. The explanations are partly overlapping. Surely they have each had their say in the marked downshift in growth that followed in 1970. Many analyses have also been made over the years of what might explain this trend reversal. One explanation that I intend to focus on here today is that production in the Swedish business community gradually gained such a composition that competitiveness on the world market decreased. As a result, Swedish business gradually fell behind and lost the good leading position it had after the end of the Second World War. As development in the industrialized countries took off after the end of the war and competition increased, among other things, as a result of the removal of trade barriers, the new situation demanded a change in the production direction in Swedish business. At the same time, wage costs rose at a rapid pace for much of this period. Profitability in Swedish business was thus squeezed both as a result of increased competitive pressure from the outside world and by rising wage costs. Companies faced the pressure of profitability by trying to reduce production costs through rationalizations rather than investing in new products. At first, most of it still looked good. The 1960s were a fantastic decade in terms of growth. But it turned out to be a defensive strategy. In the 1970s came a stagnation. Rationalizations as a growth strategy have their limit. If there is no renewal, there will normally be a slowdown in growth sooner or later. Economic policy responded in the 1970s by carrying out a series of devaluations of the crown to try to keep growth up. The latest devaluation was always said to be the last, but the pattern of rising wage costs and devaluations was repeated time and time again. All this seemed to preserve the business structure, dragging up inflation expectations and gradually creating a speculative investment climate. Real estate and shares temporarily became more advantageous than investments in new products and production technologies. Rapid expansion of the public sector also helped to sustain growth and employment, but even that strategy has its limitations. In the long run, a tax-funded part of the economy cannot grow faster than the part that forms the basis for tax payments. Somewhere, a limit is reached where it becomes difficult to maintain the driving forces on which every market-based economy rests. The attempts to compensate for the lack of transformation in Swedish business that has its roots back to the 1960s simply did not work. Rather, devaluations tended to amplify the problems. There were no longer any clear rules of the game for wage formation. The public expansion presupposed tax levels that the tax system had difficulty coping with and also contributed to higher inflation. High levels of public expenditure made central government finances vulnerable to cyclical fluctuations Through a combination of the exclusion of the most labour-intensive enterprises, investment in capital-intensive technology and moderate growth in the private sector, employment there fell from the mid-1960s onwards. The absence of investments in new products and the dependence on a gradually outdated production structure helped to force an adjustment of the material standards of the whole country. Growth in Sweden was weaker for many years than in the world around us. But the stagnation in employment in business did not become apparent until the early 1990s, when public employment expansion also stopped. Unemployment in our country rose to levels that had not occurred since the 1930s. New trends in the 1990s However, something seems to have happened in the last five years, even if the period is too short to draw any more far-reaching conclusions. Nevertheless, some indications are interesting enough for them to be worth highlighting as a basis for further economic analysis and debate. Since the economy turned up after the crisis in the early 1990s, GDP growth has averaged around 3% per annum. That in and of itself is not a remarkably high figure compared to the upturn after the devaluation in 1982. What is interesting, however, is that growth has been borne entirely by an expansion in the business sector, especially in industry. Industrial output has grown by around 45 per cent or by about 8 per cent year-on-year. This is the most expansive five-year period for Swedish industry in over 30 years. One would think that the upturn in industry is mainly due to the deep decline of the early 1990s and that what has happened since then is that only spare capacity has been used. In parallel with the increase in production, however, there has been a significant increase in investment. It is difficult to find a five-year period from the 1950s onwards when investments have increased by the same amount measured by annual percentage increases. It is mainly machine investments that have been responsible for the upturn, but investments in buildings and facilities have also increased somewhat. That in itself could be an indication that it has mostly been a question of continued investment aimed at rationalising away labour, let us call them defensive investments, in order to reduce wage costs. But other statistics suggest that capital intensity has not increased during this period, which could be an indication that there may have been more aggressive investments. An unchanged capital intensity means that the inputs of labor and capital increase approximately equally. If this is correct, it will be the first time it has happened since the 1960s. Further indications that there have been more aggressive investments are that the competitive part of the Swedish economy has increased its relative size significantly, something that has been called for in the economic policy discussion over the past 25 years. Industry has grown from under 20 percent to just over 23 percent of GDP over the past five years. This is also confirmed by the fact that Sweden's current account balance now shows significant surpluses, something we have not been used to for several decades. At the same time, the public sector's share of GDP has fallen from 29% to 27%. If we look at the composition of Swedish goods exports, the trade in cars, iron, forest and steel a significant stability. Sweden was simply dependent on its basic industry. Since the late 1980s, however, a new pattern can be discerned. New sectors are expanding and old ones are declining in a relative sense. For example, there has been a doubling of the importance of medical and telecommunications products in foreign trade over the past ten years. This suggests that a renewal of Swedish business may have begun as early as the 1980s. The long-term fall in corporate profits relative to the value of production, which has been going on since the early 1950s, seems to have ended. There is an upward trend since the late 1970s. It is not dramatic, but it is still clear. The improved profitability is probably an important explanation for the fact that the capital stock has increased faster after the more than ten-year stagnation between the mid-1970s and the mid-1980s. All of this taken together may be an indication that growth overall could be faster than the historical trend. This is particularly true as wage formation has improved in recent years and seems to be gradually adapting to the new low-inflation regime and inflation has become lower than estimates based on historical correlations. What is the explanation? Some might argue that the development I have just pointed out is only a result of the marked weakening of the krona that occurred when the krona fell in the autumn of 1992. The old common pattern repeats itself from previous devaluation cycles. For a short period of time, the economy is stimulated and it may initially look as if new patterns are emerging. But soon, however, the setback will come. A new period of price and wage rises is beginning and the problems are reappearing. In the debate, there are those who believe that the development will be the same again this time. But the fact is that recent developments cannot be explained solely by the fact that the cost situation improved when the krona fell in November 1992. The positive elements of economic development appear to be more pervasive than those noted in connection with the previous write-downs of the value of the krona. The underlying patterns also look, as I've previously shown, different. It took almost ten years, from the mid-1960s to the mid-70s, before the tendencies towards more subdued Swedish growth really made themselves felt. Similarly, the measures taken in the second half of the 1980s and in the 1990s can only be expected to have an effect many years later. The rising profit share as well as a more stable macroeconomic regime in the 1990s are one of several features of this picture. It takes a long time to build up a new capital stock that can form the basis for new products that stand up well in the increasingly fierce international competition. Conclusion Today I have very briefly touched on the Swedish economy and the signs that may indicate that the Swedish economy is heading in a more favorable direction than before. Of course, one should not draw too far-reaching conclusions solely on the basis of a few years of observations. At the very least, it should be stated with absolute certainty that we are now facing a new type of economy. It is always important to be careful when trying to interpret new long-term trends based on a few observations At the same time, there is no getting away from the fact that there are signs that the Swedish economy today has a better long-term growth force than in the 1970s and 80s. Several - let me call it infrastructural issues - have already been resolved. The division of responsibilities in the Swedish economy is clearer today; with fiscal policy geared towards sound public finances and monetary policy geared towards low inflation and thus the main instrument of stabilisation in the economy. Other measures have also been taken; key markets have been liberalised at the same time as major changes have taken place, not least in the public sector. The statistics now also show that there may be conditions for a trend reversal for growth in Sweden after a couple of decades of weak development. Nevertheless, much remains to be done. The high level of unemployment calls for continued measures to improve the functioning of the labour market and wage formation. It is difficult to see how a mere economic upturn can bring unemployment down to levels that are talked about in the political system. At the same time, no economist or central bank can be absolutely sure where the cyclical part of unemployment ends and the structural one begins. All signs also indicate that the competitive climate in the world economy is becoming increasingly harsh. With increased opportunities to locate even relatively advanced production in countries with significantly lower wages than in the Western world, greater and greater demands will be placed on more human capital in the "old" industrialized countries. But human capital is extremely mobile across borders. This apparently places tough demands on old industrialised countries that claim to both maintain and further expand the material standards of their inhabitants. These include the functioning of the education system and the scope and structure of taxation.

Title: Current monetary policy
text: Persson: Current monetary policy Date: 2001-10-30 Speaker: Deputy Governor Kristina Persson Location: Finansanalytikernas forening Thank you for the invitation to come here to the Financial Analysts' Association. I was going to start by discussing the role of monetary policy on a slightly more general level. This also brings me to some economic policy issues that I have been interested in for a long time. The latter part of my speech I intended to devote to the assessments that formed the basis for the Riksbank's latest repo rate decision. An hour ago, the minutes of our last monetary policy meeting were published. The executive board's decision this time was - as you may have already suspected - unanimous. In this sense, it was a fairly simple decision. At the same time, uncertainty about where economic development is heading was greater than it has been for a long time. I will therefore comment in particular on the risk picture and give my views on the current monetary policy situation. The inflation target makes savings and investment decisions safer The Riksbank has since 1 January 1999 a statutory obligation to maintain a fixed monetary value. In the preparatory work for the legislative text, there is relatively little guidance on how this task should be interpreted more precisely, which means that the Riksbank itself must define what is meant by a fixed monetary value and decide more precisely how the task is to be handled. The Riksbank has chosen to operationalize the task as an inflation target, specified as a target for the consumer price index (CPI) of 2 per cent with a tolerance range of plus/minus 1 percentage point. Monetary policy must thus be conducted in such a way that the purchasing power of the krona is kept in a stable relation to the shopping basket that Swedish households buy on average. This means that when a wage agreement is established, the average wage earner should be able to be fairly sure what a certain nominal salary increase gives for purchasing power development during the contract period. A predictable inflation rate can also serve as a steering oar when domestically oriented companies set their prices. Low and stable inflation expectations reduce uncertainty about the real effects of borrowing and saving in sek for households and companies that have their costs and income in Sweden. This allows the resources of the economy to be distributed in a better way than if consumer prices fluctuate. A monetary policy that is credibly geared towards an inflation target can thus be assumed to contribute to creating good conditions for growth. In addition, a monetary policy, conducted by means of a symmetric inflation target, often operates countercyclically. It acts as a stimulus to the economy in recession because inflation is then normally low and vice versa. In short, this is the philosophy behind the Riksbank's inflation target. ... but the krona exchange rate creates uncertainty A complication for monetary policy in recent times has been that the krona exchange rate has not reflected so-called fundamentals in the Swedish economy. The exchange rate has therefore been difficult to forecast. Of course, this creates problems when we have to take decisions on interest rates, because decisions must be based on assumptions about exchange rate developments for one to two years. forward. But in addition, a long-term undervalued and fluctuating krona exchange rate can lead to socio-economic costs and lower growth in the long run. As we all know, the nominal krona exchange rate has recently developed weaker than the Riksbank has expected and significantly weaker than most economists consider to be fundamentally justified in the long term. For companies with production in Sweden but with sales revenues in foreign currency, the krona development has been favorable, albeit uncertain. High profits in these companies may have led to wage increases being greater than justified by productivity growth in the industry. The uncertainty has made investment decisions in export companies more difficult. Some may have invested in investments where profitability calculations were based on expectations of continued weak krona exchange rates, while others, due to uncertainty, may have refrained from investments that were justified. For companies with large imports but with sales revenues in Sweden, on the contrary, the development of the krona has been unfavorable. Competition reasons and low inflation expectations , not least at the consumer level - have made it difficult for these companies to compensate for high import costs with increased selling prices. In those companies, profit margins have decreased in that case. These examples illustrate the problems that a fluctuating and unjustifiably weak crown can create. They show that a krona development that for a long time deviates from what is fundamentally justified can distort resource allocation. In a market economy, it is, of course, the price system - to which the exchange rate belongs - that should give signals as to where capital and labour are most useful. A long-term weak krona can provide a composition of production and exports that requires low costs and prices and in the long run thus lead to poorer welfare relative to other countries. In the early 90s, when the credibility of the inflation target was still low and at the same time there was great uncertainty about how government finances would develop, many economists assumed that the krona would strengthen when the fiscal problems were resolved and inflation expectations had ended up at low and stable levels. The fluctuations around the new level would then be moderate. According to the theory of purchasing power parity, if inflation is the same in countries with roughly the same business structure, the nominal exchange rate between the two currencies should be stable. In the industrialized countries, the business structures are quite similar and the technology the same. That is why many believed that once inflation had stabilised at a low level, it would also lead to stability in the foreign exchange markets. Since the central banks have managed to achieve price stability in both Sweden and the euro area in recent years, the krona should, according to this analysis, have developed fairly stable against the euro. So many thought, but no stabilization of the krona exchange rate has yet taken place. It is also not possible to find explanations for the weak krona exchange rate in recent years in differences in productivity, cyclical development or changing household preferences. Sweden's current account has also been in surplus for several years. It is against this background that the Riksbank makes its assessment that the krona will strengthen in the long run. I think it is quite certain that the adjustments to the financial markets following liberalisation and the rapid process towards greater integration and globalisation that have followed have, in the short term, affected pricing in the foreign exchange market in a way that cannot be explained by conventional economic theory. The models explaining exchange rate changes are usually based on the real economy and are adapted to economies with nationally based enterprises. As a result, they do not appear to fully capture the impact of portfolio decisions taken in integrated financial markets. This does not prevent the fact that it should still be the fundamental economic conditions that govern the exchange rate in the long term. Large capital flows due to relocations in the financial of international investors portfolios seem to be able to overshadow, over a fairly long period, the movements in the foreign exchange market resulting from exports and imports of goods and services. An example of this is that the US dollar has been strengthening for many years, despite the fact that trade deficits have grown. At the same time, the Swedish krona has weakened despite current account surpluses and low inflation. Especially in times of turmoil, a small currency finds it difficult to hold its own against the large or traditionally "safe", such as the Swiss franc. Other countries such as Canada, New Zealand and Australia have experienced the same thing. However, the solution to the problem of fluctuating exchange rates - despite stable inflation expectations and orderly public finances - should not be sought in a return to old regimes. Well-developed and deregulated international financial markets make it possible to raise capital for investments that increase world production and thus raise welfare. Reintroducing regulation is therefore not a solution to the problem. Introducing a fixed-rate regime and unilaterally trying to defend it in a deregulated economy can also lead to major socio-economic costs, such as unemployment. In my opinion, therefore, participation in EMU would be a better solution. The need for stability in the exchange rate is certainly not the most important reason why I personally advocate EMU membership, but the development of the krona in recent years has strengthened my convictions. As a very large part of our trade is directed towards the euro area, it is desirable that the value of money is stable also against the goods traded on the euro market. Inflation targeting policy and the economy As long as Sweden remains outside EMU, a monetary policy geared towards a price stability objective makes the best possible contribution to our welfare. Low inflation is the stable bottom plate that all other social economies need to function well. The inflation target normally also means that monetary policy can help stimulate the economy in a recession and vice versa in a boom. While in the long term, changes in interest rates cannot affect growth, in the short term monetary policy has real effects. The main determinants of inflation are assumed to be resource utilisation, import prices and inflation expectations. When resources are fully exploited and inflation expectations are in line with the target, inflation is also assumed to be on target. This means that then the interest rate changes that are decided should also not conflict with what is desirable from a growth or economic perspective. Unfortunately, the reality is not so simple - for example, temporary price changes from imported goods can lead to inflation exceeding the target even when there is spare capacity in the economy. In order to avoid unnecessary fluctuations in growth, the Riksbank has normally chosen to aim to achieve its inflation target in one to two years' time. But the inflation target means that a cyclical slowdown in itself is not a sufficient motive to stimulate the economy . First, we need to conclude that inflation is likely to fall below the 2% target. There is a certain difference here compared to, for example, the US Federal Reserve. The Federal Reserve does not have as clear a target for its monetary policy as the Riksbank, and interest rate decisions are therefore not as clearly structured around an openly reported framework of thought. For example, the US Federal Reserve has justified the many interest rate cuts that have taken place since the beginning of the year on the grounds that there was room for and need for stimulus to the US economy. Since growth began to slow at the turn of the year, the FED seems to have viewed inflation in its signalling rather as a constraint than as a target. In fact, in practice, the difference is probably not so great, even the Swedish Riksbank takes into account economic developments as this is an important component that determines inflation. The difference may mainly consist in how a monetary policy measure is justified. For a small country like Sweden with a rather problematic inflationary history, there has hardly been an alternative. To achieve and ensure the credibility of price stability, it has been necessary to have a clear and consistently implemented inflation target combined with transparency about the thinking framework that served as the basis for decisions. The current situation After several years of very strong growth, the economy turned downwards at the turn of the year. The slowdown started in the United States, which throughout the long upswing phase has been the locomotive of the world economy. Optimistic expectations based on the fact that information technology would make it possible to increase production for a long time had driven up stock prices, investments and consumption. At the same time, strong interest in investing money in US investments and stocks had greatly strengthened the dollar exchange rate. During the spring, the economic indicators were interpreted by most as meaning that the upturn in the US economy would soon come and that stock prices - which had fallen very sharply - would recover. Growth would, many believed, soon be back at the previous high levels. But during the summer, it became increasingly clear that the slowdown was a reality and that it had spread rapidly to the rest of the world. The economic slowdown was unexpectedly synchronised, the downturn in Europe seems to have actually occurred around the same time as in the US. Uncertainty about the depth and duration of the economic slowdown increased. Here at home, the monetary policy assessments were complicated by the fact that the exchange rate at the beginning of June had weakened sharply and by the fact that the CPI at the same time showed a higher rate of increase than the Riksbank expected. The uncertainty in the projections was reflected in the monetary policy decision of 5 July. At the time, the majority considered that the risk outweighed that the weak exchange rate, combined with the high outcome for inflation, would lead to inflation expectations and to the inflation target being exceeded. My assessment - and that of two members - was that there was a significant risk of weaker international demand developments and that it balanced the risk of inflation. Because the uncertainty was so great, we felt it was better to hold off on a change in interest rates. In late summer, statistics continued to come in that prompted downward revisions of growth forecasts, both in terms of growth in the Swedish economy and in the world around us. Several indicators pointed to a deteriorating demand situation in the United States even before the terrorist attacks on September 11. The uncertainty created by the attacks and the security policy situation that followed naturally further increased the risk of a demand slowdown in the world around us. Household confidence was considered to be crucial for future demand developments and there was much to suggest that uncertainty would increase savings and thus reduce demand. It was against this background that the Riksbank decided on 17 September to lower its repo rate by 50 basis points. In the main scenario in the Riksbank's October inflation report, GDP growth in Sweden was expected to pick up again as early as next year, increasing from 1.3 per cent this year to 2.2 per cent and 2.8 per cent respectively over the next two years. The assessments were based on the fact that the expansionary monetary and fiscal policy in the rest of the world would stimulate demand and that an upward turn would also take place in the US economy. At the same time, a weaker exchange rate development than the Riksbank had previously expected is expected to give some impetus to Swedish exports. Fiscal easing was also expected to increase Swedish households' disposable income sharply and lead to both annual consumption growth of a couple of percent and a rising savings rate over the next two years. In the main scenario, the resources of the Swedish economy are assumed not to be fully utilized in the near future, but by the end of the forecast period, i.e. 2003, growth should have increased so much that we will again have full capacity utilisation. Despite the low resource utilisation, inflation is expected to remain above target at the beginning of the period, but then gradually come down to close to 2 per cent over a 2-year horizon. In the near term, inflation will be affected by increases in the prices of goods and services that are not expected to have a lasting impact on inflation. The low resource utilization in Sweden and in the rest of the world, inflationary pressures are simultaneously dampening. Against this background, the Executive Board decided on 15 October to leave the repo rate unchanged. However, the main scenario assumes that the international crisis and conflict situation does not worsen. How likely this is is debatable, and it makes it more difficult than in a very long time to make assessments of how the economy and inflation will develop over the next two years. The funnel showing the spread in the risk assessment is thus wider than ever. The downside risk, of course, primarily concerns the assessment of demand developments. The terrorist attacks occurred in a very delicate situation, after all, it was the American consumers who everyone expected would relaunch world demand. Even before the terrorist attacks of September 11, there was uncertainty about how deep and prolonged the economic slowdown would be. One source of uncertainty was whether the "new economy" would create higher growth in the long term. The previously widespread optimism about future growth had strongly stimulated investment and consumption, as well as increased debt, especially in the United States. This increased the risk that the pessimism of households would now drive up household savings, reduce corporate profits and create increased unemployment. The terrorist attack and the security situation that followed further fuelled this uncertainty. Integrated commodity and financial markets have meant that economic fluctuations in recent years have been synchronised and quickly spread to the rest of the world. Expansionary fiscal and monetary policy is assumed to be an important driver of demand developments over the coming year. The fiscal stimulus in the US alone is equivalent to 2% of GDP, which can be said to be a very powerful Keynesian stimulus policy. Also in Europe, many countries, including Sweden, are reducing taxes. Real interest rates are historically very low worldwide, which also has a stimulating effect. Within the European Commission, the possibility of pursuing a coordinated stimulus policy through increased investment is being discussed, including with financing by the European Investment Bank (EIB). All this should have a sharply stimulating effect on household consumption and lead to an upturn sometime in the second half of the year. At the same time, it cannot be excluded that household uncertainty will increase further, for example as a result of new acts of terrorism, thus counteracting the effects of the stimulus. In the Riksbank's risk assessment, the price-dampening effects that weaker international growth can lead to are offset partly by the fact that the weak krona may generate more inflation than predicted and partly by the fact that inflationary pressures in the Swedish economy may not be sufficiently dampened by the low resource utilisation. A weak exchange rate will have an impact on inflation partly through higher import prices and partly by stimulating export demand. But the pass-through to consumer prices from a weakening krona exchange rate has so far been moderate. Increased competition may have made it difficult to pass on increased costs of imported goods to the consumer. However, falling demand may make it more difficult for companies to squeeze profit margins further. In conclusion, right now I do not see an immediate threat to price stability, but lots of uncertainty about the future. An excessively rapid deceleration of the world economy today seems to be a greater threat to stability than an overly stimulative monetary and fiscal policy. But for Sweden, we must still take into account the risks of a weak krona and higher domestic inflationary pressures than we expected in the main scenario. Therefore, the risk picture for inflation seems balanced after all. I can assure you that we at the Riksbank are currently following developments with a great deal of attention. Each new statistical data is part of the puzzle that is being put together so that we can assess inflation developments as accurately as possible. We will do what we can to ensure that the 2% target is neither exceeded nor undercut. On 5 December, you will know what our next monetary policy decision will be.

Men dessutom kan en lngvarigt undervrderad och fluktuerande kronkurs leda till samhllsekonomiska kostnader och lgre tillvxt p sikt. Fr fretag med produktion i Sverige men med frsljningsintkter i utlndsk valuta har kronutvecklingen varit gynnsam om n osker. Fr fretag med stor import men med frsljningsintkter i Sverige har kronans utveckling tvrtom varit ogynnsam. Konkurrensskl och lga inflationsfrvntningar inte minst i konsumentledet - har gjort det svrt fr dessa fretag att kompensera hga importkostnader med hjda frsljningspriser. I de fretagen har vinstmarginalerna i s fall minskat. De hr exemplen illustrerar de problem som en fluktuerande och omotiverat svag krona kan skapa. De visar att en kronutveckling som under lng tid avviker frn vad som r fundamentalt motiverat kan snedvrida resursallokeringen. I en marknadsekonomi r det ju prissystemet - dit vxelkursen hr - som skall ge signaler om var kapital och arbetskraft gr bst nytta. En lngsiktigt svag krona kan ge en sammansttning av produktion och export som frutstter lga kostnader och priser och p sikt drmed leda till en smre vlfrd relativt andra lnder. I brjan av 90-talet nr trovrdigheten fr inflationsmlet fortfarande var lg och det samtidigt fanns en stor oskerhet om hur statsfinanserna skulle utvecklas var det mnga ekonomer som utgick ifrn att kronan skulle strkas nr de statsfinansiella problemen var lsta och inflationsfrvntningarna hade hamnat p lga och stabila niver. Fluktuationerna kring den nya nivn skulle sedan bli mttliga. Enligt teorin om kpkraftsparitet skall - om inflationen r densamma i lnder med ungefr samma nringslivsstruktur - den nominella vxelkursen mellan de bda valutorna vara stabil. I de industrialiserade lnderna r nringslivsstrukturerna ganska lika och teknologin densamma. Det var sklet till att mnga trodde att nr inflationen hade stabiliserats p lg niv skulle det ocks leda till stabilitet p valutamarknaderna. Eftersom centralbankerna under senare r lyckats uppn prisstabilitet i svl Sverige som i euro- omrdet borde allts kronan enligt den analysen ha utvecklats ganska stabilt mot euron. S tnkte mnga, men nnu har inte ngon stabiliseringen av kronkursen skett. Det gr heller inte att hitta frklaringar till den svaga kronkursen under senare r i skillnader i produktivitet, konjunkturutveckling eller frndrade preferenser hos hushllen. Sveriges bytesbalans har ocks under flera r uppvisat verskott. Det r mot den bakgrunden som Riksbanken gr bedmningen att kronan p sikt kommer att strkas. Jag tror att man kan vara ganska sker p att anpassningarna av de finansiella marknaderna efter avregleringarna och den snabba process mot kad integration och globalisering som har fljt, p kort sikt har pverkat prissttningen p valutamarknaden p ett stt som inte lter sig frklaras av gngse nationalekonomisk teori. De modeller som frklarar vxelkursfrndringarna utgr vanligen frn den reala ekonomin och r anpassade till ekonomier med nationellt baserade fretag. De tycks drmed inte fullt ut fnga in effekterna av portfljbeslut som tas p integrerade finansiella marknader. Detta hindrar inte att det fortfarande br vara de fundamentala ekonomiska frhllandena som styr vxelkursen p lng sikt. Omfattande kapitalflden p.g.a. omflyttningar i internationella investerares finansiella portfljer tycks under en ganska lng period kunna verskugga de rrelser p valutamarknaden som hrrr frn export och import av varor och tjnster. Exempel p det r att den amerikanska dollarn har frstrkts under mnga r, trots att underskotten i handelsbalansen har vuxit. Samtidigt har den svenska kronan frsvagats trots bytesbalansverskott och lg inflation. Srskilt i tider av oro fr en liten valuta svrigheter att hvda sig mot de stora eller traditionellt "skra", typ schweizerfrancen. Andra lnder som t.ex. Kanada, Nya Zeeland och Australien har upplevt samma sak. Lsningen p problemet med fluktuerande vxelkurs - trots stabila inflationsfrvntningar och ordnade statsfinanser - br emellertid inte skas i en tergng till gamla regimer. Vlutvecklade och avreglerade internationella finansmarknader gr det mjligt att skaffa kapital till investeringar som kar produktionen i vrlden och drmed hjer vlfrden. Att terinfra regleringar r drfr ingen lsning p problemet. Att infra en fastkursregim och ensidigt frska frsvara den i en avreglerad ekonomi kan ocks leda till stora samhllsekonomiska kostnader, t.ex. arbetslshet. Enligt min uppfattning skulle drfr ett EMU-deltagande vara en bttre lsning. Behov av stabilitet i vxelkursen r visserligen inte den viktigaste orsaken till att jag personligen fresprkar ett EMU-medlemskap, men kronans utveckling under senare r har strkt min vertygelse. Eftersom en mycket stor del av vr handel riktas mot euroomrdet r det nskvrt att penningvrdet r stabilt ocks mot de varor som handlas p euromarknaden. Inflationsmlspolitik och konjunkturen S lnge Sverige str utanfr EMU ger en penningpolitik inriktad mot ett prisstabilitetsml det bsta mjliga bidraget till vr vlfrd. Lg inflation utgr den stabila bottenplatta som all annan samhllsekonomi behver fr att fungera vl. Inflationsmlet innebr normalt ocks att penningpolitiken kan bidra till att stimulera ekonomin i en lgkonjunktur och tvrtom i en hgkonjunktur. P lng sikt kan visserligen inte rntefrndringar pverka tillvxten, men p kort sikt har penningpolitiken reala effekter. De viktigaste bestmningsfaktorerna fr inflationen antas vara resursutnyttjandet, importpriserna och inflationsfrvntningarna. Nr resurserna r fullt utnyttjade och inflationsfrvntningarna ligger i linje med mlet antas inflationen ocks hamna p mlet. Det innebr att d br de rntefrndringar, som beslutas inte heller st i konflikt med vad som r nskvrt ur ett tillvxt- eller konjunkturperspektiv. Verkligheten r dessvrre inte s enkel - t.ex. kan tillflliga prisfrndringar frn importerade varor leda till att inflationen verskrider mlet ven nr det finns ledig kapacitet i ekonomin. Fr att undvika ondiga fluktuationer i tillvxten har Riksbanken valt att i normala fall sikta p att uppn inflationsmlet p ett till tv rs sikt. Men inflationsmlet innebr att en konjunkturavmattning i sig inte utgr ett tillrckligt motiv fr att stimulera ekonomin . Frst mste vi konstatera att inflationen sannolikt kommer att hamna under 2 %-mlet. Hr finns en viss skillnad gentemot t.ex. den amerikanska centralbanken. Federal Reserve har inte ett lika entydigt ml fr sin penningpolitik som Riksbanken och rntebesluten r drfr inte lika tydligt uppbyggda kring en ppet redovisad tankeram. Den amerikanska centralbanken har t.ex. motiverat de mnga rntesnkningar som skett sedan brjan av ret med att det funnits utrymme fr och behov av stimulans av den amerikanska ekonomin. Sedan tillvxten brjade vika vid rskiftet verkar FED i sin signalering ha betraktat inflationen snarare som en restriktion n som ett ml. I sjlva verket r skillnaden nog i praktiken inte s stor, ven den svenska riksbanken tar hnsyn till konjunkturutvecklingen eftersom denna r en viktig komponent som bestmmer inflationen. Skillnaden kanske frmst bestr i hur en penningpolitisk tgrd motiveras. Fr ett litet land som Sverige med en tmligen problematisk inflationshistoria har det knappast funnits ngot alternativ. Fr att uppn och skerstlla trovrdigheten fr prisstabiliteten har det varit ndvndigt att ha ett tydligt och konsekvent genomfrt inflationsml i kombination med ppenhet om den tankeram som tjnat som grund fr besluten. Det aktuella lget Efter flera r av mycket stark tillvxt vnde konjunkturen vid rskiftet nedt. Avmattningen startade i USA, som under hela den lnga uppgngsfasen utgjort lokomotivet i vrldsekonomin. Optimistiska frvntningar baserade p att informationsteknologin skulle gra det mjligt att under lng tid ka produktionen hade drivit upp aktiekurser, investeringar och konsumtion. Ett starkt intresse fr att placera pengar i amerikanska investeringar och aktier hade samtidigt kraftigt strkt dollarkursen. Under vren tolkades konjunkturindikatorerna av de flesta som att vndningen uppt i den amerikanska ekonomin snart skulle komma och att aktiekurserna - som hade fallit mycket kraftigt - skulle terhmta sig. Tillvxten skulle, trodde mnga snart vara tillbaka p de tidigare hga niverna. Men under sommaren blev det allt tydligare att avmattningen var en realitet och att den ftt en snabb spridning till resten av vrlden. Konjunkturavmattningen var ovntat synkroniserad, nedgngen i Europa tycks i sjlva verket ha skett ungefr samtidigt som i USA. Oskerheten om djupet och varaktigheten i konjunkturavmattningen kade. Hr hemma komplicerades de penningpolitiska bedmningarna av att vxelkursen i brjan av juni hade frsvagats kraftigt och av att KPI samtidigt uppvisade en hgre kningstakt n vad Riksbanken frvntade sig. Oskerheten i bedmningarna avspeglades i det penningpolitiska beslutet den 5 juli. Majoriteten ansg d att risken vervgde fr att den svaga vxelkursen i kombination med det hga utfallet fr inflationen skulle leda till inflationsfrvntningar och till att inflationsmlet skulle verskridas. Min - och tv ledamters till - bedmning var att det fanns en betydande risk fr en svagare internationell efterfrgeutveckling och att den balanserade risken fr inflation. Eftersom oskerheten var s stor ansg vi att det var bttre att avvakta med en rntefrndring. Under sensommaren fortsatte det att komma in statistik som franledde nedrevideringar av tillvxtprognoserna, bde vad gller tillvxten i den svenska ekonomin och i vr omvrld. Flera indikatorer pekade mot ett frsmrat efterfrgelge i USA redan innan terrordden den 11 september. Den oskerhet som attackerna skapade och det skerhetspolitiska lge som fljde kade givetvis ytterligare risken fr en efterfrgedmpning i vr omvrld. Hushllens frtroende bedmdes vara avgrande fr den framtida efterfrgeutvecklingen och mycket talade fr att oskerheten skulle ka sparandet och drmed minska efterfrgan. Det var mot den bakgrunden som Riksbanken den 17 september tog beslut om att snka reporntan 50 punkter. I huvudscenariot i Riksbankens inflationsrapport frn oktober bedmdes BNPtillvxten i Sverige vnda uppt igen redan nsta r och ka frn 1,3 procent i r till 2,2 procent respektive 2,8 procent under de nrmaste tv ren. Bedmningarna byggde p att den expansiva penning- och finanspolitiken i omvrlden skulle stimulera efterfrgan och att en vndning uppt skulle ske ocks i den amerikanska ekonomin. En svagare vxelkursutveckling n Riksbanken tidigare hade rknat med frvntas samtidigt ge en viss draghjlp t den svenska exporten. Finanspolitiska lttnader bedmdes vidare ka de svenska hushllens disponibla inkomster kraftigt och leda till svl en rlig konsumtionstillvxt p ett par procent som en stigande sparkvot de nrmaste tv ren. I huvudscenariot antas resurserna i den svenska ekonomin under den nrmaste tiden inte tas i ansprk fullt ut, men mot slutet av prognosperioden, allts 2003 br tillvxten ha kat s mycket att vi ter har fullt kapacitetsutnyttjande. Trots det lga resursutnyttjandet bedms inflationen fortsatt ligga ver mlet i brjan av perioden, men sedan successivt komma ner till nra 2 procent p 2 rs sikt. Under den nrmaste tiden pverkas inflationen av priskningar p varor och tjnster som inte bedms pverka inflationen varaktigt. Det lga resursutnyttjandet i Sverige och i omvrlden dmpar samtidigt inflationstrycket. Mot den bakgrunden beslutade direktionen den 15 oktober att lmna reporntan ofrndrad. Riskbilden Huvudscenariot frutstter emellertid att det internationella kris- och konfliktsituationen inte frvrras. Hur sannolikt detta r kan diskuteras, och det gr det svrare n p mycket lnge att gra bedmningar av hur konjunktur och inflation kommer att utvecklas de nrmaste tv ren. Tratten som visar spridningen i riskbedmningen r drmed vidare n ngonsin. Nedtrisken gller frsts i frsta hand bedmningarna av efterfrgeutvecklingen. Terrorattackerna intrffade i ett mycket knsligt lge, det var ju de amerikanska konsumenterna som alla frvntade sig skulle dra igng efterfrgan p nytt i vrlden. Redan fre terrordden den 11 september fanns en oskerhet om hur djup och lngvarig konjunkturavmattningen skulle bli. En klla till oskerhet var om den "nya ekonomin" skulle skapa en lngsiktigt hgre tillvxt. Den tidigare s utbredda optimismen om framtida tillvxt hade kraftigt stimulerat investeringar och konsumtion samt kat skuldsttningen srskilt i USA. Det kade risken fr att pessimismen hos hushllen nu skulle driva upp hushllssparandet, minska fretagens vinster och skapa kad arbetslshet. Terrorattacken och det skerhetspolitiska lget som fljde spdde ytterligare p denna oskerhet. Integrerade varu- och finansiella marknader har gjort att konjunktursvngningarna under senare r varit synkroniserade och snabbt ftt spridning till resten av vrlden. Den expansiva finans- och penningpolitiken antas vara en viktig drivkraft fr efterfrgeutvecklingen det nrmaste ret. Enbart den finanspolitiska stimulansen i USA motsvarar 2 % av BNP vilket fr sgas vara en mycket kraftfull keynesiansk stimulanspolitik. Ocks i Europa snker mnga lnder, inklusive Sverige skatterna. Realrntorna r historiskt sett mycket lga vrlden ver vilket ven det har en stimulerande effekt. Inom EU-kommissionen diskuteras mjligheten att fra en samordnad stimulanspolitik genom kade investeringar, bl.a. med finansiering av Europeiska investeringsbanken (EIB). Allt detta br f en kraftigt stimulerande effekt p hushllens konsumtion och leda till en uppgng ngon gng under andra halvret. Samtidigt kan det inte uteslutas att hushllens oskerhet kommer att ka ytterligare, t.ex. till fljd av nya terrorhandlingar och drmed motverka effekterna av stimulansen. I Riksbankens riskbedmning uppvgs de prisdmpande effekterna som en svagare internationell tillvxt kan leda till, dels av att den svaga kronan kan generera mer inflation n frutsett, dels av att inflationstrycket i den svenska ekonomin kanske inte kommer att dmpas tillrckligt mycket av det lga resursutnyttjandet. En svag vxelkurs fr effekter p inflationen dels via hgre importpriser dels genom att exportefterfrgan stimuleras. Men genomslaget p konsumentpriserna frn en frsvagad kronkurs har hittills varit mttligt. kad konkurrens kan ha gjort det svrt att fra ver kade kostnader fr importerade varor p konsumenten. En vikande efterfrgan kan emellertid gra det svrare fr fretagen att pressa vinstmarginalerna ytterligare. Sammanfattningsvis ser jag just nu inget omedelbart hot mot prisstabiliteten men massor av oskerhet nr det gller framtiden. En alltfr snabb inbromsning av vrldsekonomin tycks idag vara ett strre hot mot stabiliteten n en alltfr stimulerande penning- och finanspolitik. Men fr Sveriges del mste vi nd beakta riskerna med en svag krona och ett hgre inhemskt inflationstryck n vad vi rknat med i huvudscenariot. Drfr ter sig riskbilden fr inflationen trots allt som balanserad. Jag kan frskra er om att vi p Riksbanken just nu fljer utvecklingen med mycket stor uppmrksamhet. Varje ny statistikuppgift utgr en del i det pussel som lggs fr att vi s korrekt som mjligt ska kunna bedma inflationsutvecklingen. Vi kommer att gr vad vi kan fr att 2%- mlet varken ska ver- eller underskridas. Den 5 december fr ni veta vad vrt nsta penningpolitiska beslut kommer att bli. Title: The current economic situation
text: Persson: The current economic situation Date 2006-09-13 Deputy Governor Kristina Persson spoke on Wednesday about the current state of the world economy, the Swedish economy and monetary policy at a meeting organized by the Building Materials Distributors. "The world economy has performed very strongly in recent years with growth averaging 5 percent per year. The United States and parts of Asia, especially China, have served as growth engines in the world economy. In the euro area, developments have been subdued in recent years, but even there the recovery seems to have started. This has contributed to strong growth in exports and GDP in Sweden and now household consumption is also increasing at a faster pace. An important factor behind this is likely to be that the labour market has improved gradually over the past year. Profits and investments are also showing strong growth. Not least housing construction has really taken off," Persson began. "Globalisation has been a key driver of this broad and strong economic upturn. Over the past 15-20 years, there have been major and profound changes in the world economy that have opened up for greater trade and made national economies increasingly integrated. China's, India's and Eastern Europe's increased economic openness to the outside world has created both new markets and increased competition," Persson continued. "While demand growth in the world economy has been strong, consumer price pressures have been contained. There has been a downward shift in inflation rates globally since the early 1990s. In the industrialised countries, the rate of price increase has averaged 2% in recent years. The main reasons are that monetary policy is now aimed at low inflation and that more and more countries are participating in world trade, which has contributed to increased competition and increased production in low-cost countries. Globalisation has thus helped to hold back wages and prices in the industries exposed to global competition, while at the same time making it possible to import products from low-cost countries to an increasing extent. The increased competition has also pushed companies in the old industrialized countries to increase productivity, which also dampens inflation," Persson said. "In recent years, inflation in Sweden has surprised on the downside and significantly below the Riksbank's target of 2 percent. In 2004-2005, inflation (as measured by UND1X) averaged 0.8 percent. This year there has been a gradual increase in inflation, but it remains below target. This development can hardly be due to too low demand, as GDP growth has been stronger than expected. Inflationary pressures have been held back by supply factors, in particular high productivity growth and weak import price developments," Persson noted. "Despite the strong growth in recent years, the labour market has been weak, but in 2005 employment started to pick up again after falling for two years. In recent months, there has been a clear increase in the number of employed persons. At the same time, more and more people have entered the labour market as the job outlook has improved, which means that unemployment is falling relatively slowly. The improved labour market outlook is also supported by the national institute of economic research's latest barometer, which shows continued positive hiring plans in the construction industry and parts of the private service industries in the third quarter of this year," Persson said. "At the last monetary policy meeting on 29 August, the Riksbank's Executive Board decided on an increase in the repo rate by 0.25 percentage points. The background to this decision was, among other things, strong GDP growth so far this year, primarily in Sweden but also in the rest of the world. The picture of a strong demand situation is also supported by continued high lending to households and rapid house price increases. GDP growth appears to be higher this year and next year compared to our forecast in June. Productivity has developed significantly stronger than expected, with a dampening effect on unit labour costs. However, the pick-up in productivity growth is considered to be largely temporary. As the economy continues to improve, the labour market will strengthen and productivity growth will thus moderate. As a result, inflation will gradually rise," Persson continued. "In connection with the decision, the Riksbank stressed that it is reasonable to assume that the repo rate will need to be raised further, approximately in the way that the market expects, to ensure inflation in line with its target over a couple of years' time. I share that assessment," Persson said. "This assumes that the economy develops in much the way we imagine, namely that the world economy will reach the peak of the economy this year and that there will then be a slow adjustment to slightly lower growth. However, it cannot be ruled out that the global economy will decelerate much faster. What could trigger such a scenario is that the ongoing slowdown in the housing market in the US, together with high oil prices and higher interest rates, leads to a stronger slowdown in household consumption and thus growth. At the same time, the higher inflation means that the Federal Reserve does not have the same opportunities as before to stimulate the economy through interest rate cuts. Another risk factor is that the rapid growth in China risks leading to setbacks later on," Persson concluded.

Den skrpta konkurrensen har ocks pressat fretagen i de gamla industrilnderna till kad produktivitet, vilket ocks dmpar inflationen, sade Persson. Inflationstrycket har hllits tillbaka av utbudsfaktorer, framfrallt en hg produktivitetstillvxt och svag importprisutveckling, konstaterade Persson. Trots de senaste rens starka tillvxt har arbetsmarknaden varit svag men under 2005 brjade sysselsttningen ta fart igen efter att ha fallit i tv r. De senaste mnaderna har det skett en tydlig uppgng av antalet sysselsatta. Samtidigt har allt fler personer skt sig till arbetsmarknaden i takt med att jobbutsikterna frbttrats, vilket innebr att arbetslsheten sjunker relativt lngsamt. De frbttrade utsikterna p arbetsmarknaden stds ocks av Konjunkturinstitutets senaste barometer som visar p fortsatt positiva anstllningsplaner inom byggindustrin och delar av de privata tjnstenringarna under det tredje kvartalet i r, sade Persson. Vid det senaste penningpolitiska mtet den 29 augusti beslutade Riksbankens direktion om en hjning av reporntan med 0,25 procentenheter. Bakgrunden till detta beslut var bl.a. en stark BNP-tillvxt hittills i r framfrallt i Sverige men ven i omvrlden. Bilden av ett starkt efterfrglge stds ocks av en fortsatt hg utlning till hushllen och snabba huspriskningar. BNP-tillvxten verkar bli hgre i r och nsta r jmfrt med vr prognos i juni. Produktiviteten har utvecklats betydligt starkare n vntat, vilket har en dmpande effekt p enhetsarbetskostnaderna. Uppgngen i produktivitetstillvxt bedms emellertid till stor del vara tillfllig. I takt med att konjunkturen fortstter att frbttras kommer arbetsmarknaden att strkas och produktivitetstillvxten drmed att dmpas. Det leder till att inflationen gradvis stiger, fortsatte Persson. Riksbanken framhll i samband med beslutet att det r rimligt att anta att reporntan kommer att behva hjas ytterligare, ungefr p det stt som marknaden frvntar sig, fr att skerstlla en inflation i linje med mlet p ett par rs sikt. Jag delar den bedmningen, sade Persson. Detta frutstter att konjunkturen utvecklas ungefr s som vi frestller oss, nmligen att vrldsekonomi nr konjunkturtoppen i r och att det sedan sker en lngsam anpassning till en ngot lgre tillvxt. Det gr dock inte att utesluta att den globala ekonomin bromsar in betydligt snabbare. Det som skulle kunna utlsa ett sdant scenario r att den pgende avmattningen p bostadsmarknaden i USA, tillsammans med ett hgt oljepris och ett hgre rntelge, leder till en kraftigare dmpning av hushllens konsumtion och drmed tillvxten. Samtidigt gr den hgre inflationen att Federal Reserve inte har samma mjligheter som tidigare att stimulera ekonomin genom rntesnkningar. Ytterligare en riskfaktor r att den snabba tillvxten i Kina riskerar att leda till bakslag lngre fram, avslutade Persson. Title: Globalisation contributes to low inflation
text: Persson: Globalisation contributes to low inflation Date 2005-03-08 Deputy Governor Kristina Persson spoke today about globalization and low inflation in Sweden at Foreningssparbanken's annual conference Our Economic Situation. "Over the past decade or so, inflation has gradually fallen back, both in Sweden and globally. The main reason is a change in monetary policy in more and more countries with independent central banks steering towards a price stability objective. But the downshift in inflation has also been facilitated by globalization, which, among other things, brought with it increased competition from low-wage countries and pushed old industrialized countries to increased productivity. This development is reinforced by the opportunities created by the new information technology," Persson began. "The low inflation in Sweden today has surprised many forecasters, including the Riksbank. The explanation seems to be partly to be found in the fact that productivity has become higher than expected at the same time as imported inflation has been unexpectedly low. The low inflation is thus a consequence of so-called positive supply shocks and is not due to the Riksbank tightening monetary policy and dampening demand," Persson continued. "The fact that prices of imported goods and services (excluding oil) have fallen more than expected is partly due to the strengthening of the krona in recent years. But there are also signs that increased globalization and intensified competition from large low-wage countries such as China and India have had some impact on development. Surveys indicate that consumers look at the price of the product rather than the country of origin. This in turn makes it more difficult for companies to pass on cost increases to consumers and must rationalize if they want to maintain good profit margins," Persson said. "In the longer term, it is difficult to assess the significance of China's and India's integration into the world economy for inflation developments in Sweden. On the one hand, Chinese manufacturing has for several years helped to push down the prices of many types of industrial goods and consumer products on the world market, and India now looks set to embrace a corresponding role in the service sector. Continued trade liberalisation, most recently the abolition of teko quotas within the EU, and global competition also suggest that this positive supply shock may lead to continued low imported inflation over the next few years. On the other hand, it is important to remember that the growing participation of China and India in international exchanges will not only lead to a sharp increase in the supply of cheap goods and services, but that these countries will also contribute with a high demand for raw materials, goods and services from the rest of the world. For example, as China approached overheating in the construction sector and car production last year, the need for raw materials became so great that the country was forced to import 4 percent of total global steel production. This helped drive up metal prices, which in turn affected producer prices for Swedish industry," Persson said. "There are signs that the increasingly globalized world economy we live in, with the dismantling of trade barriers, deregulation of product and financial markets and the integration of more and more countries into international exchange, led to strong pressure for transformation in Sweden in recent times. While traditional industrial sectors are able to produce more and more with fewer and fewer employees, some sectors of the service sector appear to be creating jobs regardless of the economic cycle, as confirmed by surveys on companies' hiring plans. Service production now makes the biggest contribution to overall growth," Persson noted. "Structural change means, among other things, that production and jobs are moved abroad. A week rarely passes without us being made aware of new company decisions on the relocation of certain work steps. The process is largely driven by the possibility of significant cost savings. However, many studies published find no evidence that the development would lead to increased unemployment and poorer economic growth in the country from which production is relocated. On the contrary, they suggest that a better division of labor between countries leads to lower costs and productivity gains, which in turn means that labor and investments in the industrialized countries can be moved to more highly processed products," Persson emphasized. "As a small open economy, Sweden has had a lot to gain from increased global integration, but the transition process can often be demanding. Problems arise especially if new establishments and job changes are made more difficult. There must therefore be sufficient incentives to set up businesses, to train and to look for work outside one's own industry instead of being stuck in long-term unemployment. For Sweden's economic development in the future, it will be crucial that we succeed in meeting the demands for adjustment and adaptation that globalization and structural change place on both businesses and individuals," Persson concluded.
