Title: Globalization and Sweden - A discussion of new conditions and opportunities
text: Persson: Globalisation and Sweden - A discussion about new conditions and opportunities Date: 2002-02-20 Speaker: Deputy Governor Kristina Persson Location: Social Democrats Thank you for the invitation, fun to revisit so many people who played an important role for me in my active, political years in the 70s and 80s. My speech here today consists of two different parts: First, a look back and an attempt at analysis of what has really happened, politically and economically in Sweden since the early 70s. Then I go through what globalisation really means. Are there problems - and if so, how can they be dealt with? Finally, I comment on the criticism of globalisation, including the demands made at the recent World Social Forum in Porto Alegre. Record years come to an end The 1970s meant that an in many ways outstanding period of economic growth in Sweden was coming to an end. 100 years of industrial revolution had lifted Sweden from being one of Europe's poorest countries to becoming one of the world's richest. Growth created the conditions for a welfare policy that aroused admiration in the outside world, and welfare development in many ways supported economic growth. Sweden became famous throughout the world for its political and social successes - the concept of the Swedish model became part of our self-image. I traveled a lot during the 60s and 70s and I was very proud to be Swedish. Perhaps that was precisely our mistake, that we felt so successful, almost invulnerable. Anyone who has not humbly seen and listened to others will inevitably be less equipped when the crises come. Exactly what had built our welfare throughout the 1900s, from the 70s onwards, also became part of our problem and a threat to welfare. The oil price increases that came in the early 70s triggered a structural crisis that knocked out large parts of Swedish industry. The shipyards and the textile industry disappeared almost completely. International competition forced a far-reaching rationalisation of the industry. But the people who were no longer needed in the industry did not start new companies, but were mainly sucked up by the public sector, which continued to grow, even though the resources had actually begun to run out. Sweden had deficits in the state budget and in trade with the rest of the world current account. The renewal of business that we would have needed then in the form of new technology and new products with a greater knowledge content did not materialise. This did not create the basis for a continued increase in prosperity. But wages increased in any case, inflation amounted to an average of about. 8 % per year between 1975 and 1995. The value of wages eroded; those who benefited were those who owned real capital, real estate, or shares. Other countries did better, and Sweden quickly plummeted downhill in the prosperity league. Even vis-a-vis our neighbours, we lost position; if we had had the same growth as Norway, Denmark and Finland between 1975 and 1995, our standard of living would have been about. 20% higher today. The solution that was resorted to - this applied to both bourgeois and social democratic governments - was devaluations. No less than five between 1976 and 1982. The crown lost 40% of its value. In part, the write-downs of the exchange rate were necessary because Sweden had lost so much in competitiveness, but as a solution to the problems they were deeply inadequate. The idea behind the great so-called competitive devaluation in 1982 was that Sweden, by selling its goods cheaply abroad, would boost production. But devaluing more than necessary is a short-term medicine that risks making the patient really bad because it slows down the transformation and renewal required for sustainable competitiveness and growth. The boom of the 80s, the high profits and the deregulation of the credit and foreign exchange markets gave rise to a sharp expansion of credit lending in the 80s. We had a real estate boom in Sweden and a rapid increase in investments abroad, not least in real estate. Liberalisation was necessary for three main reasons: firstly, IT, electronic money and new financial instruments had already seriously hampered and partly made it impossible to regulate the currency and capital markets; The problems were exacerbated by the fact that deregulation and major tax reform came in the wrong order. Real interest rates after tax were for a period even negative for households, thereby driving up demand for credit very strongly. In that situation, a substantial tightening of fiscal policy would have been needed. The fixed exchange rate meant that monetary policy was locked in, the responsibility for conducting an economic policy that was consistent with a fixed exchange rate thus rested on fiscal policy. The fixed exchange rate is abandoned The overheating of the economy (when all attempts at austerity had failed) led to rapid wage increases and exports began to stagnate anew towards the end of the 80s. As growth slowed and weak competitiveness became apparent, clouds began to loom. The turnaround was quick and dramatic, the reasons were both international and domestic. German reunification led to inflationary pressures in Germany that were met with rising interest rates, which in turn triggered a recession in Europe. Here at home, the decline was amplified by the tax rescheduling that led to a sharp increase in savings - a correction to the high level of indebtedness that had previously arisen. The bubble in the real estate industry was punctured and a long series of bankruptcies hit the real estate and financial sectors. The stability of the banking sector was threatened and the state had to provide a general guarantee to the banking sector to prevent a breakdown in the payment system. The recession now hit the Swedish labour market with full force. Deficits in the state budget and public debt also began to increase sharply. Since 1991, Sweden had unilaterally tied the krona to the EC, in order to make it clear to the outside world that the policy of devaluation was now over. In that situation (1992), the turmoil in the foreign exchange markets began to spread. Today we know that having a small currency, deregulated foreign exchange market and fixed exchange rate is a delicate combination. After a heroic but fruitless defense of the krona with massive interventions and marginal interest rates up to 500%, the Riksbank was forced to give up. The crown began to float (which was the first time since the 30s) and in the first year lost 30 percent of its value. The competitiveness of Swedish industry was restored, but Sweden had once again become poorer in comparison with other countries. An inflation target was introduced instead of the exchange rate target defined by the Riksbank at 2%. New terms I've given this pretty detailed description of the economy in the 70s to 90s because it is important to understand the economic events that constitute the new conditions of politics. The Swedish development can be said to have been part of the international trend towards increasing globalization. It is possible that the cover was particularly noticeable in Sweden, as we postponed some of the changes for the longest time. The financial imbalances that accumulated during the late 1980s were also a major reason for both the banking crisis and the weakness of economic development in the early 90s. It wasn't just an economic transition of great scope. At least as noticeable was the political and (in a broad sense) cultural transition. One question that many people probably ask themselves is whether it could have been avoided. In my opinion, the demands on the Swedish economy and politics could not be avoided, but Sweden, by acting differently, could have prevented and at least mitigated the course of the crisis. But it's easy to be hindsight. Liberalisation and adaptation to the requirements of international competition were and are inevitable. The conditions are determined in a global environment over which Sweden alone has very little influence, where markets of various kinds set limits and create opportunities. Sweden's dependence on this market for its welfare is very large; That is not to say that we have to constantly adapt to the regulatory systems that are most liberal, there are several examples of the opposite, i.e. other industrialised countries having stricter rules. But to put it simply: we have to accept the situation, deal with the problems and seize the opportunities and, in collaboration with others, try to change the conditions - to the extent that we think they are not reasonable. Both in terms of trade openness and deregulation on the capital market, Sweden chose in 1992 to take large socio-economic costs in the form of production losses and mass unemployment in order to achieve long-term good development. The strategy paid off and in the second half of the 90s, the clouds began to dissipate. Today, government finances are in good shape, the current account has for several years shown a surplus, inflation expectations are stable around 2 percent and unemployment is down to around 4 percent. Perhaps we are at the beginning of a new stable period of growth. But the question is whether this will not require at least as great a change in the institutional field as those that characterized the post-war period. The meaning of globalisation Although globalisation is the factor that has changed the conditions of economics and politics more than others over the past 25 years, it is not a new phenomenon. As early as the 1870s and until the end of World War II, Sweden's foreign trade comprised about 20 percent of the Swedish economy. After the end of the Second World War, trade increased sharply and today it amounts to about 40 percent of our total production. This means that Sweden is a very open economy, exposed to competition on the world market. The IMF has a definition of globalization as "the growing interdependence of countries worldwide through the increasing volume and amount of cross-border transactions of goods, services, and flows of capital." Pope John Paul has expressed that "globalization is present in every aspect of human life" and that "solidarity must also become global." What we mean by globalisation in everyday terms is surely primarily the strong growth of the international financial markets. The increased movement of capital across borders and the increased size of the capital market over the past 20 years are linked, on the one hand, to deregulation and, on the other, to the development of electronics and information technology. It is difficult to find comparative figures over time, but in the UK, trading in stocks and bonds across the national border rose from almost nothing to 10 times GDP between 1970 and 1993. The new is not the movement of capital per se, the new thing is the scale - especially in relation to the trade in goods and services. Before 1914, capital also moved freely and there was extensive direct investment across national borders. At their peak around the turn of the last century, outflows from the UK accounted for 9% of their GDP, which is about twice as much as the record-high flows from Japan and West Germany in the 80s. The Swedish railway network and hydropower were expanded largely with the help of foreign capital. The mobility of capital also allowed the emergence of large multinational companies with production units in many different countries. The industrialization of Sweden accelerated, it has been calculated that the Swedish productive capital stock became 50 percent larger between 1870 and 1914 through the import of foreign capital than it would otherwise have been. As the boundaries of capital were torn down in the 80s, Sweden was also the subject of close scrutiny by international investors and capital owners. The slightest hint of mismanagement of economic policy, such as growing budget deficits, too rapidly rising wages or inflation, risks leading to foreign investors selling off their holdings of Swedish government bonds and shares. Signs of mismanagement can also lead to Swedish households and companies choosing to invest their money abroad instead of at home. It was this, combined with Sweden's history of high inflation and other imbalances, that made it impossible for us to maintain the fixed exchange rate in 1992. Financial capital is very volatile, not to say "nervous". The speed and herd behaviour of financial markets means that progress can be excessively dramatic before action is taken. As a rule, what sets speculators in motion is that an economy is out of balance, such as high public debt, weak public finances or weak competitiveness due to high cost situations. A recent example is Argentina. The series of examples where speculation has made it impossible to maintain a fixed exchange rate is long: After Sweden, Finland and the United Kingdom in 1992, Mexico was hit in 1994-95, Southeast Asia in 1997, Russia in 1998, Brazil in 1999, Turkey and Argentina in 2001. All these crises share at least one characteristic: the countries had fixed exchange rates. Why are the financial markets so important? A well-functioning financial sector is an important part of a country's economic infrastructure. If it ceases to function properly, it could have serious consequences for economic development. But it is of course much easier to see the benefits of, for example, transport and energy. The liberalisation of international capital markets means that savings capital can today be moved quickly and almost free of charge between different continents. Capital isn't really that different from other commodities: Some people have a need for capital and are willing to pay to borrow. Others have a savings and can sell the opportunity to use it for a period. Liberalisation has meant that savings can be channelled to a greater extent where it is most useful. Emerging economies today finance their emerging industries and infrastructure using savings capital from us in the rich part of the world, just as we borrowed money from abroad during our industrialization process. At the same time, savers can benefit from the growth potential that exists beyond their own borders. Free movement of capital has also made it possible to spread savings capital and thus reduce risks. It provides financial security both for those who invest and those who make use of loan capital. As pension savers (which we all are), we want to feel confident that our capital retains its value, ideally it should grow as much as is compatible with a safe investment. In this way, we also become the owners of the volatile capital, which immediately flees a country that no longer inspires confidence among the asset managers. The question is how good these fluctuations are for the national economy. Liberalisation has not gone hand in hand with the corresponding development of financial control mechanisms in national economies, let alone the emergence of international regulatory systems or control institutions. Therefore, there is so far an imbalance worldwide between the freedom enjoyed by capital and the forces that can balance and counteract the socially harmful effects. Are poor countries affected by globalisation? A common objection has been that globalisation may benefit the already rich countries but hit the poor all the harder. Let's look at the economic growth of recent decades when the pace of globalization has been particularly high: Since the early 80s, purchasing power per capita has more than doubled in the world as a whole. In Asia, the development has been particularly breathtaking: in 1975, six out of ten people in Asia lived in absolute poverty - under a dollar a day. Today it is two out of ten. In China alone, the number of poor people has fallen from 60% to just under 30% in less than twenty years. While many have improved, the differences between countries and within countries are still large. Nearly three billion people are trying to survive on a daily income that is less than two U.S. dollars. 1 billion people live in absolute poverty. The largest proportion of absolute poverty is found in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia (46 and 40% of the region's inhabitants, respectively). In Africa, even per capita income fell by an average of 1% in 1975-99. The reasons for the poor development in Africa are, of course, multiple and complex: deteriorating prices for raw material exports, trade barriers, corruption, weak governance, failed reforms, climate, AIDS, internal conflicts, population growth, etc. Africa's outlook for the next few years is uncertain. The fall in commodity prices and the recent decline in tourism have hampered development. If growth is only between 3%3.5% per year, there is no possibility of achieving the goal of halving poverty by 2015, which is one of the UN's Millennium Development Goals. So what is behind the rapid growth in other parts of the world? The two main explanations are technological progress and the rapid increase in trade as a result of the dramatic reduction in tariffs and other barriers to trade. World trade has increased by 6% annually for the past 20 years while growth has increased by 3%. The markets have thus become many times larger, which has meant that workers and companies in different parts of the world have been able to concentrate on the production at which they are relatively best. Specialisation and increased competition have put pressure on prices. Household cash lasts longer. The increased economic growth has led to better education and health care. Globalisation also brings with it other benefits: increased contacts with the outside world have made it increasingly difficult to isolate a country, which was a major factor behind the fall of the Iron Curtain. And that was before the Internet, which is a difficult-to-control and extremely powerful tool for disseminating information - even for those who are against globalisation. Criticism of globalisation Despite the positive effects of globalisation in many respects, many see it mostly as a threat. As a rule, it is about one of the following: Trade and new technologies increase competition. Companies are closing down because profitability is higher elsewhere. (Gislaved is a recent example.) Other companies cannot cope with competition and workers and white-collar workers become unemployed. Some believe that the poorest countries would benefit from joining forces with the outside world and building up their own industries in protection against the overwhelming competition from the rich countries, only to eventually be incorporated into the world economy. Free movement of capital makes countries more vulnerable if they pursue a policy less credible in the eyes of the owners/managers. Just as quickly as investment flows in when the economic outlook is good, just as quickly it flows out when financiers suspect that growing problems threaten the value of capital. Although more and more people are better off, the gap between the poor is still growing and rich. 20% of the world's population receives more than 80% of the global income generated. Many countries are at risk of falling further and further behind for various reasons. How can we deal with the downsides/challenges of globalisation? There is ample evidence that countries that pursue a more open and outward-looking policy are growing faster than those that choose to isolate themselves from the outside world. Nor is the problem that the poorest countries cannot compete with developed countries. Companies tend (at least for some production) to look to the countries with the lowest labour costs. This means that globalization places high demands on structural change and processing in the rich countries, i.e. that we seek out those niches where our higher costs matter less. Rather, the problem is that the rich countries still protect their own production to such an extent. Although barriers to trade between countries have generally declined sharply in recent decades, there is still a great deal to be done, especially in the food and textile industries, where the poorest countries have their greatest comparative advantages. For example, the EU spends 2.7 billion a year to keep EU sugar production profitable for European farmers. This is happening in parallel with the poorest countries being kept out of European markets. The UNITED STATES pursues a similar policy, in total, developed countries spend more than 300 billion US dollars a year to protect their own agriculture from competition. You get an idea of the amounts involved if you compare the EU's agricultural aid, USD 42 billion, with the total aid in the world, which is USD 56 billion. It is estimated that a 50% reduction in trade barriers would generate welfare gains of over USD 400 billion per year, a third of these profits could accrue to developing countries. Rather than being a threat, trade is a prerequisite for prosperity, especially for small countries, not least we ourselves have experience of this. Trade is also an important channel for the transfer of knowledge between countries through technologies and innovations of various kinds that are disseminated and conducive to economic development. Until the beginning of the 1990s, it was development assistance that was the most significant capital injection to the developing countries, after which private capital flows have gained the greatest importance. In total, development assistance today accounts for only 18% of the financial flows to developing countries. However, aid is still most important for the poorest developing countries. The second objection was about the mobility of international capital, which means that any hint of problems with growth or stability can quickly have negative effects on the real economy. At the same time, we have seen that countries that have good macroeconomic policies can also suffer from the spillover effects. We saw this, for example, in connection with the financial crisis in Asia and Brazil. What, then, have we learned from the international financial crises of the last decade and what can be done to prevent similar crises in the future? Here I limit myself to addressing the efforts that are ongoing in contexts where the Riksbank is concerned: Better crisis prevention and management Firstly, we have learned that greater transparency in economic policy and statistics is important. Economic information today guides the actions of the financial markets. By telling the outside world what economic policy a country intends to pursue, better predictability is created - uncertainty is reduced. The crisis in Asia was largely rooted in a lack of accounting for economic conditions, which led to incorrect credit assessments and capital flight. For example, by publishing information about its member countries on the Internet, the IMF contributes to transparency. Secondly, we have learned that internationally accepted norms and standards are needed in various areas, such as transparency in monetary policy and banking supervision. The work of creating these standards has come a long way, now the focus is on ensuring that compliance is promoted. It is not always this work gets a prominent place in the globalisation debate, but the more countries that live up to the current standards and standards, the better equipped the financial system would be to prevent financial crises. A financial crisis in Southeast Asia is also taking effect in Sweden. That is why we too benefit from countries on the other side of the globe acquiring better systems for, for example, banking supervision and bankruptcy legislation. Thirdly, we have learned that, in the long run, it is not possible to combine a fixed exchange rate in a world of free movement of capital with an economy in imbalance. Common to almost all of the recent international financial crises is that countries have been forced to abandon a fixed exchange rate, often at very high cost. Fourthly, we have learned that private investors must realise that they are taking risks and taking responsibility for the losses. Large loan packages from, for example, the IMF can create the wrong incentives in that private investors may believe that the international community will always ultimately bail out countries in crisis and that it is therefore not very risky to invest or lend to these countries. There is currently extensive work going on in all these areas in organizations such as the IMF, the World Bank and the BIS to find rules and methods to prevent crises and protect innocent people from the consequences. The demands of the anti-globalization movement The third objection concerned the situation of the poorest countries. The calls for a more equitable globalization were also the theme at the World Social Forum that a large number of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) held in Porto Alegre, Brazil recently. 60,000 people attended, including 6 French ministers. It was a kind of "counter-forum" to the World Economic Forum meeting in New York. The demands were many, including the immediate cancellation of debt for developing countries and the introduction of a tax on foreign exchange transactions (the "Tobin tax"). Of course, the debt situation in many developing countries is an obstacle to growth and combating poverty, but it is not as simple as simply writing the debts and believing that it solves the problems. Moreover, much work has already been done: in 1996, the joint IMF-World Bank initiative for debt relief for the poorest and most indebted countries, the HIPC initiative, was launched. The difference from previous efforts in the debt sector was that the initiative brought together all one country's lenders (including the international financial institutions) with the aim of reducing the external debt of poor and heavily indebted developing countries. In 1998, it was decided to take further action within the framework of this initiative. So far, 24 countries have received debt relief decisions equivalent to just over USD 20 billion. The total cost of debt relief for all 34 countries included in the initiative is estimated at USD 33 billion. The funds released by these debt reliefs will be used to step up efforts to combat poverty. Why do we not write off the debts of the poorest countries altogether, someone might ask. The funds that the IMF lends on soft terms to the poorest member countries consist of loans and grants from individual member countries. A total cancellation of the countries' debts would mean that all the funds for this soft (1) lending would have to be used. Other poor, but less indebted Member States would thus not be able to obtain grants and loans on soft terms. Recently, various proposals have been made to try to generate more money for the benefit of the poorest countries. For example, the income from a currency exchange tax, a so-called currency exchange tax, would be reduced. Tobin tax could be used for aid. George Soros has also proposed the use of imf special drawing rights for aid activities. However, both of these proposals are fraught with great difficulties. The Tobin tax would reduce liquidity and risk appetite in capital markets and thus likely help to reduce the flow of capital, including to developing countries. In addition, it is difficult to implement, it must preferably apply to everyone countries of the world to be effective. Even Soros' proposal is probably not realistic; already today there is a decision from 1997 to increase the IMF's special drawing rights that have not been adopted by the US Congress, which is a condition for implementation. It is therefore difficult to see why new proposals in this direction would be better placed. The problem is that the political will is lacking, especially among the largest and richest countries in the world to increase resources for aid. Today, only five OECD countries (Denmark, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden) have achieved the target of 0.7% of GDP for foreign aid. But even if more money is needed, even that is not always a sufficient solution; Good quality of development projects and plans in developing countries and competence in the management of resources are at least as important. Concluding remarks It may sound to some as if I have almost sung the praises of globalisation. That wasn't my point. There are lots of big, unresolved problems associated with globalisation. One , which concerns me a lot as a private person concerns the conditions of democracy. But what I want to say is that it is not possible to roll back the sequence of events, neither in Sweden nor in the world at large. And that there are also great benefits from globalization. Instead, the question we must ask ourselves is how globalisation/the international market economy can be reconciled with respect for human dignity, care and long-termism in our economies. Today, in my opinion, there is a significant imbalance between the strength and speed of global financial and corporate markets and societal, human considerations. It will be like when the gazelle competes with the turtle. Not least in the environmental field, the conflict becomes clear. As has been shown, I do not believe that the Tobin tax, a radical cancellation of debt or a return to the old national regulatory systems will solve the problems. Part of the solution is simply "unsexy": It is internationally covered rules for transparency, supervision, accounting, sound public finances and, not least, functioning democracies that take responsibility for distribution and welfare issues. But there is also a need for international rules for, among other things, the environment and for how people are treated. Not least, resources are required for follow-up and sanctions if they are not complied with. In addition to this laborious and often slow international cooperation that governments engage in, there are of course other arenas for political influence: Consumers, popular movements and trade unions could work together more to create a counterforce. In order to gain and maintain the trust of citizens, the business community must also actively contribute with efforts to increase the long-term and social responsibility of entrepreneurship and financial markets. The legal route is too slow and difficult to get comprehensive. The customers, who are ultimately all citizens and the media - who have a great responsibility for the spread of so-called quarterly capitalism - must also contribute by rewarding socio-economically sustainable performance. The events in Seattle, Prague, Gothenburg and, not least, in New York on 11 September have, in any case, brought the issues of globalisation higher up the agenda. Which I think is good and necessary. Thank you. Footnote 1) Soft or concessional lending by the Monetary Fund, i.e. loans with a long maturity (10 years), a long grace period (51/2 years) and a very low interest rate (0.05%). To compare with the fund's regular lending, which is usually to be repaid after 5 years and where the interest rate is market-determined.

Nya villkor Jag har gett den hr ganska utfrliga beskrivningen av ekonomin under 70- till 90-tal fr att det r viktigt att frst det ekonomiska skeende som utgr politikens nya villkor. Kraven p svensk ekonomi och politik kunde enligt min mening inte undvikas, dremot hade Sverige, genom att agera annorlunda kunnat frhindra och i vart fall mildra krisfrloppet. Som regel handlar det om ngot av fljande: Handel och ny teknik kar konkurrensen. Fretag lggs ner drfr att lnsamheten r strre p annat hll. (Gislaved r ett frskt exempel.) Vissa menar att de fattigaste lnderna skulle vinna p att sluta sig mot omvrlden och bygga upp sina egna industrier i skydd mot den vermktiga konkurrensen frn de rika lnderna, fr att frst s smningom inlemmas i vrldsekonomin. Mnga lnder riskerar av olika skl att hamna allt lngre p efterklken. Hur kan vi hantera globaliseringens avigsidor/utmaningar? Det finns gott om bevis fr att lnder som fr en mer ppen och uttriktad politik vxer snabbare n de som vljer att isolera sig mot omvrlden. Problemet r inte heller att de fattigaste lnderna inte kan konkurrera med i-lnderna. Det gr att globaliseringen stller hga krav p strukturomvandling och frdling i de rika lnderna, d.v.s. att vi sker oss till de nischer dr vra hgre kostnader spelar mindre roll. Problemet r snarare att de rika lnderna i s hg grad fortfarande skyddar sin egen produktion. ven om handelshindren mellan lnderna generellt sett har minskat kraftigt under de senaste decennierna finns fortfarande en hel del kvar, det gller srskilt inom livsmedel- och textilindustri dr de fattigaste lnderna har sina strsta komparativa frdelar. T.ex. satsar EU 2,7 miljarder euro per r fr att hlla sockerproduktionen inom EU lnsam fr europeiska bnder. Detta sker parallellt med att de fattigaste lnderna hlls utanfr de europeiska marknaderna. USA fr motsvarande politik, totalt anvnder industrilnderna mer 300 miljarder US dollar per r fr att skydda det egna jordbruket frn konkurrens. En uppfattning om vilka belopp det rr sig om fr man om man jmfr EU:s jordbruksstd, 42 miljarder US dollar med det samlade bistndet i vrlden som r 56 miljarder dollar. Man rknar med att en 50% minskning av handelshindren skulle generera vlfrdsvinster p ver 400 miljarder USD per r, en tredjedel av dessa vinster skulle kunna tillfalla u-lnderna. Snarare n att vara ett hot, r handeln en frutsttning fr vlstnd, srskilt fr sm lnder, det har inte minst vi sjlva erfarenheter av. Handeln r ocks en viktig kanal fr kunskapsverfring mellan lnder genom teknik och innovationer av olika slag som sprids och gynnar den ekonomiska utvecklingen. Fram till brjan av 1990-talet var det bistndet som var det mest betydelsefulla kapitaltillskottet till u-lnderna, drefter har de privata kapitalfldena ftt strst betydelse. Totalt svarar bistndet idag fr endast 18% av de finansiella fldena till ulnderna. Bistndet r dock fortfarande viktigast fr de allra fattigaste u-lnderna. Den andra invndningen handlade om det internationella kapitalets rrlighet, som innebr att varje antydan om problem med tillvxten eller stabiliteten snabbt kan ge negativa effekter p den reala ekonomin. Samtidigt har vi sett att ocks lnder, som fr en god makroekonomisk politik kan drabbas av spridningseffekterna. Det sg vi t.ex. i samband med den finansiella krisen i Asien och Brasilien. Vad har vi d lrt oss av det senaste decenniets internationella finansiella kriser och vad kan man gra fr att frhindra liknande kriser i framtiden? Hr begrnsar jag mig till att ta upp de insatser som pgr i sammanhang dr Riksbanken r berrd: Bttre krisfrebyggande och krishantering Fr det frsta har vi lrt oss att det r viktigt med kad ppenhet nr det gller ekonomisk politik och statistik. Genom att tala om fr omvrlden vilken ekonomisk politik ett land har fr avsikt att fra skapas bttre frutsgbarhet - oskerheten minskar. Krisen i Asien bottnade mycket i bristande redovisning av de ekonomiska frhllandena, vilket ledde till felaktiga kreditbedmningar och kapitalflykt. Genom att publicera information om sina medlemslnder bl.a. p Internet bidrar t.ex. IMF till ppenheten. Fr det andra har vi lrt oss att det behvs internationellt accepterade normer och standarder inom olika omrden, t.ex. fr ppenhet inom penningpolitiken och fr banktillsyn. Arbetet med att skapa dessa normer har kommit lngt, nu r fokus p att se till att frmja efterlevnaden. Det r inte alltid detta arbete fr en framskjuten plats i globaliseringsdebatten men ju fler lnder som lever upp till de aktuella normerna och standarderna desto bttre rustat skulle det finansiella systemet vara att frebygga finanskriser. En finansiell kris i Sydostasien slr igenom ven i Sverige. Drfr fr ven vi nytta av att lnder p andra sidan klotet skaffar sig bttre system fr exempelvis banktillsyn och konkurslagstiftning. Fr det tredje har vi lrt oss att det i lngden inte gr att kombinera en fast vxelkurs i en vrld av fria kapitalrrelser med en ekonomi i obalans. Gemensamt med nstan samtliga av den senaste tidens internationella finanskriser r att lnderna har tvingats verge en fast vxelkurs, ofta till mycket hg kostnad. Fr det fjrde har vi lrt oss att privata investerare mste inse att de tar risker och ta ansvar fr frlusterna. Stora lnepaket frn t.ex. IMF kan skapa felaktiga incitament genom att privata investerare kan tro att det internationella samfundet alltid i slutndan kommer att lsa ut lnder i kris och att det drfr inte r srskilt riskfyllt att investera eller lna till dessa lnder. Det pgr idag ett omfattande arbete inom alla dessa omrden i organisationer som IMF, Vrldsbanken och BIS fr att finna regler och metoder fr att dels frebygga kriser dels skydda oskyldiga mnniskor frn konsekvenserna. Kraven frn anti-globaliseringsrrelsen Den tredje invndningen rrde de fattigaste lndernas situation. Kraven p en mer rttvis globalisering var ocks temat vid World Social Forum som ett stort antal enskilda organisationer (NGOs) hll i i Porto Alegre, Brasilien nyligen. 60 000 mnniskor deltog, dribland 6 franska ministrar. Det var ett slags "motforum" till World Economic Forums mte i New York. Kraven var mnga, bl.a. en omedelbar skuldavskrivning fr u-lnderna och infrande av skatt p valutatransaktioner ("Tobin-skatten"). Naturligtvis utgr skuldsituationen i mnga utvecklingslnder ett hinder fr tillvxt och bekmpning av fattigdom men det r inte s enkelt som att bara skriva skulderna och tro att det lser problemen. Mycket arbete har dessutom redan skett: 1996 sjsattes IMF:s och Vrldsbankens gemensamma initiativ fr skuldlttnader fr de fattigaste och mest skuldsatta lnderna, HIPC-initiativet. Hittills har 24 lnder ftt beslut om skuldlttnader som motsvarar drygt 20 miljarder USD. Den totala kostnaden fr skuldlttnaden fr samtliga 34 lnder som ingr i initiativet berknas uppg till 33 miljarder USD. De medel som frigrs genom dessa skuldlttnader skall anvndas fr att ka insatserna fr fattigdomsbekmpning. Varfr skriver vi inte av de fattigaste lndernas skulderna helt och hllet kan ngon frga sig. De medel som IMF lnar ut p mjuka villkor till de fattigaste medlemslnderna utgrs av ln och bidrag frn enskilda medlemslnder. En total avskrivning av lndernas skulder skulle medfra att samtliga medel fr denna mjuka (1) utlning skulle behva tas i ansprk. Andra fattiga, men mindre skuldtyngda medlemslnder skulle drmed inte kunna erhlla bidrag och ln p mjuka villkor. Under den senaste tiden har olika frslag rests om att frska generera mer pengar till frmn fr det fattigaste lnderna. T.ex. skulle inkomsterna frn en skatt p valutavxling, en s.k. Tobinskatt kunna anvndas till bistnd. George Soros har ocks freslagit anvndande av IMF:s srskilda dragningsrtter fr bistndsverksamhet. Bda dessa frslag r emellertid frknippade med stora svrigheter. Tobinskatten skulle minska likviditeten och riskvilligheten p kapitalmarknaderna och drmed sannolikt bidra till att minska kapitalfldet, ocks till utvecklingslnderna. Dessutom r den svr att genomfra, den mste helst avse alla lnder i vrlden fr att vara effektiv. ven Soros frslag r frmodligen inte realistiskt; redan idag finns ett beslut frn 1997 om att ka IMF:s srskilda dragningsrtter som inte har antagits av den amerikanska kongressen, vilket r ett villkor fr genomfrande. Det r drfr svrt att se varfr nya frslag i denna riktning skulle ha bttre frutsttningar. Problemet r att den politiska viljan fattas, srskilt bland de strsta och rikaste lnderna i vrlden att ka resurserna fr bistnd. I dag r det endast fem OECD-lnder (Danmark, Luxemburg, Holland, Norge och Sverige) som har uppntt mlet med ett ulandsbistnd som uppgr till 0,7% av BNP. Men ven om mer pengar behvs r inte heller det alltid en tillrcklig lsning; god kvalitet p utvecklingsprojekten och planerna i u-lnderna och kompetens i hanteringen av resurserna r minst lika viktigt. Avslutande kommentar Det kanske fr en del kan lta som om jag nrap har sjungit globaliseringens lov. Det var inte min mening. Det finns massor av stora, olsta problem som r frknippade med globaliseringen. Ett , som engagerar mig mycket som privatperson rr demokratins villkor. Men vad jag vill ha sagt r att det inte gr att rulla tillbaka hndelsefrloppen, varken i Sverige eller i vrlden i stort. Och att det ocks finns stora vinster med globaliseringen. Den frga som vi i stllet mste stlla oss r hur globaliseringen/den internationella marknadsekonomin kan frenas med respekten fr mnniskovrde, omtanke och lngsiktighet i vra ekonomier. Det finns i dag enligt min mening en betydande obalans mellan de globala finans- och fretagsmarknadernas styrka och snabbhet och de samhlleliga, mnskliga hnsynen. Det blir som nr gasellen tvlar med skldpaddan. Inte minst inom miljomrdet blir konflikten tydlig. Title: Women, growth and welfare  an equation that must come together
text: Persson: Women, growth and welfare - an equation that must go together Date 2004-03-08 Deputy Governor Kristina Persson spoke on International Women's Day, 8 March, about the threats to welfare and women's work "If today's trends continue, demographic trends mean that we will be fewer and fewer in working life and more and more people who need to be supported. The number of people over the age of 64 will increase by about 40% by 2030, while people of working age will only increase by just under 5%. This means that the state and municipalities receive increasingly lower revenues at the same time as the need for welfare services increases sharply. For example, the number of people over the age of 80 is expected to almost double by 2030. With unchanged ambition, the public sector would need an addition of 130,000 new employees in the next ten years alone. This raises the question of how welfare support in the event of unemployment and ill health, pension, health care, child and elderly care - can be maintained in the future. The issue is of particular importance to women because they are the ones who largely work in the public sector (about 75 percent of the employees in that sector are women) and to a large extent stand up as private, unpaid carers when the public sector is not enough," Persson began. "The amount of resources in a society is determined by economic growth which in turn is determined by how much we work (the labor supply) and how productive we are (productivity). There is very likely to be potential for increasing productivity in the services sector. But in areas such as health care, care and education, this is limited by the fact that human labor cannot be so easily replaced by machines. In addition, increased productivity in the private sector is putting upward pressure on wages in the public sector as well. Therefore, increased productivity alone is not enough to improve public sector finances," Persson said. "The Riksbank's statutory task is to work for price stability, i.e. low inflation, which the Riksbank has defined as an increase in CPI of 2 percent. While low inflation creates favourable conditions for good economic growth, what determines the pace at which the economy can grow without inflationary pressures is a country's long-term ability to grow. This is determined by action in many different areas, such as investment in education, research and development, the design of social security systems and the conditions under which entrepreneurs are provided. A higher long-term growth capacity means that the economy can grow more in the coming decades without the Riksbank having to tighten monetary policy. The efforts required are not within the Riksbank's area of responsibility. It is the politicians in the government and the Riksdag who can create favorable conditions for an increased labor supply and increased productivity, and thus ensure the survival of the welfare state in the long run," Persson said. "The range of work depends on how many people work and how many hours each one works. From an international perspective, Sweden has a high labour force participation rate both among men and among women. Thus, we do not have the reserve of labour that many other European countries have in the form of women. Increased labour supply requires that everyone works more and that labour migration increases. We live healthy much longer than before, but the time spent in working life has decreased. Many go into work late and stop working around 60. More than 1 million people are inactive, while 300 000 people are not working because they are ill. If the ratio between breadwinners and breadwinners is not to deteriorate, many more people will have to work significantly longer," Persson said. "Although the female labor force participation rate in Sweden is high, women work significantly fewer hours than men in the paid labor market - about 40 percent work part-time. By making it easier for women to increase their working hours, reducing unsanitary rates and taking measures to enable people on sick leave to start working again, the number of hours worked could increase. Many different efforts are required to succeed in this, which in my opinion mainly concern, among other things, the organization and management of the public sector and people's incentives to work," Persson said. "Today, women do most of the homework and most of the care work. This is one of the explanations for why women have significantly lower labour incomes than men. The public sector enables a high labor force participation rate for both men and women in Sweden by taking great responsibility for, among other things, elderly care and child care. If the resources for this were no longer sufficient, it could make it more difficult to continue to have a high labour force participation rate and have distributional consequences. In summary, long-term sustainable growth is a prerequisite for a well-functioning welfare society in the future. That society is able to meet these challenges is of great importance to women", Persson concluded.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Persson: Kvinnor, tillvxt och vlfrd  en ekvation som mste g ihop Datum 2004-03-08 Vice riksbankschef Kristina Persson talade p den internationella kvinnodagen, den 8 mars om hoten mot vlfrden och kvinnors arbete "Om dagens trender hller i sig innebr den demografiska utvecklingen att vi blir allt frre i arbetslivet och allt fler som behver bli frsrjda. Antalet personer ver 64 r kommer att ka med ungefr 40 procent fram till 2030, samtidigt som personer i yrkesverksam lder endast kar med knappt 5 procent. Det innebr att stat och kommuner fr allt lgre intkter samtidigt som behoven av vlfrdstjnster kar kraftigt. Exempelvis berknas antalet personer ver 80 r nstan frdubblas till r 2030. Med ofrndrad ambitionsniv skulle offentlig sektor behva ett tillskott av 130 000 nya anstllda bara de nrmaste tio ren. Detta vcker frgan hur vlfrden std vid arbetslshet och ohlsa, pension, sjukvrd, barn- och ldreomsorg - ska kunna upprtthllas i framtiden. Frgan har srskild betydelse fr kvinnorna eftersom det r de som till stor del arbetar i offentlig sektor (ungefr 75 procent av de anstllda i den sektorn r kvinnor) och i stor utstrckning stller upp som privata, obetalda vrdare nr offentlig sektor inte rcker till", inledde Persson. "Mngden resurser i ett samhlle bestms av den ekonomiska tillvxten som i sin tur avgrs av hur mycket vi arbetar (arbetsutbudet) och hur produktiva vi r (produktiviteten). Det finns med stor sannolikhet en potential fr att hja produktiviteten inom tjnstesektorn. Men inom omrden som vrd, omsorg och utbildning begrnsas denna av att mnsklig arbetskraft inte s ltt kan ersttas med maskiner. Drtill kommer att kad produktivitet i det privata nringslivet stter en press uppt p lnerna ocks inom den offentliga sektorn. Drfr rcker det inte med enbart kad produktivitet fr att frbttra den offentliga sektorns finanser", sade Persson. "Riksbankens lagstadgade uppgift r att arbeta fr prisstabilitet, d.v.s. lg inflation, vilket Riksbanken har definierat som en kning av KPI med 2 procent. En lg inflation skapar visserligen gynnsamma frutsttningar fr en god ekonomisk tillvxt, men det som avgr i vilken takt ekonomin kan vxa utan att det uppstr ett inflationstryck r ett lands lngsiktiga tillvxtfrmga. Denna bestms genom insatser inom mnga olika omrden, exempelvis satsningar p utbildning, forskning och utveckling, socialfrskringssystemens utformning och av de villkor som rder fr entreprenrer. En hgre lngsiktig tillvxtfrmga innebr att ekonomin kan vxa mer under kommande decennier utan att Riksbanken behver strama t penningpolitiken. De insatser som krvs ligger inte inom Riksbankens ansvarsomrde. Det r politikerna i regering och riksdag som kan skapa gynnsamma frutsttningar fr ett kat arbetsutbud och en kad produktivitet, och drmed skra vlfrdsstatens fortlevnad p sikt", sade Persson. "Arbetsutbudet beror av hur mnga personer som arbetar och hur mnga timmar som var och en arbetar. I ett internationellt perspektiv har Sverige ett hgt arbetskraftsdeltagande bde bland mn och bland kvinnor. Sledes har vi inte den arbetskraftsreserv som mnga andra europeiska lnder har i form av kvinnor. kat arbetsutbud frutstter att alla arbetar mera och att arbetskraftsinvandringen kar. Vi lever friska mycket lngre n frr men tiden i arbetslivet har minskat. Mnga gr ut i arbetslivet sent och slutar arbeta kring 60. Drygt 1 miljon mnniskor str utanfr arbetskraften, samtidigt som 300 000 mnniskor inte arbetar drfr att de r sjuka. Om kvoten mellan frsrjda och frsrjare inte ska frsmras mste mnga fler mnniskor arbeta betydligt lngre", sade Persson. "ven om det kvinnliga arbetskraftsdeltagandet i Sverige r hgt arbetar kvinnorna betydligt frre timmar n mnnen p den betalda arbetsmarknaden - ca 40 procent arbetar deltid. Genom att underltta fr kvinnor att g upp i arbetstid, minska ohlsotalen samt vidta tgrder fr att sjukskrivna personer kan brja arbeta igen skulle antalet arbetade timmar kunna ka. Det krvs mnga olika insatser fr att lyckas med detta, som enligt min mening frmst rr bl.a. den offentliga sektorns organisation och ledning samt mnniskors incitament att arbeta", sade Persson. "Idag utfr kvinnor det mesta av hemarbetet och merparten av vrdarbetet. Detta r en av frklaringarna till varfr kvinnor har vsentligt lgre arbetsinkomster n mnnen. Den offentliga sektorn mjliggr ett hgt arbetskraftsdeltagande fr bde mn och kvinnor i Sverige genom att ta ett stort ansvar fr bl.a. ldrevrd och barnomsorg. Om resurserna fr detta inte lngre skulle rcka till kan det frsvra ett fortsatt hgt arbetskraftsdeltagande och f frdelningspolitiska konsekvenser. Sammanfattningsvis r en lngsiktigt uthllig tillvxt ett villkor fr ett vl fungerande vlfrdssamhlle i framtiden. Att samhllet klarar av att mta dessa utmaningar r av stor betydelse fr kvinnorna", avslutade Persson. Title: Monetary policy  experiences and thoughts on the future
text: Persson: Monetary policy  experiences and thoughts on the future Date 2007-01-12 Deputy Governor Kristina Persson will speak on Saturday in Lulea at a seminar organized by Swedbank on Swedish monetary policy, the experiences of inflation targets and her thoughts on the future. "Initially, I would like to comment on the monetary policy minutes published early last week. All of us on the Executive Board agreed that a 25 basis point increase in the repo rate was appropriate. The continued strong economy is expected to lead to rising inflation in the coming years. The repo rate, as we see it now, will also need to be raised further in order for inflation to be in line with the target in a few years' time. However, the pace at which, as usual, depends on how the economy develops in the future. At present, not least the development of the labor market is in focus," Persson began. "There are many indications that there are still available resources in the labour market. The proposals that the government has now put forward should, at least in the long term, lead to an increase in the supply of labour. The key to good labour market development going forward is that the matching of supply and demand works well," Persson continued. "A major challenge, for both the government and the social partners, will be to facilitate the transitions needed for the matching to succeed. This requires a good business climate and willingness to invest in both knowledge and capital. A functioning match also requires flexibility in the labor market so that employees can train as quickly and smoothly as possible, apply to new industries and places," Persson said. "Responsibility for the development of employment and unemployment rests with the social partners and the government. What the Riksbank can do is to conduct a well-balanced monetary policy in line with the intentions of the Riksbank Act, so that inflation is low and stable while the short-term cyclical variations do not become unnecessarily large. By stabilising inflation expectations, monetary policy contributes to more stable economic developments. The Riksbank has largely succeeded well in this so far since the inflation target was introduced," Persson said. "Two professors, Francesco Giavazzi and Frederic Mishkin, have examined how well the Riksbank has succeeded in its monetary policy over the past 10 years. As the Riksbank has an independent position, it is important that monetary policy is regularly reviewed and evaluated. The evaluation's overall impression of Swedish monetary policy and the Riksbank is positive. However, the authors put forward criticism on some points, aimed at both the Riksdag and the government as well as the Riksbank," Persson said. "In my opinion, the criticism of the Riksbank is partly justified. Giavazzi and Mishkin believe that the Riksbank should pay more attention than has been the case to the development of the real economy and the labor market. I agree with that. To this end, I took various initiatives during the years 2002-2004 to highlight the so-called structural issues in the Riksbank's work. They also believe that: inflation reports should more clearly set out what the flexibility of inflation targeting policies means. We have certainly discussed this in various contexts, including in the publication "Monetary policy in Sweden", which explains how the Riksbank can take into account the development of employment and growth in setting interest rates. But we should, in my opinion, be able to become even better at communicating to the outside world what this means in practice. I also agree with Giavazzi and Mishkin that the Riksbank should publish forecasts based on its own assessment of the future repo rate instead of the technical assumption that is being made now and which is based on what the players in the financial markets expect. This is an issue that has been being prepared within the Executive Board for some time," Persson pointed out. "Giavazzi and Mishkin also criticize the Riksbank for lowering inflation targets in recent years. To compensate for this, inflation, if I interpret the evaluation correctly, should be allowed to exceed the target for some time. But with such an approach, it is, in my view, very difficult to anchor public expectations about future inflation. However, when it comes to the criticism of the Riksbank for inflation in recent years undercut the inflation target, I agree that we should have lowered interest rates faster and earlier. But it should be remembered that the reasons for the low inflation had nothing to do with weak demand in the economy, i.e. the conditions that the Riksbank can fend off with its repo rate changes. Instead, the low inflation was due to favorable supply conditions such as surprisingly high productivity and low, even falling, import prices," Persson continued. "If the Riksbank had been able to predict the development of productivity and import prices, the improvement in the labour market would probably have started somewhat earlier. But we should not exaggerate the effects of a lower policy rate in the years 2002-2004. It is not obvious that an even lower interest rate would have had a particularly large impact on consumers' willingness to consume and employers' propensity to hire," Persson noted. "When the Riksbank was to formulate an inflation target in the early 1990s, we could not foresee the price-dampening effects that information technology and globalisation would give rise to. Then it was above all important to formulate a simple goal that the public could understand and absorb. Succeeding in anchoring inflation expectations and creating great credibility for monetary policy was very important. Perhaps, with today's knowledge, in my view, we would not have chosen to specify a precise target of 2% with a tolerance range of plus minus 1%, but more concerned with the range itself, that inflation should be between 1% and 3%, but that we normally aim to reach 2%. The difference is not large, but given that deviations from the target will always exist, especially in situations when major structural changes occur, it would be more adapted to what is reasonable to expect from an inflation targeting policy," Persson concluded.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Persson: Penningpolitiken  erfarenheter och tankar om framtiden Datum 2007-01-12 Vice riksbankschef Kristina Persson talar p lrdag i Lule vid ett seminarium anordnat av Swedbank om den svenska penningpolitiken, erfarenheterna av inflationsml och sina tankar om framtiden. Inledningsvis vill jag kommentera det penningpolitiska protokollet som publicerades i brjan av frra veckan. Vi var alla i direktionen eniga om att en hjning av reporntan med 25 punkter var lmplig. Den fortsatt starka konjunkturen bedms leda till en stigande inflation de kommande ren. Reporntan kommer, som vi ser det nu, ven att behva hjas ytterligare fr att inflationen ska bli i linje med mlet p ngra rs sikt. I vilken takt beror dock som vanligt p hur ekonomin utvecklas framver. Fr nrvarande str inte minst utvecklingen p arbetsmarknaden i fokus, inledde Persson. Mycket tyder p att det fortfarande finns lediga resurser p arbetsmarknaden. De frslag som regeringen nu har lagt fram br tminstone p sikt leda till att utbudet av arbetskraft kar. Nyckeln till en god arbetsmarknadsutveckling framver r att matchningen av utbud och efterfrgan fungerar bra, fortsatte Persson. En stor utmaning, fr s vl regeringen som fr parterna p arbetsmarknaden, blir att underltta de omstllningar som behvs fr att matchningen ska lyckas. Det krver ett bra fretagsklimat och vilja att investera i bde kunskap och kapital. En fungerande matchning krver ven flexibilitet p arbetsmarknaden s att arbetstagarna s snabbt och smidigt som mjligt kan utbilda sig, ska sig till nya branscher och orter, sade Persson. Ansvaret fr hur sysselsttning och arbetslshet utvecklas vilar p arbetsmarknadens parter och regeringen. Det Riksbanken kan gra r att fra en vlavvgd penningpolitik i linje med riksbankslagens intentioner, s att inflationen blir lg och stabil samtidigt som de kortsiktiga konjunkturmssiga variationerna inte blir ondigt stora. Genom att stabilisera inflationsfrvntningarna bidrar penningpolitiken till en mer stabil ekonomisk utveckling. Det har Riksbanken i stora drag lyckats vl med hittills sedan inflationsmlet infrdes, menade Persson. Tv professorer, Francesco Giavazzi och Frederic Mishkin, har granskat hur vl Riksbanken har lyckats med den frda penningpolitiken under de senaste 10 ren. Eftersom Riksbanken har en sjlvstndig stllning r det viktigt att penningpolitiken regelbundet granskas och utvrderas. Utvrderingens helhetsintryck av den svenska penningpolitiken och Riksbanken r positivt. Frfattarna fr dock fram kritik p ngra punkter, riktad till svl riksdag och regering som Riksbanken, sade Persson. Enligt min mening r kritiken mot Riksbanken delvis befogad. Giavazzi och Mishkin anser att Riksbanken i strre utstrckning n vad som varit fallet borde uppmrksamma utvecklingen av den reala ekonomin och arbetsmarknaden. Detta hller jag med om. I detta syfte tog jag olika initiativ under ren 2002-2004 fr att lyfta fram de s.k. strukturfrgorna i Riksbankens arbete. De anser ven att inflationsrapporterna tydligare br redovisa vad flexibiliteten i inflationsmlspolitiken innebr. Detta har vi visserligen i olika sammanhang diskuterat , bl.a. i skriften Penningpolitiken i Sverige som frklarar hur Riksbanken i rntesttningen kan ta hnsyn till utvecklingen av sysselsttning och tillvxt. Men vi br, enligt min mening, kunna bli nnu bttre p att kommunicera till omvrlden vad detta i praktiken innebr. Jag hller ocks med Giavazzi och Mishkin om att Riksbanken borde publicera prognoser baserade p en egen bedmning av den framtida reporntan istllet fr det tekniska antagande som grs nu och som utgr frn vad aktrerna p de finansiella marknaderna frvntar sig. Detta r en frga som bereds inom direktionen sedan en tid tillbaka, ppekade Persson. Giavazzi och Mishkin kritiserar ven Riksbanken fr att inflationen underskridit inflationsmlet de senaste ren. Fr att kompensera fr detta br inflationen, om jag tolkar utvrderingen rtt, tilltas verskrida mlet en tid. Men med en sdan metod r det, enligt min uppfattning, mycket svrt att frankra allmnhetens frvntningar om den framtida inflationen. Nr det gller kritiken mot Riksbanken fr att inflationen de senaste ren underskridigt inflationsmlet hller jag dock med om att vi borde ha snkt rntan snabbare och tidigare. Men man br komma ihg att orsakerna till den lga inflationen inte hade med en svag efterfrgan i ekonomin att gra, allts de frhllanden som Riksbanken kan parera med sina reporntefrndringar. Istllet berodde den lga inflationen p gynnsamma utbudsfrhllanden ssom verraskande hg produktivitet och lga, till och med sjunkande, importpriser fortsatte Persson. Om Riksbanken hade kunnat frutse utvecklingen av produktiviteten och importpriserna skulle frbttringen av arbetsmarknaden sannolikt ha kommit igng ngot tidigare. Men vi ska inte verdriva effekterna av en lgre styrrnta under ren 2002-2004. Det r inte sjlvklart att en nnu lgre rnta skulle ha haft srskilt stort genomslag p konsumenternas vilja att konsumera och arbetsgivarnas bengenhet att anstlla, konstaterade Persson. Nr Riksbanken i brjan av 1990-talet skulle formulera ett inflationsml kunde vi inte frutse de prisdmpande effekter som informationsteknologin och globaliseringen skulle ge upphov till. D var det framfrallt viktigt att formulera ett enkelt ml som allmnheten kunde frst och ta till sig. Att lyckas frankra inflationsfrvntningarna och skapa stor trovrdighet fr penningpolitiken var mycket viktigt. Kanske hade vi med dagens kunskap, enligt mitt stt att se det, inte valt att precisera ett exakt ml p 2 procent med ett toleransintervall p plus minus 1 procent utan mer tagit fasta p sjlva intervallet, att inflationen ska ligga mellan 1 och 3 procent men att vi normalt siktar p att n 2 procent. Skillnaden r inte stor men med tanke p att avvikelser frn mlet alltid kommer att finnas, speciellt i situationer d stora strukturella frndringar sker, vore det mer anpassat till vad som r rimligt att frvnta sig av en inflationsmlspolitik, avslutade Persson. Title: Regional balance and sustainable growth
text: Persson: Regional balance and sustainable growth Date 2004-04-21 Deputy Governor Kristina Persson spoke today at a conference in Stockholm under the auspices of Statistics Sweden on the theme of regional growth The Riksbank's responsibility is to maintain price stability and to contribute to a secure and efficient payment system. Regional balance is thus not the Riksbank's responsibility, but imbalances between regions can make the Riksbank's work more difficult. The same problem that was discussed before the EMU vote last autumn applies to Sweden, which, as a currency area with regional differences, may suffer from both unemployment and regional overheating. In light of the fact that interest rates and the currency cannot be adjusted based on developments in different regions of the country, other mechanisms must work," Persson began. "During the second half of the 1990s, Swedish growth was mainly concentrated in the metropolitan regions such as Malardalen, Skane and Western Sweden, which showed a higher growth rate than the rest of the country. Growth in Malardalen and Stockholm, which were the centres of ICT and financial companies, was around 4.5 per cent per year between 1994 and 2000. This was clearly above growth in other regions of Sweden. The economic slowdown of recent years and the decline of the ICT sector have meant that Malardalen's advantage has at least temporarily changed to its opposite, while the two other metropolitan regions have weathered the economic downturn relatively well," Persson said. "The metropolitan regions will of course, not least because of the size and function as a center for research and development, continue to be of great importance for Sweden's growth. But neither do they benefit from overly unbalanced growth or can grow unlimitedly. When the economy turns upwards, Sweden's economy may end up in a situation where there is a shortage of certain types of labor, which can generate bottleneck problems and regional overheating. This is what happened, especially in the Stockholm region in 1999-2000. Even when unemployment, as it is now, appears relatively high, labour shortages can quickly arise in certain regions or occupations. This poses a risk to wage formation and thus to inflation," Persson said. "From about 2008 and for a long time to come, net additions to the workforce are predicted to decline sharply, which means that fewer and fewer people will support more and more people. At the same time, the need for welfare services is increasing. These developments will put great strain on the social security system, among other things, making new, longer-term solutions necessary. Demographic developments also pose a risk of even greater problems for those areas that are already sparsely populated and have a skewed age distribution. This applies not least to the northern hinterland, where it will take a lot of entrepreneurial spirit and social innovation capacity to stop further depopulation. For this reason, municipalities and companies should be encouraged, among other things, to work for an increased labor supply and increased labor immigration from other countries," Persson emphasized. "As a result of extensive immigration, from both other regions and other countries, for a long time, Stockholm has a privileged starting point. In addition, receives Stockholm as the capital much more of publicly funded activities than others, not least those that are today considered important to stimulate growth. In the Stockholm region, there is no less than 40 percent of the total resources for research and development, as well as a large part of the publicly funded culture", Persson said. "The intensifying competition that arises in the wake of globalisation can also have regional consequences. The new technology means that sectors that were previously not exposed to foreign competition are now so. Large differences in labour costs mean that labour-intensive and less skilled production is taken over by or relocated to the eu's new member countries, India or China. The solution to this problem is for Swedish production to advance up the value chain and increasingly orient itself to new and growing product areas that are able to bear high wages. I do not believe that a reduction in wages is a solution! On the other hand, it is important that young people are allowed into the labor market, how this is achieved is another issue", Persson said. "The key to regional growth in an increasingly globalized economy, whether in large cities or sparsely populated areas, is attractiveness. Efforts to increase mobility both geographically and between occupations and sectors are also important. Good infrastructure, entrepreneur-friendly rules and laws, access to skills and labor, collaboration between business and research, and a good quality of life govern where people and investments end up. It is also required that there is access to venture capital for companies, which today can be a problem, especially for the sparsely populated parts of the country," Persson concluded.
