Title: The impact of the euro
text: Persson: The impact of the euro Datum: 2003-10-29 Talare: Vice riksbankschef Kristina Persson Plats: Women's Economic Round Table, New York City OBS: Talet finns endast pa engelska. Allow me first to extend special thanks for this invitation. It is particularly important for me personally as well as for the Riksbank to be given this opportunity to meet women economists and discuss current economic issues. I am privileged to be one of three women on the Riksbank's Executive Board, which has a total of six members. At the Riksbank we strive to attain an even distribution of men and women at all levels. This is a deliberate policy but also reflects the sharp rise in the proportion of women among qualified economists entering the Swedish business sector in recent decades. If this trend is to continue, and more women are to take the chance of achieving success in this traditionally male profession, we will need more role models like you here today. The subject of my speech is "The impact of the euro", a topic that was decided before 14 September 2003, when Sweden held a referendum on introducing the single currency. Personally I am convinced for many reasons that Sweden should introduce the euro, and made no secret of that. However, as many of you know, the result was a clear 'no' to the euro. The question of the economic advantages and disadvantages of the euro often resembles a tug-of-war between the short- and long-term perspectives. The risks, when highlighted, often temporarily overshadow the long-term gains, which arise in small incremental doses over a long period. Unfortunately, short-term conditions came sharply into focus just when the Swedish people were about to vote, as attention was turned to the global economic slowdown and its effect on the euro area, particularly in the major countries. GDP growth in Germany and France is forecast to decline from 0.2 per cent and 1.3 per cent respectively in 2002 to 0.0 and 0.3 per cent in 2003 (Riksbank forecast). This is the poorest rate of growth in these countries in over a decade. In the debate on the euro, this contraction in growth was largely attributed to the limitations imposed on these countries' economic policies, as they did not have a national monetary policy, and to the fiscal policy constraints of the Stability and Growth Pact. As we know, the budget deficits of both Germany and France have in both 2002 and 2003 exceeded the reference value of 3 per cent of GDP, which was established in the EU's Stability and Growth Pact. At the same time, attention in the debate was drawn to the temporary and one-off rise in prices of certain goods that occurred when prices were rounded after the introduction of the euro. In light of this, it is understandable that many voters got the impression that there were no economic benefits of participation in the euro. Furthermore, those that voted against the single currency may have been strengthened in their belief by the fact that the 'no' vote was not followed by any speculation against the krona, which instead has appreciated against both the euro and the dollar since the referendum. What didn't feature in the same way in the debate was the longer-term perspective and it is this perspective that I believe speaks in favour of the euro. It proved difficult to explain that the underlying causes of the crisis in Germany and France were mainly domestic structural problems, partly in the labour market. Those problems had existed long before EMU and could not be remedied by a separate currency and monetary policy. At the same time, the economic slowdown overshadowed the longterm transaction gains of a single currency for trade and the financial markets. In earlier economic research, the gains associated with a single currency were often viewed as uncertain and very small at best. As there were very few contemporary examples of currency unions, comparisons were made instead between fixed and floating exchange rates, in which fixed exchange rates did not appear to result in any definite welfare gains. More recent research has concentrated on the smaller currency unions that have nevertheless existed, and has excluded other factors in so-called gravitation models. This research has pointed to quite substantial gains from currency unions (a shift in the magnitude of 50 per cent or even more according to researchers such as Andrew K Rose, at Berkeley). Even conservative estimates indicate a considerable rise in trade within currency areas, and attendant welfare gains. Other studies, which are directly based on trade dynamics in the last decade, suggest that trade between the euro area countries may have increased by 5-10 per cent as a result of the euro. Another long-term gain is in price competition. The limited and temporary rise in prices of certain goods and services in conjunction with the introduction of the euro notes and coins should be weighed against the long-term gains from price transparency, the effect of easier price comparisons when prices in the entire euro area are expressed in the same currency. Previously, this particular gain was also perceived as minimal as cross-border trade is relatively small and companies themselves are said to be capable of converting prices regularly between currencies without suffering any major efficiency losses. However, at the same time, there were price differences in the EU of 20-30 per cent on a number of goods (cars, for example) that should be relatively easy to both transport over the border and compare in terms of price. These differences appear to have diminished quicker since euro banknotes and coins were introduced in 2001. New research also suggests that the effects of a common currency on prices may have been underestimated. For instance, Charles Engel from the University of Wisconsin compared price differences for the same goods in cities on both sides of the Canadian and US border with price differences between different cities in the US. Although US and Canadian cities have largely the same language and culture, as well as free trade, the different currencies cause prices to vary as much on each side of the border as between cities at opposite ends of the US. Finally, of course, there is the increasingly important role of the euro as a dominant international currency. The most immediate gain from this is an increase in seignorage income to the extent that the euro is more widely held outside the euro area than the sum of the currencies that preceded it. Taken as a whole, the euro area is the world's largest exporter and importer, accounting for about one-fifth of international trade. Despite this the US dollar is still the most common counterparty in foreign exchange trading and the widespread use of the dollar as a 'vehicle currency' in itself reinforces its status. Given that the euro is still a young currency it is likely to grow in importance and may in time have the potential to catch up with the dollar's share in the foreign exchange markets. Furthermore, by replacing 12 currencies, in particular the German mark and the French franc, the euro was used immediately as a reserve currency by central banks and became part of a currency basket (for example in Morocco) or a solitary anchor for the exchange rate policy of some countries (like Estonia, Bosnia and Bulgaria). Nevertheless, two-thirds of world reserves are still held in US dollars compared with less than 15 per cent in euros, although since the euro's introduction there appears to have been a gradual shift in the composition of the reserves of large economies such as Russia, and even China, towards an increased share for the euro. All this points to larger income to the euro area from external holders of the euro, a small but not insignificant gain given that estimates of US seignorage income from external holders of the dollar is estimated at almost 1 per cent of GDP. The euro is also bound to increase the efficiency of euro area financial markets. The use of the euro in the international debt market has increased compared with the joint share of its preceding currencies. The share of international bonds denominated in euros and issued by non-euro area residents has increased to about 30 per cent, compared with 20 per cent for the currencies that preceded the euro. Important factors behind this development are the larger home-currency investor base and the better issuing conditions for international borrowers provided by the unified European money market, which is now more liquid and efficient than the markets in the individual countries before the introduction of the euro. Needless to say, European equity markets have also been affected by the disappearance of currency risk within the euro area. There appears to be a gradual shift from the domestic focus in the euro area countries to a euro area-wide, sectorrelated, view. Integration is likely to attract a broader range of potential investors and benefit the development of private equity and financing opportunities for new firms. In addition to these economic advantages, we must naturally also include what I consider to be the decisive political arguments in favour of Sweden participating fully in the political and economic cooperation with a view to attaining a position of influence in a strong and prosperous Europe. The fact that the Swedish krona has not been more negatively affected by the result of the referendum, despite the foregone advantages, could in turn be due to longterm factors that are independent of EMU. The political uncertainty ahead of the referendum should indeed have contributed to the somewhat weaker krona during the summer. However, the krona has been considered undervalued for a long time. So, one reason for the krona's current recovery is that the markets are once again focusing on Sweden's long-term, stable macroeconomic policy, which has remained in place regardless of EMU. This policy includes the Riksbank's inflation target and a budgetary framework that has the support of all parliamentary parties. Thus, Sweden will remain outside the euro for the time being, together with its fellow EU countries Denmark and the UK. But as early as May next year the EU will have ten new Member States and around 100 million new inhabitants, the vast majority from Central and Eastern Europe. Of these ten, nine have expressed their desire to join monetary union as soon as they meet the convergence criteria. Contrary to many people's expectations, several of these countries appear fully capable of meeting the criteria in the next few years. After a decade of reforms leading from planned economy to market economy, inflation and budget deficits have been cut and debt levels have been kept in check in a number of the smaller countries, while for the bigger countries, such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, budget consolidation is their last remaining obstacle. So it is not unrealistic that a handful of new countries could introduce the euro as early as 2006-2007, or in any case 2-3 years later. It may be that Sweden, Denmark and the UK will have to discuss their future relationship to the euro at the same time as the euro area expands to include half a dozen new countries. The Central and Eastern European countries will also have to weigh the long-term gains of adopting the euro against the risks of asymmetric shocks. The advantages for these countries are perhaps even clearer than for Sweden. Particularly substantial gains may arise from increased financial integration through the euro. Thanks to the fact that banks from EU countries have acquired large sections of the banking system in eastern Europe, the financial sector there has been able to evolve relatively quickly. But the new Member States' financial systems are still rather undeveloped, with credits in relation to GDP of between one-eighth and one-quarter of that in the euro area. Sweden's Baltic neighbour Estonia is one example of how currency integration can help the financial system to evolve. The Estonians have pegged their currency to the euro for over a decade and are keen to quickly take the step into monetary union. Their banking system is owned by Swedish-Nordic banks and credit volumes are growing by 20-30 per cent a year - most of which is denominated in euro. In some countries, the euro can also help to cement the macroeconomic discipline that is still a relatively new phenomenon there. Meanwhile, the risks that stem from the countries possibly diverging from the euro area average are perhaps also clearer than for Sweden (which is a country that is unusually well-integrated with euro area countries and has a similar economic structure). But some factors suggest that the new Member States in central Europe do not need a different monetary policy than that of the euro area. These countries also have close ties with the rest of the EU, which is their biggest trading partner by far, accounting for some 50-70 per cent of imports and exports. Having said that, the countries are still undergoing a period of quick change; it is conceivable that any potential shocks during such a transitional period would be managed better through a national monetary policy. Their growth is and should be considerably higher than the EU average as long as they continue to reduce the differences in their standard of living compared with the rest of the EU. This always entails risks of overheating similar to that experienced by the fast-growing Irish economy. The assessment of the risks related to the process of change and of the long-term gains varies between the different candidate countries depending on how open and flexible their economies are. Nevertheless, it seems that the advantages of integration will outweigh the disadvantages when the new countries have assessed the euro, even if it is likely that some of the new Member States will have to wait longer than others before introducing the euro. If there are such gains to be made from a common currency in a reunified Europe, would it not be possible that such gains may also be attained on a global level? Should we continue on a path towards more global monetary cooperation? There are many arguments both for and against such an arrangement. In recent years we have seen substantial exchange rate fluctuations between some of the world's large economic blocs. These have largely been related to developments in the US dollar. The dollar's weakening against the euro has recently gained impetus once again; in two years, the euro/dollar exchange rate has gone from a low of 84 cents to 1.18 dollars in recent weeks - a rise of just over 40 per cent. Discussions of the implications of an overvalued dollar for the US current account deficit have quickly turned into concern over the effects of the rapid fall in the dollar on euro area growth. Should there be a quicker correction in the US current account deficit due to diminishing interest among international investors in US assets, the dollar could weaken further. A fast and dramatic depreciation of the dollar could derail Europe's fragile recovery. But in addition to this concern over excessively sharp movements in exchange rates, an equally heated discussion has flared up in recent months, both in the US and Europe, as to whether the perhaps most important fixed peg that exists today between two major international currencies, that between the US dollar and the Chinese renminbi, should be abandoned. For the past decade, the Chinese currency has been pegged by the People's Bank of China at a rate of around 8.28 renminbi per dollar. Critics of this policy, mainly leading US politicians and some industrialists, believe that Chinese exports have been given an unfair advantage when the renminbi has tracked the dollar's fall against the euro. The most drastic answer to these exchange rate issues would be to propose a new global monetary system of the kind that existed after the Second World War and up to the early 1970s in the shape of the Bretton Woods Agreement and the link via the dollar to gold. This kind of solution has actually been recommended by Robert Mundell, a currency area theorist and winner of the 1999 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Even Keynes considered the establishment of a global currency, the bancor. Mundell points to transaction gains for trade and the financial markets, but also other arguments. One of these is that the signalling of international relative prices is distorted by exchange rate fluctuations caused by capital flows. Another is that the global economy has led to increasingly weak money illusion, the illusion that prevents wage-earners from immediately perceiving a deterioration in their purchasing power following a depreciation, and from demanding compensation that would render the depreciation ineffectual. Despite the intellectual appeal of such arguments, it is not difficult to see that during the past decade, the US, Europe and Japan have had very different growth rates and their business cycles have been highly unsynchronised. Given that monetary policy would be dictated by the monetary system, a tremendous burden would be placed on fiscal policy to stabilise the economy when the differences across the common monetary area are too great. The large real adjustments that would be required in wages and relative prices in the US and Europe - instead of an adjustment in the exchange rate - would probably cost more than the gains derived from having fixed global exchange rates. Therefore, the requirements necessary to make such a system work, which in reality are the factors that determine what constitutes an optimal currency area, indicate that such a solution is a distant prospect, if it should become reality at all. In addition, there are the practical and administrative problems of organising such a global monetary system, indeed even a global central bank with representation from all countries. A middle ground between a single currency or single monetary standard such as Bretton Woods, and fully floating exchange rates, would be intervention bands and controlled exchange rates between, for instance, the euro and the dollar. However, this would partly suffer from the same problems as a fully fixed regime. Furthermore, we would encounter the same dilemma that characterised all semi-fixed, or fixed but adjustable exchange rate arrangements, which failed so miserably over the past ten years. The list is long, from Sweden's and the ERM countries' crisis at the beginning of the 1990s, to the crises in Mexico, Asia, Russia and Brazil during the subsequent decade. All displayed some similar characteristics, which a controlled exchange rate between the dollar and euro would also be unable to escape. At some point in time, the market becomes aware that the political gains of avoiding painful real adjustments are probably less than the costs and loss of prestige associated with an exchange rate adjustment. Once the market realises this, speculation follows and the costs of defending the exchange rate mount, at the same as the potential loss of prestige from adjustment diminishes. In the end, an exchange rate adjustment becomes economically unavoidable and politically acceptable - regardless of whether politicians wanted it. Of course, such a spiral is not possible with a single currency where adjustments must occur without devaluation and where speculation of this kind is impossible. Do not these arguments lead us to conclude that China too should let its currency float? After all, China is one of the world's largest economies that in spite of its increasing openness follows a course of its own. Critics of the dollar peg believe that if the renminbi were allowed to float, it would appreciate, thus reducing China's current account surplus and shrinking the US deficit. In the long term, I believe that it is right to allow the renminbi to float. In the short term, however, it is difficult to see this as the appropriate solution. The main reason for not floating the renminbi yet is the Chinese financial system. The Chinese banking system is still a long way from being adapted to market conditions, and a large proportion of its lending is still made to state-owned companies that are often unable to honour their payment obligations. If we take into account all the hidden and disclosed non-performing loans in the banking system, these are estimated to be equal to as much as half of China's GDP, and they are continuing to grow. Were the currency allowed to float before addressing these problems, it is just as likely to depreciate as appreciate since the Chinese public could take advantage of the opportunity to transfer its assets abroad instead of saving at low interest rates in the weak domestic banking system, a system that would then be rocked to its foundations. The experiences of many countries, including Sweden at the beginning of the 1990s, show that the foreign exchange market should not be deregulated until the banking system has been reformed. Could China not revalue then and adapt the exchange rate to its trade surplus without floating its currency? In my opinion, this would not be such a wise decision either. It is wrong to attribute China's trade surplus with the US to the currency issue. The surplus is probably best explained by the cost advantages enjoyed by Chinese producers in labour-intensive goods compared with the US. China's trade surplus can be seen as a natural consequence of the division of labour within the Pacific region where China's position as supplier and sub-supplier of low value-added goods is highly favourable for US productivity. This is a segment in which the Chinese compete with very few US producers, which is why an exchange rate adjustment would have only a marginal impact. In actual fact, an excessively large one-off adjustment would be required to have any effect at all on the US-Chinese trade balance. Such a large correction would in turn give rise to problems for Chinese trade elsewhere. It is with the US that China enjoys a large surplus, while the trade balance is close to zero or is negative with many other areas, including the euro area. This picture is confirmed by many fundamental analyses of an equilibrium exchange rate for China, which come relatively close to China's fixed exchange rate today. Furthermore, China currently has either very low inflation or deflation, which normally points to devaluation pressure rather than revaluation pressure (a need for real depreciation). Finally, China and other the Asian economies that are trying to prop up the value of their currencies are the main purchasers of US Treasury bonds. So, in a situation where the US government finances are deteriorating, the Chinese exchange rate regime is actually helping to depress US long yields and indirectly bolstering the US recovery. My conclusion is that China in the short term should retain its fixed exchange rate until such time as its financial system has undergone more substantial reform, which is something that nevertheless must be done in the coming years. In the long term, however, a floating exchange rate appears unavoidable for a country that is on the way to becoming one of the world's leading economies. It is only in the much longer term, when China is highly integrated with the world economy, that fixed exchangerate cooperation can become a possibility once again. This conclusion brings me back to the main line of my argument: Europe can gradually be enlarged to become a relatively big currency area that includes all the countries, from Ireland in the west to Estonia in the east, where the long-term microeconomic gains outweigh the recurring but temporary macroeconomic costs. As the representative of a central bank, I must add that it is interesting to at least toy with the idea of how a global currency and global monetary policy would look. But for the time being this will probably remain no more than an intellectually stimulating vision. At global level, integration needs to go much further, and the economies become more synchronised, if the long-term gains of fixed exchange-rate cooperation are to outweigh the risks. In the long term, it is not inconceivable that a trend will arise towards large regional currency blocs with single currencies, but with flexibility between them. Within these blocs, it will be possible to reap the advantages of integration fully, while the risks will be limited by increasingly similar conditions in the countries taking part in the common currency. Competition between these areas regarding which has the dominant reserve currency may increase gradually. The dollar's unique position will weaken, just as we are seeing today with a number of Asian central banks planning to increase their assets in euro and reduce those in dollars. Let us hope that there will also be cooperation between the regions, so as to give the world greater stability, development and continued integration.

Title: What happens to jobs in an increasingly globalized world?
text: Persson: What happens to jobs in an increasingly globalized world? Date 2005-04-11 Deputy Governor Kristina Persson today gave a talk at Mid Sweden University in ostersund on what is happening to employment in an increasingly globalized world. "Global trade contributes to economic growth through increased specialization and thus more efficient use of production resources. Examples of this are companies in the US and Europe increasingly moving production of goods and services to low-wage countries such as China, India or the new EU members in Eastern and Central Europe. However, this does not necessarily mean lower growth or higher unemployment in the country from which the relocation takes place. On the contrary, lower costs and productivity gains can enable new investments and jobs in the production of other, in many cases more value-added products and services," Persson began. "Sweden has so far handled quite well the transformational pressure that this development has entailed. Sweden, as a small open economy with production that is at the forefront of the value chain, should have good conditions to meet the pressures of transformation also in the future," Persson continued. "Structural change is an ongoing process and Sweden has already adapted to changing competitive conditions for a long time. Concrete examples are the exodus of the textile industry in the 60s and that of shipbuilding in the 70s. Industrialization and globalization have gone hand in hand: Just under a hundred years ago, about half of the working people in Sweden were employed in agriculture and forestry, today the proportion is only 2 percent. The services sector has gone in the opposite direction. In 1910, 23 percent worked in service or public administration, 90 years later the figure was 75 percent. It is the service sector that today makes the biggest contribution both to economic growth and to the increase in jobs. Services cannot be rationalized as easily and the richer a country's population becomes, the more services you want to consume," Persson continued. "Although the relocation of some jobs leads to increased productivity and lower costs, which in turn give rise to new jobs and incomes elsewhere in the economy, in the short term the effects may be high unemployment in some sectors or regions. It is important that the creation of new jobs keeps pace with the jobs that are being eliminated and that vacant labour can move to the industries where new jobs are created. The demands for flexibility  mobility between sectors and regions  increase with globalisation," Persson said. "There is much to suggest that the pressure for transformation in Sweden is growing as a result of the accelerating integration that globalization entails. Among other things, international competitive pressure increases when the cost differences between Sweden and the countries with which we compete are large at the same time as the differences in education levels decrease. Even more skilled jobs, such as in research, development, design, etc., are today competitive. So far, the expanding services sector has created new jobs when, for example, industrial jobs have disappeared. Today, not least, the new information technology enables services to be moved out as well. To create the best possible conditions for new jobs to arise, it is important to facilitate innovations and entrepreneurship in Sweden. It is particularly important that a good business and investment climate prevails in industries with high growth potential," Persson continued. "The overall unemployment rate is already high and risks worsening if we do not cope with the demands for change that globalization brings. Open unemployment in Sweden averaged about 2 percent from the early 1960s until the 1990s crisis. Since the crisis of the early 1990s, it has averaged around 6%. Despite a prolonged period of high growth in the late 1990s, open unemployment fell no more than to about 4 percent at its lowest. There is much to suggest that today's unemployment is largely of a structural nature and not an expression of the fact that the demand for goods and services in the economy is too low. The fact that the level of unemployment has shifted up and stayed at a high level is a sign of this. Another is the large differences in unemployment that exist between counties and between different occupational categories," Persson said. "Monetary policy cannot be used to deal with structural problems. In order to have a long-term impact on employment, completely different measures are required. The instruments for increased growth and new jobs are mainly found in the policy areas that the government and parliament control. In addition to the fact that existing companies simply have to want to (dare) to hire more people, there must be incentives to start new companies, get training and to seek new industries instead of remaining in long-term unemployment or livelihood in other ways than with paid work. More new jobs in the service industries must also be created outside the public, tax-funded sector. In this connection, it is worth thinking about what the high tax wedges on labor mean for the possibility of increasing the demand for services. Continued growth also requires us to address the problem of too many people of working age being on long-term sick leave or early retirement, for example. The situation will become more serious in line with demographic developments, which create an imbalance between the proportion of the elderly in the population and those of working age," Persson said. "How well different regions and countries position themselves in international competition determines growth rates, employment and income development. This adaptation presupposes changes in society as a whole. Here, both labour market policy and the ability to engage constructively interact between business and society play important roles in the future," Persson concluded.

Title: The interest rate and the krona
text: Interest and the krona Date: 1996-01-30 Speaker: Deputy Governor Lars Heikensten Location: Stockholm Chamber of Commerce and Veckans Affarer conference at Grand Hotel Let me start by thanking you for being able to come here and talk about the Swedish economy. I was going to dwell on three main things today. First, I wanted to explain in some detail the reasons for the interest rate cut that the Riksbank implemented a couple of weeks ago. This also gives you a picture of how we see the inflation outlook going forward. Next, I thought I would slightly deepen the discussion of a couple of different features of economic development in the future that are of importance for inflation, among other things. Finally, I wanted to briefly touch on the events of the past week in the bond and foreign exchange markets and the implications they may have for monetary policy. Inflation in line with target The reason why we lowered the repo rate on 9 January is basically self-evident: We believe that the probability of inflation in line with the price stability objective is good. The target, as you all know, is 2% (with a tolerance range of plus/minus 1%). It is the conditions for achieving this goal that guide our action. In various contexts, the Riksbank has emphasized that inflation is determined by demand and supply conditions in the economy and by inflation expectations. The crown plays a central role in both of these contexts. It affects demand, for example, in the competitive sector and is an indicator of inflation expectations. Therefore, it is educational to conduct the discussion in terms of three factors; demand and supply conditions, expectations and the crown. The importance of these three factors for monetary policy may vary from time to time. In general, the more established low inflation is in a country, the greater the room for manoeuvre there is for monetary policy. More concretely: The Bundesbank and (now) the Federal Reserve can, if they want to, take greater account of, for example, the economic picture than the central bank in a country that has recently pushed down inflation. They can do so because few or no one suspects them of letting go of price developments. Let me now briefly set out the arguments behind the repo rate reduction, starting with the demand and supply conditions. Weaker economy The international economy has weakened during the autumn. This applies in particular to Europe. Growth has also slowed down in Sweden. Gdp grew by 0.3 per cent between the second and third quarters, corresponding to an annual rate of 1.2 per cent. However, compared with the third quarter of 1995, growth was 4.4%. The part of the economy that has grown the fastest is industry. There has been a change here. Both industrial output and new orders appear to have peaked in June. Since then, industrial output has stagnated while new orders have fallen (see Chart 1). This weaker picture was confirmed by ki's business cycle barometer. It also gradually became increasingly clear during the autumn that the exchange ratio between growth and inflation in the Swedish economy last year would be better than expected. The forecasts for autumn 1994 were generally around 2 per cent growth and 3-4 per cent inflation. Although growth now seems to have been 3.5-4 percent, inflation fell within the tolerance range, i.e. lower than 3 percent. Lower expected inflation The information received in the latter part of the autumn has also given grounds for increased optimism with regard to expected inflation. Let me take a couple of examples: in December households expected an inflation rate of 2.5% in 1996. That was 0.2 percentage points lower than they predicted in November. Financial market participants expected an inflation rate of 2.8 percent per year for the next two years, according to Aragon's survey published in November. This was 0.6 percentage points lower than at the last measurement in August 1995. It was also 0.2 percentage points lower than in Prospera's October survey. The same picture gives the development of long-term interest rates. The differential against German 10-year bond yields had fallen from its highest level of just over 450 basis points to just over 230 basis points, at the time the repo rate was cut (see Chart 2). The development of the crown supports the picture. From the end of May, the krona had appreciated by 14 percent. However, it may be worth underlining that inflation expectations, as they could be measured at the time of the repo rate cut, were not yet at 2% or below this level. However, as we saw it, there were reasons to believe in a further change in the expectation picture in the right direction. Stronger crown The krona had thus strengthened markedly (see Chart 3). At the time of the repo rate cut, it had fallen to a level that was a couple of percentage points below the level on which the November Inflation Report was based. As we know, it continued down further, but has recently swung back both as a result of factors in the international currency market and as a result of specific Swedish conditions, which I will return to. The slowing growth in the industry, which could be traced in the autumn, probably stemmed to a limited extent from the stronger krona. But it is likely that such an impact is now gradually coming. The risk of inflationary tendencies in - and inflationary spread from - industry has thus subsided. We have also revised down our assessments of wage slippage and, from what I understand, we are not alone in that. The strengthening of the krona is responsible for a larger part of the clear decline we have seen in producer prices (see Chart 4). Import prices are now increasing by about 2 percent compared to around 10 percent at its worst. This has had - and will have an increasing impact on consumer price developments if the krona is strong. So much about our arguments at the time of the reduction. Our decision was followed by a lively debate. I'm not going to review all the elements of this one at all. Let me just comment on perhaps the most common point, that we lowered too late. During the latter part of the autumn, there was a rapid reassessment of the Swedish economy. Both growth and inflation forecasts were cancelled. The fact is, however, that as recently as November, very few people expected inflation below 2.5% in Sweden in either 1996 or 1997. Thus, most of the forecasters - some of whom, incidentally, argued vehemently in favour of lowering interest rates - did not expect us to meet the inflation target. Although the inflation picture improved during the autumn, we had a picture similar to that of other analysts. But we had (and have) no thought of shifting our gaze away from the goal. The rate cut thus indicates that we have revised our economy - and inflation assessment somewhat. When we lowered the repo rate, we marked that we saw the conditions for a certain recovery in growth in the latter part of the year. This is an issue that has attracted some attention in recent weeks. It is, of course, also of great interest for stock market development. Let me therefore now move on to the next item on the agenda, a discussion on some elements of the business cycle and economic developments that have an impact on inflation going forward. Slowdown in Europe It is currently booming for gloomy assessments of the economy. After almost only happy faces during the beginning of autumn, the development is now painted in ever wider, black brushstrokes. Let me begin by commenting on the European economic picture. The decline last year could be explained by the exchange rate turbulence that prevailed primarily in 1994, but also in the spring of 1995. Among other things, it contributed to a marked appreciation of the D-mark block in relation to the dollar area (America and Asia except Japan). "Another explanation is the development of interest rates. As we all remember, long-term interest rates in Europe were driven up in the spring of 1994 by the rise in long-term interest rates in the United States, even though the continental European economic upturn was then only in its infancy (see Chart 5). If old truths apply, it does not seem unreasonable that this should have a tangible dampening effect a few years later - that is, right now - on the European economy. But since then, especially last year, we have seen a marked cut in both short and long-term interest rates, which will eventually affect the economy in the opposite direction. "There is also evidence that profit levels are still relatively good in European industry. Also in good condition are, on the whole, household balance sheets. Neither tends to characterize economic downturns. Nor is there a need for monetary tightening as inflation remains low in most places. "In the end, there are reasons to pay attention to the stock cycle. It helped to dampen growth in the autumn, despite the fact that final demand in Europe was somewhat similar (see Chart 6). In due course, however, stock decommissioning should be slowed down. I don't want to harden these arguments. It may, of course, turn out that the economic downturn in Europe will continue. That there may be some probability of this shows, not least, the better inflation picture and the interest rate cuts implemented at the end of last year. But of course it's not. In the case of Japan, there is reason for some optimism. Here, the forecasts are revised up. By contrast, the projections for the US appear to be reasonably stable (see Chart 7). Consumption recovery in Sweden? The issue of consumption in Sweden is of a partly different nature. There has been no significant upturn here, as is the case for the international economy in 1994-1995. Nor are there clear signs of a recent decline. The question is rather whether the cautious recovery that has been going on for a couple of years should be broken. Consumption is a basically fairly stable variable. Unless something happens that radically changes households' picture of future income conditions, consumption tends to slip on (see Chart 8). Fluctuations in income between years seem to be largely absorbed into savings. It is likely that income growth will be better this year and in 1997 than last year, despite the fact that fiscal policy is also now biting quite considerably (about 3.5 percent of household income is being withdrawn this year compared with 5 percent last year). The decent income development this year and next is due to wages increasing relatively rapidly while keeping inflation in check. What, then, to believe about saving? This has been the "ten thousand crown question" in all economic assessments in recent years. Certainly, there are arguments that savings will remain at relatively high levels in a historical perspective (uncertainty about public finances and social security systems, the new tax system, high unemployment, etc.) But there are also reasons for some reduction in savings in the coming years. Household balance sheets are currently in relatively good shape. The debt ratio has fallen significantly for the average household (see Chart 9). The picture looks somewhat worse if you look at e.g. interest expenses after tax, but even with this modification, conditions are significantly better than in the early 90s. Interest rates have come down markedly. This is particularly true of long-term interest rates, which are of great importance to households (about 2/3 of the loans are tied up). The co-variation between households' own assessments of the economy and long-term interest rates has previously been high. Households are also more optimistic today than they were in late 1994 and early 1995, although pessimism has increased slightly recently. At the same time, there are risks. If we get a significantly worse development in various respects, at home and / or abroad, which leads to lower employment, consumption is also affected. My conclusion, however, is that the night-black pessimism that has spread recently in this area is a little difficult to understand. Less propensity for inflation Let me conclude the discussion of demand and supply conditions by briefly touching on one more aspect, the idea that the propensity for inflation in the economy has decreased. An indication of this, as I have previously mentioned, is the development at the overall macro level. Although growth was significantly higher than expected by most forecasters, inflation was lower. The standard argument for this is that consumption developed weakly. Therefore, the trade could not raise its prices. Against this, however, one can object that consumption last year also actually increased more than most people thought. It is precisely incorrect consumption assumptions that cannot explain the excessively high inflation forecasts. However, the latter does not, of course, prevent a larger increase in consumption from hitting prices. But we do not know how great the built-up price increase needs are - seen from the cost side. Productivity growth has been substantial in industry, but not only there but also in trade (see Chart 10). A significant structural change has taken place and is taking place in trade. Now, if import and producer prices go down, profit margins may be able to be kept up even in the event of limited price increases. The picture includes that there has been some competition in the Swedish economy. One of the real engines of inflation in the 80s, the construction sector, have changed radically. In other parts of the economy, import penetration has increased. There are also reasons to hope for further positive effects, for example, of EU membership. However, wage formation remains a concern. Despite the rise in unemployment, wage growth was higher than in the rest of the world (see Chart 11). So far, the impact of this on competitiveness and inflation has been limited by productivity growth, but this trend cannot continue indefinitely. In any event, wage growth has limited the room for manoeuvre in monetary policy while resulting in weaker employment growth. In conclusion, then, there are several question marks when it comes to assessing demand and supply conditions in the coming years. As I see it, they primarily concern the European economy, the development of consumption in Sweden and the economy's propensity to inflation. The probability of ending up at the inflation target should be good even if growth develops decently. The fact that the krona has strengthened is an advantage from an inflation point of view. It is precisely in the competitive sector that the clearest inflationary tendencies have existed in recent years. With more balanced growth, inflation risk is less. Let me conclude by noting that confidence in Swedish economic policy increased during the second half of 1995. The risk of a relapse into the old inflationary economy is perceived to have decreased. The opportunity has thus improved for sustainable and balanced growth in the Swedish economy. However, this does not mean that the risks of a less good development in the future have disappeared. Concern for confidence in economic policy must remain a high priority. The convergence programme specifies a mechanism to deal with any recurrent fiscal problems. It is also important that wage formation is improved so that accelerating wage increases do not counteract a decline in unemployment. Lower wage increases would have given more room in interest rate policy. In the past week, market interest rates have risen and the krona has fallen. There can be many different reasons why markets react the way they do and that seems to have been the case this time as well. Experience shows that fluctuations can sometimes be exaggerated in the financial markets. Some short-term traders tend to want to take profits quickly. The future is likely to show whether the market situation has changed permanently or whether the rise in interest rates and the fall in the krona were temporary in nature. Nevertheless, it can be stated that this week's events are a reminder that a clear and consistent development towards sound government finances is of great importance for confidence in the Swedish economy and thus, in the long run, for growth and employment. The basis for sustainable stable growth and employment is sound public finances and price stability. This has been shown not least by developments in the second half of 1995. At that time, confidence in Swedish economic policy increased significantly. Crucial for the continuation of monetary policy is the overall assessment of the inflation outlook. This, in turn, is affected by, among other things, cyclical developments, inflation expectations and exchange rate developments. The important thing, then, is the longer-term processes. Individual figures or short-term movements in the financial markets are therefore not decisive. It is against this background that we have today given some relief to monetary policy.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Rntan och kronan Datum: 1996-01-30 Talare: Vice riksbankschef Lars Heikensten Plats: Stockholms Handelskammares och Veckans Affrers konferens p Grand Hotel Lt mig brja med att tacka fr att jag ftt komma hit och tala om svensk ekonomi. Jag tnkte idag uppehlla mig vid i huvudsak tre saker. Frst tnkte jag relativt utfrligt redovisa sklen till den rntesnkning som Riksbanken genomfrde fr ett par veckor sedan. Drmed fr ni ocks en bild av hur vi ser p inflationsutsikterna framver. Drefter tnkte jag ngot frdjupa diskussionen av ett par olika drag i den ekonomiska utvecklingen framver som r av betydelse bl.a. fr inflationen. Slutligen tnkte jag kort berra den senaste veckans hndelser p obligations- och valutamarknaden och de implikationer de kan ha fr penningpolitiken. Inflation i linje med mlet Sklet till att vi snkte reporntan den 9 januari r i grund och botten sjlvklart: Vi anser att sannolikheten fr en inflation i linje med prisstabilitetsmlet r god. Mlet r som ni alla vet 2 procent (med ett toleransintervall p plus/minus 1 procent). Det r frutsttningarna att n detta ml som vgleder vrt agerande. Riksbanken har i olika sammanhang framhllit att inflationen bestms av efterfrgeoch utbudsfrhllandena i ekonomin och av inflationsfrvntningarna. Kronan spelar en central roll i bda dessa sammanhang. Den pverkar efterfrgan bl.a. i den konkurrensutsatta sektorn och den r en indikator p inflationsfrvntningarna. Drfr r det pedagogiskt att fra diskussionen i termer av tre faktorer; efterfrge och utbudsfrhllandena, frvntningarna och kronan. Betydelsen av dessa tre faktorer fr penningpolitiken kan variera frn tid till annan. Allmnt gller att ju mer etablerad den lga inflationen r i ett land desto strre manverutrymme finns fr penningpolitiken. Mer konkret: Bundesbank och (numera) Federal Reserve kan om de vill ta strre hnsyn till t.ex. konjunkturbilden n centralbanken i ett land som nyligen pressat ner inflationen. Det kan de gra drfr att f eller inga misstnker dem fr att slppa taget om prisutvecklingen. Lt mig nu kort redogra fr argumenten bakom reporntesnkningen och d brja med efterfrge- och utbudsfrhllandena. Svagare konjunktur Den internationella konjunkturen har frsvagats under hsten. Srskilt gller detta Europa. Ocks i Sverige har tillvxten dmpats. kningen i BNP mellan andra och tredje kvartalet blev 0,3 procent, motsvarande en rstakt p 1,2 procent. Jmfrt med tredje kvartalet 1995 var emellertid tillvxten 4,4 procent. Den del av ekonomin som vuxit snabbast r industrin. Hr har skett en frndring. Svl industriproduktionen som orderingngen frefaller ha haft sin toppniv i juni mnad. Drefter har industriproduktionen stagnerat medan orderingngen fallit (se diagram 1). Denna svagare bild bekrftades av KI:s konjunkturbarometer. Det blev ocks gradvis under hsten alltmer tydligt att utbytesfrhllandet mellan tillvxt och inflation i svensk ekonomi under fjolret skulle komma att bli bttre n vntat. Prognoserna hsten 1994 lg i allmnhet kring 2 procents tillvxt och 3-4 procents inflation. Trots att tillvxten nu verkar ha blivit 3,5-4 procent hamnade inflationen inom toleransintervallet, dvs. lgre r 3 procent. Lgre vntad inflation Ocks nr det gller den vntade inflationen har den information som kommit under senare delen av hsten givit skl fr kad optimism. Lt mig ta ett par exempel: Hushllen vntade sig i december en inflationstakt p 2,5 procent under 1996. Det var 0,2 procentenheter lgre n de frutsg i november. Aktrerna p de finansiella marknaderna vntade sig en inflationstakt p 2,8 procent per r de nrmaste tv ren enligt Aragons underskning publicerad i november. Detta var 0,6 procentenheter lgre n vid frra mttillfllet i augusti 1995. Det var ocks 0,2 procentenheter lgre n i Prosperas underskning i oktober. Samma bild ger de lnga rntornas utveckling. Differensen mot tyska 10riga obligationsrntor hade fallit frn sin hgsta niv drygt 450 punkter till drygt 230 punkter, vid den tidpunkt d reporntan snktes (se diagram 2). Kronans utveckling understdjer bilden. Frn slutet av maj hade kronan apprecierat med 14 procent. Det kan dock vara vrt att understryka att inflationsfrvntningarna, som de kunde uppmtas vid tiden fr reporntans snkning, inte nnu lg p 2 procent eller under denna niv. Det fanns dock, som vi sg det, skl att tro p en ytterligare frndring av frvntningsbilden i rtt riktning. Starkare krona Kronan hade allts frstrkts markant (se diagram 3). Vid tidpunkten fr snkningen av reporntan hade den kommit ned p en niv som var ett par procentenheter under den niv som inflationsrapporten i november baserats p. Den fortsatte som vi vet ner ytterligare, men har p senare tid svngt tillbaka bde som en fljd av faktorer p den internationella valutamarknaden och som resultat av specifika svenska frhllanden, som jag ska terkomma till. Den avtagande tillvxt i industrin, som kunde spras under hsten, hrrrde antagligen i begrnsad utstrckning frn den starkare kronan. Men det r troligt att ett sdant genomslag nu gradvis kommer. Risken fr inflationstendenser i - och inflationsspridning frn - industrin har drmed avtagit. Vi har ocks reviderat ner vra bedmningar av lneglidningen och det r vi efter vad jag frstr inte ensamma om. Kronans frstrkning ligger bakom en strre del av den tydliga nedgng vi sett i producentpriserna (se diagram 4). Importpriserna kar numera med ca 2 procent jmfrt med runt 10 procent nr det var som vrst. Detta har ftt - och kommer om kronan r stark att f - ett allt strre genomslag i konsumentprisutvecklingen. S mycket om vra argument vid tillfllet fr snkningen. P vrt beslut fljde en livlig debatt. Jag ska inte alls recensera alla inslag i denna. Lt mig bara kommentera den kanske vanligaste synpunkten, att vi snkte alltfr sent. Under senare delen av hsten skedde en snabb omvrdering av svensk ekonomi. Svl tillvxt- som inflationsprognoser stlldes ner. Faktum r dock att s sent som i november var det vldigt f som rknade med en inflation under 2,5 procent i Sverige vare sig 1996 eller 1997. De flesta prognosmakarna - varav en del fr vrigt livligt argumenterade fr snkt rnta - rknade allts inte med att vi skulle klara inflationsmlet. ven om inflationsbilden frbttrats under hsten hade vi en bild liknande vriga bedmares. Men vi hade (och har) inte ngon tanke p att flytta blicken frn mlet. Rntesnkningen indikerar allts att vi reviderat vr konjunktur - och inflationsbedmning ngot. Nr vi snkte reporntan markerade vi att vi sg frutsttningar fr en viss terhmtning av tillvxten under senare delen av ret. Detta r en frga som rnt en del uppmrksamhet under de senaste veckorna. Den r naturligtvis ocks av stort intresse fr brsutvecklingen. Lt mig drfr nu g vidare till nsta punkt p dagordningen, en diskussion om ngra inslag i konjunkturen och den ekonomiska utvecklingen av betydelse fr inflationen framver. Avmattning i Europa Det r just nu hgkonjunktur fr dystra bedmningar av konjunkturen. Efter nstan bara glada miner under brjan av hsten mlas nu utvecklingen i allt bredare, svarta penseldrag. Lt mig brja med att kommentera den europeiska konjunkturbilden.  Nedgngen under fjolret skulle kunna frklaras med den vxelkursturbulens som rdde i frsta hand under 1994, men ven vren 1995. Den bidrog bl.a. till en markant appreciering av D-marksblocket i frhllande till dollaromrdet (Amerika och Asien utom Japan).  En annan frklaring r rnteutvecklingen. Som vi alla minns drevs de lnga rntorna i Europa upp under vren 1994 av lngrnteuppgngen i USA, trots att den kontinentaleuropeiska konjunkturuppgngen d bara befann sig i sin linda (se diagram 5). Om gamla sanningar gller verkar det inte orimligt att detta skulle f en ptagligt dmpande effekt ngot r senare - dvs. just nu - p den europeiska konjunkturen. Men sedan dess har vi, srskilt under fjolret, sett en markant neddragning av bde korta och lnga rntor, som s smningom kommer att pverka konjunkturen i motsatt riktning.  Fr en snar terhmtning talar ocks att vinstniverna fortfarande r frhllandevis goda i europeiskt nringsliv. I bra skick r ocks p det hela taget hushllens balansrkningar. Ingetdera brukar knneteckna konjunkturnedgngar. Inte heller finns det behov av ngon monetr tstramning eftersom inflationen r fortsatt lg p de flesta hll.  Till slut finns det skl att uppmrksamma lagercykeln. Den bidrog till att dmpa tillvxten under hsten, trots att slutlig efterfrgan i Europa rullade p ngot snr (se diagram 6). Inom sinom tid borde dock lageravvecklingen bromsas upp. Jag vill inte hrdra dessa argument. Det kan naturligtvis visa sig att konjunkturnedgngen i Europa hller i sig. Att det kan finnas en viss sannolikhet fr detta visar inte minst den bttre inflationsbilden och de rntesnkningar som genomfrts under slutet av fjolret. Men sjlvklart r det inte. Nr det gller Japan finns det anledning till viss optimism. Hr revideras prognoserna upp. Prognoserna fr USA frefaller dremot vara ngorlunda stabila (se diagram 7). Konsumtionsterhmtning i Sverige? Frgan om konsumtionen i Sverige r av delvis annan art. Ngon markant uppgng har hr inte skett, p det stt som gller fr den internationella konjunkturen under 1994-1995. Inte heller finns tydliga tecken p en nedgng under senare tid. Frgan r snarast om den frsiktiga terhmtning som pgtt i ett par r ska brytas. Konsumtionen r en i grunden ganska stabil variabel. Om inget intrffar som radikalt frndrar hushllens bild av de framtida inkomstfrhllandena tenderar konsumtionen att lunka p (se diagram 8). Svngningar i inkomsten mellan ren verkar i stor utstrckning absorberas i sparandet. Troligt r att inkomstutvecklingen kommer att bli bttre i r och 1997 n i fjol trots att finanspolitiken ocks nu biter ganska rejlt (ca 3,5 procent av hushllens inkomster dras i r in jmfrt med 5 procent under fjolret). Den hyfsade inkomstutvecklingen i r och nsta r beror p att lnerna kar frhllandevis snabbt samtidigt som inflationen hlls i schack. Vad ska man d tro om sparandet? Detta har varit "tiotusenkronorsfrgan" i alla konjunkturbedmningar under de senaste ren. Visst finns det argument fr att sparandet kommer att ligga kvar p i ett historiskt perspektiv relativt hga niver (oskerhet om statsfinanserna och trygghetssystemen, det nya skattesystemet, hg arbetslshet etc.) Men det finns ocks skl fr en viss neddragning av sparandet under de nrmaste ren. Hushllens balansrkningar r idag i relativt gott skick. Skuldandelen har fallit ptagligt fr genomsnittshushllet(se diagram 9). Bilden ser ngot smre ut om man ser p t.ex. rnteutgifter efter skatt, men ven med denna modifiering r frhllandena vsentligt bttre n i brjan av 90-talet. Rntorna har kommit ner markant. Srskilt gller detta de lnga rntorna, som har stor betydelse fr hushllen (ca 2/3 av lnen r bundna). Samvariationen mellan hushllens egna bedmningar av ekonomin och de lnga rntorna har tidigare varit hg. Hushllen r idag ocks mer optimistiska n de var under slutet av 1994 och brjan av 1995, ven om pessimismen kat ngot p allra senaste tiden. Samtidigt finns risker. Fr vi en betydligt smre utveckling i olika avseenden, hemma och/eller utomlands, som leder till lgre sysselsttning, pverkas ven konsumtionen. Min slutsats r nd att den nattsvarta pessimism som spritt sig p senare tid p detta omrde r lite svr att frst. Mindre inflationsbengenhet Lt mig avsluta diskussionen av efterfrge- och utbudsfrhllandena med att kort berra ytterligare en aspekt, tanken att inflationsbengenheten i ekonomin minskat. En indikation p detta, som jag tidigare nmnt, r utvecklingen p vergripande makroniv. Trots att tillvxten blev betydligt hgre n vad de flesta prognosmakare vntat blev inflationen lgre. Standardargumentet fr detta r att konsumtionen utvecklades svagt. Drfr kunde inte handeln hja sina priser. Mot detta kan man dock invnda att ven konsumtionen ifjol faktiskt kade mer n de allra flesta trott. Just felaktiga konsumtionsantaganden kan allts inte frklara de alltfr hga inflationsprognoserna. Det senare hindrar dock naturligtvis inte att en konsumtionsuppgng av strre omfattning kan tnkas sl p priserna. Men hur stora de uppbyggda prishjningsbehoven r - sedda frn kostnadssidan - vet vi inte. Produktivitetstillvxten har varit omfattande i industrin men inte bara dr utan ocks i handeln (se diagram 10). En betydande strukturomvandling har skett och sker i handeln. Om nu import- och producentpriser gr ner kanske vinstmarginalerna kan hllas uppe ven vid begrnsade prishjningar. Till bilden hr att det skett en del med konkurrensen i svensk ekonomi. En av de verkliga inflationsmotorerna under 80-talet, byggsektorn, har frndrats radikalt. Inom andra delar av ekonomin har importpenetrationen kat. Det finns ocks skl att hoppas p ytterligare positiva effekter bl.a. av EU-medlemskapet. Lnebildningen r emellertid ett fortsatt bekymmer. Trots uppgngen i arbetslsheten blev lnekningarna hgre n i omvrlden (se diagram 11). Hittills har effekterna av detta p konkurrenskraft och inflation begrnsats av produktivitetstillvxten, men denna utveckling kan inte fortstta hur lnge som helst. I alla hndelser har lnekningarna begrnsat handlingsutrymmet i penningpolitiken samtidigt som de resulterar i en svagare sysselsttningstillvxt. Sammanfattningsvis finns det allts flera frgetecken nr det gller bedmningen av efterfrge- och utbudsfrhllandena de nrmaste ren. De gller som jag ser det i frsta hand den europeiska konjunkturen, konsumtionsutvecklingen i Sverige och ekonomins inflationsbengenhet. Sannolikheten att hamna vid inflationsmlet br vara god ven om tillvxten utvecklas hyggligt. Det faktum att kronan har frstrkts r en frdel ur inflationssynpunkt. Det r just i den konkurrensutsatta sektorn som de tydligaste inflationstendenserna funnits under senare r. Med en mer balanserad tillvxt r inflationsrisken mindre. Lt mig avslutningsvis konstatera att frtroendet fr svensk ekonomisk politik kade under andra halvret 1995. Risken fr ett terfall i den gamla inflationsekonomin upplevs ha minskat. Mjligheten har drmed frbttrats fr en uthllig och balanserad tillvxt i svensk ekonomi. Det innebr dock inte att riskerna fr en mindre bra utveckling framver frsvunnit. Omsorgen om frtroendet fr den ekonomiska politiken mste alltjmt ges hg prioritet. I konvergensprogrammet preciseras en mekanism fr att hantera eventuella terkommande statsfinansiella problem. Det r ocks angelget att lnebildningen frbttras s att inte accelererande lnekningar motverkar en nedgng av arbetslsheten. Lgre lnekningar skulle givit strre utrymme i rntepolitiken. Den senaste veckan har marknadsrntorna stigit och kronan fallit. Det kan finnas mnga olika skl till att marknader reagerar som de gr och s frefaller det ha varit denna gng ocks. Erfarenheten visar att svngningarna ibland kan bli verdrivna p de finansiella marknaderna. Vissa kortsiktigt inriktade aktrer har en bengenhet att snabbt vilja ta hem vinster. Framtiden lr komma att visa huruvida marknadslget varaktigt frndrats eller om rnteuppgngen och kronfallet var av tillfllig art. nd kan man konstatera att veckans hndelser r en pminnelse om att en tydlig och konsekvent utveckling mot sunda statsfinanser har stor betydelse fr frtroendet fr svensk ekonomi och drmed p sikt fr tillvxten och sysselsttningen. Grunden fr en uthlligt stabil tillvxt och sysselsttning r sunda statsfinanser och prisstabilitet. Det har inte minst utvecklingen under andra halvan av 1995 visat. D kade frtroendet fr svensk ekonomisk politik ptagligt. Avgrande fr den fortsatta penningpolitiken r den sammantagna bedmningen av inflationsutsikterna. Den pverkas i sin tur av bl.a. konjunkturutveckling, inflationsfrvntningar och vxelkursutveckling. Det viktiga r d de mer lngsiktiga frloppen. Enskilda siffror eller kortsiktiga rrelser p de finansiella marknaderna r drfr inte avgrande. Det r mot denna bakgrund som vi idag givit en viss lttnad i penningpolitiken. Title: The interest rate corridor will be reduced by 0.5 percentage points
text: Interest rate corridor to be reduced by 0.5 percentage points Date: 1996-08-15 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Press conference The Riksbank has today decided to cut its borrowing and lending rates by 0.5 percentage points each. The deposit rate is set at 4.75 percent and the lending rate at 6.25 percent. The Decision shall enter into force on 21 August 1996. The information on, among other things, Swedish price and economic developments published during the summer is in line with the main scenario presented in the Riksbank's inflation report in June. In 1996, the repo rate was reduced relatively rapidly. The pace of the Riksbank's rate cuts has recently slowed somewhat. It is essential that the conditions for monetary policy going forward are carefully analysed in the light of incoming information. There may continue to be some room for easing monetary policy. Increased stability provides better conditions for sustainable growth Low inflation is a means of creating the conditions for growth and employment. All extended periods of high and stable growth and employment in Sweden have been characterized by low inflation. An unambiguous inflation target is a means of stabilising expectations of economic policy. If the central bank acts with the key interest rate so that the target is achieved, the credibility of low-inflation policy gradually increases. The paradox of monetary policy is that the more credible economic policy is to achieve and maintain low inflation, the greater the chances of also taking growth aspects into account in the short term. The reverse is also true. The more importance a central bank is known to place on short-term growth stimulus, the less opportunities there are to promote high and stable employment. Inflation expectations risk increasing, which could lead to rising interest rates, falling currencies and price and wage rises. Attempts to increase demand when inflation expectations are high rather lead to increased inflation and not growth. The benefits of keeping inflation under control have become particularly evident over the past six months. In connection with international slowdown phases during the 1970s and 80s, the Swedish economy has often found itself in situations of high and rising inflation. It then tended to amplify the downturns in the economy. Low inflation has now provided a better starting point. During the spring, the Riksbank has been able to lower its repo rate at a relatively rapid pace. Although exact comparisons are always difficult to make over long periods of time, it can be said that the Riksbank's key interest rates have come down to 1950s and 60s levels. In recent years, significant results have been achieved to link the Swedish economy on a trajectory with a longer period of lastingly high growth and employment while keeping inflation low. There has also been a reassessment of Swedish economic policy and economy in the financial markets. Macroeconomic stability has increased and the conditions for sustainable growth and employment have thus improved. This does not mean that the adjustment has been completed, but the Swedish economy has come a long way. Sweden is in the fourth year of economic growth after the deep and severe downturn in the early 1990s. Since the turnaround in the summer of 1993, year-on-year growth has averaged about 2.5 percent. A comparison shows that this is about the same rate as in the economic upturn in the early 1980s. Preliminary figures from Statistics Sweden indicate that growth continued in the spring of 1996, albeit at a slightly weaker pace. The difference from the 1980s and also from the 1970s is that inflation has been significantly reduced. Prices are now changing trend-wise at a pace that corresponds to a good European level. Households, businesses, social partners and financial market participants are increasingly beginning to expect persistently low inflation. The general government deficit is gradually decreasing at a faster pace than most analysts expected. There is also considerable political agreement on the objective of balance by 1998. The current account shows large surpluses. The conditions for monetary policy The inflation rate (measured by the consumer price index) was 0.6% in July 1996. The strengthening of the krona over the past year and falling mortgage rates have dampened the inflation rate. However, these effects are mainly considered to be of a transitory nature. Domestically generated inflation, i.e. the part of the CPI that does not consist of imported goods and interest expenses for own homes, stood at 1.9 percent in June and has been stable around 2 percent for a long time. Despite this, the latest inflation figures have been slightly lower than what the Riksbank expected in the latest inflation report. At the heart of monetary policy-making are assessments of future inflation. Main factors in such an analysis are: Inflation expectations The development of the krona Demand situation and supply factors Inflation expectations have developed favourably. They have continued to decline in recent months and are around the inflation target and, for some groups, even below target. The krona has continued to strengthen during the summer, but rebounded slightly in early August. For the future inflation assessment - and thus for the structure of monetary policy - it is more persistent trends that matter. Given the improved stability of the Swedish economy, it is reasonable to assume that the krona exchange rate will continue to be adjusted to its equilibrium level. During the winter and spring, the demand situation in the Swedish economy has been characterized by a weaker international economy in Europe and a domestic adjustment in inventories downwards. The international economic picture is fragmented. In the US, UK and Norway, the level of activity is strong. The economy in Japan is steadily improving. On the other hand, the development has been weak in several continental European countries, although there are now some signs of an improved economic situation in, for example, Germany. It is reasonable to expect a recovery ahead, although the strength and timing of this is still uncertain. According to Statistics Sweden's preliminary statistics, growth in the Swedish economy during the spring appears to have amounted to 1.5 percent compared with the first half of 1995. Both gross capital formation and net exports contributed to this development. Private consumption also grew to some extent. It is still too early to draw any firm conclusions about the course of the Swedish economy, although stabilisation and possibly some recovery in the economy can be discerned. This, in turn, may suggest that the risk of a scenario with significantly weaker demand than in the main option discussed in the June Inflation Report has decreased. An improved international economy, slowing inventory adjustment and a slight increase in demand from the domestic market suggest a recovery in the Swedish economy. However, the economy is unlikely to reach its full capacity utilisation in 1997. The stronger krona and lower interest rates have increased the conditions for a more even use of spare capacity. In the autumn of 1996, it is estimated that inflation, as measured by the CPI, will rise slightly as a result of the absence of temporary effects. Decided increases in indirect taxes can also be expected to affect price developments. The changes in the various measures of underlying inflation that the Riksbank is working on are expected to be limited. It cannot be excluded that the high wage growth relative to the inflation target may have some impact on inflation rates, as domestic demand improves. A weight of evidence assessment of the factors determining inflation rates suggests that the conditions are good that inflation will develop in line with the inflation target over the next two years. In 1996, the repo rate was reduced relatively rapidly. The pace of the Riksbank's rate cuts has recently slowed somewhat. It is essential that the conditions for monetary policy going forward are carefully analysed in the light of incoming information. There may continue to be some room for easing monetary policy.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Rntekorridoren snks med 0,5 procentenheter Datum: 1996-08-15 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Bckstrm Plats: Presskonferens Riksbanken har idag beslutat att snka in- och utlningsrntan med 0,5 procentenheter vardera. Inlningsrntan stts till 4,75 procent och utlningsrntan till 6,25 procent. Beslutet trder i kraft den 21 augusti 1996. Den information om bland annat den svenska pris- och konjunkturutvecklingen som publicerats under sommaren r i linje med det huvudscenario som presenterades i Riksbankens inflationsrapport i juni. Under 1996 har reporntan snkts frhllandevis snabbt. Takten i Riksbankens snkningar har p senare tid avtagit ngot. Det r vsentligt att frutsttningarna fr penningpolitiken framver noga analyseras i ljuset av inkommande information. ven fortsttningsvis kan det finnas ett visst utrymme fr lttnader i penningpolitiken. kad stabilitet ger bttre frutsttningar fr varaktig tillvxt Lg inflation r ett medel att skapa frutsttningar fr tillvxt och sysselsttning. Alla lngre perioder av hg och stabil tillvxt och sysselsttning i Sverige har prglats av lg inflation. Ett entydigt inflationsml r ett medel fr att stabilisera frvntningarna om den ekonomiska politiken. Om centralbanken agerar med styrrntan s att mlet uppns kar trovrdigheten successivt fr lginflationspolitiken. Penningpolitikens paradox r att ju mer trovrdig den ekonomiska politiken r att uppn och vidmakthlla lg inflation desto strre blir mjligheterna att i det korta perspektivet ocks vga in tillvxtaspekter. Det omvnda gller ocks. Ju mer vikt en centralbank r knd fr att lgga vid kortsiktig tillvxtstimulans, desto mindre r mjligheterna att verka fr hg och stabil sysselsttning. Inflationsfrvntningarna riskerar att ka, vilket kan leda till stigande rntor, fallande valuta samt till pris- och lnestegringar. Frsk att ka efterfrgan d inflationsfrvntningarna r hga leder snarast till kad inflation och inte till tillvxt. Frdelarna med att hlla inflationen under kontroll har blivit srskilt tydliga under det senaste halvret. I samband med internationella avmattningsfaser under 1970- och 80-talen har ofta svensk ekonomi befunnit sig i situationer med hg och stigande inflation.
