Title: Relationship between the 'ins' and the 'outs'
text: Relationship between the 'ins' and the 'outs' Datum: 1996-11-13 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Backstrom Plats: Institute of Economic Affairs i Bryssel Let me start by thanking you for this invitation, enabling me to elaborate somewhat on the relationship between the 'ins' and the 'outs'. First, however, I would like to say a few words about the situation in Sweden. In recent years the imbalances in the Swedish economy have been reduced and the conditions for stability have improved. Since the upturn around mid 1993, growth in annual terms has averaged 3 per cent. There are encouraging signs of a renewed recovery after the recent slowdown and the associated stock adjustment process that began towards the end of last year. At the same time inflation is among the lowest in the European Union. For the whole of 1996, inflation is estimated at about 1 per cent. The possibility is also good that inflation will be in line with the price stability target of 2 per cent in the next 6 to 8 quarters. The general government deficit is diminishing successively, with most of the evidence pointing to a level below 3 per cent in 1997 and balance in 1998. The developments in the past year have been accompanied by a reassessment of the Swedish economy, manifested in a strengthening of the exchange rate and a fall in bond rates. Admittedly, the situation is not bright in every respect. Unemployment is still high. Wage formation has not yet adapted in full to an economy with low inflation. Government debt is still relatively high, slightly less than 80 per cent of GDP, but it is expected to go on falling relative to GDP. On the whole, substantial improvements have occurred. It is my assessment that Sweden stands a good chance of meeting the convergence criteria for participation in the EMU right from the start. The discussion is now in full swing on our country's future relationship to the European Monetary Union. The debate is about whether Sweden will belong to the first group of countries that establish the EMU or whether the political process leads us to wait. A decision by the Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, is scheduled for next autumn. In the meantime, the Swedish Central Bank, the Riksbank, is taking an active part in the preparations so that our parliament is in a position to choose either way. Europe is now fully engaged in the creation of a single market with freedom of movement for goods, individuals, services and capital. The establishment of the Monetary Union will be an important and natural step in this process. Most of the evidence also suggests that this third stage will begin on 1 January 1999. The idea of closer economic and monetary cooperation in Europe is by no means new. It was enshrined in the Treaty of Rome, signed in 1957. For various reasons, however, it was not until the second half of the 1980s that the process really got going. With the establishment of a monetary union, cooperation in Europe will also enter a new phase. It will become more intensive but because - for economic or political reasons - the monetary union will not include every country from day one, the process of integration could be disturbed. The relationship between Ins and Outs therefore needs to be thoroughly discussed because it involves a number of aspects on different planes. Permit me to consider some of them briefly. One such aspect is the need to coordinate monetary and exchange rate policy between 'ins' and 'outs'. This issue has featured prominently in the general debate as well as in the work of the EU's institutions. It is also on agenda for this December's meeting of Heads of State and Government in Dublin. A close policy co-ordination between euro-area and non-euro-area Member States from the very start of Stage Three of EMU is a matter of common interest and forms an integral part of the completion of the EMU process. In order to ensure the efficient functioning and development of the Single Market, it is especially important that real exchange rate misalignments between the euro and non-euro-area currencies can be avoided, as well as nominal exchange rate fluctuations, which would disrupt trade flows between Member States. Under Article 109m of the Treaty there is an obligation to treat exchange rate policy as a matter of common interest. It is important to bear in mind that the lasting convergence of eco-nomic fundamentals, in particular price stability, is a prerequisite for sustained exchange rate stability. Mo-reover, sound fiscal and structural policies in Member States are equally essential for sustainable price and exchange rate stability. In the absence of a convergence of fundamentals, any attemt to co-ordinate exchange rate policies is bound to be unsuccessful. Exchange rate policy co-operation cannot be a substitute for stability-oriented domestic policies. Let me also add that I believe that monetary and exchange rate policy co-operation should be flexible enough to accommodate different degrees and strategies of economic convergence. A second aspect, which has not been discussed so much, is the decision-making process. There is, of course, a risk that what was intended to be increased integration in Europe will turn out in practice to contain divisive tendencies between euro-area and non-euro-area Member States. It is reasonable that countries which naturally belong to the Monetary Union right from the start are so open that even countries joining later are in a position to influence the Union's construction. In this respect there is a high degree of openness, as is evident not least from the work being done under the auspices of the EMI. In one specific matter, however, there is a tendency that seems disturbing. This is the question of how to treat non-euro countries with respect to the TARGET system - the future European network of national systems for large-value payments. There is a desire among some countries to postpone the decision about this until the ECB has been established and to provide full access to the system only to EMU countries. That would mean that only those countries which participate in EMU from the start will be able to influence this matter and that financial institutions will be hit by negative competitive conditions because some countries do not belong to EMU initially. That clearly must not happen. This is an example of a disturbing tendency in the relationship between 'ins' and 'outs'. I find it hard to believe that this matter will not be resolved in a forum that includes all the EU's Member States, or that some countries will be excluded from the system. Neither do I expect that the question of TARGET will be followed by more tendencies in the same direction. What is at stake is potential conflicts between the EU's Member States and their respective financial systems, entirely contrary to the overriding purpose of the European process. If we construct irrelevant barriers and restrictions for the financial sector within Europe, there are reasons to believe that we will not be shifting activity from one European country to another, but could instead be shifting activity away from Europe altogether. Let me, as an example, remind you of what happened in the 1960s when US regulations gave rise to the Europe based Eurodollar market. This brings me to a third aspect, namely how to treat non-EU countries. The euro holds the potential for becoming a major world currency, which will then reduce transaction costs for European corporates, due to less FX risk and a more liquid money market. This may increase the potential for invoicing cross-border trade in the (new) home currency. To establish this it is important to help the financial industry in providing an efficient financial environment and a very open attitude towards countries outside the currency area itself. Let me, as an example, again take a closer look at this aspect with respect to TARGET and the collateral issues. In Stage Three of the EMU all central bank credit, both intraday and overnight, is to be fully collateralised. EU countries are to have a payment system based on the RTGS principle, which means that payment orders entering the system are settled one by one on a continuous basis during the system's operating hours. These systems are very much dependent on liquidity with a liquidity shortage they can give rise to disturbances in financial activity, since payments can be delayed, or cannot be made in the extreme case. Sweden was the first country to introduce a fully collateralised RTGS system, in January 1995. This has given us some valuable experience. We have noted that branches of foreign banks sometimes can have difficulties in meeting their intraday liquidity needs. We have, therefore, recently decided to accept foreign denominated securities as collateral for intraday credit, if the central bank of the location of these securities acts as our correspondent or guarantor. This has been quite controversial for some EU countries which insist on only accepting euro denominated securities issued by EMU entities and located in the EMU area. Even if there will be enough eligible euro paper, our experience shows that there could be circumstances when participants do not have the relevant papers. Consequently, I advocate an open attitude, which I think will favour a sound and stable fi-nancial system in Europe. It is also, in my view, important that the future ECB does not force banks to restructure their portpolios in a direction that they might not favour themselves. The above-mentioned example illustrates the point that potential tensions may arise between a globalisation and regionalisation approach. I am convinced that a regionalisation approach would hamper the evolution of a sound and prosperous financial system in an integrated Europe, and thereby Europe's competitive edge in the global financial system.

Title: Hearing on monetary policy
text: Ingves in the Finance Committee: Hearing on monetary policy Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Henry Ohlsson today visited the Riksdag's Finance Committee for the first hearing of the year on the Riksbank's monetary policy. Date: 2018-03-06 09:00 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Skandiasalen, Riksdagen, Stockholm Published 2018-03-06 Ingves began the hearing by outlining the background to the last monetary policy decision in February, when the repo rate was left unchanged at -0.50 percent, and the trade-off that the Executive Board then faced. On the one hand, the economy in Sweden and the rest of the world is strengthening and inflation is close to the target. On the other hand, recent statistics suggest that price and wage pressures in Sweden have weakened and that inflation is expected to be somewhat lower in the coming year. Inflation is expected to be close to 2% from 2019, but this is based on continued support from monetary policy. It has taken a long time to bring inflation back up to the 2% target. The uncertainty surrounding inflation developments means that monetary policy needs to proceed cautiously, says Ingves. "In the situation we are in, I see little risk in being cautious." Title: The Riksbank and stock market turmoil
text: The Riksbank and stock market turmoil Date: 1997-11-11 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Stora Aktiekvallen in Gothenburg Thank you for the invitation to come to Gothenburg and speak at the Big Share Evening. During the autumn, share prices have fallen on a number of stock exchanges around the world. It is natural that dramatic stock price changes have a great news value and that they attract the public's attention on a broad front. Of course, public interest has also increased as a result of the fact that more and more people have invested at least part of their savings in shares, either directly through their own share purchases or through investments in mutual funds. A stock market crash can also be a dramatic event. One example is the fall of 1929 in New York, which was the beginning of a very deep recession and thus had serious real consequences. In modern times, there is Black Monday in 1987 when the New York Stock Exchange fell by just over 22% in one day, but that decline had no lasting effect on economies. What determines whether a sharp stock market downturn risks having serious consequences for the real economy is how the financial system is affected. While many banks in the UNITED STATES, among others, ran into major problems in 1929, the financial system did quite well in 1987. There are several different reasons why changing stock prices in one country spread to other countries. Large international companies operate in the same world market. If the actual or expected economy goes up or down in key growth areas in any part of the world, it affects - at least to some extent - the valuation of the major international companies and their shares. This applies regardless of whether their shares are listed in New York, Tokyo, Hong Kong or in Stockholm. Even in industries where companies are more dependent on the domestic market, many companies are subcontractors to the large export companies. As a result, both businesses and consumers are indirectly dependent on what happens on the world market. An increase or decrease in world trade can affect employment and real incomes and thus consumer behaviour. There are also financial mechanisms. With the type of global financial markets that exist today, savers and investors can choose between many different international forms of investment and financing. The statistics show how a growing number of Swedes have invested savings in, for example, Southeast Asia. The same applies to savers in other countries. Changes in stock prices in one country can thus affect savers and stock prices in other countries. In my speech today, I will discuss how the Riksbank views the stock market turmoil during the autumn and what it means for our two tasks: to promote a secure and stable payment system and to safeguard the value of money. The last few weeks The month of October ended with drama on the world's stock exchanges. On Monday on October 28 and Tuesday, October 29, stock markets fell sharply across the globe. After turbulence in Southeast Asia late in the previous week, the Hong Kong stock exchange fell 14 percent on Monday. The Hong Kong Stock Exchange is today the seventh largest stock exchange in the world. The fall in the stock market in Hong Kong should be seen in the light of the economic crisis and currency turmoil that have affected a number of economies in Southeast Asia. The problems in South-East Asia are linked to deteriorating competitiveness, falling property values, past lending expansion, problem bank credit and short-term foreign borrowing. These are problems that we have seen in other parts of the world and not least in our own country in the early 1990s. This means that certain patterns of development in Southeast Asia in many respects feel familiar. The Swedish stock market fell 4.4 percent on Monday, October 28. Later in the evening, Swedish time, the Dow Jones index in New York fell by just over 7%, the twelfth largest share price drop in the history of the New York Stock Exchange and the biggest fall since 1987. Trading on the New York Stock Exchange was halted on Monday on two occasions as a result of the rules on stock market stops in the event of sharp price falls that were introduced after the events of October 1987. The idea of the stopgap rules is to give the market time to come to its senses and to avoid panicked behaviour. As a small digression, one might ask whether in New York on Monday it didn't have the opposite effect. If the development leads to a halt in the stock market, it seems likely that the price decline will continue after it has reopened. The system is then overloaded with sell orders and the prices are pushed further downwards. This behavior could be observed on the New York Stock Exchange on Monday. Even the dramatic development on European stock exchanges in the first half hour after they opened on Tuesday, when most European stock exchanges fell by about 10%, are examples of how prices can develop when great expectations of price falls exist just after trading starts. There is therefore reason to be hesitant about the introduction of stop rules on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, which is something that has been discussed in some quarters. After the fall in New York, expectations of sharp price falls were high on the European stock markets. After the initial collapse of 10 percent, however, the performance of the Stockholm stock exchange stopped at a decline of 4.3 percent, a development similar to that on the other European stock exchanges. Overall, prices on the Stockholm stock exchange fell by 10 percent in October. Perspectives on stock market performance The fact that the Stockholm stock exchange falls by 10 percent in one month is quite unusual. Historically, the stock market has fallen by 10 percent or more in a single month on a total of 15 occasions since the early 1920s. But there are also months when it has risen by 10 percent or more. It has happened 25 times. During a single month, the prices on the Stockholm Stock Exchange have thus, on average, risen more times by at least 10 percent than it has fallen correspondingly. It illustrates in a nutshell, I think, what stock investing is all about. The experienced share saver knows that, in the long term, stock investments usually give a higher return than other financial investments. But at the same time, the yield varies significantly between individual months and years. In other words, stock prices can go up sharply, but they can also fall significantly in the short term. These variations do not have to be so important if you have a fairly long investment horizon. It is important to put the events of autumn into context. Share prices have risen on average by several hundred percent in Sweden during the 1990s and the increase has continued almost continuously since the autumn of 1992. At the same time, however, it should be noted that overall the stock market upturn in the 1980s was substantially larger than it had been so far in the 1990s. So far, despite this autumn's fall in the stock market, share prices have risen by an average of about 20 percent. History teaches us that stock prices do not continue to rise indefinitely. Sooner or later, a period of calmer development and lower yields occurs. Sometimes such a correction becomes more rapid and sometimes a longer period of adaptation takes place. Earlier this autumn, the overall valuation of corporate profits was at relatively high levels. This means that the price level that prevailed at the time presupposed continued rapid profit growth for several years to come. In such situations, stock prices tend to be sensitive to various types of disruptions. The Riksbank monitors the stability of the financial system In addition to monetary policy and the task of safeguarding monetary value, the Riksbank will work for a stable financial system. How the Riksbank views this task has been explained in the first Financial Market Report published on Friday. The task is based on the Riksbank providing the central payment system in Sweden through which virtually all payments in Sweden pass. The turnover in the so-called. The RIX system is around SEK 300 billion per day. Disruptions in this payment system can have serious consequences for the wider economy. Disruptions in the payment system are primarily at risk if any of the companies directly linked to the payment system suffers problems. The companies in question are the banks as well as some clearing houses, such as OM. When assessing the effects of a stock market fall, it is therefore the effects on these companies that are the focus of the Riksbank's immediate analysis. Market conditions are currently so favorable that the entire payment system including the banking system should be able to cope with a stock market downturn. Unlike the stock market downturn in 1987, the loan-to-value ratio is low. Today, just under 1% of the market capitalization is leveraged. Available statistics show that securities companies' lending against collateral in shares in relation to market capitalization was 12 times greater at the end of the 1980s than today. The lower loan-to-value ratio means that vulnerability is reduced in the event of large price adjustments. The financial institutions operating on the stock exchange and derivatives markets are generally solid and have good liquidity. For example, in the first nine months of the year, the four largest banking groups showed an average return on equity of 18%. Credit losses are low and capital adequacy remains good. The banks' holdings of shares are very small, as is the part of lending where the collateral consists of shares. Overall, this exposure corresponds to approx. 1-2% of the asset mass of the big banks. Securities companies have a greater exposure to the stock market, but even in their case it is not significant. At the time of the stock market crash in 1987, investment firms had a significantly higher level of their own exposure to the stock market. It is also worth noting that the high turnover on the stock exchange that occurs during periods of high volatility is positive for the earnings of investment firms, as this is primarily generated by commission income. On Tuesday, October 29, for example, the stock exchange broke sales records with a trade of just over SEK 11 billion, compared with the normal trading that usually amounts to about. 5 billion kr. It is important for both banks and investment firms that they have sufficient liquidity in a situation when the stock market falls and turnover increases so that they can cover their commitments. The banks' liquidity, measured as their liquid assets minus their short-term funding, has been above SEK 100 billion over the past 18 months. The liquidity of investment firms is also good, even if it is considerably less than that of banks. But they also don't have to have the same high liquidity. Investment firms do not have the same exposure to liquidity risks on their balance sheets. Nor are they payment intermediaries in the same way as banks. The liquidity of investment firms has been over SEK 6 billion over the past 18 months and has averaged SEK 12 billion. This can be compared with the average daily turnover on the stock exchange which is about. SEK 5 billion. What does the Riksbank do when the stock market falls? The Riksbank routinely intensifies its monitoring if there is a stock market fall of the type we saw at the end of October. Acute problems are primarily at risk of arising in financial firms. Therefore, the monitoring of them is tightened. In particular, the Riksbank makes assessments of the effects that the development may have on the equity/assets ratio and liquidity of companies. The most acute problems for the Riksbank arise if the banks have problems with liquidity. Such problems are primarily likely to arise if the functioning of the interbank market as a distributor of overall liquidity deteriorates. This can happen, for example, if a bank finds it difficult to borrow on the interbank market as a result of other banks experiencing its position as uncertain. The Riksbank has a central role in the payment system by controlling the total liquidity of the banking system. Normally, lending to the banks takes place from the Riksbank against full collateral. If a bank cannot obtain cash to carry out its payments and also cannot deliver normal collateral, the Riksbank's role as lender of last resort may arise. However, this happens only in very special situations. Since it is in this function that the Riksbank can primarily have an active role, it is natural that the emphasis in the intensified monitoring is on the banks' liquidity. An exchange of information between the competent authorities in this area takes place routinely when turbulence increases. In addition, there is intensified monitoring of payment traffic in the Riksbank's payment system, the RIX system. Given the limited impact of falling stock prices, at least for the time being, on the companies, banks and some clearing houses, the recent turbulence on the Stockholm Stock Exchange does not pose a concern for the stability of the financial system. Stock market falls have major effects on many investors, but this time they have not given reason for the Riksbank to take any actual measures, except for increased surveillance. During the stock market turmoil, the Riksbank's payment system worked according to expectations and without problems or delays, despite the large price adjustment. The financial system has also otherwise functioned properly. Moreover, market conditions are so favourable that the payment system as a whole and banks individually should be able to cope with a stock market downturn. Good equity/assets ratio and vitality, small exposures to the stock market and a low loan-to-value ratio give the financial system good resilience to the negative effects of a stock market fall. Implications for growth and inflation outlook As we reported in September's inflation report, the economy continues to recover. Private consumption as well as investment and exports are contributing to ever stronger growth. An increasing number of indicators confirm such a development. In addition, public finances are heading for surpluses. Our combined business with the rest of the world has been in surplus for several years. Both households and firms have low indebtedness ratios. Most of it also indicates good profits in the private sector. As I pointed out earlier, the financial system is stable and there has been a marked recovery since the banking crisis years of the early 1990s. Confidence in the willingness and ability of economic policies to pursue low inflation in line with the price stability objective has also increased in recent years. Monetary policy has for some time supported expansionary development of the economy, as inflation risks have been moderate. I have said before that monetary policy cannot take this direction throughout the economic cycle. Riksbank is working consistently to ensure that monetary policy continuously achieves its target of inflation of 2%. In the Riksdag's Finance Committee the other week, I talked about how the Riksbank may need to "lighten the gas so that it is no longer forced to pull the handbrake hard". Thus, at some point - although it is unclear when - monetary policy will have to be reoriented in a more neutral direction. The timing of this is determined by the inflation outlook 12 to 24 months ahead. We're not there yet. The reasoning about having to "ease up the throttle" at some point going forward is in line with the latest inflation report. As activity in the economy strengthens and time passes, the sights of monetary policy must gradually shift forward in time. So in the next Inflation Report, we need to look further ahead than we did in the previous one. If the economy grows faster than its potential, we are gradually approaching the point where the degree of spare capacity decreases by moving the perspective forward, given that the previous forecast still holds. What we now have to assess is whether the stock market turmoil will have such effects that the economic picture changes and the inflation outlook is affected. In addition, we must ask ourselves whether other factors have been added that influence the analysis. The question, then, is whether the growth and inflation outlook remains in line with the previous Inflation Report or whether the picture has changed? Today I intend to briefly say something about the stock market turbulence impact on the basis of the information available so far. First, it can be stated that the financial system, both in Sweden and in other industrialized countries, seems to be able to cope with the stock market falls without suffering from disruptions. Although we do not know if we have seen the end of the correction in the stock market, it can be stated that the Swedish economy and its financial system have good conditions to cope with this type of price movement. The stability of the financial system contributes to the fact that the autumn events are unlikely to have any more significantly negative real economic effects. The question is then whether the effects of weaker exports to Southeast Asia, lower wealth values and possible household uncertainty as a result of the incident are of such magnitude that the economic cycle is affected. Although the share of Swedish exports that go to Asia has increased in recent years, it still does not amount to more than about 10 percent. However, a certain impact on exports cannot be excluded. If the crisis continues and worsens, the negative effects could be greater on, for example, Japan's economy. One possible real economic effect of a fall in the stock market is that household wealth is adjusted as the value of the shareholding falls. It cannot therefore be ruled out that private consumption will moderate somewhat, but at the same time we must remember that the stock market has risen overall this year, including the fall in the autumn. On the whole, based on the information the Riksbank currently has, it is unlikely that recent events in Southeast Asia and on the stock markets will have more than marginal effects on the Swedish economy. However, the Riksbank will have reason to return to this issue as well as other factors affecting the growth and inflation outlook, most recently in connection with the Inflation Report in December.

Vid ngon tidpunkt - ven om det r oklart nr - mste allts penningpolitiken lggas om i mer neutral riktning. Frst kan konstateras att det finansiella systemet, svl i Sverige som i andra industrilnder, verkar klara brsfallen utan att drabbas av strningar. ven om vi inte vet om vi sett slutet p korrigeringen p aktiemarknaden kan konstateras att svensk ekonomi och dess finansiella system har goda frutsttningar att klara den hr typen av kursrrelser. Stabiliteten i det finansiella systemet bidrar till att hstens hndelser troligen inte kommer att f ngra mer ptagligt negativa realekonomiska effekter. Frgan r sedan om effekterna av en svagare export till Sydostasien, lgre frmgenhetsvrden och en eventuell oskerhet hos hushllen till fljd av det intrffade r av den storleksordningen att konjunkturfrloppet pverkas. Title: The Riksbank and the future European Monetary Union
text: The Riksbank and the future European Monetary Union Date: 1996-05-22 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Place: Annual Meeting of the Swedish Veterans' Association Mr President, first of all I would like to thank you for the invitation to discuss the future of European Monetary Union (EMU). Sweden has been a member of the EU since the beginning of 1994 and is now being prepared probably the biggest currency reform ever in history - the European Monetary Union. The debate on the advantages and disadvantages of the European Monetary Union is now taking place at its best in our country. The overarching objective of the single monetary policy in EMU is price stability. It is sometimes argued that this very thing makes participation in the Union a serious risk. Had it been the case that inflation is a prerequisite for growth and employment, that objection would have been natural, but that is not the swedish experience. There is a special reason that makes the EMU project interesting to discuss here in the traditional premises of the Riksdag. Throughout our Swedish history and the centuries, the Riksdag and its members have taken it as their task to protect the value of money. After all, this is also an important objective of European Monetary Union. It provides a framework for how European monetary policy is to be conducted in the future so that inflation can be kept under control in the long term. In my speech, I will point out two conditions that speak in favour of Swedish accession to EMU. Firstly, monetary union ties in with the Swedish tradition of striving to safeguard the value of money. Secondly, membership makes it easier for a country to achieve this stability, especially as rapid financial developments place stricter demands on economic policy discipline. Before I get into these two questions, it is appropriate to discuss in more detail what is at the heart of monetary policy. What does a central bank do? The basic function of a central bank is to provide final means of payment, i.e. what we colloquially call money. With its monopoly position in this area, a central bank has a decisive influence over the amount of money that is in the economy. In everyday work, however, it is not the amount of means of payment that we are trying to control. Somewhat simplified, it can be said that monetary policy is about raising or lowering the interest rate we charge in order to lend the notes and coins to the public. It is this policy rate that we in Sweden call the repo rate. If the Riksbank provides excessive amounts of money and the repo rate is consequently kept unnaturally low, it will not result in long-term economic growth. Instead, prices are rising. Inflation is the same as falls in value on the means of payment provided by the Riksbank. A deterioration in the value of money means that every penny is enough for the purchase of fewer goods. The fact that this is the case is due to the fact that today's banknotes and coins do not have the net asset value indicated on them. In this regard, they differ from old copper, silver and gold coins. The banknotes are actually small white sheets of paper, on which there have been often very beautiful motifs printed including an amount. Everyone realizes that, against this background, it is not the amount of paper banknotes, or for that matter the repo rate, that determines the development of a country's prosperity. But if too many banknotes are printed, inflation will arise. Therefore, there must be some kind of rule of action for how monetary policy is to be conducted so that the value of money is safeguarded and so that public confidence in this value is maintained over time. Fixed exchange rate against the currency of another country is an example of such a rule of action that can govern the structure of monetary policy. The Riksbank then undertakes to redeem Swedish kronor for foreign currencies at a predetermined rate. The value of the krona can also be tied to a precious metal e.g. gold, something that has previously occurred. Now that the value of the krona is floating freely against other currencies, the Riksbank has an inflation target. The repo rate is then determined so that inflation in Sweden ends up at 2 percent, with a tolerance of /- 1 percentage point. Thus, regardless of whether we have a fixed or floating exchange rate, it is a way to achieve the same thing - preserve the purchasing power of the crown. At a fixed exchange rate, the value of the krona is pegged to the currency of another country. We must then, in principle, pursue the same monetary policy. If the external value of the krona is preserved, it will in the long run mean that its purchasing power within the country is also preserved, provided that the monetary policy of the countries against which the krona is pegged is in turn geared towards price stability. In the case of floating exchange rates, policy focuses instead directly on domestic price stability. Monetary union is a system in which exchange rates are irrevocably fixed against each other. However, instead of all countries pursuing a similar monetary policy on their own, i.e. issuing approximately the same amount of money and setting the policy rate at roughly the same level, it goes a step further and forms a single central bank. This central bank conducts a single monetary policy and determines a repo rate common throughout the geographical area covered by monetary union. It is easiest to understand if we look at Sweden, where all provinces, counties and municipalities form a currency area and we have a common central bank, the Riksbank. The crown is valid everywhere and we do not have to switch at the provincial border if we go between eg. Smaland and Skane. Stability favors growth Inflation is not a recipe for success for growth, employment and prosperity. On the contrary, the economic performance of countries that, with inflation, have sought to achieve short-term benefits in terms of growth and employment is disappointing. In the longer term, such countries have had a worse development in almost all areas of the economy. It is these experiences that are the reason why the countries of Europe have come to emphasise that a stability-oriented economic policy is a prerequisite for high and stable economic growth and employment. That inflation is harmful has long been known. Periods of very high inflation have actually also existed in Sweden, although not during the 1900s. We have to go back to the early 1800s in the context of the war against Russia. The 1700s were also marked by recurring periods of inflation. Germany, on the other hand, in the early 1920s suffered a thousandfold in a few months. In order to buy bread, they had to fill sacks with banknotes. This experience has also been gained in some other countries during the 1900s. However, we do not need to take the most extreme examples from history to illustrate the harmfulness of inflation. It is enough to look at our own development in the 1970s and 1980s. The repercussions of these decades of economic development are illuminating. Recurrent devaluations, fiscal overstimulation, jerky economic development, misinvestment, inflation and speculation were characteristic. As a direct result, in the early 1990s, Sweden experienced the deepest downturn since the 1930s and perhaps the most severe banking crisis of this century. Swedish history shows that periods of low inflation coincided with times of favorable and stable economic development. Sweden had second only Japan to the highest economic growth in the world from the breakthrough of industrialism in the mid-1800s until the late 1960s. During this period, the annual average inflation was around 2%, even though I also included the years around the war periods and other temporary inflation periods. Parliament protects the value of money In the old days, the trade in precious metals often took place. Later came so-called value coins, i.e. a certain specified amount of precious metal minted to mark authenticity and value. The Mint of Avesta began issuing tin coins in 1644. They were large unmanageable copper coins and could weigh up to 20 kilograms. It is said to have been enough to buy a cow at the time. However, Johan Palmstruch, the founder of Sweden's first bank, Stockholm Banco, launched an idea in 1661 that would facilitate money management by issuing the first banknotes, so-called credit notes. These notes were interest-free debt securities of fixed amounts that would correspond to money deposited in the bank. The banknotes were initially a success, as they were easier to handle than the coins. It all ended in a bank crash anyway, after Palmstruch was tempted to issue too many notes in relation to the underlying values deposited in the bank. This was to be an important experience. The effort to try to counteract the temptation to let too much money circulate in the economy runs like a red thread through Swedish history. Parliament and its members have taken it as their task to protect the value of money. This was expressed for the first time when the Riksbank was formed in 1668, which incidentally makes it the world's oldest central bank. It became, after a lot of disagreements, then the body of the Reichstag to prevent the King's government from eroding the value of money. Kings, as is well known at that time, waged a great deal of costly wars. As early as 1677, however, the bank was put to a severe test. In a letter dated January 4, 1677, The King requested. May a loan of 200,000 daler silver coins to be able to continue with the war that was then waged. In dealing with this case, historians clearly emphasize the importance of the bank being stripped of the government's sphere of power and placed under the care of the Estates. It is further emphasized in the literature that if the Riksbank had been a government's work, there is no doubt that it has come to issue banknotes for the financing of war. When Gustav III suspended the Riksdag in 1772, its members responded by appointing their own auditors with the task of auditing and supervising the Riksbank. Through the actions of the then Banking Committee and the parliamentary auditors, the bank's credibility was strengthened because the King was not allowed to use it. The 1700s were nevertheless marked by recurring periods of inflation, mostly associated with war because the banknote presses were used. The last of these periods occurred during the war with Russia in 1808-1809. As usual, the same pattern was repeated during periods of inflation, which is valid to this day. A strong monetary expansion is followed by rising prices, speculation, rising land values, falling exchange rates and then a setback in the form of a period of weak and even negative economic growth. The experience of the early 1990s after the 1980s thus, the inflation bubble is far from new. After the long period during the 1700s - with more or less uncertain monetary value - the Reichstag and its members became increasingly determined to return to a definite footing, despite the King's reluctance. In 1830, the Riksdag decided on the introduction of a silver standard. The issue of the gold standard in Sweden became relevant after the formation of the so-called Latin Coin Union in December 1865. It was France, Italy, Belgium and Switzerland that formed a confederation to have a common unit of coinage. Later, Greece also joined. In a motion in the First Chamber of the 1868 Riksdag, the bank manager Andre Oscar Wallenberg raised proposals for the introduction of a new mint foot based on francs as a unit and on gold as a value equalizer. However, parliament rejected the motion but requested an investigation from the government. A committee submitted its report in August 1870 and believed that Sweden should go ahead and join the gold-franc system. However, with the defeat of France in the German-French war of 1870-1871, the proposal for accession to the franc system lost its timeliness. However, an inter-Scandinavian commission was appointed on a Danish initiative in the summer of 1872. Later that year, it came up with a proposal that the three Nordic countries should form a monetary union based on gold. After the usual consultation, the government returned with a bill in 1873 which stated that ""gold alone shall be the measure of value in the kingdom and thus form the basis of its coinage""". The unit of counting would be called a crown and divided into 100 cents. In addition, Sweden would enter into a coinage convention with Denmark and Norway. In its report on this bill, the Banking Committee proposed that the banknotes should have a text that reads as follows: Sveriges Riksbank redeems, on demand, this banknote with gold coins. During the following 100 years, Sweden had, with some interruptions - mainly caused by world wars and the depression of the 1930s - the value of the currency tied to gold. This is also true under the so-called Bretton Woods system until its collapse in the early 1970s. Formally, the crown was then pegged to the US dollar, but the dollar, in turn, was pegged to gold. Today's monetary policy regime is no longer based on a value standard, such as gold. Nor is the krona pegged to any other currency. The Riksbank can therefore, in principle, decide how much money is to be produced or, or more specifically, what policy rate should apply. This gives agency, but it is wrong to think that it is unlimited. Just as in the old days, if the Riksbank spends too much money, i.e. sets interest rates lower than is compatible with economic balance, inflation threatens. Consequently, monetary policy must be constantly balanced in such a way as to keep inflation and inflation expectations under control. General confidence in the objective of price stability is a prerequisite for favourable economic developments. Otherwise, wages, prices and market interest rates rise and the exchange rate comes under pressure. Then problems soon arise but low growth and high unemployment. A new global capital market The mid-1800s have been referred to by historians as the time of the Industrial Revolution. The question is whether the historians of the future will not refer to the late 1980s and early 1990s as the time of the financial revolution in the world. However, the financial system is not a new innovation, nor has it been developed for its own sake. Its structure has evolved over the centuries as a means of facilitating the production of and trade in goods and services. The development of the financial system must be seen as part of a larger process that has been going on since the breakthrough of industrialism, but development has accelerated significantly from the mid-1980s. It is technological forces that have been behind the development and specialisation of the real economy over the decades. Although the development of world trade required political decisions in the form of the removal of trade barriers, the globalisation of technological innovations, which were the prerequisite for more efficient communications, was made possible. As transportation became cheaper, ranging from the steamboat to the jet, the trade in goods and services also increased rapidly. Technological development also laid the foundation for the development of new and more efficient production processes. Today we see the same type of pattern in the financial field. Technological advances in the telecommunications, communications and computing fields have also formed the basis of financial globalisation. Turnover in trading in the financial markets has increased very rapidly in just one decade, since the mid-1980s. The development of new financial instruments is also moving fast. Globalization and expansion required political decisions in the form of abolished regulations in the financial field, driven by technological development. The financial internationalization process over the past decade is fundamentally natural. New financial opportunities and solutions are necessary to facilitate international trade in goods and services. The expansion is a logical consequence of the effort to develop the range of products for payments, investments and savings. Here, too, the new derivative instruments play an important role as they make it possible to separate and price risks. That way, those who have the best ability to bear risks can do so too. Derivative products already play, but will in the future play an even greater role, not only for financial investments, but also for entrepreneurship and employment. It is easier to see if we consider that a regular fire or accident insurance is actually a derivative product. By severing risks, i.e. in my example of shifting the risk of fire or accidents to an insurance company, an entrepreneur can devote all his energy to the management of his business and use his capital for investments without having to build up a buffer in the event of a disaster. With the expanding derivatives market, one can imagine severing the risks in a variety of areas that are difficult to overview for an individual entrepreneur. These risks are then pooled with other actors who have the skills and financial resources to meet them. Financial developments thus contribute to facilitating the continued development of the real economy towards greater specialisation and efficiency. However, these developments have created a new and more difficult environment for regulators and economic policy makers. Experience shows that economic policy plays an important role in price developments on the financial markets, as it does on the real markets. The kind of abrupt corrections and - as it can sometimes be experienced - excessive fluctuations in interest rates, stocks and exchange rates that we have experienced can often be traced back to economic policy. Admittedly, in times of turbulence, price movements in financial markets may become excessive and temporarily go beyond what can be justified by fundamental economic factors. The important thing, however, is to ask what the underlying reason is for financial turbulence to occur in the first place. We have clearly seen in recent years that doubts about stability-oriented policies, as well as imbalances in the state budget or in the current account, give rise to often not insignificant tensions and financial turmoil. The new global financial environment has thus increased the demand for discipline in economic policy. The scope for missteps has simply been significantly reduced. It is not just a question of preserving the value of money as it was in the old days for a central bank, or indeed for the political system. This now also applies to more than earlier to make credible that this will characterize economic policy for a long time to come. It is precisely the uncertainty surrounding this confidence that can often explain the extensive movements in exchange rates and long-term interest rates in recent years. Not least the developments in our own country confirm this. It is also in the light of these developments that the plans for a European Monetary Union should be seen. It provides a monetary policy framework that increases the long-term credibility of economic policy discipline and stability-oriented policies. Of course, it is also possible for a country in the new global financial environment to establish credibility around its currency and the future monetary value. This is shown not least by the experience in Switzerland. My point, however, is that the difficulties of such an option for action must not be underestimated. Such a path does not offer an easier option, on the contrary, it is in all likelihood more laborious. That is why it is important to take into account the costs associated with exclusion in the discussion on EMU. In this context, the costs should be estimated for the longer adjustment period and the greater sacrifices required to achieve the same credibility for the future monetary value that a European Monetary Union can offer. Conclusion The debate on the advantages and disadvantages of the European Monetary Union is now taking place at its best in our country. It is an important discussion because it is a position that requires careful consideration. For its part, the Riksbank council has come to the conclusion that  there are predominant advantages to Swedish accession to a European Monetary Union. In my speech, I have pointed out two factors that speak in favour of Swedish accession to a European Monetary Union. Firstly, our monetary policy history shows a long tradition of the unification of price stability and favourable economic development. The importance of using different frameworks to protect the value of money is something that runs like a red thread throughout Swedish history. The role and position of the Riksdag has been prominent in this area. Secondly, a global financial market has emerged over the past decade, which places stricter demands on economic policy discipline. It is therefore not free of charge for a country, in this new financial environment, to maintain the freedom of action to be able to devalue its currency. This is a cost that must also be taken into account in the ongoing discussion on EMU.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Riksbanken och den framtida europeiska monetra unionen Datum: 1996-05-22 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Bckstrm Plats: Riksdagens Veteranfrenings rsmte Frst vill jag tacka fr inbjudan att diskutera den framtida Europeiska Monetra Unionen (EMU). Ibland hvdas att just detta gr att ett deltagande i unionen r frknippat med allvarliga risker. Hade det varit s att inflation r en frutsttning fr tillvxt och sysselsttning hade den invndningen varit naturlig, men det r inte den sven-ska erfarenheten. Det finns ett srskilt skl som gr EMU-projektet intressant att diskutera hr i Riksdagens traditionsrika lokaler. Riksdagen och dess ledamter har genom vr svenska historia och rhundradenas lopp tagit som sin uppgift att vrna penningvrdet. Det r ju ocks detta som r ett viktigt syfte med den Europeiska Monetra Unionen. Den erbjuder ett ramverk fr hur den europeiska penningpolitiken skall bedrivas framver s att inflationen lngsiktigt ska kunna hllas under kontroll. Jag kommer i mitt anfrande att peka p tv frhllanden som talar fr en svensk anslutning till EMU. Fr det frsta anknyter en monetr union till den svenska traditionen att strva efter att vrna penningvrdet. Fr det andra gr ett medlemsskap det lttare fr en land att stadkomma denna stabilitet srskilt som den snabba finansiella utvecklingen stller strngare krav p ekonomiskpolitisk disciplin. Innan jag kommer in p dessa tv frgor r det p sin plats att nrmare diskutera vad som r penningpolitikens innersta krna. Vad gr en centralbank? En centralbanks grundlggande funktion r att tillhandahlla slutliga betalningsmedel, dvs det som vi i vardagligt tal brukar kalla fr pengar. Med sin monopolstllning p detta omrde har en centralbank ett avgrande inflytande ver den mngd pengar som finns i ekonomin. I det vardagliga arbetet r det dock inte mngden betalningsmedel som vi frsker styra. Ngot frenklat kan man sga att penningpolitik handlar om att hja eller snka den rnta vi tar ut fr att lna ut sedlarna och mynten till allmnheten. Det r denna styrrnta som vi i Sverige kallar repornta. Om Riksbanken tillhandahller alltfr stora mngder pengar och reporntan fljaktligen hlls onaturligt lg, resulterar det inte i ngon lngsiktig ekonomisk tillvxt. Fljden blir istllet att priserna stiger. Inflation r detsamma som fall i vrdet p de betalningsmedel som Riksbanken tillhandahller. En frsmring av penningvrdet innebr att varje krona rcker till kp av frre varor. Att s blir fallet hnger samman med att dagens sedlar och mynt inte har det substansvrde som finns angivet p dem. I detta avseende skiljer de sig frn gamla koppar-, silver- och guldmynt. Sedlarna r egentligen sm vita pappersark, som det har tryckts ofta mycket vackra motiv p inklusive ett belopp. Var och en inser att det mot denna bakgrund inte r mngden papperssedlar, eller fr den delen reporntan, som bestmmer utvecklingen av ett lands vlstnd. Men trycks det dremot fr mycket sedlar uppkommer som sagt inflation. Drfr mste det finnas ngon form av handlingsregel fr hur penningpolitiken skall bedrivas s att penningvrdet vrnas och s att allmnhetens frtroende fr detta vrde vidmakthlls ver tiden. Fast vxelkurs mot ett annat lands valuta r exempel p en sdan handlingsregel som kan styra penningpolitikens upplggning. Riksbanken frbinder sig d att lsa in svenska kronor mot utlndska valutor till en i frvg bestmd kurs. Kronans vrde kan ocks vara knuten till en delmetall t.ex. guld, ngot som tidigare frekommit. Nu nr kronans vrde flyter fritt mot andra valutor har Riksbanken ett inflationsml. Reporntan bestms d s att inflationen i Sverige hamnar p 2 procent, med en tolerans om +/- 1 procentenhet. Oavsett om vi har fast eller flytande vxelkurs r det allts ett stt att stadkomma samma sak - bevara kronans kpkraft. Vid fast vxelkurs knyts kronans vrde till ett annat lands valuta. Vi mste d i princip bedriva samma penningpolitik. Om kronans yttre vrde bevaras kommer det i lngden att innebra att dess kpkraft inom landet ocks bevaras, under frutsttning att penningpolitiken i de lnder mot vilka kronan r knuten i sin tur r inriktad p prisstabilitet. Vid flytande vxelkurs inriktas politiken istllet direkt p den inhemska prisstabiliteten. En monetr union r ett system d vxelkurserna r oterkallerligen lsta mot varandra. I stllet fr att alla lnder p egen hand bedriver en likartad penningpolitik, dvs ger ut ungefr lika mngd pengar och stter styrrntan p i stort sett samma niv, gr man dock ett steg lngre och bildar en gemensam centralbank. Denna centralbank fr en gemensam penningpolitik och bestmmer en repornta som r gemensam i hela det geografiska omrde som omfattas av den monetra unionen. Det r enklast att frst om vi ser till Sverige, dr alla landskap, ln och kommuner bildar ett valutaomrde och vi har en gemensam centralbank, Riksbanken. Kronan r giltig verallt och vi behver inte vxla vid landskapsgrnsen om vi ker mellan t.ex. Smland och Skne. Stabilitet gynnar tillvxt Inflation r inte ngot framgngsrecept fr tillvxt, sysselsttning och vlstnd. Tvrtom r de ekonomiska resultaten i lnder som med inflation skt uppn kortsiktiga frdelar nr det gller tillvxt och sysselsttning nedslende. Sdana lnder har i ett lngre perspektiv haft en smre utveckling p snart sagt alla ekonomiska omrden. Det r dessa erfarenheter som r grunden till att Europas lnder kommit att betona att en stabilitetsinriktad ekonomisk politik r en frutsttning fr en hg och stabil ekonomisk tillvxt och sysselsttning. Att inflation r skadligt har lnge varit knt. Perioder med mycket hg inflation har faktiskt funnits ocks i Sverige om n inte under 1900-talet. Vi mste g tillbaka till i brjan av 1800-talet i samband med kriget mot Ryssland. ven 1700-talet prglades av terkommande inflationsperioder. Tyskland dremot rkade i brjan av 1920-talet ut fr att priserna tusenfaldigades p ngra mnader. Fr att kunna handla brd fick man fylla sckar med sedlar. Den erfarenheten har man ocks gjort i en del andra lnder under 1900-talet. Vi behver dock inte ta de mest extrema exemplen frn historien fr att illustrera inflationens skadlighet. Det rcker med att se till vr egen utveckling under 1970och 1980-talen. terverkningarna av dessa decenniers ekonomiska utveckling r belysande. terkommande devalveringar, finanspolitisk verstimulans, ryckig ekonomiska utveckling, felinvesteringar, inflation och spekulation var knnetecknande. Som en direkt fljd fick Sverige i brjan av 1990-talet uppleva den djupaste nedgngen sedan 1930-talet och den kanske svraste bankkrisen under detta sekel. Den svenska historien visar att perioder med lg inflation sammanfallit med tider av gynnsam och stabil ekonomisk utveckling. Sverige hade nst Japan den hgsta ekonomisk tillvxten i vrlden frn industrialismens genombrott i mitten av 1800-talet fram till slutet av 1960-talet. Under denna period uppgick den rliga genomsnittliga inflationen till omkring 2 procent, trots att jag d ocks inrknat ren kring krigsperioderna och andra temporra inflationsperioder. Riksdagen vrnar penningvrdet I gamla tider skedde handeln ofta med delmetaller. Senare kom s.k. vrdemynt, dvs. en viss angiven mngd av delmetall som prglats fr att markera kthet och vrde. Myntverket i Avesta brjade ge ut pltmynt 1644. Det var stora ohanterliga kopparmynt och kunde vga upp emot 20 kilo. Det lr ha rckt till att kpa en ko p den tiden. Johan Palmstruch, grundaren till Sveriges frsta bank, Stockholm Banco, lanserade dock 1661 en id som skulle underltta penninghanteringen genom att ge ut de frsta sedlarna, s.k. kreditivsedlar. Dessa sedlar var rntefria skuldfrbindelser p bestmda belopp som skulle motsvara insatta pengar i banken. Sedlarna blev inledningsvis en succ, eftersom de var enklare att hantera n vrdemynten. Det hela slutade nd med en bankkrasch, sedan Palmstruch frestats att ge ut fr mnga sedlar i frhllande till de underliggande vrden som fanns deponerade i banken. Detta kom att bli en viktig erfarenhet. Strvan att ska motverka frestelsen att lta alltfr mycket pengar cirkulera i ekonomin gr som en rd trd genom den svenska historien. Riksdagen och dess ledamter har tagit som sin uppgift att vrna penningvrdet. Det kom till uttryck fr frsta gngen nr Riksbanken bildades 1668, vilket fr vrigt gr den till vrldens ldsta centralbank. Den blev, efter en hel del meningsskiljaktigheter, d riksdagens organ fr att frhindra Kungens regering att urholka penningvrdet. Kungar frde som bekant p den tiden en hel del kostnadskrvande krig. Redan 1677 sattes dock banken p ett hrt prov. I en skrivelse daterad den 4 januari 1677 begrde Kungl. Maj:t ett ln p 200.000 daler silvermynt fr att kunna fortstta med det krig som d frdes. Vid behandlingen av detta rende framhller historikerna klart betydelsen av att banken undandragits regeringens maktomrde och stllts under stndernas vrd. Det framhlls i litteraturen vidare att om Riksbanken hade varit ett regeringens verk r det inget tvivel om att den kommit att ge ut sedlar fr krigets finansiering. Nr Gustav III 1772 suspenderade riksdagen svarade dess ledamter genom att tillstta egna revisorer med uppgift att granska och utva tillsyn ver Riksbanken. Genom det dvarande bankoutskottet och riksdagens revisorers agerande strktes bankens trovrdighet eftersom Kungen inte tillts anvnda sig av den. 1700-talet prglades nd av terkommande perioder med inflation, fr det mesta i samband med krig eftersom sedelpressarna anvndes. Den sista av dessa perioder infll under kriget med Ryssland 1808-1809. Som vanligt upprepades samma mnster under inflationsperioder, vilket r giltigt n i vra dagar. En stark monetr expansion fljs av stigande priser, spekulation, stigande markvrden, fallande valutakurs och drefter ett bakslag i form av en period av svag och rentav negativ ekonomisk tillvxt. Erfarenheterna vid 1990-talets inledning efter 1980-talets inflationsbubbla r sledes lngt ifrn ny. Efter den lnga perioden under 1700-talet - med mer eller mindre oskert penningvrde - blev riksdagen och dess ledamter alltmer beslutna att terg till en bestmd myntfot, trots Kungens motvillighet. r 1830 beslt riksdagen om infrandet av en silvermyntfot. Frgan guldmyntfot i Sverige blev aktuell efter bildandet av den s.k. latinska myntunionen i december 1865. Det var Frankrike, Italien, Belgien och Schweiz som bildade ett frbund fr att ha en gemensam myntenhet. Senare anslt sig ocks Grekland. I en motion i frsta kammaren vid 1868 rs riksdag vckte bankdirektren Andr Oscar Wallenberg frslag om infrande av en ny myntfot grundad p franc som enhet och p guld som vrdelikare. Riksdagen avslog dock motionen men begrde en utredning av regeringen. En kommitt avlmnade sitt betnkande i augusti 1870 och ansg att Sverige borde g vidare och ansluta sig till guld-francsystemet. Med Frankrikes nederlag i det tysk-franska kriget 1870-1871 frlorade dock frslaget om anslutning till franc-systemet sin aktualitet. Dremot tillsattes en interskandinavisk kommission p danskt initiativ p sommaren 1872. Senare samma r kom denna med ett frslag om att de tre nordiska lnderna borde bilda en monetr union som var grundad p guld. Efter sedvanlig remissbehandling terkom regeringen med en proposition 1873 dr det framkom att """guld skall ensamt vara vrdemtare i riket och sledes utgra grunden fr dess myntvsen""". Rkneenheten skulle kallas fr krona och delas i 100 ren. Dessutom skulle Sverige ing i en myntkonvention med Danmark och Norge. I sitt betnkande med anledning av denna proposition freslog bankoutskottet att sedlarna skulle ha en text med fljande lydelse: Sveriges Riksbank inlser, vid anfordran, denna sedel med guldmynt. Under de fljande 100 ren hade Sverige med vissa avbrott - frmst orsakade av vrldskrig och 1930-talsdepressionen - valutans vrde knutet till guldet. Det gller ven under det s.k. Bretton Woods-systemet fram till dess sammanbrott i brjan av 1970-talet. Formellt var kronan d knuten till den amerikanska dollarn, men dollarn var i sin tur knuten till guldet. Dagens penningpolitiska regim bygger inte lngre p en vrdemyntfot, som t.ex. guld. Inte heller r kronan knuten till ngon annan valuta. Riksbanken kan drfr i princip bestmma hur mycket pengar som skall produceras eller, eller mer konkret, vilken styrrnta som skall glla. Detta ger handlingsfrihet, men det r fel att tro att den r obegrnsad. Precis som i gamla tider gller att om Riksbanken ger ut fr mycket pengar, dvs. stter rntan lgre n vad som r frenligt med ekonomisk balans, hotar inflation. Penningpolitiken mste fljaktligen hela tiden avvgas s att inflationen och inflationsfrvntningarna hlls under kontroll. Allmn tilltro till prisstabilitetsmlet r en frutsttning fr en gynnsam ekonomisk utveckling. I annat fall stiger lner, priser och marknadsrntor och valutakursen kommer under press. D uppstr snart problem men lg tillvxt och hg arbetslshet. En ny global kapitalmarknad Mitten av 1800-talet har av historikerna kallats fr tiden fr den industriella revolutionen. Frgan r om inte framtidens historiker kommer att benmna slutet av 1980-talet och brjan av 1990-talet som tiden fr den finansiella revolutionen i vrlden. Det finansiella systemet r dock inte ngon ny innovation, inte heller har det utvecklats fr sin egen skull. Dess struktur har utvecklats ver rhundradenas lopp som ett medel fr att underltta fr produktion av och handel med varor och tjnster. Utvecklingen av det finansiella systemet mste ses som en del av en strre process som pgtt sedan industrialismens genombrott, men utvecklingen har accelererat ptagligt frn mitten av 1980-talet. Det r teknologiska krafter som legat bakom utvecklingen och specialiseringen av den reala ekonomin under decenniernas lopp. ven om vrldshandelns utveckling frutsatte politiska beslut i form av slopade handelsbarrirer s mjliggjordes globaliseringen av de teknologiska innovationer, som var frutsttningen fr effektivare kommunikationer. I takt med att transporter blev billigare, allt ifrn ngbten till jetflyget, kade ocks handeln med varor och tjnster snabbt. Det teknologiska utvecklingen lade ocks grunden fr utvecklingen av nya och effektivare produktionsprocesser. Vi ser idag samma typ av mnster p det finansiella omrdet. Teknologiska framsteg p tele-, kommunikations- och dataomrdet har utgjort grunden ven fr finansiella globaliseringen. Omsttningen i handeln p de finansiella marknaderna har p bara ett decennium, sedan mitten av 1980-talet, kat mycket snabbt. Ocks nr det gller utvecklingen av nya finansiella instrument gr det nu fort. Globaliseringen och expansionen frutsatte politiska beslut i form av slopade regleringar p det finansiella omrdet, med drivs av den teknologiska utvecklingen. Den finansiella internationaliseringsprocessen under det senaste decenniet r i grunden naturlig. Nya finansiella mjligheter och lsningar r ndvndiga fr att underltta den internationella handeln med varor och tjnster. Expansionen r en logisk konsekvens av strvan att utveckla utbudet fr produkter fr betalningar, investeringar och sparande. Hr spelar ocks de nya derivatinstrumenten en viktig roll eftersom de gr det mjligt att separera och prisstta risker. P det sttet kan de som har bst frmga att bra risker ocks gra det. Derivat produkterna spelar redan, men kommer i framtiden att spela en nnu strre roll, inte bara fr finansiella placeringar utan ocks fr fretagande och sysselsttning. Det r lttare att se om vi tnker p att en vanlig brand- eller olycksfallfrskring egentligen r en derivatprodukt. Genom att avskilja risker, dvs i mitt exempel att flytta risken fr brand eller olyckor till ett frskringsbolag, kan en fretagare gna all sin kraft t sktseln av sitt fretag och anvnda sitt kapital fr investeringar utan att behva bygga upp en buffert i hndelse av att en katastrof intrffar. Med den expanderande derivatmarknaden kan man tnka sig att avskilja riskerna p en mngd olika omrden som r svra att verblicka fr en enskild fretagare. Dessa risker samlas sedan hos andra aktrer som har kompetens och finansiella resurser att mta dem. Den finansiella utvecklingen bidrar p s stt till att underltta en fortsatt utveckling i den reala ekonomin mot kad specialisering och effektivisering. Den hr utvecklingen har dock skapat en ny och svrare milj fr tillsynsmyndigheter och fr ekonomisk-politiska beslutsfattare. Erfarenheten visar att den ekonomiska politiken spelar en betydelsefull roll fr prisutvecklingen p de finansiella marknaderna, liksom den fr vrigt gr det p de reala marknaderna. Den typ av abrupta korrigeringar och - som det ibland kan upplevas - verdrivna svngningar av rnte-, aktie- och valutakurser som vi upplevt kan ofta spras tillbaka till den ekonomiska politiken. I tider av turbulens kan visserligen prisrrelserna p finansiella marknader bli verdrivna och tillflligt g lngre n vad som kan motiveras med hnsyn till fundamentala ekonomiska faktorer. Det viktiga r dock att frga sig vad den bakomliggande orsaken r till att finansiell turbulens ver huvudtaget uppstr. Vi har klart sett under de senaste ren att tveksamheter om den stabilitetsinriktade politiken, liksom obalanser i statens budget eller i bytesbalansen ge upphov till ofta icke obetydliga spnningar och finansiell oro. Den nya globala finansiella miljn har p s stt kat kravet p disciplin i den ekonomiska politiken. Utrymmet fr felsteg har helt enkelt minskat avsevrt. Det handlar inte bara om att fr en centralbank, eller fr den delen fr det politiska systemet, att bevara pengarnas vrde som i gamla tider. Det gller nu ocks mer n tidigare att gra trovrdigt att detta kommer att prgla den ekonomiska politiken under lng tid framver. Det r just oskerheten kring denna tilltro som ofta kan frklara de omfattande rrelserna i valutakurser och lnga rntor under senare r. Inte minst utvecklingen i vrt eget land bekrftar detta. Det r ven i ljuset av den hr utvecklingen som man br se planerna p en Europeisk Monetr Union. Den erbjuder ett ramverk fr penningpolitiken som lngsiktigt kar trovrdigheten fr den ekonomisk-politiska disciplinen och den stabilitetsinriktade politiken. Det gr naturligtvis fr ett land ocks i den nya finansiella globala miljn att skapa trovrdighet kring sin valuta och det framtida penningvrdet. Det visar inte minst erfarenheterna i Schweiz. Min pong r dock att svrigheterna med en sdant handlingsalternativ inte fr underskattas. En sdan vg erbjuder inte ett enklare alternativ, tvrtom r den med all sannolikhet mer arbetsam. Drfr r det viktigt att i diskussionen om EMU beakta ocks de kostnader som r frknippade med att st utanfr. I det sammanhanget br kostnaderna uppskattas fr den lngre anpassningsperiod och de strre uppoffringar som krvs fr att stadkomma samma trovrdighet fr det framtida penningvrdet som en Europeisk Monetr Union kan erbjuda. Avslutning Diskussionen om fr- och nackdelar med den Europeiska Monetra Unionen pgr nu som bst i vrt land. Det r en viktig diskussion eftersom det handlar om ett stllningstagande som frutstter ett noga vervgande. Fullmktige i Riksbanken har fr sin del kommit till slutsatsen att  det finns vervgande frdelar med en svensk anslutning till en Europeisk Monetr Union. Jag har i mitt anfrande pekat p tv frhllanden som talar fr en svensk anslutning till en Europeisk Monetr Union. Fr det frsta visar vr penningpolitiska historia p en lng tradition nr det gller freningen av prisstabilitet och gynnsam ekonomisk utveckling. Vikten av att med olika ramverk vrna penningvrdet r ngot som gr som en rd trd genom den svenska historien. Riksdagens roll och stllningstagande har p detta omrde varit framtrdande. Fr det andra har en global finansmarknad vuxit fram under det senaste decenniet, som stller strngare krav p ekonomisk politisk disciplin. Det r drfr inte kostnadsfritt fr ett land att i denna nya finansiella milj bibehlla handlingsfriheten att kunna devalvera sin valuta. Det r en kostnad som ocks mste vgas in i den pgende diskussionen om EMU.
