Title: The Riksbank's forecasts and current monetary policy
text: Rosenberg: The Riksbank's forecasts and current monetary policy Date 2006-06-08 Deputy Governor Irma Rosenberg spoke thursday at a meeting organized by Danske Bank. One topic was the low inflation in recent years and the Riksbank's forecasts, another was the current monetary policy. "Over the past two years, inflation has been significantly lower than the Riksbank's inflation target of 2 per cent. This has led to a discussion about the quality of our forecasts. We have also been criticised for the fact that monetary policy has been too tight. To try to somewhat nuance this debate, I will start by looking back at our forecasts for 2004 and 2005 and how well they compare with other people's forecasts and with outcomes. I would also like to give my view on how it could have affected monetary policy in recent years if we had more accurately predicted inflation developments. In conclusion, I will look ahead and say a few words about the current monetary policy situation," Rosenberg began. "Let me start by noting that inflation averaged under the inflation targeting regime until a few years ago was very close to the target. 19952004, inflation as measured by the underlying measure of inflation UND1X averaged 1.9% (Table 1). Given that the Riksbank lowered the repo rate by almost 7 percentage points during these years, I think it is reasonable to look at the achievement of its target based on the UND1X measure of inflation, where the direct effects of these interest rate cuts, i.e. that interest costs for mortgages fell, are not included," Rosenberg said. "However, in 2004 and 2005, inflation was significantly below target. Inflation fell sharply at the beginning of 2004. One explanation was that energy prices, which had been pushed up sharply at the beginning of 2003, fell back slightly again. We had foreseen this and, therefore, already in the first Inflation Report in 2003, we envisaged inflation to fall below the target in 2004. As fluctuations in energy prices were considered temporary, we considered neither the pick-up in inflation at the beginning of 2003 nor the projected decline in 2004 to be grounds for taking monetary policy measures. We also expressed this clearly in the context of our monetary policy decisions. The Riksbank's forecasts for UND1X inflation in 2004 were thus well in line with the final outcome from the beginning of 2003 (Chart 1)," Rosenberg continued. "Thus, the forecast errors for inflation in 2004 were relatively small, but domestic cost pressures were significantly lower than expected. Important reasons for this were that productivity developed stronger than expected, while imported inflation was significantly lower than expected. These are factors that have been shown to help hold back inflation more sustainably than we expected. The forecasts we made especially in 2003 but also in 2004 for UND1Xinflation in 2005 therefore represented a clear overestimation. The assessment was that growth would increase and that inflationary pressures would simultaneously rise in accordance with traditional economic patterns. However, while growth strengthened significantly more than we expected, inflation remained low and our view of international and domestic cost pressures was gradually reassessed. It wasn't until early 2005 that we did a relatively sharp downward revision of the inflation forecast, but then, on the other hand, we took in a lot, as shown in Chart 1," Rosenberg said. "But why did inflation get so low in 2005? As I have mentioned, inflation has been held down by high productivity growth and weak import price developments. This is apparently linked to changes of a structural nature. One is undoubtedly increased global competition. Probably part of the explanation also lies in the rather extensive investments that have taken place in new technology in recent years. The low level of inflation is thus largely a consequence of a number of changes on the supply side of the economy. A natural follow-up question is whether the Riksbank should have been able to predict this development and thus the low inflation. Of course, it is not easy to answer these types of questions afterwards, but one possibility is to compare our forecasts with those of other forecasters to see how well we stand," Rosenberg said. "In an appendix to the Riksbank's first annual inflation report, a basis is published for a review of the monetary policy that has been conducted over the past 23 years. There, for example, our forecasts are compared both with those of other forecasters and with outcomes. The data in our latest Inflation Report show that most forecasters in 2004 greatly overestimated CPI inflation in 2005 and that our forecast compares well with others (Chart 2). With regard to GDP growth, all forecasters underestimated the strength of developments in 2004 and other analysts did not differ significantly from the Riksbank (Chart 3). This is likely an expression of the fact that changes of a structural nature are difficult to capture at an early stage in forecasting work," Rosenberg said. "A reasonable interpretation is that the Riksbank has not made worse forecasts than other forecasters and in some respects even slightly better. Similar conclusions are also drawn by the Parliamentary Finance Committee in its evaluation of monetary policy, which has recently been published. From the end of 2002, when the last period of interest rate cuts began and until the summer of 2005, the repo rate was reduced by a total of 2.75 percentage points to 1.5%. This has meant a strong stimulus to the economy. With the benefit of hindsight, it can certainly be said that the interest rate cuts could have been implemented even more quickly. But one might question whether it would have been appropriate to cut interest rates more, given that demand was already developing strongly in 2004. The rapid increase in household indebtedness and house prices testified to the fact that monetary policy was very expansionary. Driving up demand further when the economy was already growing strongly could have posed risks to the stability of the real economy down the line," Rosenberg said. "Let me now turn to the current inflation outlook and monetary policy. The development that we saw in front of us in the Inflation Report in February was that growth in the rest of the world would remain good. The new information received since then suggests that the world economy has even developed somewhat stronger than expected. New national accounts data show high growth in the U.S. in the first quarter of this year. The indicators that have emerged during the spring give somewhat mixed signals, but mainly indicate a continued good development in the future. In the euro area, developments in the fourth quarter were roughly in line with expectations, but the indicators that have emerged since then point to a somewhat more favourable development this year than we saw ahead of us in February. In Asia, the picture of stronger development is even clearer. There has been a clear upturn in Japan, while growth in China and the rest of Asia has remained high," Rosenberg said. "In February, we also saw continued strong growth in the Swedish economy ahead of us. According to the preliminary national accounts just published, GDP growth in the first quarter was a little higher than expected. However, household consumption was weaker than we expected, which is partly offset by slightly stronger investments. Other information over the past month also indicates a continued good development. According to the Business Cycle Barometer for May, companies in both manufacturing and construction report increased order intake and higher production volumes. In addition, construction companies are beginning to have major problems finding suitable workers. The retail sector is showing strong sales and in the private service sector, all industries are reporting increased demand. In addition, households are optimistic about both their own and the country's economy," Rosenberg said. "It has been turbulent in the financial markets recently with a relatively large fall in the price of equities. Changes in asset prices may reflect or lead to increased uncertainty about future developments, which may dampen firms' willingness to invest and lead households to increase their prudential savings. However, stock prices can go up significantly for a longer period of time and then get some rebound without it having to be a sign of a more lasting decline. At the moment, it is not possible to draw any more far-reaching conclusions from recent developments in the stock market globally," Rosenberg noted. "With regard to the situation in the labour market, there was much to suggest in February that employment would continue to increase in the future. New information that has come since then about e.g. newly registered vacancies and notice points in the same direction. According to the National Institute of Economic Research's barometer data, the increase in the number of employed persons will continue also in the second quarter. All in all, this suggests that the Swedish economy has rather developed somewhat stronger than our assessment in the latest inflation report in February," Rosenberg pointed out. "With regard to the inflation outlook, the inflation report estimates that inflation would rise to approach 2 per cent over a couple of years' time, provided that the repo rate is gradually raised over the forecast period. Recently, inflation has become higher than we expected in the Inflation Report, mainly as a result of unexpected price increases for a limited number of goods such as gasoline, domestic oil and electricity. There is reason to expect high oil and petrol prices for some time to come, which is reflected, among other things, in the fact that futures prices have risen. But unless energy prices continue to rise, the effect on inflation will, by all accounts, be temporary," Rosenberg said. "Gdp growth thus looks to be somewhat stronger than we expected in February, but productivity growth remains good and cost pressures moderate. The fundamental assessment of inflation developments over the next few years is fairly accurate in view of the new information received since the Inflation Report. Over a couple of years, inflation is estimated to be close to two per cent. At the same time, monetary policy remains very expansionary, which is expressed, among other things, in continued rapid credit growth and the pace of housing price increases  although we can now, for the first time in a long time, possibly see some signs that the growth rate of loans is slowing down. All in all, this suggests, I think, that it may now be time to take another step towards a less expansionary monetary policy in order to ensure inflation developments close to the target and balanced real economic developments. This also aligns well with current market expectations," Rosenberg concluded.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Rosenberg: Riksbankens prognoser och den aktuella penningpolitiken Datum 2006-06-08 Vice riksbankschef Irma Rosenberg talade under torsdagen p ett mte anordnat av Danske Bank. Ett mne var den lga inflationen de senaste ren och Riksbankens prognoser, ett annat var den aktuella penningpolitiken. "De tv senaste ren har inflationen varit betydligt lgre n Riksbankens inflationsml p 2 procent. Detta har lett till en diskussion om kvalitn p vra prognoser. Vi har ocks kritiserats fr att penningpolitiken skulle ha varit fr stram. Fr att ngot frska nyansera den hr debatten tnker jag brja med att blicka tillbaka p vra prognoser fr 2004 och 2005 och hur vl de str sig jmfrt med andras prognoser och med utfall. Jag vill ocks ge min syn p hur det skulle ha kunnat pverka penningpolitiken de senaste ren om vi mer korrekt hade frutsett inflationsutvecklingen. Avslutningsvis kommer jag att blicka framt och sga ngra ord om det aktuella penningpolitiska lget", inledde Rosenberg. "Lt mig brja med att konstatera att inflationen i genomsnitt under inflationsmlsregimen fram till fr ngot r sedan legat mycket nra mlet. 19952004 var inflationen mtt med det underliggande inflationsmttet UND1X i genomsnitt 1,9 procent (tabell 1). Med hnsyn till att Riksbanken snkte reporntan med nra 7 procentenheter under dessa r tycker jag att det r rimligt att se p mluppfyllelsen utifrn inflationsmttet UND1X dr de direkta effekterna av dessa rntesnkningar, det vill sga att rntekostnaderna fr boln sjnk, inte rknas in", sade Rosenberg. "Under 2004 och 2005 blev inflationen emellertid vsentligt lgre n mlet. Inflationen fll kraftigt i brjan av 2004. En frklaring var att energipriserna, som hade pressats upp kraftigt i brjan av 2003, fll tillbaka ngot igen. Detta hade vi frutsett och redan i den frsta inflationsrapporten 2003 rknade vi drfr med att inflationen skulle underskrida mlet 2004. Eftersom svngningarna i energipriserna bedmdes som tillflliga ansg vi varken att uppgngen i inflationen i brjan av 2003 eller den frutsedda nedgngen 2004 utgjorde skl fr att vidta penningpolitiska tgrder. Detta uttryckte vi ocks klart i samband med vra penningpolitiska beslut. Riksbankens prognoser fr UND1X-inflationen 2004 lg allts redan frn brjan av 2003 vl i linje med det slutliga utfallet (diagram 1)", fortsatte Rosenberg. "Prognosfelen fr inflationen 2004 var allts relativt sm men det inhemska kostnadstrycket blev betydligt lgre n vntat. Viktiga skl till detta var att produktiviteten utvecklades starkare n vi rknat med, samtidigt som den importerade inflationen blev betydligt lgre n frutsett. Detta r faktorer som visat sig bidra till att hlla tillbaka inflationen mer varaktigt n vi rknade med. Prognoserna som vi gjorde srskilt under 2003 men ven 2004 fr UND1Xinflationen 2005 innebar drfr en tydlig verskattning. Bedmningen var att tillvxten skulle ka och att inflationstrycket samtidigt skulle stiga enligt traditionella konjunkturmnster. Men samtidigt som tillvxten frstrktes betydligt mer n vi rknat med frblev inflationen lg och vr syn p det internationella och inhemska kostnadstrycket omvrderades gradvis. Det var frst i brjan av 2005 som vi gjorde en frhllandevis kraftig nedrevidering av inflationsprognosen, men d tog vi  andra sidan i vl mycket, vilket ocks framgr av diagram 1", sade Rosenberg. "Men varfr blev inflationen s lg 2005? Som jag varit inne p har inflationen hllits nere av en hg produktivitetstillvxt och svag importprisutveckling. Detta hnger av allt att dma samman med frndringar av strukturell karaktr. En r utan tvekan kad global konkurrens. Sannolikt ligger ocks en del av frklaringen i de ganska omfattande investeringar som skett i ny teknik p senare r. Den lga inflationen r drmed i mngt och mycket en fljd av ett antal frndringar p ekonomins utbudssida. En naturlig fljdfrga r om Riksbanken borde ha kunnat frutse den hr utvecklingen och drmed den lga inflationen. Det r frsts inte ltt att besvara den hr typen av frgor i efterhand, men en mjlighet r att jmfra vra prognoser med andra prognosmakares fr att se hur vl vi str oss", menade Rosenberg. "I ett appendix till Riksbankens frsta inflationsrapport varje r publiceras underlag fr en granskning av den penningpolitik som frts de senaste 23 ren. Dr jmfrs t.ex. vra prognoser bde med andra prognosmakares och med utfall. Av underlaget i vr senaste inflationsrapport framgr att de flesta prognosmakare under 2004 verskattade KPI-inflationen 2005 kraftigt och att vr prognos str sig vl jmfrt med andras (diagram 2). Nr det gller BNP-tillvxten underskattade samtliga prognosmakare styrkan i utvecklingen under 2004 och andra bedmare skiljde sig drvid inte frn Riksbanken p ngot avgrande stt (diagram 3). Detta r sannolikt ett uttryck fr att frndringar av strukturell karaktr r svra att fnga p ett tidigt stadium i prognosarbete", sade Rosenberg. "En rimlig tolkning r att Riksbanken inte har gjort smre prognoser n andra prognosmakare och i vissa avseenden till och med ngot bttre. Likartade slutsatser drar ocks riksdagens finansutskott i sin utvrdering av penningpolitiken, som nyligen publicerats. Frn slutet av 2002, nr den senaste rntesnkningsperioden inleddes och fram till sommaren 2005, snktes reporntan med sammanlagt 2,75 procentenheter ned till 1,5 procent. Det har inneburit en kraftig stimulans av ekonomin. Med facit i hand kan man visserligen sga att rntesnkningarna hade kunnat genomfras nnu ngot snabbare. Men man kan ifrgastta om det hade varit lmpligt att snka rntan mer med tanke p att efterfrgan redan 2004 utvecklades starkt. Den snabba kningen i hushllens skuldsttning och huspriserna vittnade om att penningpolitiken var mycket expansiv. Att driva upp efterfrgan ytterligare nr ekonomin redan vxte starkt skulle ha kunnat innebra risker fr stabiliteten i den reala ekonomin lngre fram", sade Rosenberg. "Lt mig nu verg till de aktuella inflationsutsikterna och penningpolitiken. Den utveckling som vi sg framfr oss i inflationsrapporten i februari var att tillvxten i omvrlden skulle bli fortsatt god. Den nya information som inkommit sedan dess tyder p att vrldsekonomin t.o.m. har utvecklats ngot starkare n vntat. Nya nationalrkenskapsdata visar p hg tillvxt i USA det frsta kvartalet i r. De indikatorer som kommit under vren ger lite blandade signaler men tyder i huvudsak p en fortsatt god utveckling framver. I euroomrdet var utvecklingen fjrde kvartalet ungefr i linje med frvntningarna, men de indikatorer som kommit sedan dess pekar mot en ngot gynnsammare utveckling i r n vad vi sg framfr oss i februari. I Asien r bilden av en starkare utveckling nnu tydligare. Det har skett en tydlig uppgng i Japan, samtidigt som tillvxten i Kina och vriga Asien har varit fortsatt hg", framhll Rosenberg. "Vi sg i februari ven framfr oss en fortsatt stark tillvxt i den svenska ekonomin. Enligt de preliminra nationalrkenskaper som just publicerats blev BNP-tillvxten frsta kvartalet lite hgre n vntat. Hushllens konsumtion blev dock svagare n vi rknade med, vilket delvis balanseras av ngot starkare investeringar. Annan information den senaste mnaden tyder ocks p en fortsatt god utveckling. Enligt Konjunkturbarometern fr maj rapporterar fretagen inom svl tillverkningsindustri som byggverksamhet kad orderingng och strre produktionsvolym. Byggfretagen brjar dessutom f stora problem att hitta lmplig arbetskraft. Detaljhandeln visar stark frsljning och i den privata tjnstesektorn rapporterar samtliga branscher kad efterfrgan. Drtill r hushllen optimistiska bde nr det gller den egna och landets ekonomi", sade Rosenberg. "Det har varit turbulent p de finansiella marknaderna den senaste tiden med ett relativt stort prisfall p aktier. Frndringar i tillgngspriser kan avspegla eller leda till en kad oskerhet om den framtida utvecklingen vilket kan dmpa fretagens investeringsvilja och medfra att hushllen kar sitt frsiktighetssparande. Aktiepriser kan dock g upp markant under en lngre tid fr att sedan f en viss rekyl utan att det behver vara ett tecken p en mer varaktig nedgng. Det gr just nu inte att dra ngra mer lngtgende slutsatser av den senaste tidens utveckling p aktiemarknaden globalt", konstaterade Rosenberg. "Nr det gller situationen p arbetsmarknaden fanns det i februari mycket som talade fr att sysselsttningen skulle fortstta ka framver. Ny information som kommit sedan dess om t.ex. nyanmlda lediga platser och varsel pekar i samma riktning. Enligt Konjunkturinstitutets barometerdata kommer uppgngen i antal sysselsatta att fortstta ven under andra kvartalet. Sammantaget tyder detta p att svensk ekonomi snarast utvecklats ngot starkare n vr bedmning i den senaste inflationsrapporten i februari", ppekade Rosenberg. "Nr det gller inflationsutsikterna var bedmningen i inflationsrapporten att inflationen skulle stiga fr att p ett par rs sikt nrma sig 2 procent under frutsttning att reporntan successivt hjs under prognosperioden. Den senaste tiden har inflationen blivit hgre n vad vi rknade med i inflationsrapporten frmst till fljd av ovntade prisuppgngar p ett begrnsat antal varor ssom bensin, villaolja och el. Det finns anledning att rkna med hga olje- och bensinpriser ven en tid framver, vilket bl.a. avspeglas i att terminspriserna har stigit. Men frutsatt att inte energipriserna fortstter att stiga blir effekten p inflationen av allt att dma tillfllig", sade Rosenberg. "BNP-tillvxten ser allts ut att bli ngot starkare n vi rknade med i februari men produktivitetsutvecklingen r fortfarande god och kostnadstrycket mttligt. Den grundlggande bedmningen av inflationsutvecklingen de nrmaste ren str sig rtt vl med hnsyn till den nya information som inkommit sedan inflationsrapporten. P ett par rs sikt bedms inflationen vara nra tv procent. Samtidigt r penningpolitiken alltjmt mycket expansiv vilket bland annat kommer till uttryck i en fortsatt snabb kredittillvxt och priskningstakt p bostder  ven om vi nu fr frsta gngen p lng tid mjligen kan se vissa tecken p att kningstakten i utlningen avtar. Sammantaget talar detta, tycker jag, fr att det nu kan vara dags att ta ytterligare ett steg mot en mindre expansiv penningpolitik fr att skerstlla en inflationsutveckling nra mlet och en balanserad realekonomisk utveckling. Detta stmmer ocks vl verens med rdande marknadsfrvntningar", avslutade Rosenberg. Title: Finance Committee: Hearing on financial stability
text: Ingves in the Finance Committee: Hearing on financial stability Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves today participated in the Riksdag's Finance Committee's open hearing on financial stability. Date: 2020-01-28 09:00 Speaker: Governor Stefan Ingves Place: Parliamentary Finance Committee "Expectations of low interest rates for a long time can lead to challenges to financial stability." This is what Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves said when he began his report on the current stability situation in the Finance Committee. Furthermore, Ingves highlighted that household indebtedness constitutes a major vulnerability in the Swedish economy and advocated measures in housing and tax policy to reduce risks. Ingves also pointed to the vulnerabilities of a large, concentrated and interconnected banking system such as the Swedish one, where banks also have limited capital levels. In addition, banks are exposed to falls in the price of real estate through their lending to both households and companies. The Finance Committee also discussed how Fintech and cyber threats can affect financial stability. Ingves stressed that the cyber threat is inherently global and that the consequences of cyberattacks can easily spread across national borders. This, combined with the fact that financial firms are becoming more and more cross-border, increases the importance of international cooperation in this area. In addition, a cyberattack can potentially pose a systemic risk and therefore close cooperation between the private and public sectors is necessary to address the growing cyber threat. Furthermore, Ingves advocated that financial firms continue to strengthen their resilience to cyberattacks. "An important starting point is that cyberattacks will succeed and that organizations must therefore prepare to deal with intrusions," the governor said. Ingves said that the Riksbank recently decided to adopt the TIBER-EU (Threat Intelligence-based Ethical Red Teaming) framework, which makes it possible to test the resilience of actors in the financial system in an orderly manner. "Through this initiative, the Riksbank will coordinate cybersecurity tests of key players in the Swedish financial system in the coming years," Ingves concluded. Minister of Finance and Housing Per Bolund, Director General of the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority, Erik Thede9en, and Director General of the Swedish National Debt Office Hans Lindblad also participated in the committee's hearing. Title: Adapting to new conditions - monetary policy freedom under responsibility
text: Skingsley: Adapting to new conditions - monetary policy freedom with responsibility "The pandemic outbreak demonstrates the importance of agency. The fact that we have had the freedom to choose tools ourselves and quickly deploy them has been absolutely crucial during the past year. Without that freedom, we wouldn't have been able to do as much good for the economy." This is what First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley said when she spoke today at SEB's digital webinar about the Riksbank's experiences during the pandemic. Date: 2021-05-20 13:30 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: SEB (digital) With independence comes the demand for evaluation - freedom with responsibility "The conditions for monetary policy change over time and the tools therefore need to be updated with the changes in order for us to maintain the ability to manage future crises," she continued. But, she noted, our strong independence means freedom with responsibility and the Riksbank has over the years worked to increase transparency around monetary policy. It's no coincidence that the international trend of increased independence among central banks has gone hand in hand with increased transparency and clarity, Skingsley said. In recent years, we have had new challenges to deal with. "Our goals and mandates remain unchanged, but our toolbox has needed to change," Skingsley said. In previous periods, we could immediately see the effect of a 0.25 percentage point lower repo rate on the inflation forecast. But when the toolbox is larger, it becomes much more difficult to know how big the effect on goal fulfillment will actually be. Our challenge today is to become better at understanding, clarifying and explaining the effects of the new monetary policy tools so that we facilitate the democratic scrutiny of our work. The importance of agency was reinforced during the pandemic The financial markets are constantly evolving, as are the ways in which companies finance themselves. This means that the environment in which monetary policy operates is also changing. During the pandemic, we have had to put in place many measures to keep interest rates low and maintain credit supply so that the real economy is kept going. We have purchased government bonds, municipal bonds, covered bonds and corporate securities in the form of bonds and certificates. "I believe the measures have worked as intended. We have been able to avoid a financial crisis," Skingsley noted. In order to continue to deliver a monetary policy with price stability as its objective, we need to accept that conditions are changing and that the tools need to be updated with the changes. Independence is a great trust to manage. "With continued freedom with responsibility, the Riksbank can contribute to good economic development going forward," Skingsley concluded. Title: Banks' cash service needed
text: Skingsley: Banks' cash service needed Date: 2015-11-04 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Place: Bank meeting 2015, Swedish Bankers' Association, Grand Hotel, Stockholm "In order to meet the rapid technological development in the payment market, it is important to have collaboration between market participants but also that the market takes responsibility and does not abandon cash and paper giro payments before there are realistic alternatives for all people everywhere" Says Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley when she today participates in a panel debate, organized by the Bankers' Association, about how the rapid technological development, changes in customer behaviour and new players affect the development of the financial market. Sweden has one of the world's most efficient payment markets  among the highest number of card payments per capita in the world. But still a huge amount of transactions with cash takes place. Almost 90 percent of the Swedish people state that they have used cash in the past month. Many people even save in cash. However, the payments market is changing rapidly, partly due to digitalisation, which in itself is positive. New services appear and old ones disappear, such as the checks. "It's possible that the cash and giro forms are heading in the same direction," skingsley said. At the same time, there are specific groups in Swedish society, geographical areas and situations where cash (and giro forms) are still the only option. "It is therefore important that banks take responsibility for their customers' needs and continue to provide cash services as long as their customers want to continue to use cash. But those who demand cash services should also be prepared to pay for them," Skingsley concludes.

Men de som efterfrgar kontanttjnster br ocks vara beredda att betala fr dem", avslutar Skingsley. Title: Skingsley visits London
text: Skingsley visits London Date: 2015-09-04 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Deutsche Bank, London On Friday, Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley will be in London where she will, among other things, give a presentation at Deutsche Bank. Skingsley justifies the latest interest rate decision and shows that the Riksbank's very expansionary monetary policy, with a negative repo rate and purchases of government bonds, contributes to a strengthening of the economy and that there is a clear upward trend in inflation. She points out that monetary policy needs to remain very expansionary so that inflation continues to rise towards the target and that the risks associated with too low inflation decrease. At the same time, Skingsley points out that there are risks to inflation developments. "It is important that the trend of rising inflation continues. We therefore remain highly prepared to make monetary policy even more expansionary if necessary," says Skingsley. In connection with the monetary policy reports, the members of the Executive Board carry out visits to various locations in Sweden and abroad to present the conclusions of the monetary policy decisions. The members then give lectures and depending on the occasion they meet financial market participants, the business community, municipal representatives, media and / or higher education institutions on the plastic in question. Title: The importance of the inflation target
text: Skingsley: The importance of the inflation target Date: 2015-04-14 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Industriarbetsgivarna, Skogsnaringsveckan. Munchenbryggeriet, Stockholm Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley will participate on Tuesday at the Industrial Employers' seminar on wage formation at the Forest Industry Week held at Munchenbryggeriet in Stockholm. Skingsley talks there about the importance of inflation rising towards the target. "The inflation target is a cornerstone of Swedish economic policy that actors in the economy should be able to rely on. It creates stable rules of the game and contributes to good and long-term sustainable growth." In her presentation, she points out how the inflation target has contributed to more stable wage growth and higher real wages than during the more volatile environment of the 70s and 80s. In order to safeguard its inflation target, the Riksbank is pursuing a very expansionary monetary policy. "By keeping interest rates very low, we create the conditions for inflation to rise towards the target. We are also prepared to take further action if necessary," Skingsley stresses. Title: Economic situation and monetary policy
text: Skingsley: Economic situation and monetary policy "With such a deep crisis, it is reasonable to think that it may take some time for inflation to return to the inflation target, both here and in the world around us. But that's not the same as saying you're giving up on the inflation target. The inflation target always guides monetary policy, even now." This is what First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley said when she spoke today at Dagens industri's digital event Omstart Sverige. Date: 2020-09-03 09:50 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Dagens industri's digital event Omstart Sverige The world economy has been hit hard by the ongoing pandemic, as confirmed in the second quarter's outcome for GDP and the labour market. However, business confidence and other indicators of the situation have improved during the summer, both here and abroad. This is encouraging, says Skingsley, but at the same time points out that the pandemic is not over. "We are still in a serious economic situation and the way forward is lined with a lot of uncertainty, not least in terms of the spread of infection and restrictions to curb it." In the context of economic policy as a whole, a wide range of measures of historic proportions have been deployed to support the economy's ability to overcome this shock. "The Riksbank's measures have contributed to a reduction in market interest rates that rose sharply at the beginning of the crisis, to creating security that there is access to financing at a low cost and to keeping lending to households and companies up. In doing so, we are supporting economic activity and inflation," Skingsley said. Inflation is expected to gradually rise towards 2%. However, the depth of the crisis means that it takes some time. "But it should not be perceived as a sign that we have abandoned the inflation target. On the contrary, the effects of the pandemic on the economy show how important it is that monetary policy continues to be geared towards maintaining the role of the inflation target as an anchor in price and wage formation," skingsley stresses. "Monetary policy plays an important role in alleviating recessions. It can be inserted quickly and is powerful. But the global low interest rate environment is a challenge and a large number of countries and central banks are now in the same boat," Skingsley said. "We all have to deal with low inflation with key interest rates at or near the lower bound. Other monetary policy tools such as securities purchases can and should be used. But there is also a need to consider whether the monetary policy strategy can be developed so that monetary policy continues to have the potential to counteract recessions and high unemployment. This is not a new issue, but the ongoing crisis has brought it even more to the fore," Skingsley concludes. Title: Hearing on monetary policy
text: Skingsley in finance committee: Hearing on monetary policy Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves and Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley visited the Riksdag's Finance Committee today for a hearing on the Riksbank's monetary policy. Date: 2019-03-07 09:00 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Swedish Parliament, Stockholm In his introduction, Skingsley discussed the distributional effects of monetary policy, in the light of the debate that has taken place around this. However, the effects of an expansionary policy are not unambiguous in terms of distribution. Some groups have benefited from rising asset prices. At the same time, employment has increased to a historically high level. "The fact that the labour market has become stronger and that the risk of unemployment has decreased plays a major role for individuals with weak attachment to the labour market," Skingsley said. "Fundamentally, monetary policy is not an appropriate distributional policy tool, partly because the distributional effects are unclear and partly because it would be difficult to combine with the task of monetary policy to maintain a fixed monetary value," Skingsley concluded. Title: Economic activity is improving
text: Skingsley in Skara and Boras: The economy is improving Date: 2015-09-10 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Skara and Boras "The Swedish economy is strengthening and inflation is moving upwards in trend terms. Although uncertainty in the external environment remains high, the economic and inflation outlook remains broadly unchanged since the monetary policy decision in July. Monetary policy needs to remain very expansionary so that inflation continues to rise towards the 2% target and that the risks associated with inflation that are too low are reduced. If the measures we have implemented so far are not enough for inflation to rise, we remain highly prepared to do more." This is what Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley says when she visits Skara and Boras on Thursday and Friday. She talks about the economic situation and the latest interest rate decision, including at a breakfast with representatives from companies, organizations and the municipality in the region. Skingsley also makes a company visit and gives a presentation at Boras Industri och handelsklubb by invitation from Swedbank Sjuharad. On 2 September, the Riksbank's Executive Board decided to leave the repo rate unchanged at -0.35 per cent. In addition, the Riksbank will continue to buy government bonds until the end of the year. The repo rate is expected to be 0.35 per cent for about a year and the repo rate path reflects that it is possible that the repo rate will be lowered further. In the link are the pictures that Cecilia Skingsley shows at her presentation at, among others, Sparbanken in Skaraborg. In connection with the spring and autumn monetary policy reports, the members of the Executive Board carry out visits to different locations in the country where they present the monetary policy decisions. The members then give lectures and meet with the business community, municipal representatives, media and universities in the locality in question. Cecilia's Skingsley visits are hosted by Sparbanken in Skaraborg and Boras industrial and trade club.

Title: Low interest rates contribute to a strong economy and inflation rising
text: Skingsley: Low interest rates contribute to a strong economy and inflation rising Date: 2015-11-17 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Garnisonen, Stockholm "The expansionary monetary policy with low interest rates contributes to a strong economy and that inflation has been rising since last year," says Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley when she gives a presentation today at the SIMRA Swedish Society of Business Economists. Skingsley points out that the Riksbank's monetary policy with interest rate cuts and bond purchase programs is having an effect. The low interest rate situation in Sweden has contributed to a relatively strong economy with stable GDP growth, falling unemployment and inflation rising since last year. "The economy is developing according to the Riksbank's forecasts, including the latest inflation survey, for the month of October," says Skingsley. But the readiness to take further monetary stimulus needs to remain high, given the international uncertainty and that inflation has been low for a long time, Skingsley points out. She also commented on the recent debate on both the monetary policy regime and the monetary policy framework. She believes that the inflation target has contributed to stable expectations for price and wage formation, which has been favorable for economic development. "Changing the target because we're coming from a period of prolonged low inflation would not contribute to greater confidence in the inflation target," Skingsley said. She also welcomes the upcoming evaluation from finance committee special investigators Professor Mervyn King and Professor Marvin Goodfriend. "Their report will be an interesting contribution to the Swedish discussion of the inflation target," Skingsley concludes.

Title: Strong recovery with weak inflationary pressures
text: Skingsley on summer developments: Strong recovery with weak inflationary pressures "It's been a high-pressure summer even from an economic perspective." This is what First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley said when she opened Danske Bank's Group Treasurer seminar today with a summary of this summer's economic development. Date: 2021-08-27 13:00 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Danske Bank The rapid recovery from the pandemic that we've seen ahead of us is well underway, Skingsley said. Economies have even grown a little faster than expected during the summer, both in the euro area and in Sweden. At the same time, the spread of the coronavirus has increased again in several countries and large differences in vaccination rates between different countries create uncertainty about the continued course of the pandemic. Both households and businesses are optimistic about developments going forward, which is a sign of the high growth we expect in the recovery phase. Inflation has also been slightly higher than expected this summer. This is mainly due to the unexpected increase in electricity prices. Without energy prices, inflation is low, 0.5 per cent, and cost pressures are weak. "Overall, I don't think the picture of the economic situation changed in any dramatic way this summer," Skingsley said. "On the one hand, the Swedish economy is now growing a little faster and inflation has become slightly higher than our forecast in July. On the other hand, inflationary pressures remain weak and uncertainty about the pandemic can be said to have increased". "We concluded at our July monetary policy meeting that monetary policy persistence is needed for inflation to be permanently close to 2 percent. At our next meeting, at the end of September, we will have to weigh up the information that has come to light until then and assess how monetary policy will best contribute to good economic development and continued confidence in the inflation target," Skingsley concluded. Title: Reforms in housing and tax policy needed to solve the problems of the housing market
text: Skingsley: Reforms in housing and tax policy are needed to solve the problems of the housing market "The financial system has, with the help of extensive support measures, done relatively well through the pandemic and we have managed to avoid a financial crisis. However, risks to financial stability remain elevated. High household indebtedness and large exposures of big banks to residential and commercial real estate increase vulnerabilities". This is what First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley said when she spoke today at a webinar at DI's stock exchange day. 2021-05-27 Cecilia Skingsley interviewed about the problems in the housing market (4:15) Date: 2021-05-27 09:30 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Place: Dagens Industri's conference Borsdagen (digital) "Despite the crisis, house prices have risen sharply over the past year, not only in Sweden but also in other countries. At the same time, mortgage rates have not fallen but have remained relatively stable. Therefore, it is difficult to conclude that the Riksbank's monetary policy has been a decisive factor behind the sharp rise in prices in the housing market during the pandemic," Skingsley said. Instead, other pandemic-related factors seem to have played a bigger role. "Many Swedes work more at home and may therefore want a larger home. In addition, the negative effects of the crisis on the labour market have had little impact on households in permanent employment, which normally find it easier to obtain mortgages. The pandemic has amplified the insider/outsider issues we have in the housing market," Skingsley noted. Monetary policy is too blunt a tool to deal with the problems of the housing market The fact that house prices have increased for many years is largely due to the structural problems that have long characterized the Swedish housing market. "We at the Riksbank have been talking about these problems for over a decade. But we have no legal mandate or appropriate tool to deal with it and here monetary policy becomes too blunt a tool. Our monetary policy measures provide broad support to the recovery that is now well underway. For example, if we were to sharply raise interest rates to bring down house prices, economic activity would slow down, resulting in higher unemployment and lower inflation," Skingsley said. "To solve the fundamental problems of the housing market, broad reforms are needed in housing and tax policy that improve the balance between supply and demand in the housing market," Skingsley said. "Possible measures to improve the housing market include reviewing the regulatory framework around new housing construction, the rent-setting system, the taxation of capital gains on home sales, the property tax and interest deductions," Skingsley continued. A crisis in the real estate market can threaten the financial system In addition to residential, banks are also heavily exposed to commercial real estate companies, which means that problems in the real estate sector can cause banks large credit losses. Many real estate companies are highly leveraged and are vulnerable if interest rates were to rise rapidly or property prices fall sharply. The pandemic may also have accelerated a transition from retail to e-commerce and it is uncertain what lasting needs for office space tenants will have after the pandemic. "The Riksbank is paying attention to the real estate market and the problems it may pose to the banking sector," Skingsley concluded. Updated 2021-05-27

Vi p Riksbanken har pratat om dessa problem i ver ett decennium. Men vi har inget lagligt mandat eller lmpligt verktyg fr att hantera det och hr blir penningpolitiken ett allt fr trubbigt verktyg. Vra penningpolitiska tgrder ger ett brett std till den terhmtning som nu r p god vg. Fr att lsa de grundlggande problemen p bostadsmarknaden behvs breda reformer inom bostads- och skattepolitiken som frbttrar balansen mellan utbud och efterfrgan p bostadsmarknaden, sa Skingsley. Pandemin kan ocks ha pskyndat en omstllning frn butikshandel till e-handel och det r oskert vilka varaktiga behov av kontorsytor som hyresgster kommer att ha efter pandemin. Title: Challenges in the payments market need to be solved
text: Skingsley: Challenges in the payments market must be solved Date: 2015-03-19 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Place: First Chamber Hall in parliament "It is positive that the market for payments is developing and can meet new needs. But the challenges that arise also need to be addressed so that people don't get caught." This is what Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley said when she answered questions about cash management today in an open hearing in parliament's finance committee. The Riksbank looks at the payments market as a whole. Collaboration is required to solve the challenges that exist. Positive development in the payment market Consumers need simple, fast and secure payment services and companies are continuously streamlining their work processes. This means that the market for payments is changing rapidly. Sweden is already at the forefront when it comes to developing and using electronic payments. Cash has therefore encountered stiff competition from new innovative ways of paying. This development is in many ways positive but, like all changes, it also brings challenges. Difficult in some situations Without cash, it can be difficult to pay for coffee at the children's football game, an item at the flea market or to pay in places where mobile coverage is lacking. People who, for various reasons, cannot or do not want to pay in any other way than with cash may find it difficult to shop at all. For example, minors who cannot have cards, those who cannot afford a smartphone or those who find it difficult to absorb new technologies. There are also problems with depositing cash as the number of deposit sites has decreased. It mainly affects associations with temporary needs and small business owners in places where there is no deposit service via bank or atm and where daily bag services become expensive. "These are complex challenges that require different solutions. All players in the payment market must work together to find solutions. The Riksbank does not take a position on which payment methods are used as long as they are safe and bear their costs," says Cecilia Skingsley. FACTS Most common way to pay The most common ways to pay with in Sweden are cards, cash and credit transfers. Cash is used relatively little in Sweden compared to other countries, while cards are very common. The development is fast. New payment services are launched on the market and new players establish themselves. Card payments and payments via mobile phones are growing fastest while the technical systems that mediate the payments are constantly being improved. Title: Developing central banks' mandates
text: Skingsley: Developing central bank mandates Date: 2016-09-13 Speaker: Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: Oesterreichische Nationalbank, Bank for International Settlements NB! The Riksbank has brought forward this publication due to the fact that the material has been published by a third party. Publication was scheduled for 2:30 p.m. "We need to strike a balance between, on the one hand, the will of the legislature to give the central bank a clear mandate and mandate and, on the other hand, the ability of the central bank to carry out its work independently and flexibly," said Cecilia Skingsley in a speech at the conference to be held on the occasion of the 200th anniversary of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank. Since the start of the global financial crisis in 2007, central banks have focused on stabilising financial systems and achieving inflation targets. Their actions have triggered a broad and lively discussion about the role of central banks in the national economy, their mandates and opportunities to carry out their tasks. "It's not surprising and I welcome the discussion, many central banks have been forced into new and new measures in partly new areas on a large scale. It is good that these issues are being discussed, it deepens the knowledge in society about the role, goals and means of central banks and I hope it leads to well thought-out reforms," said Skingsley. The discussion is intense, not only in Sweden, where a new parliamentary inquiry into the Riksbank is to be initiated, but also in a number of other countries where the central banks' efforts are discussed in relation to their statutory duties, Skingsley notes. When it comes to financial stability work, Skingsley points out that there is not yet an international consensus on what the division of responsibilities between legislators and different authorities should best look like. As stability measures can be unpopular, there is a risk that measures that preserve stability in the long term will not come about because they are not popular in the short term. "An interesting model is that macroprudential decisions are made by a decision-making committee with a clear goal, where members sit on personal and long-term mandates and where the activities have a high level of transparency. It could ensure both democratic control and operational decision-making," Skingsley concludes.

Title: The road from the financial crisis onwards  Monetary policy developments
text: Skingsley: The road from the financial crisis onwards  Monetary policy developments The inflation target - in combination with a number of other reforms during the 1990s, such as the budget framework - has contributed to favourable economic development in Sweden; low inflation, high GDP growth, stable real wage increases, current account surpluses and low government debt. And inflation targeting remains the dominant regime among virtually all central banks in countries with variable exchange rates. This was stated by First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley when she spoke on Tuesday about the economic development of recent decades in Sweden at the seminar ohman Perspektiv in Stockholm. Date: 2020-01-28 17:15 Speaker: First Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley Location: ohman, Berns, Berzelii park, Stockholm However, the conditions for monetary policy changed with the global financial crisis of 2008 and the subsequent debt crisis in the euro area in 2010-2012, which left a mark in the form of sharply falling GDP growth and lower productivity developments both in the rest of the world and in Sweden. In addition, global interest rates have fallen to exceptionally low levels since the 1980s, partly as a result of an ageing population and increased savings. "The low interest rate environment has made it more challenging for central banks to conduct monetary policy," Skingsley points out. In order to be able to contribute with sufficient stimulus to maintain low and stable inflation, the Riksbank and many other central banks have in recent years lowered their key interest rates to historically low levels, but also supplemented by extensive purchases of government bonds. "Our monetary policy has contributed to the strong economy we have had in Sweden and to inflation being at our inflation target in recent years." "The Riksbank does not lack opportunities to counteract future recessions, but the low interest rate environment makes it more difficult. It is therefore important that the Riksbank continues to have access to a complete toolbox. But the fact that monetary policy can become more expansionary if necessary does not necessarily mean that it is the best medicine. Many of the problems facing the world economy today are largely structural and other policy areas are likely to be more effective, although monetary policy can also contribute to some extent," Skingsley said. Skingsley also commented on the Riksbank's latest interest rate decision in December. "With good inflation target achievement since 2017, I saw compelling reasons to raise the policy rate to zero percent." The Riksbank's forecast is that its key interest rate will remain stable in the coming years. "We're in a wait-and-see mode, Skingsley said. Since the monetary policy meeting in December, developments in the world mainly look set to continue to stabilise, although uncertainty remains high".
