Title: Some comments on Professor Charles Bean's paper - Aggregate-Demand Policies and Labour Market Reform
text: Some comments om Professor Charles Bean's paper - Aggregate-Demand Policies and Labour Market Reform Datum: 1998-05-25 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Backstrom Plats: Economic Council Conference Introduction I would like to begin by thanking the Economic Council for the invitation to take part in this conference. Unemployment in Europe is not only high, but it has persisted over as long a period as a couple of decades. A discussion of what can be done to overcome this problem is therefore very relevant. This discussion is also important viewed from a central bank perspective. It is important to clarify what central banks can and cannot do to contribute to increased employment and reduced unemployment. I would also like to thank Professor Charles Bean for an interesting and thoughtprovoking essay. The starting point of his paper is the need for structural reforms to combat unemployment. In other words, he views unemployment in Europe as primarily structural and not cyclical. Professor Bean discusses in detail what should be done if such reforms are to lead quickly to the desired result. He also takes up how the establishment of the EMU may affect the prospects for success. I am grateful for valuable comments from the following members of staff at the Riksbank: Mikael Apel, Eva Udden-Jondal, Staffan Viotti and Anders Vredin. Special thanks are due to Yngve Lindh who gave useful suggests and together with Magnus Jonsson and Jonny Nilsson contributed the result of model simulations that have served as the basis for this work. In my comments, I intend to take up three aspects of the problem area identified by Professor Bean. I would first like to underline Professor Beans starting point, namely the need for structural reforms to be able to overcome the high level of unemployment. I then comment on the role of monetary policy in connection with the implementation of structural reforms. Finally, I take up the EMU perspective and the possibility of carrying out successful, structural reforms. How can increased employment and reduced unemployment be achieved? If we assume a simple model where goods and services are produced with the input of the factors of production, labour and capital, the level of employment can in principle be affected in two different ways.(1) 1. A growing economy where capital and labour increase at the same rate 2. Changed capital intensity with a given total production If we examine the actual development since the first oil crisis in 1973/74, the diagram (2)shows that the differences in the development of employment between EU and the USA can be explained by the different development of the capital intensity in the production process rather than by large differences in growth. Capital intensity in the EU has increased. The increase in production has entailed, in relative terms, a reduction in the use of labour compared with capital.(3) As shown in the diagram, labour productivity has increased considerably more in Europe than in the USA during the period 1974 to 1995. The productivity of labour measured ex post reflects not only the changes in an exogenously determined growth in labour productivity but also is to a great extent the result of high wage costs which favour capital intensive technology and force less efficient operations to stop production or shrink. In the USA the inputs of capital and labour have increased to about the same extent. Employment has therefore also increased more rapidly without growth overall having been markedly higher than in the EU. It is close at hand to explain the increased capital intensity in the EU with a rise in the total price of labour in relation to the price of capital. The real wage prices (including wage-related taxes) have increased more quickly in the EU than in the USA. A further indication of this development is that the return on capital in the USA has been higher than in the EU. On the whole, it seems that the relative price of labour has been higher in Europe than in the USA, and that this can be an important explanation for the weaker growth of employment. In Sweden, this trend seems to have been stronger than in the rest of the EU. This can have contributed to our countrys weak economic growth during recent decades. A more stable macro-economic regime-- of the type which was established in Sweden during the 1990sis itself a structural reform which can lead to a growth rate which will be higher than that of the 1970s and 1980s. Structural reforms  a path to increased employment There are many indicators that the possibilities for overcoming employment problems in Europe are connected with the possibilities of achieving both an increased production potential and a more balanced use in future of the production resources, labour and capital. Structural measures are of strategic importance for the labour market, including wage formation, to be able to function better and for employment to increase. This is also Professor Beans starting point in his paper. He points out that the flexibility of real wages needs to increase and that mobility on the labour market needs to be stimulated. It is not clear to me that Professor Beans analysis considers the effects on the employment level of a more balanced use of labour and capital. The focus of the analysis, if I have understood it correctly, is rather on how an increase can be achieved in overall growth, and in this way also in employment (4). However, a reform of the operation of the labour market should also affect the capital intensity of production. Even if this mechanism is not explicitly contained in Beans paper, it may very well follow from the structural reforms he advocates. It is in this case something that can soften the apparent conflict between the short-term and long-term effects that Bean analyses. If growth has a somewhat different content, with a greater input of labour for each unit produced, the time perspective for the increase in employment can be affected in a favourable direction. The role of monetary policy in carrying out structural reforms Basically, Beans view of the macroeconomic dynamics after the implementation of structural reforms seems to be reasonable. Both due to the individuals uncertainty about the reform, and its effects and the fact that prices and wages adapt slowly, it may, as Bean points out, lead to a short period of increasing unemployment. Subsequently, however, demand in the economy increases due to the capital stock being built up, and production and income will after a time be higher than before the structural reform was carried out. Employment increases and unemployment falls. I would like to point out two factors that mitigate or even eliminate the problem that Bean highlights. My first point illustrates the advantage of a monetary policy directed at explicit inflation targets, which partially takes care of the problem indicated by Bean. The second point deals with the importance of taking into consideration the extent to which the actors in the economy anticipate the structural reforms and their effects. A reform of the labour market that leads to an increase in the supply of labour can, according to Bean, lead to a reduced use of resources in the short-term and thus exert a downward pressure on prices. This naturally affects monetary policy, which is focused on an explicit inflation target. An inflation rate that is lower than the target normally leads to the central bank reducing the instrumental rate. Total demand and employment consequently increase. The negative effects that may arise are thus softened within the framework of the current monetary policy approach. If the instrumental horizon for monetary policy is one to two years, the central bank will accordingly be able to take into consideration the effects of the structural reform in good time. This will be the case if the political situation is such that it is highly probable that the reform will really be carried out. However, I would like to warn against carrying out a monetary policy that entails risks in the area of inflation (5). An expansive monetary policy approach can lead to inflationary expectations being adjusted upwards. This would in turn entail that the costs in terms of reduced employment to get back to the inflation target would exceed the short-term gains in the level of employment of such a policy. How high the costs of an expansive policy would be would depend on the how inflation expectations are formed. For a country which, for a long run of years, has carried out a policy that led to high inflation and quite recently come down to lower levels, the risks of such a policy are probably even higher. Neither, in my view, is the type of package solution that Bean seems to recommend especially practicable. His idea is that a supply reform should be announced at the same as the central bank provides assurances on increasing demand by reduced instrumental interest rates. The whole idea of separating monetary policy decisions from other political decisions by increasing the independence of the central banks is to counteract such confusion. Most countries  not least Sweden  have poor experiences of such arrangements. It can lead to periods of overheating, inflation and unstable growth. If the effects of a package of this type with stimulating monetary policy are built into wage contracts, nothing will be achieved. It would rather lead to other types of costs. The EMU perspective A central mechanism behind the initial problems which structural reforms are said to entail depends on the implicit assumption that these reforms come as a surprise. This explains the fact that there will arise a delay between the effects on potential and actual production respectively. This is exactly why the need for demand policy arises in Beans opinion. In an EMU perspective, this will, in his view, be an even greater problem since monetary and foreign exchange policy are carried out together and the probability for co-ordinated reforms in all eleven EMU countries is low. Moreover, fiscal policy is restricted by the Stability and Growth Pact. A basic issue is how probable it is that structural reforms will come unexpectedly. It does in fact play a large role for the development of the economy if the reforms are instead foreseen.(6) Then it is on the contrary reasonable to assume that the positive effects will appear more quickly. Labour market reforms are discussed and investigated from all appearances for a rather long time before being implemented. The whole process is probably long and drawn-out and employers, workers and unions together as well as other economic agents should at least be able to foresee in part the way things are moving. It is then not unreasonable to think that the positive effects of the reform will come earlier than would be the case if they came as a surprise. There will then be less need for demand stimulation than Bean anticipates. The fact that a country is a member of the EMU should therefore neither prevent nor make it more difficult to carry out structural reforms, provided that the reforms are to a reasonable extent expected. In addition, a EMU country has the option of using fiscal policy to support the work of reform if it nevertheless should prove necessary. Beans starting point is that fiscal policy is strictly limited by the Stability and Growth Pact. It is worth emphasising that this is only the case if the countries permanently balance at the utmost limits of the Stability and Growth Pact. It is not a law of nature that this should be so. Swedish economic policy, for instance, aims at building up a surplus in public finances. If other countries adopt the same approach, there is a scope for action also for fiscal policy. Summary It is important to discuss what can be done to reduce the high level of unemployment in Sweden and in Europe as a whole. Many factors indicate that measures are required that affect wage formation and the working of the labour market as a whole in order for employment to increase permanently to a significant extent. Professor Bean advocates such reforms and discusses in an interesting paper how they are to be implemented in the best possible way. In my comments, I have tried to take up a couple of aspects that show that the implementation of such reforms need not be linked with the type of difficulties that Bean supposes. This is especially the case since they partially operate through other mechanisms than those that Bean explicitly discusses. Structural reforms of the labour market do not lead to increased employment only by increased economic growth but can also change the way in which this growth is achieved. A more balanced mix of capital and labour is also a way to increase employment. Furthermore if structural reforms are more or less expected, which is probably the case, the positive effects will likely be felt relatively soon. Otherwise such a situation with initial negative effects, like the one that Bean visualises, can be dealt with within the framework of a monetary policy focused on an explicit inflation target. Member countries of the Monetary Union can use fiscal policy since countries need not necessarily stay at the at the limits of the Stability and Growth Pact. Sweden is an example of a country with a goal of achieving a surplus in public finances. (1) The relationship between the rate of increase of production, factor inputs and productivity can be expressed as Q PF TFP w*L (1-w)* K TFP, i.e. the increase of production (Q) is equal to the sum of the increase of the production factors (PF) and total factor productivity (TFP). The increase of the production factors is in turn a weighted sum of the increase of labour (L) and capital (C) where the weights consist of the wage portion of the value-added (w). The growth in production can also be calculated as the sum of the growth rate of employment and the growth rate of labour productivity. The growth rate of labour productivity can be written as: Q  L TFP (1-w) * (K-L), i.e. the increase in labour productivity [the difference between the increase of production (Q) and of employment (L)] is the equal to the sum of the increase in total factor productivity (TFP) and the increase in capital intensity [the difference between the increase in the capital input (K) and employment (L)] multiplied by the capital portion of value-added (1-w). (2) The figures for USA and EU in the diagram have been taken from European Economy, Annual Economic Report for 1997, No. 63, 1997. The figures for Sweden are based on statistics from Statistics Sweden and calculations made at the Riksbank. It should be emphasised that the estimates for Sweden are approximate since they are based on measurements of the capital stock which only cover the business sector. The period is 1974 to 1995. Development is stated as an annual average in per cent. Rounding-off errors may occur. For figuers, see the Word-file (3) An increasing capital intensity is not negative per se. On the contrary, it can drive up labour productivity, thus providing scope for high growth and a rising standard of living. In a situation with high unemployment and a weak growth of employment, it can, however, be a source of problems on the labour market. (4) In the first paragraph on page 3 of his essay Bean writes: the increase in equilibrium supply of output that follows from the structural reform. This should reasonably be interpreted as meaning that the way to increased employment and reduced unemployment is through increased potential and actual production viewed as a whole  and not through a reduced capital intensity. (5) This is something that Bean takes up on page 4 in the third paragraph of his paper when he writes that With a fixed money wage, this requires a temporary increase in domestic inflation, and a fortiori in consumer price inflation. Bean refers in this context also to an earlier paper where a temporary increase of inflation is directly advocated. His analysis of this is relevant for todays discussion since Bean in the third paragraph on page 6 explicitly refers to Sweden and the United Kingdom being outside the EMU and states that it should be possible to carry out a monetary policy that stimulates demand in these countries. (6) In the simulations made at the Riksbank in the macro-model RIXMOD 2.0, it clearly emerges that the development of unemployment and the economy as a whole is different depending on whether the structural reform is totally unexpected or whether it is fully anticipated. In reality, it is difficult to see that a reform of this kind could come as a total surprise Neither does it seem probable that the reform would be fully expected. The probable effect is rather somewhere between these two extremes. My point is, however, that the short-term negative effects will be smaller, the less unexpected the implementation of the reform is. This insight is therefore something that could be used by the political system if it is thinking of carrying out a reform.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Some comments om Professor Charles Bean's paper - Aggregate-Demand Policies and Labour Market Reform Datum: 1998-05-25 Talare: Riksbankschef Urban Bckstrm Plats: Economic Council Conference Introduction I would like to begin by thanking the Economic Council for the invitation to take part in this conference. Unemployment in Europe is not only high, but it has persisted over as long a period as a couple of decades. A discussion of what can be done to overcome this problem is therefore very relevant. This discussion is also important viewed from a central bank perspective. It is important to clarify what central banks can and cannot do to contribute to increased employment and reduced unemployment. I would also like to thank Professor Charles Bean for an interesting and thoughtprovoking essay. The starting point of his paper is the need for structural reforms to combat unemployment. In other words, he views unemployment in Europe as primarily structural and not cyclical. Professor Bean discusses in detail what should be done if such reforms are to lead quickly to the desired result. He also takes up how the establishment of the EMU may affect the prospects for success. I am grateful for valuable comments from the following members of staff at the Riksbank: Mikael Apel, Eva Uddn-Jondal, Staffan Viotti and Anders Vredin. Special thanks are due to Yngve Lindh who gave useful suggests and together with Magnus Jonsson and Jonny Nilsson contributed the result of model simulations that have served as the basis for this work. In my comments, I intend to take up three aspects of the problem area identified by Professor Bean. I would first like to underline Professor Beans starting point, namely the need for structural reforms to be able to overcome the high level of unemployment. I then comment on the role of monetary policy in connection with the implementation of structural reforms. Finally, I take up the EMU perspective and the possibility of carrying out successful, structural reforms. How can increased employment and reduced unemployment be achieved? If we assume a simple model where goods and services are produced with the input of the factors of production, labour and capital, the level of employment can in principle be affected in two different ways.(1) 1. A growing economy where capital and labour increase at the same rate 2. Changed capital intensity with a given total production If we examine the actual development since the first oil crisis in 1973/74, the diagram (2)shows that the differences in the development of employment between EU and the USA can be explained by the different development of the capital intensity in the production process rather than by large differences in growth. Capital intensity in the EU has increased. The increase in production has entailed, in relative terms, a reduction in the use of labour compared with capital.(3) As shown in the diagram, labour productivity has increased considerably more in Europe than in the USA during the period 1974 to 1995. The productivity of labour measured ex post reflects not only the changes in an exogenously determined growth in labour productivity but also is to a great extent the result of high wage costs which favour capital intensive technology and force less efficient operations to stop production or shrink. In the USA the inputs of capital and labour have increased to about the same extent. Employment has therefore also increased more rapidly without growth overall having been markedly higher than in the EU. It is close at hand to explain the increased capital intensity in the EU with a rise in the total price of labour in relation to the price of capital. The real wage prices (including wage-related taxes) have increased more quickly in the EU than in the USA. A further indication of this development is that the return on capital in the USA has been higher than in the EU. On the whole, it seems that the relative price of labour has been higher in Europe than in the USA, and that this can be an important explanation for the weaker growth of employment. In Sweden, this trend seems to have been stronger than in the rest of the EU. This can have contributed to our countrys weak economic growth during recent decades. A more stable macro-economic regime-- of the type which was established in Sweden during the 1990sis itself a structural reform which can lead to a growth rate which will be higher than that of the 1970s and 1980s. Structural reforms  a path to increased employment There are many indicators that the possibilities for overcoming employment problems in Europe are connected with the possibilities of achieving both an increased production potential and a more balanced use in future of the production resources, labour and capital. Structural measures are of strategic importance for the labour market, including wage formation, to be able to function better and for employment to increase. This is also Professor Beans starting point in his paper. He points out that the flexibility of real wages needs to increase and that mobility on the labour market needs to be stimulated. It is not clear to me that Professor Beans analysis considers the effects on the employment level of a more balanced use of labour and capital. The focus of the analysis, if I have understood it correctly, is rather on how an increase can be achieved in overall growth, and in this way also in employment (4). However, a reform of the operation of the labour market should also affect the capital intensity of production. Even if this mechanism is not explicitly contained in Beans paper, it may very well follow from the structural reforms he advocates. It is in this case something that can soften the apparent conflict between the short-term and long-term effects that Bean analyses. If growth has a somewhat different content, with a greater input of labour for each unit produced, the time perspective for the increase in employment can be affected in a favourable direction. The role of monetary policy in carrying out structural reforms Basically, Beans view of the macroeconomic dynamics after the implementation of structural reforms seems to be reasonable. Both due to the individuals uncertainty about the reform, and its effects and the fact that prices and wages adapt slowly, it may, as Bean points out, lead to a short period of increasing unemployment. Subsequently, however, demand in the economy increases due to the capital stock being built up, and production and income will after a time be higher than before the structural reform was carried out. Employment increases and unemployment falls. I would like to point out two factors that mitigate or even eliminate the problem that Bean highlights. My first point illustrates the advantage of a monetary policy directed at explicit inflation targets, which partially takes care of the problem indicated by Bean. The second point deals with the importance of taking into consideration the extent to which the actors in the economy anticipate the structural reforms and their effects. A reform of the labour market that leads to an increase in the supply of labour can, according to Bean, lead to a reduced use of resources in the short-term and thus exert a downward pressure on prices. This naturally affects monetary policy, which is focused on an explicit inflation target. An inflation rate that is lower than the target normally leads to the central bank reducing the instrumental rate. Total demand and employment consequently increase. The negative effects that may arise are thus softened within the framework of the current monetary policy approach. If the instrumental horizon for monetary policy is one to two years, the central bank will accordingly be able to take into consideration the effects of the structural reform in good time. This will be the case if the political situation is such that it is highly probable that the reform will really be carried out. However, I would like to warn against carrying out a monetary policy that entails risks in the area of inflation (5). An expansive monetary policy approach can lead to inflationary expectations being adjusted upwards. This would in turn entail that the costs in terms of reduced employment to get back to the inflation target would exceed the short-term gains in the level of employment of such a policy. How high the costs of an expansive policy would be would depend on the how inflation expectations are formed. For a country which, for a long run of years, has carried out a policy that led to high inflation and quite recently come down to lower levels, the risks of such a policy are probably even higher. Neither, in my view, is the type of package solution that Bean seems to recommend especially practicable. His idea is that a supply reform should be announced at the same as the central bank provides assurances on increasing demand by reduced instrumental interest rates. The whole idea of separating monetary policy decisions from other political decisions by increasing the independence of the central banks is to counteract such confusion. Most countries  not least Sweden  have poor experiences of such arrangements. It can lead to periods of overheating, inflation and unstable growth. If the effects of a package of this type with stimulating monetary policy are built into wage contracts, nothing will be achieved. It would rather lead to other types of costs. The EMU perspective A central mechanism behind the initial problems which structural reforms are said to entail depends on the implicit assumption that these reforms come as a surprise. This explains the fact that there will arise a delay between the effects on potential and actual production respectively. This is exactly why the need for demand policy arises in Beans opinion. In an EMU perspective, this will, in his view, be an even greater problem since monetary and foreign exchange policy are carried out together and the probability for co-ordinated reforms in all eleven EMU countries is low. Moreover, fiscal policy is restricted by the Stability and Growth Pact. A basic issue is how probable it is that structural reforms will come unexpectedly. It does in fact play a large role for the development of the economy if the reforms are instead foreseen.(6) Then it is on the contrary reasonable to assume that the positive effects will appear more quickly. Labour market reforms are discussed and investigated from all appearances for a rather long time before being implemented. The whole process is probably long and drawn-out and employers, workers and unions together as well as other economic agents should at least be able to foresee in part the way things are moving. It is then not unreasonable to think that the positive effects of the reform will come earlier than would be the case if they came as a surprise. There will then be less need for demand stimulation than Bean anticipates. The fact that a country is a member of the EMU should therefore neither prevent nor make it more difficult to carry out structural reforms, provided that the reforms are to a reasonable extent expected. In addition, a EMU country has the option of using fiscal policy to support the work of reform if it nevertheless should prove necessary. Beans starting point is that fiscal policy is strictly limited by the Stability and Growth Pact. It is worth emphasising that this is only the case if the countries permanently balance at the utmost limits of the Stability and Growth Pact. It is not a law of nature that this should be so. Swedish economic policy, for instance, aims at building up a surplus in public finances. If other countries adopt the same approach, there is a scope for action also for fiscal policy. Summary It is important to discuss what can be done to reduce the high level of unemployment in Sweden and in Europe as a whole. Many factors indicate that measures are required that affect wage formation and the working of the labour market as a whole in order for employment to increase permanently to a significant extent. Professor Bean advocates such reforms and discusses in an interesting paper how they are to be implemented in the best possible way. In my comments, I have tried to take up a couple of aspects that show that the implementation of such reforms need not be linked with the type of difficulties that Bean supposes. This is especially the case since they partially operate through other mechanisms than those that Bean explicitly discusses. Structural reforms of the labour market do not lead to increased employment only by increased economic growth but can also change the way in which this growth is achieved. A more balanced mix of capital and labour is also a way to increase employment. Furthermore if structural reforms are more or less expected, which is probably the case, the positive effects will likely be felt relatively soon. Otherwise such a situation with initial negative effects, like the one that Bean visualises, can be dealt with within the framework of a monetary policy focused on an explicit inflation target. Member countries of the Monetary Union can use fiscal policy since countries need not necessarily stay at the at the limits of the Stability and Growth Pact. Sweden is an example of a country with a goal of achieving a surplus in public finances. Title: A reunited Europe  opportunities and risks
text: Srejber: A reunited Europe  opportunities and risks Date: 2005-10-18 Speaker: First Deputy Governor of the Riksbank Eva Srejber Location: Ekonomidagarna i orebro The eu's new member states and their importance for a europe-wide recovery First, I would like to thank you for the opportunity to come here to orebro and participate in ekonomidagarna. I will talk about some of the challenges we face in a reunited Europe. It is now more than a year and a half since ten new countries joined the EU  eight of them countries that fifteen years earlier had freed themselves from the yoke of the Communist dictatorship. During these years, perspectives have shifted. Once these countries were described as recipients of emergency aid and advice. Today, several of them are examples of how reforms can create rapid growth and thereby lift the population out of poverty. Sometimes the new Member States are even portrayed as an economic threat when their labour force with a lower wage position is rhetorically contrasted with the weak development of employment in many of the old Member States. The enlargement of the EU has been a boost for the old Member States at a time when growth and employment have stagnated. Ever since the customs barriers were torn down between the EU and the future Member States in the mid-1990s, trade between the old and new Member States has been an engine for growth in Europe. For Sweden, the upturn in trade with countries such as Poland and the Baltic states has continued steadily over the economic cycles and has been a particularly important driver of growth in recent years, when several of the large European countries have performed weakly. There is rightly a lot of talk about China's role in globalisation, but in Sweden's case, the new EU Member States are actually more important for our exports, despite the fact that these countries are so much smaller than China. In the decade since the tariff walls were torn down, the new member states' share of Sweden's exports has risen steadily from just over 2 percent to well over 4 percent, while exports to China have only increased from 1 to 2 percent as a share of our total exports; moreover, that increase has been replaced by stagnation in recent years. It is also in the new Member States that many of the most successful Swedish foreign investments have taken place, investments that have also significantly developed these countries' economies. An important example is swedish banks' acquisition and consolidation of almost the entire banking system in the Baltic countries. This has contributed to the rapid modernisation of the banking system and rapid credit expansion in the Baltic countries. As the new Member States grow, their potential as an export market for Sweden also increases. Sweden's export growth benefits from the fact that exchanges with the new Member States, and also other European neighboring countries outside the EU, continue. I therefore wanted to deal briefly here with four challenges over the next few years for integration between old and new Member States: a common labour market, the continuation of financial integration, the introduction of the euro and the further enlargement of the Eu ropean Union. A single labour market The movement of goods and capital between the old and new Member States has thus been beneficial for both groups of countries. How has labour market mobility influenced the development? In the run-up to the enlargement of the EU in 2004, the political debate painted threatening scenarios in which citizens from the new Member States would move to the old ones and take over low-skilled jobs. Concern was expressed that the citizens of the new Member States would come to the old countries in order to raise generous subsidies in the first place. This debate was one reason why several countries in the EU created transitional rules under which the citizens of the new Member States would only gradually have access to the labour market of these old EU countries. Admittedly, almost all qualified estimates showed that, on the contrary, there would be quite a few who moved permanently, for cultural and housing reasons. Countries such as Sweden, which eventually did not introduce transitional rules, have also been able to note that the permanent inflow has been very small. There has been too little inflows into skilled occupations, where there is a shortage of key personnel in the old Member States and more than enough of that workforce in the new countries as the work requires language skills and cannot be done in short bursts but requires more long-term accommodation in the host country. On the contrary, the employers of the old Member States have had to advertise and actively recruit in the new Member States in order to attract such key personnel from the large pool of well-trained people there. When it comes to the less skilled professions, the trend that has long applied to Sweden continues, i.e. that production but not the labor force moves abroad. There are several advantages to moving production to the new Member States, such as the proximity to Sweden and the cultural ties, which contributed to the transition being smoother and that key functions have been able to stay in Sweden. Such emigration is nothing new, but, like trade, has for a long time contributed to increased prosperity and better wages in Sweden. But for the less skilled professions, a newer trend also applies, namely that people move to production because citizens of the new Member States work to a greater extent temporarily in Sweden but keep the permanent residence in their home country. The latter means that completely new industries are exposed to the type of competition that previously mainly the export industry was exposed to. However, the size of the influx of temporary foreign workers is very uncertain. It is clear that those who work temporarily in Sweden cannot be included in the LFS selection framework. They should be included in measurements of employment through companies, but it is difficult to deduce from there how many of the employed people live abroad and work temporarily in Sweden. I think it would be good to have a broad discussion about how to statistically measure the number of people living abroad who temporarily work in Sweden. Some of the influx of these jobs is probably still a growing phenomenon, but with better measurement methods we can get a more clear picture of the phenomenon. In addition, it is important that it should be clear what legal rules apply to those who work temporarily in other countries. From an economic point of view, the increasing element of temporary foreign labor in Sweden is in practice the same thing that the export industry's labor has long been faced with, namely that less qualified parts of production are carried out by people in other countries. What is new is that with the freer labor market, production in Sweden is also carried out by labor that is not permanently resident here. Basically, it provides the same opportunity, at least in the long run, for increased prosperity and higher wages in Sweden. But if the trade unions demand the same average wages for those who work temporarily in Sweden as for those who live here permanently, the situation is complicated if their productivity is not the same. Let me elaborate on this. A driving force behind the export industry's previous use of foreign labor, through the relocation of less qualified production to other countries, has been that although wages and productivity have been lower among the host countries' labor than among the Swedish one, it has paid off for companies to use highly productive better-paid Swedish labor for more skilled tasks and outsource less skilled production in other countries. The comparative advantages of each country have been exploited. Swedish productivity and wage levels have thus been able to rise. The new trend of people temporarily moving to production is driven by the same business incentives as when production is moved to people in other countries. If temporary foreign workers in Sweden with lower productivity and qualification rates have to be paid the higher wages that Swedish labor receives, the majority of this simpler production will not take place in Sweden. Instead, the largest part will take place in other countries and be imported to Sweden, for example for house construction by prefabricating the parts abroad and that only the composition takes place in Sweden. For many services, on the other hand, the purchaser and the producer of the service have to meet physically, but with the development of IT and telecom technology, an increasing part of the service sector has become the subject of cross-border trade. An example of this is call-centers in other countries. For other services such as some medical care and dental care, the result may instead be that production takes place abroad and customers become cross-border as travel costs are no longer so high. This is a development that we have already seen the beginning of. Simply put, the competition exists all the time - either here in our midst or slightly further away. It is an important challenge for the social partners to respond to this fundamentally wealth-enhancing new situation in the flexible way that has happened in the past for the traditional export industry. There is no doubt that Sweden has a lot to gain from open trade in services in the EU, as we have done for the trade in goods. Sweden is one of the countries with the largest share of services in the economy and already today a large share of trade in services as a result of the fact that large parts of the service sector are linked to industry. The EU's so-called Services Directive, which aims to make it easier for service companies to establish themselves and to perform temporary services in other Member States, has been questioned by several EU countries and it remains to be seen whether a solution can be found. Sweden is in favour of the Services Directive, but with changes that ensure that workers' rights and the Swedish collective agreement model are not eroded. Continued financial integration Let me now turn to another challenge  the impact of financial integration on supervision, depositor protection and crisis management. Swedish and Finnish banks currently jointly own over 95 percent of the banks' assets in Estonia and Lithuania. Integration has also spread to other parts of the financial system; The stock exchanges in Sweden, Finland, Denmark and all three Baltic countries are now merged into a single exchange, OMX. But this development is not unique to the northern part of Europe. There are currently 43 banks in Europe with extensive cross-border operations and all signs point to financial integration continuing within the EU. Foreign ownership of banks in the new Member States currently averages 70%, compared with 24% for the 15 'old' EU countries. In the insurance sector, too, foreign ownership is particularly evident in the new Member States, over 90% in several countries. This development means improved competition and thus better and cheaper services. However, the integration places new demands on us who work at various authorities with responsibility for regulations, etc. for the financial companies: supervisory authorities (such as the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority), central banks and ministries of finance. Companies operate according to "business lines", while the authorities still follow national borders. It is we as authorities who need to change the way we work to cope with the new challenges. We need to find new ways of supervising cross-border financial companies, to ensure that financial stability and efficiency are good and, not least, to be able to deal with financial crises. In the search for new forms of work, we must not forget that companies integrate across national borders because governments and parliaments have made it possible because it contributes to increasing competition and therefore more efficient companies and, ultimately, to higher growth. Let me start with the issue of supervision. Today, EU supervision is based on the so-called home country principle. This means that the country in which a bank has its legal seat is responsible for supervision, both by the parent bank and by its branches in other countries. Subsidiary banks, on the other hand, are provided by the host country, as they are banks with the approval of the host country's authorities. With this division of supervisory responsibilities, there is a risk that no one really has a particularly good picture of the entire banking group, which could lead to miscalculations of the banks' financial situation and risks. The development has also taken another step; banks are trying to streamline operations by specializing certain functions to a specific part of the bank, common examples are risk and liquidity management. As a result, the distinction between branches and subsidiaries has increasingly blurred, underlining the risk that supervisors will not take a sufficiently holistic view under the current rules. It The current regime means that the bank's choice of organisation governs where the supervisory responsibility lies. The EU is therefore now taking a first step towards "bringing together" supervision so that the home country authorities have a holistic view in their assessments of a bank. As I see it, it is a step in the right direction, but leaves some outstanding issues. It is a classic example of responsibility being different from competence, because even if the home country supervisor detects a problem that requires action in a subsidiary bank, it may be impossible for the home country to intervene in a subsidiary bank in another country. For the host country, too, the new regime could pose a dilemma; they remain responsible for safeguarding the stability of their financial systems, but responsibility for the supervision of the central companies, the banks, is partly handled by someone else. The unclear division of responsibilities and powers also risks complicating crisis management capabilities if a bank with cross-border operations encounters problems. During the summer, a step was taken to improve the joint ability to handle crises in cross-border financial firms; the 25 EU countries' finance ministries, central banks and supervisory authorities signed an agreement, a so-called Memorandum of Understanding, on the exchange of information in the event of financial crises. There is already a corresponding so-called. MoU between central banks and supervisory authorities in the EU. Within the Nordic region, there has been an agreement between central banks for a couple of years on cooperation in the event of a crisis in cross-border banking groups. Financial integration also poses new challenges for depositor protection, which I would like to touch on briefly. Today, on the basis of a directive, all EU countries have introduced depositor protection, which is exactly what it sounds like; in the event of a bank failure, the depositors' money is partially protected. In Sweden, amounts up to SEK 250,000 are guaranteed for transaction accounts. The only similarity between EU countries is that they have depositor protection systems, otherwise depositor protection differs in terms of scope, level and form of funding. This leads to shortcomings in both competitive neutrality and the ability to handle crises. A bank that wants to start operations in the form of a subsidiary in another country is then subject to different rules than in its home country. If the bank instead chooses to establish itself through branches, the rules of the home country apply, but they compete with the host country's banks. This may make things easier for the bank, but means that that bank's customers in branches in the host countries are covered by different protection than other bank customers in that country. It also means that the bank's choice of organizational form governs where the responsibility for the depositor guarantee lies. In my opinion, the different regulations could be obstacles to further integration. In addition, the current regime means a more complicated situation for the authorities involved in managing crises. No country's depositor protection has enough money to cover a major banking crisis. In the end, therefore, the responsibility for financing the depositor protections rests with each country's government as it may need to replenish the depositor guarantee by borrowing on behalf of the depositor guarantee authority. In the end, then, taxpayers are always at risk. And since depositor protection in the home country covers branches in other countries, the home country's taxpayers also bear the risk to the foreign depositors. And for the host country, the overall supervision now means that their ability to see the subsidiary banks is reduced, while retaining responsibility for depositor protection for them. These issues are now being discussed within the EU. I myself am convinced that it is possible to find solutions to these challenges, which involve both competitive neutrality, in order to stimulate further integration, and a strengthened capacity for crisis management. The introduction of the euro in the new Member States The entry of the new Member States into the EU is completed by the future introduction of the euro. At least four of them, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Slovenia, are, according to their own timetables, only a little over a year from the introduction of the euro. Even if Sweden has not adopted the euro, it is important for the Swedish economy how this process will develop, due to the importance of these countries as trading partners and also because Swedish banks are so deeply involved in the Baltic banking system. In a way, the Baltic states are already using the euro. Estonia and Lithuania have so-called euro currency currency, i.e. units of their own currency are only issued in the same amount as the euro exchanged, each unit's own currency thus has a backing in euros and its own currency is in practice a kind of "shadow euro". Latvia has a very close system. Euro currency board funds have contributed to a fall in inflation at low levels and to a stable investment climate. These economies have enjoyed high flexibility in wages and prices, thus being able to cope with situations where developments in the Baltic countries have deviated from those in the euro area, while public finances have been in relatively good order. The fact that they can now also introduce the euro itself is expected to bring additional benefits to trade and price comparisons. Of course, in order to be included in the monetary union and to adopt the euro, countries must fulfil all the so-called convergence criteria in the EU Treaty in a sustainable way. The economic convergence criteria concern public finances, interest rates, inflation and currency stability. With regard to the inflation criterion, the requirement is that inflation must not exceed that of the three EU countries with the best performance in terms of inflation. "Best performance" is interpreted as the lowest inflation (however, in practice countries with deflation are excluded). It may seem quite normal that countries should not be allowed to participate in the euro zone if they cannot keep inflation down, but here there is a dilemma. Countries with fixed exchange rates that grow faster than average, as the Baltic countries fortunately do, to some extent automatically experience higher inflationary pressures according to the so-called Balassa-Samuelson theorem. This theorem, very simply, means that high productivity and wage growth in the export sector pushes up wages in the less productive domestic services sector and thus inflation. Of course, other factors in the economy can hold back this inflationary impulse and cause overall inflation to be low anyway. At present, this is not the case, but inflation has increased through temporary effects of rising oil prices. Together, these effects have meant that the inflation upturn that came in, for example, the Baltic countries after eu entry, has not slowed down as quickly as expected. There is a risk here that this could delay the entry of several countries into the euro area, despite the fact that they have nevertheless had surprisingly low inflation rates given their high growth rates in GDP. In order to accommodate the current interpretation of the convergence requirement, countries would need to moderate their growth strongly in order to bring inflation down to line with the three EU countries with the lowest inflation rates The current interpretation of the convergence requirement for inflation is, in my view, questionable on economic grounds now that the euro has been introduced. It may be considered strange that the comparison is made with all EU countries when convergence should take place with the euro area countries. To single out three individual countries with the lowest inflation, I think, is also strange. After all, the goal is not to have as low inflation as possible. It would be more reasonable for the requirement to be close to the ECB's price stability objective, one part of which is now defined as just below 2% inflation as measured by the HICP. Several of the larger countries, Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, have a different situation in the run-up to joining the euro. In several of these countries, it is public finances that are the biggest problem with large budget deficits and, at least so far, not very ambitious consolidation. The large countries do not have currency board funds, but their currencies, like Sweden's, flow freely. In order to adopt the euro, they need to move to a fixed exchange rate regime within ERM2 to be approved for the requirement of currency stability. Weak public finances are not a good starting point for a currency peg like ERM2, which must constantly be credible in order to last (unlike a single currency that is credible because it simply cannot be changed). As we in Sweden experienced in the early 1990s, government finances in poor condition can erode the credibility of a fixed-rate regime and create expectations that the currency link will be released. If expectations are strong enough, they can become self-fulfilling, as they were in Sweden in 1992. The problem in several Central European countries is that public finances have deteriorated drastically in the early 2000s. Thus, if they were to peg their currency to the euro within ERM2 before public finances are in good shape, they could risk currency speculation. If the fixed-rate regime does not help to speed up fiscal consolidation, they risk remaining in the precarious position for a long time before they are approved for the introduction of the euro; another of the requirements for the introduction of the euro is precisely the maximum public deficit of 3%. Now the risk of premature entry into ERM2 seems to have decreased. The four largest new member states, led by the Czech Republic, have declared that public finances must be put in order before the process of entering the euro zone begins. New savings plans have been put in place to clean up public finances so that, after a few years, countries can take the next step towards the introduction of the euro and peg the currency ahead of the euro entry. However, it does not dispel all the concerns on the way to the euro. For example, it is not enough just to save so that, in a boom, the public budget deficit just reaches the requirement of 3% of GDP. The Stability Pact requires that the budget be kept at least close to balance over a business cycle. Above all, there must be margins in the budget to cope with situations when a country develops weaker than the euro area as a whole. Otherwise, the new countries risk ending up in Germany's or France's position today, saving in an economic downturn when the economy would really need to be stimulated. Therefore, the deficit in boom times should be significantly less than 3 percent, preferably instead be a surplus, so that there is "air above the bar" so that the budget deficit does not become greater than 3 percent when the economy is put to the test more severely in periods of low growth. Overall, there is concern that the pressure to put public finances in order will ease when the goal of introducing the euro is postponed. The future will tell whether the necessary fiscal consolidation is actually carried out as planned. I hope that this will be the case because it has value in itself, regardless of the introduction of the euro or not, because macroeconomic stability is the basis for good growth. Further enlargement The fourth major challenge, as I see it, is to take note of the success of enlargement and to continue to broaden the circle of EU Member States, as long as they meet the entry requirements of democracy and the market economy (the so-called Copenhagen criteria). Even if we take a narrow economic perspective and completely ignore the security policy and democratic dimension, it is clear that the possibility of entry into the EU motivated the countries to reform their economies  this is evident, for example, in the gap in economic reforms and the prosperity of the population between the Baltic states and Russia, between Romania and its neighbour Moldova. In addition, it is, of course, unreasonable to ignore the value, both economically and humanly, for both us in the old EU countries and the people of the new Member States, of the fact that the transformation from a planned economy and dictatorship to a market economy and democratic governance has taken place so quickly and peacefully. I believe that this is a clearly underestimated effect of the Eu ropean Union that its attractiveness has made this peaceful transformation possible in our neighbouring countries. Next in line are Bulgaria and Romania, which are scheduled to join in 2007. Their average income is well below the EU average. However, these two countries have made and continue to make strenuous efforts in recent years to reform their economies and meet EU requirements. Should this process be delayed because of political tactics to fulfil other purposes, what is sometimes referred to in Brussels by the strange term 'enlargment fatigue', progress would be jeopardised. In the next step, there are even greater potential members: Turkey, which has already formally started its negotiations, and Ukraine, which, after the "orange revolution", hopes to enter the EU as a democratic and free country. Several of the former Yugoslav republics are also next, closest to the relatively prosperous Croatia. Here, too, apart from all geopolitical considerations, the economic reform ambitions depend on the EU not closing the door. Ukraine's reform programme is still in its infancy, but those in favour of strong action have not benefited from the rejectionist attitude shown by the Eu ropean Union. The discussions that took place before the start of Turkey's EU accession negotiations illustrate the political complexity of the EU's further enlargement. Turkey, with its large population and cultural and religious differences from the current EU, obviously raises fears as to whether future cooperation will be made more difficult by full membership. The negotiations will probably take a long time, but already some quarters are signalling in countries that are now in the EU that the final accession treaty will require it to be supported in referendums  something that has never happened before in the EU. However, a crucial argument for still taking the step of starting negotiations for Turkish membership was precisely that this would constitute an important incentive for continued reform efforts in Turkey and create a politically safer development in what is today the EU's immediate area. Discussions on where the line is drawn for further enlargement of the EU will certainly continue. A particular reason for this is that enlargement is often set against deepening cooperation, where different Member States have quite different ambitions and visions. The recent failure of the Treaty establishing an EU Constitution was an attempt to manage a Union of more than 27 Member States, and so, after Bulgaria and Romania, the Treaty must in any case be revised in order to accommodate more members. Conclusion In the daily detailed discussion on common rules and further steps in integration within the EU, the overall perspective is often forgotten: that EU cooperation has helped to create new opportunities for people to operate and businesses to develop within the Union, that reunification is a great opportunity for higher growth both for us in the old Member States and in the new Member States - an opportunity that has already brought benefits to economic development.

I dagslget r det inte s utan inflationen har kat genom tillflliga effekter av stigande oljepriser. Tillsammans har dessa effekter, gjort att den inflationsuppgng som kom i t ex de baltiska lnderna efter i EUintrdet, inte avtagit s snabbt som frvntat. Det finns hr en risk fr att detta kan frdrja flera lnders intrde i euroomrdet trots att de nd haft frvnansvrt lg inflation med tanke p sina hga tillvxttakter i BNP. Lnderna skulle, fr att tillgodose den nu gllande tolkningen av konvergenskravet, behva dmpa sin tillvxt kraftigt fr att f ner inflationen till att vara i linje med de tre lnder i EU som har lgst inflation Den nuvarande tolkningen av konvergenskravet fr inflationen anser jag kan ifrgasttas p ekonomiska grunder nu nr euron vl r infrd. Det fr anses mrkligt att jmfrelsen grs med alla EU-lnder nr konvergensen br ske mot eurolnderna. Att singla ut tre enskilda lnder med lgst inflation, menar jag ocks r mrkligt. Mlet r ju inte att ha s lg inflation som mjligt. Mer rimligt vore att kravet skulle vara att vara nra ECB:s ml fr prisstabilitet vars ena del numera definieras som strax under 2 procents inflation mtt som HIKP. Flera av de strre lnderna, Polen, Tjeckien, Ungern och Slovakien har en annan situation infr eurointrdet. I flera av dessa lnder r det statsfinanserna som r det strsta problemet med stora budgetunderskott och tminstone hittills inte srskilt ambitis konsolidering. De stora lnderna har inte sedelfonder utan deras valutor flyter, likt Sveriges, fritt. Fr att infra euron behver de verg till en fastkursregim inom ERM2 fr att godknnas fr kravet p valutastabilitet. Svaga statsfinanser r inget bra utgngslge fr en valutaknytning som ERM2, som stndigt mste vara trovrdig fr att hlla (till skillnad frn en gemensam valuta som r trovrdig eftersom den helt enkelt inte gr att ndra). Som vi i Sverige fick erfara i brjan av 1990-talet kan statsfinanser i dligt skick urholka trovrdigheten fr en fastkursregim och skapa frvntningar om att valutaknytningen skall slppas. r frvntningarna tillrckligt starka kan de bli sjlvuppfyllande, som de blev i Sverige 1992. Problemet i flera centraleuropeiska lnder r att statsfinanserna frsmrats drastiskt i brjan av 2000-talet. Om de skulle knyta sin valuta till euron inom ERM2 innan statsfinanserna r i gott skick kan de allts riskera valutaspekulation. Om fastkursregimen inte skulle bidra till att skynda p budgetkonsolideringen riskerar de att bli kvar i den prekra sitsen lnge, innan de fr godknt fr euroinfrande; ett annat av kraven fr euroinfrande r ju just maximalt offentligt underskott p 3 procent. Nu tycks risken fr att ett alltfr tidigt intrde i ERM2 skall intrffa ha minskat. De fyra strsta nya medlemslnderna, med Tjeckien i spetsen, har frklarat att statsfinanserna mste komma i ordning innan processen fr att trda in i eurozonen pbrjas. Nya besparingsplaner har lagts fr att sanera statsfinanserna s att lnderna efter ngra r kan ta nsta steg mot euroinfrande och knyta valutan infr eurointrdet. Det skingrar dock inte alla orosmoln p vgen till euron. Det rcker t ex inte att bara spara s att det offentliga budgetunderskottet i en hgkonjunktur precis nr kravet p 3 procent av BNP. Stabilitetspakten stller krav p att hlla budgeten tminstone nra balans ver en konjunkturcykel. Framfrallt mste det finnas marginaler i budgeten fr att klara situationer nr ett land utvecklas svagare n euroomrdet i stort. Annars riskerar de nya lnderna att hamna i Tysklands eller Frankrikes sits idag, att spara i en konjunkturnedgng nr egentligen ekonomin skulle behvt stimuleras. Drfr br underskottet i hgkonjunktur vara betydligt mindre n 3 procent, grna i stllet vara ett verskott, s att det finns luft ver ribban s att budgetunderskottet inte blir strre n 3 procent nr ekonomin stlls p svrare prov i perioder med lg tillvxt. verlag finns det en oro fr att trycket att f ordning p statsfinanserna lttar nr mlet om att infra euron skjutits p framtiden. Framtiden fr utvisa om den ndvndiga budgetkonsolideringen verkligen genomfrs som planerat. Jag hoppas att det blir s eftersom den ju har ett vrde i sig oavsett euroinfrande eller ej eftersom makroekonomisk stabilitet r grunden fr en god tillvxt. Den fortsatta utvidgningen Den fjrde stora utmaningen, som jag ser det, r att ta fasta p framgngen fr utvidgningen och fortstta bredda kretsen av medlemslnder i EU, s lnge dessa uppfyller intrdeskraven p demokrati och marknadsekonomi (de s.k. Kpenhamnskriterierna). ven om vi tar ett snvt ekonomiskt perspektiv och helt bortser frn den skerhetspolitiska och demokratiska dimensionen r det uppenbart att mjligheten till intrde i EU motiverat lnderna att reformera sina ekonomier  detta r t ex tydligt i gapet i ekonomiska reformer och befolkningens vlstnd mellan baltstaterna och Ryssland, mellan Rumnien och grannen Moldavien. Drtill r det naturligtvis orimligt att bortse frn vrdet, bde ekonomiskt och mnskligt, fr bde oss i de gamla EU-lnderna och mnniskorna i de nya medlemslnderna, av att omvandlingen frn planekonomi och diktatur till marknadsekonomi och demokratiskt styrelseskick skett s snabbt och fredligt. Det menar jag r en klart underskattad effekt av EU att dess dragningskraft mjliggjort denna fredliga omvandling i vra grannlnder. Nrmast p tur str Bulgarien och Rumnien som planeras bli medlemmar 2007. Deras medelinkomst ligger lngt under EU:s snitt. Men dessa bda lnder har de senaste ren gjort och fortstter att gra kraftanstrngningar fr att reformera sina ekonomier och uppfylla EU:s krav. Skulle denna process frsenas p.g.a. politisk taktik fr att uppfylla andra syften, det som ibland i Bryssel benmns med den mrkliga termen enlargment fatigue, ventyras framstegen. I nsta steg finns nnu strre potentiella medlemmar: Turkiet som redan formellt startat sina frhandlingar och Ukraina, som efter den oranga revolutionen hoppas kunna trda in i EU som ett demokratiskt och fritt land. Flera av de tidigare jugoslaviska delrepublikerna str ocks p tur, nrmast det relativt vlmende Kroatien. ven hr hnger, bortsett frn alla geopolitiska hnsyn, de ekonomiska reformambitionerna p att EU inte stnger drren. Ukrainas reformprogram befinner sig nnu i sin linda, men de som frordar kraftfulla insatser har inte gynnats av den avvisande instllning som EU visat. De diskussioner som gde rum fre startskottet fr Turkiets frhandlingar om EUintrde illustrerar den politiska komplexiteten i EU:s fortsatta utvidgning. Turkiet, med sin stora befolkning samt kulturella och religisa skillnader i frhllande till det nuvarande EU, vcker uppenbarligen farhgor om det framtida samarbetet kommer att frsvras vid ett fullt medlemskap. Frhandlingarna kommer nog att ta lng tid, men redan signaleras frn en del hll i lnder som nu befinner sig i EU att det slutliga anslutningsfrdraget kommer att frutstta att det fr std i folkomrstningar  ngot som aldrig tidigare frekommit i EU. Ett avgrande argument fr att nd ta steget att inleda frhandlingar om ett turkiskt medlemskap var dock just att detta skulle utgra en viktig sporre fr fortsatta reformanstrngningar i Turkiet och skapa en politiskt tryggare utveckling i det som idag r EU:s nromrde. Diskussionerna om var grnsen gr fr EU:s fortsatta utvidgning kommer skert att fortstta. En srskild anledning till det r att utvidgning ofta stlls mot frdjupning av samarbetet, dr skilda medlemslnder har rtt olika ambitioner och visioner. Det nyligen havererade frdraget om en EU-konstitution innebar ett frsk att hantera en union med fler n 27 medlemslnder, och efter Bulgarien och Rumnien mste allts frdraget under alla omstndigheter ses ver fr att man skall kunna ta in fler medlemmar. Slutsats I den dagliga detaljdiskussionen om gemensamma regler och ytterligare steg i integrationen inom EU glms ofta det vergripande perspektivet bort: att EUsamarbetet bidragit till att skapa nya mjligheter fr mnniskor att verka och fretag att utvecklas inom unionen, att terfreningen r en stor mjlighet till hgre tillvxt bde fr oss i de gamla medlemslnderna och i de nya medlemslnderna - en mjlighet som redan inneburit frdelar fr den ekonomiska utvecklingen.
