Title: Swedish economy
text: Swedish economy Date: 1997-04-18 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Place: Equity and finance seminar in Pitea Let me begin by thanking you for allowing me to come here and talk about the Swedish economy. First of all, I shall put the current economic situation into a broader perspective. Next, I come to the way in which the price stability objective works. Finally, the current state of play is commented on. Perspectives on the Swedish economy In the early 1990s, the Swedish economy went through a deep crisis. Over three years, production fell by around 5 per cent. The open unemployment rate rose to nearly 9 percent. At the same time, general government finances weakened and the budget deficit peaked at just over 12 per cent of GDP. We also experienced severe problems in the banking sector. In order to put into perspective the causes of the economic crisis, it is important to put it in a wider context. During the 1950s and 1960s, the Swedish economy showed high and steady growth. At the same time, both inflation and unemployment were low. The state's finances and Sweden's business with foreign countries were in balance. But in the next two decades, the car-it changed radically. Several interacting factors contributed to this. 1. Exchange rate policy failed. The background is that Sweden was a member of the so-called Bretton Woods system for much of the post-war period, which was a system of fixed exchange rates. The crown was pegged to the dollar whose value, in turn, was based on that of gold. When the Bretton Woods system broke down in the early 1970s, it proved difficult to establish a fixed exchange rate regime with a corresponding statute. There was thus no longer a clear "anchor" for economic policy in general or for wage formation. Devaluation cycles followed each other, uncertainty increased, with consequences for investment, growth and employment, among others. 2. Poorly functioning wage formation. A major reason for the recurrent devaluations was problems with wage formation. Productivity growth slowed down and was not followed by a correspondingly lower rate of wage growth. Instead, there were tendencies toward increasing nominal wage increases as employees in different parts of the economy competed for the smaller wage space. In parallel, labour costs also rose as a result of increases in employers' social security contributions. 3. Weak fiscal policy. Government expenditure rose without the budget strengthening at the same rate and deficits arose. The state's debt therefore reached ever higher levels. 4. Many structural problems. The public sector grew rapidly. One effect was that the distortive effects of taxes and public expenditure on the economy increased. Some sectors were heavily regulated such as housing and agriculture. In both sectors, the subsidy element was also high. Competition was also weak in other parts of the economy. This was the case, for example, in parts of the trade in goods and, until at least the mid-1980s, also in the financial sector. 5. The liberalisation of the financial sector reinforced imbalances in the short term. Indebtedness of both firms and households increased dramatically in the second half of the 1980s. Monetary policy was tied up by the fixed exchange rate and, there-not, dampened developments. It also proved difficult to bring about fiscal-political austerity. The end result was that Swedish growth weakened in relation to developments in other countries. Nevertheless, the economy overheated, which, together with the expansion of public activity, temporarily held back unemployment. However, the development was not sustainable. An inflationary and speculative bubble cannot become as big as it gets without it bursting sooner or later. Similarly, the scope for additional publicly funded employment was limited. Towards the end of the 1980s, the Swedish economy was also in need of structural changes. A change of policy became inevitable. However, the downturn was deeper than anyone imagined, largely due to the fact that the imbalances in the economy had to build up for so long and that the changes coincided with weak international development. Reorienting economic policy The 1970s and 1980s are an illustration of how an inflationary period leads to an uncertain and unstable economic environment. Inflation often also leads to a speculative climate and to short-term economic thinking. Step by step, in this way, long-term production conditions deteriorate. High and rising inflation is due to households and firms becoming accustomed to ever-rising prices, as well as underlying tensions between demand and the productive capacity of the economy. Such a development requires measures to avoid setbacks in economic development. If economic policy reacts too late to various warning signs - as was the case in the second half of the 1980s - tensions have time to become high and negative repercussions on growth and employment threaten. This is the grim experience we have experienced after the longest inflationary period in Swedish history since the early 1800s. An economic policy geared towards low and stable inflation cannot prevent cyclical fluctuations. On the other hand, such a policy can contribute to a more sustainable development. Experience also suggests that production will increase over time, as a more stable environment facilitates the financial planning of households and businesses and stimulates productive investment. It was against this background, among other things, that Swedish economic policy was changed in the shift between the 1980s and 1990s. The focus on price stability has gradually gained broad support in Swedish society and among political parties in the Swedish Parliament. 60 percent of Swedes think it is right to have 2 percent inflation as a target for monetary policy, while only 12 percent are negative. The Riksdag has stated that there is general support for the value of price stability and that such a focus provides the conditions for growth and employment. The government has explicitly supported the Riksbank's target of 2 per cent inflation. However, the severe economic problems at the start of the 1990s, the memories of the inflationary years and the large budget deficits made it difficult to quickly establish credibility for the new economic policy line. This has been shown from time to time, among other things, in the form of turbul-lens in the fixed income and foreign exchange markets. Developments in the financial markets can, in the slightly longer term, be seen as a gauge of the confidence that exists in the will and ability to pursue a consistent and stability-oriented economic policy. Experience from other countries shows that it takes time and effort to build confidence in a low-inflation regime. Efforts to keep inflation low and the state's finances in order is a process that never ends if the aim is to have low interest rates, a stable currency and ultimately favourable growth and good employment. Decisive policy After the crown began to float in the fall of 1992, it weakened significantly. The depreciation, as is usually said when the exchange rate is variable, gave a strong demand impulse to primarily the export-oriented sectors of our country. The result was not long in coming. For a couple of years, we had one of the strongest upturns in the industrial economy that Sweden has experienced in a long time. Short-term and long-term market interest rates fell, which contributed to other parts of Swedish business being able to increase their production as well. However, this happened to a much lesser extent than in the sectors that benefited from the weak krona. The economy was divided into two parts, but the growth figures overall were probably stronger than many noted. Credit losses declined and the banking sector emerged from the crisis. During the first half of 1994, the credibility of Swedish economic policy deteriorated again. There was growing concern that the old pattern would once again make itself felt. Fiscal consolidation was insufficient. Inflationary tendencies began to emerge. Would the economic upturn once again be allowed to result in an inflation bubble? In other words, would we have a repeat and a continuation of what regularly happened in the 1970s and 1980s, with the risk of subsequent setbacks for growth and employment? During the summer of 1994, more and more people began to expect rising inflation again. In addition, the long-term interest rate rose in the spring from just under 7 to almost 12 percent. The krona's share price continued to weaken as a confirmation of inflation uncertainty. The pass-through of increases in import prices at the consumer price level began to increase. In addition, inflationary pressures in industry became more pronounced. Cost awareness waned and the likelihood of a difficult collective bargaining process increased. (Something that we also got when multi-year contracts were signed in the spring of 1995 at a far too high level). In other words, more and more elements in the patterns of the 1970s and 1980s could be discerned. In that situation, a passive economic policy would have confirmed the fears and meant a continuation in the old rut. Economic policy was thus at a crossroads. It was either a question of confirming past patterns or of consistently pursuing a stability-oriented policy and breaking with the old experience. The government, the Riksdag and the Riksbank chose to show determination. The government and parliament worked to get public finances in order. This led, via a number of "savings packages", eventually to the convergence programme, which was presented before the summer of 1995. The objective of this programme is to bring public finances into balance by 1998. The programme is followed up semi-annually. In addition, in the 1997 Spring Economic Bill, the government states that the long-term objective of budgetary policy should be a general government surplus of 2% of GDP on average over a business cycle. It also specifies how the gradual adjustment to this is to take place. The Riksbank started from the situation in force in mid-1994. Given the inflation risks that existed, it was necessary to establish higher key interest rates to show that the price stability objective was serious. In mid-August 1994, therefore, the repo rate was raised. This gradually increased the likelihood that the old pattern would not be repeated. Inflation remained at a low level and confidence increased step by step that this would also be the case for a long time to come. Easing interest rate policy It is the stronger government finances and the break with the history of inflation, which have been behind the lower market interest rates in recent years. The starting point for the future is therefore different and better now compared to the corresponding phases of the economic cycle in the 1970s and 1980s. In simple terms, the reasons for the easing of interest rate policy in 1996 were the favourable outlook for inflation going forward. Continuous falls in inflation expectations as well as subdued demand conditions gradually improved the inflation outlook for 1997 and 1998. The repo rate was lowered from 8.91% to 4.1% in 1996. This is the lowest level of the policy rate in over 30 years. The interest rate policy of recent years is a clear illustration of how monetary policy works with a price stability objective under a floating exchange rate regime. The more negative inflation forecasts generally made in mid-1994 meant that it was necessary to start a period of increases in the key interest rate. The sooner monetary policy reacts, the less interest rates need to be raised. Now that the inflation outlook has improved, the repo rate has been lowered. If the price stability objective is met, there is a basis for stable and sustainable growth and employment. If there is confidence in low inflation policy, there is also room for monetary policy to contribute in the short term to supporting the recovery in the Swedish economy. Prisstabilitetsmalet On Tuesday, Statistics Sweden published the consumer price index for March. The statistics showed that the level of consumer prices had fallen by 0.4 per cent. Does this mean, then, that the Riksbank has undercut its monetary policy target? Before answering that question, it's important to see how the goal works. 1. The price stability objective implies inflation at 2%, with an upward and downward tolerance of 1 percentage point. 2. The target should be seen in a slightly longer, annual perspective and thus not as a single monthly figure. 3. Furthermore, it is important to distinguish between underlying inflation and consumer price index developments. Temporary effects such as changes in interest rates or indirect taxes and subsidies can cause the general price level to jump up or down. It is therefore important to monitor underlying inflation in the implementation of monetary policy. Temporary effects play a subordinate role to the extent that they do not affect inflation expectations and thus underlying inflation. The tolerance range aims, among other things, to capture the most common temporary effects. Formally, the price stability objective has been undercut even if inflation is measured in a longer-term perspective, but not in a real sense. The weak development of the consumer price index is not due to the fact that monetary policy has previously been too tight and that the repo rate has been too high, but on the contrary, mainly because the repo rate was lowered so sharply last year. When homeowners convert their loans at a lower interest rate, a temporarily reducing effect on inflation arises. However, the most recent monthly figures for the consumer price index mean that underlying inflation has come down to around 1 per cent. If it falls further and then remains there for a long time, then you can talk about the price stability objective being undercut in a more real sense. However, neither the Riksbank nor any other economic assessor believe this. The current situation Let me now turn to the inflation outlook for the next few years by addressing: The Riksbank's latest inflation report and something about what has happened since then. In order to explain as openly and clearly as possible how the Riksbank analyses the future inflation outlook and looks at the structure of monetary policy, we publish special reports four times a year. The analyses in the inflation reports serve as a basis for the council's monetary policy discussion and the conclusions of this discussion are also regularly presented in a separate chapter. The latest Inflation Report, published in March, estimated GDP growth to be 2% and 3% respectively for 1997 and 1998. Furthermore, it was stressed that no more significant capacity constraints should arise during the period. Given that households and firms continue to expect continued low inflation, domestic underlying inflation (as measured by consumer price index developments adjusted for temporary effects on inflation) was estimated to be between 1.5 and 2 per cent in two years' time with unchanged monetary policy. As we all know, forecasting economic and price developments is not easy. Since such assessments cannot be made with great accuracy, it is rather a matter of weighing risks and opportunities. The Riksbank's latest inflation report therefore discussed two side options and in which situations inflation could be both lower and higher than in the main scenario in the future. In the first option, inflation could be lower than in the main scenario, owing to weaker consumption developments. In the second option, the opposite was true, inflation could be higher. The reason could be a weaker krona development, which entails faster export growth and GDP development and thus higher inflationary pressures. So far, what trends can be discerned in economic statistics? Simply put, on the one hand, it could be said that exports appear to be developing somewhat better than expected, even if the deviations are not so great. On the other hand, the signals of private consumption suggest a development either in line with the main scenario or a somewhat weaker course. This past winter saw signs of a slowdown in the industrial economy. The NIER's December barometer gave the picture of stagnant new orders and subdued production expectations. Statistics Sweden's order statistics, which show fairly large variations between the months, showed that order intake was relatively weak during the 4th quarter. During December and January, however, order intake has increased. Recent barometer-type studies have also shown a brighter picture of the industrial economy. It is mainly the export side that has been responsible for the improvement, although there is also some optimism about future developments in the domestic market as well. Against this background, export developments and industrial production could develop somewhat better than previous estimates. The changes are not so big, but various indicators, including the still undervalued krona, are still pointing in the same direction so far. The indicators of private consumption are so far not unambiguous. On the one hand, the number of new registrations on private individuals has increased by more than 60% year-on-year in the first three months of the year, although from a low level. Statistics Sweden's (SCB) survey on households' purchasing plans also shows that expectations about their own economy have shifted in a positive direction since last autumn. The development of banknotes and coins in circulation also indicates rising private consumption. On the other hand, Statistics Sweden's retail sales statistics and quick index from the Swedish Trade Research Institute indicate that retail sales performed relatively weakly during the 1st quarter. The weaker labour market may also suggest slower growth in private consumption. Actual cyclical developments form a basis for the assessments of future supply and demand conditions in the economy, which, together with inflation expectations, form the basis for the inflation forecast, which in turn guides the structure of monetary policy. The latest Inflation Report concluded that monetary policy is well balanced. It must be borne in mind that major changes have this has taken place in, among other things, the repo rate during the past year and time is needed to evaluate the effect of these and how the economy as a whole develops. Conclusion In recent years, the adjustment to a low-inflation economy has come a long way. The whole economy is gradually adjusting to the conditions that prevail in such an environment. Inflation is low and government finances are steadily improving. There also seems to be some new thinking on the part of the social partners. Let us hope that this new thinking goes so far that employment can also increase and unemployment can fall in the next few years. Overall, since the summer of 1993, the economy has grown faster on average than in the inflationary years of the 1970s and 80s. The fact that we had a temporary slowdown last year is not an unusual phenomenon in the business cycle when companies temporarily trim their inventories. This year and next year, most indications are that growth will pick up again. There is a possibility that growth in the future will be more stable in the long term than we have previously been used to. This is also what characterises a low-inflation economy based on disciplined economic policies.

De temporra effekterna spelar nmligen en underordnad roll i den mn de inte pverkar inflationsfrvntningarna och drmed den underliggande inflationen. Toleransintervallet syftar bl.a. till att fnga upp de vanligaste temporra effekterna. Title: Swedish economy and wage formation
text: Swedish economy and wage formation Date: 1997-05-22 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: SAF Annual Meeting Introduction First of all, I would like to thank you for the invitation to come here and discuss the Swedish economy and wage formation. It is an urgent subject. Although the economy has improved step by step in recent years, the still high unemployment rate shows that the labour market is not functioning satisfactorily. Total output has recovered from the decline at the beginning of the decade and is now at a higher level than in the previous peak year of 1990. GDP has also grown faster in recent years than we have been used to in the 1970s and 1980s. Moreover, the upturn in industrial output has been the largest since the early 1960s. Yet employment, measured by the number of people, is at its lowest level since 1974. An employment gap has emerged. In other words, Sweden is experiencing what characterizes many other Western European countries, jobless growth, i.e. growth without employment. Weak employment and persistently high unemployment are, as I see it, mainly due to wage formation - because it is precisely price formation that is the central market mechanism. However one looks at the causes of high unemployment, the functioning of the labour market and the climate between the social partners play an important role in reversing the trend. In other words, the role of the Swedish Employers' Association in this area is important. As Governor of the Riksbank, it is important for me to discuss the labour market and wage formation for several reasons. First, too high wage increases can fuel the inflation process  and fighting inflation is a central bank's most important task. Secondly, it is important to explain what monetary policy can and cannot do to contribute to growth and employment. Most people today believe that it is not possible to achieve a permanently low unemployment rate by accepting high inflation. Demand policy must be adapted to what the economy has the long-term ability to produce. If structural unemployment has risen - and there are many indications that this has happened in Sweden, measures must be aimed at bringing it down. This is something that is beyond the reach of monetary policy. Thirdly, favourable employment and unemployment developments help to increase long-term confidence in a low-inflation regime. Conversely, a poorly functioning labour market can affect the views of savers and investors regarding the sustainability of the low-inflation regime and thus the stability of long-term interest rates and exchange rates. One could also put it that macroeconomic stability is facilitated by microeconomic flexibility. Wage formation in focus The labour market, like the economy at large, has long been characterised by rapid transformation. Manual labour in industry has been replaced by machines and competition from countries with significantly lower wage levels has increased. In Sweden, this has been met with an expansion of both the private and public service sectors. Jobs have become fewer in industry and more in the private and public service sectors. However, for many decades there have been no net jobs in the private sector. Employment expansion has been borne entirely by the public sector, where one million new jobs were created between 1960 and 1990. Now that the political system has been forced to break the expansion in the public sector for various reasons, employment has declined overall. The process in western industrialised countries towards so-called deindustrialisation is generally a sign of successful economic development and rising living standards. 'Deindustrialisation' means a development in which the number of jobs in industry stagnates or even decreases as a result of rapid productivity development. This process has long been going on in "old" industrialized countries. More recently, the same tendency is also visible in "new" industrialized countries. As the share of industrial jobs in total employment becomes smaller, productivity developments in the industrial sector will become less and less important for the economy as a whole. Productivity developments, and therefore real wage developments, are increasingly dependent on conditions in the services sector, where average productivity growth is lower. For some countries, the reduction in the number of industrial jobs could create problems if the service sector does not expand and can employ those who are made redundant. The speed of deindustrialisation and the degree of expansion in the services sector are determined, among other things, by the way in which wage formation operates. The changed conditions on the labour market therefore place demands on wage formation in order for the dismantling of old jobs to be met with the development of new ones. Although good real wage growth is desirable, the average real wage trend cannot be higher than creating a balance between the process of dismantling old jobs and creating new ones. Wage developments must also take into account productivity developments in different sectors and sectors. In the US, average real wages overall have increased by 15% over the last 25 years, while they have risen by as much as 60% in the EU. The trend in employment has been reversed; A 60% increase in the US compared with 15% in the EU. It says something about the importance of wage formation for jobs. A particular problem on the European labour market - and at least so far also on the Swedish market - is that it does not seem that an increase in unemployment will lead to wage growth being held back. One explanation may be that the unemployed in practice have a very limited influence in wage negotiations. Instead of a moderate rate of wage growth with lower costs for companies and the possibility of an increased number of employees, wage increases remain high and unemployment high. A spectacular example is the construction sector in Sweden. Unemployment in this area is well over 20%. Yet wages there are increasing almost in line with the average for wage earners as a whole. This is an illustration of what economists call the theory of "insiders" and "outsiders" in the labor market. It is beyond the reach of monetary policy to eliminate the effects of a lack of wage formation and the structural unemployment it leads to. On the other hand, it is something that can be very much influenced by the social partners - i.e. representatives of both employers and employees. The free negotiations, which are based on a long Swedish tradition, mean that the parties are responsible for wage formation in free negotiations. One problem is that the parties do not bear the costs in full of the consequences of poorly functioning wage formation. The 1995 wage round must reasonably be described as yet another failure. Despite a very high unemployment rate for Sweden, wage increases were negotiated that drove up costs for companies and forced new rationalizations and discouraged new hires. Employment fell and unemployment increased. Certainly, there is a great deal of innovation in the area of wage formation. But the intended wage formation standard seems to be to negotiate wage increases at a Western European level and even there we are not yet. Has no one considered that it could also lead to a permanentisation of unemployment at a Western European level? From cooperation to breakdown In 1938, the so-called Saltsjobad agreement was added. Sweden was characterized by organizational skills, pragmatism, cooperation and firm rules of the game. To this, in 1938, a positive climate of cooperation in the labor market was formalized. It is likely that the Saltsjobad agreement itself was a reflection of the prevailing order with a clear insight on both sides of the realities of the economy. During the 1920s and 30s, the Swedish economy and its labour market had experienced great difficulties. Unemployment reached very high levels in the early 1930s. There was great insight that wage formation played an important role in reversing the trend. The results were not long in coming. As soon as the war was over, the Swedish economy underwent a very successful economic development in the following decades. Inflation was low, growth was high, and the prevailing labor peace brought great benefits. The unemployment of the 1930s turned into full employment. Saltsjobadsandan's most important element was consensus and respect for the other party. Workers and employers negotiated with each other in a spirit where costs and revenues were weighed against each other on both sides. SAF's Bertil Kugelberg has consequently also described LO's August Lindberg with great respect and full of admiration for his character and personality. At the beginning of the 1970s, the consensus was broken. There were several different explanations for that. One of these was the collapse of the so-called Bretton Woods cooperation in the field of currency between the world's industrialised countries. During the post-war period until the beginning of the 1970s, this monetary system had fully regulated not only the scope for Swedish stabilization policy, but also served as a clear benchmark for wage formation and consensus in the labor market. After the collapse, it proved difficult to establish a fixed exchange rate regime with the corresponding charter. There was no longer a clear "anchor" for economic policy as a whole or for wage formation. Various attempts were made to restore the old spirit and responsibility, but it turned out not to work. The reasons for this were many, one of which was that the underlying consensus was lacking. It is not possible to cooperate for the sake of cooperation. There must be a set of common insights. The unclear stabilization policy regime probably did its part. The 1970s and 80s meant that devaluation cycles followed each other, fiscal policy was expansionary, structural problems built up and wage formation worked very poorly. By the mid-1980s, the liberalisation of the financial sector came and this gradually made the economic problems obvious. Swedish growth weakened during the 1970s and 1980s in relation to developments in other countries. Nevertheless, the economy overheated, which, together with the continued expansion of the public sector, temporarily - and I would like to emphasise temporarily - held back unemployment. The problems with the poorly functioning wage formation and the economy's other problems were hidden and too many were lulled into the belief that inflation and overexpansion had made the Swedish economy immune to the laws of the economy. The development turned out not to be sustainable. An inflationary and speculative bubble cannot be inflated indefinitely. Sooner or later it cracks. Similarly, the scope for publicly funded employment was limited. The problems could no longer be hidden. In the late 1980s, the Swedish economy was in dire need of change. The process led to a deep crisis in the early 1990s. Over three years, output decreased by around 5 per cent. Open unemployment rose to almost 9 percent and the total to about 13 percent, which are figures that have been completely foreign to modern Sweden. Public finances weakened sharply, partly as a result of the enormous costs of rapidly rising unemployment. The budget deficit peaked at just over 12 percent of GDP - a figure that was almost unique in the industrialized Western world. In the midst of the crisis, there was also a time when almost the entire banking system was in danger of collapse. A new direction of economic policy Towards the end of the 1980s, it thus became obvious that Swedish economic policy had to be changed. Structural changes and a return to the old stabilization policy regime with low inflation were characteristic of the reorientation of economic policy. However, the extensive economic problems made it difficult to quickly establish credibility for the new economic policy line. The road was lined with the vagaries and doubts of the economic actors. Still in the memory are the spectacular currency turmoil in the autumn of 1992, the dramatic rise in long-term interest rates in the spring and summer of 1994 and also the failed wage round in the spring of 1995. However, the government, parliament and the Riksbank showed perseverance and determination through the work to consolidate public finances and through a relatively tight interest rate policy focused on price stability. This eventually led to a growing credibility for the new economic policy regime. Since the autumn of 1995, we have been able to observe a sharp fall in interest rates, a more stable exchange rate and tendencies towards innovation on the part of the social partners. The Riksbank's inflation target has received clear support from the political system and society at large. This, in combination with the work to achieve healthier state finances, means a return to the stabilization policy regime that was long characteristic of Swedish tradition. I am thinking not only of the time when the Saltsjobad agreement came into being and the time after the Second World War until the beginning of the 1970s, but also of the conditions that prevailed during the many decades when today's prosperity was founded. As early as 1830, the Riksdag decided that the Swedish currency should be pegged to a silver standard. It was replaced in 1863 by a gold standard and after World War II by the Bretton Woods system. For more than 100 years, the crown was thus tied to gold, with the exception of the war periods and the depression of the 1930s. The low inflation rate of an average of 2% during this period provided a stable basis for the emerging prosperity. A five-party agreement has been reached on new legislation for the Riksbank. These proposals will further enhance the credibility of the new stabilisation policy regime. The settlement reflects a willingness on the part of the political system to return to what once proved to be a successful Swedish tradition, which led to low inflation, a better functioning economy and thus the opportunity for favorable growth and employment. An independent and independent Riksbank, as it is usually called, does not mean that monetary policy is placed out of democratic control. On the contrary, such legislation entails a clear delegation of the design of monetary policy within the framework of a goal decided under democratic forms by the Riksbank's principal, the Riksdag. It is important to realise that such a delegation of monetary policy to an independent central bank is a way of creating confidence that the policies that the state authorities want to pursue will also be pursued. New spirit of cooperation in the labour market? With a return to the old Swedish tradition of stabilization policy regime, the question arises of how cooperation between the social partners will be shaped in the future. The old spirit of cooperation was abandoned when the stabilisation regime collapsed in the early 1970s. Now that a similar stabilisation policy regime is being re-established, what degree of consensus will then characterise social relations. After all, the freedom to reach agreements is reasonably based on also taking greater responsibility for the consequences that the agreements entail. Is there a common view of the fundamental links that underpin a well-functioning market economy? As Governor of the Riksbank, I cannot, of course, comment in detail on how such a possible spirit of cooperation should be developed. On the other hand, I can allow myself to hope for the same kind of respect and esteem that characterized the interaction between the parties after the Saltsjobad agreement and that the same spirit can be created where costs and revenues were weighed against each other on both sides. The Netherlands is one of the few Western European countries where employment has risen and unemployment has fallen over the past decade. An important part of the successful development in the Netherlands in the field of labour market is the developed common understanding between the partners. In a clear way, employment is clearly prioritised in wage formation. It has also paid off, not only in terms of high and sustained economic growth, but also in a marked upturn in employment and a fall in unemployment. The contribution of monetary policy to better wage formation The Riksbank will make its contribution to better functioning wage formation by striving for a stable inflation rate at the level set by its inflation target, which can be characterised as a good European level. It increases predictability in the economy and reduces uncertainty in decision-making.

Det r ett angelget mne. Trots att ekonomin frbttrats steg fr steg under de senaste ren, visar den alltjmt hga arbetslsheten att arbetsmarknaden inte fungerar tillfredsstllande. Totalproduktionen har terhmtat fallet frn nedgngen i brjan av decenniet och ligger nu p en hgre niv n vid det tidigare toppret 1990. Uppgngen i industriproduktionen har dessutom varit den strsta sedan brjan av 1960-talet. nd ligger sysselsttningen, mtt i antalet personer, p den lgsta nivn sedan 1974. Det har uppsttt ett sysselsttningsgap. Sverige upplever med andra ord det som karaktriserar mnga andra vsteuropeiska lnder, jobless growth, dvs tillvxt utan sysselsttning. En svag sysselsttning och en varaktigt hg arbetslshet har sin grund, som jag ser det, framfr allt i lnebildningen - eftersom just prisbildningen r den centrala marknadsmekanismen. Hur man n ser p orsakerna till den hga arbetslsheten spelar arbetsmarknadens funktionsstt och klimatet mellan parterna p arbetsmarknaden en viktig roll fr att vnda utvecklingen. Svenska Arbetsgivarefreningens roll inom detta omrde r med andra ord viktig. Det r fr mig som Riksbankschef viktigt att diskutera arbetsmarknad och lnebildning av flera skl. Fr det frsta kan fr hga lnekningar driva p inflationsprocessen - och inflationsbekmpning r en centralbanks viktigaste uppgift. Fr det andra r det viktigt att frklara vad penningpolitiken kan och inte kan gra fr att bidra till tillvxt och sysselsttning. De flesta anser idag att det inte gr att uppn en varaktigt lg arbetslshet genom att acceptera en hg inflation. Efterfrgepolitiken mste anpassas till vad ekonomin lngsiktigt har frmga att producera. Om den strukturella arbetslsheten stigit - och mycket talar fr att det har skett i Sverige mste tgrder inriktas p att f ned den. Det r ngot som ligger utom rckhll fr penningpolitiken. Fr det tredje bidrar en gynnsam utveckling av sysselsttning och arbetslshet till att ka det lngsiktiga frtroendet fr en lginflationsregim. Omvnt kan en dligt fungerande arbetsmarknad pverka synen hos sparare och investerare vad gller uthlligheten i lginflationsregimen och drmed stabiliteten i lnga rntor och valutakurs. Man skulle ocks kunna uttrycka det som att makroekonomisk stabilitet underlttas av mikroekonomisk flexibilitet. Lnebildningen i fokus Arbetsmarknaden har lnge prglats, liksom ekonomin i stort, av snabb omvandling. Manuella arbeten inom industrin har ersatts med maskiner och konkurrensen frn lnder med betydligt lgre lneniv har kat. I Sverige har detta mtts med en expansion av svl privat som offentlig tjnstesektor. Jobben har blivit frre i industrin och fler i privat och offentlig tjnstesektor. Det har dock under mnga decennier inte blivit fler arbetstillfllen netto i den privata sektorn. Sysselsttningsexpansionen har helt och hllet burits upp av den offentliga sektorn, dr en miljon nya jobb skapades mellan 1960 och 1990. Nr nu det politiska systemet av olika skl tvingats bryta expansionen i den offentliga sektorn har sysselsttningen totalt sett minskat. Processen i de vstliga industrilnderna mot en s.k. avindustrialisering r allmnt sett ett tecken p en framgngsrik ekonomisk utveckling och stigande levnadsstandard. Med "avindustrialisering" menas en utveckling dr antalet arbetstillfllen inom industrin stagnerar eller rentav minskar till fljd av en snabb produktivitetsutveckling. Denna process har lnge pgtt i "gamla" industrilnder. P senare tid syns samma tendens ocks i "nya" industrilnder. I takt med att industrijobbens andel av total sysselsttning blir mindre kommer produktivitetsutvecklingen i industrisektorn att bli allt mindre betydelsefull fr ekonomin i stort. Produktivitetsutvecklingen och drmed reallneutvecklingen blir i vxande utstrckning beroende av frhllandena i tjnstesektorn, dr den genomsnittliga produktivitetsutvecklingen r lgre. Fr en del lnder kan minskningen av antalet industrijobb skapa problem om servicesektorn inte expanderar och kan anstlla de som fristlls. Hastigheten i avindustrialiseringen och graden av expansion i tjnstesektorn bestms bl.a. av lnebildningens stt att fungera. De ndrade frutsttningarna p arbetsmarknaden stller drfr krav p lnebildningen fr att avvecklingen av gamla jobb skall kunna mtas med utveckling av nya. ven om en god reallneutveckling r nskvrd kan inte den genomsnittliga reallneutvecklingen vara hgre n att det skapas en balans mellan den process som innebr att gamla jobb avvecklas och nya kommer till. Lneutvecklingen mste ven beakta produktivitetsutvecklingen i skilda branscher och sektorer. I USA har de genomsnittliga reallnerna totalt sett kat med 15 procent under de senaste 25 ren, medan de stigit med hela 60 procent i EU. Utvecklingen av sysselsttningen har varit den omvnda; 60 procents kning i USA mot 15 procent i EU. Det sger ngot om lnebildningens betydelse fr jobben. Ett srskilt problem p den europeiska arbetsmarknaden - och i vart fall hittills ven p den svenska - r att det inte verkar som om en kning av arbetslsheten leder till att lneutvecklingen hlls tillbaka. En frklaring kan vara att de arbetslsa i praktiken har ett mycket begrnsat inflytande i lnefrhandlingarna. Istllet fr en terhllsam lnekningstakt med lgre kostnader fr fretagen och mjlighet till ett kat antal anstllda, frblir lnekningarna hga och arbetslsheten hg. Ett spektakulrt exempel r byggsektorn i Sverige. Arbetslsheten inom detta omrde ligger en bra bit ver 20 procent. nd kar lnerna dr nra nog i takt med genomsnittet fr lntagarna i stort. Detta r en illustration p vad ekonomerna kallar fr teorin om "insiders" och "outsiders" p arbetsmarknaden. Det ligger utom rckhll fr penningpolitiken att eliminera effekterna av en bristande lnebildning och den strukturella arbetslshet den leder till. Dremot r det ngot som i allra hgsta grad kan pverkas av arbetsmarknadens parter - dvs fretrdare fr bde arbetsgivare och arbetstagare. De fria frhandlingarna som bygger p en lng svensk tradition innebr att parterna har ansvaret fr lnebildningen i fria frhandlingar. Ett problem r att parterna inte br kostnaderna fullt ut av konsekvenserna av en dligt fungerande lnebildningen. Avtalsrrelsen 1995 mste rimligen betecknas som nnu ett misslyckande. Trots en fr svenskt vidkommande mycket hg arbetslshet frhandlades lnekningar fram som drev upp kostnaderna fr fretagen och tvingade fram nya rationaliseringar och motverkade nyanstllningar. Sysselsttningen minskade och arbetslsheten kade. Frvisso sker det en hel del nytnkande p lnebildningsomrdet. Men den tnkta lnebildningsnormen tycks vara att frhandla fram lnekningar p en vsteuropeisk niv och inte ens dr r vi nnu. S snart kriget var ver genomgick svensk ekonomi under de fljande decennierna en mycket lyckosam ekonomisk utveckling. En ny inriktning av den ekonomiska politiken Mot slutet av 1980-talet blev det slunda uppenbart att svensk ekonomisk politik mste lggas om. Strukturella frndringar och ett tervndande till den gamla stabiliseringspolitiska regimen med lg inflation var knnetecknande fr omlggningen av den ekonomiska politiken. De omfattande ekonomiska problemen gjorde det dock svrt att snabbt skapa trovrdighet fr den nya ekonomisk-politiska linjen. Vgen kantades av tevksamhet och tvivel hos ekonomins aktrer. Regering, riksdag och Riksbank visade dock uthllighet och beslutsamhet genom arbetet med att konsolidera de offentliga finanserna och genom en relativt stram rntepolitik inriktad p prisstabilitet. Det ledde s smning om fram till en vxande trovrdighet fr den nya ekonomisk-politiska regimen. Jag tnker d inte bara p den tid som gllde d Saltsjbadsavtalet kom till och tiden efter det andra vrldskriget fram till brjan av 1970-talet utan ocks p de frhllanden som var frhrskande under de mnga decennier d dagens vlstnd grundlades. Dessa frslag kommer att ytterligare ka trovrdigheten fr den nya stabiliseringspolitiska regimen. En, som det brukar heta, oberoende och sjlvstndig Riksbank innebr inte att penningpolitiken stlls utom demokratisk kontroll. Tvrtom innebr en sdan lagstiftning en tydlig delegering av penningpolitikens utformning inom ramen fr ett ml som beslutats under demokratiska former av Riksbankens huvudman riksdagen. Det r viktigt att inse att en sdan delegering av penningpolitiken till en sjlvstndig centralbank r ett stt att skapa frtroende fr att den politik som statsmakterna vill fra ocks kommer att bedrivas. Ny samarbetsanda p arbetsmarknaden? Med en tergng till den gamla svenska traditionen nr det gller stabiliseringspolitisk regim uppstr frgan om hur samarbetet mellan arbetsmarknadens parter skall formas framver. Den gamla samarbetsandan vergavs nr den stabiliseringspolitiska regimen brt samman i brjan av 1970-talet. Title: Swedish economy and monetary policy
text: Swedish economy and monetary policy Date: 1997-11-19 Speaker: Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Stora Aktiekvallen, Stockholm Thank you for the invitation to Stora Aktiekvallen. In my speech today, I will discuss the structure of monetary policy and developments in the Swedish economy. The Riksbank protects the value of money The Riksbank manufactures and distributes money. Moreover, it is our task to preserve their value - we safeguard the value of money. If the Riksbank spends too much money, in practice setting the repo rate lower than is compatible with the national economic balance, inflation threatens. Conversely, if the Riksbank spends too little money, i.e. sets the repo rate too high, the result could be deflation. Both inflation and deflation are undesirable and lead to unstable economic development. Monetary policy is thus largely about spending the right amount of money. The typically Swedish word "lagom" comes in handy here. The repo rate must be set on an ongoing basis so that both inflation and deflation are avoided and stability in price developments is achieved. The Riksbank's target of 2 per cent inflation, with a tolerance up and down of 1 percentage point, is quite close to what is usually called price stability. Sometimes the Riksbank is criticized for concentrating too one-sidedly on the price stability objective. It may be said that we should also take growth into account. Our answer is that we do too. It is, in fact, built into the way monetary policy is conducted by means of an inflation target. Once a low-inflation regime is established and the public sets itself up for long-term inflation of 2 percent, inflation will be determined by how demand in the economy relates to production capacity. If demand risks becoming too high and the economy overheats, the repo rate will be raised. Conversely, if the economy slows down and risks going into a recession, the repo rate is lowered. This means that, in the long run, a monetary policy guided by an inflation target tends to smooth out the fluctuations of the economy. It thus contributes to a more sustainable growth and is in line with the economy's long-term growth trajectory. The inflation target thus helps the economy to expand as quickly as it can, taking into account, for example, technological developments, the amount of investment made, the well functioning of the labour market, the training of the labour force and other factors that determine the long-term growth trajectory of the economy. In addition, low inflation in itself means that the economy works better and that it can thus grow somewhat faster in the long term. Expectations also guide inflation The Swedish economy is now in its fifth year of economic expansion since the deep crisis at the beginning of the 1990s. Since the turnaround in the summer of 1993, GDP has risen by just over 2.5% per annum on average. Over the same period, inflation has averaged about 2 percent per year. This development is in sharp contrast to the 1970s and 1980s when growth was about 2 percent and inflation about 8 percent. In one area, however, things still look bleak. I am thinking of the labour market and employment. If an economy has had good growth for several years, but still weak employment growth and persistently high unemployment, there is much to suggest that structural problems in the labour market are in the picture. This applies both to how the labour market works overall and, more specifically, to how wage formation appears. However, there is nothing monetary policy can do anything about. A monetary policy that is expansionary for too long leads to inflation. Experience has taught us that an inflationary economy sooner or later leads to such disruptions that unemployment rises. It is therefore not possible to achieve a lasting reduction in unemployment by accepting higher inflation. Although growth has been satisfactory in recent years, it still proved difficult to bring about a broader upturn in economic activity. Gdp growth initially came to about three quarters from the industrial sector, which makes up only 20 percent of the Swedish economy. It pretty quickly created bottleneck problems and various kinds of inflationary impulses. It goes without saying that the relatively small industrial sector cannot sustain the entire growth in the long run. The problem of the two-tier economy - a thriving export-oriented industrial sector and a rather weak recovery in more domestically oriented sectors - was linked, among other things, to lingeringly high inflation expectations. The public simply did not believe that the Riksbank would keep inflation in line with its target in the long term. This was shown, for example, in the form of high long-term market interest rates, a weak krona, high wage increases, etc. Monetary policy therefore had to be geared towards demonstrating the seriousness of the price stability objective. The repo rate was raised in several stages between the summer of 1994 and 1995. At the same time, a far-reaching fiscal adjustment was carried out. The alternative to this direction of economic policy would have been a gradual rise in inflation, but not higher growth in the long term. This period shows that it is not only the resource utilization of the economy, i.e. whether there is a boom or a recession, that determines inflation. Also important are the public's expectations about future inflation. In the spring of 1996, households, firms, savers and investors began to seriously believe that inflation would continue to be around 2% in the future. Gradually, therefore, the repo rate could be lowered to 4.10 percent - the lowest level of the Riksbank's policy rate since the early 1960s. Persistently low inflation is the best guarantee of low interest rates. Low interest rates support the upturn Most of the assessments currently being made suggest that the Swedish economy is heading into a boom with both strong domestic demand and strong export growth. The expansionary monetary conditions are thus starting to have a full impact on demand developments in the economy. The Riksbank's key interest rate is at a relatively low level, which has contributed to low market interest rates. In addition, the krona's share price is weaker than we think it should be in the long term. Thus, the krona also has a stimulating effect. The combined effects of short-term interest rates and exchange rates thus seem to support the upturn in the Swedish economy. Monetary policy cannot take such a stance over the entire business cycle while maintaining price stability. Expansionary monetary conditions lead to demand gradually accelerating so that it grows faster than the economy's long-term growth trajectory. At first, such a process leads to the use of spare capacity, but over time, sooner or later the resources of the economy will come under such pressure that inflationary tendencies arise. But, someone can say, there is probably no risk today of overheating and rising inflation. It is precisely on this plane that the pedagogical difficulties lie for a central bank. The reason is that monetary policy measures are characterised by a long backlog. It can take between one and two years for the effects to have a full impact on the economy. The Riksbank must therefore assess where the economy is towards the end of 1999 and what resource utilisation might then look like. Given that a central bank acts in a timely manner, major changes in interest rates can be avoided. This often has to be done in a situation where current inflationary pressures are still low. When most people think that everything still looks good and the central bank still raises the key interest rate slightly, it is usually said that we are chasing ghosts. But if we succeed in our work, inflation will never rise. As I have said before, it is in this way that the Riksbank supports continued sustainable economic growth. Work on a new inflation report In the Inflation Reports, we thoroughly review our views on economic developments, resource utilisation, inflation expectations and the inflation outlook for the whole economy. In the Inflation Report presented earlier this autumn, it was estimated that the Swedish economy would grow by 2 percent in 1997 and about 3 percent in 1998. In 1999, GDP was expected to grow by just over 3%. With a gap between total demand and total production resources of around 2% and a long-term potential growth rate of 2%, the gap would gradually close sometime in 1999, at least towards the end of that year. The Riksbank concluded in September that the gap would not be closed during the period of one to two years that was then relevant for monetary policy. At the same time, it was pointed out that monetary policy is conducted against the background of a rising economy. Inflation risks should not only be assessed in the light of the degree of slack, but the speed at which the output gap is closed must also be taken into account. The pace of CPI growth was estimated to be slightly increasing in 1998 and 1999. In the next Inflation Report, the aim of monetary policy must be moved forward, to the end of 1999. This means that if the previous forecast for the economy holds up, the period of time will be included when the gap between total demand and total production resources is closed. This has also been stated in speeches given by the Riksbank during the autumn. Thus, if a central bank is to be out in good time, such an analysis means that the time is approaching when it is necessary to slightly reduce the stimulative effect. For savers and investors in the market, this reasoning is no stranger. The question for them is not if - but when - the Riksbank will raise its key interest rate. An expected increase in the repo rate can also be deduced from the structure of market interest rates. The overall view among financial players seems to be that an increase in the repo rate is likely sometime in the coming winter. All this is the starting point when the Riksbank is now currently working on a new Inflation Report, as a basis for the discussion that will be held by the Riksbank's council and the conclusions that will be drawn. Some important problem areas The Riksbank must analyse whether the forecast of demand development stands up or whether factors have arisen that make it necessary to change it. One factor, which at least so far, seems to be of minor importance is the stock market turmoil in Southeast Asia. But it is also important to assess whether other factors have been added. The question is also how resource utilisation develops. In industry, capacity utilisation is high. The NIER's quarterly barometer shows that the availability of available resources is decreasing. Although there is not yet a general lack of labor, such signs are found in specific areas. An increasing number of companies are indicating increased delivery times, although pressure to raise prices so far appears to be limited. Against this background, the flexibility of the economy comes at the centre. How smoothly will resources be able to be transferred in the next few years to areas that meet good demand? Similarly, we must take account of wage negotiations, which, together with wage slippage, will determine the overall wage increases. Will there be a full adjustment to what is needed to achieve the inflation target? Or will wage increases put pressure on profit margins and thus lead to upward pressure on prices from the cost side? In a situation where the economy is in balance, a rate of wage growth consistent with the inflation target, and the continued equilibrium of the real economy, is the sum of the inflation target and the long-term trend growth rate of labour productivity. It is therefore important to distinguish between the long-term trend and the cyclical productivity component. The slightly higher productivity we can deduce from the national accounts for the first half of this year can apparently be explained by the fact that the economy is at the beginning of a broader expansion, probably not by an increasing trend trend. At present, however, the economy is not in equilibrium. The high unemployment rate is one such sign. In this situation, therefore, it is not obvious that the wage space is the same as when the economy is in equilibrium. More restrained wage developments may be required to support a balanced employment upturn while maintaining price stability. The evolution of inflation expectations, and thus confidence in economic policy, is another heavy component in assessing future inflation. Europe is now entering a period when EMU will be formed. This spring, important decisions will be made about which countries will participate from the start. By 1 July at the latest, the new central bank will begin its work. In just over a year's time, EMU will apparently begin to pursue a single monetary policy for the participating countries. The credibility of Swedish monetary policy must not be questioned in connection with the run-up to EMU, since most indications are that we will not participate from the start. There must be no doubt whatsoever that the Swedish inflation target is serious. Conclusion Monetary policy operates with a delay on inflation. Therefore, it must necessarily be forward-looking. The Riksbank is now working on the upcoming inflation report. The period ahead of us will involve several complicated trade-offs. It is about weighing up the probabilities of different scenarios into an overall assessment of the inflation outlook. In the light of what I have said about demand developments and resource utilisation, etc., it is clear that at some point in the future it will be necessary to move monetary policy in a somewhat less expansionary direction. By consistently working to achieve the inflation target of 2 percent, the Riksbank is making its best contribution to sustained high and stable growth in the Swedish economy.

Title: Swedish economy
text: Swedish economy Date: 1997-03-20 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Chalmers university of technology in Gothenburg Thank you for the invitation to discuss the Swedish economy and monetary policy. Today in the morning, the Riksbank's inflation report was presented. It analyses developments in Sweden as well as future inflation developments. This means that the Riksbank's view of future monetary policy is known. I will therefore paint with a little wider brushstrokes tonight. Positive development in the Swedish economy There is a lot that is positive in the Swedish economy. Slowly but surely, we are moving away from the recurring economic problems of recent decades, which in the early 1990s led to a deep crisis. Since the summer of 1993, GDP growth has been about 2.8% annual, which is significantly higher than the average growth rate we have been accustomed to over the past 25 years. Similarly, the surpluses in our business with foreign countries are greater than they have been for a very long time. Investment is at a high level and government deficits have gradually decreased. Inflation has not been so low for decades. Since last autumn, we have had a few months when consumer prices have been lower than a year earlier. However, this does not mean that Sweden has suffered from deflation in its true sense. An important reason for the decline in the consumer price index is that the Riksbank has lowered the repo rate and that this has reduced housing interest rates, which in turn has a temporary dampening effect on inflation. If we in Sweden continue to pursue a disciplined budget and monetary policy and also otherwise build confidence in economic policy, most of the evidence suggests that growth will gradually strengthen, from the slowdown in 1996, without inflation picking up. It is in many ways a new situation in our modern history. I compare that to the 1970s and 80s. However, the low inflation we have now ties in well with an older and very long Swedish tradition. From the beginning of the century until 1970, GDP growth averaged around 3.5% per annum. This made the Swedish economy one of the fastest growing in the industrialized Western world. Over the same period, inflation averaged around 2.5% per annum. Even during these 70 years, our country experienced some problems in connection with the periods around the two world wars and the international depression at the beginning of the 1930s. But the economy recovered relatively quickly and continued to show good growth in an environment of stable prices. Sweden's historical development shows that low inflation is not an obstacle but rather a prerequisite for favorable economic development. Why did there be a change after the 1960s? The early 1970s mark a tangible change. The Swedish economy came to suffer from problems, which eventually led to the deep crisis in the early 1990s. Various types of disruptions, both domestic and foreign, were met with both expansionary fiscal policy and devaluations of the krona. It favoured output and employment in the short term, but led to inflation, speculation, recurring economic setbacks, new devaluations and further short-term expansion. It became a vicious circle and the results for this period are disappointing. One inflation and devaluation cycle followed the other. It was the longest inflationary period since the first decades of the 1800s. Inflation from 1970 until the early 1990s averaged 8% per annum. The state's lenders compensated for the higher inflation as well as for the krona's eroded value. Market interest rates were therefore high compared to many other countries. At the same time, investments and savings were low. Growth was weak and economic development was jerky. Why did that happen? Something obviously happened towards the end of the 1960s in our country. Although many factors contributed to the poor development over the next 20 years, it is important to point to a new way of thinking that made itself felt in economic policy. It was that fiscal policy as well as monetary and exchange rate policy should be used more actively to counteract disruptions. The approach was based on a widespread view that inflation must be accepted in order to keep unemployment down and the economy to grow. In other countries, too, a similar change occurred, which was based on the same approach, but unlike these countries, the perception of the connection between unemployment and inflation lingered in Sweden. What also allowed for a more active economic policy in this view was the release of an important restriction on economic policy. The so-called Bretton Woods system broke down in the early 1970s. Under this currency system, the value of the crown was pegged to that of the dollar, and the American currency, in turn, was pegged to gold. This international exchange rate arrangement, which prevailed after the Second World War, placed great demands on economic policy discipline and therefore contributed to stability to development while inflation became low. When the Bretton Woods system broke down, the demands for discipline in economic policy seemingly disappeared. Sweden could pursue its own policy, it was believed. Inflation was not seen as something harmful, but more as a side effect of a proper economic policy, which had to be accepted. The problem was that the theory didn't deliver what it promised. It ignored the importance of expectations. For an expansionary economic policy to have any effect on production and employment, it is assumed that wage increases do not adapt to higher inflation, but they did. Let me take a simple example that illustrates this. Suppose inflation is at 2 percent in the starting position and economic policy is shifted in an expansionary direction without considering the underlying productive capacity of the economy. If wage agreements were concluded for a longer period, an increase in inflation to say 5% could at best contribute to a short-term increase in employment, as real wage costs are reduced for companies (prices are rising faster than wages). Eventually, however, 5% inflation will be perceived as normal and wage demands will be based on this level. With higher nominal wage increases, real wages increase again and unemployment tends to return to its original level, while inflation has risen to 5%. The level of unemployment to which the economy returns when inflation expectations are adjusted to actual inflation is usually referred to as equilibrium unemployment. It cannot be influenced by demand expansion in the form of, for example, monetary and exchange rate policy, but is mainly determined by structural factors. It there is therefore no long-term exchange relationship between inflation and unemployment. It is not possible to bring down unemployment permanently by means of a generally expansionary policy so that it falls below the level of equilibrium. However, we can have different levels of inflation. Problems, on the other hand, arise if inflation rises, as this makes the economy work worse and negatively affects production. Put another way: Fiscal policy and monetary and exchange rate policy can, under certain conditions, influence the fluctuations of the economy around the long-term growth path, although it should not be expected that it will be possible to fine-tune demand. But if demand growth is pushed too far, inflation is rising, which risks damaging the economy. This is probably what happened in the 1970s and 1980s, in addition to the fact that the economy was also affected by structural problems. There is also a lesson here for the current situation. I initially pointed to a lot of positive conditions in the Swedish economy. However, there is one circumstance that is less bright. That is the high unemployment rate. Although wage formation will sooner or later adapt to the current low inflation, it is worrying that progress is so slow. The recovery in employment has so far been very slow despite a rather favourable economic climate over the past three years. Most of the evidence suggests that equilibrium unemployment has risen, which means that unemployment risks remaining high if nothing is done even if the economy improves. This, in turn, is a sign of a poorly functioning labour market, which is rooted in wage formation - because price formation is the central market mechanism. If equilibrium unemployment has risen, measures should be aimed at reducing it. However, it is something that is beyond the reach of monetary policy and demand policy. What monetary policy can contribute with is to try to keep low and stable inflation and thus indirectly also contribute to stable growth and employment growth in the Swedish economy. Low inflation - a long Swedish tradition I mentioned earlier that Sweden has a long tradition of low inflation. Low inflation has gone hand in hand with good economic growth since the breakthrough of industrialism in the mid-1800s. The effort to use various means to counteract the risk of inflation and create confidence in the value of money runs like a red thread throughout Swedish history. Ultimately, inflation is about eroding the value of money if there is too much money or means of payment in the economy. The banknotes and coins issued by the Riksbank do not have the net asset value indicated on them. The metal in a five-crown is not worth five crowns if it is melted down and sold. Nor is the paper worth 50 crowns in the 50-note. It costs the Riksbank a very small amount to print a thousand dollars. In principle, therefore, we could make any amount of money. This sometimes affects the view of the Riksbank. How often are cries for a lower repo rate heard no matter where it is located? However, our repo rate is nothing more than the fee we charge for lending the notes and coins to the public. A low repo rate means that more money comes into circulation, something that can degrade its value and consequently lead to inflation. There are many examples in history of the temptation to produce too much money and erode its value becoming too great. During the 1700s and early 1800s, Sweden waged war and war cost money. The Riksbank was then forced to contribute with financing and the result was very high inflation. In 1830, the Riksdag decided to introduce a so-called silver standard to create stability in the value of money. The possibility of issuing banknotes and coins was thus linked to the possession of silver. As a result, it was no longer possible to make "cheap money" for the state authorities. There was an anchor, a restriction and a rule of action for monetary policy. It created public confidence in the monetary system and in the value of money, which formed the prelude to a very long period of low inflation in our country and created conditions for growth and employment. In 1873, Sweden switched to the gilding standard and introduced crowns and pennies. The banknotes were given a text that reads as follows: "Sveriges Riksbank redeems, on demand, this banknote with gold coins". It created further confidence in the monetary system, in the value of money and in economic policy. During the following 100 years, with the exception of the war years and the depression of the 30s, the value of the Swedish krona was directly or indirectly tied to gold and this created stability both in terms of the value of money and in the economy as a whole. This shows how important a rule of action for monetary policy is. Today, the rule of action is to keep inflation at 2 percent, with a tolerance up and down by one percentage point. We must be as careful to cope with that task as previous generations were to keep the value of the crown on par with the silver and gold. Having a silver or gold standard or an inflation target means that the Riksbank's commitments and responsibilities are clear. This also means that it will be extra clear whether the Riksbank will deviate from its commitment. Such a rule of action can help create confidence in low inflation not only this year and next, but for a long time to come. In our days, such confidence is the basis for a stable currency and for persistently low market interest rates. Financial turmoil is about uncertainty A poor inflationary history as well as weak government finances are two factors that can weaken confidence in economic policy and in the value of money. The periods of interest rate and currency turbulence that we experienced earlier in the 1990s had their origins in savers and investors doubting Sweden's will and ability to break with the historical inflation pattern from the 1970s and 80s and to overcome the problems in the state's finances. In short, one can speak of uncertainty and the state's lenders sought to compensate for the risks they experienced. Tendencies towards financial fluctuations in other countries have sometimes been the trigger behind financial turmoil, but often it has been about uncertainty at home. In the latter part of 1995 and in 1996, several pieces fell into place. A rise in inflation in connection with the economic upturn had been prevented and the strong measures taken over several years to address the deficits in the state budget paid off. Inflation expectations fell, long-term interest rates fell and the krona strengthened. Rising confidence in economic policy was an important factor in the Riksbank being able to cut its repo rate last year from just under 9 per cent to 4.10 per cent. The results of the past year demonstrate the importance of consistently and sustained economic policies aimed at price stability and sound public finances. The government's convergence programme, with its six-monthly checkpoints, enables various actors to follow the political system's will to complete the budgetary consolidation and to achieve the goal of balance in 1998. Government representatives have also stated the ambition to reach surpluses thereafter. We must remember that building trust is an arduous process, which does not end. There are additional ways to contribute to confidence in the future value of money and thus seek to reduce the risks of sharp reversals in long-term interest rates and the krona's exchange rate. I am not thinking, then, of a commitment similar to that in the old days that: 'Sveriges Riks-bank redeems, on demand, this banknote with gold coins' but rather of the kind of institutional changes that are now being discussed. The idea of, for example, setting the Riksbank's objectives in parliament through a law and introducing a direct ban on monetary policy instructions other than those that exist by law is not an end in itself. These are additional ways to create trust, but they are based on the same principle as the measures taken in the 1800s when the value of the crown was tied to the silver and gold, respectively. A serious problem in the discussion with clearly delegating monetary policy to the Riksbank is the proposal that the so-called . The currency competence inquiry recently arrived it proposes that decisions on exchange rate policy be transferred from the Riksbank. The investigator seems to have overlooked that monetary policy and exchange rate policy are two sides of the same coin. The problem with the inquiry's proposal is that it would make it more difficult to achieve credibility around sustainable price stability. Thus, the proposal risks counteracting other proposals for legislation in the Riksbank's area that are being discussed. Therefore, it is of course important that the investigator's proposal is rejected. The purpose of new legislation for the Riksbank is, of course, to increase confidence in economic policy and thus to contribute to both a more stable economy and more stable financial markets. It is also in the light of different ways of trying to create confidence that one should see the plans for the formation of EMU. This Union offers a monetary policy framework that increases the long-term credibility of the discipline of economic policy and stability-oriented policies. Conclusion My speech tonight can be summed up in three points: there is much that is positive in the Swedish economy. Slowly but surely, we are moving away from the recurring economic problems of recent decades, which in the early 1990s led to a deep crisis. However, unemployment remains at a high level. There are many indications that equilibrium unemployment has risen. It cannot be influenced by fiscal policy or monetary and exchange rate policy. If equilibrium unemployment has risen, measures should be aimed at reducing it. Experience has taught us that financial turmoil has often had to do with uncertainty. Developments in 1996 show that disciplined monetary policy and consistent budgetary consolidation are leading to good results. Building trust is a laborious process, which has no end. At the same time, institutional changes can further contribute to financial stability. However, it is important not to take steps back, which The currency competence inquiry suggests. It sees through and diminishes the results that other measures may have and that clearly delegate monetary policy to the Riksbank. EMU should also be seen in the light of measures that increase financial stability.

Lg inflation - en lng svensk tradition Jag nmnde tidigare att Sverige har en lng tradition av lg inflation. Finansiell oro handlar om oskerhet En dlig inflationshistoria liksom svaga statsfinanser r tv faktorer som kan frsvaga tilltron till den ekonomiska politiken och till penningvrdet. De perioder av rnte- och valutaturbulens som vi upplevt tidigare under 1990-talet hade sitt ursprung i att sparare och investerare tvivlade p Sveriges vilja och frmga att bryta med det historiska inflationsmnstret frn 1970- och 80-talen och att komma till rtta med problemen i statens finanser. Kort uttryckt kan man tala om oskerhet och statens lngivare skte kompensera sig fr de risker man upplevde. Regeringsfretrdare har ven uttalat ambitionen att n verskott drefter. Vi mste komma ihg att det r en mdosam process att bygga frtroende, som inte tar slut. Det finns ytterligare stt att bidra till frtroendet fr det framtida penningvrdet och drmed ska minska riskerna fr tvra kast i lnga rntan och kronans kurs. Jag tnker d inte p ett tagande liknande det i gamla tider om att: "Sveriges Riks-bank inlser, vid anfordran, denna sedel med guldmynt" utan snarare p den typ av institutionella frndringar som nu diskuteras. Detta r ytterligare vgar att skapa frtroende, men de bygger p samma princip som de tgrder som gjordes p 1800-talet d kronans vrde knts till silvret respektive guldet. Ett allvarligt problem i diskussionen med att tydligt delegera penningpolitiken till Riksbanken r det frslag som den sk. Valutakompetensutredningen nyligen kommit med. I den fresls att besluten ver valutapolitiken skall flyttas frn Riksbanken. Utredaren tycks ha frbisett att penningpolitik och valutapolitik r tv sidor av samma mynt. Problemet med utredningens frslag r att det skulle frsvra mjligheterna att uppn trovrdighet kring en varaktig prisstabilitet. Drmed riskerar frslaget att motverka andra frslag om lagstiftning p Riksbankens omrde som diskuteras. Drfr r det naturligtvis viktigt att utredarens frslag avvisas. Denna union erbjuder ett ramverk fr penningpolitiken som lngsiktigt kar trovrdigheten fr den ekonomiskpolitiska disciplinen och den stabilitetsinriktade politiken. Avslutning Mitt anfrande ikvll kan sammanfattas i tre punkter: Det finns mycket som r positivt i svensk ekonomi. Sakta men skert r vi p vg bort frn de senaste decenniernas terkommande ekonomiska problem, som i brjan av 1990-talet ledde till en djup kris. Arbetslsheten ligger dock kvar p en hg niv. Mycket talar fr att jmviktsarbetslsheten stigit. Den kan inte pverkas av finanspolitiken eller penning- och valutapolitiken. Har jmviktsarbetslsheten stigit br tgrder inriktas p att f ned den. Att bygga frtroende r en mdosam process, som inte har ngot slut. Samtidigt kan institutionella frndringar bidra ytterligare till finansiell stabilitet.
