Title: Sweden and the preparations for EMU
text: Sweden and preparations for EMU Date: 1997-02-26 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Location: ABF Goteborg Mr President, let me begin by thanking you for being able to come here and talk about EMU. Interest in these issues is increasing and I now spend a lot of time out there informing about the preparations for EMU. It is usually representatives from the financial sector that we at the Riksbank meet in our information work. It is therefore especially fun to come here to ABF and get the chance to speak in front of a new audience for me. It is also my conviction that more and more people, not just people from the financial sector, need to understand what EMU is and how EMU will affect Europe. What I will be talking about here tonight is primarily what the timetable looks like for EMU, what changes we already know will occur today and what practical preparations the Riksbank is making for EMU. I would also like to mention something about the consequences of EMU for the financial sector in Sweden and, where possible, also mention something about how we as individuals will be affected by this process. I will start with the slightly larger socio-economic features and then go into the practical aspects of the EMI. Monetary union or not? Monetary union will soon become a fact. Therefore, debating whether the project is reasonable or not has lost topicality. What we should be asking ourselves now is instead whether we want to be involved or not? Sweden should participate from the start As for the Riksbank's view of whether Sweden should participate in the currency union, the council has concluded that we should be involved from the start in 1999. We believe that the economic and political benefits of joining the Union have been underestimated in the debate, while the so-called 'European Union' has been underestimated. stabilization policy costs exaggerated. Let me explain in more detail. One of the most common arguments against monetary union is that it is believed that we must retain the possibility of devaluation in order to cope with the so-called 'currency'. asymmetric shocks, i.e. disruptions in the economy that unilaterally affect Sweden. In the event of such a disturbance in the economy, there is a great risk of an increase in unemployment and, in order to prevent this, we must be able to adjust the exchange rate, i.e. devalue. This argument is also commonly referred to as the insurance argument. In a monetary union with fixed exchange rates, we do not have this 'insurance' to be able to adjust the exchange rate in the event of future economic shocks. In EMU, Sweden cannot devalue itself from economic problems. Surely this is where our views on economic policy differ from those who say 'no' to the Union. The Riksbank believes that we cannot continue to use monetary policy to cope with problems, which have often in practice been due to the economic policy pursued and to lingering structural problems that we ourselves have created. The problems highlighted by the emu inquiry appointed by the government, such as increased unemployment, deserve to be taken very seriously but cannot be solved by monetary policy in the first place. Employment issues must be resolved with measures aimed, for example, at: wage formation and the functioning of the labour market, i.e. through structural changes. We do not believe that remaining outside EMU will facilitate these reforms. We also see it as less likely that Sweden would be unilaterally affected by a number of external disturbances to a greater extent than the other countries in Europe. The Swedish economy does not differ significantly from the EU's core countries and the reorientation of fiscal and monetary policy that has been made in recent years probably reduces the sensitivity to disturbances. In the Riksbank's response to the EMU inquiry, we have also pointed to negative effects on the Swedish financial system of remaining outside, or joining at a later stage, which the investigation has not significantly touched on. I will come back to that question later. The political consequences The economic effects of EMU are, of course, important to discuss, but also difficult to overview in the current situation. What also matters is the political effects of being involved or being left out. Here we share the view of the EMU inquiry; being outside the Union entails political costs. In the event of exclusion, we will be outside the innermost circle of countries that will bring Europe into the future. Our ability to influence important decisions is probably also reduced in areas other than monetary policy. Should Sweden opt out of the currency union for good, there is a risk that we will be marginalized as an "outdoor country". We should also be aware that the countries that join EMU from the outset will have a greater say in how the new European Central Bank, The ECB will develop in the first important years when it will find the forms of its work. In Swedish debates, the EU is often portrayed as bureaucratic and sometimes as almost ridiculous, a ban on snus, or the size of strawberries are things that recur in the reference. However, I do not think we should forget that the aim of the European Union and monetary union is improved European cooperation with objectives such as greater integration, growth, employment, peace and prosperity. Goals that I think we can all set ourselves. What kind of Europe do we want to develop, and how can we participate in that process? We can, of course, also choose to stand by and watch as the other countries move forward in this cooperation. But, we should be aware that it is a choice we are making. I find it difficult to see that Sweden would like to remain outside a functioning EMU in the long run. The countries of Europe will grow together. The question is thus not if but when Sweden should join. This was also the conclusion of the EMU study. When the question is formulated, the debate is somewhat de-dramatized. Let me now turn to the more practical aspects of this project. Timetable In all EU agencies and member states, preparatory work is in full swing. In May 1995, the Commission presented a Green Paper on the practical arrangements for the changeover to a single currency. In Madrid in the same year, the European Council adopted a transition scenario setting out the key decision-making dates. It was agreed that EMU should start on 1 January 1999. As early as possible in 1998 (probably February-April), the Council of Ministers decides which countries are participating in the Union. The decision is based on which countries have fulfilled the convergence conditions on the basis of the 1997 statistics. On the first of January 1999, exchange rates will be fixed and the European Central Bank, the ECB, will take over monetary policy. The euro is introduced as its own currency and all monetary policy operations are conducted in euros. Until 1 January 2002 at the latest, both euros and crowns will exist in parallel. However, in a legal sense, it will be a currency. It is no stranger than that Swedish krona can be expressed both as pennies and crowns. However, we will not have euros in our wallets during this time, but only by 1 January 2002 will euros be available as notes and coins. When euro banknotes and cents are put into circulation, a large exchange of notes and coins begins over six months. No later than 1 July 2002, kronor will lose the status of legal tender, but the Riksbank will of course also exchange sek for euros after this date. Who will be involved? Eu countries are now making efforts to meet the economic requirements for being part of the monetary union. At the same time, intensive political work is being carried out to remove any remaining obstacles. Following the last meeting of heads of state and government in Dublin in December 1996, there are political agreements on, inter alia, the Stability and Growth Pact, the agreement to ensure stability and convergence between the economies of the Member States even after the union is formed, and on the relationship between the new currency and external currencies. The agreement known as ERM2. However, some important issues still remain to be resolved. One of these concerns what the path into EMU might look like for those who do not join the first wave. There are also many technical details to be tweaked but the big pieces of the puzzle are in place. As has been said, the countries are working hard to meet the convergence conditions. Just a year ago, things looked rather bleak. Only a few countries met the criteria for inclusion. Major changes took place in 1996. Both the Commission and the EMI presented forecasts last autumn showing that most countries are likely to meet the convergence conditions. However, I would like to point out that it is important not to focus on individual statements and individual figures. Forecasters throughout Europe are likely to be strictly busy presenting progress reports on the participation prospects of different countries throughout 1997. What I can say now is that we will not actually know which countries will be part of the Union until spring 1998, when the Heads of State or Government sit down and analyse the figures then available on the economic development of the candidate countries. Speculating now is therefore unnecessary. What I can generally say, however, is that it seems more and more likely that the number of anatal members will be more than we previously thought. As far as the convergence conditions are concerned, these do not imply a new direction of economic policy in Sweden. Three of the criteria directly concern the Riksbank's area, namely the inflation criterion, the long-term interest rate criterion and the exchange rate criterion. At the moment, Sweden has europe's lowest inflation and we expect Sweden to meet the inflation criterion in 1997 as well. We are also likely to meet the interest rate criterion. There has been a lot of discussion about the exchange rate criterion. Some believe that a country must participate in exchange rate cooperation within the ERM for at least two years before the pre-EMU test in order to qualify, while others argue that it is the stability of the currency in practice that is essential. From the Swedish side, we subscribe to the latter view. With regard to the remaining criteria, the forecast is that the budget deficit will remain close to 3% for 1997. The government has stated that it is prepared to take action if the deficit develops in an unfavourable direction. On the other hand, we will probably not be able to reduce the ratio of public debt to GDP, which is currently around 80 percent, to the stated 60 percent already by 1997. However, the Maastricht Treaty allows for a flexible interpretation on this point. For example, it is acceptable for a country to be above 60% in debt ratio if it shows a satisfactoryly fast and stable rate of reduction. All in all, therefore, the situation looks as if we will actually meet the convergence conditions. This, of course, makes it even more interesting to start preparations even for those who were previously hesitant. What do we do for preparations at the Riksbank? Well, first of all, like the other European central banks, we are involved in the EMI's work to prepare for the single monetary policy. We participate in a number of working groups that work with everything from statistics to monetary and exchange rate policy and every month the Governor of the Riksbank goes to Frankfurt and participates in EMI's Council meetings. Some ninety projects are underway currently where we actively participate. In addition, we have begun work on the internal transition at our own bank. We, like all other banks, need to make some changes to computer systems, for example. In addition to this, work is also underway to inform the financial sector here at home in Sweden. Preparations in Sweden It is the Riksdag that decides on Sweden's membership of EMU. The Riksbank's task is to contribute to Sweden really being able to join if the Riksdag's majority so wishes. That is why preparations are needed now. Both the Ministry of Finance and the Riksbank have their own organisations for the practical introduction of the euro. A fundamental principle of this work is that voluntarism should prevail. It is therefore up to each organization to decide for itself what changes it wants to make. All parties involved must also resolve for themselves the possible problems they face as a result of EMU. The Ministry of Finance coordinates the overall Swedish transition. So far, citizens' issues, legal aspects, business issues and the public sector have been looked at. The Riksbank has taken on the task of informing and consulting the financial sector on transitional issues. To achieve this, we have formed a Comprehensive Consultation Group for the Financial Sector (SIFS) and five sub-groups working on practical preparations together with the financial sector. One result of the work so far is the report "The euro in the Swedish financial sector a progress report", which was published in early February. The report has been prepared together with representatives from the financial sector and therefore reflects both our view on the transition issues and the views of another 12 organisations via annexed opinions. It is the first report where a review and compilation has been made of the EMU preparations in the Swedish financial system. In the report, we conclude that the preparatory work in the Swedish financial sector has come a long way. Timetables and appropriate solutions have been developed in most areas. The Riksbank's assessment is therefore that the financial sector will be able to cope with a changeover to the euro on 1 January 1999. We also see that a later membership can in some cases facilitate and in other cases complicate the preparatory work. The worst option is a long period of uncertainty as to whether or not we should participate, what we usually call a 'soft no'. Double costly systems will then become a reality in several areas. We have also seen concern in the financial sector about increased costs, competitive disadvantages and the risk of various forms of discrimination against being outside EMU. This is pointed out both in our progress report and in our consultation response to the EMU study. Our work on the preparations will continue in the spring. We have recently sent our progress report to some fifty organisations with which we have not previously cooperated in order to give other interests in society the chance to give their views on the EMU transition. In addition to substance, we have also asked for comments on our continued work. The answers will be taken into account when we intend to continue the work on a new report in the spring. What will change? How will we feel about EMU? What changes will be of greatest importance to the financial system? What will we as citizens notice? I will briefly review some of the changes we know will occur for a number of important areas. 1. Monetary and exchange rate policy A single currency presupposes a single monetary policy. In EMU, this will be determined by the ECB. The riksbank and the other national central banks will have the role of implementing this monetary policy. For Swedish banks and financial institutions, the difference is unlikely to be so great. It is likely that the Riksbank will continue to be the financial sector's counterparty. The biggest difference compared to today for Swedish banks is that the overnight market will be significantly larger and that counterparties will be located throughout Europe. How monetary policy in all details will be conducted is not yet clear. It was not until 1998, when the ECB was formed, that the final decisions were taken. It will therefore be the countries that join from the outset that will be able to influence the policies pursued and the organisation of the work of the new European Bank. There are tendencies that those who belong to the "intended" core of member states have more influence over the process already today. 2. Betalningssystem In order to be able to conduct a single monetary policy, a single payment system is required, otherwise it will not be possible to process the payments associated with monetary policy. Target is the name of the system that is now under construction and which will link all national systems into a common one. A payment from one bank, say in Gothenburg to another bank in Milan, should normally be made in a matter of seconds. Today, this often takes a whole day or more. The main purpose of TARGET is to enable the ECB to conduct monetary policy, but at the same time the new system establishes a new "motorway" for commercial transactions as well. How much banks and companies will use the system is likely to be determined by the price. We do not yet know what it will cost to use the system, but full cost recovery must prevail. The central banks of all EU countries should be able to join Target whether they are in the monetary union or not. Discussions on the design of the system clearly show that there is a significant risk that countries outside the euro area will be less able to use TARGET, for example through restrictions on borrowing in euros during the day, which is important in order to be able to fend off fluctuations in payment flows. Among other things, it has been discussed that the so-called outsbanks should close the system earlier. The Riksbank has worked vigorously to prevent this type of discrimination that threatens here, but decisions on this issue, as in some others, have been postponed and will now be taken by the countries that are members of EMU from the start. Target will be tested by the summer and will be ready for full use by 1 January 1999. 3. The laws Everyone must be able to trust that the euro has a solid legal basis on which to stand. Economic values in, for example, contracts, bank accounts and pension contracts must be guaranteed during the period between 1999 and 2002, when we have both the euro and national currencies in circulation. Companies and individuals must be sure that the contracts that were concluded in sek also apply when we have received euros, i.e. contract continuity should prevail. This and much more is regulated in the so-called. the euro regulations. This legislation must be directly applicable in all Member States and therefore applies in Sweden if we become members. It is also likely that we will have to amend our national legislation. One such national legal issue concerns the role of the Riksbank. The Maastricht Treaty means that the Riksbank must be made more independent in law. This means, among other things, that the position of the Governor of the Riksbank must be clarified. He or she should only be able to be removed if there are exceptional reasons such as gross misconduct, etc. The Riksbank should also not be able to receive directives, other than by law, from someone else, such as the government. In our Riksbank Council, MPs are also represented according to Swedish tradition. This is against the traditions that exist in Central Europe where our order is seen as a risk to political control of monetary policy. 4. Banknotes and coins As mentioned, only in early 2002 banknotes and coins will be introduced. For some time, therefore, the trade will be forced to work with some kind of double price information. The exchange of banknotes and coins will take place according to a timetable set by each country, and the Riksbank's hope is that we in Sweden will manage the transition in a significantly shorter time than the six months available. In good time before the exchange of notes and coins, the public will be informed of how this will be done. Information on security features and appearance will also be provided over time. What we already know today is that we get seven notes and eight coins. So slightly more denominations than we have today. The coins will have a national side where we decide for ourselves the motifs. The banknotes may also acquire a national symbol. What's going on beyond these areas? Securities - Countries joining EMU can, and should, carry out new issues of their euro-denominated sovereign debt. If any Member State wants to convert its outstanding debt into euros, it may also do so. We can also make it possible, for example, for the stock exchange, OM and VPC, to switch to euros as early as 1999. This is also what many institutions and actors wish to do. The players in the Swedish securities market, banks, financial institutions, VPC, the OM stock exchange and others unanimously advocate a "big bang solution", i.e. a quick and comprehensive transition from sek to euro already at the turn of the year 1998/1999. When monetary policy becomes common and currency risk disappears, interest rate differentials between sovereign debt will only reflect credit risk. The market for Swedish government securities will be more or less fully integrated into a government securities market for the euro. Therefore, if the debt situation is reasonably similar, the government bonds of different countries will be able to be traded in a uniform manner. We ordinary citizens should be able to choose whether we want to use the euro from the start on 1 January 1999 or whether we want to wait until the changeover is fully completed in 2002. No one should be forced to use the euro during this period. However, its use will be encouraged. In 1996, the banks worked on various strategies and procedures for the conversion to the euro. It has been agreed that the banks, the post office, the bank giro and the privatgirot will handle both the krona and the euro during the transition period. At checkout, you will make a payment to the currency you use in your own systems regardless of what we as a customer have used for currency. At the bank branches there will also be two different types of forms, one for SEK and one for euro. New cheque forms, giror forms, deposit and payment balances will therefore be produced. On our bank statements, it will be stated that the currency has been converted at the established rate xxx. ATMs and the Minuten system will also have to be converted. Banks must also be prepared for the fact that private individuals want to make euro payments as early as 1/1 1999 as a giro payment. Similarly, some large companies may wish to pay salaries in euros before the euro is available as notes and coins. How much demand for euro services will be and how fast companies and individuals will switch from kronor to euros is difficult to see. Finally, there is reason to believe that EMU is likely to change the financial map significantly. Globalisation, concentration and integration in the world's financial markets are nothing new, but it is reasonable to believe that the process will accelerate with EMU. Summary and conclusions Today, there is every reason why economic and monetary union will get under way as planned on 1 January 1999. For Sweden, the question is whether we should be involved from the beginning, wait a while or try to stay out for good. My hope is that in the future we will have an increased debate on this very important decision. The discussion leading up to this position should then not focus solely on the question of monetary policy autonomy. It is not just a question of economics, although we believe that the economic arguments speak in favour of membership. It is also about the fact that EMU is an important part of the European development cooperation in which Sweden now participates. Sweden's economy demands changes Sometimes in the discussion one gets the impression that in the event of exclusion there is an easy way for Sweden to go. Outside of this European cooperation, we would be spared all the adaptation requirements that are imposed. That's not the case. In any case, we must now continue to work on reorganising the state's finances and creating long-term confidence in the stability of the Swedish economy. It will hardly be easier outside EMU. If we are a small neighbour of a large currency, we are fit and then we have to take care of ourselves. The world will not be the same A 'no' to EMU does not mean the status quo. By creating a monetary union just beyond our borders, the world will not be the same. Both individuals and businesses will feel the introduction of the euro, whether we are involved or not. In our work to inform the financial sector about EMU, we see that the preparations have gone a long way. We also see a strong desire from the parties involved to be involved as quickly as possible so as not to be left behind. Swedish financial institutions and companies want to be given the opportunity to compete on the same terms as other European companies and they do not want to risk losing business opportunities. A common transition or a two-tiered society? What we risk with an exclusion, which I do not think has been up for debate before, is the risk of a "two-divided" Sweden. The financial players together with the large companies declare that they will technically "join" EMU" regardless of whether Sweden joins or not. From a competition point of view, they cannot risk being outside a large and influential euro area. At the same time, the public sector and consumer organisations declare that they want to wait as long as possible. This comes to light in, among other things, The Ministry of Finance's report on the practical preparations in Sweden. The question to be asked is what kind of society we will have if this becomes a reality. What does it mean for businesses to adapt to the euro while we citizens continue to live in a crown world? Such a development may mean greater losses than shifting monetary policy to the ECB. Would it probably be best if the whole society changes together and at the same time? In any case, this is one aspect of EMU worth discussing. Further preparations Regardless of the political discussion, practical preparations must continue. The EMI will continue to resolve the issues on which it has not yet taken a position. We will continue to participate in that work. Here at home, the Cabinet Office will continue to provide information on its level and we will continue our cooperation with the financial sector. In the autumn, we have the ambition to write a new report on emu preparations. After the Riksdag has taken a position on Swedish participation or not, we will also have the opportunity to give clearer and clearer information about what preparations will be needed. We are facing a dynamic process both in the world around us and here at home.

Frberedelserna i Sverige Det r Riksdagen som beslutar om Sveriges medlemskap i EMU. Riksbankens uppgift r att bidra till att Sverige verkligen kan g med om Riksdagens majoritet s nskar. Det r drfr frberedelser behvs redan nu. Svl Finansdepartementet som Riksbanken har sina egna organisationer fr det praktiska infrandet av euron. En grundlggande princip i detta arbete r att frivillighet skall rda. Det r allts upp till varje organisation att sjlv bestmma vilka omstllningar man vill gra. Alla inblandade parter mste ocks sjlva lsa de eventuella problem de stlls infr till fljd av EMU. Finansdepartementet samordnar den samlade svenska vergngen. Hittills har man tittat p medborgarfrgor, lagliga aspekter, nringslivsfrgor och offentlig sektor. Riksbanken har tagit p sig uppgiften att informera och samrda med den finansiella sektorn i vergngsfrgor. Rapporten har utarbetats tillsammans med representanter frn finansiella sektorn och speglar drfr bde vr syn p vergngsfrgorna och ytterligare 12 organisationers syn via bilagda yttranden. Jag tnker kortfattat g igenom en del av de frndringar vi vet kommer att intrffa fr ett antal viktiga omrden. 1. Penning- och valutapolitiken En enda valuta frutstter en gemensam penningpolitik. Denna kommer i EMU att bestmmas av ECB. Riksbanken och de andra nationella centralbankerna roll blir att genomfra denna penningpolitik. Fr svenska banker och finansinstitut blir sannolikt skillnaden inte s stor. Troligen kommer Riksbanken ven i fortsttningen att vara den finansiella sektorns motpart. Den strsta skillnaden jmfrt med idag fr svenska banker r att dagslnemarknaden kommer att vara betydligt strre och att motparterna kommer att finnas i hela Europa. Hur penningpolitiken i alla detaljer kommer att bedrivas r nnu inte klart. Frst 1998 nr ECB bildats fattas de slutgiltiga besluten. Det blir allts de lnder som gr med frn brjan som kommer att kunna pverka vilken politik som frs och hur arbetet skall organiseras i den nya europeiska banken. Det finns tendenser till att de som tillhr den "tilltnkta" krnan av medlemslnder har strre inflytande ver processen redan idag. 2. Betalningssystem Fr att kunna bedriva en gemensam penningpolitik krvs ett gemensamt betalningssystem, annars gr det inte att hantera de betalningar som sammanhnger med penningpolitiken. Target heter det system som nu r under uppbyggnad och som kommer att lnka samman alla nationella system till ett gemensamt. En betalning frn en bank, sg i Gteborg till en annan bank i Milano skall normalt ske inom loppet av ngra f sekunder. I dag tar detta ofta en hel dag eller mer. Syftet med Target r frmst att ECB ska kunna bedriva penningpolitik, men det nya systemet innebr samtidigt att en ny "motorvg" etableras ven fr kommersiella transaktioner. Hur mycket banker och fretag kommer att anvnda sig av systemet avgrs troligen av priset. Vad det kommer att kosta att utnyttja systemet vet vi inte n, men full kostnadstckning skall rda. Alla EU-lnders centralbanker skall kunna ansluta sig till Target vare sig de r med i valutaunionen eller inte. Diskussionerna om systemets utformning visar klart att det finns en betydande risk att lnder utanfr euro-omrdet kommer att f smre mjligheter att anvnda Target, genom t.ex. begrnsningar att lna i euro under dagen vilket r viktigt fr att kunna parera svngningar i betalningsfldena. Det har bl.a. diskuterats att de s kallade outsbankerna skall stnga systemet tidigare. Riksbanken har med kraft arbetat fr att hindra denna typ av diskriminering som hr hotar, men beslut i denna frga, liksom i en del andra, har skjutits p och kommer nu att fattas av de lnder som r med i EMU frn starten. Target kommer att testkras till sommaren och skall vara frdigt att anvndas fullt ut 1 januari 1999. 3. Lagarna Alla mste kunna lita p att euron har en stabil laglig grund att st p. Ekonomiska vrden i t.ex. kontrakt, bankkonton och pensionsavtal mste garanteras under perioden mellan 1999 och 2002, d vi har bde euron och nationella valutor i omlopp. Fretag och privatpersoner mste vara skra p att de kontrakt som ingicks i kronor ven gller nr vi har ftt euro dvs. kontraktskontinuitet skall rda. Title: Sveriges Riksbank, EMU and the European Central Bank
text: Sveriges Riksbank, EMU and the European Central Bank Date: 1996-10-23 Speaker: Deputy Governor Stefan Ingves Location: Sveriges Riksbank IRR conference on the Euro currency I would first like to thank you for being invited to speak about the Riksbank and the EU process. EMU issues have ended up higher and higher on the agenda, not only with us at the Riksbank but also in society. I notice this because I spend more and more of my working time talking about EMU preparations, not only internally but more and more often outside the Riksbank, as I do today. I also notice that only in the last six months has knowledge of EMU increased significantly, which I am pleased about. More and more people are now becoming familiar with the broad outlines of the process towards the single currency. There is still uncertainty among many about the details of this process and, above all, how the transition as a whole will work. I would therefore like to try here today to concretize what lies ahead of us in the transition work and the Riksbank's role in the transition work. I would also like to point out at the beginning of my speech that time is moving fast and we are soon approaching the time when we can no longer postpone practical planning. If we want to have an opportunity to participate in monetary union from its inception in 1999, now is the time to prepare. It will soon be 1997, when TARGET, Europe's new payment system, will be tested and tested. In 1997, the Swedish Parliament will also decide whether sweden should participate in EMU or not. In addition, economic developments in 1997 will be particularly interesting as it is statistics from this year that will form the basis for assessing which countries meet the convergence criteria. Then many technical preparations will also need to be made in the financial sector. The question that is often encountered is whether it is really necessary to make any preparations and whether there really is a Union. The answer from me is that just a year ago monetary union felt rather distant and only a few countries could present an economy in line with the convergence requirements. Most important decisions remained to be taken in Frankfurt and most of the countries had done limited preparatory work at home. Today, the situation is different. The countries of Europe are competing to meet the convergence conditions, our neighbouring country to the east Finland decided last week to participate in the ERM, most countries have begun extensive work to implement and plan for the transition to the new currency also at home. The state authorities in most European countries have become more and more involved in the transition work, including in Sweden. Last summer, the government decided to appoint an EU coordinator and since then it has been working intensively on a ministry memorandum on the transition issues. Last but not least, the market has also begun to believe that EMU will start on time. Convergence trading (i.e. interest rates converge) has started in Europe's financial markets. All in all, this makes my belief that we have a monetary union in Europe in 1999. The debate in Sweden should therefore concentrate more on how should we prepare for this new situation. Regardless of whether Sweden is involved from the start or not. Before I tell you about what needs to be done in the future, I would just like to briefly mention something about the fulfilment of the convergence conditions for Sweden. After all, that is what determines whether we can participate from the start in 1999 or not. The convergence conditions must be fulfilled if membership is to be offered to us in 1998, when the Heads of State or Government are to decide which countries will be included in EMU. As far as the convergence conditions are concerned, these do not imply a new direction of economic policy in Sweden. Three of the criteria directly concern the Riksbank's area, namely the inflation criterion, the long-term interest rate criterion and the exchange rate criterion. After all, it is the Riksbank's task to keep inflation down and thus give the market incentives to maintain a low level of long-term interest rates, which are partly due to the public's expectations of the future rate of price rise. At the moment, Sweden has europe's lowest inflation and we expect Sweden to meet the inflation criterion in 1997 as well. The recent decline in interest rates shows that we are also likely to meet the interest rate criterion. There has been a lot of discussion about the exchange rate criterion. Some believe that a country must participate in exchange rate cooperation within the ERM for at least two years before the pre-EMU test in order to qualify, while others argue that it is the stability of the currency in practice that is essential. From the Swedish side, we subscribe to the latter view. With regard to the remaining criteria, the forecast is that the budget deficit will remain close to 3% for 1997. The government has stated that it is prepared to take action if the deficit develops in an unfavourable direction. On the other hand, there should be no possibility of reducing the public debt/GDP ratio, which is currently around 80 percent, to the stated 60 percent already by 1997. However, the Maastricht Treaty allows for a flexible interpretation on this point. For example, it is acceptable for a country to be above 60% in debt ratio if it shows a satisfactory rapid and stable rate of reduction ("if the ratio is sufficiently diminishing and approaching the reference value at a satisfactory pace" as stated in the Maastricht Treaty). All in all, therefore, the situation looks as if we will actually meet the convergence conditions. This, of course, makes it even more interesting to start preparations even for those who were previously hesitant. To return to this planning work, I usually start by saying that we have to do everything three times. Firstly, in Frankfurt in the EMI. Where we, together with the other 14 Member States, will agree and take decisions. Secondly, the changes will take place in the respective central banks. Central banks are also facing major changes as monetary policy will be steered from Frankfurt. In addition, we as a bank must also be able to handle, for example, TARGET. Thirdly, we must also implement the changes in our respective countries. At the Riksbank, we do everything we can to sort out the first two parts in time. I can promise you that we will do everything we can to help with the last thing, but here it is not we who are responsible, but it is actually up to everyone in the community to prepare. How, then, are we to know what is to be done? In order to keep preparations together for the introduction of the single currency, the EMI - the forerunner of the European Central Bank - is carrying out work on a large number of projects in several areas of expertise. The work of the EMI is monitored by monthly Council meetings. It decides on the timetable and guidelines and takes the final positions. The meetings are prepared by subcommittees and working groups in which representatives from the Riksbank and the other central banks participate. List areas of work within the EMI are long and, in addition, there are a large number of projects in each area. According to the latest list, some 90 different projects are being worked on in the run-up to EMU at the same time. Other projects have already been completed and further projects will certainly be added later on. Much will be fully discussed and decided already this year, other things can wait until 1999 or even later. What subject areas are discussed in the Masterplan? Let me do a quick review of some areas that we are working on in EMI to give you an idea of the current issues: Monetary policy Monetary policy will be centrally controlled by the ECB in Frankfurt. A single monetary policy is a cornerstone of monetary union. However, there are many indications that the actual execution of monetary policy operations will, at least initially, take place in a decentralised manner at the central bank of each country. As has been shown in the press, there is an ongoing discussion about the strategy that should be applied in order for monetary policy to lead to the ultimate objective of price stability. Should there be an explicit inflation target, similar to the one the Riksbank is now applying, or should inflation be tackled indirectly by directing liquidity towards a so-called intermediate target? From the Swedish side, we believe that the difference is not as big as it may sometimes seem. The goal in both cases is to secure a stable monetary value. The instruments of monetary policy also need to be harmonised between countries. In addition to repos and other direct market operations by the central bank, as well as standing loan facilities, reserve requirements are also used in some countries. It is also likely that such instruments will be part of the single monetary policy. The matter will be decided as early as 1997. The management of foreign reserves is another major issue on which it is still open whether management should be centralised or decentralised. Payment. In order to be able to conduct a single monetary policy throughout EMU, it must be possible to operate in euros quickly throughout the area. This requires interconnected payment systems across national borders. The project is called TARGET. In practice, this means that the national systems for large payments, in Sweden the Riksbank's so-called RIX system, are harmonized so that they can communicate with each other. All countries' systems must work according to the RTGS principle, which the Swedish RIX system has been doing for several years. RTGS stands for "Real Time Gross Settlement" and means that the payment orders that enter the system are settled one by one, and continuously during the time the system is open during the day. This network of national RTGS systems, named TARGET, will make it possible to initiate and settle payments in euro across land borders within seconds. The Council of the EMI decided on the design of TARGET in the summer of 1996. It is now up to central banks, banks and clearing houses to rebuild their own payment systems so that they can handle euros and otherwise meet the requirements for participating in TARGET. The Euro function is necessary to be able to make and receive payments via RIX, which becomes the Riksbank's TARGET connection. TARGET is complemented by specific systems for the management of securities as collateral for the provision of credit in the payment system and for the implementation of monetary policy. In several EU countries, central banks own securities settlement systems, in whole or in part. This is not the case in Sweden, but because the Riksbank has a close and close consultation with VPC, the mutual exchange of information works well. The RIX system will have different designs depending on whether Sweden will join EMU or not. Banks and clearing houses must therefore also prepare for alternative solutions. Regardless of whether Sweden joins EMU or not, we will be able to use TARGET to send and receive euro payments. The Riksbank also intends to provide euro accounts in parallel with krona accounts on Sweden ends up outside. A concrete sub-question is how payments and accounts are to be made during the period when we still have kronor, but when the euro is increasingly being used as a unit of valuation for the state, companies and other parties. Banks must then be prepared to receive, for example, payments in sek, but to make the corresponding payment in euros. Somewhere in the system, then, there must be a conversion mechanism, popularly known as the 'black box', in which the crowns are converted into euros at the fixed rate. With this conversion, the recipient may even be able to receive a payment notice that makes it possible to choose whether she wants payment in sek or euros. Of course, a euro payment can only be made before 2002 by crediting an account, because physical notes and coins are still missing. It is planned that public authorities will gradually start using the euro as a valuation unit from 1999. For example, all monetary policy operations must be carried out and expressed in euro and new government loans are issued in this currency unit from the outset. This should show, among other things, that the authorities are behind the new currency. Private sector operators may switch to using the euro as a valuation unit whenever they see fit (but no later than 2002). However, central banks will create incentives for such a transition, including by using the euro in transactions between them and banks, as well as in the money and foreign exchange markets. (However, this does not prevent banks from carrying out transactions among themselves also in sek). For the Riksbank, this transition will take place as early as 1 January 1999. From that point on, the Riksbank's accounts will be made in euros. Banknotes and coins. It takes a long time from the start of planning a new banknote until the first copies are printed and issued. Work on the euro banknotes has already been going on for some time, although they are unlikely to have to be issued until 1 January 2002 (the ECB will take the final decision on the date of issue in 1998). A design competition has recently ended. A number of companies in Europe have proposed the appearance of banknotes with two different motifs: one is different cultural styles in European history, in the form of architecture, art or otherwise. The second area of motifs is abstract patterns. As far as the coins are concerned, they will have a national side and a European side. For the Riksbank, it is also important to plan for how this huge "exchange project" will take place. All Swedish kronor must be deposited to the Riksbank and exchanged for euros. It is important that the transition takes place as quickly as possible, as there are practical problems with dual currency means of payment. This will require, among other things, large transport and storage facilities. As banknotes will be widely distributed, probably also outside the EMU area, designers will take the opportunity to introduce the latest in terms of protection against counterfeiting. This applies to traditional watermarks, security wires and other things, but also to advanced optical protection mechanisms. Statistics This summer, much of the preparation of statistics within the EMI was completed, and I think you are already aware that EMU will mean changed and also increased reporting requirements. A larger number of contributors will be an effect of the fact that, by definition, we will have more monetary financial institutions, so-called MFIs, which have reporting requirements. The basic purpose of banking statistics is to provide a basis for the single monetary policy. In order to measure liquidity in the financial sector, the ECB needs to be aware of developments in account balances and other financial dealings. Furthermore, the ECB must have access to other balance sheet data showing the overall stability of the payment system or if there are tensions. If the data collected are to be summed up within EMU and form the basis for monetary policy, the statistics must be harmonised so that each country reports the same things according to the same principles. Extensive harmonisation work is underway and the rapporteurs are currently working on to be informed in detail of the changes so that they can take the necessary action. Ins and Outs. Sweden's preparations are also made on the basis that we will become EMU members as early as 1 January 1999, but Sweden may of course end up among the EU countries that are voluntarily or involuntarily outside EMU. There will be different categories of outs. Partly those who have not passed the requirements but have to wait, and partly those who have passed the requirements but themselves have chosen to remain outside. The United Kingdom and Denmark, unlike Sweden, have this possibility enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty. An important issue to be resolved before 1999 is what relations should prevail between the countries that are inside and the countries that are outside. Those who remain outside are, of course, still MEMBERS of the EU and are part of the common market. Nevertheless, this market must continue to function. It is therefore in the interests of all countries to create monetary stability between ins and outs as well. For example, a devaluation of an outside country's currency would create problems for the in-country countries. After all, the latter cannot protect themselves by their own compensatory depreciation other than by a depreciation for the entire euro area, which could jeopardise price stability. Intensive discussions are under way to determine which arrangements, involving both ins and outs, can ensure such stability. Of course, this is also in the interests of the ute countries themselves, especially those countries that are striving to stabilise their own economies so that they can participate in EMU at a later stage. The design of the final arrangement, called ERM2, will be completed in the autumn. We can expect that the euro will be the anchor of this new exchange rate arrangement, that the bands will be wide, perhaps as at present /15%. There will be a duty to intervene, individual countries can negotiate tighter ties if desired, and participation will be voluntary, but it is 'expected' that outs will participate. In addition to exchange rate arrangements, it is also essential that fiscal policy is managed satisfactorily for the functioning of EMU. The economies of the countries must be somewhat convergent even after the introduction of the Union. Public finances must be sound and the balance of payments stable. A so-called. the Stability Pact shall be introduced to ensure this. The forms of this are not entirely clear, but we know today that some form of fine will be imposed on those countries that let their deficits run away. The amount of these fines and when they are to be enforced is currently under discussion. By the time of the Dublin Summit in December, however, the structure should be ready. One conclusion for Sweden is that we can hardly expect to be able to pursue a less stability-oriented economic policy if we end up outside EMU. This is then due not only to the fact that the outside world would react with a flight from krona investments and thus increased Swedish interest rates, but also because we would be covered by the economic policy surveillance of all EU countries. Other areas As I showed just now, the Master plan covers a very large number of sub-areas. In addition to those I have examined in particular, mention can be made of the establishment of the European Central Bank and its relations with the national central banks. It should be noted here that the requirements for the national central banks to be independent within each country, for example vis-e0-vis the government, apply regardless of whether the country becomes a member of EMU or not. Within each sub-project there are also many legal issues to be resolved. A special group of legal experts from the central banks has therefore been set up to deal with them. An important legal issue is the so-called contract continuity. Contracts currently stipulating that payments or other transactions are to be carried out in national currency will, after 2002, only be able to be executed in euro (for the EMU countries) as the national currency has ceased to be a means of payment. The lawyers are now considering how to make it easier for the courts, at least in the EU area, to regard payments in euros as the fulfilment of the contractual obligation to pay in national currency. The Euro Regulation, which will be finalised in the autumn, will clarify the legal status of the euro. A legal issue, of less fundamental importance but of great practical importance to all of us, is what rounding rules should be applied when moving from national currency to euro. Since the changes are to be made at fixed rates, it is understood that it is of the utmost importance to: rounding rules are uniform and precise regardless of the currency or currencies used for a given transaction. There is also the question of the Riksbank Act - does it need to be amended? Is the Riksbank as independent as required by the Treaty? The Governor of the Riksbank must be made virtually irreplaceable and it shall be prohibited for the Governor of the Riksbank to take instructions from, for example, the Riksbank's Delegate before taking decisions in the ECB. It shall also be prohibited to give instructions. Another crunch question is whether MPs should be able to sit on the council. The other EU countries say no, but we are pushing the view that the MPs should be able to participate. Other areas where it is important to have certain uniform rules are accounting and IT. For example, how are we going to exchange information between the national central banks in order to be able to carry out monetary and exchange rate policy transactions, and how are we going to link the payment systems in practical terms? After this brief presentation on what is going on in Frankfurt, I would like to say to those who still have doubts. The master plan is followed and the work will be completed on time. What will happen to the Riksbank if we join the Union? Of course, monetary policy will be decided by the European Central Bank ECB in Frankfurt, but by and large all operational functions will remain for the Riksbank. We must continue to distribute money even if it is called euros instead of crowns. The RIX system will remain. We will continue to have opinions on monetary policy and the Governor of the Riksbank will be involved in making the ECB's monetary policy decisions. The implementation of monetary policy will also be carried out by the national central banks. It is also to be expected that we will want to keep analysis activities, e.g. regional analyses or analyses of particular interest to Sweden. In addition, there is currently a debate on whether the single exchange reserve should be managed centrally in Frankfurt or whether it should be decentralised at the respective national central banks. In addition, we will remain responsible for the national payment system. To this can also be added responsibility for the distribution of banknotes and coins. It is today a very large part of our business to ensure that there are means of payment throughout the country. This will continue to be the case in the future, even if in the future it is the euro that we are dealing with. These tasks will closely monitor the future development of the financial sector with a view to promoting a secure and efficient payment system. This means that great demands will also be made in the future on the Riksbank's work, even though we, like many others, will change and adapt resources and tasks to the new requirements that the formation of EMU will give rise to. After this description of what is happening in Frankfurt and how the Riksbank will be affected by membership of EMU, I want to return to the preparations in Sweden. How are we doing with the preparations and where are the preparations for EMU taking place in Sweden? Information and consultation in Sweden As the EMI's work is not yet complete in all areas, we have so far been cautious about trying to influence the financial sector in any particular direction. We have been content to disseminate information in those areas where the contours of future decisions have been discernible. The need has proven to be great and the Riksbank has been overwhelmed with requests to inform about the EMU process, generally or within specific issues of fact. The requests have come from very different parts of society: authorities, the financial sector, trade unions, business organisations, journalists, students, the general public, etc. We regard it as an obvious task for the Riksbank and other authorities that as far as we can, for reasons of confidentiality, and are able, for resource reasons, we should provide information. For democratic reasons, the greatest possible information on the consequences of EMU participation should be disseminated before the Riksdag's position in 1997. This facilitates a serious debate. Both the Ministry of Finance and the Riksbank have their own organisations for the practical introduction of the euro. I do not want to give the impression that the opportunities for being flexible in the face of EMU are particularly great. A fundamental principle of the work is to allow the parties, as far as possible, to resolve for themselves how they wish to adapt to the requirements of EMU. This may mean, for example, that the main thing is to achieve the intended objective, such as a certain statistical product, while the technical methods of getting there may be freely chosen. Despite this principle, many of the requirements of EMU will probably have to be formulated in such detail that the room for manoeuvre will in practice be limited. Otherwise, the desired degree of harmonisation will not be achieved. At the national level, the Ministry of Finance (under Claes Ljung) is responsible for ensuring that preparations and planning are carried out in the areas, business, the public sector, law and "the citizen and the euro". The Riksbank is responsible for the financial sector and we have had a consultation organisation SIFS since last spring. (Consultation and Information for the Financial Sector). SIFS consists of a parent steering group under the leadership of the Riksbank. Representatives of the Ministry of Finance, the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority and the Swedish National Debt Office participate in this. In addition, the Banking Association and various groupings of non-banking financial institutions, insurance companies, securities institutions, finance companies, clearing and settlement institutions, etc. are included. Furthermore, the group is used for a mutual exchange of information about the organizations' own preparations for EMU. The practical work is conducted in five underlying working groups. The division follows the master plan's most important areas such as Monetary and Exchange Rate Policy, Payment Systems, Statistics, Banknotes and Coins and Law. In these working groups, the ongoing work of preparation takes place. The Riksbank will provide detailed information on what is happening in EMI as soon as possible. We also inform about how we as a Riksbank intend to adapt ourselves as a result of the decisions. On this basis, the banks and other interested parties can then start their work. Should difficulties arise in the preparation, these can be discussed in the groups. 'Voluntarism' is the motto of the transitional period and also of our consultation work. This requires that the financial actors themselves are active and identify issues and problems that they need to solve. The work has worked very satisfactorily so far and we are grateful for the response given to us by the financial players. The collaboration will continue in the work on a Swedish plan for the transition of the financial sector. Some kind of coordinated document on how a changeover to the single currency could take place is a necessity. We have thought that the plan should consist of two parts; main text and attachments. In the main texts, we will try to describe how the transition may take place in a number of different areas: statistics, monetary policy, means of payment, payment systems and legal changes. IT issues and accounting will also be taken into account. But in order to further increase the detail of this transition plan and to be able to get down to the concrete practical problems, we have invited 16 different interest groups and authorities to write annexes to this work. There we hope that the organizations will be able to present the most important details of how to view the transition for their respective organizations and when to take action changes of various kinds. It all boils down to providing as much information about how a transition might take place as possible. Perhaps we can agree that the entire securities side will switch to the euro on a set date. Perhaps we can agree on how the exchange of banknotes should take place in practice, etc. Our hope is that sometime at the turn of the year, we can present a ready-made plan for the transition of the entire financial sector. We believe this can make it easier for all of us in the great work ahead of us. Summary Finally, I would like to briefly summarise; The situation today is different than it was just six months ago. It looks as if Sweden will be able to cope with the convergence conditions. Other EU countries are making every effort to meet these conditions and preparatory work is now underway throughout Europe. We have to do everything three times; Frankfurt Riksbanken Out in the community In Frankfurt, preparations are made in the EMI, in which the Riksbank also participates. 90 different projects are currently underway in the various subject areas, monetary policy, statistics, means of payment, payment systems, law, etc. Out in the community, the Ministry of Finance coordinates the Government Offices and the Riksbank is working within the framework of the SIFS structure During the autumn, a Swedish plan for the transition of the financial sector will be completed.
text_original: UTSKRIFT FRN WWW.RIKSBANK.SE Sveriges riksbank, EMU och den europeiska centralbanken Datum: 1996-10-23 Talare: Vice riksbankschef Stefan Ingves Plats: Sveriges riksbank IRR-konferens om Eurovalutan Jag vill frst tacka fr att jag blivit inbjuden att tala om Riksbanken och EMUprocessen.
