Today the Government and the Riksdag are firmly intent on meeting the budget criterion by 1997 and on reducing government debt, as demonstrated most recently in this April's economic policy bill. Conditions exist for fulfilling the convergence criteria by 1997. The creation of a successor to the current form of exchange rate cooperation, the ERM, is a reasonable step towards phasing in national exchange rates in the run up to EMU. In our opinion, however, it should be possible for a country to have an inflation target, of the type used at present in Sweden, as a direct policy goal. Our basis for this view is that price stability is the paramount goal for EU monetary policy. The ultimate foundation for exchange rate stability lies in the ability to keep inflation down. Sweden's experience from 1992 supports this opinion. We have also taken note of the subsequent success in restricting inflation and creating economic stability. The road to a stable currency must be travelled, under any circumstances, by directing economic policy in general for stability and not just by issuing declarations about a fixed rate. From these starting points and considering that the ERM is no longer what it was at the time of the Maastricht Treaty, we have rejected a strict interpretation of the membership criterion which stipulates that any country wishing to participate in EMU must previously have been a participant in the ERM for two years. Neither do we consider that membership of a new exchange rate system should be mandatory for countries that remain outside EMU. It should also be possible, provided all criteria including the stable currency provisions - are fulfilled, to become an EMU member at a later date. At the same time we appreciate that there is concern in Europe that the so-called outs might use their situation to devalue their way out of problems, although what happened when the ERM collapsed in 1992-93 can hardly count as competitive devaluation. Consequently we have indicated a willingness to support a system with strict oversight, with the continuous monitoring of both inflation and budget policy. It is hard to see why a country that properly abides by EMU standards in both these respects should have problems with its exchange rate. What really matters, in our opinion, is thus that a country has instilled fundamental stability into its economy and its currency. Only then does exchange rate cooperation become meaningful. We have also said that this stability may need to be confirmed by participation in the exchange rate cooperation for a period prior to actually joining EMU. This applies both in connection with the establishment of EMU and later, when the Union is already functioning. 7. Conclusion The first half of the 1990s has been a dramatic period for Sweden's economy. A policy realignment - aimed at creating stable conditions for production, with low inflation and an improvement in the workings of the economy - was implemented at the beginning of the decade. The purpose was to break away from the partially destructive line of economic policy that had been followed in the 1970s and '80s and adhere instead to the good economic development which Sweden had previously experienced for almost a century. The realignment was also inspired by developments in the EU and its implementation coincided with Sweden's application for membership of and accession to the Union. Steps have been taken to make the economy function more efficiently but more can and should be done. This applies primarily perhaps to the labour market and wage formation, where major adjustments are now required so that unemployment can be reduced. But public sector activities and the public expenditure systems in other respects also need to undergo considerable changes so that good conditions can be created for growth. To sum up, in recent years Sweden has become more like other countries in northern Europe.

Introduction I should like to begin by expressing my thanks for the invitation to talk today about Sweden's path towards European Monetary Union. My talk is arranged as follows: First I shall discuss the crisis which the Swedish economy endured in the early 1990s. In my view, the crisis was partly a consequence of economic policy's realignment. This realignment was necessary in order to achieve greater stability, with better conditions for long-term growth. It also represented an adjustment to the policy which had been conducted in much of Europe in the 1980s. Then I shall review what has happened in the Swedish economy in recent years and say something about the future. Higher growth, in conjunction with extensive budgetary measures and a consistently tight monetary policy, has created a foundation for a more stable or, if you like, a more Continental development. Finally I intend to say something about our view of European monetary integration. 2. In the next two decades, however, the picture was very different. Opinions differ about the reasons for this but it is clear that they included both political and economic factors. Without claiming to present a full account or to know all the answers, I should like to mention some of the main causes. Exchange rate policy failed. When the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates collapsed, it proved difficult to establish an alternative arrangement that gave the same stability. This meant that no firm benchmark existed for either economic policy or wage formation. A series of devaluation cycles led to widespread uncertainty, with repercussions on such factors as investment and productivity. An important cause of the recurrent devaluations lay in problems with wage formation. Productivity growth slowed without a corresponding retardation in the rate of wage increases. Instead, nominal wage increases actually tended to accelerate as employees in different parts of the economy competed for the smaller wage share. This was accompanied by further additions to labour costs in the form of increased social charges. Fiscal policy was weak, for both economic and political reasons (e.g. a more fragile parliamentary base for the Government). When economic activity turned downwards, it proved impossible to reinforce the budget to match rising expenditure and diminishing revenue. Government debt rose higher and higher. Structural problems were also at work in the economy: a) With the rapid expansion of the public sector, the distortionary economic effects of taxes and public spending grew. b) Certain sectors, such as agriculture and housing, were heavily regulated. In both these cases there was also a large element of subsidies. c) Competition was also inadequate in other parts of the economy, for instance in parts of trade in goods and, at least until the mid '80s, in the financial sector. The imbalances were accentuated when the financial sector was deregulated in the mid '80s. Households and firms both accumulated debts on a dramatic scale. Being confined by the fixed exchange rate, monetary policy was not in a position to curb this tendency. All this meant that Sweden's standing in the international prosperity league slipped. Thanks to the expansion of public activities, unemployment was held back. But by the end of the 1980s, the scope for continuing the fiscal financing of employment was very limited. At the same time, inflation had accelerated. The need for a policy realignment was evident. The devaluation policy had come to a dead-end. 3. The policy realignment 1990-91 Early in 1990 the Government of the day signalled a change of course in economic policy. Priority would now be accorded to price stability, with a view to establishing more stable conditions for growth. Work would also be stepped up on improving the Swedish economy's structure. An awareness that policy should take this course had gradually emerged in Swedish society and the changes were also broadly supported by Swedish economists. Developments in Europe had also contributed to the new picture. Inflation there had been pressed down in the course of the 1980s and after a difficult period in the '70s, some countries - of which Denmark, the host country for this conference, is one had succeeded in generating a stable economic development. In this situation, when Sweden applied for membership of the European Union, it was even more natural to opt for a more long-term, "European" economic policy. As confirmation of the endeavour to achieve price stability, in June 1991 the Swedish krona was tied to a basket of European currencies. In the following years, however, economic development in Sweden changed dramatically. Industrial production faltered first, due to a combination of weaker export demand and an excessively high level of costs. Investment followed the downward path and unemployment started to rise. This tendency was reinforced both by a far-reaching tax reform, which included decreased tax deductions for interest expenditure, and by a rising real interest rate. The development of household income was weak, partly due to the high unemployment and sizeable fiscal withdrawals to reinforce the government budget, particularly from 1995 onwards. Moreover, the current account has begun to show substantial surpluses. One drawback, on the other hand, is that the increased production has generated just a marginal fall in unemployment; neither is there much likelihood of an appreciable change in this respect as long as domestic demand remains weak. Shortly after that the Government presented a major programme for budget consolidation. Between them, the measures of fiscal and monetary policy helped to break the rise in bond rates and the krona became somewhat stronger. In the referendum on EU membership, moreover, a majority voted in favour. However, the movement towards stability did not last. Bond rates rose and the exchange rate weakened again in the spring of 1995. The period from 1993 to mid 1995 was thus marked by unrest, particularly in financial markets. There was, however, a notable recovery in the real economy and the combination of fiscal and monetary policies helped both to turn the budget deficit downwards and to establish a low rate of inflation. 5. The stabilisation Since the summer of 1995 it seems that confidence in the Swedish economy and in Swedish policy has improved. The krona has become appreciably stronger and both long and short rates of interest have fallen. There are plausible explanations for this: Public finance has developed better in 1994 and 1995 than many observers expected. This has to do both with the strong economic development and with the extensive budget reinforcements. Relative to GDP, the deficit peaked in 1993 at 12.3 per cent; the level for 1995 was 8.1 per cent and for 1997 the most recent official forecast , including new budget measures presented in April 1996, is 2.7 per cent. If the present economic slowdown turns out to be deeper than expected, additional budget reinforcements may be needed. The Government and the Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, are firmly committed to the goal of balanced public finance in 1998. The situation is being followed continuously in accordance with the principles incorporated in Sweden's convergence programme. On each occasion in the six-monthly monitoring process the Government has tightened its policy to the requisite extent. The picture of inflation has also improved in the past six months. Title: Growth and high unemployment
text: Growth and high unemployment Date: 1999-03-15 Speaker: Deputy Governor Villy Bergstrom Location: University of Visby I intend to talk about two dominant problems in the Swedish economy: The statistics indicate that Sweden has fallen from a leading position in the standard league - we were third or fourth in 1970 - to a place below the average for the OECD countries - position 17-18. That's one thing. The second is that we have been faced with mass unemployment, since the early 1990s. I am going to start talking about the lagging growth. The second problem, mass unemployment, must be kept separate from weak growth. These are two, at least in part, different problems. Sweden's weak growth All developed countries suffered from lower productivity growth in connection with the first oil crisis in 1974-75. In many cases, it was a question of halving growth. Sweden was no exception. On the contrary, our growth slowed down a little more than that of many other leathers. Maybe there wasn't much to worry about at first. But if a country has only marginally lower growth than other countries for a long time, it has effects. A worrying indicator that things have gone downhill is the development of the exchange rate. When Sweden was forced to release the fixed krona exchange rate at the end of 1992, the krona first fell 10-12 percent and at most by just over 30 percent. But note that the reduction in 1992 started from a cost situation which, measured in the single currency, was 25% lower than it had been before the devaluation period began in 1976. The krona has depreciated more than would have occurred just because of relative inflation. So it wasn't just wage inflation that drove devaluations. Sweden was forced to accept real reductions in the level of costs, because the efficiency and structure of the economy could not defend the old standard of living. A lot of resources have been spent on clarifying why things have gone relatively badly for us. At the invitation of Sweden, two American research institutes have analyzed the Swedish economy, namely the Brookings Institution, 1987, and the National Bureau for Economic Research, 1994-95. In addition, there is the Lindbeck Commission appointed by the government in 1993 and a number of investigations carried out by the SNS Economic Policy Council. Throughout these studies, one does not find "the smoking gun" but that the analyzes point to many, interacting factors. Some we are responsible for ourselves, others we have suffered, more or less through no fault of our own. 1. Most people point to a lack of "flexibility" in the labour market, as an overall explanation for the problems. We have had wage formation that is too rigid and the labour market has been inflationary. Thus, relative wages are too locked and compressed and wage levels rise too much at a given unemployment rate. There is too much job security, so that employers are reluctant to hire new employees. It is too good compensation in the event of unemployment, which keeps up the wages of the low-skilled and means that the unemployed do not make enough effort to take up new jobs. It is precisely these conditions that are referred to when more 'flexibility' is demanded in the labour market. There are not enough job changes, not enough geographical relocations. Structural changes are slowed down, start-ups are not flourishing. One of the annexes to the Lindbeck Commission shows that Sweden is not distinctive in these respects. We are roughly in the middle of a spectrum where either union agreements or legislation restrict flexibility in the labor market, much like in Sweden. But things have also gone badly in many European countries. Continental Europe has problems similar to those of us with slow growth and structural problems. But we have lost lives even relative to the European countries. Therefore, it is difficult to see the lack of flexibility as crucial. There are two clear exceptions, the US and the UK. There, employment relations are more unprotected and the mobility in wages and between jobs is much greater than in Sweden and continental Europe. These countries  the US and the UK  also have lower unemployment rates, but at the cost of weaker safety nets for the population and, in the worst case, the proletarianisation of parts of the workforce. These countries, on the other hand, represent an extreme that hardly anyone in Sweden  not even the SAF  wants to copy. No one wants America's social conditions. The risk of this is small in a small, democratic and homogeneous country like Sweden, with strong popular movements. But it cannot be ignored that trade union policy and legislation on the labour market create security for employees. These are welfare values that we all strive for. Therefore, they are difficult to change. 2. The second criticism concerns Social Security as it was designed in the 1970s and well into the 1980s. In Sweden, you could stay home from work for a week without any reduction in income, just by calling and calling in sick. The number of sick days per insured rose from just over 10 days in 1955 to 25 days by the end of the 1980s. With each reform that made insurance more affordable, the number of sick days rose. Nearly five per cent of the labour force was absent due to illness during some part of a working week in 1988. We were one of the sickest peoples in the world. So we were one of the world's sickest people, even though other indicators indicated that we were one of the healthiest in the world. Life expectancy was and is one of the longest in the world as was child mortality. Nevertheless, companies must keep up to 100,000 extra staff to fill all sick vacancies. This wasn't just a direct cost. It also led to disorganization and inefficiency in production, with constant substitutes and extra employees. I think this slowed growth. Benefits increased gradually and utilisation gradually increased through habituation. But this problem is now reasonably solved. We have both waiting periods and reduced allowances. The Swedish people have recovered significantly. We had obvious overuse of health insurance in the early 1980s but maybe we got an underutilization. It costs to be at home. People go to work with a cold and infect each other. In social security, one has to choose between high compensation and strict controls or no controls and high deductibles. We had no controls and no deductibles. We couldn't handle that. This held back growth and the productivity of the Swedish economy, although no one has managed to quantify the effects. The overly lax rules were driven by the difference between workers' and white-collar workers' sickness benefits. You have to have approximately the same rules for different groups, at least in a society like the Swedish one with strong equality traditions, otherwise the differences drive improvements for the disadvantaged groups. The austerity that eventually came took over everyone getting unsustainably generous rules. Another lesson is that you have to have the same rules in the different insurances, otherwise there is a risk that there will be an overflow from one insurance to another. So I think the second factor, the design of health insurance, was a problem for the growth of the Swedish economy. The first factor, "flexibility," may not have directly hindered growth, but hiring is dampened in economic peaks as well as layoffs are slowed in recessions. That's what the researchers have come up with. But it should be borne in mind that in the case of health insurance, the social experiment was done through drastic changes in insurance conditions. Therefore, we can read a result. As for the labor market, the experiment has not been done. Therefore, research has a hard time coming up with pregnant results. It is clear that employment would rise if it became so miserable to be unemployed that people are forced to take almost any job hoarsely and at any salary, for example by drastically reducing the level of unemployment insurance benefits. Unemployment would fall but growth would hardly rise. But to deregulate the labour market, for example to produce what are called household services cleaning jobs, gardening and the like - is to create conditions that allow for lower productivity in the labour market than is now normal. The existing wage and employment conditions now place such high demands on productivity that this type of job does not arise. It is therefore a question of creating more jobs, but not higher growth, when we propose deregulation of the labour market. Other proposals with the same aim are to introduce tax breaks for domestic services. The objections are both principled and practical. Having different taxes for different sectors of production has many disadvantages. There are hardly economic arguments for favoring some consumption over others. Why would I be tempted to hire cleaning help through tax subsidies if I would rather spend the money on going to Visby for a few weeks in the summer? And think of all the boundary-drawing problems. It is easy to see how it would arise itinerant car repair shops, who come home and fix the car, or hairdressers, who, with scissors in bag, start cutting at home. Catering would knock out restaurants. The demarcation problems would become legio. Employment would increase with the tax authorities. I hereby come to the subject of taxes in general. 3. Tax wedges are highlighted as growth brakes. The tax wedges are the difference between the productivity required to hire a person on the margin and the money he or she brings home because of the employment. It is easiest to illustrate with the cost of hiring a person for another hour for a salary of say 100 kr. For the employer, the cost will be at least SEK 133 plus any contract insurance costs. The employee receives SEK 40 home after tax or for a low-income person just over SEK 60. The productivity requirement is SEK 133, "take home pay" is between SEK 40 and SEK 60. The difference in between, SEK 70  90 is the so-called tax wedge. It places great demands on the productivity of the employee and it gives little in return. It is therefore considered to have both an anti-demand effect on the labour market and an anti-supply effect. One could possibly make the observation that the wedges are now smaller than before the tax reform of 1991 and that they are not very different from the tax wedges in other northern European countries. But 60 percent of GDP in public spending enables only marginal changes to the tax wedges, through the redistribution of taxes to "less harmful taxes". But this problem has another dimension. Capital investments are moving from Sweden, large companies are changing nationality, wealthy people are fleeing Swedish taxes and highly educated people seem to increasingly choose to work abroad, at least for some part of their lives. The share of public spending in GDP will be forced down by increasingly mobile tax bases. The fact that many low-income people have a hard time in today's Sweden, not least because of high tax pressure on them, will not prevent those who want and can move to countries with a lower tax burden. Moralization does not help. 4. One factor behind the weak growth, which was overlooked by the Lindbeck Commission but observed by the National Bureau study in 1994, is the - judging by the "eye-econometrics" - perfect correlation between the drastic reduction in the rate of capital formation in Sweden and the slowdown in growth. It is, of course, a deeper question, what has caused the decline in the rate of capital formation and thus, ultimately, growth. But it is difficult to get past the superficial observation that investment growth in the Swedish economy has been significantly lower from the mid-1970s than it was during the golden years of the 1950s and 1960s. I am showing a graph which is a little special, but which streamlines the growth aspect, namely the link between net investment - in other words, the contribution to the capital stock - and Sweden's disposable income. (That's GDP minus depreciation, interest payments to the rest of the world and development aid, "net national income.") (Image source, Associate Professor Lennart Berg, Uppsala University.) In the good years 1950-1970, we spent 15-18 per cent of our disposable income on capital formation. By the mid-1970s, capital formation halved to 7-8 percent of our country's disposable income. This immediately affected growth. On the one hand, capital input per worker, or per hour worked, grew more slowly than before. The interaction between capital and labour is an important factor in the growth of labour productivity. Productivity growth went down. New capital is an important source of introduction of technological changes, new organization, new rational methods of production. In this respect, too, weak investment growth played a negative role in growth. I therefore believe that a major reason for the weak growth from the early 1970s is the lower investment activity actually strangely overlooked in the debate about our lagging growth. In any case, economic policy has not been specifically focused on boosting capital formation in recent decades. The debate mainly highlights other factors, such as rigidities in the labour market, high tax burdens and security legislation. The growth problem is difficult. There are no quick fixes. The solutions reasonably involve capital formation and skills building - i.e. investments in physical capital as well as in human capital. Innovation and entrepreneurship are required. Education policy has not been successful in recent decades. Above all, we must increase the volume of technical and scientific education in Sweden, something that has already begun. And it's not just a question of taxes and regulations in the labor market. It is also a question of culture and the environment, of the right to go bankrupt and to try again, without being stigmatised. Sweden has the disadvantage of a peripheral location in relation to the major markets in Europe. We are a small country with a small market. Sweden lacks depth and breadth as a financial center in comparison with the large countries. And it's dark, cold and wet at home. Perhaps the disadvantages are so great that they are difficult to compensate for with tax cuts and measures in the area of labour law? I am now rehearsing to talk about unemployment. Mass unemployment A country does not have to have mass unemployment because growth is low. Low productivity growth should not be an obstacle to high employment, because rapid productivity growth means precisely the rationalisation of labour. Given the growth of productivity, demand must grow fast enough to absorb a growing labour supply and to engage the unemployed in production. But weak long-term productivity growth, such as the one we have had, is not opposed to full employment. It was difficult to point to the decisive factors behind the weak growth in Sweden. On the other hand, it is easy to identify how mass unemployment arose in the early 1990s. Sweden had experienced severe overheating in the late 1980s. The open unemployment rate was down to 1.3% on average in the country in 1989 and 1.5% in 1990. In Malardalen it was down to 0.5%. No wage formation system can work in such a labour market. Throughout the 1980s, after the "super devaluation" of 1982, the government had been trying to bring down the rate of wage rise: Roundtables, income-based tax policies, the launch of inflation norms, appeals to the social partners. The background, then, is all the failed attempts to bring down inflation and nominal wage increases. During the 1980s, total hourly labor costs for industrial workers increased between 8 and 12 percent per year. Between 1975 and 1991, the real gross wage of industrial workers fell by 7%, while the nominal increase was 248%! In 1994, an industrial worker had SEK 11 lower hourly wages at 1994 prices than he or she had in 1975. In truth, no successful outcome of the parties' actions and the government's stabilization policy. But the overheating towards the end of the 1980s thwarted all stabilization attempts. Competitiveness began to erode significantly from 1987, when the fall in the dollar ended. (Sweden's currency policy, with "double dollar weight" in the currency basket, entailed an automatic general depreciation of about 10 percent, when the dollar fell about 40 percent. This helpfully compensated for the high wage increases of 1985-87. After that, competitiveness quickly eroded.) In 1991, the government gave up. Bringing down inflation through consensual solutions would have proved impossible. In the Financial Plan in January, the government wrote that the fight against inflation would take precedence over all other economic policy objectives. For several decades, full employment (more or less explicitly) had been an overriding goal (subject to different restrictions in different time periods). Despite declining economic conditions, appropriations for emergency preparedness work were cut by almost 40 per cent from the level of the economic boom. Unemployment began to rise in the spring of 1991. Exports fell 2.3 percent in volume. This was the worst export trend since 1976. For the first time in decades, the government failed to counteract an economic downturn based on exports. Unemployment rose every month. The government resigned. For the new attitude to unemployment, a whole philosophy had developed among Swedish economists, mainly under the auspices of the so-called Economic Policy Council under the auspices of SNS. Swedish economists there launched the new ideas about the possibilities of stabilization policy. In short, it was about establishing a norm of low inflation and tying sanctions to the norm. The most important norm, of course, was the fixed exchange rate. And the government talked a lot about norms. A standard was introduced, which also entailed sanctions, namely that the state should not finance current account deficits by borrowing abroad. It was the so-called foreign loan snake. Interest rates would then be forced up in the event of a deterioration in competitiveness and current account deficits. The private sector would be induced to take the currency risk. High Swedish interest rates would be required compared to, for example, the German ones, so that it paid off for private players to borrow in German marks and buy Swedish securities, thus taking the currency risk. It would be punishing to drive up wage costs too much through high interest rates in Sweden. There was a whole philosophy around this that the government should commit itself so that the actors in the Swedish labor market would realize that the state would no longer counteract unemployment in the event of cost crises or other reasons for rising unemployment. The Social Democratic government allowed unemployment to rise in the spring of 1991. Many leading economists applauded and urged the incoming nonsocialist government to pursue the Social Democrats' "non-compromise", not to change policies to counteract unemployment. The new government announced cuts in transfers and public consumption. Subsidies for construction investments were cut. A great deal of uncertainty spread among households, which radically increased their savings. The following year in 1992, the Swedish crown came under attack. The defense of the fixed exchange rate resulted in interest rates of 15  at worst 25 percent over a short period  for fixed home loans. In the autumn of 1992, the government and the Social Democratic opposition announced a couple of savings packages, which strengthened household uncertainty about the future by tightening household incomes. The high interest rate policy continued in the spring of 1993. Only the industrial sector - 20 percent of GDP - eventually began to grow as a result of falling krona exchange rates. But it wasn't far enough to stabilize GDP. Let's look at a joint position: Housing construction 1990-1995: -72%; From 70,000 apartments started to under 10,000. Household savings, savings rate 1989 -4.9%; 1994 8.3%; Cover 13.2 percentage points of households' disposable income. Together with the fall in exports, only the rise in household savings represents a demand shock to GDP of almost 10 percent. In addition, there are the consequences in the form of failed investments. At the same time, a wave of rationalizations was triggered. (Picture of household savings and unemployment) The interesting thing here is that economic policy reinforced the economic downturn instead of counteracting it in the traditional way and stabilising GDP. This was, of course, due to the fact that the government carried out structural reforms, which had long been planned, but which happened to coincide with a general economic downturn. The development of the budget balance was devastating. In the calendar year 1993, the budget balance was 14.3% of GDP. In 1995, the interest rate debt reached over 80% of GDP and interest costs 120 billion. The situation was unstable, verging on uncontrollable. The overall unemployment rate  the openly unemployed and people in action  rose from 2.6 percent of the labor force in 1990 to 12.7 in 1994. GDP fell by five per cent between 1990 and 1993. We have clear evidence in these data that unemployment rose due to an outright "Keynesian" demand shock. At the same time, public finances and public debt had developed at such a pace  partly as a result of austerity itself  that traditional stabilization policies became counterproductive. Increased public spending or tax cuts would only further impair the credibility of the Swedish economy and drive up interest rates. From 1993, stabilization policy instead became a matter of austerity of public spending and tax increases. As a result, unemployment did not fall in the first round, but an improvement in public finances promised to lower the skyrocketing real interest rates and thus counteract the austerity effects of the state budget. We also lived in an international environment with weak public finances and the 'Maastricht conditions' forced a policy of restructuring in the large countries of Europe, while in our country we moved quickly with the policy of restructuring. In the financial year 1992/93, the state budget deficit was 188 billion. In 1997 it was down to 60 billion and now there is talk of having a budget surplus. In five years, a heavy-handed adjustment of public finances was carried out, which kept down household disposable income and private consumption - and thus kept up unemployment. This whole process, with high economic and social costs, was part of the attempts to restore a stable macroeconomic regime. It has now been established with low interest rates and growing credibility for Swedish economic policy. Mass unemployment remains the big blot on the record. It is not until recent years that private consumption has begun to grow. Since private consumption accounts for about half of GDP, growth in private consumption is a prerequisite for increasing capacity utilisation and pushing down unemployment. It is not enough to grow industrial production, which is instead important for the external balance. Employment also increased in Sweden by over 100 00 people in the course of 1998. This described development has meant that Sweden has not emerged from the misery of unemployment. Still in the winter of 1999, over 6 percent are openly unemployed and the overall unemployment rate is almost 10 percent. The share of the employed among people of working age is good 70 per cent, compared with 83 per cent ten years ago. These figures indicate resource losses and load on state and municipal budgets. With some technological development that in the long term drives up productivity by 1.5 to 1.7 percent (the technology factor), and some growth in the labor force of that 0.5 percent, we have a "spontaneous" long-term growth of 2-2.2 percent without increased input of either capital or labor. In order for unemployment to fall, demand and the economy in such conditions must temporarily grow well above these figures. We need a year of growth around 3% to bring down unemployment. This is precisely why the government will launch a growth target in the spring budget of 2.75% by 2004. But not all unemployment is dependent on low demand. An undetermined part of Swedish unemployment is structural. The longer unemployment persists, the greater the risk of the structural element of unemployment. A couple of years ago, the Economic Policy Council's report from SNS estimated the part of unemployment that is due to too low demand at 2-3 percentage points of the open unemployment rate. The Riksbank estimates cyclical unemployment at not much more than one percentage point of total unemployment. This is in line with what LO's PO Edin recently stated, that we have to get used to just over 8 percent total unemployment. Unemployment below that level would boost inflation. It's a kind of surrender. Closing comment In order to raise Swedish growth and claim Sweden as one of the richest countries in the world, productivity growth must be raised in the long term, not just during an economic upturn. There is now a gathering of forces around various policy measures to increase growth in Sweden. It is education policy  more technology and science than social sciences  it is a question of shifting tax policy. This is not least about society's view of inventions, entrepreneurship and entrepreneurship. And it is a social climate with collaboration between the trade union movement and the employer parties. Things are happening in all these areas in Sweden. It is also a monetary policy of low, stable inflation. The Riksbank is facing a growing understanding of efforts to stabilise inflation at two per cent within the two-year time horizon. No attempt at persuasion from the Riksbank can be more effective than the experiences now being made in the Swedish economy. Under the murmur, low contracts were struck last year. They ended up with about 3 percent annual wage increases. But by pushing inflation out of the Swedish economy, this 3 percent represents the highest real wage increase achieved by wage earners in decades. But this does not necessarily mean higher employment. For that, the labour market needs to withstand higher capacity utilisation in the economy than we currently have, without wage inflation. For a number of quarters, demand had to rise above capacity growth, in order to absorb the unemployed, who are unemployed for economic reasons. Unfortunately, we do not know how large groups have been permanently harmed by mass unemployment, so that they cannot be drawn into productive employment. But the discussion has focused almost exclusively on the supply side of the economy. The notion that equilibrium unemployment is now very high  Edin says just over 8 percent  has led to caution in demand policy. But developments in the US seem to indicate that the so-called NAURU, the unemployment rate that does not drive up the inflation rate, may fall as unemployment goes down. Perhaps structural unemployment is overestimated? We do not know much about how great structural unemployment is and how large the cyclical one is. In any case, one can hope that inflation expectations are driven out of the economy, which should increase the chances of getting closer to full employment without inflation picking up. Let me end in a positive spirit! Why should things continue to go badly for Sweden? Swedes are open to news. We have a wide spread of computers in the country and the knowledge to use them. We have large IT investments, on a par with the US but much more than in continental Europe. We were quick to embrace the cell phones. Foreign companies use Sweden as a test market for news. Sweden is in practice bilingual. We have a higher GDP share of research than any other country in the world. We are at the top in terms of the number of patents per 100,000 inhabitants (patents in at least two countries): USA Japan Germany Sweden 1980 16,71 20,65 38,41 39,82 1996 29,47 33,09 49,40 46,89 Let me conclude by saying that Sweden has all the prerequisites to regain a leading position in terms of growth and eventually living standards.

Utbildningspolitiken har inte varit framgngsrik under de senaste decennierna. Frmst mste vi utka den tekniska och naturvetenskapliga utbildningens volym i Sverige, ngot som redan har pbrjats. Och det r inte bara en frga om skatter och regler p arbetsmarknaden. Det r ocks en frga om, kultur och milj, om rtten att gra konkurs och att frska igen, utan att stigmatiseras. Sverige har nackdelen av ett perifert lge i frhllande till de stora marknaderna i Europa. Vi r ett litet land med en liten marknad. Sverige saknar djup och bredd som finansiell centrum i jmfrelse med de stora lnderna. Och det r mrkt, kallt och bltt dr hemma. Kanske r nackdelarna s stora att de svrligen kompenseras med skattesnkningar och tgrder p arbetsrttens omrde? Jag vargr nu till att tala om arbetslsheten. Massarbetslshet Ett land behver inte ha massarbetslshet drfr att tillvxten r lg. Lg produktivitetstillvxt borde inte vara ngot hinder fr hg sysselsttning, eftersom snabb produktivitetsstegring betyder just bortrationalisering av arbetskraft. Givet produktivitetens tillvxt mste efterfrgan vxa tillrckligt snabbt, fr att absorbera ett vxande arbetsutbud och fr att engagera de arbetslsa i produktionen. Men en svag lngsiktig produktivitetstillvxt, som den vi har haft, str inte i motsttning till full sysselsttning. Det var svrt att peka p de avgrande faktorerna bakom den svaga tillvxten i Sverige. Det r dremot ltt att identifiera hur massarbetslsheten uppstod i brjan av 1990-talet. Sverige hade haft en kraftig verhettning i slutet av 1980-talet. Den ppna arbetslsheten var nere p 1,3 % i genomsnitt i riket 1989 och 1,5 % r 1990. I Mlardalen var den nere i 0,5%. Inget lnebildningssystem kan fungera i en sdan arbetsmarknad. Hela 1980-talet, efter superdevalveringen 1982, hade regeringen frskt att f ner lnestegringstakten: Rundabordskonferenser, inkomstbaserad skattepolitik, lansering av inflationsnormer, vdjanden till arbetsmarknadens parter. Title: What happens to inflation and interest rates?
text: What happens to inflation and interest rates? Date: 1997-09-30 Speaker: Governor Urban Backstrom Location: Stora Rantedagen in Stockholm First of all, I would like to thank you for the invitation and the opportunity to discuss the Swedish economy and how the Riksbank views the inflation outlook. In the Inflation Report that the Riksbank presented last week, it was concluded that monetary policy is currently well balanced. In this context, the report makes the technical assumption that monetary policy remains unchanged, i.e. that the repo rate remains at 4.10%, until 1999 in order to analyse the effects this will have on demand and price developments. Of course, this assumption does not mean that we can promise that the repo rate will remain unchanged in the coming years. By a well-balanced monetary policy, we mean that the repo rate does not need to be changed in the near future in order for the inflation target of 2 percent to be achieved within the time horizon that monetary policy operates, i.e. usually between 1 and 2 years. But our analysis of the economy and inflation risks for the coming years is not without reservations. The report states that, with current economic developments, it is particularly important to closely monitor incoming information in order to assess whether the inflation picture changes. This is only natural in the light of the upturn in the economy and our determination to meet the price stability objective. There are uncertainties and there are a few of them that I intend to discuss today. However, this discussion must not detract from the main impression that the Swedish economy today has a much better starting point than it has been for a long time. We are well placed to experience a time of sustained high growth and continued low inflation. It is something that must be well managed. A first uncertainty factor that is central to inflation developments is the course of the economic cycle. This, in turn, raises the question of whether and how resource utilization develops in the economy. A second factor is the evolution of inflation expectations and a third is wage formation. Let me take these factors in turn, but first repeat something about the fundamentals of the price stability objective. Prisstabilitetsmalet Leaving aside various factors that have caused one-off changes in the price level upwards or downwards, and thus only temporarily affected inflation rates, it can be concluded that both actual and expected inflation in the 1990s have gradually moved closer to the price stability objective. We are thus moving from a situation where economic policy needed to be geared towards bringing down inflation to a situation where it is important to keep price developments in line with the price stability objective in the long term. Central to such a policy is the capacity of the economy to produce goods and services. This one is not without limits. History teaches us that when demand increases faster than the economy is able to sustainably produce, the risk that capacity constraints and bottlenecks lead to rising prices and wages increases over time. If a situation of this type is at risk of arising, it is better to at an early stage seek to slow down the process somewhat with a small rate hike so that demand growth is in line with the expansion of the economy's production capacity. Then the growth can be sustainable. By acting predictably and in good time, it is hoped that sharp changes in interest rates can be avoided and, at the same time, economic actors can continue to assume stable low inflation. It is important to note that the long-term growth trajectory is determined by factors such as the construction and use of physical capital, by the way in which the skills of the workforce are developed and used, as well as by technological developments. None of these fundamental growth factors can be directly affected by the change in the Riksbank's repo rate. What monetary policy can do is provide certainty about future inflation developments and thus probably indirectly contribute to raising growth potential. A jerky and undisciplined monetary policy can similarly lower output potential. A monetary policy aimed at maintaining low inflation does not have to be incompatible with an economy that is growing by, for example, 4% or 5%. However, the prerequisite for such high growth is that the supply side of the economy works so well that growth does not give rise to inflationary impulses. If, on the other hand, the structure of the economy only allows for growth of 1% or 2%, then demand and therefore monetary policy must be adjusted accordingly. Once the price stability objective has been established as a credible benchmark, it can be said that the objective of inflation not rising above or falling below the target on a sustained basis is normally matched by an effort to ensure that the economy produces neither above nor below its long-term sustainable capacity. The orientation of monetary policy to contribute to stable and sustainable growth is facilitated by the construction of the price stability objective. When the economy weakens, inflationary pressures are normally lower. That could leave room for rate cuts. Similarly, there are usually reasons to tighten monetary policy after a period of rising demand if it is increasing faster than the expansion of the economy's capacity. It is therefore wrong to say that monetary policy does not take account of employment and growth. The organisation of monetary policy means that production and employment are taken into account as long as it does not jeopardise low inflation. This type of consideration is automatic with the symmetrical orientation of a price stability objective. Disturbances involving one-off changes in the price level and leading to temporarily higher or lower inflation should normally be able to be captured by the tolerance range. However, sometimes such disruptions can become so severe that inflation falls outside the range and that the inflation target, which is to be evaluated in a longer, annual perspective, is not met. As is well known, this happened in 1996 when inflation, measured for the year as a whole, was a few tenths below the lower tolerance limit. An important reason was that the sharp fall in interest rates contributed to a decrease in interest costs for single-family homes. In situations where inflation falls outside the range, it is the Riksbank's task to provide an explanation for what is happening and to make it credible that the structure of monetary policy is such that inflation gradually returns to its target of 2 per cent. This applies regardless of whether it is a question of exceeding the upper tolerance limit or of exceeding the lower tolerance limit. The decline in CPI figures that led to inflation falling below the lower bound of the price stability objective tolerance range last year was temporary. Registered inflation is now again approaching underlying inflation around 2 per cent. So this is a predicted increase and fundamentally not something that affects monetary policy and neither did the temporary downturn last year. Our action is therefore symmetrical in this respect. The business cycle and resource utilisation The Inflation Report presented last week states that the recovery in the Swedish economy continues. As in the past, the Riksbank estimates that GDP growth could be around 2 per cent this year and around 3 per cent in 1998 and 1999. Despite the fact that the increase in demand in the economy is thus likely to be above the growth rate that the supply side of the economy is able to meet in the long run, no general capacity shortages should arise in the next few years. Most of the evidence suggests that there are spare resources in the economy that can be used in the event of such an increase in demand. In addition, the upturn looks set to be relatively evenly divided between export and domestic markets, which also helps to counter inflationary bottleneck problems. In the absence of serious tensions between the demand and supply sides of the economy, underlying inflation should remain broadly constant over the time horizon that monetary policy is working on, i.e. one to two years from now. The fact that the rate of increase in the consumer price index will nevertheless increase somewhat in the future has to do with temporary factors, which I pointed out earlier. That process has already begun. The recorded inflation rate has gradually risen this year from a low of 0 percent this spring to 1.5 percent, according to the latest figure. Average inflation according to the CPI is expected to rise from around 1% in 1997 to around 2% in 1998 and 1999. As a result of the fact that the pass-through of monetary policy to demand is characterized by a long lag, we are forced to work with more or less uncertain forecasts of economic developments over the next two years. We are not alone in working with forecasts. This is something that many actors in the economy do. We publish four Inflation Reports per year to continuously monitor developments and, if necessary, to revise the assessments. We don't know exactly how much the economy can produce without inflation rising. So-called output gap calculations - i.e. attempts to measure the difference between actual output and the level of output at which inflation is at risk of rising - are fundamentally too uncertain to be an exact steering oar for monetary policy action. Therefore, it is also important to see how resource utilization in the different parts of the economy develops. Various measures for industry show a slightly rising capacity utilisation between the first and second quarters of this year in the Swedish economy. In the NIER's Business Cycle Barometer, the share of enterprises that reported that it was the availability of factors of output that limited output has grown slightly. In addition, in the second quarter there was a slight increase in the shortage rates for skilled workers and technical officials. In the services sector, too, there has been an increase in capacity utilisation. Similarly, delivery times increased slightly during the second quarter. Further signs that capacity utilisation has increased in the economy is that the proportion of companies intending to raise their prices in the third quarter is slightly larger than those that say they will lower prices. Thus, most evidence suggests that resource utilisation in the economy has risen slightly, but the main hypothesis is still that the supply of resources is still good enough to be able to meet rising demand. A rapidly growing economy may experience temporary bottleneck problems because new plants cannot always be put into operation at exactly the time when the increase in demand arrives. Admittedly, the experience of the upturn in 1994 and 1995, which was mainly located in the industrial sector, suggests a higher degree of flexibility than in the past both in the use of the existing capital stock and in investing rapidly in new plant and machinery when demand rises. But demand was then so strong in the industrial sector that there were still capacity problems, resulting in an acceleration in producer prices. It may also take some time for companies to have their labour needs met as a result of "matching problems" in the labour market. It is not necessarily the case that demand now comes in exactly the industries and regions that suffered a loss of demand in the early 1990s. The unchanged level of remaining vacancies suggests some matching problems in the labour market. The complex structure of an economy makes it necessary to follow many different factors in order to form a picture of resource use in the economy and to be able to assess whether there is a risk of bottleneck problems that can lead to an acceleration of Inflation. So far, developments do not suggest that inflation risks in the future would be too great. But we are in an upturn and it is necessary to be vigilant if the picture changes. Inflationsforvantningarna The importance of bringing inflation expectations down to a level consistent with the price stability objective was demonstrated in the 1990s by a series of economic policy decisions. The formulation of the objective of the Riksbank's monetary policy, the tightening of monetary policy between the summer of 1994 and 1995 and the multi-party agreement on the Riksbank's position are examples of this. Fiscal consolidation has also been influenced by the price stability objective, although it has also been guided by other motives. This emphasis on price stability has also led to results. Inflation expectations, as shown in various surveys, have fallen markedly in recent years. The decline in long-term interest rates, as well as the stronger krona, are also a reflection of this. The contrast is now great with the inflation of the 1970s and 1980s of an average of 8 percent per year. We have come a long way towards establishing confidence in low-inflation policy. However, it is essential to closely monitor developments in inflation expectations in the context of the current economic upturn. There must be no doubt about the important role of the price stability objective in overall economic policy and that the Riksbank takes this task very seriously. In an environment where inflation expectations are firmly anchored to the inflation target, monetary policy has some room for manoeuvre and can support the recovery in the economy. This is shown not least by developments in the countries where low inflation has characterized the development for a longer period. It may seem a paradox that the more credible a central bank is in its fight against inflation, the greater the room for manoeuvre to support general economic policy. But the order must be exactly this. First comes credibility and then room for manoeuvre - not the other way around. It was this approach that guided the Riksbank when we waited to cut its key interest rate until January 1996 - we wanted to work with safety margins and confirm the focus on low inflation. Those who did not see monetary policy in this way in the debate at the time, I hope, do so today. It is through price stability, low inflation expectations and thus low market interest rates across the yield curve that monetary policy can contribute to sustainable - let me stress sustainable - growth. Without the credibility of inflation expectations in line with the target, monetary stimulus risks bringing the economy back into the inflationary end with negative consequences for output and employment. Not necessarily because a marginal deviation from 2% inflation would be disastrous for the functioning of the economy, but because we would then lose the clear anchor that a price stability objective entails for both economic policy and for the actors in the economy. We only have to go back to the early 1970s to see what such a loss meant for the development of the many areas of the economy. The collapse of the Bretton Woods system, of which Sweden was a member, formed the prelude to a long period of variable and high inflation. It is for this reason that the inflation target must be nurtured with care. It provides a clear point of reference and a clear message to various decision-makers in the economy about the direction of economic policy. In Sweden, the low-inflation regime began to be established only in the early 1990s, which means that we must be especially vigilant about whether the policies being pursued spill over into rising inflation expectations. The risk of this has in all likelihood diminished in recent years, partly because inflation has been low and partly because the government has shown in action that price stability is a central part of economic policy. But there must be vigilance, especially as now that monetary policy has a stimulating impact on the economy. With inflation expectations in line with the target, stable conditions are created for the many contracts that are concluded every day in a dynamic economy. This applies not least to the labour market, which is becoming clear now that we are facing a very important round of collective bargaining. Wage Wage formation is, of course, significantly affected by how high inflation is expected to be in the future. The relatively large wage increases in recent years, despite the high unemployment rate, are probably largely explained by the fact that when the agreements were concluded, inflation was expected to be significantly higher than it actually was. Wage growth thus reached a level that did not allow for a decline in unemployment. In addition to inflation expectations, institutional conditions in the labour market, or, more generally, the functioning of the labour market, play a major role in wage developments. It is difficult today to have a clear idea of whether the talks that have taken place about future wage formation and the cooperation agreements reached in certain parts of the labour market will lead to better functioning wage formation from 1998. Basically, it is the result that counts and the level of unemployment gives an indication of the problems in wage formation. Of great importance for the future wage space is how productivity will develop. The average growth in labour productivity has been considerably higher in the 1990s than in the 1980s. The question, however, is whether this is a question of a lasting increase that can be used as a basis for future wage formation or whether there are explanations of a more temporary nature. Although the changes in the Swedish economy in recent years are likely to result in improved future productivity, it seems too early today to draw far-reaching conclusions about a structural trend reversal in productivity development. The higher productivity in the 1990s seems to be partly explained by factors of a temporary nature. In connection with the cost crisis and the large decline in production at the beginning of the decade, major rationalizations were carried out in Swedish business. As a result, employment, measured both in terms of the number of employees and in hours worked, fell more than output in the early 1990s, which could be seen in an increase in labour productivity. Another effect of a transitory nature that may have contributed to the high recorded productivity in recent years is that as the economy rises, companies can normally cope with the increase in demand at the beginning of the upswing with the existing workforce. Historically, economic upturns have been associated with greater improvements in productivity. However, over the business cycle, such variations in productivity tend to even out. Moreover, it cannot be ruled out that the higher wage increases in recent years have led to rationalisation aimed at counteracting an increase in costs. This, too, is not a productivity effect that can be used as an argument for wage increases, especially if the aim is to bring down unemployment. Future wage formation is thus another risk factor that the Riksbank must take into account. There are encouraging signs that wage formation is on the right track, but it is necessary that unemployment also falls permanently in order to be able to say that wage formation is not a problem. Conclusion The Riksbank's assessment is that monetary policy is currently well balanced. A monetary policy guided by a price stability objective means that it is primarily domestic developments and the assessment of future inflation in Sweden that determine the need for a change in interest rates. We are therefore not directly affected by whether interest rates are raised or lowered in other countries. This was shown earlier when other countries lowered interest rates and the Riksbank remained at a higher level, and it is now evident now that Finland has raised its key interest rate while we keep interest rates unchanged. The Swedish economy is well placed to enter a phase of sustained high growth based on stable macroeconomic conditions. For this to be possible, we must be vigilant if there are changes that could cause inflation to rise. This is particularly important now in the coming years, when growth is expected to be above trend. At this point, it is important to discuss some of the risks that may lie ahead, even though the situation seems good even in view of these risks as they appear today. If the division of labour is such that we in the Riksbank have the task of identifying potential risks, then hopefully everyone else can devote themselves to taking advantage of the stable economic development that price stability offers. It is several decades since the Swedish economy experienced such favorable conditions that now prevail. If the labour market functions satisfactorily, developments could also lead to a sustained decline in unemployment over the next few years. The impending upturn will show whether that will be the case.
